design_detail: Naturalistic within-person comparison, pooled from three studies at one university: 52 young drivers each drove a 20-minute simulated commute (STISIM fixed-base simulator, mixed rural and urban route with hazards and a divided-attention task) on the morning after a self-chosen night of social drinking and on a morning after no alcohol, in counterbalanced order. Drinking was not observed or assigned. After testing, participants were split by morning breath alcohol into a zero group (n = 26) and a residual-alcohol group (n = 26). Outcomes: 15 driving variables, NASA Task Load Index (workload) and the Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale.
can_establish: Whether the same young drivers drove worse in a demanding simulator on the morning after a night of social drinking than after a night without alcohol, including those whose breath alcohol was zero, and how they rated their own workload.
cannot_establish: Whether the impairment is due to alcohol itself rather than shorter or poorer sleep, the night out or expectation (sleep was not recorded, drinking amounts are not reported, and nobody was blind to condition); how it compares with legal blood alcohol limits (no alcohol-dose benchmark was run in this study); whether it applies to older or experienced drivers or to real roads; and whether residual alcohol adds risk (the residual and zero groups were formed after the fact and already differed on the control day).

sample.recruitment: Students and other people recruited through the experimenters' contacts, University of the West of England; unpaid; data from three studies with separate ethics approvals combined.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Driving licence holders aged 18 to 25 with 1 to 6 years of driving experience, self-reported good health, not pregnant, not using illicit drugs, non-smokers, fewer than 5 caffeinated drinks a day, social drinkers who reported having hangovers regularly; a short familiarization drive screened for simulator sickness.
sample.demographics: Mean age 20.9 years (range 18 to 25); 21 men and 31 women.
sample.attrition: Not reported: no drop-outs, exclusions or missing data are described, and how many people were enrolled across the three studies is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Young, inexperienced drivers who drink socially and often have hangovers; participants chose the drinking night and could postpone a test morning depending on whether they had drunk, so the hangover mornings were self-selected. The split into zero and residual groups depended on how much and how late people drank.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported night of social drinking, recalled with a retrospective diary (some could not recall amounts); breath alcohol measured with a Lion Alcometer immediately before driving, with readings hidden from participants; hangover severity rated on the Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale after the drive.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: drinks and amounts chosen by participants and not reported. Morning breath alcohol in the residual group averaged 0.047% (range 0.01 to 0.08%); all 52 had zero breath alcohol after the no-alcohol night. Mean hangover severity 4.7 (SD 1.8) on a 0 to 10 scale; 5.1 in the zero group and 4.3 in the residual group.
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug use and smoking excluded at screening (self-report); caffeine withheld on test mornings until after testing; other drug use on the drinking night not recorded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Half the sample had zero breath alcohol at testing; the other half had residual alcohol up to 0.08%. Breath readings were not confirmed in blood, which the authors note may misclassify some participants.

comparison.controls: The same participants on a morning after no alcohol (all with zero breath alcohol).
comparison.matching: Within-person; condition order and driving-scenario order counterbalanced, although participants could rearrange test days.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep on both nights, time drinking ended, food and how much was drunk were not recorded or not reported; the authors name sleep loss as a likely part of the effect.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable within person; other drug use on the drinking night not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: STISIM Drive simulator, 60,000-foot scenario (about 20 minutes, 50 mph limit, UK road layout) recording divided attention (response time and its variability, correct, incorrect and missed responses), vehicle control (mean speed and speed variability, mean lane position, lane deviation, centre-line crossings, time off road, lane excursions) and violations (accidents and collisions, speed-limit exceedances, tickets such as failing to stop or running red lights); NASA Task Load Index (six dimensions, 0 to 100); Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale (12 symptoms rated 0 to 10), with fatigue analysed separately.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors describe the one-hour highway test and its standard deviation of lateral position as the reference standard for driving impairment; this shorter urban scenario has no published benchmark against blood alcohol levels.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment means a significant difference in the poorer direction between the hangover and control mornings on a paired comparison, after a significant MANOVA and ANOVA; effect sizes as Cohen's d.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: MANOVA gating before separate ANOVAs and paired tests; no correction across the 15 driving variables and 6 workload dimensions; correlations shown only if p < 0.01 with nonparametric support, from an unreported number tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Simulator measures were recorded automatically; participants and experimenters knew which morning was which; participants did not see their breath readings.

analysis.effect_sizes: Combined group (n = 52), hangover against control, means (SD): divided-attention response time 3.5 (1.8) against 2.4 (1.3), d = 0.55; incorrect responses 0.2 against 0.0, d = 0.21; missed responses 2.1 against 1.1, d = 0.30; mean speed 35.9 against 31.7 mph, d = 0.42; centre-line crossings 7.8% against 4.0%, d = 0.36; time off road 1.6% against 0.6%, d = 0.68; lane excursions 18.9 against 10.6, d = 0.58; tickets 1.2 against 0.8, d = 0.34. Not significant: response-time variability, correct responses, speed variability, mean lane position, lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), accidents (1.8 against 1.3), speed exceedances. Zero group (n = 26): response time d = 0.69, mean speed d = 0.40, centre-line crossings d = 0.48, time off road d = 0.61, lane excursions d = 0.64; accidents 1.1 against 1.6 (not significant). Residual group (n = 26): response time d = 0.50, mean speed d = 0.45, time off road d = 0.72, excursions d = 0.51, accidents 2.5 against 0.9, d = 0.74. Workload (NASA-TLX overall) 53.8 against 38.4, d = 0.99. Multivariate effect of alcohol on driving F(1,50) = 19.4, p < 0.0001.
analysis.covariates: Gender and study entered as exploratory factors and dropped after non-significant multivariate tests; no other covariates.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 15 driving variables are tabulated. The correlations between self-ratings and driving are shown only when significant at p < 0.01 with nonparametric support, without the number tested, and it is not stated whether they used hangover-morning scores or differences from the control morning. The abstract does not mention that lane deviation, the measure closest to the reference standard, did not change.
analysis.power: Not reported; 26 per group for the residual comparison.

interpretation_gap.results_show: On the morning after a night of social drinking, the same young drivers responded more slowly to a divided-attention task, drove faster, crossed the centre line and left the road more often, made more lane excursions and collected more tickets in a 20-minute simulated commute than after a night without alcohol, with small to medium effects (d 0.21 to 0.68), while lane deviation, speed variability and accidents did not differ overall. The pattern was similar in the 26 whose breath alcohol was zero. They also rated the drive as needing more effort and workload. The residual group drove faster and got more tickets than the zero group on both mornings, not only after drinking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions state that the impairment reflects that seen with alcohol-impaired driving and was comparable to driving with a blood alcohol level at or above the legal limit used in several countries, even with zero breath alcohol. Gaps: (1) no alcohol-dose benchmark was run in this study; the comparison rests on another study (Mets et al., 2011) of a highway test whose main measure, lane deviation, did not change here; (2) the Results state that residual alcohol resulted in faster driving, more speed exceedances and more tickets, but Table 1 shows the residual group already drove faster (34.3 against 29.1 mph), exceeded speed limits more (10.4 against 7.0) and got more tickets (1.0 against 0.6) on the no-alcohol morning, with no alcohol-by-group interaction for these measures, so the difference is between people, not an effect of residual alcohol; (3) a lack of awareness of impairment is inferred from a few correlations selected by significance that differ between groups; (4) the effect is attributed to hangover although sleep was not recorded, which the authors acknowledge.

timeline.event: Laurell and Törnros: impaired vehicle control on a hangover morning in a naturalistic driving study (summarized in Gunn et al., 2018).

Verster et al.: greater weaving (standard deviation of lateral position) on a one-hour simulated highway drive during hangover, mostly in the second half (as described in this paper and in Gunn et al., 2018); Verster is a co-author of this paper.
Gunn et al. systematic review: driving studies too different to pool; two of three found impaired vehicle control.

Robbins et al.: student drivers the morning after drinking drove faster and exceeded limits longer in a 15-minute simulator test, mostly with residual alcohol, without impaired visual attention (as described in this paper).
This study: impairment on a 20-minute urban commute, also in participants with zero breath alcohol.

replication.where_it_stands: Several simulator and naturalistic studies, from overlapping and independent groups, report poorer driving the morning after drinking, but the measures differ: weaving on a long highway drive in one, lane excursions, time off road and speed on a short urban drive here, where weaving itself did not change. None has measured sleep alongside driving, and none links the urban-route measures to blood alcohol levels in the same scenario.

funding.funder: No external funding.
funding.declared_conflicts: C.A. has done sponsored research or consultancy for companies and organizations including Airbus Group Industries, Astra, BAe Systems, the UK Civil Aviation Authority, Duphar, Farm Italia, Carlo Erba, Ford Motor Company, ICI, Innovate UK, Janssen, LERS Synthélabo, Lilly, Lorex/Searle, the UK Ministry of Defence, More Labs, Quest International, Red Bull GmbH, Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, Sanofi Aventis and Vital Beverages. S.J. has done sponsored research for Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Merck, Gilead, Novartis, Roche, Red Bull GmbH, the Department for Transport and the Road Safety Trust. J.C.V. has in the past three years received grants or research support from the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and the Environment, Janssen Research and Development and Sequential, and consulted for Clinilabs, More Labs, Red Bull GmbH, Sen-Jam Pharmaceutical, Toast! and ZBiotics.
funding.affiliations_note: J.C.V. is also first author of the 2014 simulator study this paper cites as agreeing with it and of the methods paper it cites in support of naturalistic designs.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover study in which the same drivers drink a measured amount of alcohol or a placebo, with sleep held equal and recorded, then drive the same urban scenario at zero blood alcohol (confirmed in blood) the next morning, with a third session at a known blood alcohol level on the same scenario to calibrate the size of any impairment, in drivers of different ages and experience.

domains.note: The within-person comparison removes stable differences between people, and both tests were in the morning with caffeine withheld. Sleep, food and the night out itself were not recorded and travel with the hangover. For the zero-versus-residual contrast the risk is high: the groups formed after the fact already differed in speed, speeding and tickets on the control morning.

Drinking was self-reported and unobserved, amounts are not reported and some could not recall them; residual alcohol by breath only. Zero alcohol after the control night was confirmed by breath test, and hangover severity was rated.

Volunteers from students and the experimenters' contacts who report regular hangovers; participants chose and could postpone their test mornings; three studies combined without describing how many were enrolled.
None; participants did not drive or ride to the university after drinking.
No information on drop-outs or exclusions across the three studies; consumption data are missing for some participants.
Driving measures were recorded automatically, but participants knew their condition, which may affect effort and motivation; workload and hangover ratings were given after the drive.

All driving variables are tabulated, but 21 outcomes were tested without correction and nothing was preregistered. The correlations between self-ratings and driving were selected by significance from an unreported number of tests and are at high risk.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the main within-person contrast (driving after a night of social drinking against after no alcohol), the design is reasonably protected: same people, counterbalanced order, automatic measures and all driving variables reported. What remains uncertain is attribution, since sleep and drinking amounts were not recorded and nobody was blind, and the result describes a night out drinking, not alcohol alone. The card may be cited for poorer simulated driving and higher workload the morning after drinking, including at zero breath alcohol. It should not be cited for an effect of residual alcohol (the groups differed already on the control morning), for equivalence with a blood alcohol level (not measured here), or for a lack of awareness of impairment (selected correlations).

key_findings.finding: Combined group (n = 52): on the hangover morning, divided-attention response time was slower (3.5 s, SD 1.8, against 2.4, SD 1.3; d = 0.55), with more incorrect (d = 0.21) and missed (d = 0.30) responses; mean speed was higher (35.9 against 31.7 mph; d = 0.42), centre-line crossings (7.8% against 4.0%; d = 0.36), time off road (1.6% against 0.6%; d = 0.68) and lane excursions (18.9 against 10.6; d = 0.58) increased, and tickets rose (1.2 against 0.8; d = 0.34). Eight of the 15 driving variables differed.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Combined Groups columns; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The printed d values cannot be reproduced from the table means and SDs with a simple pooled SD (for example 0.70 against the printed 0.55 for response time; editors' calculation), presumably because the method accounts for the within-person correlation, which is not reported; most printed values are smaller.

key_findings.finding: Lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), speed variability, mean lane position, response-time variability, correct responses, accidents (1.8 against 1.3) and speed-limit exceedances did not differ significantly between hangover and control mornings in the combined group.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Combined Groups columns

key_findings.finding: Zero breath alcohol group (n = 26): response time slower (3.4 against 2.3; d = 0.69), faster driving (33.7 against 29.1 mph; d = 0.40), more centre-line crossings (6.0% against 3.8%; d = 0.48), time off road (1.3% against 0.5%; d = 0.61) and lane excursions (20.2 against 9.7; d = 0.64); accidents 1.1 against 1.6 (not significant); incorrect and missed responses and tickets not significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Zero BAC Group columns; Results › 3.1, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Residual alcohol group (n = 26, with alcohol still measurable in the breath; values in the exposure field): response time slower (d = 0.50), faster driving (d = 0.45), more time off road (d = 0.72) and excursions (d = 0.51), and more accidents and collisions (2.5 against 0.9; d = 0.74), the only measure with an alcohol-by-group interaction.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3 (opening paragraph); Table 1, Residual Alcohol Group columns; Results › 3.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: On the no-alcohol control morning the residual group already drove faster than the zero group (34.3 against 29.1 mph), exceeded speed limits more often (10.4 against 7.0) and got more tickets (1.0 against 0.6); the authors' significant group contrasts for speed (F(1,50) = 4.28), exceedances (F(1,50) = 4.59) and tickets (F(1,50) = 4.17) are main effects of group, not interactions with drinking.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Control columns of the Zero BAC and Residual Alcohol groups; Results › 3.1, 2nd paragraph (last two sentences)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Table 1: the group difference is present without alcohol, so it reflects differences between people rather than an effect of residual alcohol.

key_findings.finding: Perceived workload rose on the hangover morning: NASA-TLX overall 53.8 (SD 13.6) against 38.4 (12.8), d = 0.99; effort 60.5 against 41.6, d = 0.80; all six dimensions significant (for example temporal demand F(1,50) = 37.8).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Subjective Assessments rows; Results › 3.2 Subjective Measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mean hangover severity was 4.7 (SD 1.8) on the 0 to 10 scale (5.1 in the zero group, 4.3 in the residual group); some participants could not recall how much they had drunk, and amounts are not reported; sleep was not recorded.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3 (opening paragraph); Discussion, 6th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Correlations between self-ratings and driving (selected at p < 0.01): in the combined group lower hangover ratings went with faster driving (r = −0.359) and lower fatigue ratings with faster driving (r = −0.460); the associations differed between the zero and residual groups, and hangover ratings were not associated with workload ratings.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › 3.3 Associations Between Measures, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that residual alcohol resulted in greater speed, more speed exceedances and more tickets, but Table 1 shows these group differences on the no-alcohol control morning too, and no alcohol-by-group interaction is reported for them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The residual-alcohol effect on speeding and tickets is not supported; claims must not cite it.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Conclusions equate the impairment with driving at or above a blood alcohol level used as a legal limit in several countries, but no blood alcohol benchmark was tested in this study; the comparison cites a highway-test study (Mets et al., 2011) whose main measure, lane deviation, did not change here.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 1st paragraph; 5. Conclusions; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The equivalence to a blood alcohol level is an extrapolation, not a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: For the group contrast in speed-limit exceedances, F(1,50) = 4.59 is printed with partial eta squared 0.10; that F gives 0.084 (editors' calculation), and the same F appears for accidents and collisions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a copying error; the statistic for exceedances is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol consumption was collected with a retrospective diary but not reported, and the number of participants enrolled, excluded or lost across the three combined studies is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure cannot be described in amounts and attrition cannot be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: The method behind the printed Cohen's d values is not reproducible from the table: a simple pooled-SD calculation gives different values for most variables (for example 1.17 against the printed 0.99 for overall workload; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes should be quoted as printed and described as the authors' calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: Whether the correlations in Table 2 used hangover-morning scores or differences from the control morning is not stated, nor how many correlations were tested before selecting those with p < 0.01.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lack-of-awareness interpretation cannot be evaluated.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 110 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7291334 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, reference list, author contributions, funding and conflicts read; Figure 1 is an image of the scenario and was not needed for values)

design_detail: Systematic review (19 studies, 1970 to 2016) with inverse-variance meta-analyses in RevMan 5.3 (Hedges' g) of next-day cognitive performance after an evening of heavy drinking. Only studies with a no-hangover control condition, a measure validating the hangover (a symptom questionnaire) and blood alcohol near zero at testing (threshold in the exposure field) were eligible. Five pooled analyses (sustained attention, divided attention, short-term memory, long-term memory, psychomotor speed), each of four or five studies; 11 studies contributed to at least one. PROSPERO CRD42017054617.
can_establish: Whether healthy adults tested the morning after heavy drinking, with blood alcohol near zero, performed worse on attention, memory and reaction-time tasks than on a control day in the small controlled literature to 2016, and roughly how large the average difference was in standardized units.
cannot_establish: What the difference means for everyday tasks (effects are standardized and no task is tied to a real-world outcome except three simulator driving studies that were not pooled); whether the impairment comes from alcohol itself rather than lost sleep, expectation or fatigue (sleep, food and smoking were not controlled in the naturalistic studies); whether people who drink heavily but feel no hangover are affected (no separate analysis); how impairment changes with the amount drunk (no dose-response analysis); and whether the pooled estimates are inflated by small-study or publication effects (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, Embase and PsycNET run between December 2016 and May 2018 with terms for alcohol and hangover, plus reference lists of articles; no date limit (included studies date from 1970 to 2016). The review does not tabulate where participants came from; the reference titles of included studies name college students (Howland et al., 2010), maritime academy cadets (Rohsenow et al., 2006) and young adults (Rohsenow et al., 2010), and one study was of women only (Kruisselbrink et al., 2006).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: healthy adults aged 18 or over; a no-hangover control condition; a measure validating the presence of hangover; blood alcohol concentration (BAC) near zero at testing (threshold in the exposure field); laboratory (alcohol given) or naturalistic (drinking at a time and place of the person's choosing) designs. Of 20 articles excluded at full text, the stated reasons were: no hangover measure at testing (12 studies), only fatigue or arousal found on the hangover measure (2), no BAC at testing (7), BAC above the threshold (2), another treatment in the design (2), and data already included (1). These reasons sum to 26 for 20 articles, so several studies were excluded for more than one reason.
sample.demographics: Not tabulated beyond per-study n (5 to 193), design, alcohol dose and BAC at testing (Table 1). Several studies averaged the dose across men and women; age, sex mix and country are not given for most studies.
sample.attrition: 1163 participants recruited across the 19 studies (assuming no attrition where none was reported) and 846 with data reported, an attrition of 27.3% (Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph). The Table 1 sample sizes sum to 846 at their upper bounds (editors' arithmetic).
sample.selection_effects: The strict definition (validated hangover, near-zero BAC) removed several studies with null results that the Introduction cites: Finnigan et al. (1998), Chait and Perry (1994) and Lemon et al. (1993) were excluded at full text, two of them because the hangover measure showed only fatigue or arousal, that is, on the strength of the hangover the study produced. Four other null studies cited in the Introduction (Carroll et al., 1964; Ideström and Cadenius, 1968; Morrow et al., 1990; Dowd et al., 1973) do not appear among the full-text exclusions, so how they were handled is not reported. In naturalistic studies people were tested after nights on which they chose to drink heavily, so the sample is people who drink heavily and agreed to be tested the next morning. Two included studies had some participants above the blood alcohol limit (Törnros and Laurell, 1991, at their earliest morning session; four participants in Verster et al., 2014).

exposure.measurement: An evening of heavy drinking before testing: alcohol given in the laboratory, or drinking chosen by the participants in naturalistic studies, with intake self-reported or peak BAC estimated. The hangover was validated by a questionnaire (Acute Hangover Scale, a 20-item hangover questionnaire, rated severity and others) and BAC was measured at testing.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1): laboratory studies 0.8 to 1.43 g/kg, naturalistic studies 1.25 to 1.77 g/kg; the Discussion gives means of 1.21 g/kg (laboratory) and 1.54 g/kg (naturalistic). One Table 1 entry reads 13 g/kg (Collins and Chiles), evidently a typesetting error. A single drinking episode, by mouth.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed beyond the limitation that three studies did not control nicotine use (Myrsten et al., 1970; Collins, 1980; Collins and Chiles, 1980). Other drug use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: BAC below 0.02% at testing by inclusion (0 to 0.012% in Table 1), with two exceptions: some participants above 0.02% at the 9 a.m. session in Törnros and Laurell (1991), and four participants in Verster et al. (2014). The time between drinking and testing, and the sleep allowed, varied between studies and are not tabulated; the authors state this makes firm conclusions difficult.

comparison.controls: A no-alcohol, placebo or no-drinking control day for the same people in most studies (within-person designs); a separate no-hangover group in the mixed designs (Finnigan et al., 2005; McKinney and Coyle, 2007; Rohsenow et al., 2006; Rohsenow et al., 2010).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison in most studies. Condition order was not randomized in one study (Kim et al., 2003) and task order was not randomized in three (McKinney and colleagues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Largely not relevant for within-person comparisons. Not controlled in naturalistic studies, and not assessed by the review: sleep duration and timing, food, expectation and the motivation to perform after a night out.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Nicotine use not controlled in three studies; other drugs not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Tasks were coded into cognitive components: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Task, Continuous Performance Test, a correction test, sustained-attention tasks), divided attention (tracking with reaction time, dual task), selective attention (flanker, Stroop), vigilance (Mackworth clock), working memory (adaptive paced auditory serial addition, visual span and auditory digit span backwards), short-term memory (word recall, probed recall, pattern memory, pattern identification), long-term memory (delayed recall and recognition, lecture material learned while sober), psychomotor speed (simple and choice reaction time), psychomotor accuracy, and real-life simulations (simulated driving, ship power-plant operation, managerial simulation, graduate record examination).
outcomes.validity_norms: Two studies used tasks from the Neurobehavioral Evaluation System 3, validated for detecting cognitive impairment; the authors note that several other tasks had never been shown to be sensitive to drug-induced state changes.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment means poorer performance (slower, less accurate, fewer items recalled) after heavy drinking than in the control condition, expressed as Hedges' g with positive values meaning worse performance in the hangover condition. Several outcomes from one study within the same component were averaged so that no study counted twice.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across the five pooled analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening by two independent reviewers (95% agreement); data extraction is not described as done in duplicate. Blinding of participants was not counted as a risk of bias because, the authors say, participants readily guess their condition.

analysis.effect_sizes: Hedges' g with 95% CI, studies weighted by inverse variance (RevMan 5.3); fixed- or random-effects model not stated. Short-term memory g = 0.64 (0.15 to 1.13), 5 studies, I2 = 73%, P = 0.01; long-term memory g = 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17), 4 studies, I2 = 84%, P = 0.05; sustained attention g = 0.47 (0.07 to 0.87), 4 studies, I2 = 50%, P = 0.02; psychomotor speed g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), 5 studies, I2 = 36%, P < 0.001; divided attention, 4 studies, described as showing no evidence of an effect with no estimate given. No tau-squared, prediction intervals, subgroup analyses or tests for small-study effects.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; laboratory and naturalistic studies were pooled together.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017054617, printed under the heading 'Pre-registered hypothesis'. The paper does not compare its methods with the registered protocol or report deviations; the record itself was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The divided-attention pooled result has no number. The four studies pooled for sustained attention are not identified in the text (two reference numbers are cited; Figure 3 is an image). One laboratory study with a null reaction-time result (Kruisselbrink et al., 2006) could not be pooled for lack of data, which the authors say may inflate the psychomotor-speed estimate.
analysis.power: Not addressed for the meta-analyses. Several laboratory studies had 5 to 15 participants; the authors name low power as a likely reason for null results and recommend a priori power analysis.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Each pooled estimate rests on four or five small studies. The morning after heavy drinking, with blood alcohol near zero, performance was worse than on control days by about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation for short-term memory, long-term memory, sustained attention and reaction-time speed, with wide intervals (the long-term memory interval reaches down to 0.01) and moderate to high heterogeneity (I2 36% to 84%). Divided attention showed no detectable effect, working memory was mixed, and the executive tasks (ship power-plant operation, a managerial simulation, examination scores) showed no clear effect. Two of three naturalistic simulator studies found poorer vehicle control, and one found no change in speed. Naturalistic studies, with more alcohol, tended to find impairments where laboratory studies often did not.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that hangovers "may involve impaired cognitive functions and performance of everyday tasks such as driving", which is suitably hedged. Gaps: (1) the abstract says 1163 participants across 19 studies were included in the analysis, while 846 had data and 11 studies entered any pooled analysis; (2) the abstract says the review suggested impaired driving, which was not meta-analysed and rests on three naturalistic studies, one of them null; (3) the Discussion explains null results by insensitive tasks and low power but does not weigh the same design weaknesses (sleep not controlled, unblinded naturalistic designs, non-randomized task order) against the positive results; (4) the Introduction states that the review examines next-day effects of heavy drinking rather than hangover as such, because people in the hangover conditions may have had no symptoms, a qualification absent from the title and abstract.

timeline.event: Stephens et al. and Prat et al. narrative reviews of the cognitive effects of hangover (cited as earlier reviews that excluded studies with any alcohol at testing).
Alcohol Hangover Research Group consensus statement on best practice (Verster et al., 2010), the basis of this review's inclusion criteria.
This review: by the authors' account the first to pool effect sizes for next-day cognitive effects.
Alford et al. simulated commute driving at zero and residual blood alcohol, a later primary study on the driving question the review could not pool.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of this question that its authors knew of. Its estimates are averages of a handful of small studies, mostly from three groups (Howland and Rohsenow; McKinney and Coyle; Verster), and the Howland et al. (2010) and Rohsenow et al. (2010) studies used the same test battery in the same group, without the review saying whether their samples overlap. The driving evidence it summarises is three naturalistic simulator studies (Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Törnros and Laurell, 1991; Verster et al., 2014), not pooled.

funding.funder: University of Bath research studentship. The acknowledgements also list funding from the British Heart Foundation, Cancer Research UK, the Economic and Social Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the National Institute for Health Research under the UK Clinical Research Collaboration.
funding.declared_conflicts: S.A. and M.R.M. are members of the UK Centre for Tobacco and Alcohol Studies; the other authors declare no relevant conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors thank R. Stephens and J. Grange, authors of an included study (Grange et al., 2016), for providing information, and obtained unpublished information from the authors of Verster et al. (2014) by correspondence.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized crossover study in which the same people drink a measured amount of alcohol or a placebo in the evening, with sleep duration and timing held equal and measured, food and smoking controlled, and validated state-sensitive tasks plus a standard driving test given at zero blood alcohol the next morning, with hangover severity recorded and analysed as a moderator; and an updated meta-analysis with random-effects pooling, separate laboratory and naturalistic estimates, and small-study tests.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Healthy adults; heavy drinking the evening before with validated hangover and BAC near zero at testing; a no-hangover control condition; cognitive performance.
PROSPERO CRD42017054617 is cited, but the paper neither reports deviations nor compares its methods with the record; the record was not read, so whether it specified the analysis plan is not known.
The Introduction explains why laboratory and naturalistic designs were both included and why studies needed a hangover measure and near-zero BAC.

Three databases with the search terms given, reference lists searched, no stated language or date restriction, and the search ended three months before publication; but no trial registries, no stated grey-literature search and no stated consultation of experts (though authors were contacted for data).
Two independent reviewers screened, with 95% agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.
Not described: the Methods say only that data were extracted.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 20 full-text exclusions are cited by reference number with their reasons in the running text (Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph). The reason counts sum to 26 for 20 articles, so several were excluded on more than one ground; this is not explained but each exclusion has a stated reason.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives n, design, alcohol dose, BAC at testing, hangover measure, tasks and main finding; age, sex mix, setting and the interval between drinking and testing are missing.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The RevMan risk-of-bias tool was applied (results in Figure 2, an image), but blinding was deliberately not assessed, and for the naturalistic studies, which are non-randomized comparisons, no confounding domain was assessed (sleep, food, smoking, expectation). The text reports only randomization of condition order, selective reporting and other bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

The model is not named (inverse-variance weights are described, which in RevMan may be fixed or random effects) despite I2 up to 84%; how g was computed for within-person designs is not described; laboratory and naturalistic designs were pooled together with no separate estimates or stated justification.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis by risk of bias or by design.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion names non-randomized condition and task order, uncontrolled nicotine and variable sleep as limits that make firm conclusions difficult. It applies these limits mainly to explain null results (insensitive tasks, low power) rather than to the positive ones.

I2 is reported for each pool and possible sources (task sensitivity, laboratory against naturalistic design, dose, auditory against visual stimuli) are discussed, but none was investigated, although the authors themselves observe that naturalistic studies tended to find impairments and laboratory studies did not.
Not assessed or discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the authors' interests are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (9: risk-of-bias assessment without blinding or confounding; 11: model not stated and designs pooled together; 15: publication bias not assessed), two are partly met (2 and 4) and two met (7 and 13), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. In practice the pooled numbers are averages of four or five small studies of mixed design, possibly from a fixed-effect model whose intervals would then be too narrow given the heterogeneity, with no check for missing null studies, and the strict inclusion criteria excluded several null studies. The review may be cited for the direction of next-day effects on memory, sustained attention and reaction time in controlled studies, and for the absence of pooled evidence on driving and executive function; its effect sizes should be cited as approximate and from small studies.

key_findings.finding: 805 records were screened, 39 full texts assessed, 19 studies included in the systematic review and 11 in at least one meta-analysis; 1163 participants were recruited across the 19 studies and 846 had data reported (27.3% attrition).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Results › Identification of studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Sustained attention: five studies (three laboratory, two naturalistic), three reporting impairment and two not; pooled over four studies, Hedges' g = 0.47 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.87), I2 = 50%, P = 0.02, worse after heavy drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Attention › Sustained attention, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Divided attention: five studies, of which only one (n = 5) found impairment; the meta-analysis of four studies showed no evidence of a next-day effect (no estimate reported). One study each of vigilance (no effect) and selective attention (slower responses and more Stroop interference) were not pooled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Attention › Divided attention, 1st paragraph; Results › Attention › Other attention, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Short-term memory: seven studies, three reporting impairment (one in women only) and four not; pooled over five studies, g = 0.64 (0.15 to 1.13), I2 = 73%, P = 0.01.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Short-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: Long-term memory: four studies; impairment in the three word-recall studies, no effect where lecture material had been learned while sober (Howland et al., 2010); pooled g = 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17), I2 = 84%, P = 0.05.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Long-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 5 legend

key_findings.finding: Working memory was mixed: no next-day effect on the adaptive paced auditory serial addition test or auditory digit span backwards, impairment on visual span backwards in one study; not pooled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Other memory, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor speed (reaction time): three naturalistic studies found slower responses and three laboratory studies did not; pooled over five studies, g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), I2 = 36%, P < 0.001. The one laboratory study that could not be pooled (Kruisselbrink et al., 2006) found no change in reaction time but lower accuracy, and the authors say its omission may inflate the estimate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychomotor performance › Speed, 1st paragraph; Figure 6 legend; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Real-life simulations were not pooled: no clear effect on solving a mechanical failure in a ship simulator, on managerial simulations, or on graduate record examination scores; in three naturalistic driving studies, vehicle control (deviation from a set course) was impaired in two (Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Verster et al., 2014) and speed did not change in one (Törnros and Laurell, 1991).
key_findings.locator: Results › 'Real-life' simulations, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Naturalistic studies involved more alcohol than laboratory studies (means in the exposure field) and were more likely to find next-day impairment; the authors read this as higher amounts being linked to greater impairment, without a formal analysis.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (Figure 2): one study did not randomize condition order, selective reporting was unclear for every study because none was preregistered, half had other risks (non-randomized task order, sampling), and blinding was not assessed because participants readily guess their condition.
key_findings.locator: Results › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: The authors state that people in the hangover conditions may not have had hangover symptoms and that, since studies did not analyse them separately, the review examines next-day effects of heavy drinking rather than hangover as such.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: condition order not randomized in one study and task order in three; nicotine not controlled in three; and the time between drinking and testing, and so the sleep allowed, varied between studies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 1163 participants across 19 studies were included in the analysis; the Results give 846 participants with data, and only 11 studies entered any meta-analysis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sample is smaller than the abstract implies; the pooled estimates rest on four or five studies each.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence giving 11 studies with sufficient data for meta-analysis cites only eight reference numbers (1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12), and the sustained-attention section says four studies were pooled while citing two (1, 7). The divided-attention, memory and speed sections name ten different pooled studies in all.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph; Results › Attention › Sustained attention
reporting_issues.consequence: The set of pooled studies cannot be fully reconstructed from the text; Figure 3, which would show it, is an image.

reporting_issues.issue: Design classification differs between places. The text counts 11 laboratory and 8 naturalistic studies, lists Verster et al. (2003) in both groups and Kim et al. (2003) as laboratory; Table 1 classes 9 studies as laboratory and 10 as naturalistic, with both of these naturalistic; the memory sections class Verster et al. (2003) as laboratory.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Results › Memory
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements contrasting laboratory and naturalistic results cannot be checked exactly; Table 1 is taken as authoritative.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives an implausible alcohol dose for Collins and Chiles, about ten times the other laboratory doses (the Discussion's range for these studies points to a misplaced decimal point; values in the exposure field), dates the study 1979 while reference 18 is 1980, and spells two author names differently from the reference list (Mrysten for Myrsten, Rohers for Roehrs).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting errors; the dose should not be quoted from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Discussion, 4th paragraph, says the laboratory reaction-time studies had 8 to 12 participants; Table 1 gives 15, 11 and 12 for the three laboratory reaction-time studies (Myrsten, Collins and Chiles, Kruisselbrink).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point that the laboratory studies were small stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The risk-of-bias method is cited as reference 56, which is an EEG study of binge drinking (Stock et al., 2016), not a risk-of-bias tool.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Reference 56
reporting_issues.consequence: The tool is identifiable only as RevMan's risk-of-bias graph; its domains are not stated in full.

reporting_issues.issue: Two included studies did not meet the stated near-zero blood alcohol criterion for all participants (Törnros and Laurell, 1991, at their earliest morning session; four participants in Verster et al., 2014, retained after correspondence with the authors).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and its footnotes a and b
reporting_issues.consequence: Some residual intoxication may contribute to the driving findings; the authors report that excluding the four participants did not change the Verster et al. result.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-analysis model (fixed or random effects) is not named, and no pooled estimate is given for divided attention.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data analysis; Results › Attention › Divided attention
reporting_issues.consequence: If fixed-effect, the intervals are too narrow given I2 of 50% to 84%; the null for divided attention cannot be quantified.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6282576 (all sections, Table 1 rendered as text, reference list, declaration of interests and acknowledgements read; Figures 1 to 6, including the PRISMA diagram, the risk-of-bias graph and all forest plots, are images and their values were not extracted; the PROSPERO record was not read)

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of one survey wave (January to June 2021) of the Happiness and Health Study, a cohort first recruited in ninth grade at ten Los Angeles high schools in 2013; 1312 respondents aged 21 to 24 who drank in the past 30 days. Exposure: ever having used hangover remedy pills (for example dihydromyricetin), yes or no. Outcomes: a modified AUDIT score (0 to 40), drinking days, binge-drinking days, drinks per drinking day, and a count of seven alcohol problems; linear and negative binomial regressions, unadjusted and adjusted for sociodemographic factors and depressive symptoms; the reverse direction in a supplement.
can_establish: How many young adults in this Southern California cohort had used, heard of, or believed in hangover remedy pills in 2021, and whether those who had used them reported more drinking problems and heavier drinking than those who had not, at one point in time.
cannot_establish: Whether remedy pills lead people to drink more, or heavier drinking leads people to try remedies (the direction is unknown and both are plausible, as the authors say); whether the pills work or are safe (not studied); and anything about regular or recent use, or about remedies other than pills (the single item asked about ever-use of pills).

sample.recruitment: Cohort originally recruited from ninth graders at ten high schools in Los Angeles in 2013 and surveyed repeatedly; this analysis uses the 2021 wave.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Respondents to the 2021 wave who reported drinking alcohol in the past 30 days and answered the remedy question.
sample.demographics: Mean age 21.8 (SD 0.4); 61.4% women, 34.8% men, 3.8% another gender identity; 25.0% non-heterosexual; 47.4% Hispanic or Latino, 18.0% white, 15.7% Asian, 18.9% another race or ethnicity; 63.7% enrolled in a degree programme, 68.6% in paid work, 60.7% not living comfortably financially; mean CES-D-10 depression score 9.9 (SD 6.2).
sample.attrition: Not reported for the cohort: the number originally recruited and retained to 2021 is not given in this paper. Covariates were missing for 158 respondents (12.0%) and multiply imputed.
sample.selection_effects: One region and one school-based cohort, with unknown attrition since 2013; past-30-day drinkers only; only 42 respondents had used remedy pills, which limits precision and generalization.

exposure.measurement: One self-report item: ever used hangover remedy pills (for example dihydromyricetin), yes or no. Awareness (ever heard of remedy pills to prevent hangovers) and belief (do you feel they work) were single yes/no items.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: no information on how often, how recently, which product or why.
exposure.polysubstance: Not considered.

comparison.controls: Past-30-day drinkers in the same survey who had never used hangover remedy pills.
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age, gender and sexual identity, race and ethnicity, enrolment, employment, financial situation and depressive symptoms; the problem-count model was further adjusted for drinking frequency, binge frequency and drinks per drinking day.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality traits such as sensation seeking, peer drinking, earlier drinking history from the cohort's own previous waves, and hangover frequency or severity were not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: A modified AUDIT (10 items, 0 to 40), with the first three consumption items converted from the survey's own response options (Supplemental Table S1, not read); past-30-day drinking days, binge-drinking days (standard sex-specific definition) and drinks per typical drinking day, recoded from ranges to midpoints; a past-year count of seven alcohol problems, called an AUD symptom count.
outcomes.validity_norms: The AUDIT is a validated screening instrument; the consumption items were converted rather than asked as in the AUDIT. The seven items of the problem count (unable to stop, failing expectations, morning drinking, guilt, blackouts, injury, others' concern) are the AUDIT's problem items, not DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder.
outcomes.operationalization: Differences in modified AUDIT score (unstandardized B) and incidence rate ratios for the counts, the ever-use group against the never-use group.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; described as exploratory.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed survey).

analysis.effect_sizes: Ever-use group against never-use group: modified AUDIT 7.7 (SD 4.7) against 5.4 (4.7), adjusted B = 2.29 (95% CI 0.82 to 3.76), unadjusted 2.45 (0.96 to 3.93); drinks per typical drinking day, adjusted IRR 1.24 (1.02 to 1.49); alcohol problem count 1.7 against 0.9, adjusted IRR 1.86 (1.18 to 3.02), after also adjusting for drinking frequency and intensity; drinking days 6.4 against 5.6, adjusted IRR 1.19 (0.94 to 1.51), and binge days 2.6 against 2.1, adjusted IRR 1.40 (0.91 to 2.23), both not significant. Prevalence: 3.2% had ever used remedy pills (42 of 1312), 18.9% had heard of them, 8.6% believed they work.
analysis.covariates: Age, gender identity, sexual identity, race and ethnicity, enrolment in a degree programme, paid employment, financial situation and CES-D-10 depressive symptoms; missing covariates handled by multiple imputation.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the authors call the study exploratory.
analysis.selective_reporting: All five outcomes are reported with intervals; the reverse-direction analyses are in a supplement that was not read.
analysis.power: Not calculated; the authors note reduced power from the small number of people who had used remedy pills (42).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2021, 42 of 1312 young adult drinkers in a Los Angeles cohort (3.2%) had ever used hangover remedy pills. Compared with those who had not, they scored about 2.3 points higher on a 0 to 40 alcohol problem scale, drank about a quarter more drinks per drinking day, and reported almost twice as many alcohol problems, but did not drink on detectably more days or binge on more days. About one in five had heard of remedy pills and fewer than one in ten believed they work.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state an association and call for scientific and regulatory attention, which is consistent with the data, and the Limitations state plainly that causal interpretation is not possible. Gaps: (1) the Discussion speculates that remedy beliefs lead young adults to drink more and raises concern that remedy marketing could increase drinking, which a single cross-sectional association involving 42 people who had used the pills cannot support, as the authors partly acknowledge; (2) the problem count is called an AUD symptom count, although its items are the AUDIT's problem items rather than diagnostic criteria; (3) the Discussion recommends strategies (pacing, alternating with non-alcoholic drinks, medical evaluation for frequent hangovers) that this study did not examine.

timeline.event: Verster et al. review of 82 hangover remedy products sold on a US retail website (cited by the authors for product ingredients and marketing claims; not read here).
This study: by the authors' account the first to examine remedy use against drinking patterns and alcohol problems.

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional association in one cohort; no longitudinal study has tested whether remedy use comes before heavier drinking or follows it.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute and FDA Center for Tobacco Products (U54CA180905), National Cancer Institute (R01CA229617) and National Institute on Drug Abuse (K24DA048160).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the University of Southern California; the cohort is run by the senior author's group.

what_would_settle_it: A longitudinal study in the same or a similar cohort measuring remedy use (type, frequency, reasons) and drinking at several waves, testing whether starting remedy use is followed by heavier drinking or follows it, with adjustment for earlier drinking, hangover frequency and sensation seeking.

domains.note: Adjusted only for sociodemographic factors and depressive symptoms; earlier drinking, hangover frequency, personality and peers were not, and heavier drinking may itself lead to remedy use.
One self-report item on ever using remedy pills, with one example product; no recency, frequency or product information.
A school-based cohort with unreported attrition since 2013, restricted to past-30-day drinkers.
Not applicable to a single survey.
17 excluded for a missing exposure; covariates missing for 12% and multiply imputed.
Self-reported drinking and problems, recoded from response ranges; consumption items converted to the AUDIT scale.
Exploratory and not registered, but all planned outcomes are reported with intervals, including null ones.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For any causal reading (remedy use leading to heavier drinking, or the reverse) the risk of bias is high: the direction is unknown and important confounders were not measured. For the association as described, the main limits are a single crude exposure item and only 42 people who had used the pills. The card may be cited for the prevalence of remedy-pill use, awareness and belief in this cohort, and for the association of ever-use with more drinks per drinking day and more alcohol problems; not for any effect of remedies on drinking.

key_findings.finding: Of 1312 past-30-day drinkers aged 21 to 24 in 2021, 42 (3.2%) had ever used hangover remedy pills, 248 (18.9%) had heard of them, and 110 (8.6%) believed they work.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The ever-use group scored higher on the modified AUDIT (7.7, SD 4.7, against 5.4, SD 4.7); adjusted difference B = 2.29 (95% CI 0.82 to 3.76) on a 0 to 40 scale.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Alcohol use problem score; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The ever-use group drank more per typical drinking day (about a quarter more; adjusted IRR 1.24, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.49) and reported more alcohol problems (1.7 against 0.9 of 7; adjusted IRR 1.86, 1.18 to 3.02, also adjusted for drinking frequency and intensity).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, drinks per typical drinking day and Past Year AUD symptom count rows; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ever-use was not detectably associated with the number of drinking days (6.4 against 5.6; adjusted IRR 1.19, 0.94 to 1.51) or binge-drinking days (2.6 against 2.1; adjusted IRR 1.40, 0.91 to 2.23).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the reverse direction, higher problem scores, more drinks per drinking day and more alcohol problems were associated with higher odds of ever having used remedy pills.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (last sentence); Supplemental Table S2 (not read)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that causal interpretation is not possible, that the exposure item cannot separate recent from past or occasional from regular use, and that the small number of people who had used the pills limits power and generalizability.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The unadjusted AUDIT difference is marked with three asterisks, a symbol the table footnote does not define (it defines one and two); its interval (0.96 to 3.93) corresponds to p of about 0.001 (editors' calculation), not clearly below 0.001.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 and its notes
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the adjusted estimate (two asterisks, p about 0.002) is the one to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The seven-item count called an AUD symptom count consists of the AUDIT's problem items (unable to stop, failing expectations, morning drinking, guilt, blackouts, injury, others' concern), not DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Alcohol use problems; Table 2, footnote d
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say alcohol-related problems, not symptoms of alcohol use disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: The proportion of missing covariate data is printed as 'n = 158.12.0%'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error, read as 158 respondents (12.0%).

reporting_issues.issue: The original size of the cohort and its retention to the 2021 wave are not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study design and participants
reporting_issues.consequence: Selection by attrition cannot be judged from this paper.

design_detail: Open-label randomized two-period crossover trial in 13 healthy Japanese men with fully active aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2*1/*1): the same amount of sake drunk with or without added mineral water taken in between, in two sessions, with standard meals, an overnight stay and repeated measures of breath ethanol and acetaldehyde, a one-minute Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) and six visual analogue symptom ratings from before drinking to the next day (schedule in the exposure field). Registered UMIN000050305. Funded by the sake brewer that made the test drink.
can_establish: Whether, in a small group of healthy men drinking a fixed amount of sake under controlled conditions, adding a large volume of water during drinking changes breath alcohol and acetaldehyde or the next-morning symptom ratings and DSST performance by a large amount.
cannot_establish: Whether water during drinking makes a small or moderate difference to hangover (13 participants; no intervals reported); whether it helps in real life, where water may reduce how much and how fast people drink (alcohol was fixed here); whether results apply to women, to people with the less active ALDH2 variant or other genetic backgrounds, to other drinks, or to smaller amounts of water; and whether people actually had a hangover (no hangover scale was used).

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond healthy Japanese men studied at the Oita University Hospital Clinical Trial Unit, January to March 2023.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: men aged 20 to 50, body mass index 18.0 to 30.0, ALDH2*1/*1 genotype (checked by PCR on cheek cells), a history of drinking more than 100 g of pure alcohol per day (as printed), and no significant health problems. Excluded: history of alcohol abuse or alcohol allergy, regular medication, liver disease, or abnormal findings at clinical examination.
sample.demographics: Mean age 36.2 years (SD 9.6), height 172.5 cm (6.0), weight 71.5 kg (8.2), body mass index 24.0 (2.0); all men, all Japanese.
sample.attrition: Of 16 who consented, 2 withdrew and 14 took part; one was excluded because severe abdominal fullness stopped him finishing the water, leaving 13 in a per-protocol analysis. When the withdrawals occurred, and the excluded man's data, are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Men only; only the fully active ALDH2 genotype, which the authors say excludes the roughly 40% of East Asians with the less active variant; people able to drink at least 100 g of alcohol in a day; a per-protocol analysis that dropped the one participant who could not tolerate the water condition.

exposure.measurement: Supervised drinking in the clinical trial unit, with the amounts of sake and water fixed by body weight and drunk at an even pace over one hour.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: Japanese sake (15% alcohol by volume) equal to 1.3 g/kg pure alcohol, drunk over one hour from 9 p.m., alone or with 15 mL/kg mineral water taken in between drinks; mean sake 749 mL (range 598 to 967) and mean water 1,072 mL (855 to 1,383). Total fluid in the water condition about 1,800 mL in the hour. About 6 hours of sleep, waking 7 hours after drinking ended. Sessions at least one week apart. Measures before drinking, immediately and one hour after drinking ended, and at several times from 7 to 15 hours after; the next-morning DSST differences discussed are at 7 and 8 hours. A standard dinner at least 2 hours before drinking and a standard breakfast 10 hours after; one 550 mL bottle of water allowed overnight and another from breakfast, in both conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Regular medication excluded; other drugs and smoking not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Next-morning measures began 7 hours after drinking ended; breath ethanol at that point is shown only in a figure.

comparison.controls: The same men drinking the same amount of sake without the added water, in the other period.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with a washout between sessions (interval in the exposure field); order randomized, method not described; the number of men in each sequence is not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant to the within-person comparison. Sleep was not measured, and expectations about water were not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde by sensor gas chromatography (detection limits 0.2 ppm and 5 ppb); DSST, number of correct symbol matches in one minute, analysed as change from the pre-drinking score; 100 mm visual analogue scales for facial flushing, headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness and feeling exhilarated; all before drinking, shortly after drinking and at several times the next morning (schedule in the exposure field).
outcomes.validity_norms: The DSST is a standard processing-speed test; the six visual analogue items are not a validated hangover scale, and no hangover severity questionnaire was used.
outcomes.operationalization: Hangover was inferred by the authors from higher headache and nausea ratings and lower concentration ratings early the next morning; a difference between conditions at any time point was the test of effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, by design (exploratory study), across nine outcomes, each tested at several time points.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open label. Symptoms were self-rated by participants who knew which condition they were in.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported numerically. Means, SDs and differences appear only in figures (images; values not extracted). Text: no significant difference in breath ethanol or acetaldehyde at any time, with acetaldehyde point estimates slightly higher with water shortly after drinking; DSST change from baseline lower with water immediately after drinking (p = 0.01) and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08, described as not significant); no significant difference in any of the six symptom ratings. The publisher's figure descriptions, which it says were written with AI support, describe the without-water curves as peaking higher in the headache, sleepiness and exhilaration panels; these were not used as data.
analysis.covariates: Linear mixed-effects model with drink condition and period as fixed effects and participant as a random effect; whether a separate model was fitted at each time point is not stated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: UMIN-CTR 000050305, registered before the trial according to the paper. The registry record was not read, so the registered primary outcome and target sample (the paper gives a target of 20 and a minimum of 6) could not be compared with the report.
analysis.selective_reporting: No numerical results for any outcome are given in text or tables; only the DSST has p-values. The target of 20 participants was not reached and no reason is given.
analysis.power: Exploratory; no formal calculation in advance. The authors state afterwards that with 13 participants power was barely 0.8 to detect an effect size of 1 at a one-sided 5% level, so smaller effects could be missed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 13 men, adding a large amount of water while drinking sake did not detectably change breath ethanol or acetaldehyde, or any of six next-morning symptom ratings, compared with the same sake without water; DSST performance was worse with water right after drinking (when several participants reported bloating) and, without reaching significance, slightly better with water the next morning. No numerical estimates or intervals are reported, so the size of any effect that was missed cannot be bounded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title states that water intake during drinking "does not alleviate hangover symptoms", and the abstract concludes it did not affect hangover. Gaps: (1) a non-significant result in 13 people, with power only for a very large effect, is read as absence of effect; (2) no hangover scale was used, and the hangover state is inferred from figure trends; (3) the conclusion speculates that water helps in daily life by limiting how much people drink, which the fixed-dose design could not test, and also suggests water may slightly improve next-morning performance from a p of 0.05 to 0.08 the authors call non-significant; (4) the funding statement says the funder had no role in analysis, while two of the four authors employed by the funder did the formal analysis. The Discussion does list the small sample, men only, open label, one genotype and one drink as limits.

timeline.event: Mackus et al. (Alcohol, 2024) on drinking water to prevent or relieve hangover, cited by the authors as agreeing; not read here and not in the library's references.
This trial: by the authors' account the first randomized crossover study of water during drinking with alcohol, water and food controlled.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small, open-label, industry-funded crossover trial. It is the only randomized test of water during drinking that the authors knew of; the earlier work they cite on water and hangover was not randomized.

funding.funder: Sanwa Shurui Corporation, a sake brewer, which made the test drink (Waka Botan sake); the statement says the funder was not involved in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to publish.
funding.declared_conflicts: Four authors (SK, AN, KM, MK) were employed by the Research Laboratory of Sanwa Shurui Co., Ltd.; the others declare no conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Per the author-contribution statement, two of the employees (SK and MK) did the formal analysis and data curation and all four contributed to conceptualization or methods, which sits uneasily with the statement that the funder had no role in design or analysis.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover trial, preregistered with a validated hangover severity scale as the primary outcome, in women and men of different genetic backgrounds, comparing water with no water at amounts people actually drink, with the alcohol fixed in one comparison and free (self-chosen) in another so that any effect through drinking less can be seen, and with sleep measured and outcomes rated blind where possible.

domains.note: Random assignment to sequence is stated, but how the sequence was generated and concealed is not, nor how many men were in each sequence.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: The washout between sessions (interval in the exposure field) is ample for a single evening of alcohol; period was in the model.
Open label. One man could not finish the water because of abdominal fullness and was dropped (per-protocol analysis); several others reported bloating during the water condition.
One of 14 participants excluded for a reason tied to the intervention, and his data are not reported; the two earlier withdrawals are not explained.

Symptoms were self-rated by participants who knew whether they had drunk water, a remedy the authors call widely believed to work. The breath measures are objective and the DSST less exposed. The expected direction of this bias favours water, so it does not explain the null result.
Registered, but the registered primary outcome could not be checked here; results are reported only as figures and p-values, at many time points without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Overall high because the symptom outcomes were self-rated without blinding; other domains raise some concerns (randomization not described, per-protocol exclusion tied to the intervention, no numerical results). For the question this card is cited for, whether water during drinking reduced next-morning symptoms, the unblinded rating would be expected to favour water, so the null finding is not likely to be an artefact of it; its main weakness is imprecision. The trial may be cited as finding no detectable effect in 13 men at one fixed amount of sake, and not as showing that water has no effect.

key_findings.finding: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde did not differ significantly between the water and no-water conditions at any time after drinking; acetaldehyde point estimates were slightly higher with water shortly after drinking, and the curves were almost identical by the next morning.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: DSST change from the pre-drinking score was lower with water immediately after drinking ended (p = 0.01) and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08), which the authors call not statistically significant; scores then returned to pre-drinking levels in both conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: No means, SDs or intervals are given in text; the 5% two-sided threshold was stated in advance, so p = 0.05 is on the boundary.

key_findings.finding: None of the six visual analogue ratings (facial flushing, headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, feeling exhilarated) differed significantly between conditions at any time point.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 4

key_findings.finding: The authors read higher headache and nausea ratings and lower concentration ratings early the next morning as a hangover state, and higher flushing and mood ratings right after drinking as intoxication; these trends are shown only in figures.
key_findings.locator: Discussions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Total fluid intake in the water condition was very large (amounts in the exposure field); several men reported abdominal bloating, and one dropped out with severe fullness; the authors suggest the bloating may explain the lower DSST score right after drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Discussions, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that 13 participants gave power barely 0.8 to detect an effect size of 1 (one-sided 5% level), so smaller effects may have been missed; and that the design cannot separate drinking water between drinks from drinking the same alcohol diluted to about half strength.
key_findings.locator: Discussions, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding came from the sake brewer that made the test drink, and four of eight authors were employed by its research laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract state that water does not alleviate hangover symptoms, a conclusion of absence drawn from non-significant differences in 13 men, with no estimates or intervals reported and power only for an effect size of 1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Title; Abstract › Conclusion; Discussions, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must say the evidence is insufficient to rule out a modest effect, not that water does not work.

reporting_issues.issue: The funding statement says the funder had no role in design, analysis or interpretation, but four authors were employed by the funder and two of them did the formal analysis and data curation (author contributions).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions
reporting_issues.consequence: The funder's involvement is larger than the funding statement says; a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount the null result, which runs against a commercial interest in neither direction obviously.

reporting_issues.issue: The model is described differently in two places: the abstract names fixed effects for the test beverages and the number of administrations, the Methods name beverage and time (first and second periods), and how the difference at each time point was tested is not stated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Methods › Statistical analyses
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysis cannot be reproduced from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: No numerical results (means, SDs, differences, intervals) are reported for any outcome; all values are in figures only. The data availability statement refers to online repositories whose names are said to be in the article, but none is named.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results; Figures 2 to 4; Data availability statement
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes cannot be computed, and the imprecision of the null result cannot be quantified.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion suggests that water may slightly improve next-morning psychomotor function, from DSST differences with p = 0.05 and 0.08 that the Results call non-significant, and attributes the popular belief in water to drinking less, which the fixed-dose design did not test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither statement is a finding of this trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the two conditions the Control group and the Water group, although every participant took part in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: Terminology only; the comparison is within-person.
