design_detail: Single-centre, open-label randomized crossover trial with matched triplets (Witten/Herdecke University, Germany, summer 2017): participants matched on age, sex, body size, drinking and hangover frequency were randomized 1:1:1 to beer then wine (study group 1), wine then beer (study group 2), or a control group drinking only beer or only wine, each to the same breath alcohol target, under medical supervision with an overnight stay; in a second session each person drank in the opposite order (or the other single drink); targets and intervals are in the exposure field. Primary outcome: Acute Hangover Scale the next day; 90 of 105 randomized completed.
can_establish: Whether drinking beer before wine, rather than wine before beer, to the same supervised level of intoxication changes next-day hangover severity by as much as the trial's prespecified difference (about 8 points on a 0 to 56 scale) in healthy young adults.
cannot_establish: Whether order makes a smaller difference (the interval of the primary comparison runs to about 4 points either way; editors' calculation), whether other drinks (spirits, red wine, dark beer) behave differently, whether results hold for unsupervised drinking without water before bed, and whether vomiting or feeling very drunk cause worse hangovers (they are exploratory correlates that are part of the same heavy intoxication).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers from Witten/Herdecke University recruited by an online survey, September 2016 to June 2017; interventions 1 July to 26 August 2017.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 to 60, drinking both beer and wine, physically fit, with two available matching partners. Excluded: aversion to beer or wine, history of drug or alcohol abuse, abstinence or alcohol intolerance, East Asian origin (because of common variants of alcohol-metabolizing genes), abnormal liver tests or liver disease, viral hepatitis, chronic pain, epilepsy, Wernicke or Korsakoff syndrome, thiamine deficiency, gastritis, bariatric surgery, immunosuppression, recent infection, pregnancy or breastfeeding, frequent use of pain medication, and medications that interact with alcohol (for example antibiotics, opioids, nitrates, antidepressants).
sample.demographics: Age 19 to 40 (group means 23.6 to 24.3); 48.4%, 48.4% and 53.6% women; mean BMI about 22.3; drinking several times a month and hangovers between rarely and a few times a month in all groups (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 105 randomized, 90 completed (14% lost), mostly because the trial overlapped with exams or holidays; if a study-group member dropped out, the whole matched triplet was excluded; per-protocol analysis. The target of 36 per study group was not reached.
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy university volunteers who drink both beer and wine and could be matched; completers only.

exposure.measurement: Supervised drinking with breath alcohol measured hourly (AlcoQuant 6020+, after 15 minutes without food or drink) and again the next morning; readings were not shown to participants. The drink of the day was disclosed only on the evening of each session.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: Carlsberg 1847 Pilsner lager (5%) and a 2015 white wine (Chasselas/Johanniter, 11.1%), served cold. Study groups drank the first drink to a breath alcohol of 0.05% or more, then the second to 0.11% (switch at about 0.06%, after 1.7 to 2.3 hours); about 1.2 to 1.4 L of beer and 0.6 to 0.7 L of wine per session; peak breath alcohol 0.12 to 0.13% in all groups after about 3.6 to 4.6 hours; controls drank about 2.6 L of beer or 1.2 L of wine (Table 2). Drinking could stop early at the person's wish or for safety. A standardized meal before drinking, 6 mL/kg of water before sleep, and an overnight stay under medical supervision; no alcohol for one week before each session. The second session was at least one week after the first.
exposure.polysubstance: Medications interacting with alcohol and frequent pain medication excluded; smoking and other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Hangover rated the next day once breath alcohol had returned to zero.

comparison.controls: Within person: the same participants drinking in the opposite order in a second session. A parallel control group drank one beverage only on each day.
comparison.matching: Triplets matched on age, sex, weight, height, BMI, drinking frequency and hangover frequency (Supplemental Table 1, not read), each triplet randomized with a six-sided die.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant within person; sleep duration was described as similar but not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Acute Hangover Scale as an 8-item compound score (thirst, fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, stomach ache, racing heart, loss of appetite), each 0 to 7, total 0 to 56; perceived drunkenness 0 to 10 at the end of drinking; vomiting; blood and urine tests before drinking and the next day (Supplemental Table 3, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: The scale is cited to its developers; Rohsenow et al. (2014, read in this round) describe the Acute Hangover Scale as nine items including an overall hangover item, while this trial used eight.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: the within-person difference in hangover score between the two drinking orders, compared between study group 1 and study group 2 (Welch two-sample t test); the defining formula is printed as an image.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One primary comparison; secondary analyses (sex, relative score per unit of peak breath alcohol, a cluster analysis, regression with backward selection on both days, laboratory panels) are numerous and several are reported as data not shown, so the number of tests cannot be counted.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open label. The authors say blinding beer and wine proved impossible in a pre-trial, and that an alcohol-free control was not feasible.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: within-person difference X in study group 1 −0.32 (SD 7.63) against Y in study group 2 0.36 (SD 6.82), P = 0.71 (editors' approximate 95% CI for X minus Y −4.4 to 3.0 points on the 0 to 56 scale). No group differed in hangover score between its two days (P > 0.05; control group beer-only against wine-only days included). Period difference ('carryover' test) P = 0.8. Women reported more severe hangovers than men (P = 0.009, data not shown), not significant after dividing by peak breath alcohol. Vomiting and perceived drunkenness were associated with higher scores on both days in regression (coefficients in Figure 5, an image; values not extracted).
analysis.covariates: Exploratory regression with backward selection by Akaike information criterion, with unadjusted 95% CIs; 89 participants on day 1 and 88 on day 2.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Approved beforehand by the Witten/Herdecke University Ethics Committee (140/2016), which the authors call prospective registration, and registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00015285) only retrospectively. No public prospective registration, so the primary analysis cannot be checked against a protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: Mean hangover scores for each condition are not given in text or tables (box plots only); the sex difference, the cluster analysis and some regressions are reported as data not shown; individual symptoms are in a supplement not read.
analysis.power: Planned for 36 per study group to detect a 14% difference (1 point per item, about 8 points) with 80% power at 5%; 31 per group completed. The observed interval excludes a difference of 8 points (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 62 young adults who drank beer and wine in both orders to the same breath alcohol, the order did not detectably change next-day hangover severity (difference between groups −0.68 points on a 0 to 56 scale, editors' 95% CI about −4.4 to 3.0, P = 0.71), and controls did not differ between a beer-only and a wine-only day. Differences as large as the trial's planned 8 points are excluded; smaller ones are not. In exploratory regressions, vomiting and feeling drunk went with worse hangovers; women reported worse hangovers than men.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings "dispel the traditional myths" and the Discussion that they "debunk" them, and the authors advise readers to heed perceived drunkenness and vomiting to reduce hangover intensity. Gaps: (1) one trial with lager and white wine, open label and per protocol, cannot debunk an effect smaller than about 4 points or with other drinks; (2) vomiting and perceived drunkenness are markers of the same heavy intoxication, found by backward selection in exploratory models, and are not shown to be causes that can be acted on; (3) the Discussion states that women and men did not differ in hangover severity, while the Results report that women's hangovers were more severe (P = 0.009).

timeline.event: This trial: by the authors' account the first data to test the beer-and-wine order sayings.

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized test of drink order and hangover; its null result is reasonably precise for large differences, for lager and white wine at the level of intoxication studied.

funding.funder: No external funding is stated; Carlsberg donated the beer free of charge and, per the paper, had no role in design, conduct or analysis.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest related to the research.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Witten/Herdecke University and HELIOS University Hospital Wuppertal.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized crossover replication at another centre with blinded outcome assessment where possible, more drink types (spirits, red wine, dark beer), more than one level of intoxication, realistic bedtimes without supplied water, prespecified secondary analyses, and full reporting of mean hangover scores by condition.

domains.note: Matched triplets randomized with a die and the drink of the day concealed until the evening; study groups balanced at baseline (Table 1). In the control group, 7 of 28 drank beer first and 21 wine first, which is unlikely under a 1:1 random choice (two-sided binomial p about 0.01; editors' calculation) and is not explained, but the control group is not part of the primary comparison.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: Washout and abstinence before each session (intervals in the exposure field); no difference between study days (P = 0.8).
Supervised drinking to breath alcohol targets with an overnight stay; open label, but no sign of departures from the assigned order.
15 of 105 randomized (14%) not analysed, mostly for exams or holidays; whole triplets were excluded when a study-group member dropped out.

Self-rated hangover by participants who knew what they drank and in what order; the folk sayings are well known, but both sequences involved mixing, and expectation would favour the saying rather than the null result.
Only retrospective public registration; condition means are not reported numerically and several secondary results are data not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-controlled supervised design with matched randomization and within-person comparison; the concerns are open-label self-rating, per-protocol analysis with 14% loss, and retrospective registration with incomplete numerical reporting. The card may be cited for no detectable effect of the order of beer and wine on next-day hangover at the amounts and drinks studied, with differences as large as the planned 8 points excluded. It should not be cited for vomiting or perceived drunkenness as causes of hangover, nor as showing no sex difference.

key_findings.finding: Primary endpoint: the within-person difference in Acute Hangover Scale score between drinking orders was −0.32 (SD 7.63) in study group 1 and 0.36 (SD 6.82) in study group 2, P = 0.71; no group's score differed between its two days.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: X minus Y = −0.68 points, approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 3.0 on the 0 to 56 scale; the planned difference was about 8 points (1 point on each of 8 items).

key_findings.finding: Control participants did not differ in hangover between a beer-only and a wine-only day (P > 0.05); 7 of 28 drank beer on day 1 and 21 wine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Drinking conditions were comparable: breath alcohol at the switch and at its peak was similar in all sequences and groups (values in the exposure field); the switch came sooner when wine was drunk first.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Trial progress specifics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Dividing each person's hangover score by his or her peak breath alcohol gave the same pattern as the uncorrected scores.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 3rd paragraph; Supplemental Figure 1 (not read)

key_findings.finding: Women reported more severe hangovers than men on both days (P = 0.009, data not shown); after dividing by peak breath alcohol the difference was a non-significant tendency (45 women, 45 men).
key_findings.locator: Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: In exploratory regressions with backward selection (89 participants on day 1, 88 on day 2), vomiting and perceived drunkenness were associated with higher hangover scores on both days; blood and urine tests did not differ between groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Figure 5 legend

key_findings.finding: Vomiting occurred more often in the control group (wine only 6, beer only 5) than in the study groups (2 to 4), and in more women than men on both days (5 against 4; 8 against 4).
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse events, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 272 screened, 247 were eligible, 105 were matched and randomized and 90 completed; the planned 36 per study group was not reached because of loss to follow-up during exams and holidays.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study population, 1st paragraph; Methods › Sample size

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that no difference between women and men in hangover severity was found, while the Results report more severe hangovers in women (P = 0.009), attenuated only after dividing by peak breath alcohol.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex finding should be taken from the Results: women reported worse hangovers, partly explained by higher breath alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The control group is 28 in the text and Table 1 but 29 in the heading of Table 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Table 2; Results › Study population
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the denominators of the drinking data.

reporting_issues.issue: Of 28 controls, 7 were assigned beer first and 21 wine first, though assignment was described as random by die; a split this uneven has a two-sided probability of about 0.01 under a 1:1 random choice (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Randomization; Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The control group's assignment may not have been 1:1 random; it does not affect the primary comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: What the paper calls a carryover test compares summed scores between the two days, which tests a period effect; and the Methods say it was done before the first intervention, which is not possible.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Biostatistical analyses, 3rd paragraph; Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Carryover was not formally assessed, though the washout makes it unlikely.

reporting_issues.issue: The formula defining the primary within-person differences is printed as an image, and mean hangover scores for each drink condition are not given in text or tables.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Biostatistical analyses, equation (1); Results; Figure 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of hangovers in each condition cannot be quoted; only the difference statistics can.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion advises readers to heed perceived drunkenness and vomiting to reduce hangover intensity, from exploratory associations after backward model selection.
reporting_issues.consequence: A correlational, exploratory result presented as practical advice; not a finding about prevention.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of a randomized laboratory trial (Howland et al., 2010, designed for simulated driving) comparing two of its parallel groups: young adults who drank beer with added caffeine (n = 28) or the same beer without caffeine (n = 36) to the same breath alcohol target, then had a supervised sleep opportunity at a clinical research centre (conditions in the exposure field); next-morning hangover (Acute Hangover Scale), self-reported sleep and sleepiness. The trial's placebo-beer groups were not analysed. Author manuscript version in PubMed Central.
can_establish: Whether adding a fixed amount of caffeine to beer, at a controlled level of intoxication and with a full night in bed, changed next-morning hangover or self-reported sleep by a large amount in healthy young adults.
cannot_establish: Whether caffeine changes hangover by a small or moderate amount (the interval for hangover incidence runs from 32 percentage points lower to 15 higher; editors' calculation); effects with energy drinks (other ingredients, other amounts), with heavier or later drinking, or with the shortened sleep typical of real nights out; or objective sleep (sleep was self-reported only).

sample.recruitment: Greater Boston, USA; 89% university students, the rest recent graduates; paid 150 US dollars.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21 to 30; no current or past drinking problems; at least one recent heavy-drinking occasion (definition in the exposure field); no health problems or medication contraindicated with alcohol, no sleep disorder, not pregnant or nursing; regular tobacco use excluded. A prescribed sleep schedule for three nights before the session (diary and time-stamped phone check); abstinence from alcohol, unapproved medication, sleep aids, recreational drugs and caffeine before the session (intervals in the exposure field).
sample.demographics: Caffeinated group: mean age 22.8 (SD 2.3), 41.4% men, 78.6% white, 96% at university; non-caffeinated group: 23.3 (2.1), 58.3% men, 83.3% white, 83% at university; all differences p > 0.20 (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Only completers are reported (28 and 36); how many were randomized to each group is not stated here (it is in the parent trial report, not read). The 41.4% men in a group of 28 is not a possible proportion (12 of 29 gives 41.4%).
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, mostly white students without drinking problems, non-smokers, with regulated sleep before the session; volunteers paid to take part.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory-administered drinks, with breath alcohol measured; caffeine added by the investigators as a tasteless solution.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: high-gravity beer (8.1% alcohol by volume) dosed to a breath alcohol of 0.12 g% (1.068 g/kg for men, 0.915 g/kg for women), on average 44 oz of beer (37 oz for women), drunk from 7:30 to about 8:30 p.m. three hours after a standard meal; caffeine added at the concentration of a commercial caffeinated beer (69 mg per 12 oz), on average 383 mg (338 mg for women). Mean peak breath alcohol 0.12 g% (range 0.08 to 0.16) in both groups. Sleep opportunity 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., monitored by an emergency medical technician; Stanford Sleepiness Scale at 8:00, 8:30 and 9:00 a.m. Inclusion required at least one occasion of 5 or more drinks (4 for women) in the previous 30 days; before the session, no alcohol, unapproved medication, sleep aids or recreational drugs for 24 hours and no caffeine for 8 hours.
exposure.polysubstance: Recreational drugs, sleep aids and unapproved medication excluded for 24 hours before the session; regular smokers excluded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; morning measures after the sleep opportunity (breath alcohol in the morning not reported here).

comparison.controls: A parallel randomized group drinking the same beer without caffeine to the same breath alcohol target.
comparison.matching: Randomized; the method of randomization and any blinding to caffeine are not described in this paper (it refers to the parent trial).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Groups were similar on age, alcohol daily volume, race and university enrolment; men were 41% of the caffeinated and 58% of the non-caffeinated group (not significant). Habitual caffeine use is not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded before the session by instruction.

outcomes.instruments: Acute Hangover Scale (nine items; incidence defined as any rating above none on the first item, severity as the mean of the nine items); six items from a post-sleep questionnaire (Roehrs et al., 1991) giving an average sleep quality score, later split into two night-time and two morning alertness and concentration items; self-reported minutes to fall asleep and minutes asleep; Stanford Sleepiness Scale three times in the morning, averaged.
outcomes.validity_norms: The Acute Hangover Scale is described as psychometrically validated (Rohsenow et al., 2007, by the same group); the sleep-quality items had previously separated heavy drinking from placebo.
outcomes.operationalization: Between-group differences in means (t tests) and proportions (chi-square), with Cohen's d and h, used to judge whether non-significant results reflected small effects or low power.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; alpha 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes were self-reported by participants; whether they knew they had caffeine is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Caffeinated against non-caffeinated, means (SD): Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 (0.84) against 1.45 (0.89), d = 0.13 (editors' 95% CI for d −0.63 to 0.38); hangover incidence 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19 (editors' risk difference −8.7 percentage points, 95% CI −32 to 15); average sleep quality 4.45 (0.41) against 4.16 (0.49), t(62) = 2.49, 95% CI of the difference 0.057 to 0.517, d = 0.64, better with caffeine; morning alertness and concentration items 4.66 (0.82) against 4.29 (0.93), d = 0.42, p < 0.10; night-time items d = 0.30; minutes to fall asleep 36.5 (67.7) against 23.2 (29.4), d = 0.28; minutes asleep 390.7 (73.8) against 404.7 (62.5), d = 0.21; Stanford Sleepiness 2.52 (1.37) against 2.78 (0.90), d = 0.23; none of these significant except sleep quality.
analysis.covariates: None; the authors argue that dosing by sex and weight and the narrow age range made adjustment unnecessary.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; this is a secondary analysis proposed after the parent trial by a co-author.
analysis.selective_reporting: The split of the sleep-quality score into night-time and morning items was decided after the main result (the Discussion calls it post hoc). The Highlights state that caffeine did not affect next-day mood, but no mood outcome is reported in the paper.
analysis.power: No calculation; the authors use effect sizes to argue that the null results reflect small effects, which the intervals (editors' calculation) do not fully support.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 64 young adults randomized to beer with or without added caffeine at the same breath alcohol, next-morning hangover severity and incidence did not differ detectably (61% against 69% with any hangover), but the intervals are wide enough to include a moderate effect either way. Caffeine did not detectably change self-reported time to fall asleep, time asleep or sleepiness, and the caffeine group rated its sleep quality better, mostly because of morning alertness items.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say mixing caffeine and alcohol does not significantly impair sleep, hangover or sleepiness in this population, which is fair; but the Discussion goes further, saying people who believe adding caffeine to alcohol affects the odds of hangover are likely misinformed and that the results probably generalize to energy drinks and heavier drinking. Gaps: (1) a non-significant difference in 64 people with an interval from 32 points lower to 15 higher cannot show absence of effect; (2) energy drinks, larger amounts and the short sleep of real nights out were not tested; (3) the Highlights report an effect on mood that was not measured in the paper.

timeline.event: Parent randomized trial of caffeinated and non-caffeinated beer on simulated driving (Howland et al., 2010), not read here.

This secondary analysis: by the authors' account the first randomized comparison of hangover after caffeinated and non-caffeinated alcohol.

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized test of caffeine added to alcohol on hangover that the authors knew of; its null result agrees in direction with an earlier student survey but is imprecise.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized, double-blind trial (with participants' guesses about caffeine recorded) comparing alcohol with and without caffeine or a commercial energy drink, at more than one amount of alcohol and caffeine, with realistic bedtimes, polysomnography or actigraphy, and a prespecified hangover outcome powered to detect a small-to-moderate difference.

domains.note: Described only as randomized, with details deferred to the parent trial; unequal group sizes (28 and 36) and an imbalance in sex (41% against 58% men) without explanation.
Drinks were given and finished under supervision to a breath alcohol target, with a monitored night in the laboratory.

A secondary analysis of a trial designed for driving outcomes, without registration of these outcomes; the sleep-quality score was split after the fact.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The administration of drinks and the night in the laboratory were well controlled, but randomization, blinding and attrition are not reported in this paper, and the outcomes are a later secondary analysis. For the hangover outcome, which is null, the main limitation is imprecision rather than bias. The card may be cited for no detectable difference in next-morning hangover or self-reported sleep after caffeinated against non-caffeinated beer at this level of intoxication, and not for showing that caffeine has no effect on hangover.

design_detail: Systematic review and fixed-effect meta-analysis of published randomized placebo-controlled trials in which people who drank alcohol just before or during the trial took repeated usual (therapeutic) doses of acetaminophen (paracetamol) and had serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) measured. Six trials met the criteria; five, with 551 people on acetaminophen and 350 on placebo, reported ALT at one common early time point and were pooled (doses, durations and measurement days in the exposure field). Funded by an investigator-initiated grant from a manufacturer of acetaminophen products. Author manuscript version in PubMed Central.
can_establish: Whether, in the published randomized trials to 2010, mostly of people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification, a short course of acetaminophen at usual doses raised ALT at an early measurement compared with placebo, and whether any liver failure was reported.
cannot_establish: The risk of rare serious liver injury (with no events among 551 people, the upper 95% limit is about 0.5%; editors' calculation by the rule of three); effects of longer use (ALT rose modestly at later measurements in three trials); effects of taking acetaminophen during a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking (no trial studied that situation); effects of larger doses or of combination products; and whether acetaminophen relieves hangover symptoms (not studied).

sample.recruitment: Searches on 17 November 2010 of MEDLINE (1950 to 2010), EMBASE (1980 to 2010) and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts (1967 to 2009) for acetaminophen terms, with the results filtered for alcohol terms in an internal database, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials to 22 November 2010; no language restriction; published trials only. Four included trials recruited people with heavy drinking admitted to detoxification centres, one moderate drinkers who kept drinking as usual, and one people taking warfarin, most of whom reported light drinking (drinking levels in the exposure field).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized placebo-controlled trials in which participants drank alcohol just before (usually by self-report) or during the trial, took multiple usual doses of acetaminophen (exposure field), and had ALT measured. Of eight randomized trials found, two were excluded because ALT was not measured (Edwards et al., 1982) or not compared between acetaminophen and placebo (Critchley et al., 1983).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated; Table 1 gives each pooled trial's dose, duration and group sizes.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; within trials, Table 2 shows numbers measured falling over time (for example from 306 to 256 in the acetaminophen group of the largest trial).
sample.selection_effects: Published trials only; five of the six included trials and all five pooled trials have authors of this review among their authors (Dart, Green, Heard, Sivilotti), and the earlier systematic review the authors cite (Dart, Kuffner and Rumack, 2000) is also theirs. Mostly people in detoxification who stopped drinking at entry; little information on people who keep drinking.

exposure.measurement: Acetaminophen or placebo given under trial conditions; alcohol use from self-report (no alcohol was allowed during the four detoxification trials).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 2 to 4 g a day by mouth for 2 to 28 days across the six trials; in the five pooled trials 4 g a day for 2, 3, 5 or 10 days, or 3.9 g a day of a modified-release form for 4 days. In the detoxification trials acetaminophen began within 24 hours of the last drink. ALT was pooled at study day 4 (after the end of dosing in the 2-day and 3-day trials). Later measurements: days 6 and 7 in Dart et al. (one and two days after a 5-day course), day 11 in Heard et al. (one day after a 10-day course), days 14 and 28 in Parra et al. (2 g and 4 g a day). Drinking levels: moderate drinkers in Heard et al. reported 1 to 3 drinks a day; most participants in Parra et al. reported less than 2 oz of alcohol a day.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; one trial was in people taking warfarin.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: In four pooled trials participants were abstinent from alcohol during dosing (the period when, the authors argue, the liver enzyme CYP2E1 is most induced); in one, moderate drinkers continued drinking.

comparison.controls: Placebo groups within each randomized trial.
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; no formal risk-of-bias assessment of the trials was done.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Nutrition, liver disease and other medicines are not summarized at review level.

outcomes.instruments: Serum ALT; other liver tests (AST, INR, total bilirubin, glutathione S-transferase) summarized narratively; liver dysfunction (bilirubin above 2 mg/dL or INR above 2.0), liver failure and death recorded.
outcomes.validity_norms: ALT is a standard marker of liver-cell injury; the review chose it as the most commonly reported and more specific than AST.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: the difference between groups in mean change in ALT from baseline at the one early time point reported by most trials (study day in the exposure field); a positive value means a greater rise with acetaminophen.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the single pooled outcome; other time points and tests are reported descriptively.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Two independent abstractors assessed eligibility with a structured form and resolved disagreements by consensus; laboratory outcomes in the trials are objective.

analysis.effect_sizes: Fixed-effect meta-analysis (Comprehensive Meta-Analysis) of five trials at the common early time point: printed as 0.0 IU/L (95% CI −0.2 to 0.1 in the abstract; called a 97% CI in the Results); Q = 1.7, p = 0.8, I2 = 0. The printed values match a standardized difference in means (editors' recalculation from Table 1: −0.04, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.10, Q = 1.6), as the forest-plot legend says, not IU/L; in IU/L the pooled difference is about 0.1 (95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; editors' calculation). Later time points, not pooled: ALT higher with acetaminophen by 12.6 IU/L shortly after the end of a course (Dart et al.), by 8.4 IU/L just after the end of a longer course, statistically significant (Heard et al.), and by 18.7 IU/L at the higher dose and 8.1 IU/L at the lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra et al.), with no difference at that trial's last measurement; measurement days in the exposure field. No liver dysfunction, liver failure or death in any trial.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the protocol, analysis methods and inclusion criteria were prespecified but not registered.
analysis.selective_reporting: Planned pooling at several time points was abandoned because trials measured ALT on different days; only one early time point was pooled. Results at other days are shown trial by trial in Table 2.
analysis.power: Not addressed; five trials, 901 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In five published randomized trials, mostly of people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification, ALT at the pooled early time point did not rise detectably more with acetaminophen at usual doses than with placebo (pooled difference about 0.1 IU/L, 95% CI about −1.3 to 1.5; editors' calculation), and no trial reported liver failure or death. In two of the five trials acetaminophen had already been stopped before that measurement. Three trials that measured later found modest ALT rises with acetaminophen (about 8 to 19 IU/L) with longer use, mostly just after dosing ended, which had gone at the last measurement of the one trial that looked.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say there was no elevation of ALT at the pooled time point at the highest usual dose, and the Discussion that concerns about liver injury from therapeutic doses in people with alcohol dependence are "overstated". Gaps: (1) the pooled estimate is printed in IU/L with an interval of −0.2 to 0.1, which is a standardized difference; (2) the Discussion describes the pooled result as the effect of a fixed number of days of use, while two pooled trials had shorter courses that had ended before the measurement; (3) ALT at one early time point in about 900 people cannot show that rare serious liver injury does not happen; (4) the review was funded by an acetaminophen manufacturer, its senior authors had consulted or testified for that manufacturer, the sponsor reviewed the manuscript, and the authors wrote all five pooled trials, with no formal risk-of-bias assessment. The authors do report the later ALT rises and say their meaning is unclear.

timeline.event: Dart, Kuffner and Rumack systematic review of acetaminophen in people with alcohol dependence (pre-1999 literature; two controlled trials), by authors of this review.
Kuffner et al. randomized trial in detoxification patients, pooled here.
Kuffner et al. multicentre trial in detoxification patients and Heard et al. trial in moderate drinkers, pooled here.
Bartels et al. trial in recently abstinent people with alcohol dependence (modified-release form), pooled here.
Dart et al. trial in detoxification patients, pooled here.
This meta-analysis.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled trials largely come from one research group and one funder, so their agreement is replication within a team rather than independent replication. No trial has studied acetaminophen taken for a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking.

funding.funder: Investigator-initiated grant from McNeil Consumer Healthcare (a manufacturer of acetaminophen products) to Denver Health; K.H. was supported by NIDA award K08DA020573. The sponsor had no stated role in design, analysis or authorship but reviewed the final manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: Five authors (K.H., J.G., B.B., D.A., R.D.) are employees of Denver Health, which has clinical, consulting and research contracts with Cumberland Pharmaceuticals (maker of intravenous acetylcysteine), Cadence Pharmaceuticals and McNeil Consumer Healthcare (makers of acetaminophen products). B.H.R. has provided consulting services to McNeil on behalf of Denver Health and testified on behalf of McNeil in litigation in 2010.
funding.affiliations_note: Review authors are authors of all five pooled trials (Dart, Green and Heard of four; Sivilotti of one) and of the earlier systematic review cited in support.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial, independent of manufacturers, in people who drink heavily on single occasions, giving acetaminophen at usual doses for hangover, with repeated liver tests afterwards; and pooling of individual participant data from all trials, published and unpublished, at every measured day with a formal risk-of-bias assessment, alongside large observational data on serious liver injury.

domains.note: People who drink; acetaminophen at usual doses; placebo; ALT and liver events.
The protocol was prespecified but not registered, and it did not include a risk-of-bias assessment.
Randomized trials only, justified by the inability of case reports and retrospective series to establish causation or rates.

Four databases including CENTRAL, keywords given, no language restriction, authors of included trials asked about unpublished work; but restricted to published trials without justification, no trial registries or grey literature, no stated reference-list search, and alcohol terms applied only within an internal database of acetaminophen records. Judged as written for publication restrictions, as for item 4 elsewhere (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Two independent abstractors assessed eligibility.
The same two independent abstractors used a structured abstraction form with consensus for disagreements; the text implies but does not state separately that extraction was done in duplicate.

A weighted fixed-effect model justified by I2 of 0. Weaknesses: a standardized difference was used although all trials report ALT in IU/L, and it is printed as IU/L; and the pooled measurement fell after the end of dosing in two of the five trials.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Interpretation rests on the trials being randomized and blinded, without assessment; the conclusion that concerns are overstated does not consider bias, sponsorship or the authors' own trials.
No heterogeneity (Q = 1.7, I2 = 0).

A funnel plot was examined and the Limitations say publication bias cannot be excluded; with five trials the plot cannot show much, despite the Results' statement that the estimate is not subject to publication bias.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Industry funding, institutional contracts and an author's litigation testimony are disclosed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2: no registered protocol; 4: published trials only without justification; 9: no risk-of-bias assessment; 13: interpretation without regard to bias), which gives critically low confidence. The pooled day-4 result itself is simple and checkable from Table 1, and recalculation confirms no detectable ALT rise at the pooled early time point (in IU/L, about 0.1 with a 95% CI of about −1.3 to 1.5). The card may be cited for that short-term laboratory finding in mostly recently abstinent people with heavy drinking, for the modest ALT rises at later measurements, and for zero reported liver failures among 551 people treated; not for the safety of acetaminophen during a hangover after a single heavy night, for the absence of rare serious injury, or for the authors' conclusion that concerns are overstated.

key_findings.finding: 184 unique records yielded eight randomized trials, of which six met all criteria; five reported ALT at a common early time point (551 people on acetaminophen, 350 on placebo) and were pooled; doses, durations and measurement days are in the exposure field. Four trials were in detoxification patients who had just stopped drinking.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that recently abstinent heavy drinkers are at maximal theoretical risk (induced CYP2E1, possible glutathione depletion) and that alcohol present at the time of dosing inhibits the toxic pathway; four of the six included trials studied that recently abstinent period.

reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical inconsistency; 95% is presumably meant.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the pooled result as the effect of a set number of days of acetaminophen, but in two of the five pooled trials the course was shorter and had ended before the pooled measurement (durations in the exposure field).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled result describes ALT at one early time point after courses of different lengths, not after a fixed period of continuous use.

design_detail: Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis with meta-regression (registered on the Open Science Framework, 10.17605/OSF.IO/EJX5Q) of controlled experimental studies in healthy adults aged 18 to 70 that gave a measured dose of alcohol before a night of sleep measured by polysomnography. 27 studies included, all crossover designs except two; pooled mean differences against control for sleep onset latency, total sleep time, REM sleep onset latency, latency to deep (N3) sleep, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency and sleep stages, with 95% prediction intervals; meta-regression on alcohol dose (g per kg), timing and the proportion of women; subjective sleep summarized narratively. Same team and methods as the caffeine meta-analysis (Gardiner et al., 2023).
can_establish: The average change in that night's objectively measured sleep after drinking alcohol in the hours before bed, compared with the same people without alcohol, in healthy adults in laboratory studies, and how the REM and sleep-onset effects change with the amount of alcohol.
cannot_establish: Effects of drinking earlier in the day (almost all studies gave alcohol within three hours of bedtime), of real-world nights out (later bedtimes, more alcohol, other drugs), in people with alcohol use disorder, insomnia, adolescents or adults over 70; whether men and women differ (only one study analysed sex); or whether alcohol changes total sleep time, sleep efficiency or night-time waking, for which the intervals and prediction intervals are wide.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies: laboratory volunteers, from 1 to 95 per study, published from 1966 to 2022 (Table 2, PDF pages 43-47, which carry no printed page numbers).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults 18 to 70; controlled experimental design; measured alcohol dose; night-time sleep measured after drinking; excluded naps under 90 minutes, alcohol more than 18 hours before or after the start of sleep, no sleep measures (pre-proof p. 6, lines 141-149). English-language peer-reviewed human studies only (lines 130-132).
sample.demographics: 12 studies men only, 4 women only, 11 mixed (45.3% men in the mixed studies) (pre-proof p. 16, lines 399-401); mostly young adults.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; several studies' data were excluded from pooling (missing variances, combined stages, implausibly small variances, part-night data) (pre-proof pp. 8-9, lines 194-205).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy laboratory volunteers drinking measured amounts shortly before a fixed bedtime, mostly vodka or other spirits with juice or tonic: real nights of drinking (later bedtimes, larger and uneven amounts, food, other drugs) are not represented.

exposure.measurement: Alcohol given as a measured dose in each study; doses in g per kg calculated by the authors for six studies (pre-proof p. 9, lines 205-208).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 37 alcohol conditions from 0.16 to 1.20 g per kg, classified as low (0.50 g per kg or less; 12 conditions), moderate (over 0.50 to under 0.75; 8) and high (0.75 or more; 17); the authors equate these to about three or fewer, three to five and five or more standard drinks of 10 g for a 62-kg adult (pre-proof pp. 10-11, lines 249-256). Mostly drunk within three hours of bedtime; four studies gave alcohol on two, three or nine nights (lines 256-258). Thresholds reported by the authors' dose models (results, not advice): REM onset delayed from about 0.35 g per kg, REM duration reduced from about 0.50, sleep onset shortened from about 0.85, latency to N3 shortened from about 0.95 (pre-proof pp. 12-14).
exposure.polysubstance: Beverage types varied (vodka, scotch, bourbon, beer, sake, shochu); the authors name this as a possible confounder (pre-proof p. 31, lines 757-758).

comparison.controls: The same participants without alcohol (placebo or no alcohol) in crossover studies; separate control groups in two studies.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison in most studies; time in bed standardized in only a few studies (pre-proof p. 19, lines 465-466; p. 26, lines 639-641).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, drinking history and ADH genotype not accounted for in most studies (pre-proof pp. 28-31).

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography for objective sleep; questionnaires, diaries and visual analogue scales for subjective sleep (Table 2).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In healthy adults drinking before bed in the laboratory, alcohol delayed the first REM sleep period by about 18 minutes and reduced REM sleep by about 11 minutes (about 3% of the night), more so with more alcohol; it did not detectably change the time to fall asleep on average (except in the dose model at larger amounts), and its effects on total sleep, waking during the night and sleep efficiency were uncertain, with prediction intervals spanning both losses and gains.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary, practice points and conclusion (pre-proof pp. 2, 32-34) say a low dose of alcohol will reduce REM sleep and that larger doses only shorten sleep onset, and they advise people seeking to protect REM sleep to be mindful of intake. The thresholds come from statistical significance in meta-regressions of mostly small studies, which the authors acknowledge (pre-proof p. 31, lines 767-769); the summary's conversion of the low-dose threshold to about two standard drinks conflicts with the authors' own conversion of about three (reporting issues). The Discussion's statement that low doses may increase total sleep time rests on one study.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (4, 7, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. Within that rating, the statistical approach is careful (multilevel models, prediction intervals, a correlation sensitivity analysis) and the REM findings are consistent in direction, but 11 of 27 included studies were at high risk of bias (no washout, part-night data, unclear protocols, one study of a single participant) and none was excluded in a sensitivity analysis. Cite it for the average effects on REM sleep and for the uncertainty about total sleep and falling asleep; do not cite its dose thresholds as safe or unsafe amounts.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA and SWiM; protocol registered on the Open Science Framework in May 2024, 10.17605/OSF.IO/K9NTY) of studies relating the alcohol hangover to negative affect (anxiety, low mood, stress, guilt, emotional dysregulation) in healthy adults, compared with a sober state or baseline. 22 studies (n = 6152): randomized and semi-naturalistic experiments, naturalistic within-person studies, cross-sectional surveys and three interview studies, synthesized narratively by theme. Risk of bias with RoB 2, ROBINS-I, the AXIS tool for cross-sectional studies and the CASP qualitative checklist.
can_establish: Which negative feelings people report the day after drinking compared with sober days or baseline, how consistently the direction of the difference appears across designs, which personal characteristics have been studied alongside it, and how people describe the experience in interviews.
cannot_establish: How large the change in mood is (no effect sizes are reported or pooled), whether the mood change is caused by the hangover itself or by sleep loss, events of the night, expectations or pre-existing mood (mostly naturalistic and cross-sectional designs), or whether any personal factor or coping strategy changes it (associations from single cross-sectional or small studies).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies: mostly young adults recruited from the general population, with 10 of 22 specifically recruiting students; most from the United Kingdom (9) and the United States (5), published 1980 to 2024 (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 18 or over with experience of a hangover; a validated hangover measure or descriptive self-report of a hangover; a relationship between hangover and negative affect; a comparison with a sober state or baseline. Excluded: reviews, grey literature and conference papers, participants under 18, current alcohol dependence, hangovers combined with other substances, no hangover-specific measure (pp. 2-3).
sample.demographics: 57% women (3531 of 6152); ages 18 to 88; mean age 26.3 (SD 7.9) in the 16 studies that reported it; individual samples from 11 to 1837 (p. 3).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Mostly students and young adults with mild-to-moderate hangovers; people with alcohol dependence excluded; English-language peer-reviewed studies only. The largest samples are retrospective surveys.

exposure.measurement: Hangover measured with a single-item severity rating (10 studies), the Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale (7) or other scales, or by asking about a recent hangover (p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: reported average consumption from 6 to 17 alcoholic units depending on the timeframe; mean units per drinking session in Table 4 from 10.6 to 19.7; estimated peak blood alcohol up to 0.22%; in the randomized trials hangover severity was weak (for example 1.4 on single-item or acute hangover scales) (p. 3; Table 4, pp. 11-12).
exposure.polysubstance: Studies combining alcohol with other substances (for example alcohol and cannabis) were excluded; other drug use in the remaining studies not summarized.

comparison.controls: A sober day or alcohol-free condition in the same people (experimental and naturalistic studies), baseline affect, or variation in hangover severity across respondents (cross-sectional surveys).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparisons in most experimental and naturalistic studies; none in the surveys.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name tolerance, sleep and pre-existing psychological conditions as unmeasured differences (p. 15); one included study suggests baseline anxiety re-emerges during hangover (p. 14).

outcomes.instruments: State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (4 studies), visual analogue mood scales (8), Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory II, Depression Anxiety Stress Scales, Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (state and trait versions), Brief-COPE, Brief Resilience Scale, single-item ratings; semi-structured and unstructured interviews (Table 1, pp. 5-7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Mostly validated scales; several single-item ratings.
outcomes.operationalization: Negative affect as higher anxiety, depression, stress, guilt or irritability, or lower positive mood, during a hangover than when sober or at baseline.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no pooling).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; outcomes are self-reported, usually by participants who knew whether they were hungover.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The review reports direction and significance as stated in each study (Table 4, pp. 11-12) and themes from the qualitative studies (Table 5, p. 13); no standardized effect, interval or pooled estimate is given, because measures and analyses were too heterogeneous (p. 3).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework, registered prospectively in May 2024 (10.17605/OSF.IO/K9NTY); search on 20 January 2025 (p. 2); deviations not discussed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; vote counting by significance as reported in each study.
analysis.power: Not applicable; included studies ranged from 11 to 1837 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across most quantitative studies, people rated their mood as worse (more anxiety, low mood, stress, guilt, irritability and less alertness or contentment) during a hangover than when sober or at baseline; in the largest survey, anxiety and depression were the least reported and least severe hangover symptoms, two smaller studies found no difference in anxiety or tension, and the size of the change is never quantified. Associations with emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, baseline anxiety, coping style and resilience come from one or two studies each, mostly cross-sectional. In interviews, people linked their distress to what they had done while drunk, memory gaps and a wasted day, and said that sharing the hangover with friends eased it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract (p. 1) says the 22 studies demonstrated a significant association, that maladaptive emotion regulation, avoidant coping, repetitive negative thinking and baseline anxiety exacerbated these experiences, and that social support and resilience were protective; the conclusion speaks of a strong link. Three of the 22 are interview studies, several found no difference for anxiety, no magnitude is reported, and the causal words (exacerbated, protective) rest on correlational single studies.

timeline.event: McKinney, narrative review of next-day effects of alcohol on subjective mood: overall decrease in mood with more anxiety and fatigue during hangover (cited as ref. 16; not in the library's references).
Gunn et al., systematic review of next-day effects of heavy drinking on cognition (a related outcome, cited as ref. 10)
This review: negative affect higher during hangover in most of 19 quantitative studies, with no pooled magnitude.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (worse mood during a hangover) is consistent across many small studies and with the earlier review, but its size, and whether it is caused by the hangover itself rather than by sleep loss or regret about the night, are not established.

funding.funder: No specific funding for the work; the first author held an Australian Government Research Training Program scholarship (pp. 1, 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: A.C.H. was supported by a Rebecca L Cooper Al and Val Rosenstrauss Fellowship (GNT: F2021894); the other authors declare no conflicts (p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Human Psychopharmacology, Swinburne University of Technology; Institute for Breathing and Sleep, Austin Hospital, Melbourne.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person study with randomized alcohol and placebo-alcohol nights, repeated standardized mood measures the next day, sleep measured objectively, and analysis of how much mood change remains after accounting for sleep loss and events of the night; plus a trial of any proposed way to ease next-day anxiety.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (4, the narrow single-person search with unjustified restrictions, and 7, no list of excluded studies), and one is met only in part (9), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The more important limitation for the site is that the review reports no magnitudes: it can support a claim about the direction of mood change during a hangover, with very low certainty, but not about how large the change is or what causes it. Its moderator findings rest on single cross-sectional studies and its qualitative findings are themes, not frequencies.

key_findings.finding: 22 studies with 6152 participants were included (individual samples 11 to 1837; 57% women; ages 18 to 88; mean age 26.3, SD 7.9, in the 16 studies reporting it); 10 recruited students; no meta-analysis was done because measures and analyses were heterogeneous.
