key_findings.finding: The authors' reading of CBI: given the naltrexone × CBI interaction, the main-effect tests for naltrexone and CBI should be interpreted with caution (Results, p. 2009); patients receiving medical management did better when they also received either CBI or naltrexone: without CBI naltrexone helped, without naltrexone CBI helped, and CBI plus naltrexone did not further improve outcomes (Comment, p. 2013). Among the placebo groups, corrected post hoc tests showed more abstinent days with placebo, medical management and CBI than with placebo and medical management (79.8 against 73.8, P=.04) (pp. 2011–2012).

key_findings.finding: The authors call the lack of acamprosate efficacy surprising and offer explanations: a higher daily dose than in most earlier trials (a study condition); only 4 days of abstinence before starting, achieved mainly as outpatients, whereas most positive acamprosate trials had a longer abstinence established during inpatient treatment; and earlier trials' less frequent assessment, non-standardised counselling and recruitment from clinical, mainly inpatient, settings.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Explanations offered, not tested; the doses are study conditions and are not recorded here.

reporting_issues.issue: The hazard ratios labelled main effects for time to first heavy drinking day (naltrexone 0.72, 0.53 to 0.98; acamprosate 0.85, 0.63 to 1.15; CBI 0.81, 0.60 to 1.10; Figure 2) come from a model fitting all main effects and 2- and 3-factor interactions (Table 4 footnote), and the coding of the factors is not stated. Editors' calculation: their 97.5% intervals imply standard errors of about 0.14 on the log scale, which corresponds to roughly 210 to 220 heavy-drinking events (4/SE²), about a quarter of the 856 events in the pill groups; MM + naltrexone against MM + placebo (no acamprosate, no CBI) has 219 events, MM + acamprosate against MM + placebo 223 and MM + CBI + placebo against MM + placebo 226 (Table 5); the 1-year naltrexone hazard ratio (0.77, 0.58 to 1.02) implies about 252 events against 250 in the same two MM-only cells (Table 9). The simple-effect hazard ratios pooled over acamprosate (0.78, 0.84, 0.91) imply about 430 to 450 events, matching their pooled cells, and the abstinent-days main effects have intervals that fit the whole factorial (d 0.06 for naltrexone, about 600 per group).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline naltrexone hazard ratio of 0.72 is probably the contrast within MM without CBI or acamprosate (154 vs 153 people), not an effect averaged over the trial; averaged over all pill groups, 68.2% vs 71.4% had a heavy drinking day. Claims should cite 0.72 with this caveat, or the per-group counts in Table 5, until the coding is confirmed from the design paper or the data.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Figure 2 and Tables 4, 5, 8 and 9 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 gives 1294 participants with data for the composite good clinical outcome. Editors' calculation: each of its nine cells reproduces exactly as a count divided by a whole-number denominator (for example 71 of 122 = 58.2%, 87 of 118 = 73.7%), these denominators sum to 1137, about 82% of 1383, and the odds ratios of Figure 4 are reproduced from the same denominators pooled over acamprosate. The numbers needed to treat printed in the text (7 for CBI, 6 for naltrexone, 7 for naltrexone + CBI) do not follow one rounding rule from the printed percentages: editors' calculation 1/(0.713−0.582) = 7.6, 1/(0.737−0.582) = 6.5, 1/(0.744−0.582) = 6.2.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 18% rather than 6% may lack composite data, so the composite results rest on those with data; Table 5 does not say whether its percentages are adjusted (its footnote says all drinking measures are). Numbers needed to treat should be quoted as printed with the editors' values beside them.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Table 5 and Figure 4 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the CBI-only group a baseline OCDS craving score of 18.9 (SD 9.98) against 24.5 to 26.3 (SDs about 7.6) in the other eight groups, with P=.47 for the comparison; editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs gives an F(8, 1374) of about 12.5, far from P=.47, and the text says only one of 76 baseline comparisons was nominally significant. The drinking-variable SDs in Table 1 are also almost identical across groups (percent days abstinent 24.68 to 24.78 in eight groups), which suggests model-based values; the table does not say how they were computed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the CBI-only value or its P value is misprinted, or that group started with less craving than the others; the paper does not allow a decision. If real, the no-pill comparison would be unbalanced on craving.

design_detail: Prospective cohort analysis of the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health study: 55,917 Danish-born people (26,696 men, 29,221 women) aged 50–64 when invited (December 1993 to May 1997), questioned and examined at baseline, and followed in national registers to 31 December 2011 (median 14.9 years; 831,285 person-years) for a first register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (257 men, 85 women). All exposures come from one baseline questionnaire: weekly amount by beverage converted to 12-g standard drinks, drinking frequency (days a week), recalled average weekly intake at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59, and the wine share of weekly intake. Sex-stratified Cox models with age as the time axis, adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference, test three stated hypotheses: daily drinking carries more risk than less frequent drinking, current intake matters more than lifetime intake, and wine carries less risk than beer and liquor. Read from the online-first (article in press) PDF, pages 1–7; the printed article is J Hepatol 2015;62:1061–1067.
can_establish: Within this middle-aged Danish cohort, how the incidence of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis over about 15 years varied with self-reported baseline amount, drinking frequency, recalled intake in earlier decades and wine share, after adjustment for smoking, education and waist circumference.
cannot_establish: That drinking frequency or wine affects cirrhosis risk beyond the amount drunk (frequency and amount are highly correlated and the authors say they cannot be separated, and wine share may stand for unmeasured habits such as drinking with meals); that cutting down removes the risk of past heavy drinking (intake was measured once, earlier decades only by recall at age 50–64, and no change in drinking was observed); that lifetime abstainers have no risk (the outcome presupposes drinking, and fewer than two cases would have been expected among them); or what holds for women (85 cases) and for heavy drinking occasions (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Community cohort. From December 1993 to May 1997, 160,725 Danish-born men and women aged 50 to 64 without a previous cancer diagnosis were invited to the Diet, Cancer and Health study, designed to study diet, lifestyle and cancer; 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part (response 35%). Participants completed a food-frequency questionnaire, a lifestyle questionnaire (alcohol, smoking, physical activity, education) and a brief physical examination with waist circumference (Materials and methods › Study population, p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: alcoholic cirrhosis diagnosed before baseline (86); missing information on alcohol amount (105), smoking (27), education (27) or waist circumference (50); conflicting answers on alcohol amount and frequency (236) or on smoking status and tobacco use (7) (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Median age 55 to 60 years across drinking-frequency groups. Men drinking daily: median 26 drinks a week (5th–95th percentile 9.4–60), 47% smokers, 33% with 7 years of schooling or less; men drinking 2–4 days a week: 8.9 drinks (3.6–13), 34% smokers. Women drinking daily: 19 drinks a week (7.3–40), 43% smokers; women drinking 2–4 days a week: 6.6 (3.0–19), 27% smokers (Table 1, p. 3).
sample.attrition: Register follow-up from baseline to diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (342), emigration (337), loss to follow-up (2), death from other causes (8132) or 31 December 2011; 831,285 person-years; median 14.9 years (14.6 men, 15.1 women) (Follow-up, p. 2; Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Deaths from other causes were censored.
sample.selection_effects: Only 35% of those invited took part, and the authors note that participants may live more healthily than non-participants and that women's incidence of alcoholic cirrhosis was somewhat lower than national data would predict (Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph, p. 6). Lifetime abstainers are very few (63 men, 265 women). Current abstainers include former heavy drinkers: their median lifetime average was 18 drinks a week in men, against 15 in daily drinkers, and 55% of them smoked (Table 1, p. 3). The listed exclusions sum to 538, but 1136 of the 57,053 participants are missing from the analysed cohort (editors' arithmetic; see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at baseline only: average weekly amount of beer (light, regular and strong, in 330 ml bottles), wine (125 ml glasses) and liquor (30 ml drinks), converted to standard drinks of 12 g ethanol; frequency in seven categories (never, less than one day a month, one to three days a month, once a week, two to four, five to six days a week, daily); recalled average weekly intake at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59, summed to lifetime drinks and a lifetime average since age 20 (Information on alcohol consumption, p. 2). No repeated measurement during follow-up and no biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Standard drink = 12 g ethanol. Amount in drinks a week, categorized <14 (reference), 14–28, 28–42, 42–56, 56–70 and >70 in men, with women above 42 grouped (Fig. 1, p. 3). Frequency analysed as <1, 1, 2–4 (reference), 5–6 and 7 days a week (Table 2, p. 4). Wine share of weekly intake <1%, 1–15%, 15–50% and 50–100% (Fig. 2, p. 5). Frequency was strongly correlated with amount: Spearman r = 0.77 in men, 0.85 in women (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Binge drinking could not be examined (Introduction, last paragraph, p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking measured and adjusted (never, former, under 10 g tobacco a day, over 10 g a day). Other drug use not measured. Hepatitis C status not available; the authors call this a minor limitation because of its low prevalence in Denmark (p. 6).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Lifetime abstainers (no alcohol over lifetime or at baseline) and current abstainers (drank in the past but not at baseline) were kept apart from drinkers (Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).

comparison.controls: The reference differs by analysis: drinkers of fewer than 14 drinks a week for amount (Fig. 1); people drinking two to four days a week for frequency (Table 2); men drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week who took 50–100% of it as wine for beverage type (Fig. 2); per-drink hazard ratios for the life-period analyses (Tables 3 and 4). Lifetime abstainers had no cases and could not serve as a reference.
comparison.matching: None. Adjustment for smoking, length of education (7 years or less, 8–10, 11 or more) and waist circumference (WHO categories), with age as the time axis; all analyses stratified by sex (Statistical analysis, 1st and 6th paragraphs, p. 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Hepatitis B and C, diabetes, diet and physical activity (both measured in the cohort but not used as covariates), heavy drinking occasions, drinking with meals (the authors' explanation for part of the wine finding, p. 6), drinking before age 20, and socioeconomic position beyond education were not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: First diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.0; ICD-10 K70.3) in the Danish National Patient Register (all somatic admissions since 1977, outpatient contacts since 1995) or the Danish Register of Causes of Death, linked by personal identifier (Follow-up, p. 2). A supplementary combined outcome added unspecified cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.9, 456.0, 785.3; ICD-10 I85.0, I85.9, K74.6, R18.9): 393 men and 229 women (Statistical analysis, 7th paragraph, p. 2; Results, p. 5). Deaths were 11% of cases (p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite earlier work for a high validity of the register diagnosis (p. 2, refs 21 and 22); no validation within this cohort is reported. Classifying a cirrhosis as alcoholic depends on clinicians knowing that the person drank, so the outcome definition is itself tied to the exposure (editors' observation).
outcomes.operationalization: Hazard ratios from Cox proportional hazards models, proportional hazards checked by parallel stratified survival curves (no violation found). Trend tests across frequency categories exclude abstainers; interaction tests by nested likelihood-ratio tests and by comparing per-drink slopes across frequency groups (Statistical analysis, p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two outcomes (alcoholic cirrhosis; alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis in the supplement), but each of three hypotheses was tested in both sexes with several adjustment levels and parametrizations (categories, per-drink slopes, trend and interaction tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: diagnoses come from routine care registers, independent of the study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Standard drink = 12 g; adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference, age as time axis. Amount against drinkers of fewer than 14 drinks a week: 14–28 drinks a week, men HR 2.33 (95% CI 1.52–3.58), women 3.49 (2.00–6.12); 28–42 drinks, men 6.98 (4.65–10.5), women 16.2 (9.16–28.7); current abstainers, men 7.58 (3.39–16.9), women 3.21 (0.77–13.4) (p. 3). Frequency against 2–4 days a week, fully adjusted (Table 2, p. 4): men daily 3.65 (2.39–5.55), 5–6 days 1.43 (0.84–2.43), 1 day 1.30 (0.59–2.87), <1 day 1.34 (0.67–2.67), current abstainers 10.0 (4.32–23.0), trend P < 0.001; women daily 1.73 (0.85–3.52), 5–6 days 2.30 (1.14–4.67), 1 day 0.81 (0.29–2.24), <1 day 1.45 (0.71–2.96), current abstainers 4.03 (0.91–17.8), trend P = 0.14. Men's daily HR was 8.29 (5.52–12.4) adjusted for age only and 4.83 (3.20–7.29) with amount added. Per additional weekly drink (Table 3, p. 4): men 1.02 (<1 day a week) to 1.05 (daily); women 1.09 (<1 day) to 1.05 (daily); interaction P < 0.0001 and P = 0.0007. Life periods (Table 4, p. 5): after adjustment for baseline intake, men 20–29 1.00 (0.99–1.01), 30–39 0.99 (0.98–1.01), 40–49 1.01 (1.00–1.02), 50–59 1.03 (1.02–1.03); lifetime average adjusted for baseline 1.03 (1.02–1.03) in men and 1.03 (1.01–1.06) in women. Wine, men at 14–28 drinks a week against men drinking <14 a week mostly as wine: <1% wine 7.47 (1.68–33.12), 1–15% 3.12 (1.53–6.39), 50–100% 1.69 (0.79–3.65); wine share × amount interaction P = 0.63 (p. 5). Editors' calculation of crude incidence per 100,000 person-years from Table 2: men daily 165, 5–6 days 45, 2–4 days 20, current abstainers 154; women daily 51, 5–6 days 36, 2–4 days 10.
analysis.covariates: Age (time axis), smoking (four categories), length of education (three categories), waist circumference (three categories), by sex; amount added for the frequency analyses; other beverages controlled in the beverage-specific models (Supplementary Table 6, not on file); baseline intake added in the life-period models. In the main frequency analysis (Table 2) amount entered as a continuous term (Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph, p. 2); because risk rises steeply across amount categories (Fig. 1), this adjustment may leave confounding by amount in the daily-drinking hazard ratios (editors' reading).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the three hypotheses are stated in the Introduction (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Estimates for the heaviest drinkers (men 42–56, 56–70 and over 70 drinks a week; women over 42) are shown only in Fig. 1, and the wine-share estimates other than three quoted in the text only in Fig. 2, which has no confidence intervals. The amount-by-frequency table that the authors say makes frequency and amount hard to separate (Supplementary Table 5), the beverage-specific models (Supplementary Table 6) and all analyses of the combined cirrhosis outcome (Supplementary Tables 2A–6A, Fig. 2A) are online supplements, not on file. The beverage analysis was not done in women because there were few cases.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 85 cases in women (30 among daily drinkers) the authors say firm conclusions for women are not possible (p. 6); with 0 cases in 4846 person-years among lifetime abstainers, their risk cannot be estimated (editors' observation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Risk of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis rose steeply with the amount drunk in both sexes. In men, daily drinking went with about 3.7 times the hazard of drinking two to four days a week after adjustment for amount and confounders; adjustment for amount alone more than halved the age-adjusted estimate (8.29 to 4.83), and the authors could not separate frequency from amount. In women, frequency showed no trend: the highest hazard was at five to six days a week and daily drinking was not significantly raised. Recalled intake in the twenties and thirties added nothing once current intake was known, but the lifetime average still did (1.03 per weekly drink in both sexes). Men drinking 14–28 drinks a week mostly as wine had a lower hazard than those drinking little wine, with wide, overlapping intervals and no significant interaction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says daily drinking was associated with an increased risk in men, that recent rather than earlier consumption was associated with risk, that wine might be associated with a lower risk, and that results were in general similar for women (p. 1). The discussion goes further: the results are said to confirm that daily drinking increases the risk (p. 6); the conclusions say daily drinking appears to raise risk regardless of amount, at least in men (p. 6); and the implications say there is gain in cutting down whatever the lifetime intake and that “daily drinkers should be advised to drink less frequently” (p. 6). Gaps: (1) causal and advisory language on frequency, although the authors themselves state that frequency and amount could not be disentangled (p. 4) and residual confounding by a self-reported amount is likely; (2) the women's frequency results do not resemble the men's (trend P = 0.14; highest hazard at five to six days; steepest per-drink slope in the least frequent drinkers); (3) 'recent rather than lifetime' overstates Table 4, where the lifetime average remains associated after adjustment for baseline, and where the recent periods overlap the baseline measure while earlier periods rest on recall over decades; (4) no participant was observed cutting down; (5) 'no risk among lifetime abstainers' is stated as a finding (pp. 1, 6) although an alcoholic-cirrhosis diagnosis presupposes drinking and fewer than two cases would have been expected among them.

timeline.event: Becker et al. (Hepatology), a Danish population study of alcohol intake, sex, age and liver-disease risk (this paper's ref 21), one of the 17 studies of the Rehm et al. (2010) meta-analysis.

Becker et al. (Hepatology): lower risk of alcohol-induced cirrhosis in wine drinkers, which this study agrees with; Pelletier et al. (Alcohol Alcohol) found no lower risk with wine in heavy drinkers, which it conflicts with (refs 18 and 19, p. 6).
Kamper-Jørgensen et al. (J Hepatol): dose–response or threshold for cirrhosis (ref 7), cited for earlier findings on frequency, recent intake and beverage type (pp. 1, 6).

Hatton et al. (Addiction), drinking patterns and lifetime drinking history in people with alcohol-related liver disease (ref 12): among the earlier studies in clinical samples that compared daily with episodic drinking (p. 6).
Rehm et al. meta-analysis: different dose–response for cirrhosis morbidity and mortality; this cohort, with deaths only 11% of its cases, could not separate the two (p. 6; card sc_rehm_2010).
This study: first comparison of daily drinking with drinking five or six days a week in a general population, by the authors' account (p. 6).

Roerecke et al. (Am J Gastroenterol), dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cirrhosis (card sc_roerecke_2019): this cohort is one of its nine studies (its Table 1), although the cohort's men contribute no estimate to its main analysis. It reports daily-drinking ratios for this cohort at the same weekly intake (men 2.25, women 1.28) that are not in this paper's main text, which gives 3.65 and 1.73 (Table 2, fully adjusted). Its Table 1 lists this cohort with 393 men and 229 women, the counts of this paper's supplementary combined outcome of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis (Statistical analysis, 7th paragraph, p. 2; pp. 5–6), so its figures probably come from that analysis (editors' reading; supplement not on file).

replication.where_it_stands: The steep amount gradient agrees with the meta-analyses (sc_rehm_2010). The association of daily drinking with alcoholic cirrhosis in men agrees in direction with earlier clinical studies the authors cite, but in this cohort it cannot be separated from amount, and in women it was not found; the wine finding agrees with one earlier Danish study and conflicts with studies of heavy drinkers. The Diet, Cancer and Health cohort is not among the 17 studies of Rehm et al. (2010), so the two are independent; the 2019 meta-analysis (Roerecke et al.) includes this cohort, so the two are not independent and are counted once when cited together.

funding.funder: Not reported. The authors declare that they have nothing to disclose regarding funding or conflict of interest with respect to the manuscript (Conflict of interest, p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Hepatology, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen; the National Institute of Public Health, University of Southern Denmark; and the Danish Cancer Society Research Center, Copenhagen, which hosts the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort (one author is credited with the acquisition of data). No industry ties are stated.

what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that measure amount and frequency repeatedly during follow-up (diaries or biomarkers of recent drinking), analysed with time-varying exposure and fine-grained adjustment for amount within frequency groups, in several populations and with enough women, using an outcome that does not depend on the clinician's knowledge of drinking (all cirrhosis with a recorded cause), would show whether frequency matters beyond amount; a cohort observing people who cut down would show whether past heavy drinking stops mattering.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, smoking, education and waist circumference only; hepatitis B and C, diabetes, diet and physical activity not adjusted. The frequency results depend on adjustment for a self-reported amount correlated with frequency (r = 0.77 and 0.85), which removed more than half of the men's age-adjusted daily-drinking excess, and the authors state the two cannot be disentangled; the wine results are open to confounding by drinking with meals and social position. For the amount gradient alone, confounding would be a smaller concern.

One self-report at baseline for a 15-year follow-up; intake in earlier decades recalled at age 50 to 64, so error grows with the distance of the period, which would by itself weaken the associations of the earlier periods; the 50–59 period overlaps the baseline measure; 236 people with conflicting answers were excluded. The judgment is driven by the life-period and frequency comparisons; current amount alone would be some concerns.

35% response, possibly healthier participants, lower than expected incidence in women; prevalent alcoholic cirrhosis excluded at baseline; 598 participants missing from the analysed cohort without explanation.
Changes in drinking during follow-up, including after early liver disease or medical advice, were not measured; baseline exposure is assumed constant.
About 1% excluded for missing covariates or inconsistent answers; register follow-up nearly complete (2 lost, 337 censored at emigration).

Register diagnoses of alcoholic cirrhosis, said to be valid; but the label 'alcoholic' requires known drinking, so classification depends on exposure (no lifetime abstainer can have the outcome, and recognised heavy or daily drinkers are more likely to be coded alcoholic). A supplementary analysis adding unspecified cirrhosis reportedly agreed (supplement not on file).

Three hypotheses stated in advance in the Introduction but no registered protocol; several adjustment levels and parametrizations; the heaviest categories and most wine-share estimates only in figures; key tables in supplements; one text value differs from its table.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The amount gradient is large, consistent in both sexes and robust to the measured confounders, and the cohort has near-complete register follow-up. The paper's own contributions, about frequency, recent against past intake and wine, rest on correlated single-occasion self-reports, recalled intake over decades, a small number of cases in women and an outcome whose definition depends on drinking; confounding by amount and measurement error are serious for each of them, so the overall risk of bias is high for those results. Citable for the association of baseline amount with alcoholic cirrhosis in middle-aged Danes and, as an association that may reflect amount, for the higher hazard in men who drank daily; not citable for advice on frequency or beverage, for the effect of cutting down, or for zero risk in lifetime abstainers.

key_findings.finding: Cohort and follow-up: 160,725 invited (December 1993 to May 1997), 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part (35%); after exclusions 55,917 were analysed; follow-up to 31 December 2011 gave 831,285 person-years (median 14.9 years); 342 developed alcoholic cirrhosis, 337 emigrated, 2 were lost and 8132 died of other causes. Incidence of alcoholic cirrhosis was 66 per 100,000 person-years in men (257 cases) and 19 in women (85 cases).

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and dose–response meta-regression of case–control, nested case–control and cohort studies of alcohol intake and 23 cancer sites. 572 unique papers (704 site-specific papers; published 1956–2012) with 486,538 cancer cases. Each study's intake categories were converted to grams of ethanol per day (one drink = 12.5 g), assigned their midpoint and grouped as light (midpoint up to 12.5 g/day), moderate (above 12.5 and up to 50 g/day) or heavy (above 50 g/day) drinking, and compared with the study's reference group of nondrinkers, or nondrinkers and occasional drinkers combined (24.1% of studies). Pooling by DerSimonian–Laird random effects; nonlinear dose–response by two-term fractional-polynomial random-effects meta-regression; subgroup analyses by design, sex and world region. No protocol registration and no assessment of primary-study quality or publication bias.
can_establish: The average association reported in 572 observational studies published before September 2012 between light, moderate and heavy drinking and the risk of each of 23 cancers, relative to nondrinkers or occasional drinkers, and how far these associations differ by study design, sex and world region.
cannot_establish: That alcohol causes any of these cancers (the conclusion's causal verbs rest on IARC's classification, not on this analysis); that the small light-drinking associations are free of confounding by smoking, of under-reporting and of former drinkers in the reference group (none is assessed study by study, and about half the contributing estimates were unadjusted); absolute risks (none are reported); whether the pooled estimates are inflated by publication bias (not assessed here); or the effect of drinking pattern and beverage type (not analysed).

sample.recruitment: Literature search in MEDLINE, ISI Web of Science (Science Citation Index Expanded) and EMBASE for epidemiological studies published online before September 2012, plus reference lists of relevant studies, reviews and meta-analyses; English only; search terms in Supplementary Material S1 (not read) (Materials and methods › Search strategy). Figure 1 (flowchart, read on the rendered page): 31,473 non-unique records; 29,786 excluded on title or abstract; 1,687 full texts retrieved plus 210 from reference lists; 1,193 excluded as not meeting the inclusion criteria (no breakdown by reason); 704 site-specific papers, 572 unique (56 papers reported on more than one site). The primary studies are hospital- and population-based case–control series and cohorts: 41.3% from North America, 32.2% Europe, 17.7% Asia, 8.9% other or mixed areas (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case–control, cohort or nested case–control studies published as original articles, reporting an OR, RR or HR (or data to compute one) for at least two levels of intake against nondrinkers and/or occasional drinkers, with a standard error or CI (or data to compute one); cancer sites with five or more papers. Excluded: abstracts, letters, reviews and meta-analyses; studies of one beverage type only, because nondrinkers of that beverage might drink others. For duplicate publications the most recent or complete was kept, and a pooled analysis was preferred to its constituent study (Materials and methods › Inclusion criteria; Data abstraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Study level (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1): 409 case–control (71.5%) and 163 cohort (28.5%) papers; 541 (94.6%) reported incidence and 31 (5.4%) mortality; 219 (38.3%) gave estimates for men, 256 (44.8%) for women and 179 (31.3%) for both sexes together (sex-specific papers counted twice); 297 (51.9%) reported adjusted estimates; 138 (24.1%) included occasional drinkers in the reference category. Largest sites: female breast 118 papers (117,317 cases in drinking categories, 48,433 in the reference category), colorectum 66, oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 54, oral cavity and pharynx 52; smallest: small intestine and cervix, 5 papers each. Participants' ages are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.
sample.selection_effects: English only, no grey literature or registries, and a search ending in September 2012 for a paper published online in November 2014. Eligibility for each site was judged by a single author (Data abstraction, 1st paragraph). Case–control studies dominate (409 of 572) and gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites (oral cavity and pharynx, heterogeneity P=0.007; heavy drinking and liver cancer 2.79 in case–control vs 1.12 in cohort studies; larynx 2.81 vs 1.12; Table 2), which points to recall or control-selection effects in the case–control literature. Many contributing estimates were not adjusted for the main site-specific confounders: adjusted estimates were reported by 41 of 118 breast, 32 of 54 oesophageal squamous cell, 21 of 41 laryngeal and 14 of 36 liver cancer papers (Table 1).

exposure.measurement: As in each primary study (self-reported current or lifetime intake by questionnaire or interview; methods are not described study by study in the main text). The reviewers converted all units to g/day (0.8 g per ml, 28 g per ounce, 12.5 g per drink), assigned each category its midpoint (open upper category: 1.2 times its lower bound), classed categories as light, moderate or heavy by midpoint, and combined several estimates falling in one class within a study with Hamling's method (Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average volume only. Light = midpoint up to 12.5 g/day (up to about one 12.5-g drink a day); moderate = above 12.5 and up to 50 g/day (about one to four drinks); heavy = above 50 g/day (more than four drinks). Drinking pattern (such as heavy drinking occasions) and beverage type could not be analysed (Discussion, 10th paragraph). The fitted dose–response curves (Figure 3) are plotted over 0–100 g/day for most sites and 0–50 g/day for melanoma, cervix, endometrium, ovary and thyroid; no numeric curve parameters are printed.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco, the main confounder for upper aerodigestive, lung and other cancers, is handled only through whatever adjustment each primary study made (main confounders by site listed in Supplementary Material S2, not read); about half the pooled estimates are unadjusted. The authors discuss residual confounding by smoking for lung and stomach cancer and cite their own earlier meta-analysis finding no association between alcohol and lung cancer in never-smokers (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Other drugs are not considered.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Former drinkers may sit in the nondrinker reference group of primary studies; the review did not record or separate them (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Each study's lowest category: nondrinkers, or nondrinkers and occasional drinkers combined in 138 of 572 studies (24.1%). Whether nondrinkers were lifetime abstainers or included former drinkers was not recorded (Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 2nd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjusted estimates were used when available; otherwise the reviewers computed crude RRs from the raw data (Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: By site: smoking, diet, obesity, diabetes, hepatitis B and C infection, reproductive and hormonal factors, socio-economic position and, in East Asian populations, ALDH2 genotype. Which were controlled varies by study and is listed only in Supplementary Material S2 (not read). The authors name under-reporting by drinkers, former drinkers in the reference group, and quitting because of early symptoms (lymphomas) as sources of misclassification.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking in the reference groups is not reported at review level; other drug use is not considered.

outcomes.instruments: Incident cancer (541 studies) or cancer death (31 studies) by site, as defined in each primary study: oral cavity and pharynx; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma; oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia; stomach; small intestine; colorectum; liver; gallbladder; pancreas; larynx; lung; melanoma; female breast; cervix; endometrium; ovary; prostate; bladder; kidney; thyroid; brain; Hodgkin's lymphoma; non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: No quality or risk-of-bias assessment of the primary studies. Only adjustment status and the inclusion of occasional drinkers in the reference group were recorded, and both were used in sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk of each site-specific cancer for light, moderate and heavy drinking against the reference group; odds ratios, risk ratios and rate ratios were treated as equivalent because cancer is rare (Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 64 counts the pooled category estimates in Figure 2 (23 sites by 3 intake categories, with heavy drinking not evaluable for 5 sites). The paper also reports 23 fitted dose–response curves, three subgroup tables (design, sex, area) with a heterogeneity test per site, and a publication-year analysis whose data are not shown.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility was judged by one author per site, with doubts resolved by consensus among all investigators; duplicate data extraction is not described.

analysis.covariates: None at review level: adjusted estimates were taken as reported (main site-specific confounders listed in Supplementary Material S2, not read), otherwise crude estimates were computed from raw data and pooled with them. Sensitivity analyses restricted to adjusted estimates, and excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference group, are reported as not materially changing the results (Supplementary Material S3, not read); the discussion gives only the pancreatic result (about a 20% increase with fully adjusted estimates).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported. MOOSE is cited only in the limitations paragraph.
analysis.selective_reporting: The main text and Figure 2 give each site's total number of studies but not the number behind each intake category. Sensitivity-analysis results are only in Supplementary Material S3, and the publication-year analysis is 'data not shown'. Two statistically significant inverse associations at light drinking that appear in Figure 2, lung cancer 0.84 (0.79–0.88) and oesophageal adenocarcinoma with gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76–0.98), are not mentioned in the text, and two significant subgroup heterogeneity tests are not discussed (ovary by design, P=0.007, Table 2; lung by area, P=0.045, Table 4).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Six sites rest on 5 to 9 studies (small intestine, cervix, brain, gallbladder, Hodgkin's lymphoma, thyroid), and subgroup analyses were limited to sites with more than 10 studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Higher risk with drinking for cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx (heavy drinking RR 5.13), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (4.95), larynx (2.65), gallbladder (2.64), liver (2.07), female breast (1.61), colorectum (1.44), stomach (1.21), pancreas (1.19) and lung (1.15), compared with nondrinkers or occasional drinkers. At light drinking (up to 12.5 g/day) the associations were small and statistically significant only for oral cavity and pharynx (1.13, 1.00–1.26), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (1.26), female breast (1.04, 1.01–1.07) and prostate (1.04). Inverse associations were found for kidney, thyroid and both lymphomas, and, at light drinking only, for lung cancer and oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Heterogeneity was high for many estimates (I² up to 91%), case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites, and about half of the contributing estimates were unadjusted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the final paragraph state that alcohol “increases risk of cancer” of six sites (oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, colorectum, liver, larynx, female breast). Gaps: (1) the causal verb comes from IARC's classification, cited in the introduction; this pooling of observational associations, with no appraisal of the primary studies, cannot by itself show causation; (2) the abstract's conclusion names the oesophagus without qualification, whereas the association was confined to squamous cell carcinoma (adenocarcinoma: no positive association, and 0.86, 0.76–0.98, at light drinking); (3) the heavy-drinking breast estimate quoted in the abstract (1.61) rests on 11 of the 118 breast studies (Table 2), and only 41 of the 118 reported adjusted estimates (Table 1); (4) the discussion reads the inverse kidney association as support for a protective effect of moderate drinking, while it explains the inverse lymphoma association by misclassification, and the final paragraph then lists kidney among cancers with no association; (5) the statement that oral, oesophageal and breast cancer were associated with drinking even at low doses sits beside the authors' concession that under-reporting by drinkers may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations (Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs). Against this, the discussion names residual confounding by smoking for lung and stomach cancer and treats the pancreas, prostate and melanoma findings cautiously.

timeline.event: IARC Working Group lists alcohol drinking as carcinogenic for the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, liver and larynx (as summarised in this paper's introduction).
Bagnardi et al., earlier meta-analysis by the same group based on 235 studies, which this paper updates.
IARC monograph volume 100E (cited in this paper as IARC Working Group, 2010) adds colorectum and female breast to the sites for which alcohol is carcinogenic.

Bagnardi et al., the group's meta-analysis of light drinking and cancer, which this paper says it updates and corroborates; it estimated about 5000 oral and pharyngeal, 24,000 oesophageal squamous cell and 5000 breast cancer deaths attributable to light drinking worldwide in 2004 (as cited in this paper's discussion).

Heinen et al., a Dutch cohort of 120,852 people (the Netherlands Cohort Study, as named in this paper's reference list), found no inverse association between alcohol and lymphoid neoplasms, against this review's inverse lymphoma estimates (as cited in this paper's discussion, which calls it a European cohort).

Rumgay et al. estimate the global cancer burden attributable to alcohol with relative risks from the WCRF Continuous Update Project rather than this review, using IARC's list of causal sites and leaving out the inverse kidney association (card sc_rumgay_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: The most comprehensive site-by-site dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cancer up to 2012, and a common source of site-specific relative risks by intake category. Its positive associations for the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, larynx, colorectum, liver and female breast agree with IARC's causal classification, which the paper cites rather than tests. Its light-drinking estimates (RR 1.04 to 1.26 at three sites) are small enough for confounding, under-reporting and former drinkers in the reference group to matter, and the review neither appraised study quality nor examined publication bias. Claims should cite it for the direction and approximate size of each site's association, stating the reference group (nondrinkers, sometimes with occasional drinkers), the 12.5-g drink and the category bounds (light up to 12.5 g/day, moderate up to 50 g/day, heavy above 50 g/day).

funding.funder: Italian Association for Cancer Research (AIRC), Project No. 10258 (My First AIRC Grant), and the Italian Foundation for Cancer Research (FIRC); FT supported by a FIRC fellowship; MR and CG supported by Fondazione Umberto Veronesi (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Milan-Bicocca, the European Institute of Oncology, the Mario Negri Institute, the University of Milan, the Besta Neurological Institute, IARC (Lyon), the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the American Cancer Society, Emory University, the Karolinska Institute, the Istituto Nazionale Tumori and Tehran University of Medical Sciences. The same group wrote most of the earlier site-specific meta-analyses this review updates, and it refers questions such as publication bias to those papers. No industry funding is stated. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the low-intake associations: a pooled individual-participant analysis of prospective cohorts with lifetime abstainers as the reference, repeated intake measures, full adjustment for smoking with results in never-smokers, and estimates by site and histology reported as absolute risks; and genetic analyses using variants in alcohol-metabolising genes (ALDH2, ADH1B) in populations where they are common, by cancer site.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (participants of human case–control and cohort studies), exposure (alcohol intake by g/day category), comparator (nondrinkers and/or occasional drinkers), outcomes (23 site-specific cancers, incidence or mortality) and eligible designs are stated (Materials and methods › Inclusion criteria).
No protocol or registration is reported.

Case–control, nested case–control and cohort studies were included without a stated reason. The choice is self-evident for an exposure that cannot be randomized, but the item asks for the explanation.

Three databases and reference lists, but English only without a justification, no grey literature or registry search, search terms only in a supplement, and a search ending more than two years before online publication (September 2012; November 2014). Under AMSTAR 2 as the project applies it (decision 21), an unjustified language limit gives 'no'.
The reports for each site were reviewed for eligibility by one author, with doubts resolved by consensus among all investigators (Data abstraction, 1st paragraph).
Duplicate extraction, or checking by a second reviewer, is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 reports 1,193 full-text papers excluded as not meeting the inclusion criteria, without reasons by category and without a list. The supplements as the paper describes them (S1 search terms, S2 confounders, S3 sensitivity analyses, S4 list of included studies, S5 study-specific estimates) include no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the main text describes the included studies only in aggregate by site (Table 1: design, outcome, area, sex, adjustment, reference group). Study-level information is in Supplementary Materials S4 (list of studies) and S5 (study-specific estimates), which were not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies; only adjustment status and the presence of occasional drinkers in the reference group were recorded.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

The techniques are appropriate in themselves: random-effects pooling (DerSimonian–Laird), Hamling's method for correlated estimates within a study, and a dose–response meta-regression that allows for within-study correlation. But the headline estimates combine adjusted estimates with crude RRs computed from raw data for about half the studies (297 of 572 reported adjusted estimates), with no reason given beyond availability; the adjusted-only analysis is a sensitivity analysis reported only in Supplementary Material S3. The methods also call the heterogeneity small while I² reaches 91% (Figure 2), and no prediction intervals are given. A close call, judged not met because crude and adjusted estimates are mixed in the main results.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses restricted to adjusted estimates and excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference group, and subgroup analyses by design, examine two main sources of bias (results reported as not materially changed; Supplementary Material S3, not read). Former drinkers in the reference group were not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion weighs residual confounding by smoking (lung, stomach) and poor diet, misclassification from under-reporting and from former drinkers among nondrinkers, and reverse causation for the lymphomas (Discussion, 5th, 7th and 10th paragraphs). The abstract's causal conclusions are not qualified by these points; judged met on balance.

I² is reported for every pooled estimate (Figure 2; Tables 2–4); heterogeneity was investigated by design, sex and area with F tests and by publication year, and high heterogeneity is acknowledged as the first limitation.
Not investigated in this paper; the authors refer to their earlier site-specific meta-analyses (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a no-conflict statement are given (Acknowledgments).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from Supplementary Materials S4–S5, which were not read; it is not a critical item and cannot change the rating. Six critical items are not met (2 protocol, 4 search, 7 excluded studies, 9 appraisal of primary studies, 11 statistical methods, a close call, and 15 publication bias), with 13 met, so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. This rates how far the pooled numbers can be taken as unbiased summaries, not the paper's usefulness. In practice: (a) the light-drinking RRs of 1.04 to 1.26 lie in a range that confounding (about half the estimates unadjusted), under-reporting and former drinkers in the reference group could produce or mask; (b) small-study and publication effects were not examined; (c) with I² up to 91%, a single pooled RR describes no particular population. The large heavy-drinking associations for upper aerodigestive cancers are consistent in direction across designs, sexes and regions (Tables 2–4) and are the most robust results. The paper may be cited for site-specific associations by intake category, with these caveats, but not as evidence of causation or of risk at very low intake on its own.

key_findings.finding: 572 unique papers (704 site-specific; 409 case–control, 163 cohort) published 1956–2012 contributed 486,538 cancer cases across 23 sites; 541 reported incidence and 31 mortality; 297 (51.9%) reported adjusted estimates and 138 (24.1%) included occasional drinkers in the reference category.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Exposure definitions used for every pooled estimate: intake in grams of ethanol per day with one drink = 12.5 g; categories by midpoint as light (up to 12.5 g/day), moderate (above 12.5 and up to 50 g/day) and heavy (above 50 g/day); reference group nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24.1% of studies; former drinkers not separated.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oral cavity and pharynx (52 studies), RR vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers: light 1.13 (95% CI 1.00–1.26), moderate 1.83 (1.62–2.07), heavy 5.13 (4.31–6.10); I² 26%, 72% and 77%. Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (54 studies): 1.26 (1.06–1.50), 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 4.95 (3.86–6.34); I² 68%, 85% and 91%. Larynx (41 studies): light 0.87 (0.68–1.11), moderate 1.44 (1.25–1.66), heavy 2.65 (2.19–3.19).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: I² values are printed in Figure 2 (read on the rendered page), not in the text. The study numbers printed beside each site (52, 54, 41) are its total at any intake; from Table 2 (editors' sums of the cohort and case–control columns) the light estimates rest on 26, 34 and 14 studies, the moderate on 52, 53 and 37 and the heavy on 38, 41 and 36. The larynx light value (0.87) is in Figure 2 only.

key_findings.finding: Female breast cancer (118 studies), RR vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers: light 1.04 (1.01–1.07), moderate 1.23 (1.19–1.28), heavy 1.61 (1.33–1.94); I² 63%, 54% and 10%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic from Table 2: the heavy-drinking estimate rests on 11 studies (6 cohort, 5 case–control), the moderate on 95 and the light on 115. Only 41 of the 118 breast studies reported adjusted estimates (Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Colorectum (66 studies): light 0.99 (0.95–1.04), moderate 1.17 (1.11–1.24), heavy 1.44 (1.25–1.65). Liver (36 studies): light 1.00 (0.85–1.18), moderate 1.08 (0.97–1.20), heavy 2.07 (1.66–2.58). Heavy drinking was also associated with stomach (1.21, 1.07–1.36; 39 studies), pancreas (1.19, 1.11–1.28; 39), lung (1.15, 1.02–1.30; 34) and gallbladder cancer (2.64, 1.62–4.30; 8 studies). All vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: The light values for colorectum (0.99) and liver (1.00) are in Figure 2 only; the text says light drinking was not associated with colorectal cancer. From Table 2 the heavy-drinking estimates rest on 29 colorectal and 31 liver cancer studies (editors' sums).

key_findings.finding: Prostate (43 studies): light 1.04 (1.01–1.08), moderate 1.06 (1.01–1.11), heavy 1.09 (0.98–1.21). Melanoma (14 studies): light 1.11 (0.97–1.27), moderate 1.20 (1.03–1.41), heavy not evaluable. No significant positive association for oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia, small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Inverse associations vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers: Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.73 (0.59–0.89), 0.73 (0.60–0.87) and 0.63 (0.41–0.97) for light, moderate and heavy drinking (9 studies); non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.88 (0.80–0.97), 0.87 (0.81–0.95) and 0.75 (0.64–0.88) (24 studies); kidney light 0.92 (0.86–0.99) and moderate 0.79 (0.72–0.86) (17 studies); thyroid light 0.81 (0.74–0.88) and moderate 0.81 (0.71–0.94) (9 studies). Figure 2 also shows inverse associations at light drinking for lung cancer, 0.84 (0.79–0.88), and oesophageal adenocarcinoma with gastric cardia, 0.86 (0.76–0.98), which the text does not mention.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: By design (Table 2): case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohort studies for oral cavity and pharynx (heavy drinking 5.34, 4.46–6.39, 35 studies vs 3.13, 1.59–6.19, 3 studies; heterogeneity P=0.007). Heavy drinking and liver cancer: 2.79 (2.00–3.87) in 24 case–control vs 1.12 (1.02–1.23) in 7 cohort studies; larynx 2.81 (2.33–3.39) vs 1.12 (0.75–1.67), 3 cohorts (heterogeneity tests not significant). Light drinking and liver cancer in cohorts: 0.85 (0.74–0.97). Melanoma was associated with drinking only in the 2 cohort studies (light 1.25, moderate 1.27). Light drinking, cohort against case–control studies: oral cavity and pharynx 0.86 (0.60–1.23; 4 studies) against 1.22 (1.10–1.35; 22); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.20 (0.84–1.71; 10) against 1.29 (1.07–1.55; 24); female breast 1.06 (1.03–1.10; 42) against 1.04 (0.99–1.09; 73); lung 0.85 (0.82–0.89; 18) against 0.71 (0.57–0.89; 11). Design heterogeneity P (across intake levels): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 0.157, liver 0.226, larynx 0.216.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: By sex (Table 3): the colorectal association was stronger in men (light 1.05, moderate 1.21, heavy 1.53, 1.30–1.80) than in women (0.95, 1.07, and 1.24, 0.68–2.25, from 4 studies; heterogeneity P=0.010); no significant colorectal association in women. Light drinking: oral cavity and pharynx men 1.20 (1.06–1.35; 12 studies), women 1.00 (0.78–1.27; 8), heterogeneity P = 0.165; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma men 1.39 (1.11–1.74; 16), women 1.14 (0.87–1.49; 8), P = 0.548.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: By region (Table 4): light drinking was significantly associated with oral cavity and pharynx (1.33, 1.06–1.68; 7 studies) and oesophageal squamous cell cancer (1.54, 1.18–2.00; 11 studies) only in Asian studies; melanoma (light 1.32, moderate 1.47) and prostate cancer (1.05, 1.09, 1.20) only in North American studies; the non-Hodgkin's lymphoma association differed by region (P=0.013), with no association in European studies. The between-area heterogeneity tests for these two sites were not significant (P = 0.375 and 0.503), and the discussion links the Asian finding to the ALDH2 variant carried by 28–45% of people in Asian countries.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Restricting to adjusted estimates, or excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference category, did not materially change the results; the prostate association emerged more clearly in both sensitivity analyses. For pancreatic cancer, fully adjusted estimates alone still gave a significant increase of about 20% for heavy drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Sensitivity-analysis estimates are in Supplementary Material S3, not read; only the pancreatic figure is given in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Dose–response meta-regression (Figure 3): risk rose steeply with intake for oral cavity and pharynx and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma; increased risk for stomach and liver cancer was observed at about 25 g/day (two drinks); risk of lymphomas decreased linearly with dose; lower doses were inversely associated with kidney and thyroid cancer.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Figure 3 shows curves only (log RR axis; 0–100 g/day for most sites, 0–50 g/day for melanoma, cervix, endometrium, ovary and thyroid); no values were extracted from it.

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: high heterogeneity for some cancers; drinking pattern and beverage type not analysed; under-reporting by drinkers may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations; former drinkers in the nondrinker category may dilute risks; heterogeneous exposure measurement; publication bias and control type deferred to the group's earlier site-specific meta-analyses.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest the inverse lymphoma association may partly reflect misclassification, because early symptoms may lead people to stop or reduce drinking, and they cite a European cohort of 120,852 people that found no inverse association.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says the meta-analysis supports a protective effect of moderate drinking on renal cell cancer (8th paragraph), but the concluding paragraph lists kidney among cancers with no apparent association with alcohol, while the results report significant inverse associations (light 0.92, 0.86–0.99; moderate 0.79, 0.72–0.86).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper gives two incompatible readings of its kidney result; neither can be cited as the authors' conclusion without the other, and the protective reading is not tested against the misclassification explanation the authors apply to lymphomas.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says alcohol was not significantly associated with oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia, but Figure 2 gives a light-drinking RR of 0.86 (0.76–0.98), whose interval excludes 1; the light-drinking lung cancer RR of 0.84 (0.79–0.88) is also absent from the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two significant inverse associations at light drinking appear only in the figure; they matter for judging the light-drinking category as a whole (for example confounding or reference-group effects that lower RRs at low intake).

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say random-effects models were used to allow for heterogeneity that is described as small, while Figure 2 shows I² up to 91% and the limitations call heterogeneity high for some cancers.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Discussion, 10th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency; the pooled estimates for oesophageal squamous cell, oral, laryngeal, liver and lung cancer at heavy drinking (I² 73% to 91%) summarise widely varying studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1, stomach row: 33 studies of incidence plus 5 of mortality make 38, not the 39 studies listed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting error; one stomach study is unaccounted for in the outcome columns.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 and the text label each site with its total number of studies (for example female breast, 118), but the pooled estimate for each intake category uses a subset; the heavy-drinking breast estimate of 1.61, quoted in the abstract, rests on 11 studies (editors' sum of the cohort and case–control counts in Table 2). Likewise the light-drinking estimates for the oral cavity and pharynx and for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma rest on 26 and 34 studies (Table 2), not the 52 and 54 printed beside them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers will overrate the evidence behind the heavy-drinking estimates; study counts per category are available only for sites with more than 10 studies, through Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Two significant subgroup heterogeneity tests are not mentioned in the text: ovary by study design (P=0.007, Table 2) and lung cancer by world region (P=0.045, Table 4; heavy drinking 1.26 in North American, 0.96 in European and 0.92 in Asian studies).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor selective reporting; the lung cancer association at heavy drinking may be confined to North American studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports an indication of a positive association of alcohol with melanoma and prostate cancer, whereas Results, 2nd paragraph, describing the same estimates (melanoma moderate 1.20, 1.03–1.41; prostate 1.04, 1.06 and 1.09), says there was “little indication of an association”.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper can be cited either way on melanoma and prostate; claims should give the small relative risks and their regional and design restrictions (Tables 2 and 4), not either summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The categorical and continuous analyses disagree at low intake: Figure 2 gives light-drinking estimates below 1 for lung cancer (0.84, 0.79–0.88) and for adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus and gastric cardia (0.86, 0.76–0.98), while the continuous meta-regression shows a slight but significant linear increase for lung cancer and no significant dose–response for the adenocarcinoma (Results, 3rd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The shape at low intake depends on the model used; the inverse light-drinking estimates for these two sites should not be read as protection.

design_detail: Mendelian randomization in one cohort, UK Biobank (371 463 unrelated participants of European genetic ancestry; recruited 2006-2010, follow-up to 2016), with conventional (observational) analyses in the same participants. Instruments: variants associated with alcohol use disorder (9) and with the AUDIT-C consumption score (13) in a published genome-wide study (Kranzler et al., 2019, ref 27), from which variants associated with smoking, body mass index, physical activity, vegetable or red meat intake, self-rated health, C-reactive protein or total cholesterol were removed: the primary AUD-Restricted score kept 5 variants and the secondary AUDIT-C-Restricted score 10. Analyses: Cox models of incident disease by drinking category against abstainers, with and without six lifestyle factors; linear two-sample Mendelian randomization (inverse-variance weighted, with weighted median, MR-Egger and MR-PRESSO); allele-score analyses within drinking categories; and nonlinear Mendelian randomization (fractional-polynomial and piecewise-linear models fitted to estimates within deciles of residual intake). Selected analyses were repeated in 30 716 participants of the Mass General Brigham Biobank. The sources of the variant-exposure and variant-outcome estimates for the two-sample analysis are in eMethods 8 (not read). Labelled prospective-cohort and appraised with ROBINS-E under the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization in one cohort, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether a genetic score for alcohol use disorder, which also strongly predicts weekly intake in UK Biobank, is associated with higher odds of hypertension, coronary artery disease and other cardiovascular conditions; and whether the lower cardiovascular risk of light and moderate drinkers in conventional analyses shrinks when a few lifestyle factors are taken into account.
cannot_establish: That every amount of alcohol raises cardiovascular risk: the shape at low intake comes from parametric curves fitted to stratum estimates, depends on the score shifting intake by the same amount at every level of drinking (not shown in the main text), and changed with the secondary instrument; that the score acts only through alcohol (variants for alcohol use disorder may influence other behaviours, and pleiotropy was detected for HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A); effects outside a European-ancestry UK volunteer cohort; or absolute risks.

sample.recruitment: UK Biobank volunteers (recruitment 2006-2010); unrelated participants of European genetic ancestry (eMethods 1-4, not read). Replication in the Mass General Brigham Biobank, a US hospital-based biobank (eMethods 5, not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Exclusions are described in eMethods 2 (not read).
sample.demographics: Mean age 56.97 (SD 7.93); 46.41% men; mean intake 9.16 (SD 10.61) US standard drinks (14 g) per week; mean body mass index 27.41; mean systolic blood pressure 140.23 mm Hg; 43 297 (11.66%) genotyped on the UK BiLEVE array (Table 1). Light drinkers' intake was 38% beer, 29% red wine, 24% white wine or champagne and 6% spirits; heavy drinkers' 38% beer, 24% red wine, 28% white wine or champagne and 7% spirits (Results › Characteristics in the UK Biobank).
sample.attrition: Not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: UK Biobank is a volunteer cohort; the paper does not discuss how taking part might relate to drinking or health. Only unrelated people of European genetic ancestry were analysed. The observational reference group, abstainers, is defined as 0 drinks/week and is not split into former and lifelong non-drinkers in the main analysis; lifelong abstainers (34 423) appear only as a negative control for pleiotropy. The allele-score analyses within drinking categories and the nonlinear analyses within strata of residual intake compare people grouped by a variable that the score itself influences.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported intake at baseline, converted to US standard drinks of 14 g (eMethods 3, not read), with categories abstainers (0 drinks/week), light (>0 to 8.4), moderate (>8.4 to 15.4), heavy (>15.4 to 24.5) and a highest category (>24.5) (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph). Genetic scores as described; each was standardized to a difference of 1 drink/day using UK Biobank estimates (Methods › Genetic Instruments for Alcohol Consumption).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: In grams (editors' conversion at 14 g per drink): light up to about 118 g/week, moderate about 118-216, heavy about 216-343, highest above 343. Mean (SD) intake 4.9 (2.7) drinks/week in light and 21 (3.8) in heavy drinkers. Instrument relevance: the AUD-Restricted score was associated with intake (β 7.0 drinks/week, as expected from its scaling to 1 drink/day; P<.001), with an F statistic of 780 (Results › Associations Between Genetic Instruments and Alcohol Intake Phenotypes). The linear Mendelian randomization odds ratios are expressed per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption, an SD that the main text does not define.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking: variants associated with smoking were removed from the scores; smoking was one of the six lifestyle covariates in the observational models; multivariable nonlinear Mendelian randomization adjusted for smoking, body mass index and depression (eFigure 14, not read). Other drugs: not reported.

comparison.controls: Observational: abstainers (0 drinks/week at baseline; current non-drinkers, not separated into former and lifelong non-drinkers in the main text). Linear Mendelian randomization: per unit of genetically predicted intake; Table 2's footnote says the disease associations were tested in current drinkers. Nonlinear Mendelian randomization: curves anchored at 0 drinks/week (OR 1). Pleiotropy check: 34 423 lifelong abstainers.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Observational models adjusted only for smoking, body mass index, red meat and vegetable intake, physical activity and self-rated health, some of which (body mass index, self-rated health) may lie on the path from drinking or reflect earlier illness; no adjustment for socioeconomic position or medical history is described. Genetic: confounding of the score is addressed by removing variants, by the abstainer test and by MR-Egger; how ancestry structure was handled (for example principal components) is not described in the main text.

outcomes.instruments: Six cardiovascular phenotypes (hypertension, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation; definitions in eTable 2, not read) and ten continuous traits (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, LDL, HDL and total cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoproteins A and B, γ-glutamyltransferase, C-reactive protein); 31 continuous phenotypes in eTables 7-8 (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Case definitions are in eTable 2 (not read). Table 1 reports prevalence, which suggests that the Mendelian randomization analyses counted cases present at any time, while the Cox models used incident disease.
outcomes.operationalization: Observational: prevalence and hazard ratios by drinking category against abstainers. Mendelian randomization: odds ratio per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption (linear), per 1 drink/day of allele score (within categories), or relative to 0 drinks/week along a fitted curve (nonlinear).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni within families: P<.008 for the six diseases and P<.005 for the ten continuous traits (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; outcomes from records and measurements.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Conventional; UK Biobank; reference abstainers] J- or U-shaped prevalence and hazards for all six diseases (Figure 1, eFigures 1-2; no numbers printed in the main text). [Linear Mendelian randomization; AUD-Restricted score; OR per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption] hypertension 1.28 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.39; P=1.73×10−9), coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74; P=6.00×10−3), myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05 to 1.78; P=2.00×10−2), stroke 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54; P=2.10×10−2), heart failure 1.39 (1.08 to 1.78; P=9.00×10−3), atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08 to 1.44; P=3.00×10−3) (Table 2). [Allele score per 1 drink/day, within categories] hypertension: light 1.3 (1.1 to 1.5), moderate 1.7 (1.3 to 2.2), highest category 2.6 (1.6 to 4.2); coronary artery disease: light 1.7 (1.2 to 2.4), moderate 1.8 (1.1 to 2.8), highest 5.7 (2.4 to 13.5). [Nonlinear Mendelian randomization] quadratic models fitted better than linear ones for hypertension and coronary artery disease (P<.001) and for systolic and diastolic blood pressure and LDL cholesterol; the curves are plotted without printed values (Figures 2-3). Replication cohort: quadratic association with diastolic blood pressure (P<.001), none with systolic.
analysis.covariates: Observational adjusted model: six lifestyle factors (covariates of the baseline model in eMethods 7, not read). Multivariable nonlinear Mendelian randomization: smoking, body mass index and depression.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is reported; the paper states that it followed the STROBE reporting guideline.
analysis.selective_reporting: Nonlinear results are shown in the main text for hypertension and coronary artery disease only, with the other diseases and all-cause mortality in eFigures 6-7. Results with the secondary score that suggested a threshold (no rise in risk until about 7 to 14 drinks/week) or slight decreases in risk at modest intake are reported in one paragraph and attributed to pleiotropy in that score, while the primary score's assumptions for nonlinear analysis are not examined in the main text. The text says that analyses of the other cardiovascular phenotypes supported the primary results, although three of them did not reach the paper's own threshold of P<.008.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors say the sex-stratified nonlinear analyses had reduced power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Conventional analyses reproduced J-shaped associations, and light and moderate drinkers had healthier lifestyles than abstainers; adjustment for six lifestyle factors made the inverse associations of moderate intake with hypertension and coronary artery disease non-significant, while in Figure 1 the light-drinking category still appears below 1 after adjustment. Genetically predicted higher intake was associated with higher odds of hypertension and coronary artery disease, and quadratic curves fitted better than straight lines. With the secondary score, piecewise analyses suggested no rise in risk below about 7 to 14 drinks/week.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points describe a "consistently risk-increasing association between all amounts of alcohol consumption" and hypertension and coronary artery disease, and the Discussion says the results substantiate earlier claims that no amount of alcohol protects against cardiovascular disease. Gaps: (1) the conclusion about light drinking comes from fractional-polynomial curves fitted to stratum estimates and fixed at OR 1 for zero intake; stratified estimates of this kind are valid only if the score changes intake by the same amount at every level of drinking, which the main text does not test, and the secondary score gave a threshold instead; (2) the primary score is built from variants for alcohol use disorder, which the authors concede is an indirect measure of usual intake; (3) the fitted curves imply very large effects (odds ratios of roughly 4 to 5 for hypertension and roughly 9 for coronary artery disease at 21 drinks/week, read approximately from Figure 2, which prints no values), far beyond the linear estimates (1.28 and 1.38 per SD) and the observational hazard ratios near that intake in Figure 1, and the paper does not reconcile them; (4) lifestyle adjustment attenuated rather than removed the lower risk of light drinkers, and the suggestion that unmeasured factors would remove it is speculation; (5) the published correction (Error in Abstract, April 2022) reworded the first sentence of the abstract's conclusions to attribute the attenuation to adjustment for lifestyle factors, which matches the data; the PMC text still carries the original sentence.

timeline.event: Holmes et al. (European ancestry, ADH1B rs1229984): carriers of the intake-lowering allele had lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90); cited here as earlier Mendelian randomization evidence.
Millwood et al. (China Kadoorie Biobank): in men, genotype-predicted intake was associated log-linearly with stroke but not with myocardial infarction; cited here.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease, listed in the project's DOI list as answering items 13-15, which include this paper; it was published online in November 2019 (in print in February 2020), about two years before this paper (online March 2022), and so cannot address it.
Larsson et al. (European two-sample Mendelian randomization, up to 94 variants): associations with stroke and peripheral artery disease, borderline with coronary artery disease; cited here.

This study, with a replication in the Mass General Brigham Biobank inside the paper: the quadratic association with diastolic blood pressure was reproduced, systolic blood pressure was not significant, and disease outcomes were not tested.

Correction, "Error in Abstract" (JAMA Netw Open 2022;5(4):e2212024; doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.12024; read on PMC, PMC9021906): the first sentence of the abstract's Conclusions and Relevance was reworded to say that adjustment for coincident favourable lifestyle factors attenuated the observational benefits of modest intake. No number was changed; the PMC full text read for this card still shows the original sentence.

replication.where_it_stands: The linear Mendelian randomization associations agree in direction with other European-ancestry studies for coronary disease and stroke (Holmes et al., 2014; Larsson et al., 2020), but not with the null east Asian result for myocardial infarction (Millwood et al., 2019). The paper's distinctive claim, that risk rises from the very first drinks, rests on nonlinear Mendelian randomization with one score and was not robust to the choice of score; it should be presented as contested until nonlinear methods that do not need a constant genetic effect across intake levels are applied and replicated. Larsson et al. (2020) also used UK Biobank outcome data, so the two are not independent.
