what_would_settle_it: Nonlinear Mendelian randomization of incident cardiovascular events using instruments for usual consumption that are shown to shift intake equally across the intake range (or methods that do not need this assumption), applied in several cohorts including ones with many lifelong abstainers, and reporting the stratum-specific estimates as well as fitted curves; agreement across instruments at 0 to 14 drinks/week would show whether light drinking carries a measurable cardiovascular risk.

domains.note: Instrument independence and exclusion restriction: variants associated with eight risk factors were removed; the scores did not appear to be associated with confounders (eTables 4-6, not read); in 34 423 lifelong abstainers the score was not associated with the continuous traits reported except HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A, a pleiotropic signal (no disease results for abstainers are printed); MR-Egger intercepts were non-significant, and weighted median and MR-PRESSO agreed. Variants for alcohol use disorder may act on other behaviours, which the authors concede could mean a shared genetic basis rather than a causal effect. Ancestry: European only; the handling of population structure is not described in the main text. The observational analysis is at high risk of confounding (six covariates; whether former drinkers were excluded from the abstainers is not stated in the main text).

Relevance: strong (F=780). The primary score tracks susceptibility to alcohol use disorder more than usual intake; intake was self-reported once; and the scale of the linear estimates (per SD, undefined) cannot be converted into grams.

For the results that carry the paper's conclusions (the curves and the category-specific estimates), participants are compared within strata of observed or residual intake, which the score influences. Shape at low intake: this is valid only if the score shifts intake by the same amount at all levels, which is not shown, and the threshold found with the secondary score suggests it may not hold. Selection into the cohort: UK Biobank volunteers of European ancestry; Table 2's footnote restricts the disease analyses to current drinkers, which would condition on a variable influenced by genotype.
Not applicable in the usual sense: the score is fixed at conception.
Exclusions and missing intake or covariate data are not reported in the main text.
Definitions in eTable 2 (not read); prevalent and incident cases appear to be mixed in the genetic analyses; misclassification is unlikely to depend on genotype.

No registered plan; nonlinear results for two of six diseases in the main text; contrary results with the secondary score reported in one sentence each, with their figures only in the supplement, and explained after the fact as pleiotropy; phenotypes that missed the stated threshold described as supporting the main results.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The linear associations of the alcohol-use-disorder score with hypertension and coronary artery disease are reasonably well protected (strong instrument, several pleiotropy-robust methods, an abstainer negative control), with some concerns about pleiotropy of behavioural variants. The paper's distinctive conclusions, risk at all levels of intake and the shape of the curve, rest on stratified nonlinear analyses whose key assumption is not examined, whose results changed with the score used, and whose fitted curves imply implausibly large effects; for those, the risk of bias is high, and the overall judgment reflects them because they are the paper's headline. The conventional analyses are at high risk of confounding and serve only to show the attenuation of the J-shape. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: attenuation of UK Biobank J-shaped associations by lifestyle adjustment, and linear genetic associations of an alcohol-use-disorder score with higher odds of hypertension and coronary artery disease. Do not cite it for: risk at specific intakes such as 7 or 14 drinks/week, the statement that any amount raises cardiovascular risk, or the size of the odds ratios read from the fitted curves.

key_findings.finding: 371 463 UK Biobank participants of European genetic ancestry (mean age 57.0, SD 7.9; 172 400 men, 46%) drank a mean of 9.2 (SD 10.6) US standard drinks (14 g) per week; 121 708 (32.76%) had hypertension, 27 667 (7.45%) coronary artery disease, 14 503 (3.90%) myocardial infarction, 8710 (2.34%) stroke, 5812 (1.56%) heart failure and 14 367 (3.87%) atrial fibrillation.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics in the UK Biobank, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Drinking categories (US standard drinks of 14 g per week): abstainers 0; light >0 to 8.4; moderate >8.4 to 15.4; heavy >15.4 to 24.5; highest >24.5. Observational hazards were estimated with abstainers as the reference, then re-estimated adjusting for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable intake, red meat intake and self-rated health.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conventional analyses reproduced J- or U-shaped associations of intake with the prevalence and hazards of all six diseases. Light and moderate drinkers reported better health, smoked less, had lower body mass index, more physical activity and more vegetable intake than abstainers. Moderate intake had significantly lower hazards of hypertension and coronary artery disease in the baseline models, and these differences lost significance once the six lifestyle factors were added.
key_findings.locator: Results › Observational Associations With Cardiovascular Diseases and Lifestyle Factors, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Figure 1 prints no values. Read approximately from the enlarged figure image: at light intake (about 5 drinks/week) the hazard ratio for hypertension is about 0.78 in the baseline model and about 0.90 adjusted, and for coronary artery disease about 0.76 and 0.85, with adjusted intervals that appear to exclude 1; at moderate intake (about 13 drinks/week) the adjusted ratios are about 1.00 and 0.96. Adjustment thus removed the moderate-intake association but only attenuated the light-intake one.

key_findings.finding: The primary AUD-Restricted score was strongly associated with intake in UK Biobank (β 7.0 standard drinks per week; P<.001; F statistic 780), was also associated with other alcohol measures, and showed no apparent association with confounders (eTables 4-6, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations Between Genetic Instruments and Alcohol Intake Phenotypes

key_findings.finding: Pleiotropy checks: the score was not associated with the continuous traits reported in that paragraph (γ-glutamyltransferase, blood pressure, LDL cholesterol) in 34 423 lifelong abstainers (no disease results for abstainers are printed in the main text, although the Table 2 footnote says abstainers were used to test for pleiotropy), and MR-Egger intercepts were non-significant, but among lifelong abstainers the score was associated with HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A, which the authors call a potential pleiotropic effect. Genetically predicted intake was associated with higher γ-glutamyltransferase, systolic and diastolic blood pressure and LDL cholesterol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Traditional MR, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Linear two-sample Mendelian randomization (inverse-variance weighted; OR per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption): hypertension 1.28 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.39; P=1.73×10−9); coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74; P=6.00×10−3); myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05 to 1.78; P=2.00×10−2); stroke 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54; P=2.10×10−2); heart failure 1.39 (1.08 to 1.78; P=9.00×10−3); atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08 to 1.44; P=3.00×10−3). The abstract rounds the first two to 1.3 (1.2 to 1.4; P<.001) and 1.4 (1.1 to 1.8; P=.006). Weighted median, MR-Egger, MR-PRESSO and analyses excluding abstainers were in the same direction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Traditional MR, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: By the paper's stated threshold for the six diseases (P<.008), myocardial infarction, stroke and heart failure are not significant. The SD is not defined in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Allele-score analyses within drinking categories (OR per 1 drink/day increase in the allele score): hypertension in light drinkers 1.3 (1.1 to 1.5; P=.003), moderate 1.7 (1.3 to 2.2; P<.001), highest category 2.6 (1.6 to 4.2); coronary artery disease in light drinkers 1.7 (1.2 to 2.4; P<.001), moderate 1.8 (1.1 to 2.8; P=.02), highest 5.7 (2.4 to 13.5). In male light drinkers, hypertension 1.4 (1.1 to 1.8; P=.01); in female light drinkers, coronary artery disease 1.7 (0.9 to 3.0), not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Traditional MR, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nonlinear Mendelian randomization with the primary score: three tests favoured nonlinear over linear models for hypertension and coronary artery disease, quadratic models fitted best (both P<.001), and every amount of intake was associated with higher risk, rising more steeply at higher intake, including between 1 and 2 drinks per day; similar quadratic shapes for systolic blood pressure (P<.001), diastolic blood pressure (P=.001) and LDL cholesterol (P<.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Evaluating Association Shapes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 2 and 3
key_findings.note: The fitted curves print no values. Read approximately from the enlarged Figure 2 image (log scale): hypertension OR about 1.2 at 7, 2 at 14 and 4 to 5 at 21 drinks/week; coronary artery disease about 1.3, 2.8 and 9; the curves are fixed at OR 1 at zero intake. Figure 3 (approximate) shows systolic blood pressure about 12 mm Hg and LDL cholesterol about 35 mg/dL higher at 21 drinks/week.

key_findings.finding: With the secondary AUDIT-C-Restricted score, piecewise-linear analyses suggested a threshold: intake was not associated with higher cardiovascular risk until roughly 7 to 14 drinks/week, and slight decreases in risk with modest intake were seen for hypertension and in some analyses in women. The authors attribute these to residual pleiotropy in that score and to low power in sex-stratified analyses, because they were not seen with the ADH1B variant alone, after removing abstainers, or in other analyses. Multivariable nonlinear analysis adjusted for smoking, body mass index and depression supported the primary results.
key_findings.locator: Results › Evaluating Association Shapes, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Replication in 30 716 Mass General Brigham Biobank participants: the primary score was strongly associated with intake; nonlinear analysis again favoured a quadratic model for diastolic blood pressure (P<.001); the result for systolic blood pressure was not significant. No disease outcomes were analysed there.
key_findings.locator: Results › Nonlinear Genetic Associations in the Mass General Brigham Biobank

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that the associations may reflect genes that influence both drinking and cardiovascular disease rather than an effect of alcohol itself, and that the primary score rests on variants for diagnosed alcohol use disorder, an indirect proxy for usual intake.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations

It changes wording only; all numbers on this card are unaffected.

design_detail: Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2020 analysis by the GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators (575 named collaborators; led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, Seattle). It re-estimates the theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) of GBD 2016 and adds the non-drinker equivalence (NDE), the intake at which the weighted risk returns to that of a non-drinker, separately for 21 regions, 5-year age groups from 15 to 95 and older, sex and year, 1990–2020. Relative-risk curves for 22 outcomes: five (ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, type 2 diabetes, tuberculosis) re-fitted with 71 additional studies (update to 31 December 2019, English only) using the MR-BRT meta-regression tool with bias covariates chosen by a Lasso; lower respiratory infection dropped for insufficient evidence; the other 17 curves carried over from GBD 2016; alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy left out for lack of dose–response studies. Weights: each cause's share of DALYs among the 22 causes in each region, age, sex and year, from GBD 2020 (unpublished when the paper appeared). The number and share of people whose average intake exceeds the NDE ('harmful amounts') was estimated for 204 countries and territories from GBD 2020 consumption estimates (data to 2019, forecast to 2020). Design 'modelling' as the round brief directs for attributable-burden estimates: no risk-of-bias instrument applies, so the card states the design's limits (METHODS §5.3).
can_establish: How the intake that minimises a DALY-weighted average of 22 cause-specific relative-risk curves (TMREL), and the intake at which that average returns to a non-drinker's risk (NDE), change when the weights are each region's, age group's, sex's and year's own disease mix, under GBD 2020's inputs; and the modelled number and share of people whose average intake exceeds the NDE.
cannot_establish: Whether low intake actually protects older people (the J-shapes come entirely from the protective dips of observational cause-specific curves, chiefly ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes, which the Mendelian-randomization studies the authors cite mostly do not support); any individual's risk (the authors put individual-level risk outside the study's scope); the effect of drinking patterns (not modelled); or that thresholds are the same for women and men (sex differences were not significant, which is not the same as shown to be absent).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (modelling). The update searched PubMed and previously published meta-analyses for studies published up to 31 December 2019, in English only, for the six outcomes with the most alcohol-attributable DALYs (Research in context › Evidence before this study; Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 2nd paragraph). Search strings, inclusion criteria and PRISMA diagrams are in appendix 1 (pp 18–47), which was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Outcomes: the 23 GBD 2016 outcomes without lower respiratory infection; alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy left out of the weighted curves for lack of dose–response studies and tested in a sensitivity analysis (Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 2nd paragraph); depression, anxiety and dementia not included because evidence was scarce and reverse causation possible (Discussion, 8th paragraph). Ages 15 to 95 and older.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. TMREL and NDE for 21 regions; harmful-use estimates for 204 countries and territories; both sexes; 5-year age groups from 15; 1990–2020.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: English-language publications only, with PubMed and earlier meta-analyses as the only sources; 17 of the 22 curves were not updated since GBD 2016. The relative risks come from observational studies of self-reported intake; between-study bias was handled with candidate covariates (study reference group, adjustment for sick-quitter bias, sex, age, population representativeness, outcome reporting method, timing of exposure measurement, geographical representativeness, incidence versus mortality, adjustment for confounders) selected by a Lasso, the selected sets being given only in appendix 1 (p 15) (Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Modelled. GBD 2020 estimates (cited as unpublished) of average grams of ethanol a day among current drinkers by country, age, sex and year, combining supply-side, household-survey and administrative data with adjustments for under-reporting in surveys, unrecorded alcohol and tourists' consumption (Methods › Estimating prevalence of alcohol use and alcohol consumption). Data were collected through 2019 and forecast to 2020, so changes during the COVID-19 pandemic are not reflected (Discussion, 8th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Standard drink = 10 g of pure ethanol; current drinker = at least one standard drink in the past 12 months; exposure = average daily volume. Relative-risk draws were sampled at 1 g steps from 0 to 100 g a day. Drinking patterns (heavy episodic drinking) were not modelled (Discussion, 8th paragraph). 'Harmful amounts' = average intake above the NDE for the person's region, age, sex and year; Figure 4's legend specifies the mean NDE.
exposure.polysubstance: Not modelled. Tobacco and other drug use enter only through the underlying studies' own adjustment; 'adjustment for confounders in risk estimation' is one of the candidate bias covariates.

comparison.controls: Relative risks are against non-drinkers, as in GBD 2016 (Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 3rd paragraph), with the study's reference group and sick-quitter adjustment among the candidate bias covariates. Whether the reference is lifetime abstainers or all current non-drinkers is not stated in the main text. TMREL and NDE are read from the weighted curve relative to zero intake.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at model level. The authors name residual confounding, selection bias, measurement bias and reverse causation in the underlying studies as possibly unadjusted (Discussion, 8th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: GBD 2020 DALY rates by cause (cited as unpublished) as weights; 22 cause-specific relative-risk curves (17 from GBD 2016, five updated with MR-BRT). DALYs = years of life lost plus years lived with disability (Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper states adherence to GATHER and production under the GBD Protocol (Introduction, 5th paragraph; Methods › Overview). The weighted curves are not checked against observed all-cause mortality.
outcomes.operationalization: TMREL = intake minimising the weighted all-attributable-cause curve; NDE = the intake above zero at which that curve again equals the risk at zero intake; weights = each cause's share of the DALYs from the 22 causes in that population (Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend). 'Alcohol-related DALYs' in the Results are DALYs from these 22 causes whatever their cause, not DALYs attributable to alcohol (Figure 2 legend: the proportions are the weights).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable. Differences by sex, year and age are called significant or not without a stated method, apparently from the uncertainty intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: All intervals are 95% uncertainty intervals, in standard drinks (10 g) a day, relative to zero intake (non-drinkers). 2020 TMREL across all regions, ages and sexes: 0 (0–0) to 1.87 (0.500–3.30). Ages 15–39 across regions: TMREL 0 (0–0) to 0.603 (0.400–1.00), NDE 0.002 (0–0) to 1.75 (0.698–4.30); globally, males 0.136 (0–0.400) and 0.249 (0–1.00), females 0.273 (0–0.500) and 0.546 (0–1.30). Ages 40–64, global: TMREL 0.527 (0.400–1.00) males and 0.562 (0.400–0.800) females; NDE 1.69 (0.800–3.20) and 1.82 (1.00–3.10). Ages 65 and older: TMREL 0.636 (0.500–1.00) and 0.656 (0.500–1.00); NDE 3.19 (1.50–5.20) and 3.51 (1.70–5.50). Ages 40 and older across regions: TMREL 0.114 (0–0.403) to 1.87 (0.500–3.30); NDE 0.193 (0–0.900) to 6.94 (3.40–8.30). Global, age-standardised, both sexes (Table 2): TMREL 0.511 (0.400–0.700) and NDE 1.72 (0.80–3.30); with GBD 2016 curves and 2020 weights 0.534 (0–1.00) and 0.669 (0–1.40); GBD 2016 as published 0 (0–0.800). Above the NDE in 2020: 1.03 billion (0.851–1.19) males, 35.1% (29.1–40.7) of males aged 15 and older; 312 million (199–432) females, 10.5% (6.72–14.6); 1.34 billion (1.06–1.62) in all, against 983 million (718–1,190) in 1990; 59.1% (54.3–65.4) aged 15–39 and 76.9% (73.0–81.3) male. Sensitivity with hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy: TMREL lower on average by 0.058 (0.00–0.30), 0.092 (0.00–0.50) and 0.146 (0.00–0.60), NDE by 0.188 (0.00–0.90), 0.310 (0.00–1.30) and 0.508 (0.00–2.10) drinks a day in scenarios A, B and C.
analysis.covariates: Candidate MR-BRT bias covariates as listed under selection effects, selected by a generalised Lasso; the sets kept for each of the five updated outcomes are in appendix 1 (p 15), not read.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration of this analysis is mentioned; the paper says it was prepared within the GBD Collaborator Network under the GBD Protocol and follows the GATHER statement.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several inputs are cited as unpublished GBD 2020 work by the first author (the DALY rates used as weights, the consumption estimates, the 1.78 million alcohol-attributable deaths in 2020), so they cannot be checked from the article. The sensitivity analysis with risk-deleted DALY weights is said not to change the results, but its numbers are only in appendix 2 (pp 39–41), not read. No cause-specific curve is shown in the main text (Figure 1 is an illustrative weighted curve, image only); region-specific TMRELs and NDEs are only in Figure 3 (image) and appendix 2. Data for this analysis were offered, before the full GBD 2020 publication, on request to Emmanuela Gakidou (Data sharing).
analysis.power: Not applicable. Intervals come from 1000 draws of each cause-specific curve, which include between-study heterogeneity, and 1000 draws of the DALY rates, propagated to the TMREL and NDE (Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 1st paragraph). The main text does not say whether the uncertainty of the NDE was carried into the harmful-use prevalence, which Figure 4 defines by the mean NDE; structural choices and residual bias in the underlying studies are not stated to be included.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With weights from each population's own disease mix, the weighted curves had their minimum at or close to zero intake for ages 15–39 (TMREL 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions) and above zero for ages 40 and older (0.114 to 1.87), where ischaemic heart disease and stroke make up more of the burden. The global, age-standardised minimum was 0.511 (0.400–0.700) drinks a day against GBD 2016's zero; recomputing with the 2016 curves and the 2020 weights gave 0.534 (0–1.00). Differences by sex and by year were not significant. About 1.34 billion people were estimated to drink more than their population's NDE in 2020, most of them men aged 15–39.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The interpretation finds “strong evidence to support recommendations on alcohol consumption varying by age and location” (Summary › Interpretation); the discussion and conclusion add that guidelines should not differ by sex and that existing low-risk thresholds are too high for young people in all regions. Gaps: (1) the variation by age and region comes mainly, as the Results say, from applying the same cause-specific curves (one per outcome for all regions) to different disease mixes, not from age- or region-specific risk data, so 'strong evidence' describes a consequence of the model; (2) every non-zero TMREL comes from the protective dips of observational curves for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes, while the discussion itself reports that most Mendelian-randomization studies of cardiovascular disease (67%) and diabetes (75%) found no association; (3) the case against sex-specific guidelines rests on non-significant differences whose point estimates were higher for women in every age group (for example NDE 0.546 against 0.249 drinks a day at 15–39); (4) 'harmful amounts' means average intake above the population's NDE, which for men aged 15–39 worldwide is 0.249 standard drinks (about 2.5 g) a day; by such thresholds 83.2% of men and 77.7% of women aged 15–39 in Australasia drink harmful amounts; (5) the discussion's 'conservative approach' of using the lower bound of the interval strengthens rather than tests the conclusion that thresholds are too high, while the upper bounds (up to 4.30 drinks a day for the NDE at 15–39) are not discussed; (6) the abstract calls the curve J-shaped in every region at 40 and older, but the lowest regional TMREL in that group, 0.114, has an interval reaching zero. Against this, the paper states openly that GBD 2016's global zero does not survive updated weights.

timeline.event: GBD 2016 (Griswold et al.): one globally weighted curve, TMREL zero (0–0.8) standard drinks a day (card sc_griswold_2018).

Letters on GBD 2016 (Shield & Rehm; Di Castelnuovo, Costanzo & de Gaetano) criticise the global DALY weighting; this paper's population-specific weights address the cause-mix part of that criticism. Simona Costanzo, a co-author of the second letter, is among the GBD 2020 collaborators.

Correction (Lancet 2022;400:358; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)01389-7): appendices 1 and 2 corrected as of 19 July 2022; the notice does not say what changed and the main text is not mentioned, so the numbers on this card, all from the main text, are unaffected as far as the notice shows.

Linked comment by Burton & Sheron (Lancet 2022;400:141–43; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)01288-0): its first paragraph says the findings seemingly contradict GBD 2016's message that any amount leads to health loss; the rest is paywalled and was not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent GBD alcohol-threshold analysis read for this project. It reverses GBD 2016's global zero (0.511 drinks a day) while keeping minima close to zero for young adults, and it shows that GBD thresholds depend on the weights as much as on the relative risks. Its J-shapes at older ages stand or fall with the protective cardiovascular and diabetes associations, appraised separately on the cohort and Mendelian-randomization cards (Wood et al., 2018; Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019; Biddinger et al., 2022; Larsson et al., 2020). Later GBD rounds were not read.

A collaborator declaring ERAB and Brewers of Europe ties (S Costanzo) co-wrote a 2019 letter criticising GBD 2016's method. what_would_settle_it: Age-specific, cause-specific dose–response curves at low intake from designs less exposed to confounding and abstainer bias, above all non-linear Mendelian randomization in large cohorts of several ancestries that separate lifetime abstainers from former drinkers, for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in people over 40; data on drinking patterns; and a weighting scheme fixed in advance with all sensitivity analyses reported in the main text.

domains.note: DALY weights and consumption estimates were unpublished GBD 2020 work when the paper appeared; consumption data end in 2019 and were forecast to 2020; the review update covered six outcomes, English only, PubMed and earlier meta-analyses; 17 of 22 curves are unchanged since 2016.

Observational studies of self-reported intake; bias covariates chosen by a Lasso with the chosen sets only in an appendix; one curve per outcome assumed for every region; the protective dips for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes, which create every non-zero TMREL, are the contested part; alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy have no curve.

domains.domain: Theoretical minimum and non-drinker equivalence levels
domains.note: Both depend on the weights; the reference 'non-drinkers' is not defined in the main text; the weights include DALYs caused by alcohol (a risk-deleted alternative is reported only in an appendix); harmful use is defined by the mean NDE.

domains.domain: Uncertainty intervals: what they include and exclude
domains.note: Draws include between-study heterogeneity and DALY uncertainty; structural choices and residual bias are not stated to be included; it is not stated whether NDE uncertainty enters the harmful-use prevalence; sex and year comparisons are judged without a stated method.

Three sensitivity analyses are reported (risk-deleted weights, hypothetical curves for two excluded outcomes, GBD 2016 curves). Table 2 shows the global TMREL moving from 0 to 0.534 with the same 2016 curves when only the weights changed, which the paper does not explain; no sensitivity to curve form or reference group is reported.

Unpublished inputs; key sensitivity numbers only in appendices, which were later corrected without the notice saying what changed; the ambiguous term 'alcohol-related DALYs'; a trend statement that does not match Table 1 (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for burden-of-disease modelling (METHODS §5.3; the round brief sets design 'modelling' with no instrument). The editors' checklist is used with the same design-specific domains as card sc_griswold_2018; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The analysis improves on GBD 2016 by letting the weights follow each population's disease mix and by reporting the NDE, and it states that GBD 2016's global zero does not survive updated weights. Its age and region patterns are consequences of applying common observational curves to different disease mixes, and its J-shapes at older ages are only as sound as the protective cardiovascular and diabetes associations. Citable for GBD 2020's model estimates of TMREL, NDE and the number of people above the NDE, always with the definitions (standard drink 10 g; relative to non-drinkers; harmful = above the NDE) and assumptions; not citable on its own for a protective effect of alcohol in older people, for equal thresholds for women and men, or for advice to individuals.

key_findings.finding: Relative-risk update: the six outcomes with the most alcohol-attributable DALYs were re-reviewed with 71 additional studies; lower respiratory infection was dropped for insufficient evidence, leaving 22 curves (five re-fitted with MR-BRT, 17 carried over from GBD 2016); curves are relative to non-drinkers, with 1000 posterior draws sampled at 1 g steps from 0 to 100 g a day.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: TMREL and NDE come from a weighted average of the cause-specific curves, weighted by each cause's share of DALYs in each region, age, sex and year (GBD 2020); uncertainty from 1000 draws of each curve and 1000 draws of the DALY rates was propagated; estimates are given to three significant figures.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Across all regions, ages, sexes and years the 2020 TMREL ranged from 0 (95% UI 0–0) to 1.87 (0.500–3.30) standard drinks (10 g) a day; TMREL and NDE varied significantly by age but not by sex or year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ages 15–39, 2020: TMREL from 0 (0–0) to 0.603 (0.400–1.00) and NDE from 0.002 (0–0) to 1.75 (0.698–4.30) standard drinks a day across regions; globally, TMREL 0.136 (0–0.400) in males and 0.273 (0–0.500) in females, NDE 0.249 (0–1.00) and 0.546 (0–1.30); the sex differences were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Summary › Findings

key_findings.finding: Ages 15–39: injuries made up 66.3% (65.1–67.5) of alcohol-related DALYs in males and 47.9% (46.0–49.8) in females; transport injuries 25.9% (25.0–27.0) and 12.7% (12.0–13.4), self-harm 11.7% (10.1–13.3) and 12.3% (10.8–13.8), interpersonal violence 12.4% (11.8–13.0) and 6.70% (5.90–7.69).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (image) legend
key_findings.note: 'Alcohol-related DALYs' here are DALYs from the 22 alcohol-associated causes, whatever their cause (the weights), not DALYs attributable to alcohol (Figure 2 legend).

key_findings.finding: Ages 40–64, global: ischaemic heart disease made up 24.1% (23.0–25.3) of alcohol-related DALYs in males and 19.5% (18.0–21.0) in females, intracerebral haemorrhage 10.3% (9.61–10.9) and 11.7% (10.7–12.8), injuries 23.0% (21.7–24.4) and 16.7% (15.3–18.3); TMREL 0.527 (0.400–1.00) in males and 0.562 (0.400–0.800) in females; NDE 1.69 (0.800–3.20) and 1.82 (1.00–3.10) standard drinks a day.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ages 65 and older, global: ischaemic heart disease 31.5% (30.3–32.7) of alcohol-related DALYs in males and 29.7% (28.2–31.2) in females, intracerebral haemorrhage 11.6% (10.9–12.4) and 10.9% (10.1–11.8), ischaemic stroke 14.2% (13.5–14.9) and 16.0% (15.2–16.7); TMREL 0.636 (0.500–1.00) and 0.656 (0.500–1.00); NDE 3.19 (1.50–5.20) and 3.51 (1.70–5.50) standard drinks a day; sex differences not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ages 40 and older across regions: TMREL from 0.114 (0–0.403) to 1.87 (0.500–3.30) and NDE from 0.193 (0–0.900) to 6.94 (3.40–8.30) standard drinks a day; the abstract calls the weighted curve J-shaped in every region at these ages.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Findings; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Regional example, ages 55–59: in north Africa and the Middle East cardiovascular disease made up 30.7% (27.3–34.6) of alcohol-related DALYs, cancers 12.6% (11.0–14.3) and tuberculosis 0.37% (0.27–0.55), giving TMREL 0.876 (0.500–2.00) and NDE 3.89 (1.50–5.90); in central sub-Saharan Africa 20.1% (17.2–23.8), 9.80% (8.31–11.7) and 10.1% (6.03–14.1), giving TMREL 0.596 (0.300–2.00) and NDE 1.53 (0.600–4.70) standard drinks a day.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mean TMRELs and NDEs were larger for females than males of the same region, age and year, because injuries make up more of the male cause mix, but the differences were not significant once uncertainty was taken into account.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In 2020, 1.03 billion (0.851–1.19) males, 35.1% (29.1–40.7) of males aged 15 and older, and 312 million (199–432) females, 10.5% (6.72–14.6), drank more than the NDE; the number rose from 983 million (718–1,190) in 1990 to 1.34 billion (1.06–1.62) in 2020, which the authors attribute to population growth, and they state that the global proportion did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1's global rows show significant decreases since 1990 for three of six age–sex groups (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.locator: Table 1, Global rows

key_findings.finding: Of the 1.34 billion above the NDE, 59.1% (54.3–65.4) were aged 15–39, and 75.5% (70.3–80.7) of these were male; the highest shares of men aged 15–39 above the NDE were in Australasia (83.2%), western Europe (79.3%) and central Europe (78.3%); of women aged 15–39 in Australasia (77.7%), western Europe (64.3%) and southern Latin America (59.0%); 6.55% (4.79–8.43) of those above the NDE were older than 65. The text reports significant increases in 14 countries, decreases in 55 and no significant change in 135.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Table 1 (regional rows)

key_findings.finding: Adding hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL on average by 0.058 (0.00–0.30), 0.092 (0.00–0.50) and 0.146 (0.00–0.60) standard drinks a day and the NDE by 0.188 (0.00–0.90), 0.310 (0.00–1.30) and 0.508 (0.00–2.10) in scenarios with maximum relative risks of 3, 5 and 10 reached at four drinks a day; the largest changes were in men in eastern Europe and at ages 30–54.
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Global, age-standardised, both-sexes estimates (Table 2): GBD 2016 as published, TMREL 0 (0–0.800); GBD 2016 curves with GBD 2020 DALY weights, TMREL 0.534 (0–1.00) and NDE 0.669 (0–1.40); GBD 2020 curves and weights, TMREL 0.511 (0.400–0.700) and NDE 1.72 (0.80–3.30) standard drinks a day.
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The discussion notes that existing low-risk guidelines range from 8 to 42 g a day for women and from 10 to 52 g a day for men (citing Kalinowski & Humphreys, 2016), and argues that even the lower bound of the TMREL and NDE intervals implies these are too high for younger people.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Citing a systematic review of Mendelian-randomization studies (van de Luitgaarden et al., 2021), the discussion reports that 67% of Mendelian-randomization studies of cardiovascular disease and 75% of those of diabetes found no association with alcohol, and that only five of 24 studies tested a non-linear relationship.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: drinking patterns not modelled; alcohol use disorders excluded from the TMREL; possible residual confounding, selection and measurement bias and reverse causation in the relative risks; self-reported intake; no distinction by beverage type or quality; weights include alcohol-caused DALYs; consumption forecast to 2020 from data through 2019; depression, anxiety and dementia not included, whose inclusion would possibly lower the TMREL and NDE.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Correction notice (Lancet 2022;400:358; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)01389-7): appendices 1 and 2 were corrected as of 19 July 2022; the notice describes no change to the main text, from which every number on this card is taken.
key_findings.locator: Department of Error

key_findings.finding: The introduction cites unpublished GBD 2020 work by the first author for 1.78 million deaths (95% UI 1.39 to 2.27) attributable to alcohol in 2020, with alcohol the leading risk factor for death among males aged 15 to 49.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A model estimate cited to unpublished work, not a result of this paper. It is lower than the GBD 2016 figure of 2.8 million (2.4 to 3.3; sc_griswold_2018), and the two intervals do not overlap (editors' observation).

key_findings.finding: The authors say their estimates aim to minimise health loss across all alcohol-attributable outcomes in a population; that individual-level risk minimisation depends on individual factors such as other illnesses and medicines, which are more common in older people; that their results for older adults carry additional uncertainty; and that approaches to minimising individual-level risk are beyond the scope of the study.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the global proportion consuming more than the NDE has not changed significantly since 1990, but Table 1's global rows show significant decreases for males aged 15–39 (−4.62%, −6.27 to −2.64), females 40–64 (−4.22%, −6.54 to −0.279) and females 65 and older (−1.96%, −3.63 to −0.448); the text also speaks of the proportion of drinkers, the table of the population.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 6th paragraph; Table 1, Global rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The no-change statement may hold for all ages combined, which is not shown; claims about trends should use the age- and sex-specific rows.

reporting_issues.issue: The country counts (14 significant increases, 55 decreases, 135 no change) are given for 1990–2019 and attributed to Table 1, whose heading gives the percentage change since 1990 for 2020 and which reports only age- and sex-specific changes; the basis of a single country-level verdict is not stated, nor whether the change column is relative or in percentage points.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 7th paragraph; Table 1 heading and columns
reporting_issues.consequence: The country counts cannot be reproduced from the table; cite them as the authors' statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The lowest NDE at ages 15–39 is 0.002 (0–0) in the abstract and the results but 0 (0–0) in the discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding only; cite 0.002.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Alcohol-related DALYs' is used for the DALYs from the 22 alcohol-associated causes (the weights), not for DALYs attributable to alcohol; the Results do not say so, only the Figure 2 legend implies it.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements such as injuries making up 66.3% of alcohol-related DALYs in young men must not be read as shares of the harm caused by alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: This paper describes GBD 2016's curves as estimated with a Bayesian meta-regression tool (DisMod ODE), whereas the GBD 2016 paper describes mixed-effects logistic regression with non-linear splines.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The two papers disagree on how the 17 carried-over curves were fitted; the GBD 2016 appendix would settle it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 shows the global TMREL moving from 0 to 0.534 drinks a day with the same GBD 2016 curves when only the DALY weights were updated to GBD 2020, while the text says the results were not sensitive to the approach to weighting and attributes the differences to three changes without explaining this one.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 8th and 9th paragraphs; Table 2; Discussion, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The global threshold is sensitive to which year's DALY rates are used; claims comparing GBD 2016 and GBD 2020 should say so.

design_detail: Invited Comment in The Lancet (2018;392:987–88, issue of 22 September 2018, open access) published with the GBD 2016 alcohol paper (Griswold et al., 2018). Two authors; five paragraphs of running text and 14 references, one of them a review whose first author is R Burton. It restates GBD 2016's headline results, endorses its conclusions and argues for population-level alcohol policy (taxation and minimum unit pricing, marketing regulation, restricted availability). No methods, search or data of its own. Design 'narrative-review' with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for commentaries.
can_establish: How two clinicians and public-health researchers (King's College London, University of Southampton, both employed by Public Health England) read GBD 2016 on publication, and the arguments they gave for population-level alcohol policy.
cannot_establish: Anything about the health effects of alcohol beyond what GBD 2016 itself shows: every figure is second-hand from that paper; the title's statement that no level of consumption improves health is stronger than GBD 2016's own interval for the minimum-risk level (0 to 0.8 drinks a day); and the policy statements rest on one cited review rather than on any appraisal in the comment.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (comment).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; 14 references chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selective by design. The two meta-analyses reporting lower mortality or cardiovascular risk at moderate intake (Ronksley et al., 2011; Di Castelnuovo et al., 2006) are cited only as the view GBD 2016 superseded; the critiques of that view (Fillmore et al., 2006; Britton & Bell, 2017; Naimi et al., 2017; Holmes et al., 2014; Stockwell et al., 2016) are cited as the emerging literature that allows more reliable estimates; the policy paragraph rests on a single review (Burton et al., 2017, an English perspective on alcohol control policies).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; the comment restates GBD 2016's modelled exposure.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Restates the GBD 2016 minimum-risk level as 0 g of ethanol per week, without its interval (2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). The comment discusses alcohol-attributable deaths and DALYs as reported by GBD 2016, and harm beyond health (to families, through crime and disorder, in the workplace) and to people other than the drinker, without figures.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Improves health' is not defined; the comment equates it with GBD 2016's minimum of the DALY-weighted curve.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Restated from GBD 2016 and checked against that paper (card sc_griswold_2018): alcohol the seventh leading risk factor for deaths and DALYs in 2016; 2.2% (95% UI 1.5–3.0) of female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; at ages 15–49, 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; minimum-risk level 0 g of ethanol a week.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: The comment leaves out GBD 2016's interval for the minimum (0 to 0.8 drinks a day in that paper's results), its statistically significant J-shaped curve for ischaemic heart disease, and its stated limitations other than unrecorded consumption and drinking patterns; it gives no figures for harm to others or for the effects of the policies it recommends.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: GBD 2016 estimated that alcohol was the seventh leading risk factor worldwide and the leading one at ages 15–49, and that one globally DALY-weighted curve had its minimum at zero drinks a day with an interval reaching 0.8 drinks a day, while ischaemic heart disease showed a significant J-shaped association.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title states that no level of alcohol consumption improves health; the comment calls the analysis “state-of-the-art epidemiology” giving a “definitive understanding of alcohol-related harm” (3rd paragraph), calls its conclusions “clear and unambiguous” (4th paragraph), and takes them as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline, quoted as finding “no safe level of alcohol consumption”. Gaps: (1) a minimum of zero with an interval up to 0.8 drinks a day does not show that no level improves health, and the GBD authors later agreed that the risk is low across that range (authors' reply, 2019); (2) the minimum is described as minimising an individual's risk (2nd paragraph), though it comes from a curve weighted by the world population's disease mix; (3) 'definitive' is applied to a new method whose weighting four letters criticized in 2019 and whose global zero the same consortium revised to 0.511 drinks a day in 2022; (4) the policy paragraph mixes evidence (one cited review) with a prediction (that mortality in Scotland and England might diverge dramatically within a few years) and value statements (that limiting young people's exposure to marketing “has no downsides”; that these diseases are driven by commercial interests) without marking which is which.

timeline.event: Burton et al., rapid evidence review of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of alcohol control policies from an English perspective (Lancet), the comment's source for its policy ranking; not read here.
GBD 2016 alcohol paper (Griswold et al.), the paper commented on: minimum-risk level zero (0–0.8) drinks a day (card sc_griswold_2018).

Four letters on GBD 2016 and the GBD authors' reply (Lancet 2019;393:2389–92; summarized on card sc_griswold_2018). Di Castelnuovo, Costanzo & de Gaetano cite this comment's title as the conclusion that cannot be drawn from GBD 2016; the GBD authors agree the risk is low between 0 and 0.8 drinks a day.
GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al.): global minimum-risk level 0.511 (0.400–0.700) drinks a day; minima between 0 and 0.603 at ages 15–39 and J-shaped weighted curves at 40 and older (card sc_bryazka_2022).

Burton & Sheron's comment on GBD 2020 (Lancet 2022;400:141–43; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)01288-0): its first paragraph says the new findings seemingly contradict the 2018 message that any amount of alcohol leads to health loss; the rest is paywalled and was not read.
Controlled interrupted time-series evaluation of minimum unit pricing in Scotland (Wyper et al., 2023), on the project's Alcohol list, bears on the comment's prediction for Scotland; not read here.

replication.where_it_stands: A short endorsement written on publication. Its title states more than GBD 2016's own interval supports, and that paper's global minimum was revised to about half a drink a day by the same consortium in 2022, when the authors themselves described the new estimates as seemingly contradicting the earlier message. Cited for how the 'no safe level' reading was framed, not for any estimate.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement; Comment).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: RB is employed full-time at Public Health England (PHE), is a visiting researcher at King's College London, and declares no other competing interests. NS is employed part-time at PHE; has received research grants from the British Liver Trust, the Alcohol Education Research Council and other funding bodies; has done paid consultancy and received travel expenses from Gilead; has been paid for medicolegal work on hepatitis C and alcohol-related liver disease; and is clinical adviser to PHE, scientific adviser to the European Public Health Alliance, and Royal College of Physicians representative on EU alcohol-policy bodies, the EU Alcohol Forum, the Alcohol Health Alliance UK, several UK government departments, NICE, Southampton City Council and liver and gastroenterology societies. One GBD 2016 author (F Greaves) is affiliated with PHE but had no involvement in or knowledge of the Comment.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations: Addictions Department, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King's College London (RB); Clinical Hepatology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton (NS). Both authors were employed by Public Health England, a government agency; the cited policy review has R Burton as first author; no alcohol-industry ties are declared. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the health statement, the evidence named on cards sc_griswold_2018 and sc_bryazka_2022: low-intake dose–response curves from designs less exposed to confounding and abstainer bias, with a weighting scheme fixed in advance. For the policy prediction, controlled evaluations of minimum unit pricing on alcohol deaths and hospital admissions, such as the Scottish evaluation on the project list (Wyper et al., 2023).

domains.note: A two-page comment with 14 references chosen by the authors; no search or selection criteria.

GBD 2016 is called state-of-the-art and definitive without any appraisal of its weighting, of its interval for the minimum or of its reliance on observational relative risks; the J-curve meta-analyses are set aside in one sentence.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The ranking of policies rests on a single review whose first author is R Burton; the health argument rests on GBD 2016, which is not the authors' work.

A prediction (a dramatic divergence of mortality between Scotland and England within a few years) and value statements (no downsides to limiting marketing; commercial interests ahead of human consequences) are interleaved with evidence and not marked as such.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a health benefit of low-level drinking
domains.note: The side under-represented is the evidence for lower risk at low intake and the uncertainty around GBD 2016's zero: its significant J-shaped curve for ischaemic heart disease and its 0–0.8 drinks a day interval are not mentioned; possible costs or trade-offs of the recommended policies are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used (model card sc_kish_2017), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The comment is advocacy accompanying a modelling paper: it restates GBD 2016's numbers correctly (checked against that paper) but adds no evidence, and its title and characterizations ('definitive', 'clear and unambiguous') go beyond what that paper's own interval shows. Citable for how the 'no safe level' reading of GBD 2016 was framed on publication and for the authors' policy argument; not citable for any estimate (use sc_griswold_2018) or as evidence that no level of drinking improves health. A claim resting only on this comment stays at draft (METHODS §5.3, §6.3).

key_findings.finding: The title states that no level of alcohol consumption improves health.
key_findings.locator: Title

key_findings.finding: The comment restates GBD 2016's headline figures: alcohol the seventh leading risk factor for deaths and DALYs in 2016, accounting for 2.2% (95% UI 1.5–3.0) of female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; at ages 15–49 the leading risk factor, with 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths attributable.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The same paragraph calls alcohol the “leading cause of DALYs” at ages 15–49; GBD 2016 ranks it as the leading risk factor (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: It gives the GBD 2016 minimum-risk level as 0 g of ethanol a week, presented as the level minimising an individual's risk, and explains it by the lower risks estimated in women for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes being cancelled out by cancer risks that rise steadily with intake; it credits the new method with estimating rather than assuming the counterfactual level and with giving a concrete basis for low-risk drinking advice.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: It describes the analysis as epidemiology of the most advanced kind that settles the understanding of alcohol-related harm, and names remaining work: unrecorded consumption, drinking patterns and binge drinking (particularly in young people), and harm beyond health and to people other than the drinker.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: It calls the conclusions unambiguous: the small gains at low intake are more than offset by higher risks of other harms such as cancer; it takes this as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline (no safe level of consumption) and as a reason to prioritise policies that lower population consumption.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Policy argument: cutting affordability through taxes or price controls such as minimum unit pricing is ranked first for effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, ahead of marketing regulation and limits on availability (citing Burton et al., 2017), and the same measures are likened to tobacco control and to what obesity will need. The authors present Scotland's minimum unit pricing (from May 2018) as a large natural experiment with England as the comparison, and suggest that death and illness rates in the two might draw apart sharply within a few years.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Declarations: both authors employed by Public Health England (RB full-time, NS part-time); NS reports grants from the British Liver Trust and the Alcohol Education Research Council, consultancy and travel expenses from Gilead, paid medicolegal work, and advisory roles on alcohol policy; no funding statement.
key_findings.locator: Declaration of interests (end of article)

reporting_issues.issue: The comment calls alcohol the “leading cause of DALYs” at ages 15–49; GBD 2016 reports it as the leading risk factor for that age group.
reporting_issues.consequence: A risk factor is presented as a cause of disease burden; claims must use GBD 2016's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The minimum-risk level is restated as 0 g a week with no interval, following GBD 2016's abstract, which itself prints the interval per week rather than per day (see sc_griswold_2018, reporting issue 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the comment cannot see that the estimate is compatible with up to 0.8 drinks a day.

reporting_issues.issue: The Scottish policy change is described as a controlled natural experiment, with “England as the placebo control”.
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-randomized comparison between countries is described in the language of a placebo-controlled trial, which overstates what such a comparison can show.

reporting_issues.issue: The phrase attributed to the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline (“no safe level of alcohol consumption”) is cited to the 2016 report without a page.
reporting_issues.consequence: The quotation was not checked against the guideline in this reading; a claim using it should cite the guideline itself.

design_detail: Lancet Seminar (invited clinical review; Lancet 2019;394:781–92) by five authors from Toronto, Linköping, Bogotá, Dresden and Moscow, covering diagnosis, epidemiology, genetic and other risk factors, neurobiology, treatment use and the treatment gap, psychosocial and pharmacological interventions, the care pathway from primary to specialist care, and alcohol policy, with a boxed panel on Colombia. It states a focus on developments of the past 5 years not covered by the previous Lancet Seminars (Schuckit, 2009; Connor, Haber & Hall, 2016). A boxed search strategy describes searches of Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE and PsycINFO, plus the Cochrane Library and reference lists, for English-language publications from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2018, with preference for highly cited manuscripts; the search terms are in an online appendix that is not on file. No quantitative synthesis and no appraisal of the cited studies; 140 references. Design “narrative-review” with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for this Seminar.
can_establish: How five researchers in alcohol epidemiology, neurobiology and treatment summarised alcohol use disorders for clinicians in 2019: the working definition they adopt, the figures they chose for prevalence, treatment rates and treatment effects (each traceable to a cited source), and the care model and policies they recommend.
cannot_establish: Any estimate on its own authority: every figure is second-hand (WHO 2018 for prevalence, a 2004 overview for the global treatment rate, a 2010 study in the US Veterans Health Administration for prescribing rates, Jonas et al., 2014, for the naltrexone number needed to treat) and none is appraised; whether the treatments and policies it recommends work as stated (no pooling, no appraisal, the sources for Table 2 only in an appendix not on file); and anything about the management of alcohol withdrawal, which the Seminar does not review.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence from the described search and from the authors' choice; highly cited manuscripts were given higher preference for inclusion (p. 781, search box).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Search box: English-language publications from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2018 in four databases, plus the Cochrane Library and reference lists of relevant manuscripts; no further criteria and no record of what was found or left out (p. 781).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The stated window does not define the evidence base: of the 140 references, 52 are dated before 2015, 10 in 2019 and 1 is in press (editors' count from the reference list, pp. 789–792). The preference for highly cited manuscripts favours prominent findings. At least 33 references (24%) name one of the five authors, 28 of them J Rehm (editors' count; entries ending in et al. may hide more), and the four acknowledged reviewers (P Anderson, A Gual, R Room, R Wiers) are authors of further cited papers (for example refs 15, 27, 83 and 93). The primary-care figures on treatment and recognition come from a cross-sectional study led by J Rehm (ref 70), partly through the authors' own calculations.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). The Seminar notes that alcohol use is usually measured by self-report and recommends biomarkers of heavy drinking such as phosphatidylethanol in clinical settings, with costs and practical and ethical questions to be discussed with the patient (p. 782, Diagnosis, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No drinking amounts are defined. The Seminar's working definition of alcohol use disorder is compulsive heavy use with loss of control, which it equates with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 alcohol use disorder or ICD-11 alcohol dependence (p. 781, Diagnosis, 3rd paragraph); heavy use is not defined in grams or drinks. The prevalence figures it quotes come from WHO's 2018 report, whose case definition the Seminar does not state. The overall level of consumption in the policy correlation and the Colombian adult per-head figure (about 6 L a year) are given without saying whether litres of pure alcohol per adult are meant (p. 788).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that the Colombia panel reports that, according to directors of treatment institutions, most people with alcohol use disorders refused to be treated together with people who use other drugs (p. 788, Panel).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data of its own). Reference groups behind the figures it quotes: the population aged 15 and older (prevalence), people of high socioeconomic status (mortality ratios), the population average (life expectancy), and standardised instruments and general practitioners' identification as each other's reference (recognition in primary care).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. Discussed: DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria (listed in appendix pp 4–6, not on file), AUDIT and AUDIT-C for screening, phosphatidylethanol as a biomarker; treatment outcomes as reported by the cited reviews (a number needed to treat; credible intervals from a Bayesian meta-analysis).
outcomes.operationalization: Alcohol use disorder as compulsive heavy use with loss of control (p. 781); treatment success framed as reduced drinking, with abstinence said to give the largest effect on mortality (p. 782, Diagnosis, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own; all second-hand, as cited. Prevalence of alcohol use disorders in 2016, ages 15 and older: men 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); high-income countries 8.4% (8.0–8.9), upper-middle-income countries 5.4% (5.0–6.0) (p. 782). Life expectancy reduced by more than 20 years in Nordic register analyses (p. 782). Heritability: one Australian twin study 64%, range 40% to 70%, a meta-analysis about 50% (p. 783). ALDH2*2 carried by about 40% of East Asian people (p. 783). Treatment: 22.3% of patients with alcohol dependence in European primary care received interventions, 21.9% globally (p. 784); screening of eligible primary-care patients 5.9% (3.4–8.4) (p. 784); general practitioners identified 30.3% (27.1–33.7) of patients with an instrument-identified disorder, and instruments identified 39.9% (36.0–43.9) of patients with alcohol dependence identified by general practitioners (p. 785); cognitive bias modification: cognitive bias 0.23 (95% credible interval 0.06 to 0.41), relapse −0.27 (−0.68 to 0.22) (p. 785); naltrexone number needed to treat 12 to prevent return to heavy drinking (p. 786); medications prescribed to 0.07% overall and 5.8% of those seeking specialty treatment (p. 787); Spearman correlation between overall consumption and prevalence of alcohol use disorders 0.69 (0.60–0.76) (p. 788).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: An effect size is given for one approved medication only (the naltrexone number needed to treat); the strong statements in Table 2 (robust effectiveness for topiramate; sodium oxybate safe and effective; baclofen's efficacy robustly replicated in one adequately powered multicentre trial) cite sources only in the appendix, and the baclofen trial is not identified in the printed paper; no null or negative trial and no critique of the approved medications is cited; the policy section cites only supportive evidence; withdrawal management is not covered.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As presented, the cited evidence shows that alcohol use disorders affected an estimated 8.6% of men and 1.7% of women aged 15 and older worldwide in 2016 (WHO figures the authors call rough estimates); that about one in five people with alcohol dependence receive treatment (22.3% in a 2015 European primary-care study, 21.9% in a 2004 global overview); that screening in European primary care was rare (5.9% at baseline in a five-country trial); that the approved medications have meta-analytic support, with a naltrexone number needed to treat of 12 as the only effect size given; that cognitive bias modification had a small effect on cognitive bias and an uncertain effect on relapse; and that a substantial share of people recover with little or no treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says these disorders are “undertreated partly because of the high stigma associated with them” and because of insufficient screening, that effective and cost-effective interventions exist, and that primary care should be responsible for most treatment, with routine screening and a stepped response (p. 781). Gaps: (1) the causal wording for stigma and screening rests on associations (p. 784) and on reasons for the treatment gap that the body says “seem to be threefold” (p. 785, Clinical presentation and treatment use, 6th paragraph); (2) the medications are said to have “solid support for modest, but clearly clinically useful effectiveness” (p. 787), and Table 2 calls topiramate robust and sodium oxybate safe and effective, without effect sizes or identified trials in the printed paper; (3) cognitive bias modification is said to have a small effect on relapse although the credible interval includes zero (p. 785); (4) the policy argument rests on an ecological correlation (0.69) whose countries, year and method are not stated and which cannot show that lowering consumption lowers the prevalence of the disorder, and minimum unit pricing is said to have promising results on the strength of one Canadian study of consumption (p. 788); (5) prescribing rates from one 2010 study in the US Veterans Health Administration are presented as general (p. 787); (6) no outcome evidence is given for the primary-care model the summary recommends (the ODHIN trial is cited only for its baseline screening rate, p. 784); (7) heritability is described as a share of disorders (p. 783). Against this, the authors call the prevalence figures rough estimates, say the cognitive bias modification evidence is not conclusive, list caveats of the neurocircuitry model including recovery without treatment, and say systematic evidence for integrated care pathways may not yet exist.

replication.where_it_stands: A 2019 overview, not a source of primary estimates. Its prevalence figures are WHO's 2016 estimates; its treatment-gap figures date from 2004 (global) and 2015 (European primary care), and later syntheses on the project list (Mekonen et al., 2021, on treatment rates; McPheeters et al., 2023, on pharmacotherapy) should be preferred for current claims once read. It does not cover alcohol withdrawal, for which the project's withdrawal sources (Mayo-Smith, 1997; Amato et al., 2010) apply.
