what_would_settle_it: For the figures, the primary sources it cites (WHO 2018; Rehm et al., 2015; Jonas et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2010) read in full, and an appraised, up-to-date synthesis of treatment rates across countries. For the central recommendation, cluster-randomised trials of routine primary-care screening with a stepped care pathway against usual care, reporting drinking, remission of the disorder and mortality.

domains.note: A search of four databases over 2015–2018 is described (strategy in an appendix not on file), which is more than many narrative reviews offer; but nothing says which retrieved papers were cited and why, highly cited manuscripts were explicitly preferred, and 52 of the 140 references predate the window and 10 postdate it (editors' count), so the evidence base was largely chosen outside the search.

No cited study is appraised. Limitations are named for the prevalence estimates (rough, culturally specific criteria), cognitive bias modification (not conclusive) and baclofen (divergent meta-analyses of small studies), but strong efficacy wording (robust, robustly replicated, safe and effective, solid support) is applied without effect sizes, and one credible interval that includes zero is read as an effect.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 33 of 140 references name one of the authors (28 J Rehm); the primary-care treatment and recognition figures come from the senior author's study with the authors' own calculations, and the consumption–prevalence correlation uses an exposure dataset two authors co-wrote (Manthey et al., 2019).

Recommendations are mostly marked as such (should, might, probably), and experimental treatments are labelled Wave 3; but normative statements (primary care should be responsible for most treatment; inability to offer psychological support is no excuse not to prescribe) sit beside evidence without data, and an ecological correlation is presented as the basis of all policy measures.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the benefits and limits of the treatments and policies it recommends
domains.note: The side under-represented is evidence of limited, null or uncertain effect: no negative trial or critique of the approved medications is cited, harms appear only as table lists, the policy section cites supportive studies only, and recovery without treatment is acknowledged in two sentences (pp. 784, 787).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used (model card sc_kish_2017) and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. A well-referenced Seminar by experienced researchers, but the evidence was selected rather than systematically gathered, and no cited study is appraised. Citable for the authors' working definition of alcohol use disorder, for how the treatment gap and the primary-care model were framed in 2019, and as a pointer to primary sources; every figure is second-hand, and claims must cite the primary source (WHO 2018 for prevalence; Rehm et al., 2015, for European primary care; Jonas et al., 2014, for the number needed to treat; Harris et al., 2010, for prescribing rates). A claim resting only on this Seminar stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). Not citable for withdrawal management, which it does not review.

key_findings.finding: Definition: diagnoses require a minimum number of operational criteria within the same 12 months; DSM-5 diagnoses the disorder when more than one criterion is met, with severity by the number met, and ICD-11 distinguishes alcohol dependence from a harmful pattern of use. Sharing reservations about DSM-5 and calling the widening gap between DSM-5 and ICD-11 problematic, the authors use alcohol use disorder for compulsive heavy use with loss of control, which they equate with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 disorder or ICD-11 dependence.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; page checked on the rendered image)

key_findings.finding: Search: a systematic literature search per subject area of Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE and PsycINFO for English-language publications from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2018, plus the Cochrane Library and reference lists; highly cited manuscripts were given higher preference for inclusion; search terms in appendix pp 2–3.
key_findings.locator: Search strategy and selection criteria (box)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from the reference list (pp. 789–792): 52 of 140 references are dated before 2015, 10 in 2019 and 1 is in press. The appendix is not on file.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and all 140 references read; appendix not on file)

key_findings.finding: Treatment goal: the authors say reduced drinking has been linked to lower mortality and is a vital goal of any treatment, and that reductions leading to abstinence give the largest effect on mortality (citing Roerecke, Gual & Rehm, 2013); brain changes caused by alcohol are described as partly reversible after abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, 5th paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Prevalence in 2016 (adults aged 15 and older, citing WHO's 2018 global status report and Rehm & Shield, 2019): men 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); men's prevalence five times women's, with signs of the gap narrowing; highest in high-income (8.4%, 8.0–8.9) and upper-middle-income countries (5.4%, 5.0–6.0). The authors say these survey-based figures should be considered rough estimates because several criteria are culturally specific.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is a world map of 2016 prevalence by country with bands from 0.0–2.0% to 15.1–21.2%; country values were not extracted, and the caption gives no source (the text attributes it to WHO 2018). The case definition behind the WHO figures is not stated in the Seminar.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; Figure 1 seen on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Mortality: excess mortality of people with alcohol use disorders (mainly through conditions such as cirrhosis or injury) does not appear in burden-of-disease reports, where alcohol poisoning is the main cause of death listed under these disorders, but only in special analyses; register analyses in Nordic countries show life expectancy reduced by more than 20 years from the population average (citing Westman et al., 2015).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Socioeconomic gradient: people of low socioeconomic status are at higher risk of the disorders and at least twice as likely to die from them and from prolonged heavy drinking as people of high status (citing Probst et al., 2015); the low-versus-high ratio is higher for alcohol-attributable causes than for all causes, which the authors read as an interaction and as more harm per litre in people of low status.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Heritability: an Australian twin study estimated 64%; twin and adoption studies of the past 35 years report 40% to 70% with no sex difference; a meta-analysis (Verhulst et al., 2015) gives about 50%, possibly an underestimate; concordance rates below 50% are taken to show that environmental factors and gene–environment interactions also contribute.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 1st paragraph (begins p. 782; figures on p. 783)
key_findings.note: The text says “about 50% of alcohol use disorders are heritable” (reporting issue 6).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Genes: carriers of ALDH2*2, especially homozygotes, accumulate acetaldehyde when they drink (flushing, headache, sweating, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting), which protects against the disorder; the variant is carried by about 40% of East Asian people and is rare in European people; ADH variants such as ADH1B*2 are also protective; the largest genome-wide meta-analysis of AUDIT scores (2019) found ten risk loci.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Environmental and family risk factors named: permissive cultures with cheap, available alcohol and advertising, positive expectancies, poor family support, conduct and mood disorders, low self-control, perceived peer drinking, low parental monitoring, parental drinking and favourable parental attitudes; a 2018 prospective cohort found parental supply of alcohol associated with adolescent drinking, alcohol-related harms and symptoms of the disorder.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 5th–6th paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Neurobiology: alcohol facilitates GABA-A and inhibits NMDA receptor signalling, suppressing nervous-system excitability, which rebounds during withdrawal; higher than normal stimulation and lower than normal sedation predict progression to the disorder (citing King et al., 2016). The authors note caveats of the three-stage neurocircuitry model: it ignores the recovery phase, structural and functional brain changes may reverse after abstinence, and a substantial proportion of people recover with no or minimal treatment.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 7th paragraph (p. 783) and 10th paragraph (p. 784)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Treatment use: in a study of more than 13 000 patients and 358 general practitioners in six European countries, 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence received interventions; the most recent global overview gave 21.9%, and some countries such as the USA were lower; the authors infer a treatment gap larger than for any other mental disorder.
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The European figure is from Rehm et al. (2015, ref 70); the global figure and the comparison with other disorders are from Kohn et al. (2004, ref 72), 15 years before the Seminar (reporting issues 1 and 2).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Stigma: compared with people not in treatment, people in treatment show more social disintegration, drinking, comorbidity and functional loss; fear of stigma has been associated with less access to treatment; stigma towards alcohol use disorders has not improved over time while stigma towards mental disorders generally has; high stigma has been recorded among health professionals.
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 2nd–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Screening: no systematic screening exists in primary care in most countries; in five European jurisdictions, including two with the highest screening rates (Catalonia and England), 5.9% (95% CI 3.4–8.4) of eligible adult patients were screened during a 4-week baseline period (ODHIN trial, Anderson et al., 2016).
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 4th paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Recognition in primary care (six-country European study): general practitioners rely on drinking level and signs such as breath, red eyes and raised liver enzymes rather than criteria; they identified 30.3% (95% CI 27.1–33.7) of patients with an alcohol use disorder identified by standardised instruments, while the instruments identified 39.9% (36.0–43.9) of patients with alcohol dependence identified by the general practitioners (authors' own calculations from Rehm et al., 2015).
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 5th paragraph (begins p. 784; figures on p. 785)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial treatment: citing Miller and Wilbourne (2002), brief counselling, motivational enhancement therapy, the community reinforcement approach, guided self-change, behaviour contracting and social skills training were among the ten most effective interventions; the authors say little has changed, that specific well-defined therapies are more effective than unstructured therapist–patient interaction, and that their effective elements have not been identified.
key_findings.locator: Interventions, 1st paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Cognitive bias modification (the most comprehensive review, a Bayesian individual-participant meta-analysis, Boffo et al., 2019): effect on cognitive bias 0.23 (95% credible interval 0.06 to 0.41) and on relapse −0.27 (−0.68 to 0.22), none on substance use; the authors call the evidence, when added to other treatments, not conclusive and in need of more rigorous randomised trials.
key_findings.locator: Interventions, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The relapse interval includes zero although the text describes a small effect on relapse; the scale of both estimates is not stated (reporting issue 3).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Approved medications (Wave 1: disulfiram, naltrexone oral or depot, nalmefene, acamprosate) all have meta-analytic support and different indications: disulfiram only under supervision; naltrexone and nalmefene mainly prevent relapse to heavy drinking and could serve a goal of controlled drinking; acamprosate promotes abstinence in severe disorder. The authors say their effect sizes resemble those of common medical treatments, citing a number needed to treat of 12 for naltrexone to prevent return to heavy drinking (Jonas et al., 2014).
key_findings.locator: Interventions, 3rd paragraph (p. 786); Table 1 (p. 785)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Table 1 safety notes: a disulfiram–ethanol reaction may be an emergency, so disulfiram can sustain abstinence but not reduce drinking; naltrexone and nalmefene can block opioid analgesics and precipitate opioid withdrawal; acamprosate does not undergo first-pass metabolism and can be used in liver disease; listed adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, psychosis and optic neuritis for disulfiram, and diarrhoea, pruritus, rash and altered libido for acamprosate.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (Adverse effects and Observations columns)
key_findings.note: Table 1 also has a dosage column, not extracted (the project reports no dosing).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (Table 1 read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Off-label medications (Wave 2: baclofen, gabapentin, ondansetron, sodium oxybate, topiramate, varenicline) are said to have meta-analytic support. Topiramate has perhaps the strongest support but needs careful titration and causes early cognitive side-effects, so stays a specialist treatment; baclofen meta-analyses, mostly of small studies, diverge, but efficacy was robustly replicated in one adequately powered multicentre trial, with tolerance and dose escalation risking serious adverse events; sodium oxybate was safe and effective in severe dependence but has high potential for non-medical use and is reserved for specialist settings.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Interventions, 4th–5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 2's sources are only in the appendix (pp 8–9), not on file; the baclofen trial is not identified in the printed paper. A dose mentioned for gabapentin was not extracted.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (Table 2 read on the rendered page; appendix not on file)

key_findings.finding: Prescribing: several medications have solid support for modest but clinically useful effectiveness, yet are prescribed to an estimated 0.07% of patients with alcohol use disorders overall and 5.8% of those seeking specialty treatment (citing Harris et al., 2010, on the US Veterans Health Administration); the authors judge wider use of existing treatments the greatest short-term opportunity.
key_findings.locator: Interventions, 9th paragraph
key_findings.note: The source is one health system in one country (reporting issue 4).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Care pathway: primary care should be the entry point and the site of most treatment, with regular checks of drinking like blood-pressure checks, brief advice first, then lifestyle interventions, then psychological and pharmacological treatment; specialist referral when drinking stays high or comorbidity exceeds primary care; inability to offer psychological support should not stop prescribing. Figure 2 sets out a stepped model from screening of all adults to specialised care. An important proportion of these disorders improve without formal intervention (citing Walters, 2000).
key_findings.locator: Acute and long-term management, 1st–4th paragraphs; Figure 2
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; Figure 2 read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal is not reviewed: it appears only as the withdrawal or negative-affect stage of the neurobiological model and as rebound excitability (p. 783), and detoxification only as an option “if needed” in Figure 2 and in a pointer to guidelines from NICE (2011) and Rolland et al. (2016) (p. 787). No evidence on withdrawal management is given.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 7th–8th paragraphs (p. 783); Acute and long-term management, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 787)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Experimental medications (Wave 3): neurokinin-1 antagonism reduced alcohol self-administration in rodents and stress-induced craving in patients, but industry programmes stopped after depression trials; mifepristone reduced cue-induced craving and drinking in a small 1-week laboratory study in men; a ghrelin antagonist has so far proved safe; a κ-opioid antagonist trial began in 2019 (NCT03852628).
key_findings.locator: Interventions, 6th–8th paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read)

key_findings.finding: Policy: the authors base restrictions on availability, marketing bans and taxation on the association between overall consumption and the prevalence of alcohol use disorders, a Spearman correlation of 0.69 (95% CI 0.60–0.76) based on WHO's 2018 report and Manthey et al. (2019); minimum unit pricing (several Eastern European countries, Scotland, some Canadian provinces) is said to have promising results, citing one Saskatchewan study; these policies are called highly cost-effective (citing Chisholm et al., 2018).
key_findings.locator: The role of the wider environment and alcohol policy, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (the 3rd begins p. 788)
key_findings.note: The number of countries, the year and the method of the correlation are not stated (reporting issue 5).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Colombia panel: adult per-head consumption about 6 L a year; prevalence of alcohol use disorders 7% in 2016; Law 1566 of 2012 made substance use a public-health matter and gave a right to free state-of-the-art treatment, but took 5 years to implement because private institutions wanted guaranteed reimbursement; according to directors of treatment institutions, most people with alcohol use disorders refused to be treated together with people who use other drugs; and, the authors state without attribution, facilities offering inpatient treatment of up to 90 days for alcohol use disorders only remained almost empty as of May 2019.
key_findings.locator: Panel: Hazardous alcohol use and alcohol use disorders in Colombia

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 maps the 2016 prevalence of alcohol use disorders by country in bands from 0.0–2.0% to 15.1–21.2% without printing country values; the contiguous USA is shaded in the 10.1–15.0% band, Canada in the 6.1–8.0% band.

The Seminar does not say which survey or model WHO's US estimate rests on, so the map cannot be used as independent confirmation of any one US survey.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the low treatment rate in the European countries “is not common in other regions”, then that the global rate was almost the same (21.9%) and some countries' rates lower.
reporting_issues.page: p. 784, Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence contradicts the evidence that follows it (probably “not uncommon” was meant); claims should rest on the figures, not on that sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The “most recent overview” of global treatment (21.9%) and the statement that the treatment gap is larger than for any other mental disorder both rest on Kohn et al. (2004), published 15 years before the Seminar.

design_detail: Editorial (Addiction, pp. 726–727; ten paragraphs, 19 references) by six alcohol epidemiologists arguing that observed health benefits of low-volume (‘moderate’) drinking reflect confounding and selection bias from how abstainers are defined, and are contradicted by Mendelian randomization (MR) studies; it recommends that burden-of-disease estimates, drinking guidelines, clinicians and policy no longer assume protective effects. No search, selection criteria, data or synthesis. Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief directs for commentaries and debate pieces.
can_establish: Which arguments and sources a group of alcohol epidemiologists relied on in January 2015 to doubt protective effects of low-volume drinking, and the policy recommendations they drew from them.
cannot_establish: Whether low-volume drinking lowers or raises mortality or cardiovascular risk; how complete or strong the cited evidence is (no search, no appraisal, no quantitative synthesis); or the accuracy of its summaries of other studies, which must be checked against those studies.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). The 19 cited sources: a Swedish societal-cost study; a cardiology paper and the Ronksley et al. (2011) meta-analysis, cited together as arguing for a therapeutic role of alcohol; a critique of J-shaped findings (Fekjaer, 2013); confounder and selection-bias studies (Naimi et al., 2005; Ng Fat & Shelton, 2012; Fillmore et al., 2006; Liang & Chikritzhs, 2013); eight Mendelian randomization or genetic studies (refs 9 to 16: Holmes et al., 2014, and others on cognition, child academic achievement, balance, blood pressure and cardiovascular biomarkers); two observational studies of intima-media thickness and coronary calcification in young adults; and a Mediterranean-diet trial (Estruch et al., 2013).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and one-directional: no study reporting benefit is examined, Ronksley et al. being cited only as having led others to see alcohol as therapeutic. Three of the 19 references come from the authors' own group and carry the abstainer-bias argument (Naimi et al., 2005, with Naimi; Fillmore et al., 2006, with Stockwell and Chikritzhs; Liang & Chikritzhs, 2013). One cited MR source is an unrefereed working paper, and two of the four sources cited as further MR studies concern prenatal alcohol exposure and children's outcomes, according to their titles.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. ‘Moderate’ drinking is glossed as low average volume; the description of Holmes et al. mentions a cut-off of 21 g of ethanol a day.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The argument concerns the abstainer reference group of cohort studies, said to be inflated by former and occasional drinkers with poorer health.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. Outcomes discussed: cardiovascular disease and coronary heart disease (CHD), stroke, type 2 diabetes, all-cause mortality, cognitive function, children's academic achievement and balance, blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, coronary calcification and carotid intima-media thickness.
outcomes.operationalization: Protection is framed as lower risk in low-volume drinkers than in abstainers; MR evidence is treated as closer to randomization than cohort evidence.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical analysis).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The editorial reports no estimates from the studies it cites; the only number is the 21 g/day cut-off it attributes to Holmes et al.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence for protective associations is mentioned only to be set aside; limitations of the MR studies, and of the observational studies cited in support (intima-media thickness, coronary calcification), are not discussed.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Four lines of argument, each resting on a few cited studies: protective associations have been reported for implausible conditions (liver cirrhosis, fetal effects, the common cold); confounding and the counting of former and occasional drinkers as abstainers can produce the J-curve (Fillmore et al., 2006; Liang & Chikritzhs, 2013); MR studies, chiefly Holmes et al. (2014), find no benefit of low-volume drinking; and MR studies suggest HDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein and fibrinogen are not causal for CHD, while intima-media thickness and coronary calcification rise with drinking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The editorial concludes, explicitly as the authors' opinion, that the field is due for a major repositioning, invokes the precautionary principle in the absence of randomized studies (Mendelian or clinical) supporting benefit, and recommends that burden-of-disease estimates and guidelines assume no protective effect, that guidelines discourage drinking for health reasons, that clinicians not recommend moderate drinking, and that the benefit hypothesis play no role in policy. Gaps: (1) the title's collapse and the conclusion rest on a handful of studies chosen without search; (2) one MR meta-analysis is presented as closer to a randomized trial than to cohort studies without examining whether the instrument assumptions hold for alcohol variants (effects of the variant other than through the amount drunk, or analyses split by drinking status, which the variant itself influences): the editorial states the exclusion assumption but does not test it; (3) observational associations in the harmful direction (intima-media thickness, coronary calcification) are accepted at face value while those in the protective direction are attributed to bias; (4) showing that three biomarkers are not causal for CHD rules out those pathways, not protection through others, and the statement that any mortality benefit runs through cardiovascular outcomes is uncited; (5) a diet trial that did not randomize alcohol cannot show that wine has no effect; (6) two of the MR examples concern prenatal exposure, not adult low-volume drinking. The recommendations not to assume benefit and not to advise drinking for health can be defended on precautionary grounds whether or not the hypothesis has collapsed.

timeline.event: Naimi et al.: potential confounders of heart disease more common among US non-drinkers than moderate drinkers (cited; Naimi is a co-author of this editorial).
Fillmore et al.: meta-analysis grouping studies by abstainer definition (cited; Stockwell and Chikritzhs co-authored it).
Ronksley et al. meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes, cited as an example of the protective reading (carded in this round by another reader).
Holmes et al. Mendelian randomization meta-analysis, the editorial's central evidence (carded in this round by another reader).
This editorial (first published 22 January 2015); no linked comments are listed on PubMed.
Stockwell et al. meta-analysis by three of the same authors, which cites this editorial in its first sentence (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round).

On the project list: the GBD 2016 alcohol analysis (Griswold et al.), described there as the ‘no safe level’ paper; how it treated the protective effects this editorial asked burden estimates to drop is for its own card (carded in this round by another reader).
On the project list: Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm's critique of Mendelian randomization studies of alcohol and cardiovascular disease (not read).
Zhao et al. update of the abstainer-referenced meta-analysis, with Stockwell and Naimi as authors (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).

replication.where_it_stands: A position statement that framed the later debate rather than evidence in its own right. Each of its factual claims should be cited from the primary study it summarizes, several of which are carded in this round; the Mendelian randomization evidence and its published critique are appraised separately.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declaration of interests: None (as printed).
funding.affiliations_note: National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University (Chikritzhs, Liang); Centre for Addictions Research of BC, University of Victoria (Stockwell); Boston Medical Center (Naimi); Karolinska Institutet (Andreasson); Sahlgrenska Academy and University Hospital, Gothenburg (Dangardt). Three authors wrote the abstainer-bias studies the editorial relies on, and three later wrote the 2016 meta-analysis that tests its claim. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Not answerable by an editorial. The question it raises would be settled by a long-term randomized trial of low-volume drinking against abstention, or by genetic analyses able to estimate the dose–response at low intake without splitting participants by drinking status, together with cohort analyses using lifetime abstainers and lifetime drinking histories.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; 19 sources chosen by the authors.
No appraisal of any cited study; an unrefereed working paper and prenatal-exposure studies are cited as MR evidence on low-dose drinking without comment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 19 references are from the authors' group, and they carry the abstainer-bias argument; the MR evidence comes from other groups.

The conclusion is labelled as opinion and the recommendations as recommendations, but contested inferences (MR as near-randomized, the biomarker argument, the diet-trial inference) are stated as findings.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against protective effects of low-volume drinking
domains.note: Only evidence against protection is presented; the evidence for it (cohort meta-analyses, experimental biomarker studies) is mentioned only to be dismissed, and the limitations of MR are not discussed, so the case for benefit is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS §5.3). It is a clearly argued advocacy piece whose selection is unsystematic and one-sided and whose cited studies are not appraised; the overall judgment follows the worst domains. Claims should cite the primary studies it summarizes and may cite this editorial only for the position its authors took in 2015 and for its recommendations, attributed to them (for example that guidelines should discourage drinking for health reasons).

key_findings.finding: The summary line states that evolving epidemiological evidence, including better methods for assessing causality, is raising doubts about whether moderate drinking protects health.
key_findings.locator: Standfirst (summary line above the text)

key_findings.finding: The authors say protective estimates for heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes have been built into international burden-of-disease estimates, including the Global Burden of Disease project, into some national drinking guidelines and into economic cost estimates, and have led some authors to propose alcohol as a therapeutic agent for some patients.
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph (refs 1 to 3)

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that protective associations are unlikely to be causal because they have been reported for implausible conditions (liver cirrhosis, fetal effects, the common cold), and that confounding and selection bias contribute to the J-shaped curve.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (refs 4 to 7)

key_findings.finding: Fillmore et al. (2006) are summarized as finding no significant protection in studies that kept former and occasional drinkers out of the abstainer group, explained by people quitting or cutting down as they age and fall ill; Liang and Chikritzhs (2013) are summarized as removing the difference in health status between abstainers and low-dose drinkers by combining former with current drinkers and adjusting for confounding.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (refs 7 and 8)

key_findings.finding: MR is described as using genetic variants associated with exposure but not with typical confounders, assuming the genotype affects the outcome only through the exposure; Holmes et al. (2014) are summarized as showing lower cardiovascular risk in drinkers carrying a variant linked to lower consumption, in a sentence that also refers to people consuming up to 21 g of ethanol a day, with the association seen in drinkers but not in non-drinkers. The authors write that MR “resembles more closely a randomized controlled trial (RCT) than traditional observational studies”.
key_findings.locator: 4th and 5th paragraphs (ref 9)
key_findings.note: The editorial's sentence on Holmes et al. is ambiguously worded (see reporting issues); check the primary study before citing the 21 g/day subgroup.

key_findings.finding: Further MR studies are cited as finding no protective effect of low-dose alcohol on cognitive function, children's academic achievement, balance and blood pressure.
key_findings.locator: 6th paragraph (refs 10 to 13)
key_findings.note: By their titles, refs 11 and 12 concern prenatal alcohol exposure and children's outcomes, and ref 11 is a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper.

key_findings.finding: MR studies are cited as suggesting that HDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein and fibrinogen are not causally related to CHD, and observational studies as showing only positive associations of drinking with coronary calcification and carotid intima-media thickness; the authors conclude that these biomarkers cannot explain an apparent protective effect on all-cause mortality, which they say is driven by cardiovascular outcomes.
key_findings.locator: 7th paragraph (refs 14 to 18)

key_findings.finding: A trial of a Mediterranean diet (Estruch et al., 2013), not randomized for alcohol, is cited as suggesting that the French paradox may reflect diet rather than wine.
key_findings.locator: 8th paragraph (ref 19)

key_findings.finding: In the authors' stated opinion the foundations of the protective hypothesis are so undermined that the field is due for repositioning; they invoke the precautionary principle in the absence of randomized studies, Mendelian or clinical, supporting protective effects.
key_findings.locator: 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: future burden-of-disease estimates, including the Global Burden of Disease, and national guidelines should assume no protective effect of low-dose drinking; guidelines should discourage drinking for health reasons; health professionals should not recommend moderate drinking to reduce cardiovascular risk; the hypothesis of health benefits should play no role in policy decisions.
key_findings.locator: 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Declaration of interests: none. No funding statement. Six authors, 19 references.
key_findings.locator: Declaration of interests; author information; References

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence summarizing Holmes et al. is ambiguous: it says drinkers with a variant linked to lower consumption among those consuming up to 21 g a day had decreased cardiovascular risk, leaving unclear whether 21 g/day defines a subgroup of the analysis or describes the carriers' intake.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial cannot be cited for what Holmes et al. found at low intake; the primary study (carded by another reader) must be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the four sources cited as further MR studies showing no benefit of low-dose alcohol (refs 11 and 12) concern prenatal exposure and children's academic achievement or balance, according to their titles; ref 11 is an unrefereed working paper, and the title of ref 12 does not identify an MR design.
reporting_issues.consequence: These sources do not bear on adult low-volume drinking and should not be counted as MR evidence on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that any positive mortality effect of low-dose drinking is driven by cardiovascular outcomes, on which the biomarker argument depends, has no citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The step from non-causal biomarkers to no mortality benefit is the authors' assertion.

reporting_issues.issue: Several author names in the reference list are garbled: Ronksley is given the initial R (ref 3), and George Davey Smith appears as Davey S. G. (refs 13 and 14) and Dave S. G. (ref 16).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; match references by DOI, not by author name.

design_detail: Dose-response meta-analysis of 34 prospective cohort studies (56 independent curves by sex, age group, beverage or ethnic group; 1,015,835 participants, 94,533 deaths) of alcohol intake and all-cause mortality published up to December 2005, found by one PubMed search and reference lists. Curves were pooled by inverse-variance-weighted second-order fractional-polynomial meta-regression allowing for correlation within studies (best fit: log RR = b1 x^0.5 + b2 x^0.5 log x), with fixed effects as the main model and a random-effects repeat; subgroups by adjustment level, sex, region, reference group, study size, follow-up and publication year with 99% confidence intervals and Sidak-adjusted contrasts. Reference: each study's lowest-intake category. No protocol, no appraisal of the included studies, no test for publication bias.
can_establish: The shape and size of the pooled association between alcohol intake and all-cause mortality in cohort studies published up to 2005, and how it changed with adjustment for confounders, sex, region, the composition of the reference group, follow-up and publication year.
cannot_establish: That drinking at low or moderate levels lowers mortality (pooled observational cohorts; residual confounding and reference-group bias not removed, and the inverse association was smaller and ended at lower intake when former and light drinkers were excluded from the reference group); the precision of the pooled curve (the tabulated intervals are fixed-effect despite large heterogeneity); or the completeness of the evidence (one database, no appraisal of the included studies, publication bias not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Review-level: PubMed, no start date, to December 2005 (humans; title or abstract containing alcohol, beer, wine or spirits plus mortality or death), and the references of the selected articles. 73 publications identified; excluded: one risk category only (4), mortality not reported separately by sex (5), cause-specific mortality only (3), multiple reports of one cohort (9; the longest follow-up kept), reference category not the lowest intake (4), relative risks or cases and person-years unavailable (14) (Methods › Search strategy and data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Prospective studies of alcohol dose and total mortality reporting at least two intake categories, by sex, with the lowest-intake category as reference and usable relative risks or counts; no language or population restriction is stated.
sample.demographics: Study level only (Table 1): cohorts from Japan, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Poland, Germany, Russia, the United States, Sweden, France, China, Australia and Italy, published 1981 to 2005; follow-up 5.5 to 26 years; age ranges at entry from 18 to 84 where given; 37 curves in men and 19 in women. Several cohorts are occupational or volunteer samples, according to the reference titles (male British doctors, male Japanese physicians, male German construction workers, the Physicians' Health Study enrolment cohort, men enrolled in an American Cancer Society study).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the primary cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One database plus reference lists; no grey literature; excluded studies are given only as counts. The meta-analysis inherits each cohort's reference group: in 26 of 56 curves former drinkers were not excluded from it. Few cohorts adjusted for or excluded pre-existing disease (by Table 1's codes, 4 adjusted for baseline diseases and 4 for coronary disease). One cohort weighs heavily: Boffetta and Garfinkel (1990; men in an American Cancer Society cohort, adjusted for age and smoking only) contributes 239,462 of the 1,015,835 participants (23.6%) and 37,079 of the 94,533 deaths (39.2%) (Table 1, p. 2438; percentages calculated by the editors); the weights of the curves are not reported and no analysis without this cohort is given, so under fixed-effect weighting it probably carries a large share of the pooled curve. Renaud et al. (1999) contributes separate wine and beer curves from one cohort of men, which share that cohort's reference group, yet both are counted among the 56 curves the Methods call independent (p. 2438).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported baseline intake as reported by each cohort, assigned in grams a day: the midpoint of each reported range, and 1.2 times the lower bound for open-ended top categories. A drink was taken as defined by each study; where undefined (7 studies) as 10 g of ethanol, and the authors say that 12 or 14 g gave the same results (data not shown) (Methods, p. 2439).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Curves plotted from 0 to 70 g a day; the figures' drinks-per-day axis equates one drink with 10 g, so the abstract's '1-2 drinks' and '2-4 drinks' are about 10 to 20 and 20 to 40 g a day (editors' conversion from the axes). Drinking pattern and beverage were not analysed, except one cohort reported for wine and beer separately.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking adjusted in 27 of the 34 studies, by Table 1's codes; other drugs not addressed.

comparison.controls: Each cohort's lowest-intake category: no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded (30 curves), declared no alcohol use (12) or occasional use (14), with former drinkers not excluded in either (Results › All studies, 1st paragraph). Among the 48 adjusted curves, 27 were classed as without and 21 as with light and/or former drinkers in the reference group (Table 2); whether the 27 also excluded occasional drinkers is not stated consistently (reporting issue 6).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Lifetime drinking history, reasons for not drinking and pre-existing illness are not available at review level; by Table 1's codes only 4 studies adjusted for baseline diseases.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking of the reference groups not reported.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality as reported by each cohort; adjusted relative risks extracted whenever possible, otherwise crude relative risks and 95% CIs computed from the number of events (5 studies) (Methods, p. 2439).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death ascertainment as in each cohort (not described).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Protection' is a pooled RR below 1 against the reference category; 'maximum protection' is 1 minus the lowest pooled RR; the 'reversion point' is the intake above which the inverse association is no longer significant at the 99% level (Table 2 footnote).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: 99% confidence intervals in subgroup analyses and Sidak-adjusted pairwise contrasts (Methods › Data analysis); seven subgroup families were tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; data acquisition is credited to two authors, without a statement on independent or duplicate extraction.

analysis.effect_sizes: All 56 curves (fixed effects): best fit b1 = -0.1592 (SE 0.0056), b2 = 0.0421 (SE 0.0014); lowest mortality at 6 g a day, RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), i.e. maximum protection 19% (95% CI 17 to 20); inverse association significant up to 42 g a day. Random effects: same model, very similar curve, wider intervals (Figure 1 only); deviance 879.4 (fixed) against 154.0 (random). Maximum protection (99% CI) at the intake of lowest risk, and reversion point (Table 2): not adjusted (8 curves) 36% (21 to 40) at 10 g, 68 g; adjusted at least for age (48) 17% (15 to 18) at 6 g, 37 g; also for social status (28) 18% (15 to 21) at 9 g, 46 g; also for social status and diet (10) 18% (12 to 24) at 6 g, 30 g; women (16) 18% (13 to 22) at 5 g, 18 g; men (32) 17% (15 to 19) at 6 g, 38 g; women by region: US 19% (13 to 24), Europe 20% (3 to 34), Australia, Japan and China 12% (0 to 23), P > .54; men: US 16% (14 to 19) at 4 g, 27 g; Europe 24% (20 to 28) at 9 g, 58 g; Australia, Japan and China 18% (13 to 23) at 6 g, 33 g; reference group with light or former drinkers (21) 23% (20 to 26) at 8 g, 52 g, without (27) 16% (14 to 18) at 5 g, 30 g, P < .001; small studies (26) 17% (15 to 22), large (22) 15% (10 to 20), P = .61; follow-up 10 years or less (22) 21% (18 to 25), more (26) 15% (13 to 27 as printed), P < .001; published 1981-1998 (25) 15% (13 to 18), 1999-2005 (23) 21% (18 to 24), P < .001. In the 34 curves with both crude and adjusted estimates: 19% (17 to 21) crude against 16% (14 to 18) adjusted. No I2, tau-squared or prediction interval; no absolute rates.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; adjusted estimates as reported by each cohort, with adjustment sets in Table 1 ranging from age alone to 10 variables; subgroup analyses by level of adjustment.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several analyses are reported as 'data not shown' (12- or 14-g drinks; men against women within the 13 populations with both; ethnicity within US data). The random-effects results appear only as a curve in Figure 1, while all tabulated estimates and intervals are from the fixed-effect model. No test for publication bias.
analysis.power: Not addressed; subgroups with few curves have wide intervals (women in Europe, 5 curves: 3 to 34%; other countries, 4 curves: 0 to 23%).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In cohorts published up to 2005, the pooled fixed-effect relative risk of death fell steeply from the reference category to its lowest point at 5 to 6 g a day (about half a 10-g drink; RR 0.81) and then rose, with the inverse association no longer significant above 42 g a day (37 g in adjusted curves; 18 g in women, 38 g in men). It was smaller and ended at lower intake when former and light drinkers were excluded from the reference group (16% at 5 g, significance lost at 30 g) than when they were included (23% at 8 g, lost at 52 g); it was larger in unadjusted curves (36%, different studies), in European than US men, in shorter follow-up and in more recent publications. Heterogeneity was large, and the random-effects intervals are wider than the tabulated ones.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion speak of 'protection' and of windows of intake that may confer a "net beneficial effect of moderate drinking" (abstract, p. 2437; similar wording in the conclusion, p. 2444); the Comment calls the 15 to 18% benefit of undoubted public health value and judges residual confounding very unlikely to change the picture substantially (p. 2442); the conclusion recommends that people who already drink low to moderate amounts regularly "should be encouraged to continue" (p. 2444). Gaps: (1) causal and advisory language from pooled observational cohorts; (2) the residual-confounding argument assumes unmeasured confounding no stronger than measured confounding and rests on the 34 curves with both crude and adjusted estimates, an assumption that cannot be tested; (3) the reference-group result, which the Comment itself calls important, is absent from the abstract and the conclusion, although it moves the reversion point from 52 to 30 g a day; (4) the abstract's windows (1 to 2 drinks for women, 2 to 4 for men, in 10-g drinks) lie where the fitted curves are returning towards 1, not where mortality was lowest (editors' calculation: men 0.88 to 0.99 at 20 to 40 g a day, women 0.86 to 0.95 at 10 to 20 g), and the abstract's limit of 4 drinks a day in men differs from the limit of 3 given in the Results; (5) most of the fitted reduction lies between the reference category and the first grams of intake (RR 0.85 at 1 g a day, editors' calculation), the contrast most exposed to reference-group bias; (6) the tabulated intervals are fixed-effect and understate uncertainty; (7) publication bias is dismissed by argument, not tested.

timeline.event: White, Altmann and Nanchahal (BMJ), described here as a meta-analysis finding a J-shaped relation only in men over 34 and women over 54 (ref. 9).
Gmel, Gutjahr and Rehm: precision-weighted hierarchical meta-analysis of the alcohol and all-cause mortality curve (ref. 10).
Bagnardi et al.: the flexible meta-regression method used here, co-developed by the third author (ref. 11).
This meta-analysis (accepted 30 August 2006; issue of 11/25 December 2006).
Fillmore et al.: meta-analysis grouping studies by abstainer definition (Addiction Research and Theory; cited by Stockwell et al., 2024, not read).

Stockwell et al.: 87-study meta-analysis with lifetime-abstainer and bias-adjusted analyses, which according to its card does not cite this paper; the project list presents items 5 to 7 as critiques of it (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round).
Wood et al.: individual-participant analysis restricted to current drinkers, avoiding the abstainer reference group (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Di Castelnuovo et al.: MORGAM analysis of 142,960 individuals by the same first author, one of the 20 cohorts added in Zhao et al. (2023) and Stockwell et al. (2024) (title as cited there; not read).
Zhao et al.: 107-cohort meta-analysis with study-level adjustment for abstainer biases (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).

Stockwell et al.: in the 6 cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger with lifetime-abstainer references, low-volume RR 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 in older cohorts with both abstainer biases (card sc_stockwell_2024, this round).

replication.where_it_stands: The standard citation for the J-shaped all-cause mortality curve in cohorts published up to 2005. Its own subgroup analysis anticipated the later critique: excluding former and light drinkers from the reference group reduced the inverse association and moved its end from 52 to 30 g a day. Later meta-analyses with stricter reference groups (Stockwell et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2023; Stockwell et al., 2024, one group with overlapping data) found no significant reduction in the least-biased subgroups, and the Mendelian randomization studies carded in this round test the question differently. Claims may cite this paper for what the pre-2006 cohort literature showed and for how sensitive the curve was to the reference group, not for a protective effect of drinking.

what_would_settle_it: A pooled individual-participant analysis of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories, using lifetime abstainers and stable occasional drinkers as separate references, excluding or modelling baseline illness, reporting random-effects intervals and absolute death rates; together with genetic analyses able to estimate risk at low intake, which test the question without an abstainer reference group.

The dose-response method is appropriate in itself (weighted, allowing for correlation within studies), and adjusted estimates were preferred, but every tabulated estimate and interval comes from the fixed-effect model although the authors found substantial heterogeneity (deviance 879.4 against 154.0 with random effects); random-effects results appear only as a curve, and the main analysis mixes crude and adjusted curves.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are 'no' (2, 4, 7, 11 and 15), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The judgment concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries: a single-database search, no appraisal of the cohorts, fixed-effect intervals despite large heterogeneity and no check for publication bias. The paper remains useful for what it shows about its own inputs: the J-shape in the pre-2006 cohort literature and its sensitivity to the reference group, to adjustment and to region. It may be cited for those descriptive points, attributed to the cohorts it pooled, and not for a causal effect or for the recommendation to keep drinking.

key_findings.finding: Main curve (56 curves, fixed effects): best fit log RR = b1 x^0.5 + b2 x^0.5 log x with b1 = -0.1592 (SE 0.0056) and b2 = 0.0421 (SE 0.0014); mortality lowest at 6 g a day, about half a drink, RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), a maximum 'protection' of 19% (95% CI 17 to 20); the inverse association remained significant up to 42 g a day (about 4 drinks). The random-effects repeat selected the same model and gave a very similar curve with wider intervals; the deviance fell from 879.4 to 154.0 (P < .001), which the authors read as heterogeneity among studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's maximum-protection values for small (17%, 99% CI 15 to 22) and large studies (15%, 10 to 20) do not match Table 3's parameters, which give about 14% for small and 17% for large studies (editors' calculation), nor Figure 4B, in which the small-study curve is the shallower one (lowest RR about 0.85) with the wider interval; the reversion points (26 and 36 g) do match the figure. Smaller mismatches: the intake of lowest risk for women is about 3.4 g a day by Table 3 (5 in Table 2), and about 7.4 g for social-status-adjusted curves (9 in Table 2), where the curves are flat.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two maximum-protection values for study size appear transposed; the authors' conclusion of no difference by size (P = .61) is unaffected, but size-specific values should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Two intervals in Table 2 are not compatible with their estimates on a symmetric (log) scale: not adjusted 36% (21 to 40), that is RR 0.64 (0.60 to 0.79), and follow-up over 10 years 15% (13 to 27), that is RR 0.85 (0.73 to 0.87); the row for all curves uses a 95% interval while every other row uses 99% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably typographical (for example 31 to 40 and 13 to 17); these intervals should not be cited as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 4D the dashed curve labelled 'Follow-up >10 y' is the deeper one (lowest RR about 0.78) with the wider interval, while Table 2, Table 3 and the text give greater protection with follow-up of 10 years or less (21% against 15%); the longer-follow-up group also has more deaths (61,532 against 25,409), which should give it the narrower interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure legend appears swapped; the tables and text should be cited for the direction of the follow-up difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts in the text do not all match the tables: the text gives 28 European, 17 American and 11 other curves, while Table 1 and Table 2 (adjusted curves plus the 8 unadjusted European curves) imply 27, 16 and 13; Table 1 places Goldberg et al. (1994), whose reference title names the Honolulu Heart Program, under Japan, although Honolulu is in the United States; the adjustment codes in Table 1 give 27 curves adjusted for social class against 28 in Table 2; and Tolstrup et al. (2004) carry no age code although all adjusted curves are described as adjusted at least for age (editors' counts).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the pooled curve; the regional comparison in men may include two US curves in the 'Australia, Japan, China' group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the inverse association extended up to 4 drinks a day in men and 2 in women, and its conclusion names 2 to 4 drinks for men and 1 to 2 for women; the Results say up to 3 drinks a day in men and 2 in women, and Table 2's reversion points are 38 and 18 g a day. The drinks are 10-g drinks (figure axes), which the abstract does not say.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should use grams a day and the reversion points; in standard drinks of 14 g, 38 g is under 3 drinks (editors' conversion).

reporting_issues.issue: The subgroup without light or former drinkers in the reference group is described as using no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded (Results › Other subgroup analyses), as excluding 'either ex-drinkers or very light drinkers' (Comment), and as 'No Drinkers in Reference Group' (Figure 4A legend).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether occasional drinkers were excluded from the reference group in these 27 curves is unclear, so the 16% estimate may still carry some reference-group contamination.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's standard error for b1 in large studies, 0.0664, gives z of about 2.2, inconsistent with the printed P < .001 and four times the small-study value (0.0160) despite 16 times the participants; the P values for women in Europe and in other countries match one-sided rather than two-sided tests (for example b2 0.0295, SE 0.0149: two-sided P about .048, printed .02); and the women's regional P value is printed as > .54 while one Sidak-adjusted pairwise P is .53 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; signals transcription errors in the statistical tables, consistent with reporting issues 1 and 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Text against Table 3: the Results say adjustment for social status and dietary markers did not affect the results, but Table 3 reports significant differences between the curves (adjusted for social status, 28 curves, against the other 20 adjusted curves: P < .001; adjusted also for diet, 10 curves, against social status without diet: P = .03), and its footnote gives n = 8 for the curves adjusted for social status but not diet, where 28 − 10 = 18 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that social status and diet made no difference holds for maximum protection (17%, 18%, 18%) but not for the shape of the curve (reversion points 37, 46 and 30 g a day); claims should not cite it as showing that this adjustment did not matter.
