design_detail: Cross-sectional national household survey (NESARC-III): face-to-face interviews with the AUDADIS-5, a fully structured interview, of 36,309 US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 or older, April 2012 to June 2013. Weighted 12-month and lifetime prevalence of DSM-5 alcohol use disorder (AUD), overall and by severity (mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe 6 or more of 11 criteria); sociodemographic correlates and psychiatric comorbidity as adjusted odds ratios; current mental-health-related functioning (SF-12v2, 12-month AUD only); treatment or help seeking. DSM-IV AUD was also derived for comparison with the 2001-2002 NESARC. Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as this round's brief directs for national prevalence surveys.
can_establish: The weighted prevalence of DSM-5 alcohol use disorder, as diagnosed by a fully structured interview given by interviewers who were not clinicians (as the companion paper states), among US adults living in households and selected group quarters in 2012-2013, overall, by severity and by sociodemographic group, together with the cross-sectional adjusted associations of AUD with other psychiatric disorders and with self-rated mental-health functioning, and the share of people with AUD who reported ever seeking treatment or help.
cannot_establish: The direction or cause of any comorbidity or functioning association (one interview, with lifetime diagnoses and ages of onset recalled); prevalence among people the frame does not cover (homeless people, prisoners and most people in treatment, as the authors state) or among the 40% of sampled people who did not take part; whether the higher DSM-IV prevalence than in 2001-2002 reflects real change rather than differences between the two surveys (not analysed here; see Grant et al., 2017); or functioning beyond SF-12v2 self-ratings.

sample.recruitment: National multistage probability sample: counties or groups of contiguous counties, then groups of census blocks, then households, then a randomly selected adult. Hispanic, black and Asian respondents were oversampled, and two respondents were selected in households with at least four eligible minority adults (n = 1661). Frame: US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 or older, including selected group quarters such as group homes and worker dormitories. Fieldwork by Westat; respondents received $90; oral consent was electronically recorded (Methods › Sample, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 or older in sampled households and selected group quarters. Not covered by the frame: homeless people, prisoners and most people in treatment, which the authors say may lead to underestimation (Discussion, 7th paragraph). No clinical exclusions.
sample.demographics: Weighted (Table 1): men 48.1%, women 51.9%; white 66.2%, black 11.8%, Native American 1.6%, Asian or Pacific Islander 5.7%, Hispanic 14.7%; aged 18-29 21.7%, 30-44 25.7%, 45-64 35.0%, 65 or older 17.6%; married or cohabiting 57.8%; less than high school 13.0%; annual family income below $20,000 22.8%; urban 78.8%.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). Response: screener level 72.0%, person level 84.0%, total 60.1% as printed (the product of the two printed component rates is 60.5%, editors' arithmetic). Data were weighted for oversampling and for screener- and person-level non-response, then post-stratified to the 2012 American Community Survey (Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.selection_effects: Four in ten sampled people did not take part. The authors judge that weighting compensated adequately, from comparisons of respondents with the full eligible sample on segment-level characteristics (Hispanic, black and Asian composition, population density, vacancy, group quarters, renters) and on individual Hispanic ethnicity, sex and age; respondents included slightly more men (48.1% vs 46.2%) and more people aged 60-69 (13.7% vs 12.6%) than the eligible sample. These checks cannot show whether people who declined drink differently. The frame omits groups with high AUD rates (homeless, incarcerated and most treated people), which biases prevalence downward, as the authors state. The effect of the $90 incentive and face-to-face interviewing on disclosure is unknown.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the AUDADIS-5, a fully structured interview developed by the NIAAA, given by interviewers who were not clinicians (stated in the companion paper, Grant et al., 2017; this paper does not describe the interviewers); no biological or record verification. Lifetime DSM-5 AUD required at least 2 of 11 criteria in the past 12 months or earlier, with earlier diagnoses requiring the criteria to cluster within one year. Reliability, from the investigators' own general-population studies: test-retest kappa 0.60 (AUDADIS-5 AUD) and 0.62 (DSM-5 AUD), intraclass correlations 0.83 and 0.85 for the dimensional scales; blind clinical reappraisal with the PRISM-5 gave kappa 0.49 and 0.62 (fair to good) and intraclass correlations 0.81 and 0.85 (Methods › Alcohol Use Disorders, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No measure of alcohol consumption is analysed for the 2012-2013 sample and no drink size is defined: AUD is a count of criteria, not an amount. The Discussion cites the first author's unpublished data on past-year drinking of at least 5, 8 and 10 drinks per day as having risen from 31.0%, 15.6% and 11.5% in 2001-2002 to 39.6%, 20.8% and 15.5% in 2012-2013, without stating the denominator or the drink size (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Nicotine use disorder and any drug use disorder (sedative or tranquilizer, cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine, club drug, opioid, heroin, hallucinogen, solvent or inhalant) were diagnosed with the AUDADIS-5 and entered as covariates in the comorbidity models; they do not restrict the prevalence estimates (Methods › Other Psychiatric Disorders, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis).

comparison.controls: The prevalence estimates have no comparison group. Correlates are adjusted odds ratios against reference categories in the same sample: women; white respondents; age 65 or older; married or cohabiting; some college or higher; family income $70,000 or more; rural; West. Comorbidity and functioning compare people with and without the AUD category in question (Tables 3 to 5).
comparison.matching: None. Sociodemographic odds ratios are mutually adjusted; comorbidity odds ratios are further adjusted for other substance use and psychiatric disorders (versions adjusted for sociodemographics only are in supplementary eTables 1 and 2, not read); SF-12v2 comparisons are adjusted for sociodemographics and 12-month psychiatric comorbidity (Methods › Statistical Analysis).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant to the prevalence estimates. For the comorbidity and functioning associations, childhood adversity, family history and the order of onset of AUD and the other disorders are not used, and lifetime associations depend on recalled onsets, which the authors say may be subject to recall bias.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other substance use disorders are adjusted for, not excluded.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-5 diagnoses: DSM-5 AUD (2-3 criteria mild, 4-5 moderate, 6 or more severe); DSM-IV abuse (1 or more of 4 criteria) and dependence (3 or more criteria); DSM-5 nicotine and drug use disorders; mood disorders (major depressive, persistent depressive, bipolar I and II), anxiety disorders (panic, agoraphobia, social and specific phobia, generalized anxiety), posttraumatic stress disorder, eating disorders and antisocial, borderline and schizotypal personality disorders, all excluding substance- and medical-illness-induced disorders; SF-12v2 Mental Health, Social Functioning, Role Emotional and Mental Component Summary scores (norm-based, mean 50, SD 10, lower scores meaning more disability); seeking treatment or help for AUD (Methods).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability and validity evidence comes mainly from the investigators' own NESARC-III-associated studies: DSM-5 AUD test-retest kappa 0.62 and agreement with clinician reappraisal kappa 0.49 to 0.62; other psychiatric diagnoses test-retest kappa 0.35 to 0.54 and clinician agreement kappa 0.20 to 0.59; DSM-IV and DSM-5 AUD concordance in NESARC-III kappa 0.76 (12 months) and 0.61 (lifetime). The SF-12v2 is described as reliable and valid, with population norms (Methods).
outcomes.operationalization: AUD is a criteria count, not an amount of drinking. Disability is a lower SF-12v2 norm-based score and was analysed for 12-month AUD only (Methods › Statistical Analysis; Table 5). Treatment is any reported seeking of treatment or help for AUD, including 12-step groups (Results › Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; P < .05 throughout. 24 counts the distinct outcome measures (12-month and lifetime AUD; the 17 disorders in Table 4; 4 SF-12v2 scales; help seeking). The paper reports about 350 adjusted contrasts: 152 sociodemographic odds ratios in Table 3, 136 comorbidity odds ratios in Table 4 and 60 functioning comparisons in Table 5 (editors' count).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: a fully structured instrument given by interviewers who were not clinicians (Grant et al., 2017); how diagnoses were derived from the answers is not described in this paper; random respondent callbacks verified data (Methods › Sample, 3rd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Prevalence, % (SE) (Table 2): 12-month AUD 13.9 (0.31), of which mild 7.3, moderate 3.2, severe 3.4; lifetime 29.1 (0.48), of which mild 8.6, moderate 6.6, severe 13.9. By group, 12-month and lifetime: men 17.6 and 36.0, women 10.4 and 22.7; white 14.0 and 32.6, black 14.4 and 22.0, Native American 19.2 and 43.4, Asian or Pacific Islander 10.6 and 15.0, Hispanic 13.6 and 22.9; ages 18-29 26.7 and 37.0, 30-44 16.2 and 34.4, 45-64 10.0 and 28.2, 65 or older 2.3 and 13.4; never married 25.0 and 35.5. Adjusted odds ratios for 12-month AUD (Table 3): men vs women 1.9 (1.72-2.01); black vs white 0.8 (0.67-0.90), Native American 1.3 (0.99-1.76), Asian or Pacific Islander 0.5 (0.42-0.64), Hispanic 0.7 (0.58-0.72); ages 18-29 vs 65 or older 13.9 (11.57-16.67); for severe 12-month AUD, lowest vs highest income 1.8 (1.38-2.24). Comorbidity, adjusted odds ratios for 12-month and lifetime AUD (Table 4): any drug use disorder 3.3 (2.88-3.76) and 4.1 (3.72-4.57), up to 6.4 (5.76-7.22) for lifetime severe AUD; nicotine use disorder 2.5 (2.24-2.69) and 3.2 (2.95-3.42); major depressive disorder 1.2 (1.08-1.36) and 1.3 (1.15-1.39); bipolar I 1.4 (1.08-1.78) and 2.0 (1.59-2.44); antisocial personality disorder 1.6 (1.28-1.94) and 1.9 (1.67-2.26); borderline 1.9 (1.66-2.23) and 2.0 (1.74-2.19); generalized anxiety 1.0 (0.86-1.22) and 1.2 (1.05-1.39); posttraumatic stress 1.0 (0.86-1.22) and 1.3 (1.10-1.48). SF-12v2 Mental Component Summary for no 12-month AUD vs any, mild, moderate and severe AUD: 51.4, 47.6, 49.6, 47.2, 43.8 (Table 5); on the norm SD of 10 these differences are 0.18 SD (mild) to 0.76 SD (severe) (editors' calculation). Help seeking: 7.7% of people with 12-month AUD and 19.8% with lifetime AUD; lifetime by severity 4.4%, 8.7% and 34.7% (Results › Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
analysis.covariates: Sociodemographic models: sex, race or ethnicity, age, marital status, education, family income, urbanicity and region, each adjusted for the others. Comorbidity models: the same plus other substance use and psychiatric disorders, with eating disorders used only as covariates. Disability models: sociodemographics and 12-month psychiatric comorbidity.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Analysis of a national survey; no protocol or analysis plan is referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Functioning was analysed for 12-month AUD only, though the abstract also links disability to lifetime AUD. Supplementary eTables 1 to 4 (comorbidity adjusted for sociodemographics only; treatment sources) are in a PDF supplement that was not read. Tables 3 and 4 say significant estimates are in boldface, which the PMC author manuscript does not render; significance on this card is judged from the printed confidence intervals. The Methods do not say how the complex sample design was handled in variance estimation, although standard errors are printed.
analysis.power: Not discussed. Overall prevalence is precise (SE 0.31 and 0.48 points), small groups are not: estimates for Native American respondents (511 unweighted) have SEs of 1.09 to 2.81 points, and rare cells give wide intervals (12-month severe AUD at ages 18-29 vs 65 or older, adjusted odds ratio 44.0, 22.98-84.09; Table 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2012-2013, 13.9% of US household-dwelling adults met DSM-5 AUD criteria for the past year and 29.1% at some time; about half the past-year cases were mild. Past-year AUD was most common at ages 18-29 (26.7%) and least common at 65 or older (2.3%); after adjustment, odds were higher for men and lower for black, Asian or Pacific Islander and Hispanic than for white respondents. AUD went with drug and nicotine use disorders (adjusted odds ratios 2.0 to 6.4), with bipolar I disorder and borderline and antisocial personality disorders, and more weakly or inconsistently with depressive and anxiety disorders. People with past-year AUD scored lower on SF-12v2 mental-health scales, by about 2 to 4 points overall and 5 to 8 points for severe AUD (norm SD 10), while mild AUD differed by 0 to 1.9 points. One in five people with lifetime AUD (19.8%) had ever sought treatment or help.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Several abstract statements do not match the paper's tables. (1) It gives 1.8% and 1.5% as the prevalence of 12-month and lifetime severe AUD in the lowest income group; these are the adjusted odds ratios (Table 3), and the prevalences are 5.2% and 16.1% (Table 2). (2) It lists white respondents among those with the highest prevalence, though black respondents had a higher 12-month prevalence (14.4% vs 14.0%); white respondents had higher adjusted odds. Previously married respondents are also listed, though their lifetime prevalence (27.1%) is below that of married respondents (27.2%). (3) It reports associations with major depressive and bipolar I disorders and antisocial personality disorder across all levels of AUD severity, as do the Results; in Table 4 the intervals include 1 for major depressive disorder with mild (1.1, 0.91-1.29) and moderate (1.2, 0.97-1.56) 12-month AUD, for bipolar I with mild 12-month AUD (1.2, 0.84-1.81) and for antisocial personality disorder with mild lifetime AUD (1.3, 0.98-1.60). (4) It links significant disability to lifetime AUD, which was not analysed. (5) It says 19.8% were ever treated; the measure is seeking treatment or help, including 12-step groups. (6) The conclusion calls DSM-5 AUD a "highly prevalent, highly comorbid, disabling disorder" (Abstract), but mild AUD, half of past-year cases, differed from no AUD by less than 2 SF-12v2 points. (7) The Results (Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 1st paragraph) derive a 3-year lag between onset and treatment by comparing mean age at onset in everyone with AUD (26.2 years) with mean age at first treatment among those treated (29.4 years), two different groups. (8) The Discussion calls the DSM-IV rise from 8.5% (2001-2002) to 12.7% substantial while also reporting that the NSDUH showed a stable 12-month AUD prevalence of about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013 and listing differences in survey methods between NESARC and NESARC-III as a limitation. The headline prevalence figures themselves are reported faithfully.

timeline.event: National Comorbidity Survey Replication (Kessler et al., 2005): 12-month DSM-IV AUD 4.4%, lifetime 18.8%; this paper attributes the lower rates to skipping the dependence questions when no abuse criterion was endorsed (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).
Hasin et al. (2007), NESARC 2001-2002: 12-month DSM-IV AUD 8.5%, lifetime 30.3%, the comparison for this paper's DSM-IV figures (on the alcohol evidence map, Tier C).
SAMHSA, NSDUH 2013: 12-month AUD 7.0% (Introduction); the Discussion adds that NSDUH 12-month AUD was stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013, against NESARC-III's DSM-IV 12.7%.

Methods papers by the same group cited as the instrument's evidence: AUDADIS-5 reliability (Grant et al., 2015), procedural validity against the PRISM-5 (Hasin et al., 2015) and DSM-IV versus DSM-5 nosology in NESARC-III (Goldstein et al., 2015).
This study (NESARC-III): DSM-5 AUD 13.9% (12 months) and 29.1% (lifetime); DSM-IV AUD 12.7% and 43.6%.
Grant et al. (2017), the companion trend analysis: 12-month DSM-IV AUD 8.5% in 2001-2002 vs 12.7% in 2012-2013 (this round's list; card sc_grant_2017).

replication.where_it_stands: NESARC-III gives the most-cited US DSM-5 AUD prevalence (13.9% past year, 29.1% lifetime) and, in this paper, the first national DSM-5 figures. Its DSM-IV past-year figure is well above the contemporaneous NSDUH figure (12.7% vs about 7.0-7.5%), a discrepancy the authors call for research on but do not explain; the surveys differ in instrument, sponsor and design. Claims should cite the figures as NESARC-III estimates of interview-diagnosed AUD in the household population (60.1% response) and say that another national survey gives lower AUD prevalence. No correction notice or letter is linked on the PMC or JAMA Psychiatry pages (checked 27 October 2026).

funding.funder: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) and National Institute on Drug Abuse; National Institutes of Health grant K05AA014223 (Dr Hasin); Intramural Research Program of the NIAAA. The funding sources are stated to have had no role in design, conduct, data collection, management, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, review or approval, or the decision to submit (Acknowledgments › Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor).
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported (Conflict of Interest Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: Ten of the 11 authors are at the Laboratory of Epidemiology and Biometry, Division of Intramural Clinical and Biological Research, NIAAA (NIH), the institute that conducted NESARC-III and developed the AUDADIS-5; the 11th is at Columbia University and the New York State Psychiatric Institute. The no-role statement thus sits beside the fact that the funding institute's own staff designed, ran and analysed the survey, and the reliability and validity studies cited for the instrument are largely the same group's. No industry funding or ties are declared. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A bridging study that fields the NESARC-III and NSDUH alcohol use disorder measures (or the two surveys' full protocols) in randomly split samples of the same population in the same year, with blind clinical reappraisal of a random subsample, would show how much of the gap between their AUD prevalences comes from instrument, sponsor and fieldwork; for the comorbidity and functioning associations, prospective cohorts with repeated diagnostic interviews would establish the order of onset.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National frame of US civilian non-institutionalized adults including selected group quarters; homeless people, prisoners and most people in treatment, groups with higher AUD rates, are not covered, as the authors state.
Multistage probability sampling with random selection of adults within households, oversampling of minority groups and weights for unequal selection.
36,309 respondents give SEs below half a percentage point for national prevalence; estimates for Native American respondents (511) and for severe AUD in older adults are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives weighted and unweighted composition by sex, race or ethnicity, age, marital status, education, income, urbanicity and region; field procedures and dates are described.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Weighting for screener- and person-level non-response and post-stratification; respondents compared with the eligible sample on a few segment-level and individual characteristics only, with small differences in sex and age.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-5 criteria applied by a structured instrument with test-retest kappa 0.62, but agreement with clinician reappraisal was only fair to good (kappa 0.49 to 0.62); interviewers who were not clinicians (stated in Grant et al., 2017, not in this paper); self-report only; validity evidence mostly from the same group.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same structured instrument for every respondent, with interviewer training, supervision and callback verification.

Weighted prevalence with SEs and mutually adjusted logistic models are appropriate, but the Methods do not state how the complex design entered variance estimation, about 350 contrasts are tested at P < .05 without correction, and significance marks are not rendered in the PMC version.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Total response 60.1%, managed by non-response weighting; whether people who declined differ in drinking is unknown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large, well-documented national probability survey with a structured instrument of published reliability. Its limits come from the design rather than its conduct: 60.1% response managed by weighting on a few characteristics; a household frame that leaves out homeless, incarcerated and most treated people; diagnosis by interviewers who were not clinicians (Grant et al., 2017), with only fair-to-good agreement with clinicians; and estimates that depend on the survey (the NSDUH gives lower AUD prevalence). The prevalence figures can be cited as NESARC-III estimates. Several abstract statements on correlates, comorbidity and disability must be checked against the tables (see reporting issues), and the cross-sectional associations cannot support causal claims about comorbidity or disability.

key_findings.finding: NESARC-III interviewed 36,309 US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 or older face to face from April 2012 to June 2013; screener-level response 72.0%, person-level 84.0%, total 60.1%; data were weighted for oversampling and non-response and post-stratified to the 2012 American Community Survey.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The product of the two printed component rates is 60.5% (editors' arithmetic); the companion paper prints the total as 60.0% in its Methods and 60.1% in its Limitations (Grant et al., 2017).

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of DSM-5 AUD, % (SE): past 12 months 13.9 (0.31), of which mild 7.3 (0.19), moderate 3.2 (0.13), severe 3.4 (0.12); lifetime 29.1 (0.48), of which mild 8.6 (0.18), moderate 6.6 (0.18), severe 13.9 (0.31). Unweighted cases: 5133 past-year (2624 mild, 1186 moderate, 1323 severe) and 10,001 lifetime. The authors translate the rates into about 32,648,000 and 68,485,000 US adults.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 1st paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mean age at AUD onset was 26.2 years, younger with greater severity: 30.1 (mild), 25.9 (moderate) and 23.9 years (severe).
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: DSM-IV AUD derived from the same interviews: 12-month 12.7% and lifetime 43.6%, against 8.5% and 30.3% in the 2001-2002 NESARC. Without the three abuse questions added in NESARC-III, 12-month DSM-IV AUD was 12.2% (kappa 0.98 with the full version). Concordance of DSM-IV with DSM-5 AUD in NESARC-III: kappa 0.76 (12 months) and 0.61 (lifetime).
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 1st paragraph; Methods › Alcohol Use Disorders, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sex and age: past-year AUD 17.6% in men and 10.4% in women (lifetime 36.0% and 22.7%); adjusted odds ratio for men vs women 1.9 (1.72-2.01) for 12-month and 2.0 (1.87-2.11) for lifetime AUD, 2.2 (1.90-2.50) for 12-month severe AUD. Past-year AUD by age: 26.7% at 18-29, 16.2% at 30-44, 10.0% at 45-64, 2.3% at 65 or older; severe past-year AUD 7.1% at 18-29. Adjusted odds ratio for ages 18-29 vs 65 or older: 13.9 (11.57-16.67) for any and 44.0 (22.98-84.09) for severe 12-month AUD.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Table 3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Race and ethnicity, 12-month and lifetime prevalence: white 14.0% and 32.6%, black 14.4% and 22.0%, Native American 19.2% and 43.4%, Asian or Pacific Islander 10.6% and 15.0%, Hispanic 13.6% and 22.9%. Adjusted odds ratios against white respondents for 12-month AUD: black 0.8 (0.67-0.90), Native American 1.3 (0.99-1.76), Asian or Pacific Islander 0.5 (0.42-0.64), Hispanic 0.7 (0.58-0.72); Native American respondents had higher adjusted odds of severe AUD (12-month 2.1, 1.32-3.23; lifetime 1.8, 1.40-2.31).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Table 3; Results › Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Native American estimates rest on 511 unweighted respondents (Table 1), with SEs of 1.09 to 2.81 points in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Income: severe 12-month AUD in 5.2% of respondents with family income below $20,000 vs 2.1% at $70,000 or more, adjusted odds ratio 1.8 (1.38-2.24); severe lifetime AUD 16.1% vs 12.4%, adjusted odds ratio 1.5 (1.33-1.79). Income was not associated with any 12-month AUD after adjustment (1.1, 0.97-1.23).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Table 3
key_findings.note: The abstract prints 1.8% and 1.5% as the prevalence of severe AUD in the lowest income group; those values are these adjusted odds ratios (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Other correlates of 12-month AUD (adjusted odds ratios): never married vs married or cohabiting 1.6 (1.45-1.75), prevalence 25.0%; widowed, separated or divorced 1.6 (1.46-1.81), prevalence 11.4%; urban vs rural 1.4 (1.20-1.55), but not for lifetime AUD (1.1, 0.96-1.19); less than high school vs some college: higher odds of severe (1.3, 1.02-1.61) and lower odds of mild 12-month AUD (0.7, 0.61-0.84).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Table 3; Results › Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Comorbidity, adjusted for sociodemographics and other disorders (reference: respondents without the AUD category in question), 12-month and lifetime AUD: any drug use disorder 3.3 (2.88-3.76) and 4.1 (3.72-4.57), rising to 5.3 (4.52-6.27) and 6.4 (5.76-7.22) for severe AUD; nicotine use disorder 2.5 (2.24-2.69) and 3.2 (2.95-3.42); major depressive disorder 1.2 (1.08-1.36) and 1.3 (1.15-1.39); bipolar I 1.4 (1.08-1.78) and 2.0 (1.59-2.44); antisocial personality disorder 1.6 (1.28-1.94) and 1.9 (1.67-2.26); borderline personality disorder 1.9 (1.66-2.23) and 2.0 (1.74-2.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comorbidity, 1st paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Comorbidity not significant or inverse (Table 4 intervals): major depressive disorder with mild (1.1, 0.91-1.29) and moderate (1.2, 0.97-1.56) 12-month AUD; bipolar I with mild 12-month AUD (1.2, 0.84-1.81); antisocial personality disorder with mild lifetime AUD (1.3, 0.98-1.60); bipolar II at every level; 12-month AUD with panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder and persistent depression at every level; social anxiety disorder inversely with 12-month AUD (0.8, 0.63-0.98). Lifetime AUD was associated with posttraumatic stress disorder (1.3, 1.10-1.48) and generalized anxiety disorder (1.2, 1.05-1.39).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Comorbidity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: SF-12v2 norm-based scores (mean 50, SD 10; lower means more disability) for no 12-month AUD vs any, mild, moderate and severe AUD: Mental Health 52.3, 48.6, 50.4, 48.3, 45.1; Social Functioning 50.9, 49.1, 50.9, 48.6, 45.7; Role Emotional 48.7, 46.9, 48.5, 46.8, 43.4; Mental Component Summary 51.4, 47.6, 49.6, 47.2, 43.8. By criterion count the Mental Component Summary fell from 51.5 (0 criteria) to 36.7 (11 criteria). Differences were tested after adjustment for sociodemographics and 12-month psychiatric comorbidity; only 12-month AUD was analysed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Disability, 1st paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation on the norm SD of 10: severe AUD differs from no AUD by 0.52 to 0.76 SD, mild AUD by 0 to 0.19 SD (Social Functioning 50.9 vs 50.9, not significant). The table does not say whether the printed means are adjusted.

key_findings.finding: Help seeking: 7.7% of people with 12-month and 19.8% with lifetime DSM-5 AUD had sought treatment or help for AUD (DSM-IV: 8.1% and 15.6%, against 7.2% and 14.0% in the 2001-2002 NESARC). By severity: 2.7%, 4.9% and 21.3% for mild, moderate and severe 12-month AUD; 4.4%, 8.7% and 34.7% for lifetime AUD. Among people with 12-month AUD, 4.5% used 12-step groups, 3.6% health care practitioners, 2.0% outpatient facilities and 1.8% rehabilitation programs; for lifetime AUD, rehabilitation programs 9.0% and practitioners 8.7%. Mean age at first treatment 29.4 years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: To explain the higher DSM-IV prevalence, the Discussion cites the first author's unpublished data: past-year drinking of at least 5, 8 and 10 drinks per day rose from 31.0%, 15.6% and 11.5% (NESARC) to 39.6%, 20.8% and 15.5% (NESARC-III); in the paragraph on young adults, from 60.7%, 41.0% and 33.9% to 68.2%, 46.3% and 38.0% among men and from 33.5%, 14.7% and 8.7% to 47.7%, 22.1% and 14.2% among women. It also reports that NSDUH 12-month AUD was stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No denominator (all adults, people who drink, or young adults only) or drink size is given for these unpublished figures, so they cannot be checked or cited as data.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: differences in some survey methods between NESARC 2001-2002 and NESARC-III; less than ideal reliability for a few non-AUD diagnoses; possible recall bias in lifetime comorbidity; homeless people, prisoners and most treated people not covered, so prevalence may be underestimated; cross-sectional design.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 1.8% and 1.5% as the prevalence of 12-month and lifetime severe AUD in the lowest income group. These are the adjusted odds ratios against the highest income group (Table 3: 1.8, 1.38-2.24; 1.5, 1.33-1.79); the prevalences are 5.2% and 16.1% (Table 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Anyone citing the abstract would understate severe AUD in low-income adults by a factor of about 3 (past year) to 11 (lifetime) (editors' arithmetic). Use Table 2 for prevalence and Table 3 for odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists white respondents among those with the highest prevalence (14.0% and 32.6%), but black respondents had a higher 12-month prevalence (14.4%, Table 2); it also lists previously married respondents (11.4% and 27.1%), whose lifetime prevalence is below that of married or cohabiting respondents (27.2%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract mixes crude prevalence with adjusted odds (white respondents had higher adjusted odds than black respondents, 0.8 for black vs white). Claims about which groups have the highest prevalence should use Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Results say AUD was associated with major depressive and bipolar I disorders and antisocial personality disorder across all severity levels and time frames, but in Table 4 the intervals include 1 for major depressive disorder with mild and moderate 12-month AUD, bipolar I with mild 12-month AUD and antisocial personality disorder with mild lifetime AUD.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comorbidity associations are not uniform across severity; for mild 12-month AUD, which is half of past-year cases, the association with major depressive disorder is not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's lower bound for the anxiety-disorder odds ratios, 1.2 (95% CI 1.01-1.43), matches no cell of Table 4; the nearest are 1.2 (1.03-1.43) for specific phobia with 12-month AUD and 1.2 (1.01-1.46) for generalized anxiety disorder with lifetime severe AUD.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor transcription error; cite the Table 4 values.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that significant disability was associated with 12-month and lifetime AUD, but the Methods and Table 5 analyse SF-12v2 scores for 12-month AUD only.
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim about functioning and lifetime AUD can rest on this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The total response rate is printed as 60.1%, while the product of the printed screener (72.0%) and person-level (84.0%) rates is 60.5% (editors' arithmetic); the companion trend paper gives 60.0% in one place and 60.1% in another.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the response rate should be quoted as about 60% with the components.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 3 and 4 state that significant estimates are in boldface, which the PMC author manuscript does not render, and Table 4 carries a footnote marker c on the nicotine use disorder estimate for severe 12-month AUD (3.6, 3.07-4.24) with no footnote c defined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the PMC version must judge significance from the intervals; the meaning of footnote c is lost.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe disability as greater, with few exceptions, in people with one or more AUD criteria than in those with none, but in Table 5 13 of the 44 criterion-count comparisons carry no significance marker: 8 of 11 for Social Functioning and 5 of 11 for Role Emotional (editors' count). The table also does not say whether the printed means are adjusted, while the tests are adjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The functioning gradient is consistent for Mental Health and the Mental Component Summary but not for Social Functioning or Role Emotional at lower criterion counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion uses the first author's unpublished heavy-drinking data, without denominators or a drink definition, to explain the increase in DSM-IV AUD since 2001-2002.
reporting_issues.consequence: The explanation cannot be checked from the paper; these figures should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's statement that 12-month AUD prevalence in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health stayed stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013 is cited to reference 15 (Hasin and Grant, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2004, a NESARC paper on DSM-IV abuse and dependence), which, published in 2004, cannot report NSDUH figures to 2013; the 7.0% for 2013 in the Introduction is cited to the NSDUH 2013 detailed tables (reference 16).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph; reference list, references 15 and 16)
reporting_issues.consequence: The stable NSDUH trend has no checkable source in this paper and rests on the authors' statement; claims that use it should say that the authors report it.

design_detail: Repeated cross-sectional comparison of two independent NIAAA national face-to-face surveys of US adults aged 18 or older in households and selected group quarters: NESARC Wave 1 (April 2001 to June 2002; n = 43,093; AUDADIS-IV) and NESARC-III (April 2012 to June 2013; n = 36,309; AUDADIS-5). Weighted 12-month prevalence of any alcohol use, high-risk drinking (exceeding 4 US standard drinks of 14 g in a day for women or 5 for men at least weekly), DSM-IV alcohol use disorder (AUD), and DSM-IV AUD among people who drank and among people who drank at high risk, overall and in 28 sociodemographic subgroups; differences between surveys tested with two-sided t tests on design-based standard errors (SUDAAN). Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as this round's brief directs for national prevalence surveys.
can_establish: Whether two NIAAA national surveys conducted 11 years apart with closely similar questions produced different weighted prevalences of self-reported past-year drinking, weekly high-risk drinking and interview-diagnosed DSM-IV AUD, overall and within sociodemographic groups.
cannot_establish: Whether the differences reflect change in the population rather than differences between the surveys (sampling design, review boards and fieldwork, response rates of 81.0% and about 60%, a $90 incentive reported only for NESARC-III (the paper is silent on any NESARC incentive), census weighting base and instrument version), none of which is modelled; why drinking changed; whether change differed between subgroups (no interaction tests); change within people (different people were sampled); or anything about homeless or incarcerated people, whom neither survey covers.

sample.recruitment: NESARC-III: multistage probability sample (counties or groups of contiguous counties, then groups of census blocks, then households, then adults), oversampling black, Asian or Pacific Islander and Hispanic adults; weighted to the 2012 American Community Survey; respondents received $90; protocol approved by the NIH Combined Neuroscience Institutional Review Board and the Westat Institutional Review Board. NESARC 2001-2002: multistage probability sample with counties or county equivalents as primary units, oversampling black and Hispanic adults and young adults; weighted to the 2000 Decennial Census; protocol reviewed and approved by the US Census Bureau and the US Office of Management and Budget (Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: US adults aged 18 or older living in households and selected group quarters. Neither survey covers homeless or incarcerated people, which the authors say may lead to underestimation (Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Sample composition is not tabulated in this paper; Tables 1 to 5 give prevalence for 28 subgroups by sex, race or ethnicity (white, black, Native American, Asian or Pacific Islander, Hispanic), age (18-29, 30-44, 45-64, 65 or older), marital status, education, family income, poverty threshold, urbanicity and region.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (two independent cross-sectional samples). Overall response 81.0% in NESARC (sampling frame 98.5%, household 88.5%, person 93.0%) and, for NESARC-III, 60.0% in the Methods and 60.1% in the Limitations (household 72.0%, person 84.0%).
sample.selection_effects: The overall response rate fell from 81.0% to about 60% between the surveys. Both are weighted for non-response on measured characteristics only, so a change in who agreed to take part could create or hide a change in prevalence. The authors list the lower NESARC-III response rate as a limitation and say weighting facilitated comparison; the other design differences described in the Methods (sampling stages, oversampled groups, approving bodies, incentive, census base, instrument version) are not discussed as possible sources of the change.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in lay-administered interviews: AUDADIS-IV in NESARC and AUDADIS-5 in NESARC-III. Any 12-month alcohol use was asked with identical questions. DSM-IV AUD symptom items are described as virtually identical, with 3 items slightly reworded and 3 abuse questions added in NESARC-III; DSM-IV AUD with and without the added questions was 8.5% vs 8.2% in NESARC (kappa 0.97) and 12.7% vs 12.2% in NESARC-III (kappa 0.98). No biological testing (Methods › Assessments, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: US standard drink = 14 g of pure alcohol. High-risk drinking: 4 or more drinks on any day for women and 5 or more for men, said to follow the US dietary guidelines, exceeded at least weekly in the past 12 months. Alcohol use: any drinking in the past 12 months. Volume, beverage type and other patterns are not analysed (Methods › Assessments, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: The same population subgroup in the 2001-2002 survey.
comparison.matching: None. Crude weighted prevalences for each survey, with no adjustment for changes in population composition or for differences in survey design.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The unmeasured factors that matter are the differences between the surveys (fieldwork and interviewers, sampling design, response, incentive, weighting base, instrument version), none of which is modelled or tested beyond the added abuse questions.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV (2001-2002) and AUDADIS-5 (2012-2013). DSM-IV AUD: dependence (3 or more of 7 criteria) or abuse (1 or more of 4 criteria) in the past 12 months (Methods › Assessments, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability and validity of alcohol use, high-risk drinking and DSM-IV AUD are described as fair to excellent, citing the group's own studies, with no figures in this paper. A NESARC-III validation substudy is said to show similar prevalence and good concordance between AUDADIS and clinician diagnoses of 12-month AUD, also without figures (Methods › Assessments, 4th paragraph; Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Change is reported as the relative percentage change between surveys (the 2012-2013 minus the 2001-2002 prevalence, divided by the 2001-2002 prevalence); absolute differences in percentage points are not reported. Significance refers to the difference between the two weighted prevalences.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five outcomes in the total population and 28 subgroups give 145 between-survey comparisons at P < .05 (editors' count); no test of whether change differed between subgroups.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (lay interviewers, structured instrument).

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted 12-month prevalence, % (95% CI), 2001-2002 vs 2012-2013, with the printed relative change and the absolute change in percentage points (editors' calculation): alcohol use 65.4 (64.3-66.6) vs 72.7 (71.4-73.9), +11.2%, +7.3 points; high-risk drinking 9.7 (9.3-10.2) vs 12.6 (12.0-13.2), +29.9%, +2.9 points; DSM-IV AUD 8.5 (8.0-8.9) vs 12.7 (12.1-13.3), +49.4%, +4.2 points; AUD among people who drank in the past year 12.9 (interval printed as 12.3-17.5) vs 17.5 (16.7-18.3), +35.7%; AUD among people who drank at high risk 46.5 (44.3-48.7) vs 54.5 (52.7-56.4), +17.2%. DSM-IV AUD by subgroup: men 12.4 vs 16.7 (+34.7%, +4.3 points); women 4.9 vs 9.0 (+83.7%, +4.1); ages 18-29 16.2 vs 23.4 (+44.4%, +7.2); 65 or older 1.5 vs 3.1 (+106.7%, +1.6); white 8.9 vs 13.1 (+47.2%, +4.2); black 6.9 vs 13.3 (+92.8%, +6.4); Hispanic 7.9 vs 12.0 (+51.9%, +4.1); Asian or Pacific Islander 4.5 vs 8.0 (+77.8%, +3.5); Native American 12.1 vs 16.6 and rural 8.8 vs 10.2 (both not significant); family income below $20,000 8.8 vs 14.6 (+65.9%, +5.8). High-risk drinking: women 5.7 vs 9.0 (+57.9%, +3.3 points), men 14.2 vs 16.4 (+15.5%, +2.2), 65 or older 2.3 vs 3.8 (+65.2%, +1.5), black 9.3 vs 15.1 (+62.4%, +5.8). The authors convert these to about 20.2 and 29.6 million adults with high-risk drinking and 17.6 and 29.9 million with DSM-IV AUD.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted weighted prevalences.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of two existing surveys; no protocol or analysis plan is referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only relative changes are given; absolute differences and their intervals are not. The Discussion cites other surveys' increases in drinking as corroboration (NHIS +6.0% and NSDUH +9.1% for past-year alcohol use; NHIS +17.8% for 5 or more drinks at least once a year; per capita consumption from sales +6.4%) but not the NSDUH trend in AUD, which the same authors had reported as stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013 (Grant et al., 2015, Discussion, 1st paragraph). The NESARC-III validation substudy is cited without figures.
analysis.power: Large samples; intervals are wide for Native American respondents (AUD 12.1, 9.3-15.6 vs 16.6, 12.7-21.5) and for small subgroups of people who drank at high risk (age 65 or older: 19.8, 13.7-27.8 vs 31.3, 24.8-38.7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Between the 2001-2002 and 2012-2013 surveys, weighted past-year drinking rose from 65.4% to 72.7%, weekly high-risk drinking from 9.7% to 12.6% and past-year DSM-IV AUD from 8.5% to 12.7%, with significant differences in almost every subgroup. In absolute terms the AUD difference was largest at ages 18-29 (+7.2 points), among black respondents (+6.4) and in the lowest income group (+5.8), similar in men (+4.3) and women (+4.1), and smallest at 65 or older (+1.6), whose relative increase (106.7%) is the largest only because their starting prevalence was 1.5% (editors' calculations from Tables 1 to 3).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract, Key Points and Conclusions call the increases a "public health crisis" that portends rises in chronic disease, especially among women, older adults, racial or ethnic minorities and socioeconomically disadvantaged people; the study measured no health outcome, and the Discussion's supporting trends (cardiovascular and stroke mortality, hypertension, cirrhosis deaths, emergency visits) are cited aggregate series. (2) Increases are said to be greatest among women, older adults, minorities and people with less education and income; this holds for relative change only, and no difference in change between subgroups was tested. In absolute terms women's rise in AUD matched men's, and older adults had the smallest rise in both high-risk drinking and AUD. (3) The validity of the increase is defended by coherence with other indicators, but the cited increases are much smaller than NESARC's, the stable NSDUH AUD trend the same group reported in 2015 is not mentioned, and design differences other than response rate are not discussed. (4) The Discussion's explanations of subgroup trends (more permissive norms and career stress for women, wealth inequality after the 2008 recession) were not measured. (5) The Conclusions' statements on low treatment rates (below 10%) and on costs ($250 billion) do not come from this study's data. (6) The Key Points list the relative changes (11.2%, 29.9%, 49.4%) in a way that can be read as prevalences.

timeline.event: Earlier national surveys cited in the Introduction and Discussion: between 1991-1992 and 2001-2002 past-year drinking rose from 44.0% to 65.4%, high-risk drinking from about 8.0% to 9.7% and DSM-IV AUD from 7.4% to 8.5%.
Hasin et al. (2007): NESARC 2001-2002 12-month DSM-IV AUD 8.5%, the baseline here (alcohol evidence map, Tier C).

Grant et al. (2015), NESARC-III DSM-5 AUD 13.9% past year; its Discussion reports that NSDUH 12-month AUD was stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013, against NESARC-III's DSM-IV 12.7% (card sc_grant_2015).
This study: DSM-IV AUD 8.5% to 12.7%, high-risk drinking 9.7% to 12.6%, past-year drinking 65.4% to 72.7%.

Schuckit, accompanying editorial in JAMA Psychiatry (doi 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.1981), whose freely visible opening paragraph accepts the paper's case that the US faces a crisis with alcohol use; the rest was not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The NESARC-to-NESARC-III comparison is the main source for a large rise in US past-year AUD between 2001-2002 and 2012-2013. The NSDUH showed no such rise in AUD over the same years (as the same authors reported in 2015), so the size of the change depends on which survey is believed, and this paper cannot separate change in the population from change in the survey. Claims should present the figures as differences between two surveys, give absolute alongside relative change, and say that another national survey did not show the AUD increase. No correction is linked on the PMC or JAMA Psychiatry pages (checked 27 October 2026).

funding.funder: Sponsored by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, with supplemental funding from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, and by National Institutes of Health grant K05AA014223 (Dr Hasin). The funding sources are stated to have had no role in design, conduct, data collection, management, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, review or approval, or the decision to submit (Article notes › Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor).
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported (Conflict of Interest Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: Nine of the 11 authors are at the NIAAA Epidemiology and Biometry Branch, the institute that conducted both surveys; two are at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University. As in the 2015 paper, the no-role statement refers to a sponsor whose staff designed, ran and analysed the surveys. No industry funding or ties are declared. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A bridging design in which the 2001-2002 and 2012-2013 protocols (or the NESARC-III and NSDUH protocols) are fielded on random halves of one sample in the same year would measure how much of the difference in AUD prevalence comes from survey design; a continuing series with an unchanged design would then establish the trend.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Both surveys sample the US household and group-quarters population; homeless and incarcerated people are excluded from both, and the two frames differ in sampling stages and oversampled groups.
Both are multistage probability samples with weights for unequal selection, analysed with design-based standard errors (SUDAAN).
43,093 and 36,309 respondents; small subgroups (Native American respondents; older adults who drank at high risk) have wide intervals.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Field periods, sampling and weighting are described, but the composition of each sample is not tabulated in this paper.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Both surveys are weighted for non-response; the change in response (81.0% to about 60%) between the two surveys is not examined beyond weighting.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Structured DSM-IV interview with reliability cited from the group's own work; self-report only; validity figures for NESARC-III are not given here.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Identical drinking questions and near-identical AUD items, but different instrument versions (AUDADIS-IV and AUDADIS-5) fielded under different protocols 11 years apart; only the effect of the added abuse questions was checked.

Design-based standard errors and t tests are appropriate, but change is reported only in relative terms, subgroup differences in change are asserted without tests, 145 comparisons are made without correction, and one printed interval is implausible.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: 81.0% (NESARC) and about 60% (NESARC-III), managed by weighting; differential response is a direct threat to a comparison between the surveys.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This rating concerns the paper's result, the change between surveys: each survey's own prevalence would rate as moderate (as for sc_grant_2015). The comparison is of two independent surveys whose designs differ in response rate (81.0% vs about 60%), sampling stages, approving bodies and fieldwork, census weighting base and instrument version (a $90 incentive is reported for NESARC-III only); the only comparability check reported concerns three added abuse questions, and another national survey (NSDUH) did not show the AUD rise. The direction of change in drinking is consistent with other indicators, but its size, and the subgroup pattern presented in relative terms, cannot be attributed to the population rather than to the surveys.

key_findings.finding: Samples: NESARC, April 2001 to June 2002, 43,093 adults, overall response 81.0% (sampling frame 98.5%, household 88.5%, person 93.0%), weighted to the 2000 Census; NESARC-III, April 2012 to June 2013, 36,309 adults, household response 72.0%, person 84.0%, overall 60.0%, weighted to the 2012 American Community Survey, with a $90 incentive.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The Limitations give the NESARC-III response rate as 60.1%; the product of the printed components is 60.5% (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Definitions: a standard drink is 14 g of pure alcohol; high-risk drinking is 4 or more drinks on any day for women or 5 or more for men, exceeded at least weekly in the past 12 months; DSM-IV AUD is 12-month abuse (1 or more of 4 criteria) or dependence (3 or more of 7).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Assessments, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Comparability: past-year alcohol use was asked with identical questions in both surveys; DSM-IV AUD items were virtually identical, with 3 reworded and 3 abuse questions added in NESARC-III. DSM-IV AUD with and without the added questions: 8.5% vs 8.2% in NESARC (kappa 0.97) and 12.7% vs 12.2% in NESARC-III (kappa 0.98).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Assessments, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Past-year alcohol use rose from 65.4% (64.3-66.6) to 72.7% (71.4-73.9), a relative increase of 11.2%, and rose significantly in every subgroup: women 59.6% to 69.0% (+15.8%), men 71.8% to 76.7% (+6.8%), ages 65 or older 45.1% to 55.2% (+22.4%), Asian or Pacific Islander 48.4% to 62.5% (+29.1%), black 53.2% to 66.1% (+24.2%), Hispanic 59.9% to 70.2% (+17.2%), family income below $20,000 52.4% to 64.1% (+22.3%).

key_findings.finding: Weekly high-risk drinking rose from 9.7% (9.3-10.2) to 12.6% (12.0-13.2), relative +29.9%, significantly in all subgroups except Native American respondents (12.4% to 17.4%) and rural residents (9.6% to 10.8%): women 5.7% to 9.0% (+57.9%), men 14.2% to 16.4% (+15.5%), ages 65 or older 2.3% to 3.8% (+65.2%), black 9.3% to 15.1% (+62.4%), Hispanic 9.6% to 13.5% (+40.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results › 12-Month High-Risk Drinking, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Past-year DSM-IV AUD rose from 8.5% (8.0-8.9) to 12.7% (12.1-13.3), relative +49.4%, significantly in all subgroups except Native American respondents (12.1% to 16.6%) and rural residents (8.8% to 10.2%): women 4.9% to 9.0% (+83.7%), men 12.4% to 16.7% (+34.7%), ages 18-29 16.2% to 23.4% (+44.4%), 65 or older 1.5% to 3.1% (+106.7%), black 6.9% to 13.3% (+92.8%), Hispanic 7.9% to 12.0% (+51.9%), white 8.9% to 13.1% (+47.2%), family income below $20,000 8.8% to 14.6% (+65.9%), urban 8.4% to 13.4% (+59.5%).

key_findings.finding: Conditional prevalence: DSM-IV AUD among people who drank in the past year rose from 12.9% to 17.5% (+35.7%; not significant for Native American, previously married and rural respondents); among people who drank at high risk, from 46.5% (44.3-48.7) to 54.5% (52.7-56.4) (+17.2%; not significant for Native American, Asian or Pacific Islander, previously married, less-than-high-school, rural, Northeast and Midwest respondents).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th and 5th subsections, 1st paragraph each; Tables 4 and 5
key_findings.note: The 2001-2002 interval for AUD among people who drank is printed as 12.3-17.5 in both the abstract and Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Absolute changes in percentage points (editors' calculation from Tables 1 to 3): alcohol use +7.3; high-risk drinking +2.9 (women +3.3, men +2.2, ages 65 or older +1.5, 30-44 +4.0); DSM-IV AUD +4.2 (men +4.3, women +4.1, ages 18-29 +7.2, 65 or older +1.6, black +6.4, white +4.2, Hispanic +4.1, Asian or Pacific Islander +3.5, income below $20,000 +5.8, $70,000 or more +3.7).
key_findings.locator: Tables 1 to 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation; the paper reports relative changes only.

key_findings.finding: The authors translate the prevalences into about 20.2 million (2001-2002) and 29.6 million (2012-2013) adults with high-risk drinking and 17.6 million and 29.9 million with DSM-IV AUD, and contrast the 49.4% rise in AUD with the 14.8% rise between 1991-1992 (7.4%) and 2001-2002 (8.5%).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Corroboration cited by the authors: past-year alcohol use rose 6.0% in the National Health Interview Survey and 9.1% in the NSDUH over the same period, drinking 5 or more drinks at least once in the past year rose 17.8% in the NHIS, and per capita consumption from sales rose 6.4%. No other survey's AUD trend is cited.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: no biological testing; homeless and incarcerated people not covered (possible underestimation); lay interviewers, though a NESARC-III substudy is said to show good concordance with clinician diagnoses; NESARC-III response (60.1%) lower than NESARC's (81.0%), with weighting said to facilitate comparison; validity of the increases supported, in their view, by coherence with other indicators.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The 2001-2002 prevalence of DSM-IV AUD among people who drank in the past year is printed as 12.9% with a 95% CI of 12.3%-17.5%, in both the abstract and Table 4; the upper limit equals the 2012-2013 point estimate and makes the interval about eight times wider above the estimate than below it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Almost certainly a transcription error (the same error appears on the JAMA Psychiatry page); the upper limit should not be quoted. By the widths of the neighbouring intervals the true upper limit is probably near 13.5%, but that is an inference.

reporting_issues.issue: The NESARC-III overall response rate is 60.0% in the Methods and 60.1% in the Limitations; the product of the printed household (72.0%) and person (84.0%) rates is 60.5% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote about 60% with the components.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the high school (10.4% to 14.8%) and some college or higher (9.5% to 11.6%) rows lack the significance marker, although the text says high-risk drinking rose significantly in all subgroups except Native American and rural respondents and the two years' intervals do not overlap.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting omission; both increases are significant by the paper's own test.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion refers to changes between the early 1900s and the early 2000s where the early 1990s are meant, and gives the earlier rise in DSM-IV AUD (7.4% to 8.5%) as 14.8% and, two sentences later, as 14.9% (14.9% by editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the three additional abuse questions appeared in NESARC-III, yet report a comparison of DSM-IV AUD with and without the additional questions for NESARC as well (8.5% vs 8.2%, kappa 0.97), without saying how the comparison was made in a survey that did not ask them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparability check for the 2001-2002 survey cannot be understood from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points state that alcohol use (11.2%), high-risk drinking (29.9%) and DSM-IV AUD (49.4%) increased, giving relative changes without labelling them as such.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take 49.4% for a prevalence or an absolute change; the absolute change in AUD was 4.2 percentage points.
