design_detail: Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2016 comparative risk assessment for alcohol by the GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (more than 500 named collaborators; analysis led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, Seattle). Exposure (prevalence of current drinking and average grams of ethanol a day among current drinkers) was modelled for 195 locations, 1990–2016, both sexes and 5-year age groups from 15 to 95 and older, from 694 sources (121,029 data points), combining sales data adjusted for tourism and unrecorded alcohol with survey data. Dose–response relative-risk curves for 23 outcomes were fitted to 3,992 relative-risk estimates from 592 cohort and case-control studies found in a new systematic review (details only in appendix 1). A theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) was taken as the minimum of one weighted average of the 23 curves, each weighted by that outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate in 2016 (both sexes); population attributable fractions from exposure, relative risks and the TMREL were applied to GBD 2016 deaths and DALYs, with alcohol use disorders assigned an attributable fraction of 1. Design 'modelling' as the round brief directs for attributable-burden estimates: no risk-of-bias instrument applies, so the card states the design's limits (METHODS §5.3).
can_establish: Model-based estimates, under GBD 2016's stated inputs and assumptions, of the prevalence of current drinking and average consumption by location, age and sex, of deaths and DALYs attributable to alcohol, of the shape of each cause-specific relative-risk curve as fitted to the observational studies, and of the intake that minimises one globally DALY-weighted average of those curves.
cannot_establish: That any amount of alcohol harms a given person or every population (the zero minimum comes from one globally weighted curve whose interval reaches 0.8 drinks a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group changed the weights in 2022); causal effects beyond what the underlying observational studies can support; the risk of particular drinking patterns (only average volume is modelled); or burden in people under 15 and harm to others beyond road injuries.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (modelling). Exposure sources were found through the Global Health Data Exchange (GHDx) and PubMed; relative-risk studies through PubMed, the GHDx and the reference lists of earlier meta-analyses. The relative-risk studies together covered about 28 million people and 649,000 registered cases of the outcomes (Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph). Search strategy, flow diagrams, the list of sources and the cause-specific curves are in appendix 1 (pp 52–146), which was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Outcomes were chosen by reviewing prospective and observational studies and judging causality with Bradford Hill's criteria; 23 outcomes were included (Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph). People younger than 15 were not modelled because data were sparse; outcomes with accumulating but insufficient evidence, such as dementia and psoriasis, were left out (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Eligibility criteria for individual studies, search dates and language limits are not given in the main text.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Estimates cover 195 locations, both sexes and 5-year age groups from 15 to 95 and older, 1990–2016.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Relative risks come from observational studies whose participants and reference groups differ. Whether former drinkers were counted among abstainers was tested as a study-level covariate and kept only where significant: for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes (Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph); for the other 20 outcomes no reference-group adjustment is reported. No appraisal of the quality of the 592 studies is described in the main text. Survey exposure data are self-reported and were rescaled to sales data.

exposure.measurement: Modelled. Population alcohol stock (litres per capita) came from sales data, adjusted by adding alcohol drunk abroad by residents and subtracting alcohol drunk by tourists (World Tourism Organization data), and by adding unrecorded alcohol (illicit production, home brewing, local beverages) drawn 1000 times from a uniform distribution between zero and the average of published estimates for each location, which the authors call conservative. Survey estimates of current drinking, abstention and grams a day by age and sex were rescaled to sum to that stock (Methods › Data sources, 2nd to 5th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure is average daily volume: grams of pure ethanol a day among current drinkers, reported in standard drinks of 10 g. Current drinking = at least one drink in the past 12 months; abstention = no alcohol in the past year (Introduction, 7th paragraph; Figure 1 legend). Curves were fitted between 0 and 12.5 standard drinks a day, beyond which there were no data. Drinking pattern (heavy episodic drinking) is not modelled, which the authors list as a limitation (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Survey volumes by beverage were converted to ethanol with assumed average strengths (appendix 1, p 50, not read).
exposure.polysubstance: Not modelled. Tobacco and other drug use enter only through whatever adjustment each underlying study made; joint effects (for example of alcohol and smoking on cancers of the mouth and throat) are not addressed in the main text.

comparison.controls: Two counterfactuals. For the relative risks: the abstaining or non-drinking category of each underlying study, whose make-up varied (adjusted for the inclusion of former drinkers only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes). For attributable burden: the estimated TMREL of zero standard drinks a day, which the authors present as estimated rather than assumed (Introduction, 6th paragraph; Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at model level. In the underlying studies, illness that makes people stop drinking (the sick-quitter problem) and survival bias are handled only through the reference-category covariate and the average age of participants (Introduction, 4th paragraph); other ways in which lifelong abstainers differ from people who drink are not addressed in the main text (editors' observation).

outcomes.instruments: GBD 2016 estimates of deaths and DALYs by cause, location, age, sex and year for 23 alcohol-associated outcomes (the list is in appendix 1; the GBD 2020 paper names the same 23: ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, atrial fibrillation and flutter, eight cancers, type 2 diabetes, cirrhosis and other chronic liver disease, pancreatitis, idiopathic epilepsy, tuberculosis, lower respiratory infection, transport injuries, unintentional injuries, self-harm and interpersonal violence). Road-injury burden falling on people other than the drinker was redistributed with US Fatality Analysis Reporting System data, assumed to hold everywhere (Methods › Attributable burden due to alcohol use, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper states that it follows the GATHER reporting guideline (Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph). No check of the weighted curve against all-cause mortality is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Attributable burden = population attributable fraction (from exposure, relative risk and TMREL) × deaths or DALYs for each outcome, summed over outcomes and aggregated by Socio-demographic Index (SDI) quintile. The TMREL is the minimum of a single weighted average of the cause-specific curves, weights being each outcome's global, age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016 for both sexes (Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph). 'Health loss' thus means DALY-weighted risk over 23 outcomes; all-cause mortality was not analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: estimation with uncertainty intervals; 'significant' is used only for curve shapes and for the sensitivity analysis, without stated tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: All intervals are 95% uncertainty intervals; standard drink = 10 g ethanol; current drinking = any drink in the past 12 months. Prevalence of current drinking in 2016: 32.5% (30.0–35.2) of people worldwide, 25% (23–27) of females and 39% (36–43) of males, 2.4 billion people; mean consumption 0.73 (0.68–0.78) standard drinks a day in females and 1.7 (1.5–1.9) in males. Attributable deaths 2.8 million (2.4–3.3); 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female deaths and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) of female and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of male DALYs; seventh leading risk factor. Ages 15–49: leading risk factor; 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; 2.3% (2.0–2.6) of female and 8.9% (7.8–9.9) of male DALYs. Cause-specific curves (relative to each study's non-drinking category): significant J-shape only for ischaemic heart disease, minimum relative risk 0.86 (0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 drinks a day; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; all other outcomes, including all cancers, rising with intake. TMREL of the weighted curve: zero (0.0–0.8) standard drinks a day.
analysis.covariates: In the relative-risk meta-regressions: a study-level covariate for the composition of the reference category, kept for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes, and the average age of participants (Introduction, 4th paragraph; Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph). Other covariates, and the model in detail, are only in appendix 1 (pp 51–138).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper states adherence to the GATHER statement. Raw data underlying the figures and relative-risk curves were posted on Mendeley Data on 19 September 2018, after publication, and a data-sharing statement was added by correction (Lancet 2018;392:1116).
analysis.selective_reporting: The weighted all-outcome curve on which the headline rests is shown only as an image (Figure 5); the text gives no relative risk, absolute risk or attributable rate at any intake other than its minimum. The single sensitivity analysis of the weights is reported in one sentence without numbers. The search, the study list, the cause-specific curves and model details are in appendices (4.2 MB and 21 MB PDFs) that were not read. The widely reported absolute figures (918 against 914 per 100,000 a year at one drink a day) do not appear in the article; a 2019 letter (Astrup & Estruch) attributes them to The Lancet's press release, which was not found at its cited address.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Uncertainty intervals come from 1000 draws carrying sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation, reported as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (Methods › Uncertainty analysis). The paper does not say that they include uncertainty from structural choices (the form of the curves, the weights, the outcomes included) or from residual bias in the underlying observational studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under its inputs and weights, the model attributes about 2.8 million deaths in 2016 to alcohol (2.2% of female and 6.8% of male age-standardised deaths) and ranks alcohol as the leading risk factor at ages 15–49. Of the 23 cause-specific curves, only ischaemic heart disease had a significant J-shape (minimum relative risk 0.86 in men and 0.82 in women at about 0.8–0.9 drinks a day); diabetes and ischaemic stroke dipped non-significantly; all others, including every cancer, rose with intake. The minimum of the single globally DALY-weighted curve was zero drinks a day with an interval reaching 0.8 drinks a day, and it changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the conclusion say the level that minimises health loss is zero and that “the safest level of drinking is none” (Conclusion); the discussion concludes that alcohol leads to health loss in populations whatever the amount drunk (Discussion, 2nd paragraph) and suggests considering recommendations for abstention (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the abstract gives the minimum's interval as 0.0–0.8 standard drinks per week, the results as per day, so the abstract understates the uncertainty sevenfold; on the per-day interval, intakes up to 0.8 drinks a day are compatible with the minimum; (2) a curve weighted by global population DALY rates is described as minimising an individual's total attributable risk (Introduction, 7th paragraph; Research in context), although the weights describe the world's disease mix, not a person's, and the authors' own sensitivity analysis shows the curve shifts where ischaemic heart disease and diabetes make up more than 60% of deaths; (3) the interpretation's wording that alcohol 'causes substantial health loss' rests on observational relative risks screened with Bradford Hill's criteria; (4) the discussion treats newer studies showing little or no protection as settling a literature that remains contested; (5) the Summary's Interpretation says the study found that the risk of all-cause mortality rises with consumption, although no all-cause mortality analysis is reported (the weighted curve combines 23 outcome curves weighted by DALY rates); (6) the Introduction (6th paragraph) presents the new counterfactual method as providing tangible evidence for low-risk drinking recommendations, yet the minimum it reports is zero. In their 2019 reply to letters, the authors agreed that the risk is low between 0 and 0.8 drinks a day and said that debating zero against near zero misses the point.

timeline.event: Comment by Burton & Sheron in the same issue endorses the conclusions as clear and unambiguous and as support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline (appraised on its own card, sc_burton_2018).

Correction (Lancet 2018;392:1116; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32338-9), online version corrected 27 September 2018: Alan D Lopez added to the collaborators, two names corrected, one affiliation updated, raw data for the figures and relative-risk curves posted on Mendeley Data (DOI 10.17632/5thy2mcwn7.1) and a data-sharing statement added. No numbers changed.

Letter, Abat, Roussel, Chaudet & Raoult: argue that alcohol consumption tracks life expectancy and SDI, so diseases of ageing were attributed to alcohol; the authors reply that exposure is age-specific and the relative risks control for participants' average age.

Letter, Astrup & Estruch: object that mainly ecological data and models cannot support global policy, that the pooled curve cannot be read at regional or individual level, and that the zero category spans up to 0.8 drinks a day; cite 918 against 914 per 100,000 a year at one drink a day from the press release. Declared ties, as printed: Astrup, external scientific board of and personal fees from the Dutch Beer Institute; Estruch, external scientific board of the Beer and Health Initiative (The Brewers of Europe) and lecture fees from The Brewers of Europe, Fundacion Cerveza y Salud, Pernaud-Ricard and Instituto Cervantes.

Letter, Shield & Rehm: the curves should be weighted by lifetime abstainers' DALYs, not the general population's; with those weights they find a slight net benefit of 20.8 DALYs per 100,000 at one drink (12 g) a day; heavy drinking occasions were not modelled; no competing interests declared. The authors reply that those weights would make the model circular.

Letter, Di Castelnuovo, Costanzo & de Gaetano: all-cause mortality was not analysed; the DALY weighting is unvalidated and somewhat arbitrary (heart failure excluded) and ignores the differing precision of the curves. Declared ties include grants from the European Foundation for Alcohol Research and fees from Heineken and Assobirra. The authors reply that all-cause mortality depends on each population's cause mix.

Authors' reply (Griswold & Gakidou, Lancet 2019;393:2391–92): agree the risk is low between 0 and 0.8 drinks a day, note that most current drinkers drink far more, and call the zero-versus-near-zero debate beside the point.

Second correction (Lancet 2019;393:e44; DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31050-5), online version corrected 20 June 2019: Stefan Lorkowski added to the collaborators with affiliation and declaration of interests. No numbers changed.

GBD 2020 update by the same consortium (Bryazka et al.): with 2020 DALY weights the global, age-standardised TMREL is 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the 2016 curves and 0.511 (0.400–0.700) with five updated curves; minima between 0 and 0.603 drinks a day at ages 15–39 and J-shaped weighted curves at 40 and older (card sc_bryazka_2022).
Burton & Sheron's comment on GBD 2020 describes the new estimates as seemingly contradicting the 2018 any-amount message (only its first paragraph was readable; the rest is paywalled).

replication.where_it_stands: The 2016 burden figures are model outputs revised by later GBD rounds (the GBD 2020 paper cites 1.78 million alcohol-attributable deaths in 2020 from unpublished GBD 2020 work). The headline zero minimum was not reproduced by the same group's 2022 update, in which the global minimum became about half a standard drink a day once the weights were updated, while minima stayed between 0 and 0.6 drinks a day at ages 15–39. Whether low intake truly lowers the risk of ischaemic heart disease (and of ischaemic stroke and diabetes), the dip that produces every non-zero minimum, is the subject of the cohort and Mendelian-randomization papers on the project list (Wood et al., 2018; Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019; Biddinger et al., 2022; Larsson et al., 2020), appraised by other readers.

funding.funder: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (Summary › Funding). The acknowledgments add the US National Institute on Aging (award P30AG047845) and list individual collaborators' fellowships and institutional support, mostly from public research bodies and universities. The funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Methods › Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed in the Declaration of interests: Yannick Béjot, grants and personal fees from AstraZeneca and Boehringer-Ingelheim and personal fees from Daiichi-Sankyo, Pfizer, MSD, Medtronic, BMS and Amgen; Jacek Jóźwiak, grants and personal fees from VALEANT, personal fees from ALAB Laboratoria and AMGEN, non-financial support from MICROLIFE and SERVIER; Srinivasa Vittal Katikireddi, grants from the Medical Research Council, the Scottish Government Chief Scientist Office and an NRS Senior Clinical Fellowship during the conduct of the study; Ted Miller, other support from the AB InBev Foundation (ABIF); Maarten Postma, grants, personal fees or other support from 26 pharmaceutical, research and consulting companies; Dan Stein, personal fees or grants from Lundbeck, Novartis, AMBRF, NRGF, Servier, Biocodex, MRC, Cipla and Sun. All except Katikireddi's are stated to be outside the submitted work; all other authors declare no competing interests. The 2019 correction added Stefan Lorkowski, whose declaration appears only in the corrected online version: personal fees from AMGEN, Berlin-Chemie, MSD Sharp & Dohme, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi-Aventis, Synlab, Unilever, Upfield and Akcea Therapeutics and non-financial support from Preventicus, outside the submitted work.
funding.affiliations_note: Analysis led and written at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (University of Washington); the first author developed the models and ran all analyses (Contributors). The only declared tie bearing an alcohol producer's name is Ted Miller's support from the AB InBev Foundation; one collaborator (Mete Saylan) is an employee of Bayer AG (Acknowledgments). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Cause-specific dose–response curves at low intake from designs less exposed to confounding and abstainer bias, chiefly non-linear Mendelian randomization in large cohorts of several ancestries, and cohorts that separate lifetime abstainers from former drinkers and record drinking patterns, combined with a weighting scheme fixed in advance and published with sensitivity analyses of the weights, and checked against all-cause mortality in populations with different disease mixes.

domains.note: Exposure combines sales data (adjusted for tourism and, conservatively, for unrecorded alcohol) with self-reported surveys; burden comes from GBD 2016 cause estimates; harm to others enters only through US road-injury data assumed to apply everywhere; under-15s, drinking patterns, harm to others from violence and outcomes such as dementia are left out, which the authors expect to make the burden an underestimate.

Fitted to observational cohort and case-control estimates (of self-reported intake, as the GBD 2020 paper notes of the same evidence base); reference-group bias adjusted only where a covariate was significant (three outcomes); no quality appraisal of the 592 studies described in the main text; one curve per outcome applied to every population; the low-intake shape for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes is where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed.

One global curve weighted by 2016 global age-standardised DALY rates, a choice that is not validated and was criticized in 2019 (weights should be abstainers' DALYs; precision of curves ignored); with GBD 2020 DALY weights and the same 2016 curves the global minimum became 0.534 drinks a day (GBD 2020 paper, Table 2).

domains.domain: Uncertainty intervals: what they include and exclude
domains.note: 1000 draws carry sampling error and parameter and hyper-parameter uncertainty; structural choices and residual bias in the underlying studies are not stated to be included; the minimum's interval (0–0.8 drinks a day) is printed per week in the abstract.

One sensitivity analysis (choice of weights) is reported, in a sentence without numbers: the curve changed only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease exceeded 60% of deaths. No sensitivity to curve form, reference group or outcomes included is reported in the main text; the 2022 update shows the global minimum is sensitive to the weights.

GATHER adherence stated and raw data posted after publication; but the weighted curve appears only as an image, no absolute risks are given, the headline interval has inconsistent units, appendix cross-references conflict, and the methods that matter are only in appendices.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for burden-of-disease modelling (METHODS §5.3; the round brief sets design 'modelling' with no instrument). The editors' checklist is used with domains for the inputs, the relative-risk curves, the counterfactual level, the uncertainty intervals, the sensitivity of the headline and the reporting, as in card sc_visser_2019; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The burden estimates are transparent model outputs with stated limitations. The headline zero rests on one globally weighted curve whose interval reaches 0.8 drinks a day and whose minimum moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated the weights. Citable for GBD 2016's model estimates (attributable deaths and DALYs, drinking prevalence, the cause-specific curve shapes as reported), always with their assumptions; not citable on its own for the statement that any amount of alcohol harms health or that the safest level for a person is zero.

key_findings.finding: Inputs: 121,029 exposure data points from 694 sources; 3,992 relative-risk estimates from 592 prospective and retrospective studies covering about 28 million people and 649,000 registered cases; 23 outcomes; 195 locations, 1990–2016, ages 15 to 95 and older.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In 2016, 32.5% (95% UI 30.0–35.2) of people worldwide were current drinkers (at least one drink in the past 12 months): 25% (23–27) of females and 39% (36–43) of males, 2.4 billion (2.2–2.6) people. Mean consumption was 0.73 (0.68–0.78) standard drinks (10 g ethanol) a day in females and 1.7 (1.5–1.9) in males.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global, regional, and national trends in alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text does not say whether mean consumption is per current drinker or per person; the next paragraph and Figure 2 refer to averages among current drinkers.

key_findings.finding: Current drinking was most common in high-SDI locations (72% [69–75] of females, 83% [80–85] of males) and least common in low-to-middle-SDI locations (8.9% [6.6–9.7] of females, 20% [17–22] of males); examples: Nepal 1.5% (1.2–1.9) of females against 21% (17–25) of males; Sweden 86% (84–88) against 87% (85–89).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global, regional, and national trends in alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Average consumption among current drinkers (age-standardised): high-SDI locations 1.9 (1.3–2.7) standard drinks a day in females and 2.9 (2.0–4.1) in males; lowest for males in low-SDI locations, 1.4 (0.6–2.4); lowest for females in low-to-middle-SDI locations, 0.3 (0.1–0.6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global, regional, and national trends in alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: 2.8 million deaths (95% UI 2.4–3.3) were attributed to alcohol in 2016: 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female deaths and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) of female and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of male DALYs. Alcohol ranked seventh among GBD risk factors.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st paragraph; Summary › Findings

key_findings.finding: At ages 15–49, alcohol was the leading risk factor: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths, and 2.3% (2.0–2.6) of female and 8.9% (7.8–9.9) of male DALYs, were attributed to it. The leading attributable causes of death in this age group were tuberculosis (1.4% [1.0–1.7] of total deaths), road injuries (1.2% [0.7–1.9]) and self-harm (1.1% [0.6–1.5]).
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Summary › Findings
key_findings.note: The Results call the 8.9% and 2.3% shares 'of attributable DALYs', the abstract 'attributable DALYs'; the denominator is not stated explicitly (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: At ages 50 and older, cancers made up 27.1% (21.2–33.3) of alcohol-attributable female deaths and 18.9% (15.3–22.6) of alcohol-attributable male deaths in 2016.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the burden estimates, females, particularly in high-SDI locations, had some protective effects for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes themselves beyond age 60 (negative attributable burden for those causes, not a net effect across causes); among males only high-SDI and low-SDI locations showed noticeable protective effects for ischaemic heart disease, which the authors call small compared with the total attributable burden there.
key_findings.locator: Results › Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cause-specific curves (relative to the non-drinking category of the underlying studies): only ischaemic heart disease showed a statistically significant J-shape, with a minimum relative risk of 0.86 (0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 standard drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 drinks a day; diabetes and ischaemic stroke showed non-significant J-shapes; no significant age differences were found for ischaemic heart disease or diabetes; every other outcome, including all cancers, rose monotonically with intake.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 (image; values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: The minimum of the DALY-weighted curve over all attributable outcomes (the TMREL) was zero standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0–0.8 drinks a day), and the weighted risk rose monotonically with intake; the protective associations for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes in females were offset by cancers, whose risk rose monotonically with consumption (the Discussion, 2nd paragraph, names cancer, injuries and communicable disease). In a sensitivity analysis of the weights, the curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph; Figure 5 (image; values not extracted)
key_findings.note: The abstract prints the same interval as 0.0–0.8 standard drinks per week (reporting issue 1); the GBD 2020 paper (Table 2) and the authors' 2019 reply treat it as per day.

key_findings.finding: Method of the minimum: dose–response curves were fitted with mixed-effects logistic regression and non-linear splines for 0 to 12.5 standard drinks a day; the TMREL is the minimum of a weighted average of the cause-specific curves, weights being each outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016, both sexes; a covariate for whether former drinkers were in the reference group was retained for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Uncertainty intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1000 draws that carry sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation through every step.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Uncertainty analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: unrecorded consumption may still be missed; drinking patterns were not modelled; harm to others from road injuries rests on US data; harm to others from violence was not estimated; under-15s were not assessed; outcomes such as dementia and psoriasis were excluded. The authors conclude these make the risks and burden likely underestimates.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Two correction notices changed authorship, an affiliation, a declaration of interests and data availability, not numbers: Lancet 2018;392:1116 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32338-9) and Lancet 2019;393:e44 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31050-5). The PMC text read is the uncorrected original; every decimal figure in its main text also appears in the corrected online version (editors' comparison of the two texts), so the numbers on this card are the corrected ones.
key_findings.page: PMC HTML; publisher HTML (corrected online version); PMC6902241; PMC6598857
key_findings.locator: Correction notices (Department of Error); corrected version's Data sharing and Declaration of interests

design_detail: Mendelian randomization with individual-participant data pooled from 56 studies (261 991 participants of European descent), using a single instrument: carriage of the A-allele of ADH1B rs1229984, a variant of an alcohol-metabolising enzyme, analysed as a dominant trait (carriers of one or two A-alleles, on average about 7% of participants, against GG homozygotes). Genotype associations with alcohol traits, cardiovascular biomarkers, lifestyle factors, coronary heart disease (primary outcome), stroke and type 2 diabetes were estimated within each study and combined by fixed-effect meta-analysis (random effects as a check), overall and within strata of self-reported intake (0, >0 to <21 and ≥21 UK units/week; for coronary heart disease the middle stratum was split at 7 units/week). No instrumental-variable estimate of the effect of a given amount of alcohol was computed. The studies were not found by a systematic search: the authors approached population-based studies genotyped on the IBC CardioChip array, genetic study groups they had worked with (offering new genotyping) and a few studies that had published on the variant; 56 of 59 took part. The paper calls them epidemiological studies; their individual designs are listed in an appendix that was not read, and coronary events and strokes included both incident and prevalent cases. A conventional analysis of self-reported intake against risk factors (131 490 people, 28 studies) is reported only in the appendix. Labelled prospective-cohort and appraised with ROBINS-E under the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization of pooled cohorts, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether people carrying an allele that lowers drinking (about 17% fewer self-reported units per week, more abstention, less binge drinking) have lower blood pressure, inflammatory markers, adiposity and odds of coronary heart disease than non-carriers, in a comparison that assignment of genotype at conception protects from confounding by lifestyle and from illness changing drinking, provided the variant affects these outcomes only through alcohol.
cannot_establish: What a given amount of alcohol does, or the shape of the dose-response at low intake (one binary variant shifts intake proportionally, no instrumental-variable estimate was made, and the strata are defined by self-reported drinking, which the genotype itself changes); that cutting down helps light drinkers in particular (the light and moderate strata each have intervals that include no difference); and that the variant acts only through alcohol (carriers who reported not drinking also had lower blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index).

sample.recruitment: Pooled studies identified through collaboration, not a systematic search: population-based studies genotyped on the IBC CardioChip array, genetic study groups that had worked with the authors (some genotyped anew), and a small number of European-descent studies that had published on this variant; the public CARDIoGRAMplusC4D data did not include the variant. Of 59 studies approached, 56 were included: INTERHEART and INTERSTROKE declined because of overlap with other projects, and CoLaus was excluded because the variant had not been genotyped directly (Methods › Formation of the consortium; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participants of European descent with data on rs1229984 genotype, age, sex and at least one outcome; not every study contributed to every analysis, because the variables collected differed (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; appendix figure S2, not read).
sample.demographics: 48% women; mean age per study 58 years (study means ranged from 26 to 75). Median alcohol intake by study is given only in appendix table S4 (not read) (Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a pooled genetic analysis. Of the 261 991 participants, 168 731 (from 46 studies) entered the coronary heart disease analysis. The analysis by drinking status covered 150 507 participants with 16 013 of the 20 259 coronary events, so about 4246 events (21%) had no usable alcohol data (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2).
sample.selection_effects: Studies entered because they had genotyped the variant on one array or belonged to the authors' network, mainly with unpublished genetic data, which the authors argue protects against publication bias. Coronary events and strokes included prevalent cases, so people who died before a study enrolled them are missing; if the genotype affected survival after an event, the odds ratios could be biased (not addressed). Only people of European descent were analysed. The analyses within drinking strata compare carriers and non-carriers selected on self-reported drinking, a variable the genotype affects; the authors checked only that lifestyle factors were not differentially associated with the genotype across strata (Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and lifestyle factors).

exposure.measurement: Instrument: rs1229984 genotyped directly in every study (median call rate 98.8%; platforms and Hardy-Weinberg tests in appendix table S1, not read). Alcohol: self-reported weekly volume in UK units derived from each study's questionnaire (1 UK unit = 10 mL or 7.9 g ethanol = 0.57 US units), drinking status (drinkers v non-drinkers), the study- and sex-specific top third of intake, and binge drinking (definitions in appendix table S2, not read); γ-glutamyltransferase as a marker of heavy drinking (Methods › Alcohol traits).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Instrument relevance: carriers reported 17.2% fewer units per week (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%; 46 studies, 218 969 people; P=5.5×10−76; I2 64%), were less often in their study's top third of intake (OR 0.70, 0.68 to 0.73) or binge drinkers (0.78, 0.73 to 0.84), higher odds of reporting abstention (1.27, 1.21 to 1.34), and 1.8% lower γ-glutamyltransferase (−3.4% to −0.3%) (Table 1). The proportional reduction looked constant across the range of intake (appendix figures S5 and S6, not read). No F statistic is reported. Strata used: none (0 units/week), light to moderate (>0 to <21) and heavy (≥21, about 166 g ethanol/week by the editors' conversion); for coronary heart disease, light (>0 to <7), moderate (≥7 to <21) and heavy (≥21).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking was examined as a possible confounder of the instrument: carriers had slightly higher odds of ever smoking (OR 1.06, 1.02 to 1.09), opposite in direction to the observational smoking-drinking association, and no difference in cigarettes per day, pack-years or cotinine (Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and lifestyle factors). Other drug use was not reported.

comparison.controls: Non-carriers (GG homozygotes) in the same studies, compared within each study and then pooled. In the stratified analyses the comparison is between carriers and non-carriers within the same self-reported drinking category; the non-drinker stratum is people reporting 0 units/week, and whether former drinkers were separated is defined study by study in appendix table S2 (not read); the authors note that long-term non-drinkers are hard to classify from questionnaires (Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph). The main text reports no conventional analysis of self-reported intake against cardiovascular events.
comparison.matching: None needed for the genetic comparison; estimates are crude within-study contrasts (Figure 1 legend), with adjustment for principal components of ancestry where available as a sensitivity analysis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genotype is fixed at conception, so premorbid differences between carriers and non-carriers are expected only through population structure or neighbouring variants. Checks: adjustment for principal components in studies with genome-wide data did not change the estimates (appendix figures S15-S16); no linkage disequilibrium with known cardiovascular genome-wide loci, tested in Whitehall II only (table S11). Carriers had slightly more years of education (0.04 SD, 0.01 to 0.08), which the authors say needs further study.

outcomes.instruments: Coronary heart disease (primary): incident and prevalent, fatal and non-fatal events. Stroke of all subtypes, incident and prevalent, with ischaemic stroke separately in a subsample. Type 2 diabetes: prevalent cases, except one nested case-cohort with incident cases. Study-specific definitions are in appendix table S3 (not read). Biomarkers: systolic blood pressure, hypertension, body mass index, waist circumference, interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, non-HDL and HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoprotein A1, and eight further traits (carotid intima-media thickness, electrocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor VII, fasting glucose, NT-proBNP, lipoprotein(a)).
outcomes.validity_norms: Outcome definitions and ascertainment varied by study; no central adjudication is described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Odds ratio of the outcome in carriers against non-carriers (log odds ratios pooled across studies); mean or percentage differences for continuous traits.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 22 counts the four clinical outcomes and the 18 cardiovascular traits named in the main text; the paper also reports five alcohol traits, at least six lifestyle factors, stratified analyses in three or four drinking categories, and 58 plus 48 exploratory subgroup comparisons, all judged at P<0.05 two-sided.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Genetic; carriers v non-carriers; fixed-effect pooled] Coronary heart disease OR 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96; 46 studies, 20 259 events in 168 731 people; I2 17%; P=0.001); in the four studies with ≥1000 events (8374 events) 0.81 (0.72 to 0.91; I2 0%). By self-reported drinking (UK units/week): non-drinkers 0.98 (0.88 to 1.10; 5883 events in 43 029); drinkers 0.86 (0.78 to 0.94; 10 130 in 107 478); test of difference P=0.095; light (>0 to <7) 0.90 (0.79 to 1.02; 4686 in 47 246), moderate (≥7 to <21) 0.89 (0.75 to 1.06; 3222 in 33 772), heavy (≥21) 0.97 (0.76 to 1.24; 1919 in 16 225); trend P=0.83 (Figure 2). Stroke 0.98 (0.90 to 1.07; 10 164 events in 145 063); ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72 to 0.95; subset); type 2 diabetes 1.02 (0.95 to 1.09) (Figure 3). Biomarkers: systolic blood pressure −0.88 mm Hg (−1.19 to −0.56); hypertension OR 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 104 570 cases); interleukin-6 −5.2%; C-reactive protein −3.4%; body mass index −0.17 kg/m2; waist −0.34 cm; non-HDL cholesterol −0.03 mmol/L; triglycerides +1.6%; HDL cholesterol −0.004 mmol/L (−0.012 to 0.003) (Table 2). Random-effects estimates were similar. No absolute risks and no instrumental-variable estimates are reported.
analysis.covariates: None in the main genetic contrasts (crude, within study); principal components of ancestry in the studies that had them, as a sensitivity analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported. A standard analysis protocol was sent to the participating studies (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph); it is not published with the main text (appendix not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The stratum-specific coronary estimates and the test of non-drinkers against drinkers (P=0.095) appear only in Figure 2; the text gives the non-drinker and drinker estimates without that test. The Methods describe three drinking strata (0, >0 to <21, ≥21 units/week); the coronary analysis split the middle one at 7 units/week. Several subgroup results are stated to be available on request rather than shown.
analysis.power: Not reported. The authors attribute the weak coronary association in heavy drinkers (OR 0.97, 0.76 to 1.24; 1919 events) to few events and call the number of strokes an important limitation (Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of the study, 4th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Carriers of the intake-lowering ADH1B allele drank about 17% less and had slightly lower blood pressure, inflammatory markers, adiposity and non-HDL cholesterol, and 10% lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96); there was no association with all stroke or type 2 diabetes, and lower odds of ischaemic stroke in a subset. Within drinking strata the coronary odds ratios were 0.90 (light), 0.89 (moderate) and 0.97 (heavy), each with an interval including 1, and the difference between non-drinkers (0.98) and drinkers (0.86) had P=0.095. In people reporting no drinking, carriers still had lower systolic blood pressure (−0.80 mm Hg), interleukin-6 (−7.15%) and body mass index (−0.21), about as much as light-to-moderate drinkers (Figure 1).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that reducing alcohol, "even for light to moderate drinkers, is beneficial for cardiovascular health" (Abstract, Conclusions); the summary box on what the study adds says the lower risk held at all levels of drinking, while the Discussion's section on the meaning of the study says such reductions may be beneficial. Gaps: (1) the statement about light-to-moderate drinkers rests on stratified estimates that are each compatible with no difference and on a non-significant heterogeneity test (P=0.83), which shows no detectable difference between strata, not equal benefit; (2) stratifying on self-reported drinking, which the genotype changes, can itself create bias, which the authors examined only through lifestyle factors; (3) the Discussion states that associations with the traits were null or much weaker in non-drinkers, as expected if the variant works only through alcohol, but Figure 1 shows associations of similar size in non-drinkers for systolic blood pressure, interleukin-6, body mass index and C-reactive protein, pointing either to misclassified former or occasional drinkers or to a pathway other than current drinking, which the paper does not discuss; (4) a single variant shifting intake by about 17% cannot show what happens below a given intake or compare light drinking with none, and no causal effect per unit of alcohol was estimated; (5) light to moderate here means >0 to <21 UK units/week (up to about 166 g ethanol), self-reported. The conclusion that the observational J-shape reflects residual confounding or selection bias (Discussion › Meaning of the study) is a reasonable inference, but the paper tests neither explanation.

timeline.event: This study: by the authors' account the first Mendelian randomization analysis large enough to detect an association of an alcohol-lowering genotype with coronary heart disease events (Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses in relation to other studies, 1st paragraph).

Millwood et al. (China Kadoorie Biobank; ALDH2 rs671 and ADH1B rs1229984): genotype-predicted male intake was associated log-linearly with ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage but not with myocardial infarction (RR 0.96 per 280 g/week); those authors describe their rs1229984-only coronary result as consistent with this study.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, "Genetic instrumental variable analysis: time to call Mendelian randomization what it is" (Eur J Epidemiol), listed in the project's DOI list as a critique of the Mendelian randomization studies of alcohol and cardiovascular disease; not read for this card. Two of its three authors (K Mukamal, E Rimm) are coauthors of this study.

Larsson et al. (two-sample Mendelian randomization with up to 94 variants, European ancestry): genetically predicted drinking associated with stroke (OR 1.27 per SD of log drinks/week) and borderline with coronary artery disease (1.16, 1.00 to 1.36), attenuated after adjustment for smoking liability; rs1229984 alone was associated with coronary artery disease in a dataset with about three times this study's coronary cases, by Larsson and colleagues' account.

Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank; variants associated with alcohol use disorder): linear Mendelian randomization OR for coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per SD of genetically predicted intake, and nonlinear analyses that those authors read as risk rising from the lowest intakes.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the coronary result (a genotype that lowers drinking goes with fewer coronary events) was seen again in later European-ancestry Mendelian randomization (Larsson et al., 2020, for rs1229984; Biddinger et al., 2022), but not for myocardial infarction in the east Asian two-variant analysis (Millwood et al., 2019). For stroke the studies differ: this one found no association with all stroke, while the later ones found higher genetically predicted intake associated with more stroke, especially intracerebral haemorrhage. Whether cutting down benefits light drinkers is the contested part: this design cannot show it, and the stratified estimates the abstract relies on are imprecise and open to selection bias. Millwood et al. share two authors with this study (M V Holmes, G Davey Smith), so the two are not fully independent.

funding.funder: Supported in part by British Heart Foundation programme grant RG/10/12/28456. Individual authors were funded by the UK Medical Research Council, British Heart Foundation, National Institute for Health Research (University College London Hospitals Biomedical Research Centre), Economic and Social Research Council, Netherlands Heart Foundation, NWO, Swedish Heart-Lung Foundation, Swedish Research Council, Mayo Foundation, American Heart Association, and the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, National Institute on Aging, National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, National Institute on Drug Abuse and National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities, among others. Contributing studies were funded mainly by public and charitable bodies; industry funding is printed for several: PROSPER (an investigator-initiated grant from Bristol-Myers Squibb), PROCARDIS (AstraZeneca among others), NPHS II (DuPont Pharma), TPT (DuPont Pharma and Bayer Corporation), NORDIL (Pharmacia, with the British Heart Foundation), EPIC-Potsdam (Mercodia supplied assay kits free of charge), and the department behind the UCP study, which reports unrestricted funding from public bodies and industry (GlaxoSmithKline, Pfizer and others). The paper states that the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Funding of individuals; Funding of studies; Statement of independence from funders).
funding.declared_conflicts: One author (J Whittaker) declared being 90% employed by GlaxoSmithKline and owning GlaxoSmithKline shares. All other coauthors declared no support for the submitted work, no financial relationships in the previous three years with organisations that might have an interest in it, and no other relevant relationships or activities (Competing interests). No ties to the alcohol industry are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: A consortium of more than 150 authors from the contributing studies. The author list includes K Mukamal and E Rimm, two of the three authors of the 2019 critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol named in the DOI list. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A Mendelian randomization study of incident coronary events in a population where genotype produces large absolute differences in intake down to near zero (as with ALDH2 in east Asia), using several independent alcohol variants, nonlinear methods whose assumptions are checked, and biomarker-verified non-drinkers to test whether the variant acts outside alcohol. A long-term randomized trial of light drinking against abstention with cardiovascular events as the outcome, which the authors consider not feasible, would answer the light-drinking question directly.

domains.note: Instrument independence: genotype is assigned at conception; adjustment for principal components of ancestry did not change the estimates where available, and no linkage disequilibrium with known cardiovascular loci was found (one cohort). An HDL association confined to northern European studies raised the possibility of population structure, which principal-component adjustment did not confirm. Small imbalances: education (+0.04 SD) and ever smoking (OR 1.06, in the direction that would not produce the protective result). Exclusion restriction (no other path from variant to outcome): ADH1B is an alcohol-metabolising enzyme, so a path outside drinking is less likely than for behavioural variants, and the coronary association was null in self-reported non-drinkers (0.98, 0.88 to 1.10); but its difference from drinkers was not significant (P=0.095), and in non-drinkers the variant was still associated with lower systolic blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index (Figure 1). Pleiotropy-robust methods are not possible with one variant.

Relevance: strong (17.2% fewer units per week, P=5.5×10−76, with consistent effects on abstention, binge drinking and γ-glutamyltransferase), although no F statistic is given and only about 7% of participants carry the allele. Shape at low intake: the instrument shifts intake proportionally and cannot show what happens at specific low intakes; the paper deliberately computes no causal effect per unit. Intake itself is self-reported with heterogeneous questionnaires, which matters for the strata.

Selection into the pooled data: studies chosen by genotyping platform and collaboration rather than by search, European descent only, and prevalent as well as incident events (survivors only). For the stratified estimates the risk is high: carriers and non-carriers are compared within categories of self-reported drinking that the genotype itself influences; the authors examined lifestyle factors across strata (no differential association) but not other consequences of this conditioning.
Not applicable in the usual sense: the instrument is fixed at conception, and later changes in drinking are part of what it captures.

Studies contributed according to the variables they had collected, which is unlikely to depend on genotype. About a fifth of coronary events lacked the alcohol data needed for the stratified analysis (editors' arithmetic), which affects only the stratified estimates.

Study-specific definitions of coronary heart disease, stroke and diabetes, mixing incident and prevalent and fatal and non-fatal events, without central adjudication. Misclassification is unlikely to depend on genotype and would mainly dilute associations.

No registered plan; many outcomes, strata and subgroups without correction; the coronary analysis split a stratum described in the Methods; stratified biomarker results that contradict the Discussion's account of non-drinkers are shown in Figure 1 but described inaccurately in the text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the main result, the pooled association of the alcohol-lowering ADH1B genotype with lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90) and with lower blood pressure and adiposity, the design is well protected against the confounding that affects conventional studies, the instrument is strong and tied to alcohol metabolism, and outcome misclassification would bias towards no association; the remaining concerns are pleiotropy (biomarker associations in non-drinkers), the choice of studies and the inclusion of prevalent cases. The stratified estimates, which carry the abstract's message about light to moderate drinkers, are at high risk of bias from conditioning on self-reported drinking and are imprecise. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: genetic evidence that a variant lowering alcohol intake is associated with lower coronary risk and lower blood pressure in people of European descent. Do not cite it for: a benefit of cutting down in light drinkers specifically, a dose-response or threshold, the absence of any protective effect at low intake, or stroke (null overall; ischaemic stroke only in a subset).

key_findings.finding: 56 of 59 approached studies took part, giving 261 991 participants of European descent (48% women; mean age per study 58, range 26-75) with 20 259 coronary heart disease events, 10 164 strokes (4339 ischaemic) and 14 549 type 2 diabetes cases; all studies genotyped rs1229984 directly (median call rate 98.8%).

key_findings.finding: Instrument and alcohol (carriers v non-carriers): 17.2% fewer UK units per week (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%; 46 studies, 218 969 people; P=5.5×10−76; I2 64%); top third of intake OR 0.70 (0.68 to 0.73); binge drinking 0.78 (0.73 to 0.84); self-reported abstention 1.27 (1.21 to 1.34); γ-glutamyltransferase −1.84% (−3.40 to −0.26). One UK unit is 10 mL or 7.9 g of ethanol.

Light (>0 to <7) 0.90 (0.79 to 1.02; 4686 in 47 246); moderate (≥7 to <21) 0.89 (0.75 to 1.06; 3222 in 33 772); heavy (≥21) 0.97 (0.76 to 1.24; 1919 in 16 225); P for trend across the three 0.828 (meta-regression).

key_findings.finding: The Methods state that, if the observational U-shape were causal, carriers should have higher coronary risk among light-to-moderate drinkers (>0 to <21 units/week) and lower risk among heavy drinkers (≥21), and that the variant should have no or an attenuated effect in non-drinkers.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: No protocol or registration was published, so whether the expectation was set before the analysis cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that for the traits associated with the variant overall, associations were null or substantially reduced in non-drinkers, as expected if the variant acts only through alcohol. Figure 1 shows associations in non-drinkers of about the same size as in light-to-moderate drinkers for systolic blood pressure (−0.80 v −0.68 mm Hg), interleukin-6 (−7.15% v −7.24%), body mass index (−0.21 v −0.11) and C-reactive protein (−3.32% v −3.52%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Principal findings of study, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's main check of the no-other-path assumption is weaker than described: either self-reported non-drinkers include many former or occasional drinkers, or the variant affects these traits outside current drinking. Claims should not cite the non-drinker analysis as confirming the instrument.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the protective association "remained the same across all categories" of drinking, citing P=0.83 for heterogeneity, but the stratum estimates in Figure 2 (light 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02; moderate 0.89, 0.75 to 1.06; heavy 0.97, 0.76 to 1.24) each include 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-significant heterogeneity test is presented as evidence of an equal effect; the benefit for light or moderate drinkers is not established by these estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe the null coronary association in non-drinkers and the reduced odds in drinkers as consistent with the instrument acting through alcohol, without the formal test of their difference, which Figure 2 gives as P=0.095.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The difference between non-drinkers and drinkers that supports the exclusion assumption for coronary heart disease is not statistically established.

reporting_issues.issue: The stratified coronary analysis covers 16 013 of the 20 259 events (non-drinkers 5883 plus drinkers 10 130), and the three drinker categories sum to 9827 events and 97 243 people against 10 130 events and 107 478 people for all drinkers (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2); the text does not explain the missing events.
reporting_issues.consequence: About a fifth of coronary events, and some drinkers, are absent from the stratified estimates, which are therefore based on a subset of studies or participants that may differ from the whole.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that reduction is beneficial even for light to moderate drinkers is stronger than the Discussion's corresponding sentence, which says such reductions may be beneficial.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Conclusions); Discussion › Meaning of the study
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline wording should not be carried into claims; the paper's own discussion is more tentative.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods specify three drinking strata (0, >0 to <21, ≥21 units/week) chosen to represent the U-shape; the coronary results are reported in four (with light and moderate split at 7 units/week), a subdivision introduced in the Results.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph; Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the finer split is not prespecified, and it lowers the precision of each stratum estimate.
