design_detail: Systematic review with country-specific random-effects meta-analyses (Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation) of the prevalence of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) among children and youth in the general population: 24 studies with 1416 children and youth with FASD (ages 0 to 16.4) from 8 countries, published November 1973 to June 2015, limited to active case ascertainment or clinic-based studies with a stated diagnostic guideline or case definition. The 6 countries with two or more studies were pooled; the other 181 of 187 countries, including Canada and Norway with one study each, were assigned a predicted prevalence: the drinking-during-pregnancy prevalence from Popova et al. (2017) divided by a quotient of 13 women who drank per FASD case, derived from countries with a WHO drinking-pattern score of 3 or less. Monte Carlo intervals; WHO regional and global means weighted by live births; ratios to selected special-population studies. PROSPERO CRD42016033837.
can_establish: The range of FASD prevalence found up to mid-2015 by active case ascertainment and clinic-based studies in 8 countries (below 1 to 207.5 per 1000) and pooled estimates for the 6 countries with two or more such studies, together with model-based working estimates elsewhere.
cannot_establish: Measured FASD prevalence for 181 of 187 countries, including the global and regional figures, which are predictions from self-reported and mostly modelled drinking in pregnancy; an individual's risk at any level of drinking (the 1-in-13 figure is an aggregate ratio from an unstated set of countries); effects of dose, pattern or timing; or valid comparisons between countries whose estimates differ in diagnostic system, age at assessment and ascertainment method.

sample.recruitment: MEDLINE, MEDLINE in process, EMBASE, ERIC, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Scopus, November 1, 1973 to June 30, 2015, without geographic or language restriction (keywords in eTable 1, not read); plus contents pages of major epidemiology journals, citation screening and contact with leading FASD experts and researchers about pending publications; non-English studies translated by fluent colleagues or with Google Translate checked by a native speaker (Methods › Comprehensive Systematic Search Strategy).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original quantitative research in a peer-reviewed journal or scholarly report that measured FASD (or any combination of diagnoses in the spectrum), gave a CI or SE or the sample size or case count, specified the diagnostic guideline or case definition, and used active case ascertainment or clinic-based methods; no age restriction. Excluded: pooled estimates, passive surveillance, duplicate publications (Methods › Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria). No study of adults was found (Results › Comprehensive Systematic Literature Search).
sample.demographics: Table 1: study periods from 1974-1975 to 2012-2013; sample sizes 160 to 1,533,333; ages 0 to 16.4 years, with four studies of newborns or live births; percentage male 46.1 to 63.0 where reported; 18 studies used active case ascertainment, 5 were clinic-based and 1 used mixed methods; 11 of 24 (45.8%) used the clarification of the Institute of Medicine criteria. Countries: Australia 2 studies, Canada 1, Croatia 2, France 4, Italy 2, Norway 1, South Africa 6, USA 6.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Data come from 8 countries, half the studies from South Africa and the USA; none from Asia, Latin America or the Eastern Mediterranean. The authors note that the studies were not nationally representative and that some may have been done where FASD was more prevalent; the South African studies are from selected communities in the Western and Northern Cape. Restriction to the general population removes high-prevalence groups. Two newer South African studies reporting 170 to 259 per 1000 fell outside the search window (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Maternal drinking is not extracted from the FASD studies. For prediction, each country's prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy is taken from Popova et al. (2017): self-reported and, for 158 of 187 countries, itself a model prediction.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed: the authors state that the effect of the timing, dose and frequency of prenatal alcohol exposure on FASD risk could not be examined (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (prevalence review). Special-population prevalences from select studies are expressed as multiples of the global estimate.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to prevalence. The quotient assumes the same ratio of FASD cases to women who drank in pregnancy everywhere; countries with drinking-pattern scores of 4 or 5 were left out of its derivation because they would give an unrealistically high ratio, but the resulting quotient is applied to those countries as well.

outcomes.instruments: FASD as defined in each study (Table 1): the clarification of the Institute of Medicine criteria (11 studies), Institute of Medicine criteria, the 4-digit diagnostic code, CDC diagnostic guidelines, guidelines of the Fetal Alcohol Study Group of the Research Society on Alcoholism, criteria by Sokol and Clarren, an adapted 4-digit code with American Academy of Pediatrics criteria, or a case definition stated by the authors. The breakdown into FAS, partial FAS and other diagnoses is in eTable 2 (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was appraised on seven criteria from a prevalence appraisal tool (representative sample, appropriate recruitment, sample of at least 300, description of participants and setting, coverage of the identified sample, objective standard criteria for FASD, appropriate statistics); results in eTable 3, not read; whether appraisal was done in duplicate is not stated. The authors state that the diagnostic systems overlap but lack diagnostic reliability and that their sensitivity and specificity are unknown (Methods › Critical Appraisal of Identified Studies; Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: FASD prevalence per 1000 children and youth in the general population, pooled by country; WHO regional and global means weighted by live births for the latest year available (2000-2014); the 630,000 annual births figure applies the global prevalence to live births.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. How studies were screened and selected, and by how many reviewers, is not reported. Extracted data were checked by one author (S.L.) against the original articles, with discrepancies reconciled by team discussion; who did the extraction is not stated (Methods › Data Extraction).

analysis.effect_sizes: Global FASD prevalence among children and youth in the general population 7.7 per 1000 (95% CI 4.9-11.7); European region 19.8 (14.1-28.0); Americas 8.8 (6.4-13.2); African region 7.8 (5.4-10.7); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5-11.7); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6-5.3); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1-0.5) (Table 2). Highest countries: South Africa 111.1 (71.1-158.4; meta-analysis), Croatia 53.3 (30.9-81.2; meta-analysis), Ireland 47.5 (28.0-73.6; prediction), Italy 45.0 (35.1-56.1; meta-analysis), Belarus 36.6 (23.7-53.2; prediction); 76 of 187 countries above 1%. Quotient: one FASD case per 13 women who drank during pregnancy, about 630,000 children with FASD born each year (more than 1700 a day). Study-level prevalence (Table 1) ranges from 0.1 per 1000 (Australia, national, n = 1,533,333) and 0.4 (French newborns) to 207.5 per 1000 (South Africa, Western Cape). Special populations, as multiples of the global estimate: aboriginal 15.6 to 24.6, children in care 5.2 to 67.7, correctional 30.3, low socioeconomic status 23.7, psychiatric care 18.5 (study values 40.0 to 521.1 per 1000; Figure 2 legend). Heterogeneity and publication-bias results only in eTable 5 (not read); no prediction intervals.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42016033837 (record read): registered on 31 January 2016, after the search closed in June 2015, with a review start date of 1 May 2015; version 1.1 (11 July 2017) marks the review completed. The record planned FAS and FASD prevalence in the general population and in Aboriginal or Indigenous and other special populations, ten appraisal criteria, two-reviewer selection, and exact confidence intervals for countries with a single study. The paper appraises with seven criteria, does not report how selection was done, compares special populations through select studies rather than a systematic synthesis, predicts the two single-study countries (Canada, Norway) from drinking prevalence, and adds the quotient and the drinking-pattern exclusion, which the record does not describe. The record's synthesis text refers to alcohol consumption in pregnancy, apparently copied from the companion record.
analysis.selective_reporting: Country estimates (eTable 4), forest plots (eFigure 2), heterogeneity and publication-bias tests (eTable 5), appraisal results (eTable 3), the quotient's derivation (eMethods) and the flow diagram (eFigure 1) are only in the supplement, which was not read. Special populations were compared using select studies without stated selection criteria. Publication bias was judged unlikely in advance and would not have been adjusted for if found (Methods › Meta-analyses).
analysis.power: Country pools rest on 2 to 6 studies; which countries entered the quotient, and how many, is not stated in the main text.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 24 studies in 8 countries, FASD prevalence ranged from below 1 to 207.5 per 1000, depending on country, age, setting and method: active case ascertainment studies in the USA, Italy, Croatia and South Africa found 5.1 to 207.5 per 1000, while newborn clinic studies in France and a national Australian study found 0.1 to 5.6 per 1000. Pooled national estimates exist for 6 countries; every other figure, including the global 7.7 per 1000, is the modelled drinking prevalence divided by 13 (editors' arithmetic: 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1000; European 25.2% / 13 = 19.4; Americas 11.2% / 13 = 8.6).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The Key Points present "approximately 8 of 1000 in the general population had fetal alcohol spectrum disorder" and the 1-in-13 ratio as findings of a meta-analysis of 24 studies; the first is mostly a model output and the second an aggregate ratio from an unstated set of countries, not a risk for an individual pregnancy. (2) Prevalence above 1% in 76 countries is almost entirely predicted: under the quotient any country whose drinking-in-pregnancy prevalence exceeds 13% passes 1% by construction (editors' arithmetic). (3) The Discussion compares these 76 countries' FASD prevalence with US birth-defect rates (anencephaly, Down syndrome, spina bifida, trisomy 18) on the strength of those predictions. (4) The Conclusions say FASD occurs throughout society regardless of socioeconomic status, education or ethnicity; the study analysed none of these. (5) That most affected children and youth will require lifelong care, and the 630,000 births a year, are not results of this review's data. (6) Publication bias is dismissed in advance on the argument that any unexpected prevalence would be published. The limitations paragraph does state the self-report, diagnostic, representativeness and prediction problems.

timeline.event: Hoyme et al. (2005), the clarification of the 1996 Institute of Medicine criteria, used by 11 of the 24 included studies.
Popova et al. (2017), companion FAS and drinking-in-pregnancy meta-analysis by the same team from the same FAS search; its drinking estimates drive the FASD predictions here (card sc_popova_2017).
Chudley, accompanying editorial in JAMA Pediatrics (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2017.2232), linked from the PMC page; not read.
May et al. (2018), Prevalence of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders in 4 US communities (JAMA 319:474; alcohol evidence map, Tier C), linked from the PMC page as related; not read in this session.

Pichini, Pacifici and Busardò, letter in JAMA Pediatrics (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0044) questioning that Italy was among the five countries with the highest FASD prevalence; only its opening paragraph was visible.

Lange, Rehm and Popova, reply (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0058): the Italian estimate (45.0 per 1000) pools two active case ascertainment studies with randomly selected schools, a diagnostic system endorsed by the Institute of Medicine and experienced dysmorphologists, 1519 children screened; the reply adds that the letter writers had raised a similar concern about the companion FAS paper.

replication.where_it_stands: The standard source for a global FASD prevalence of about 8 per 1000 children and youth and for 1 FASD case per 13 pregnancies with drinking. Only 6 national estimates are pooled from observations; all other figures, including the global and regional ones, are the companion paper's drinking-in-pregnancy prevalences divided by 13. Claims should cite study-level or country-pooled measured figures where possible (for example South Africa 111.1, Croatia 53.3 and Italy 45.0 per 1000 from active case ascertainment) and present the global figure as a model estimate. A later US four-community study (May et al., 2018) is linked from the PMC page; it was not read here. No correction is linked on the PMC or JAMA Pediatrics pages (checked 27 October 2026).

funding.funder: Not reported: neither the PMC full text nor the JAMA Pediatrics article page carries a funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported (Conflict of Interest Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: Five of the six authors are at the Institute for Mental Health Policy Research, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (with University of Toronto, Technische Universität Dresden and University of New South Wales affiliations); one is at the Department of Pediatrics, University of North Dakota School of Medicine. The same team wrote Popova et al. (2017), whose estimates and methods this paper builds on. No industry funding or ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Active case ascertainment studies using one validated diagnostic system in randomly sampled school populations of the countries now covered only by prediction, with maternal drinking measured in the same samples, would replace modelled with measured prevalence and show how the ratio of FASD cases to exposed pregnancies varies with drinking pattern.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (children and youth in the general population), condition (FASD), outcome (prevalence) and eligible study methods are specified.

PROSPERO CRD42016033837 was registered on 31 January 2016, after the search closed (June 2015); the paper does not state that methods were set beforehand, and it departs from the record (seven instead of ten appraisal criteria, prediction instead of exact intervals for single-study countries, the quotient, special populations by select studies) without explanation.
Restriction to active case ascertainment (described as the criterion standard) and clinic-based studies, and exclusion of passive surveillance, is explained by the quality of case ascertainment.

Eight databases with keywords in a supplement, no language restriction, journal hand-searching, citation screening and contact with experts; but the search closed about 26 months before online publication (August 2017), and two newer South African studies are acknowledged as missing.
The paper does not report how screening and selection were done or by how many reviewers (the protocol planned two).
Extracted data were checked by one author against the original articles, with discrepancies reconciled by team discussion, which meets the item's consensus criterion; who extracted is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies with reasons appears in the article; the flow diagram (eFigure 1) is in the unread supplement.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country and region, study period, sample size, cases, prevalence, diagnostic system, sex, age range and method; how communities or schools were chosen, participation and setting are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A prevalence-appropriate seven-criterion tool was used, but its results are only in eTable 3 (not read), duplicate appraisal is not stated, and diagnostic reliability and age at assessment are not addressed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of double-arcsine-transformed proportions is standard, but combining is not justified: newborn clinic studies are pooled with school-age active case ascertainment within countries (France: 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 per 1000 in newborns with 66.0 on Réunion Island), studies with data from 1974 to 2013 yield estimates labelled 2012, heterogeneity is not reported in the article, there are no prediction intervals, and the observed single studies for Canada and Norway are replaced by predictions.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how study quality affects the pooled or predicted estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations discuss self-reported drinking, varying diagnostic systems, non-representative and regionally confined samples, and prediction error.
Heterogeneity tests are only in eTable 5; the article neither reports nor discusses them, although study prevalences within France range from 0.4 to 66.0 per 1000.
Tests were run (results in eTable 5), but publication bias was judged unlikely in advance and would not have been adjusted for if found; its likely impact is not discussed on the evidence.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors report no conflicts of interest, which meets the item; there is, however, no funding statement at all.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, no protocol before the review; 7, no list of excluded studies; 11, unjustified combining and unreported heterogeneity; 15, publication bias dismissed in advance) and two are only partly met (4, the search; 9, the risk-of-bias assessment); by the AMSTAR 2 rule confidence is critically low. Beyond the instrument, the global, regional and 181 of 187 national figures are not meta-analytic results but drinking prevalences divided by a single ratio. The country pools for South Africa, Croatia, Italy and the USA rest on recognized active case ascertainment studies and are the most citable numbers in the paper.

key_findings.finding: 24 unique studies were included, covering 1416 children and youth diagnosed with FASD, aged 0 to 16.4 years, from 8 countries: Australia (2 studies), Canada (1), Croatia (2), France (4), Italy (2), Norway (1), South Africa (6) and the USA (6). 18 used active case ascertainment, 5 clinic-based methods and 1 mixed methods; 45.8% used the clarification of the Institute of Medicine criteria. No study of adults was found.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comprehensive Systematic Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Study-level FASD prevalence per 1000 (Table 1): South Africa 63.9 to 207.5 (six active case ascertainment studies, ages 4.8 to 16.4); Croatia 40.8 (urban) and 66.8 (rural); Italy 40.5 and 47.1; France 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 in newborns (clinic-based) and 66.0 on Réunion Island (active case ascertainment); Norway 1.1; Canada 5.3; USA 5.1 to 33.5; Australia 0.1 (national, 1,533,333 children) and 1.7 (Northern Territory).
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: The Réunion Island row prints 75 cases in 1320 children as 66.0 per 1000; 75/1320 is 56.8 per 1000 (editors' arithmetic; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Highest country estimates per 1000: South Africa 111.1 (95% CI 71.1-158.4) and Croatia 53.3 (30.9-81.2), both by meta-analysis; Ireland 47.5 (28.0-73.6) by prediction; Italy 45.0 (35.1-56.1) by meta-analysis; Belarus 36.6 (23.7-53.2) by prediction. 76 of 187 countries had a predicted or observed prevalence above 1%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Global FASD prevalence among children and youth in the general population: 7.7 per 1000 (95% CI 4.9-11.7). By WHO region: European 19.8 (14.1-28.0), highest; Americas 8.8 (6.4-13.2); African 7.8 (5.4-10.7); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5-11.7); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6-5.3); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1-0.5), lowest.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Abstract › Results

key_findings.finding: For countries with one or no study, prevalence was predicted from Popova et al.'s drinking-in-pregnancy prevalence using a quotient of women who drank per FASD case, derived only from countries with a WHO drinking-pattern score of 3 or less (countries scoring 4 or more were excluded as giving an unrealistically high ratio); the quotient is 1 FASD case per 13 women who drank, implying about 630,000 children with FASD born each year, more than 1700 a day.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Prevalence Estimation, 1st paragraph; Results › Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Which countries entered the quotient is given only in the eMethods (not read).

key_findings.finding: Editors' arithmetic: the regional estimates are close to the companion paper's regional drinking prevalence divided by 13 (global 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1000, printed 7.7; European 25.2% / 13 = 19.4, printed 19.8; Americas 11.2% / 13 = 8.6, printed 8.8; South-East Asia 1.8% / 13 = 1.4, printed 1.4). Set against the companion FAS quotient of 1 in 67, the two papers imply about 5 FASD cases per FAS case (67 / 13 = 5.2), whereas the companion paper cites a ratio of about 9 or 10.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic using the drinking prevalences of Popova et al. (2017), Table; the small differences come from the six meta-analysed countries.

key_findings.finding: FASD in special populations from select studies, per 1000 (Figure 2 legend): adoptees from Eastern Europe in Sweden 521.1; foster and adopted youth referred to a US children's mental health centre 285.2; a correctional population in Canada 233.5; an aboriginal population in Canada 189.7; a rural low-socioeconomic-status population in South Africa 182.4; children in a Brazilian orphanage 170.2; a US psychiatric-care population 142.4; an aboriginal population in Australia 120.4; children before adoption or in foster care in Israel 40.0. As multiples of the global estimate: 15.6 to 24.6 (aboriginal), 5.2 to 67.7 (children in care), 30.3 (correctional), 23.7 (low socioeconomic status), 18.5 (psychiatric care).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of the Global Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population With the Prevalence in Special Populations, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Publication bias was tested by funnel plot, rank correlation and weighted regression, but the authors judged it unlikely in advance, reasoning that any prevalence substantially different from earlier estimates would have been published, and did not adjust for it if found; test results are in eTable 5.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Results › Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: predictions rest on self-reported drinking in pregnancy, likely under-reported; different diagnostic guidelines and case definitions may have affected the pooled prevalence in a direction that depends on their sensitivity and specificity; not all studies were nationally representative, and some may have been done where FASD was more prevalent; predicted values carry measurement error; timing, dose and frequency of exposure could not be examined. Two newer South African studies (170 to 259 per 1000) were outside the search window.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that current diagnostic guidelines overlap but lack diagnostic reliability owing to low convergent validity, and that their sensitivity, specificity and accuracy are unknown for lack of an external standard, which can lead to misclassification.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In a published reply to a letter questioning the Italian estimate, the authors state that Italy's 45.0 per 1000 (3.5% to 5.6%) pools two active case ascertainment studies using random selection of schools, an Institute of Medicine-endorsed diagnostic system and experienced dysmorphologists, with 1519 children screened.
key_findings.locator: JAMA Pediatrics, Global Prevalence of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder in Italy, Reply (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0058), 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists the two Italian studies with 543 and 976 children (1519 in total).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the Réunion Island study (Serreau et al., 2002) as 75 FASD cases in 1320 children with a prevalence of 66.0 per 1000; 75/1320 is 56.8 per 1000 (editors' arithmetic). Every other row of Table 1 reproduces from its cases and sample size.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the sample size or the prevalence is misprinted (66.0 per 1000 would need about 1136 children); the French pooled estimate may carry the error. The same values appear on the JAMA Pediatrics page.

reporting_issues.issue: Passive surveillance was an exclusion criterion, yet Harris and Bucens (2003, Australia, Northern Territory) is included with a method described as mixed methods (passive surveillance and clinic based).
reporting_issues.consequence: The inclusion criteria were not applied strictly; Australia's pooled estimate partly rests on surveillance data.

reporting_issues.issue: Elliott et al. (2008), a national Australian study of 1,533,333 children with 92 cases (0.06 per 1000, editors' arithmetic), is classed as active case ascertainment, which the paper defines as researchers actively seeking, assessing and identifying cases; its prevalence is 18 to more than 3000 times lower than in the other active case ascertainment studies (1.1 to 207.5 per 1000; editors' arithmetic), and how cases were found is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The method label may group very different ascertainment designs; Australia's pooled estimate depends on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The two countries with a single study, Canada (5.3 per 1000) and Norway (1.1 per 1000), are assigned predicted values, which are given only in eTable 4; the main text does not show how far the predictions depart from the observed values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Observed data are set aside in favour of a model for these two countries, contrary to the registered plan of reporting single studies with exact intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend gives FASD in a Brazilian orphanage (Strömland et al.) as 170.2 per 1000, while the companion paper by the same team (Popova et al., 2017, Discussion, 3rd paragraph) gives FAS in the same orphanage as 3191 per 10,000 (319.1 per 1000), although FAS is a subset of FASD.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the two figures is wrong; neither should be cited without checking the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding statement appears in the PMC full text or on the JAMA Pediatrics article page.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding cannot be recorded; the companion paper reports institutional funding by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health only.

design_detail: Mendelian randomization, two-sample, using published summary statistics: up to 94 variants associated at genome-wide significance with alcohol consumption (log-transformed drinks per week) in a genome-wide study of 941 280 people of European descent (GSCAN; Liu et al., 2019, ref 16) as instruments, and variant-outcome associations from case-control genome-wide consortia (MEGASTROKE, CARDIoGRAMplusC4D, AFGen, ISGC) and from case/non-case analyses in UK Biobank, for eight primary cardiovascular diseases and three stroke types. Methods: random-effects inverse-variance weighted analysis (primary), weighted median, MR-PRESSO, MR-Egger, and multivariable Mendelian randomization adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation; the ADH1B rs1229984 variant alone as a secondary instrument; UK Biobank never-smokers as a sensitivity analysis. The methods are described in detail only in the Data Supplement (not read). Labelled case-control under the round brief's rule (outcome associations come from case-control genome-wide studies, with UK Biobank case/non-case data alongside) and appraised with ROBINS-E, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether people genetically predisposed to drink more, in European-ancestry data, have higher odds of stroke, peripheral artery disease and six other cardiovascular diseases, by an approach less exposed than conventional studies to confounding by lifestyle and to reverse causation.
cannot_establish: The shape of the relationship, including any J- or U-shape (the authors say they could not examine it); the effect of a given number of drinks (estimates are per SD of log-transformed drinks per week, an SD not reported in the main text); effects in non-European populations; and whether part of the association runs through smoking (the instrument predicts smoking initiation) or through education (the ADH1B variant is associated with it).

sample.recruitment: Consortium and biobank data: published genome-wide summary statistics (GSCAN for alcohol consumption and smoking initiation; SSGAC for education; MEGASTROKE, CARDIoGRAMplusC4D, AFGen and ISGC for outcomes) and UK Biobank analyses under application 29202 (Figure 1; Acknowledgments).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Variants associated with alcohol consumption at genome-wide significance in the exposure study; selection details are in the Data Supplement (not read).
sample.demographics: Exposure data from people of European descent; outcome consortia mostly of European ancestry, with stroke (MEGASTROKE) and atrial fibrillation (AFGen) results similar when restricted to European-descent participants (Table XII, not read). The alcohol-lowering rs1229984 allele has a frequency of 0.026 in UK Biobank (Discussion › Comparison With Other Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (summary data).
sample.selection_effects: UK Biobank contributes to the exposure genome-wide study and to most outcome datasets, so samples overlap (the authors note possible bias). Case definitions and case selection differ between consortia; several outcomes have few cases (aortic valve stenosis 2244, abdominal aortic aneurysm 1094, subarachnoid haemorrhage 1084), and the ISGC intracerebral haemorrhage dataset is small (1545 cases, 1481 non-cases).

exposure.measurement: Genetic instrument for self-reported alcohol consumption in drinks per week, log-transformed, from the exposure genome-wide study (how drinks were defined and whether non-drinkers were included are in that study and the Data Supplement, not read). No individual-level intake was analysed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: All estimates are per 1-SD increase in log-transformed drinks per week; the size of that SD, and the grams it corresponds to, are not given in the main text. Instrument strength (F statistics) is not reported in the main text.
exposure.polysubstance: Genetically predicted drinking was associated with smoking initiation (OR 1.24, 1.15 to 1.33; P=9.5×10−9); multivariable Mendelian randomization adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation, and UK Biobank never-smokers were analysed separately (Table XI, not read). The ADH1B variant showed no association with smoking initiation (OR 0.97, 0.89 to 1.07; P=0.57).

comparison.controls: Non-cases in each outcome dataset (consortium controls, or UK Biobank participants without the condition); the genetic estimates compare people along a continuous scale of genetic predisposition to drink, with no drinking reference group.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Education: weak association of the overall instrument with fewer years of schooling (β −0.09 years, −0.17 to 0.00; P=0.05) and a clearer one for the ADH1B variant (β −0.15, −0.23 to −0.08; P=5.4×10−5), which the authors note could create horizontal pleiotropy for coronary artery disease.

outcomes.instruments: Eight primary outcomes (stroke, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, venous thromboembolism, peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis, abdominal aortic aneurysm); secondary: ischaemic stroke (with its subtypes in MEGASTROKE), intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage; possible mediators (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, HDL and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides) and confounders (smoking initiation, education).
outcomes.validity_norms: Case definitions follow each consortium or UK Biobank coding (Data Supplement, not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Odds ratio of disease per 1-SD increase in log-transformed drinks per week (random-effects inverse-variance weighted); beta per SD for mediators.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated in the main text. 18 counts the eight primary and three secondary cardiovascular outcomes, five mediators and two confounders (plus four ischaemic stroke subtypes); associations with P near 0.05 are described as some or suggestive evidence.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Genetic; overall instrument; OR per 1-SD increase in log drinks/week; inverse-variance weighted / multivariable adjusted for smoking initiation] stroke 1.27 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.45; P=2.87×10−4) / 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40; P=0.010); coronary artery disease 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36; P=0.052) / 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27); atrial fibrillation 1.17 (1.00 to 1.37; P=0.050) / 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32); heart failure 1.00 (0.68 to 1.47) / 0.88 (0.57 to 1.37); venous thromboembolism 1.04 (0.77 to 1.39) / 1.05 (0.75 to 1.47); peripheral artery disease 3.05 (1.92 to 4.85; P=2.30×10−6) / 2.55 (1.49 to 4.35; P=6.09×10−4); aortic valve stenosis 1.03 (0.56 to 1.90) / 0.94 (0.46 to 1.91); abdominal aortic aneurysm 2.60 (1.15 to 5.89; P=0.022) / 2.29 (0.89 to 5.93; P=0.087) (Figure 3). Ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46; P=0.002) and intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32; P=0.001), combining consortium and UK Biobank data (Figure 4). Mediators: systolic blood pressure 0.12 (0.05 to 0.20), diastolic 0.15 (0.05 to 0.25), HDL cholesterol 0.39 (0.25 to 0.53), LDL cholesterol −0.01 (−0.18 to 0.16), triglycerides −0.37 (−0.67 to −0.07) (Figure 2; the units printed there are doubtful, see reporting issues). [ADH1B rs1229984 only] ischaemic stroke 1.31 (1.05 to 1.65; P=0.018), intracerebral haemorrhage 11.5 (1.31 to 101.46; P=0.027).
analysis.covariates: Multivariable Mendelian randomization adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: All eight primary outcomes are reported with both main methods (Figure 3); secondary methods, single-variant results and sensitivity analyses are in supplementary tables (not read).
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors note low precision for outcomes with few cases.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Genetic predisposition to drink more was associated with higher odds of stroke (1.27 per SD of log drinks/week), especially intracerebral haemorrhage (3.53), and of peripheral artery disease (3.05), and these associations remained after adjustment for genetic liability to smoking; associations with coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation and abdominal aortic aneurysm were weaker and lost significance after smoking adjustment; there was no association with heart failure, venous thromboembolism or aortic valve stenosis.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions report "evidence of a causal relationship" for stroke and peripheral artery disease. That wording depends on the Mendelian randomization assumptions holding; the authors' own data show that the instrument predicts smoking initiation, and the smoking-adjusted estimates are smaller. The peripheral artery disease result rests on 3415 UK Biobank cases, in a biobank that also contributed to the exposure study. The Discussion's remark that, because heavy drinking was uncommon in UK Biobank, the burden of risk is unlikely to be confined to heavy drinkers is an inference the linear analysis cannot test, since the authors concede they could not examine J- or U-shapes. The Discussion also says the overall instrument showed no association with education, where the Results report weak evidence (P=0.05). Otherwise the paper is cautious about coronary artery disease and the other outcomes.

timeline.event: Holmes et al. (European ancestry, ADH1B rs1229984): lower coronary heart disease odds in carriers of the intake-lowering allele; this paper says its own rs1229984 results for stroke and coronary artery disease largely confirm that study.

Millwood et al. (China Kadoorie Biobank, ALDH2 and ADH1B): positive genetic associations with stroke, stronger for intracerebral haemorrhage, and none with myocardial infarction; this paper says it extends the stroke findings to European ancestry.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease (listed in the project's DOI list); published before this paper and not read for this card.

Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank, scores for alcohol use disorder): linear Mendelian randomization associations with stroke (OR 1.26, 1.04 to 1.54) and coronary artery disease (1.38), citing this paper; both studies use UK Biobank outcome data, so the agreement is not independent replication.

replication.where_it_stands: For stroke, genetic studies in European and east Asian populations agree that higher genetically predicted intake goes with more stroke, more strongly with intracerebral haemorrhage (Millwood et al., 2019; this study). Peripheral artery disease and aortic aneurysm rest on single datasets with few cases and need replication outside UK Biobank. For coronary disease the genetic evidence is inconsistent across instruments and populations.

funding.declared_conflicts: Disclosures: none (as printed).
funding.affiliations_note: Uppsala University and Karolinska Institutet (S C Larsson, K Michaëlsson); Department of Public Health and Primary Care, MRC Biostatistics Unit and British Heart Foundation Cardiovascular Epidemiology Unit, University of Cambridge (S Burgess, A M Mason). According to this paper's reference list, S Burgess is also an author of Wood et al. (2018), the pooled analysis of 83 prospective studies. No ties to the alcohol industry are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Replication of the peripheral artery disease, aortic aneurysm and intracerebral haemorrhage associations in outcome data independent of UK Biobank and of the exposure study, with instruments not associated with smoking; and nonlinear analyses of individual-level data to see whether the stroke association extends down to light intake.

domains.note: Instrument independence: European-descent exposure data and partly multi-ancestry outcome consortia (restricted analyses similar); the authors say population stratification cannot be ruled out. Exclusion restriction: the instrument predicts smoking initiation (OR 1.24) and the ADH1B variant predicts education; MR-Egger indicated directional pleiotropy only for aortic valve stenosis; weighted median, MR-PRESSO and multivariable analyses were used; the stroke and peripheral artery disease associations persisted after smoking adjustment and in never-smokers.

Relevance: variants at genome-wide significance in 941 280 people, but no F statistic in the main text; overlap of UK Biobank between exposure and outcome data can bias estimates towards the conventional association if instruments are weak (the authors note possible bias). Shape at low intake: the exposure scale (per SD of log drinks per week) cannot be converted into grams and the linear analysis cannot show what happens at low intake.

Selection into the source studies: case-control consortia and UK Biobank volunteers, with overlapping samples; recruitment into these studies is outside the authors' control and could relate to both drinking and disease.
Not applicable: the instrument is fixed at conception.
Not applicable to summary data beyond the use of outcomes with available genome-wide results.
Definitions vary between consortia and UK Biobank (Data Supplement, not read); misclassification is unlikely to depend on genotype and would mainly dilute associations.
Methods only in a supplement; no registered plan; 18 outcomes without a stated correction; all primary outcomes are nonetheless reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A standard summary-data Mendelian randomization with a strong multi-variant instrument and the usual sensitivity analyses. For stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage the results are consistent across methods, after adjustment for smoking liability and with the ADH1B variant alone, and agree with the east Asian genetic data; for peripheral artery disease and aortic aneurysm they rest on few UK Biobank cases with sample overlap; for coronary artery disease and atrial fibrillation they are borderline and sensitive to smoking adjustment. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: genetic evidence in European-ancestry data that higher genetically predicted alcohol intake is associated with higher odds of stroke (particularly intracerebral haemorrhage) and of peripheral artery disease. Do not cite it for: risk at a particular intake, the shape of the relation, or a firm effect on coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, venous thromboembolism or aortic valve stenosis.

key_findings.finding: Data sources: instrument variants from a genome-wide study of alcohol consumption in 941 280 people of European descent; outcomes (cases/non-cases) stroke 76 814/812 384 (MEGASTROKE, UK Biobank), coronary artery disease 90 079/461 812 (CARDIoGRAMplusC4D, UK Biobank), atrial fibrillation 65 446/522 744 (AFGen), and from UK Biobank heart failure 6712/360 874, venous thromboembolism 14 097/353 489, peripheral artery disease 3415/364 171, aortic valve stenosis 2244/365 342 and abdominal aortic aneurysm 1094/366 492; ischaemic stroke 64 943/817 434, intracerebral haemorrhage 2609/368 003 (ISGC, UK Biobank), subarachnoid haemorrhage 1084/366 502; blood pressure up to 367 284 and lipids up to 350 162 individuals (UK Biobank); smoking initiation 632 802 (GSCAN); education 766 345 (SSGAC).

key_findings.note: Values printed in the Figure 1 diagram (an image), read from the full-size figure image.

key_findings.finding: Possible mediators (overall instrument; beta per SD increase of log drinks per week; random-effects inverse-variance weighted): systolic blood pressure 0.12 (0.05 to 0.20; P=0.001; 346 656 people), diastolic 0.15 (0.05 to 0.25; P=0.003; 367 284), HDL cholesterol 0.39 (0.25 to 0.53; P=6.10×10−8; 320 717), LDL cholesterol −0.01 (−0.18 to 0.16; P=0.900; 349 795), triglycerides −0.37 (−0.67 to −0.07; P=0.016; 350 162).

key_findings.finding: Possible confounders: the overall instrument was strongly associated with smoking initiation (OR 1.24, 1.15 to 1.33; P=9.5×10−9) and weakly with education (β −0.09 years of schooling, −0.17 to 0.00; P=0.05). The ADH1B rs1229984 instrument was associated with higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure and LDL cholesterol, not with HDL cholesterol or triglycerides, not with smoking initiation (OR 0.97, 0.89 to 1.07; P=0.57), and with less education (β −0.15, −0.23 to −0.08; P=5.4×10−5).

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular diseases (overall instrument; OR per SD increase of log drinks per week; inverse-variance weighted, then adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation): stroke 1.27 (1.12 to 1.45; P=2.87×10−4), adjusted 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40; P=0.010); peripheral artery disease 3.05 (1.92 to 4.85; P=2.30×10−6), adjusted 2.55 (1.49 to 4.35; P=6.09×10−4); coronary artery disease 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36; P=0.052), adjusted 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27; P=0.389); atrial fibrillation 1.17 (1.00 to 1.37; P=0.050), adjusted 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32; P=0.237); abdominal aortic aneurysm 2.60 (1.15 to 5.89; P=0.022), adjusted 2.29 (0.89 to 5.93; P=0.087); heart failure 1.00 (0.68 to 1.47; P=0.996), adjusted 0.88 (0.57 to 1.37); venous thromboembolism 1.04 (0.77 to 1.39; P=0.810), adjusted 1.05 (0.75 to 1.47); aortic valve stenosis 1.03 (0.56 to 1.90; P=0.926), adjusted 0.94 (0.46 to 1.91).

key_findings.note: The smoking-adjusted estimates are printed only in Figure 3 (an image), read from the full-size image; the text says only that they were somewhat attenuated.

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: directional pleiotropy was indicated only for aortic valve stenosis (the main text does not name the test; MR-Egger is the likely one, in supplement Table X, not read); weighted median and MR-Egger analyses suggested positive associations with aortic valve stenosis; stroke and coronary artery disease estimates were similar using consortium data only and UK Biobank data only; in UK Biobank never-smokers the estimates resembled the smoking-adjusted ones, except that the coronary artery disease estimate was larger (OR 1.39, 0.98 to 1.96; P=0.064).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations With CVD, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stroke types (overall instrument, per SD of log drinks per week): ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46; P=0.002) combining MEGASTROKE and UK Biobank; intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32; P=0.001) combining ISGC and UK Biobank. By source: MEGASTROKE any ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.08 to 1.48), large artery 1.30 (0.93 to 1.82), small vessel 1.20 (0.88 to 1.64), cardioembolic 1.11 (0.79 to 1.56); UK Biobank ischaemic stroke 1.24 (0.84 to 1.84), subarachnoid haemorrhage 2.47 (1.08 to 5.62), intracerebral haemorrhage 3.81 (1.57 to 9.27); ISGC intracerebral haemorrhage 3.00 (0.83 to 10.82; 1545 cases, 1481 non-cases).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations With CVD, 2nd paragraph; Figure 4
key_findings.note: Source-specific estimates are printed in Figure 4 (an image), read from the full-size image.

key_findings.finding: With rs1229984 in ADH1B as the only instrument, genetically predicted drinking was associated (all P<0.05) with higher odds of any stroke, coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm; ischaemic stroke OR 1.31 (1.05 to 1.65; P=0.018), intracerebral haemorrhage 11.5 (1.31 to 101.46; P=0.027). Excluding rs1229984 from the overall instrument gave results similar to the full set.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: low precision for outcomes with few cases; UK Biobank in the variant-discovery, exposure and outcome datasets, which may bias estimates (stroke and coronary results were similar with consortium data only, and with rs1229984, which was not discovered in UK Biobank); population stratification not excluded; and no possibility of examining U- or J-shaped associations, so no statements about moderate versus heavy drinking.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of risk differences, written as the evidence base of an American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) practice guideline on the pharmacological management of alcohol withdrawal by the society's working group (chair M. F. Mayo-Smith; JAMA 1997;278:144–151). MEDLINE from 1966 to June 1995, English only; 134 articles with original data, including 65 prospective controlled trials of 42 medications. Meta-analyses only for delirium and seizures: benzodiazepines vs placebo (6 trials, 1961–1983), long- vs short-acting benzodiazepines (3 trials), and phenothiazines vs placebo or cross-tolerant medication (4 trials); other agents and dosing strategies reviewed narratively. Recommendations graded A to C by a published system (Cook et al., 1992). AMSTAR 2 is applied to the meta-analysis, as the round brief directs; the guideline's recommendations are reported only as what it recommended, without regimens or doses. The PDF is a scan; every number on this card was checked on the rendered page.
can_establish: What the 1997 ASAM guideline recommended for the pharmacological management of alcohol withdrawal, and the pooled absolute differences in delirium and seizures between benzodiazepines and placebo, between long- and short-acting benzodiazepines, and between phenothiazines and placebo or cross-tolerant medication, in the trials found up to mid-1995.
cannot_establish: Whether those pooled estimates are unbiased or complete (single-database English-language search, no appraisal of the trials' risk of bias, no heterogeneity or publication-bias analysis, six small placebo-controlled trials from 1961–1983); the effects of particular drugs, doses or regimens; outcomes in people already in delirium or after a seizure (out of scope), or in adolescents, older people, pregnant women or people with comorbid illness (no studies found); or anything published after June 1995.

sample.recruitment: MEDLINE search with the key words substance withdrawal syndrome and ethyl alcohol, from its first entries in 1966 through June 1995, plus references of selected articles and reviews; English-language articles with original clinical data on humans (p. 145, Methods › Review of the Evidence). The pooled trials' settings, participants and recruitment are not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies with clinical data; for data extraction and meta-analysis, prospective controlled trials with methodologically sound end points and documented reporting of the end point in question (p. 145). Outside the guideline's scope: patients seen after a withdrawal seizure or with established withdrawal delirium, and the choice of inpatient or outpatient setting; phenytoin had its own earlier guideline (p. 144, Introduction, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported for any trial.
sample.attrition: Not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One database, English only. The six placebo-controlled trials date from 1961 to 1983; the pooled delirium estimate leaves out two of them (Sellers et al. and Naranjo et al., 1983) because they did not report delirium, and the seizure estimate one (Rosenfeld & Bizzoco, 1961). Kaim et al. (1969) supplies 233 of the 358 patients in the delirium analysis and 8 of its 11 placebo-arm cases, and 9 of the 17 placebo-arm seizures (editors' counts from Table 2). No studies were found in adolescents, in older people, in pregnancy or in people with coexisting medical or substance use disorders (p. 148).

exposure.measurement: The interventions as given in the primary trials: benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide in four of the six placebo-controlled trials, diazepam and lorazepam in one each; Table 2), other sedative-hypnotics (chlormethiazole, barbital, tetrabamate, paraldehyde, phenobarbital), β-blockers, clonidine, carbamazepine, neuroleptics (promazine, chlorpromazine), magnesium, ethyl alcohol, thiamine and other agents; and two ways of giving medication, on a fixed schedule or triggered by symptoms measured on a scale.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted. The trials' regimens are not described trial by trial; Table 5 gives example regimens meeting the guideline, which the project does not reproduce (no dosing information). Amounts given in one trial are reported below only as a trial outcome.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the trials. The review names concurrent non-medical sedative-hypnotic use as a risk factor for major complications and advises caution in using withdrawal scales during withdrawal from other drugs (p. 148).

comparison.controls: Placebo (Table 2); other benzodiazepines (Table 3: long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam vs short-acting lorazepam or alprazolam); placebo, or cross-tolerant medication that combines benzodiazepines and paraldehyde (Table 4); fixed-schedule dosing vs symptom-triggered dosing in two randomized trials (text only).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (review).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline withdrawal severity, history of seizures or delirium, medical and psychiatric comorbidity and other drug use in the pooled trials are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Seven outcomes: severity of withdrawal and withdrawal delirium, each as defined in DSM-IV; withdrawal seizures; completion of withdrawal; entry into rehabilitation; adverse effects; and cost (acquisition costs from wholesale prices in the 1993 Red Book) (pp. 144–145). Only delirium and seizures were meta-analysed. Withdrawal scales discussed: CIWA-A and its revision, the CIWA-Ar.
outcomes.validity_norms: The pooled trials (1961–1986) predate DSM-IV (1994); how their definitions of delirium and seizures were matched to DSM-IV is not described.
outcomes.operationalization: Delirium and seizures as numbers of patients with the event in each arm; withdrawal severity by a count of trials favouring each drug (no pooled estimate).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two-tailed tests with significance at P≤.05 (p. 145). The 7 counted here are the pooled estimates (2 in Table 2, 1 in Table 3, 4 in Table 4); 7 outcomes were also listed, of which 2 were pooled.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the trials; not applicable at review level.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects meta-analysis of risk differences (refs 13–15); single-trial comparisons by Fisher exact test with Taylor-series 95% CIs for relative risks. Benzodiazepine vs placebo: delirium −4.9 cases per 100 patients (95% CI −9.0 to −0.7), P=.04, 4 trials; seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), P<.001 in Table 2 and P=.003 in the abstract and text, 5 trials. Long- vs short-acting benzodiazepines, seizures: −6.7 per 100 (−13.0 to −0.0), P=.07, 3 trials. Phenothiazine vs placebo: delirium 0.0 per 100 (−5.8 to +6.6), P=.92; seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9), P=.19. Phenothiazine vs cross-tolerant medication: delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8), P=.002; seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6), P<.001. Kaim et al. (1969) alone: chlordiazepoxide vs placebo, delirium RR 0.16 (0.02–1.24), P=.08, seizures RR 0.14 (0.02–1.09), P=.046; chlorpromazine vs chlordiazepoxide, delirium RR 7.4 (0.9–54), P=.03, seizures RR 12.6 (1.6–95), P=.001. Editors' sums from Table 2: delirium 3/172 (1.7%) with benzodiazepines vs 11/186 (5.9%) with placebo; seizures 1/182 (0.5%) vs 17/196 (8.7%); editors' calculation from the pooled risk differences: about 20 patients treated per delirium case avoided and about 13 per seizure avoided. Symptom-triggered vs fixed-schedule dosing (two randomized trials): significantly less medication and shorter treatment (abstract, P<.001); in the larger trial, median chlordiazepoxide 100 mg vs 425 mg and median duration 9 vs 68 hours, reported as trial outcomes.
analysis.covariates: None (crude event counts).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned. The draft guideline was reviewed by first authors of included articles from the past 10 years and representatives of 68 medical organizations; the ASAM board of directors approved it in June 1996, with review and revision scheduled for June 2001 (p. 145).
analysis.selective_reporting: Delirium was not reported in two of the six placebo-controlled trials and seizures in one; withdrawal severity, completion of withdrawal, entry into rehabilitation and adverse effects are described without pooled estimates; heterogeneity is never reported; the effectiveness outcomes of the two trials of symptom-triggered dosing are not given; the minimally clinically significant benefit on which the grades depend is not stated.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The review says the trials of several agents (chlormethiazole, barbital, tetrabamate, β-blockers, clonidine, magnesium) were too small to judge effects on delirium or seizures. Event counts in the benzodiazepine–placebo analyses are low: 3 vs 11 delirium cases and 1 vs 17 seizures (editors' sums).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six small placebo-controlled trials from 1961–1983 (four of chlordiazepoxide), benzodiazepines were associated with 4.9 fewer cases of delirium per 100 patients (95% CI 0.7 to 9.0 fewer; 3 vs 11 events) and 7.7 fewer seizures per 100 (3.5 to 12.0 fewer; 1 vs 17 events). In three trials, long-acting agents had 6.7 fewer seizures per 100 than short-acting ones (P=.07). Phenothiazines did not differ from placebo in delirium or seizures but had more of both than benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. Two randomized trials found symptom-triggered dosing used less medication and shorter treatment than fixed schedules. For other agents, trials showed relief of symptoms but were too small for delirium or seizures, and no studies were found in adolescents, older people, pregnancy or comorbid illness.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and recommendations match most of this, with these gaps. (1) The text says neuroleptics “increase the incidence of seizures compared with placebo” (p. 147), and the grade A recommendation against neuroleptic monotherapy gives increased seizures as a reason (p. 149), while the pooled comparison with placebo is +4.6 per 100 (−2.6 to +11.9; P=.19); more seizures are shown only against benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. (2) The recommendations state “There is no evidence that the recommendations should change” for adolescents or older people (p. 149), after a results section that found no studies in adolescents and none of treatment approaches in older people (p. 148): an absence of studies is presented as an absence of difference. (3) The abstract says benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal severity; this rests on a count of six trials without a pooled estimate, and one of the six cited references is an evaluation of a social-setting detoxification programme (p. 145). (4) The grades depend on a minimally clinically significant benefit that is never stated, and level I labels are given to findings resting on one cited trial of 40 patients (a smoother withdrawal with long-acting agents) or partly on reviews (potential for non-medical use). (5) The grade A recommendation for individualized, scale-guided dosing rests on two randomized trials, the larger co-authored by the guideline's author, whose effectiveness results are summarized only as equivalent. The core conclusion, that benzodiazepines are suitable agents with fewer seizures and delirium than placebo, is in line with the pooled data.

timeline.event: The six placebo-controlled trials pooled in Table 2 span 1961 to 1983 (Rosenfeld & Bizzoco, 1961; Sereny & Kalant, 1965; Kaim et al., 1969; Zilm et al., 1980; Sellers et al., 1983; Naranjo et al., 1983).
Sullivan et al., the revised CIWA-Ar scale (ref 157; first author a working-group member; on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B); not read here.

Saitz et al., randomized double-blind trial of symptom-triggered vs fixed-schedule treatment (ref 146; co-authored by M. F. Mayo-Smith; on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B), the larger trial behind the grade A recommendation for individualized dosing; not read here.
Kasser et al., ASAM guideline on phenytoin in alcohol withdrawal (ref 9), written by members of the same working group.
ASAM board of directors approved this guideline in June 1996, with review and revision scheduled for June 2001 (p. 145).

Mayo-Smith et al., ASAM evidence-based guideline on the management of alcohol withdrawal delirium (on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B), the topic this paper left to a separate guideline; not read here.

Amato et al., Cochrane review of benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal (on the project's Alcohol list; card being written by another reader in this round), and Minozzi et al., Cochrane review of anticonvulsants for alcohol withdrawal (Tier B; not read here).
Schuckit, review of the recognition and management of withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens); not read here.
ASAM guideline on alcohol withdrawal management, named among the known gaps of the project's Alcohol list; not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The guideline's central pooled result (fewer seizures and delirium with benzodiazepines than placebo) rests on six small trials from 1961–1983 found by a 1995 MEDLINE search; later syntheses on the project list (Amato et al., 2010) should be preferred for current effect estimates once read. This paper is cited for what the 1997 ASAM guideline recommended and for its pooled estimates as reported, labelled as from a review rated critically low in confidence. Its secondary claims (long- vs short-acting agents, P=.07; neuroleptic seizure risk against placebo, not significant; special populations, no studies) were not settled by it. No correction notice is on file or mentioned in the PDF; none was searched for in this reading.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement. The guideline was produced for the ASAM Committee on Practice Guidelines; reprint requests to the California Society of Addiction Medicine (p. 144, first-page footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Working group (p. 149): M. F. Mayo-Smith (chair; Ambulatory Care Service, Veterans Affairs Medical Center, Manchester, NH, and Harvard Medical School), P. Cushman Jr, A. J. Hill, G. Jara (California Society of Addiction Medicine), C. Kasser, M. Kraus, D. Nauts, R. Saitz, J. W. Smith, J. T. Sullivan (Department of Clinical Pharmacology, Bayer Corporation, West Haven, Conn) and N. Thiessen. Several cited primary studies have authors whose names match working-group members: Saitz and Mayo-Smith (the 1994 symptom-triggered trial, ref 146, and a 1995 national practice survey, ref 6), Sullivan (CIWA-Ar, ref 157; ref 132), Kraus (atenolol trials, refs 86 and 115), Cushman (adrenergic-agonist and lofexidine studies, refs 82, 83 and 111), Kasser, Smith, Thiessen and Mayo-Smith (the phenytoin guideline, ref 9), and Mayo-Smith (late-onset seizures, ref 149). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A current, registered systematic review with several databases and no language limit, per-trial risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity and small-study analyses; and adequately powered randomized trials comparing benzodiazepine strategies (symptom-triggered vs fixed schedule; long- vs short-acting agents) on seizures and delirium, including older people, pregnant women and people with medical comorbidity, for whom this review found no studies.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people in alcohol withdrawal), interventions (any pharmacological agent) and seven outcomes are stated; comparators are not specified and appear only in the tables.
No protocol or a priori plan is mentioned; the review predates review registries, so this reflects the standards of its time rather than a judgment of intent.

All studies with original clinical data were reviewed and prospective controlled trials pooled, with a design hierarchy used for grading (Table 1), but no reason is given for the designs included or for pooling only prospective controlled trials.

MEDLINE only (1966 to June 1995) with one pair of key words, English only without justification, plus reference lists of selected articles and reviews; no second database, trial registry or grey literature. Partial yes needs at least two databases.
Not reported; only data extraction is said to be duplicated.
Two reviewers independently extracted data from each prospective controlled trial with sound end points (p. 145, Methods › Review of the Evidence).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies; trials were kept only if their end points were methodologically sound and documented, without saying which failed and why.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2–4 give first author, year, agents and event counts per arm only; populations, settings, severity, regimens, follow-up and whether each trial was randomized or blinded are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No trial-level assessment of randomization, allocation concealment, blinding or attrition. Table 1's levels classify designs and error rates for grading recommendations, and the paper does not say which trials were rated level I or II.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of risk differences (refs 13–15) lets trials with zero events contribute, but different drugs (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam) and comparators (benzodiazepines and paraldehyde as cross-tolerant medication) are combined without stated justification, randomized and non-randomized controlled trials are not distinguished, and heterogeneity is neither reported nor investigated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how trial quality affects the pooled estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The introduction says the trials generally involved few subjects and were of uncertain quality, and the results flag small trials for several agents, but the pooled benzodiazepine and neuroleptic results and their grades are interpreted without regard to the trials' risk of bias.
No heterogeneity statistic or discussion for any pooled estimate.
Not investigated.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement for the review; one working-group member is affiliated with Bayer Corporation, and several members wrote cited primary studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Seven critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence. This measures the review against current standards, several of which (protocol registries, trial-level risk-of-bias tools) were not usual in 1995–1997; it is not a judgment of the guideline's clinical value. Consequences: the pooled benzodiazepine estimates rest on six small trials from 1961–1983, found by a single-database English-language search and not appraised for bias; the delirium estimate rests on 3 vs 11 events; heterogeneity and publication bias are unknown; and the grade A labels depend on an unstated threshold of clinically significant benefit. Citable for what the 1997 ASAM guideline recommended, graded as it graded them, and for its pooled estimates as reported, with this rating; current claims about benzodiazepines for withdrawal should rest on later systematic reviews (Amato et al., 2010, on the project list) once read.

key_findings.finding: Methods: MEDLINE searched with the key words substance withdrawal syndrome and ethyl alcohol from 1966 through June 1995 (abstract: English-language articles published before 1 July 1995), plus references of selected articles and reviews; articles with original clinical data on humans underwent structured review; prospective controlled trials with methodologically sound end points were extracted by 2 reviewers independently; single-trial differences tested by the Fisher exact test with Taylor-series 95% CIs for relative risks; meta-analysis, when appropriate, by a random-effects model with risk differences; two-tailed tests, significance at P≤.05.

key_findings.finding: Scope and outcomes: seven outcomes (withdrawal severity and withdrawal delirium as defined in DSM-IV, seizures, completion of withdrawal, entry into rehabilitation, adverse effects, cost); not addressed: patients seen after a withdrawal seizure or with established delirium, and the choice of inpatient or outpatient setting, left to separate guidelines; phenytoin covered by an earlier ASAM guideline. The introduction says alcohol dependence occurs in 15% to 20% of primary care and hospitalized patients and that withdrawal trials generally involved few subjects and were often of uncertain quality.

Longer-acting agents are said to give a smoother withdrawal with less breakthrough or rebound (one cited trial) and, on pharmacological data and clinical experience, to risk excess sedation in older people and people with marked liver disease; there are few data on delirium.

key_findings.finding: Potential for non-medical use: the trials and reviews cited (refs 65, 151–153) show that some benzodiazepines are preferred by people with addictive disorders; agents of rapid onset (diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam) have higher potential than slower-onset agents (chlordiazepoxide, oxazepam, halazepam), which the review says may matter in outpatient settings or for people with a history of benzodiazepine or other substance use problems, while faster onset may help when rapid control of symptoms is needed.

key_findings.finding: Costs: published case reports of continuous infusions of short-acting benzodiazepines give drug costs of $50 335 for a 25-hour midazolam infusion in one patient and $26 045 for another patient's stay; no evidence was found that infusions give better outcomes than oral or intravenous bolus treatment with longer-acting agents; in one institution, a guideline favouring longer-acting agents over infusions was followed by a fall in mean costs from $1008.72 to $59.79 per patient, with equivalent outcomes and no more adverse effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The text spells midazolam as midalozam. The same paragraph lists 1993 wholesale prices per tablet at roughly equivalent doses; not extracted because they are tied to doses.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Other sedative-hypnotics: chlormethiazole was better than placebo, and barbital and tetrabamate equal to benzodiazepines, for signs and symptoms, in trials too small to judge seizures or delirium; paraldehyde has only case series and one trial (superior to promazine); barbiturates are used by about 10% of US detoxification programmes, but no controlled trial of phenobarbital was found, only uncontrolled studies in support; phenobarbital is described as long acting, inexpensive and of low potential for non-medical use, and barbiturates, phenobarbital included, as carrying a greater risk of respiratory depression, particularly with alcohol, and a lower safety margin than benzodiazepines at high doses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 5th paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal scales: the CIWA-A and its shortened revision, the CIWA-Ar, are described as reliable, reproducible and valid against ratings by experienced clinicians, usable in detoxification and psychiatric units and by nursing staff on general medical and surgical wards; high scores predict seizures and delirium.
key_findings.locator: Results › Structured Assessment Scales and Determination of Dosage, 1st paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Symptom-triggered dosing: many patients go through withdrawal with only minor symptoms despite little or no medication; in two randomized trials, giving medication only when a structured scale crosses a severity threshold was as effective as fixed-schedule dosing, with significantly less medication and a significantly shorter treatment; in the larger trial (Saitz et al., 1994), median chlordiazepoxide was 100 mg vs 425 mg and median duration of treatment 9 vs 68 hours. Seizures were not observed in series treated with symptom-triggered therapy.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Data Synthesis (p. 144); Results › Structured Assessment Scales and Determination of Dosage, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 146)
key_findings.note: Amounts are trial outcomes, not doses to use. The abstract gives P<.001 for less medication and shorter treatment; the text gives no P value and no effectiveness results (reporting issue 6). M. F. Mayo-Smith is a co-author of the larger trial (ref 146).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on pages rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: β-Blockers: some evidence that they reduce manifestations of withdrawal, mainly autonomic ones; they have no known anticonvulsant activity and no study was large enough to show whether they reduce or increase seizures; delirium is a known side effect of β-blockers that enter the brain well, such as propranolol, and was increased with propranolol in at least one study; they may mask other withdrawal signs and hinder scale-guided treatment (a case report of delayed recognition of delirium).
key_findings.locator: Results › β-Adrenergic Antagonists (begins p. 146, continued p. 147)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on pages rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Clonidine: well-designed studies consistently show symptom relief in mild to moderate withdrawal, with no study large enough for delirium or seizures. Carbamazepine: superior to placebo and equal to barbital and oxazepam in mild to moderate withdrawal, with limited data on seizures or delirium; without significant haematological or hepatic toxicity in 7-day protocols; associated with less psychiatric distress and a faster return to work; prevents withdrawal seizures in animal studies; described as not adding to alcohol's central nervous system and respiratory depression and as having no potential for non-medical use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clonidine; Results › Carbamazepine, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Neuroleptics (Table 4): Thomas & Freedman 1964, promazine 4/34 vs paraldehyde 0/33 delirium; Sereny & Kalant 1965, promazine 1/23, placebo 1/11, chlordiazepoxide 0/24 delirium and 2/23, 0/11, 0/24 seizures; Chambers & Schultz 1965, promazine 5/34, diazepam 0/35, chlordiazepoxide 0/34 seizures; Kaim et al. 1969, chlorpromazine 7/98, placebo 8/130, chlordiazepoxide 1/103 delirium and 12/98, 9/130, 1/103 seizures. Pooled risk differences, phenothiazine vs placebo: delirium 0.0 per 100 (95% CI −5.8 to +6.6), P=.92; seizures +4.6 per 100 (−2.6 to +11.9), P=.19. Phenothiazine vs cross-tolerant medication (benzodiazepine or paraldehyde): delirium +6.6 per 100 (+2.4 to +10.8), P=.002; seizures +11.4 per 100 (+6.2 to +16.6), P<.001. The agents studied, chlorpromazine and promazine, are said to be among those with the greatest effect on seizure threshold; uncontrolled experience supports neuroleptics for calming agitation.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Neuroleptic Agents
key_findings.note: The text gives 12.4 for the seizure difference against benzodiazepines (Table 4: 11.4) and says these agents increase seizures compared with placebo, which the pooled comparison with placebo does not show (reporting issues 2 and 3).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; Table 4 read on the page rendered at 600 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Magnesium: levels are usually normal on admission, fall during withdrawal and recover as symptoms subside; one double-blind placebo-controlled trial of intramuscular magnesium added to benzodiazepines found no difference in withdrawal severity, seizures or delirium, with limited power for the latter two. Ethyl alcohol: only small uncontrolled case series without objective severity measures, and no controlled trials against placebo or benzodiazepines; intravenous infusion needs close monitoring and has toxicity and infusion-site risks. Thiamine: in one large trial it did not reduce delirium or seizures, but thiamine deficiency is frequent in people with alcohol dependence and its administration prevents Wernicke disease and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Other agents: some relieve withdrawal, none has been shown to reduce delirium or seizures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Magnesium; Ethyl Alcohol (p. 147, continued p. 148); Thiamine; Other Agents (p. 148)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on pages rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Special populations: no studies were identified on withdrawal management in adolescents, on treatment approaches in older people, in pregnant women, or in people with specific coexisting medical or substance use disorders. Ethyl alcohol is called a well-known teratogen; retrospective studies associate benzodiazepines and barbiturates with congenital malformation, and a recent study associated in-utero phenobarbital exposure with intelligence deficits; the review judges these risks small against the harm to the fetus of severe withdrawal or seizures. Concurrent non-medical sedative-hypnotic use is a risk factor for major complications; one cohort of psychiatric inpatients found symptom-triggered treatment with a long-acting benzodiazepine safe and effective.
key_findings.locator: Results › Special Populations, 1st–2nd paragraphs
