design_detail: Mendelian randomization within one prospective cohort, the China Kadoorie Biobank (512 715 adults from ten areas of China, recruited 2004-2008 and followed about 10 years to 1 January 2017), set beside conventional analyses of self-reported drinking in the same cohort. 161 498 participants were genotyped for ALDH2 rs671 and ADH1B rs1229984: 151 028 chosen at random (used in all genetic analyses) and 10 470 chosen because they had a stroke or coronary event during follow-up (used only in the disease analyses). In each area, mean male intake was computed for each of the nine joint genotypes, and the 90 area-genotype combinations were grouped into six categories (cut-points 10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 g/week; category means in men 4, 18, 34, 78, 130 and 256 g/week). Disease rates were compared across categories by Cox regression stratified by area and adjusted for age; slopes per 280 g/week were fitted within each area and combined by inverse-variance weighting. Women, few of whom drink, were placed in the same categories to test for effects of the genotypes not mediated by drinking. Labelled prospective-cohort and appraised with ROBINS-E under the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization in one cohort, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether men whose genotype and area predict higher mean alcohol intake, from about 4 to about 256 g/week, have higher or lower rates of stroke and myocardial infarction, in a comparison largely free of the confounding and reverse causation that affect comparisons by self-reported drinking; and whether the U-shape seen with self-reported drinking in the same cohort reappears when people are grouped by genotype instead.
cannot_establish: Effects in women (few drink, so the design uses them only as a check for pleiotropy); effects of beverages other than spirits or of drinking patterns; whether alcohol has a modest effect on myocardial infarction in either direction (1696 genotyped cases; RR 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18 per 280 g/week); the risk at a particular individual intake (categories are group means, and the slopes assume a log-linear relation); and whether part of the genetic effect works through acetaldehyde exposure per drink or faster alcohol clearance rather than through the amount drunk.

sample.recruitment: Community: all permanent residents aged 35-74 without major disability in ten rural and urban areas were to be invited; 499 500 (28% of 1 801 167 invitees) took part, plus 13 215 people just outside the target age range (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participants who had already had coronary heart disease, a stroke or a transient ischaemic attack were left out of the incidence analyses (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph). Genetic analyses used the genotyped participants described above.
sample.demographics: Mean age 52 (SD 11); 226 182 urban and 286 533 rural residents; 41% men (editors' calculation, 210 205/512 715). Drinking was mainly of spirits, and the prevalence of weekly drinking varied widely between areas (Results, 1st paragraph; appendix pp 11-12, not read).
sample.attrition: By 1 January 2017, 4781 participants (0.9%) were lost to follow-up and 44 037 (8.6%) had died (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: 28% of invitees took part. The genotyped set adds 10 470 people selected because they had an event, used only in disease analyses; how they were handled in the Cox models is described in the appendix (pp 5-6, not read). Physiological factors other than blood pressure (HDL cholesterol, γ-glutamyltransferase and others) were measured in 18 256 participants of nested case-control studies, not in a random sample.

exposure.measurement: Conventional: self-reported drinking at baseline (main beverage, amount, frequency), classified as current drinkers (drinking in most weeks of the past year), non-drinkers (no drinking in the past year and never a weekly drinker), occasional drinkers (some drinking in the past year but never weekly) and ex-drinkers (formerly weekly drinkers who now drink occasionally or not at all); usual intake estimated from two resurveys of 4-5% of participants to correct for regression dilution (Methods › Alcohol drinking patterns). Genetic: rs671 and rs1229984 genotyped on custom arrays, with genotype frequencies in every area consistent with Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; assignment to a category depended only on genotype and area, not on a person's own drinking (Methods › Mean alcohol intake by genotype and area).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Units: grams of ethanol per week; the authors equate 100 g/week with one to two drinks per day and 280 g/week with about four drinks per day. Baseline groups of current drinkers: men <140, 140-279, 280-419 and ≥420 g/week; women <70 and ≥70 g/week. Mean usual intake was about 280 g/week in male current drinkers and about 100 g/week in all men (appendix p 12, not read). Genotype effects in men: rs671 AA, AG and GG mean 3, 37 and 157 g/week (1%, 16% and 45% current drinkers); rs1229984 AA, AG and GG 98, 106 and 157 g/week (32%, 33% and 43%). Across the six categories, men's prevalence of ever drinking in most weeks rose from 3% to 74% and mean intake from 4 to 256 g/week; in women intake was below 2 g/week in categories 1-3 and 4 to 8 g/week in categories 4-6 (Figure 2). Occasional drinkers were assigned 5 g/week and ex-drinkers were left out of the category means. No F statistic is reported; mean intake differed more than 50-fold between category 6 and category 1.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking: the conventional analyses were adjusted for smoking and, in a sensitivity analysis, excluded ever-smokers; the genetic analyses were adjusted only for age (stratified by area), with education, income and smoking added in sensitivity analyses (appendix p 25, not read), and the six categories did not differ much in smoking or other self-reported characteristics (appendix p 19, not read). A published letter (Chen et al., 2019) quotes this paper's data as 61% of men and 71% of current drinkers smoking. Other drugs: not reported.

comparison.controls: Conventional analyses: current drinkers with the lowest intake (men <140 g/week) are the reference (RR=1); non-drinkers, occasional drinkers and ex-drinkers are plotted separately, and their RRs are not printed as numbers (Figures 4 and 5). Genetic analyses: category 1 (mean 4 g/week in men; two-thirds non-drinkers and most of the rest occasional drinkers) is the reference.
comparison.matching: Genetic comparisons are within area (stratified by area) and age-adjusted; conventional comparisons are adjusted for age, area, education, income and smoking.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genetic analysis: genotype is assigned at conception; A-allele frequencies differ between areas (more common in the south), which the within-area analysis removes. Conventional analysis: reasons for not drinking (illness, former heavy drinking) and lifestyle are only partly captured; sensitivity analyses excluding early follow-up, ever-smokers and people in poor self-reported health left the U-shape in place (appendix pp 23-24, 32, not read).

outcomes.instruments: Linkage by national identification number to hospital records of the national health insurance system (more than 98% coverage in the study areas), local stroke and coronary heart disease registries and death registries; cardiovascular events reviewed and coded to ICD-10. Outcomes: ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, total stroke, acute myocardial infarction and total coronary heart disease (first fatal or non-fatal record of each). Physiological factors: systolic blood pressure at baseline; HDL and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein(a), C-reactive protein, fibrinogen and γ-glutamyltransferase in the biochemistry subsample.
outcomes.validity_norms: Details of event review are in the appendix (p 4, not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk (Cox) of each category against the reference; slope expressed as RR per 280 g/week of usual intake (conventional) or of genotype-predicted mean male intake (genetic); adjusted means of physiological factors by category.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the five diseases and eight physiological factors (13); the authors mention allowance for multiple testing only for the further physiological factors examined in women (appendix p 21, not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; record-based coding is unlikely to depend on genotype.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Conventional; men; current drinkers; RR per 280 g/week usual intake; reference lowest-intake current drinkers] ischaemic stroke 1.28 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.38), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.59 (1.37 to 1.85), total stroke 1.35 (1.27 to 1.44), acute myocardial infarction 1.15 (0.96 to 1.38; p=0.14), total coronary heart disease 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21; p=0.003); systolic blood pressure +4.8 mm Hg (4.5 to 5.1). Lower stroke and coronary risks at about 100 g/week than in non-drinkers and ex-drinkers (U-shape), shown in plots only. [Genetic; men; per 280 g/week genotype-predicted mean intake; reference category 1] ischaemic stroke 1.27 (1.13 to 1.43; p=0.0001; 5709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36 to 1.84; 2790 cases), total stroke 1.38 (1.26 to 1.51; 9189 cases); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04 to 1.14), 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24) and 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); acute myocardial infarction 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18; p=0.69; 1696 cases), total coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17; p=0.40; 6145 cases); systolic blood pressure +4.3 mm Hg (3.7 to 4.9), HDL cholesterol +0.16 mmol/L (0.13 to 0.19), γ-glutamyltransferase +44 IU/L (36 to 53). [Genetic; women; same categories; per 280 g/week of male intake] systolic blood pressure −0.6 mm Hg (−1.0 to −0.1), ischaemic stroke 0.98 (0.88 to 1.09), intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82 to 1.12), acute myocardial infarction 0.94 (0.74 to 1.20). [Single variants; men; GG v AG] rs671: stroke 1.19 (1.13 to 1.24), myocardial infarction 1.02 (0.92 to 1.13); rs1229984: stroke 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27), myocardial infarction 1.11 (0.95 to 1.31).
analysis.covariates: Conventional: area, age, education, income and smoking. Genetic: stratified by area and adjusted for age; sensitivity analyses adding education, income and smoking did not change the results materially (appendix p 25, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published analysis plan is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: All five disease outcomes are reported for both approaches. The conventional RRs for non-drinkers and ex-drinkers, on which the U-shape rests, appear only in plots. The category cut-points (10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 g/week) are not justified in the main text; a check pooling the three lowest categories is in the appendix (p 26, not read).
analysis.power: Not reported. The authors call the number of myocardial infarction cases limited, so that some real benefit or hazard cannot be excluded (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In men, self-reported drinking showed the familiar U-shape, with lower stroke and coronary risks at about 100 g/week than in non-drinkers and ex-drinkers. Grouped by genotype and area instead, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage rose steadily across 4 to 256 g/week of predicted mean intake, with no dip at moderate intake; systolic blood pressure rose by about the same amount per gram in both approaches; and myocardial infarction showed no association (RR 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18). The same genotypes showed no adverse associations in women.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Interpretation states that alcohol "uniformly increases blood pressure and stroke risk" and that its apparent protection against stroke is largely non-causal; Research in context calls the apparently protective associations with stroke largely artifacts of reverse causation and confounding. The genetic results support the absence of a protective dip for stroke, but (1) uniformity rests on a log-linear fit through six category means, and the lowest categories (means 4, 18 and 34 g/week) are estimated imprecisely; (2) the paper does not separate reverse causation from confounding as the cause of the conventional U-shape; (3) the attributable fractions (about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men) hold, as the authors say, only if there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear; (4) the excess stroke risk is about twice that expected from the blood-pressure effect, and the explanations offered are untested. Research in context (Implications) states the attributable shares without that condition (reporting issue 3). For myocardial infarction the Interpretation is appropriately limited (little net effect, in this one study).

timeline.event: Holmes et al. (European ancestry, ADH1B rs1229984 only): carriers of the intake-lowering allele had lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90) and, in a subset, of ischaemic stroke (0.83), with no association with all stroke. This paper reports its own rs1229984 coronary result as consistent with that study, and its rs671 result as not supporting earlier east Asian meta-analyses (Discussion, 10th paragraph).
This study, published with an accompanying Comment by Yeung and Lam, "Unite for a framework convention for alcohol control" (Lancet 2019;393:1778-1779; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32214-1; not read).

Letter by Chen, Ferreira, Mochly-Rosen and Gross (Lancet 2019;394:1617-1618; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31880-X; read on PMC, PMC7259464): does not dispute the estimates; argues that guidance should take account of the ALDH2 rs671 variant and of the extra acetaldehyde load when smoking and drinking are combined, and asks whether cerebrovascular risk is higher in people who both smoke and drink. Two of its authors declare patents on ALDH2 activation licensed to Foresee Pharmaceuticals.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease (Eur J Epidemiol), listed in the project's DOI list as answering the Mendelian randomization studies; not read, and whether it addresses this paper was not checked.

Larsson et al. (European two-sample Mendelian randomization, up to 94 variants): genetically predicted drinking associated with stroke (OR 1.27 per SD of log drinks/week) and more strongly with intracerebral haemorrhage (3.53); Larsson and colleagues describe this as confirming the present stroke findings in European ancestry.

Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank): linear Mendelian randomization associations with stroke (OR 1.26, 1.04 to 1.54; not significant at that paper's corrected threshold) and with coronary artery disease (1.38, 1.10 to 1.74), the latter unlike this study's null myocardial infarction result.

replication.where_it_stands: For stroke, this is the strongest genetic evidence against a protective effect of moderate drinking compared with near-abstention, and European-ancestry Mendelian randomization points the same way, more strongly for intracerebral haemorrhage (Larsson et al., 2020). For myocardial infarction and coronary disease the genetic evidence is inconsistent: null here, positive in European-ancestry studies using ADH1B or many variants (Holmes et al., 2014; Larsson et al., 2020; Biddinger et al., 2022). Two authors (M V Holmes, G Davey Smith) are shared with Holmes et al. (2014), so the two studies are not fully independent.

funding.funder: Kadoorie Charitable Foundation, Hong Kong (baseline survey and first resurvey); UK Wellcome Trust (long-term follow-up; grants 212946/Z/18/Z, 202922/Z/16/Z, 104085/Z/14/Z, 088158/Z/09/Z); National Natural Science Foundation of China; National Key Research and Development Program of China (the Summary names the Chinese Ministry of Science and Technology); GlaxoSmithKline and the UK Medical Research Council (DNA extraction and genotyping); British Heart Foundation, Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK (core funding of the Clinical Trial Service Unit and Epidemiological Studies Unit, Oxford); individual support for G Davey Smith (Medical Research Council) and M V Holmes (British Heart Foundation; NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre). The funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Role of the funding source; Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Seven authors (IYM, RGW, XWM, SP, RCl, RP, ZC) report grants from the Kadoorie Charitable Foundation, Wellcome Trust, Medical Research Council, GlaxoSmithKline, British Heart Foundation and Cancer Research UK during the study. R Collins reports support from the Nuffield Department of Population Health; grants and personal fees from the British Heart Foundation; grants from Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, Wellcome Trust, Merck & Co, the National Institute for Health Research and Medco; personal fees from UK Biobank; a Pfizer prize for independent research awarded to his department; and a patent for a statin-related myopathy genetic test licensed to the University of Oxford from Boston Heart Diagnostics, with personal benefits waived. All other authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests). No ties to the alcohol industry are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: GlaxoSmithKline part-funded the genotyping. M V Holmes, first author of Holmes et al. (2014), and G Davey Smith, an author of that study, are coauthors. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Many more incident myocardial infarctions in genotyped east Asian cohorts (longer follow-up of this cohort, or pooling with other east Asian biobanks), analysed with the same within-area genotype design, to narrow the interval around the null coronary estimate; together with calibration of genotype-predicted intake against repeated objective measures of drinking, to fix the scale of the slopes.

domains.note: Instrument independence: genotype is assigned at conception, and comparisons within area remove differences in allele frequency and drinking culture between areas; little genotype-related difference in smoking or other baseline characteristics (appendix, not read). Exclusion restriction: tested with women as a negative control, in whom the same genotypes predict almost no drinking; women showed no adverse associations with stroke, myocardial infarction, HDL cholesterol or γ-glutamyltransferase, but slightly lower blood pressure (−0.6 mm Hg) and small differences in height, waist and hip, so some path outside drinking exists, and the authors note that the two enzymes act in many pathways. A further route not through the amount drunk: rs671 raises acetaldehyde exposure per drink and rs1229984 speeds alcohol clearance. Pleiotropy-robust multi-variant methods are not applicable to two variants grouped in this way.

Relevance: very strong (category means from 4 to 256 g/week; weekly drinking in men from 3% to 74%), although no F statistic is given. The exposure scale is the self-reported mean intake of men in each category, so under-reporting would make the slopes too steep (the authors say so), and assigning ex-drinkers zero rather than leaving them out would strengthen the slopes by about 10%. Shape at low intake: six categories give a coarse picture below 50 g/week; no excess risk was seen in category 1, where two-thirds do not drink, but the lowest categories are imprecise.

Selection into the cohort: 28% of invitees, aged 35-74, with people with prior vascular disease excluded; for a genetic comparison this matters only if taking part depended on both genotype-driven drinking and vascular risk. The disease analyses add 10 470 people genotyped because they had an event, and their handling in the Cox models is described only in the appendix (not read).
Not applicable in the usual sense: genotype is fixed, and changes in drinking over life are part of the genetic contrast.
0.9% lost to follow-up; the genotyped subset was chosen at random apart from the added cases.
Record linkage to insurance hospital data with more than 98% coverage, disease registries and death registries, coded to ICD-10; unlikely to depend on genotype.

No registered plan; the category cut-points were chosen by the authors without justification in the main text, and the conventional non-drinker and ex-drinker RRs are not given as numbers; all five diseases are reported for both approaches.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The genetic stroke result is among the best-protected estimates of an effect of alcohol available: strong instruments, comparisons within area, a sex in which the genotypes barely change drinking as a negative control, near-complete follow-up by record linkage, and many events. Concerns remain about effects of the genotypes that do not run through the amount drunk (acetaldehyde per drink, small differences in women) and about the coarse resolution at the lowest intakes. The conventional analyses in the same paper are at high risk of confounding and reverse causation, as the authors themselves argue, and serve here only to show the U-shape that the genetic analysis does not reproduce. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: genotype-predicted alcohol intake in Chinese men associated log-linearly with higher risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage across 4 to 256 g/week, with no sign of a protective dip at moderate intake; similar blood-pressure effects in genetic and conventional analyses. Do not cite it for: effects in women, a precise null for myocardial infarction, wine or drinking patterns, or the attributable fractions without their stated conditions.

key_findings.finding: 512 715 adults from ten areas of China were enrolled in 2004-2008 (28% of invitees aged 35-74, plus 13 215 just outside that range; mean age 52, SD 11) and followed for about 10 years to 1 January 2017; 4781 (0.9%) were lost to follow-up and 44 037 (8.6%) died.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 33% of men (69 897/210 205) and 2% of women (6245/302 510) drank in most weeks, mostly spirits, and the proportion varied widely between areas.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Summary › Findings

key_findings.finding: Genotype and intake in men: rs671 AA, AG and GG mean 3, 37 and 157 g/week, with 1%, 16% and 45% current drinkers; rs1229984 AA, AG and GG 98, 106 and 157 g/week, with 32%, 33% and 43%. A-allele frequencies 0.21 for rs671 (0.13-0.29 by area) and 0.69 for rs1229984 (0.64-0.74). Within single areas, mean male intake ran from 2 to 443 g/week across genotypes in Sichuan and from 1 to 29 g/week in Gansu.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The six genotype-area categories had mean male intakes of 4, 18, 34, 78, 130 and 256 g/week, and the proportion of men who had ever drunk in most weeks was 3%, 15%, 20%, 39%, 60% and 74%; in women the proportions were below 1% in categories 1-3 and 2%, 5% and 6% in categories 4-6, with mean intake below 2 g/week in categories 1-3 and 4, 5 and 8 g/week in categories 4-6.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2; Figure 1; Results, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Category values are printed on the bars of Figure 2 (an image), read from the full-size figure image.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure in men: systolic blood pressure rose by 4.8 mm Hg (95% CI 4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g/week of usual intake among current drinkers (conventional; 193 003 men) and by 4.3 mm Hg (3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake (genetic; 55 897 men in Figure 3). HDL cholesterol rose by 0.19 (0.17 to 0.22) and 0.16 (0.13 to 0.19) mmol/L, and γ-glutamyltransferase by 62 (54 to 70) and 44 (36 to 53) IU/L, in the conventional and genetic analyses respectively.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: The HDL and γ-glutamyltransferase slopes and the sample sizes are printed in Figure 3 (an image), read from the full-size figure image.

key_findings.finding: Conventional stroke analysis in men: U-shaped associations of self-reported intake with ischaemic stroke (14 930 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage (3496) and total stroke (19 859), with lower risk at about 100 g/week than in non-drinkers and, even more, ex-drinkers. In current drinkers, RR per 280 g/week usual intake 1.28 (1.19 to 1.38) for ischaemic stroke and 1.59 (1.37 to 1.85) for intracerebral haemorrhage (difference p=0.01); total stroke 1.35 (1.27 to 1.44). The U-shape remained when the first years of follow-up, ever-smokers or people reporting poor health were excluded. Reference: current drinkers with the lowest intake.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 4A-C
key_findings.note: Case numbers and the total-stroke slope are printed in Figure 4 (an image); the RRs of non-drinkers, occasional drinkers and ex-drinkers are plotted without numbers and were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Genetic stroke analysis in men: no U-shape; risk rose steadily across genotype-predicted mean intake of 4-256 g/week; RR per 280 g/week 1.27 (1.13 to 1.43; p=0.0001) for ischaemic stroke (5709 cases), 1.58 (1.36 to 1.84; p<0.0001) for intracerebral haemorrhage (2790 cases; difference p=0.01) and 1.38 (1.26 to 1.51) for total stroke (9189 cases); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04 to 1.14), 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24) and 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16). Adjusting for potential confounders did not change the results materially.
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th paragraph; Figure 4D-F

key_findings.finding: There was no sign of increased stroke risk at the lowest genotype-predicted intake (category 1, in which two-thirds were non-drinkers) and no material departure from a log-linear relation; pooling categories 1-3 (about 25 g/week) against categories 4-5 (about 100 g/week) still showed adverse rather than protective associations for ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage, and findings in each area were directionally consistent.
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conventional coronary analysis in men: U-shaped associations, with substantially lower rates of acute myocardial infarction (2958 cases) and total coronary heart disease (14 326) at moderate intake than in non-drinkers or ex-drinkers; among current drinkers RR per 280 g/week 1.15 (0.96 to 1.38; p=0.14) for myocardial infarction and 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21; p=0.003) for total coronary heart disease. Reference: current drinkers with the lowest intake.
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph; Figure 5A-B

key_findings.finding: Genetic coronary analysis in men: no clear association; RR per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18; p=0.69) for acute myocardial infarction (1696 cases) and 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17; p=0.40) for total coronary heart disease (6145 cases).
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph; Figure 5C-D

key_findings.finding: Women as a check for pleiotropy (same six categories; effects per 280 g/week of mean male intake): systolic blood pressure −0.6 mm Hg (−1.0 to −0.1; men +4.3); HDL cholesterol 0.00 (−0.03 to 0.03); γ-glutamyltransferase 0 (−3 to 3) IU/L; ischaemic stroke RR 0.98 (0.88 to 1.09; men 1.27); intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82 to 1.12; men 1.58); acute myocardial infarction 0.94 (0.74 to 1.20; men 0.96). P for a larger effect in men than in women <0.0001 for blood pressure, HDL, γ-glutamyltransferase and intracerebral haemorrhage, 0.0007 for ischaemic stroke and 0.45 for myocardial infarction. After allowing for multiple testing, women showed small genotype-related increases in height, waist and hip only.
key_findings.locator: Results, 12th paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Single-variant analyses in men (one copy of the variant allele; GG v AG): rs671 stroke RR 1.19 (1.13 to 1.24), myocardial infarction 1.02 (0.92 to 1.13); rs1229984 stroke 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27), myocardial infarction 1.11 (0.95 to 1.31). In women, neither variant was significantly associated with stroke or heart disease.
key_findings.locator: Results, 13th paragraph

key_findings.finding: If, and only if, there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear, the genetic estimates imply that alcohol caused about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages among the men; the excess stroke risks are about twice what the blood-pressure effect alone would predict.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that if intake was under-reported, all their dose-response slopes are too steep, and that counting ex-drinkers as zero intake instead of leaving them out would have made the genetic slopes about 10% stronger; effects of drinks other than spirits could not be assessed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 12th and 13th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Blood-pressure and stroke slopes appeared steeper in men younger than 60 at baseline than in older men, but the authors say the numbers were insufficient for this dependence on age to be reliable (appendix p 30, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Both approaches indicated about 5 mm Hg higher systolic pressure per 280 g a week, which, in conventional analyses of blood pressure and risk in this cohort, corresponds to about 15% more ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke and about 30% more intracerebral haemorrhage; the genetic excess stroke risks are about twice what the blood-pressure effect alone would predict (key finding 12).

design_detail: Essay (European Journal of Epidemiology, section 'Essay'; online-first PDF of 5 pages, 1 figure, 23 references) arguing that Mendelian randomization (MR) is an observational instrumental-variable method that should be renamed genetic instrumental variable analysis (GIVA) and reported without the words randomization or causality. It sets out threats to validity (confounding by population structure and by parental genotype, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation over the life course, inconsistent results), illustrated mainly with two alcohol MR studies (Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019), and contrasts them with the MTHFR and folate example. No search, selection criteria, data or synthesis. Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief directs for this essay.
can_establish: Which methodological objections three Harvard nutrition epidemiologists raised in 2019 against Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease, and which features of two MR studies they offered in support.
cannot_establish: Whether these objections explain the MR findings on alcohol (the essay quantifies none of them and reports no data from the studies it criticizes), what those studies found or how they tested their assumptions (to be taken from the studies themselves), or whether moderate drinking protects the heart.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (essay). The 23 references: the two alcohol MR studies (Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019); population genetics of the ADH genes (Osier et al., 2002); ADH and ALDH polymorphisms and alcohol dependence in four Chinese ethnic groups (Shen et al., 1997); the Adverse Childhood Experiences study (Felitti et al., 1998); a validity study of self-reported drinking (Midanik, 1982); a meta-analysis of interventional studies of alcohol and coronary risk markers (Brien et al., 2011, with Mukamal); the AUDIT-C (Bush et al., 1998); binge drinking among US adults (Naimi et al., 2003); Wood et al. (2018); Roerecke and Rehm (2010) on heavy drinking occasions; a consensus statement on LDL cholesterol (Ference et al., 2017); trends in binge drinking (Grucza et al., 2018); binge drinking in Chinese, Korean and White college students (Luczak et al., 2001); a mouse study of binge drinking and plaque (Liu et al., 2011); a study of binge drinking and vascular function in young adults (Goslawski et al., 2013); three East Asian genetic studies of coronary disease (Takeuchi et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2017; Han et al., 2013); two MTHFR meta-analyses (Klerk et al., 2002; Lewis et al., 2005); a meta-analysis of folic-acid trials for stroke prevention (Hsu et al., 2018); and the VISP trial (Toole et al., 2004).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; examples chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The MR evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease is represented by two studies, each discussed only for features that support the critique; MR studies published later (Larsson et al., 2020; Biddinger et al., 2022, on the project list) could not be considered; the conventional cohort evidence that the MR studies were designed to test is not discussed.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The essay notes that self-reported drinking is misclassified in both directions and that drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity, binge drinking), which genetic variants shift together.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed (smoking is not discussed).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. Outcomes discussed: cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction and stroke, with HDL cholesterol as an intermediate; for folate, homocysteine, coronary heart disease and stroke.
outcomes.operationalization: The validity of MR is judged against the instrumental-variable conditions (an instrument strongly related to the exposure, unconfounded, acting on the outcome only through the exposure), plus adaptation over the life course and replication.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical analysis).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The essay reports no estimate from any study; its only quantitative content is Fig. 1 (relative Google search interest for terms labelled 'Causality' and 'MR', September 2009 to September 2019) and the statement that Ashkenazi Jews make up about 0.2% of Europe's population.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Features of the cited MR studies that support the critique (an association of the variant with education, a null association with HDL cholesterol, stronger associations in drinkers) are described without numbers; features bearing on the same points (the strength of the variant's association with intake, adjustment for ancestry, sensitivity analyses) are not mentioned.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A reasoned list of conditions under which MR estimates for alcohol can be biased (population structure, parental genotype, weak instruments, pleiotropy through acetaldehyde, dimensions of drinking that genes shift together, lifelong rather than adult exposure, inconsistent results), illustrated with qualitative features of two MR studies, and an example (MTHFR and folate) in which genetic findings agreed with randomized trials once folate intake was taken into account.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that examples like alcohol and cardiovascular disease "demonstrate that it must be treated with all of the circumspection" of observational epidemiology (p. 1); the Summary calls the approach's observational nature incontrovertible and urges dropping randomization and causality from its reports (p. 4). Gaps: (1) the essay shows that these biases are possible, not that they explain the alcohol MR findings: none is quantified, and no estimate, instrument-exposure association or sensitivity analysis from the criticized studies is reported; (2) weak-instrument bias is inferred from a null genotype-HDL association, although the essay itself names the genotype-exposure association as the relevant test and does not report it (the companion card sc_holmes_2014 records a strong association with intake, not checked here); a null association with one intermediate trait bears on that pathway, not on instrument strength; (3) the education association is called clearly likely to reflect ancestry, without data; (4) the alternative readings offered (variants as effect modifiers; MR results as evidence of harm from binge drinking or from drinking in youth) are possibilities, not shown; (5) the biases named for MR (confounding, misclassification, selective publication) apply equally to the conventional cohorts that show a protective association, which the essay does not discuss, so it cannot be read as evidence for protection. The central methodological point, that MR is an observational design whose assumptions must be defended, is sound.

timeline.event: Brien et al.: meta-analysis of interventional studies of alcohol and coronary risk markers, co-authored by Mukamal; the essay's source for alcohol raising HDL cholesterol (ref. 7).
Holmes et al. (BMJ): ADH1B rs1229984 Mendelian randomization analysis, the essay's main example (ref. 1; card sc_holmes_2014, this round).
Wood et al. (Lancet): cited for the different health effects of the dimensions of drinking (ref. 10; card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Millwood et al. (Lancet): China Kadoorie Biobank genetic and conventional analyses, criticized for combining genetic and ecological instruments (ref. 2; card sc_millwood_2019, this round).
This essay: received 20 October, accepted 6 November, published online 24 November 2019; printed in vol. 35 (2020), pp. 93-97, according to the reference record.
Larsson et al. (Circ Genom Precis Med): Mendelian randomization study on the project list, published after this essay and not addressed by it (card sc_larsson_2020, this round).

Biddinger et al. (JAMA Netw Open): UK Biobank Mendelian randomization study; the project list describes this essay as a critique of items 13 to 15, but item 15 (Biddinger) appeared over two years later (card sc_biddinger_2022, this round). No replies or letters are linked in the PDF; none were searched for in this round.

replication.where_it_stands: A methodological critique to be cited, attributed to its authors, for the conditions under which Mendelian randomization estimates for alcohol can be biased. What the MR studies found, and how they tested their assumptions, must be cited from the MR studies themselves (cards this round); the essay does not engage with their numbers. MR studies published after it (Larsson et al., 2020; Biddinger et al., 2022) cannot be judged by it.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PDF has no funding statement ('Acknowledgements: None').
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the online-first PDF.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Nutrition, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (all three authors) and Division of General Medicine Research Section, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Mukamal). Reference lists read in this round show the authors' earlier work on the protective side of the question: Rimm and Stampfer co-authored a 1996 review and a 1999 meta-analysis whose titles link moderate alcohol to lower coronary risk, and Stampfer a 1995 cohort study of US women, all cited by Di Castelnuovo et al. (2006); Mukamal co-authored the Ronksley et al. (2011) meta-analysis and two cohort studies in the Stockwell et al. (2024) pool, one titled for higher usual intake and lower coronary mortality (Dai et al., 2015). The essay does not mention this work. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the arguments.

what_would_settle_it: Not answerable by an essay. Its objections are testable: Mendelian randomization analyses of alcohol that report instrument strength, use within-family (sibling) designs to remove population structure and parental effects, test the variants in people who never drink, estimate non-linear effects without splitting participants by their reported intake, and separate drinking pattern from volume; and, ultimately, a long-term randomized trial of moderate drinking against abstention with cardiovascular outcomes.

domains.note: No search or criteria; two alcohol MR studies chosen as examples.

The essay is itself a critique of the two MR studies, but it describes selected features without numbers and does not report how those studies addressed the same threats (ancestry adjustment, instrument strength, sensitivity analyses); the evidence for its own counter-arguments (a mouse study, a vascular-function study, the ACE study) is not appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 23 references (Brien et al., 2011) lists an author of the essay; the main examples come from other groups. The authors' wider publication record is noted under funding.

Several alternatives are hedged ('may', 'potentially'), but others are asserted as findings: the education association as clearly likely to reflect ancestry, a stratified result as a perfect example of pleiotropy, the observational nature of MR as incontrovertible.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the validity of Mendelian randomization estimates for alcohol and cardiovascular disease
domains.note: Only the case against the MR estimates is made; their strengths (a strong, specific instrument; agreement across studies) and the weaknesses of the conventional cohort evidence they were designed to test are not discussed, so the case for the genetic evidence is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to an essay (METHODS §5.3). Its methodological arguments are coherent and referenced, but the examples are chosen without search, the criticized studies are described selectively and without numbers, and only one side is argued; the overall judgment follows the worst domains. Claims may cite it for the objections it raises to Mendelian randomization studies of alcohol, attributed to its authors; not for what those studies found, and not as evidence that moderate drinking is cardioprotective.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that Mendelian randomization carries all the limitations of instrumental-variable analysis plus genetic ones (confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation, failure of replication); that it has some use for discrete biochemical pathways such as folate metabolism; that the example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease shows it needs the circumspection due to all observational epidemiology; and that reports should drop randomization and causality and call it genetic instrumental variable analysis (GIVA).

key_findings.finding: In the authors' view the only randomization reliably present is which of the parental alleles a person inherits; the assumption that genotype is randomly assigned within a population amounts to assuming randomly assigned parents, so the name implies an unwarranted degree of causal inference.

key_findings.finding: The essay states the conditions GIVA requires: no path from genotype to outcome except through the exposure (genotype neither confounded nor acting through other pathways) and a link between loci and exposure strong enough to overcome the variability of the two-step chain.

key_findings.finding: Population stratification: the ADH1B rs1229984 variant used in alcohol MR studies is said to be most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern descent, including Jews; in Holmes et al. (ref. 1) it went with lower reported intake but also with more education, which the authors read as reflecting ancestry and a healthier lifestyle. Adjustment with 3 to 5 principal components succeeds only if the subpopulation is large enough to appear among them; Ashkenazi Jews are about 0.2% of Europe's population, and the variant is in linkage disequilibrium with nearby variants.

key_findings.finding: Parental genotype: variants that lower a person's drinking are carried by at least one biological parent; if they lower the risk of alcohol dependence ('alcoholism' in the essay), carriers are less likely to have been raised by a parent with alcoholism, itself cited as a risk factor for later cardiovascular disease (the Adverse Childhood Experiences study).

key_findings.finding: Weak instruments: the essay says GIVA should always report the genotype-exposure association, notes that self-reported drinking is misclassified in both directions, and infers likely weak-instrument bias and pleiotropy in Holmes et al. from a null association of genotype with HDL cholesterol, although alcohol raises HDL cholesterol in trials (Brien et al., ref. 7), together with the variant's association with cardiovascular disease.

key_findings.finding: Pleiotropy: the ALDH2 rs671 variant, which influences intake more strongly than ADH1B, acts on many aldehydes and raises acetaldehyde exposure in people who drink, so it may affect risk directly. In Holmes et al., genetic associations were stronger in drinkers than in non-drinkers; the essay says greater toxicity when alcohol is consumed cannot be excluded as the explanation and that such variants can be read as modifying the effect of alcohol rather than only as instruments for it.

key_findings.finding: Dimensions of drinking: frequency, usual quantity and binge drinking correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects (Wood et al., ref. 10); genetic variants lower all three, so GIVA cannot separate them, and MR studies linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking.

key_findings.finding: Adaptation: GIVA tests lifelong (and parental) differences in exposure rather than adult exposure; given heavy drinking patterns in adolescence and early adulthood, their lower prevalence among young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking initiates atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), alcohol MR may be testing youthful binge drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.
key_findings.locator: Adaptation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Inconsistency: the China study (Millwood et al., ref. 2), described as combining genetic and ecological instruments, claimed causal, dose-dependent harm for stroke with no effect on myocardial infarction, while three East Asian reports found higher coronary risk with the ALDH2 rs671 variant without claiming a causal benefit of alcohol, which the essay calls the more conservative and appropriate reading.

key_findings.finding: Appropriate role: the MTHFR rs1801133 variant is a proxy for methyl-cycle activity, not an instrument for folate intake; its association with cardiovascular disease appears only at low folate intake, which randomized folic-acid trials confirmed for stroke; the authors conclude that without knowledge of folate intake GIVA would not give reliable results (some early reports wrongly concluded the observational associations were refuted), and that this model does not extend easily to alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF on file is the online-first version (published online 24 November 2019) without volume, issue or page numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors cite PDF pages 1 to 5; the printed article is pp. 93-97 of vol. 35 (2020) according to the reference record, which could not be checked against this PDF.

reporting_issues.issue: The essay says GIVA should always report the association of the genetic instrument with the exposure, but when it judges Holmes et al. likely to suffer from weak-instrument bias it reports no genotype-intake association and argues from a null genotype-HDL association instead.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weak-instrument charge cannot be evaluated from the essay; the cited study must be read for the strength of its instrument.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 (relative changes in searches for the two terms, September 2009 to September 2019) gives only the legend labels 'MR' and 'Causality', with no query strings; the text calls it worldwide interest (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, p. 1). Each series reaches 100 at its own peak (Causality about 2011, MR about 2018; checked on the rendered p. 2), so the two appear to be scaled separately and the figure shows the trend within each term, not their relative levels; if 'MR' was the literal search term, it also captures unrelated uses of the abbreviation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot show that interest in Mendelian randomization in particular rose, or how it compares with interest in causality.

reporting_issues.issue: The essay calls itself a review ('In this review', Introduction, 4th paragraph; Summary) but describes no review methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: It should not be cited as a review of the MR evidence on alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The three East Asian reports offered as inconsistent with Millwood et al. are, by their titles, a genome-wide association study of coronary disease in Japanese people, an exome-chip meta-analysis of lipid and coronary loci, and a meta-analysis of ADH and ALDH2 polymorphisms and coronary disease, not instrumental-variable analyses of alcohol.
reporting_issues.consequence: The inconsistency described is between analyses of different design and purpose, which weakens it as an example of conflicting MR results.

reporting_issues.issue: The parental-confounding argument rests on the premise that variants that lower drinking reduce the risk of alcohol dependence, supported by a single citation (ref. 4, a study of ADH and ALDH polymorphisms among four ethnic groups in China); its bearing on the ADH1B variant in European-descent studies is not shown.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 3 and 5 of the online-first PDF (Confounding, 3rd paragraph; reference 4)
reporting_issues.consequence: Indirect support for one of the essay's arguments; like the others, it is not quantified.
