design_detail: Two systematic reviews with country-specific random-effects meta-analyses (Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation), combined with modelling: (a) prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy among women in the general population (studies published January 1984 to June 2014; 328 studies, 50 countries) and (b) prevalence of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) in the general population (November 1973 to June 2015; 62 studies, 19 countries). Drinking prevalence was pooled for the 29 countries with two or more studies and predicted for 158 countries by fractional response regression (GDP per capita, women's alcohol consumption, WHO region); FAS was pooled for 7 countries and, for 180 countries, computed by applying a quotient of 67 women who drank in pregnancy per FAS case (derived from 7 countries) to the drinking prevalence. Monte Carlo confidence intervals; WHO regional and global averages weighted by live births; all estimates labelled 2012. PROSPERO CRD42016033835 and CRD42016033837.
can_establish: Pooled prevalence of reported alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population for the 29 countries with two or more studies, and of FAS for the 7 countries with meta-analysed data, from studies published up to mid-2014 and mid-2015, together with model-based working estimates for all other WHO member states.
cannot_establish: Measured prevalence for most countries (158 of 187 drinking estimates and 180 of 187 FAS estimates are model predictions); the amount, pattern or timing of drinking (not analysed); the risk of FAS for a woman who drinks a given amount (the 1-in-67 figure is a ratio of aggregate prevalences in 7 countries, not a dose-response risk); the prevalence of FASD as a whole (FAS only); trends over time (studies from 1984 to 2014 are pooled into one estimate labelled 2012); or prevalence in special populations (excluded).

sample.recruitment: Alcohol use in pregnancy: 14 databases (Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse Library Collection Database, Campbell Collaboration, CINAHL, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CSA Sociological Abstracts, Embase, ERIC, Google Scholar, MEDLINE, NIAAA Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Science Database, PsycINFO, Scopus, Social Work Abstracts, Web of Science), January 1, 1984 to June 30, 2014, without language or geographic restriction, plus contents pages of three epidemiology journals and citation screening. FAS: 7 databases (CINAHL, Embase, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science), November 1, 1973 to June 30, 2015, without language or geographic restriction, human studies where the database allowed, plus contents pages of three paediatric epidemiology journals and citation screening (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original quantitative research in a peer-reviewed journal or scholarly report reporting the prevalence of alcohol use during pregnancy, or of FAS with a CI, SE, sample size or case count, in the general population of a country. Excluded: samples from special populations (for drinking, for example Indigenous women, adolescents, women of low socioeconomic status, women with HIV or with an alcohol use disorder; for FAS, also Indigenous and correctional populations, children in care and children of women with an alcohol use disorder), pooled estimates from several studies, duplicate publications and, for drinking, studies that excluded abstainers. Where a study gave several drinking estimates, preference went to the estimate after pregnancy recognition, over the whole pregnancy, within 6 weeks post partum, or by a validated method (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Not in the main text: characteristics of the included drinking and FAS studies are in the appendix (pp 4-16 and 28-31), which was not read. Of the 62 FAS studies, 22 used active case ascertainment, 20 passive surveillance, 14 were clinic-based and 6 used mixed methods; 40 used an established diagnostic guideline or stated their case definition (Results, 3rd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Restriction to the general population removes groups with much higher prevalence (the Discussion cites 60.5% drinking in pregnancy among Inuit women in northern Quebec and FAS at 92.6 per 10,000 in an Indigenous Australian population). FAS data come from 19 countries in four WHO regions, none in the Eastern Mediterranean or South-East Asia regions, and the authors note that FAS studies were most often regionally confined to areas where high prevalence was expected. Countries with a single study were not meta-analysed: 21 of the 50 countries with drinking data (those with one study, or a meta-analysis giving an interval of 0 to 100%) were assigned a model prediction instead of their observed estimate (editors' arithmetic: 50 minus 29).

exposure.measurement: Alcohol use during pregnancy as measured in each primary study, mostly by self-report questionnaire or interview, in some studies by a validated screening method (the appraisal scored validated method vs questionnaire). No biomarker-based estimate is reported separately in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Any amount at any time in pregnancy. Quantity, frequency, binge drinking and timing were not analysed because they were not reported or were reported inconsistently (Discussion, 5th paragraph), although the registered protocol named binge drinking (4 or more standard drinks on one occasion) as an outcome. No drink size is defined.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (prevalence review). Denominators: pregnant or recently delivered women in the general population for drinking; general-population samples of children of various ages, including newborns in clinic-based studies, for FAS.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to prevalence. The FAS quotient assumes the same ratio of FAS cases to women who drank in pregnancy in every country; drinking pattern, nutrition, smoking, stress, genetic background and diagnostic practice, which the paper names as modifiers of fetal vulnerability, are not modelled.

outcomes.instruments: Prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy (%) and of FAS (per 10,000 people), with FAS diagnosed by varied systems or case definitions. The primary FAS analysis used studies with active case ascertainment or clinic-based methods and a specified guideline or case definition; a secondary analysis added passive-surveillance studies and studies without a stated definition (Methods › Meta-analyses, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Drinking studies were appraised in duplicate on four criteria based on Wong et al. (2008): probability vs non-probability sampling, a sample of at least 300, validated method vs questionnaire, and response or participation of at least 70%. FAS studies were appraised in duplicate on the ten criteria of Munn et al. (2014). The appraisal results are in the appendix (pp 21-26 and 37-38), not read (Methods › Meta-analyses, 1st and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: FAS prevalence per 10,000 people in the general population; the annual number of births with FAS applies the global prevalence to 81,536,534 live births. All estimates are labelled 2012 although the pooled studies span 1984 to 2014 (drinking) and 1973 to 2015 (FAS).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive estimates).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two investigators did each selection step and the quality appraisal independently; one extracted the data and a second cross-checked them independently against the original studies, with discrepancies settled by team discussion; non-English studies were translated by fluent colleagues or with Google Translate checked by a native speaker (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Any alcohol use during pregnancy in 2012, weighted by live births (Table): global 9.8% (95% CI 8.9-11.1); European region 25.2% (21.6-29.6); Americas 11.2% (9.4-12.6); African region 10.0% (8.5-11.8); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5-11.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9-5.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1-0.9). Highest countries: Ireland 60.4% (42.8-76.8), Belarus 46.6% (42.4-50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9-61.2), UK 41.3% (lower limit 32.9; upper limit misprinted), Russia 36.5% (18.7-56.4); lowest, 0% by prediction: Oman, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait. FAS per 10,000 people (Table): global 14.6 (9.4-23.3); European region 37.4 (24.7-54.2); Americas 16.6 (11.0-24.0); African region 14.8 (8.9-21.5); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7-19.4); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3-8.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2-0.9). Highest countries: South Africa 585.3 (430.7-761.7), Croatia 115.2 (34.8-236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4-142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1-134.6), Belarus 69.1 (42.1-103.5; predicted). Quotient: one FAS case per 67 women who drank during pregnancy, from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA, giving about 119,000 children with FAS born each year. Heterogeneity statistics and publication-bias tests are reported only in the appendix (pp 20 and 35); no prediction intervals.
analysis.covariates: Prediction of drinking prevalence for countries with one or no study: fractional response regression (generalised linear model, binomial family, logit link) on GDP per capita at purchasing power parity (World Bank), women's mean total alcohol consumption (WHO Global Information System on Alcohol and Health) and WHO region, with the European region split into EU and non-EU states and the Americas into Canada and the USA vs the rest; other candidate variables in the appendix (Methods › Meta-analyses, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42016033835 (alcohol use in pregnancy) and CRD42016033837 (FAS and FASD), both registered on 31 January 2016 (PROSPERO records read), after the searches had closed in June 2014 and June 2015; at registration the alcohol-use record marks searching, screening and data extraction as completed. Deviations not explained in the paper: the alcohol-use protocol planned binge-drinking prevalence, estimates for Aboriginal or Indigenous and low-socioeconomic-status populations and by method of ascertainment (self-report, meconium, other biomarkers), and exact confidence intervals for countries with a single study; the paper reports any use only, excludes special populations, and replaces single-study countries with predictions (fractional response regression for drinking, the quotient for FAS), methods neither record describes. The FAS record also planned FASD estimates, reported separately in Lange et al. (2017).
analysis.selective_reporting: Binge drinking, planned in the protocol, is not reported. Country estimates, heterogeneity and publication-bias results and appraisal results are confined to the appendix and the maps. The main text does not say which seven countries had meta-analysed FAS estimates.
analysis.power: Not applicable as such. The FAS quotient rests on seven countries, and FAS meta-analyses exist for seven countries; every FAS figure outside those countries inherits the quotient's uncertainty.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling reported drinking in pregnancy from 328 general-population studies and modelling the remaining countries, about 1 in 10 pregnant women worldwide (9.8%) and about 1 in 4 in the WHO European region (25.2%) drank some alcohol during pregnancy, with estimates near zero in the Eastern Mediterranean region. FAS prevalence was estimated at 14.6 per 10,000 globally and 37.4 in the European region. Because FAS was measured in 19 countries and meta-analysed in 7, the regional and global FAS figures are in effect the drinking prevalence divided by 67 (editors' arithmetic: 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000; 25.2% / 67 = 37.6; 10.0% / 67 = 14.9).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The Summary says "one in every 67 women who consumed alcohol during pregnancy would deliver" a child with FAS, which reads as an individual risk; it is a ratio of two aggregate prevalences in seven countries, applied unchanged to 180 others, and the Discussion's own explanation of South Africa's high FAS prevalence (a binge pattern among women who drink) shows the ratio varies with drinking pattern. (2) The 119,000 births a year apply a prevalence measured in general-population samples of children, stated per 10,000 people, to live births; the paper calls the same figure per 10,000 people in the Summary, Results and Discussion and per 10,000 livebirths in the Research in context panel. (3) Estimates labelled 2012 pool studies from 1984 to 2014 without allowing for time. (4) The Interpretation and Discussion call FAS a relatively prevalent birth defect and speculate that its prevalence could increase, from mostly modelled figures, while the authors acknowledge that the FAS studies were done where high prevalence was expected. (5) The Discussion's comparison for the USA with anencephaly, spina bifida, trisomy 18 and trisomy 21 is made without the US estimate in the main text. Against this, the limitations paragraph is candid about self-report, unvalidated tools, diagnostic inconsistency and prediction error.

timeline.event: Jones and Smith (1973), Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy (Lancet 302:999-1001), cited as the first description of FAS and the start date of the FAS search; this is not the Jones et al. 1973 paper held as jones_1973.
Abel (1995): FAS in 4.3% of children born to pregnant women who drank heavily (about 1 in 23), cited in the Discussion as consistent with the quotient of 1 in 67 for any drinking.

Correction (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e276; doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30032-3; online 25 January 2017): figures 2 and 4 had been published in the wrong order, and values for Australia and China (drinking map) and for Australia, Jamaica, Kazakhstan, Lesotho, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan (FAS map) were corrected to match appendix tables A2 and A7. The notice lists no change to the text or the Table.

Tsang and Elliott, linked Comment (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e232-e233; doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30008-6): supportive; notes that few included studies were truly population-based or national, that only 16.5% used a validated method to identify the level of risk from prenatal alcohol exposure (their figure; not in this paper's main text), that patterns of exposure were not analysed and diagnostic criteria vary, and that excluding special populations may make the estimates conservative.

Lange et al. (2017), companion FASD meta-analysis by the same team from the same FAS search, using these drinking estimates: FASD 7.7 per 1000 children and youth, one FASD case per 13 women who drank (card sc_lange_2017).

In their reply to a JAMA Pediatrics letter by Pichini, Pacifici and Busardò about the Italian FASD estimate, Lange, Rehm and Popova state that the same writers had raised a similar concern about this paper's FAS estimates in The Lancet Global Health; that correspondence was not located or read.

replication.where_it_stands: The standard source for the figures that about 10% of pregnant women worldwide drink and that FAS affects about 15 per 10,000. Both are dominated by modelling: drinking prevalence is pooled from observations for 29 countries and predicted for 158, and FAS is pooled for 7 countries and computed for the other 180 as the drinking prevalence divided by 67. Claims should separate measured from modelled estimates, describe the 1-in-67 figure as an aggregate ratio from seven countries rather than a woman's risk, and keep FAS distinct from FASD. The FASD companion paper (Lange et al., 2017) inherits these drinking estimates.

funding.funder: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health; no external funding was sought (Summary › Funding). The funder had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Methods › Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: None: the authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests).
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are at the Institute for Mental Health Policy Research, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto, with University of Toronto, Technische Universität Dresden and University of New South Wales affiliations. The introduction draws on the team's own earlier FASD comorbidity and cost studies, and the same team wrote the companion FASD meta-analysis (Lange et al., 2017). No industry funding or ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Nationally representative surveys of pregnant women with validated quantity, frequency and binge measures (with biomarkers in a subsample) in the countries now covered only by prediction, and active-case-ascertainment FAS and FASD studies using one diagnostic system in randomly chosen rather than high-prevalence communities, from which a pattern-specific ratio of FAS cases to exposed pregnancies could be estimated.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (general population of each country; pregnant women for drinking), condition (any alcohol use in pregnancy; FAS), outcome (prevalence) and eligible studies are specified for both reviews.

Both PROSPERO records were registered on 31 January 2016, after the searches closed (June 2014 and June 2015), and the alcohol-use record shows searching, screening and extraction already completed; the paper does not state that methods were set beforehand and does not explain its departures from the records (binge drinking and special populations dropped; single-study countries predicted rather than reported with exact intervals).
Any original quantitative study reporting general-population prevalence, the designs a prevalence question calls for; studies excluding abstainers were excluded with an evident reason.

14 and 7 databases with search terms given, no language restriction, journal hand-searching, citation screening, Google Scholar and scholarly reports admitted; but no contact with experts is reported and the searches closed about 31 months (drinking) and 19 months (FAS) before online publication in January 2017.
Two investigators did each selection step independently, with disagreements settled by team discussion.
One investigator extracted and a second independently cross-checked against the original studies, discrepancies settled by discussion, which meets the item's consensus criterion.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flow charts (Figures 1 and 3, images) summarize exclusions; no list of excluded full-text studies with reasons appears in the article, and none of the appendix pages cited in the text is described as one (appendix not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: study characteristics are only in the appendix (pp 4-16 and 28-31), which was not read; the main text gives counts by country and FAS ascertainment method only.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Prevalence-appropriate tools applied in duplicate (four criteria based on Wong et al. for drinking studies, ten from Munn et al. for FAS studies), but the drinking checklist does not address under-reporting, the timing of the question in pregnancy or the definition of use, and the results are only in the appendix.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text.

Within-country random-effects pooling of double-arcsine-transformed proportions is a standard technique, but the paper gives no justification for pooling studies spanning 30 years into one estimate labelled 2012, or for pooling different definitions and timings of drinking; heterogeneity statistics are not reported in the article and no prediction intervals are given; observed single-study data are replaced by model predictions; and the FAS quotient assumes one ratio for all countries. Judged on the item's requirement that combining the data be justified; a close call for the within-country pooling alone.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the drinking estimates by study quality; for FAS, the secondary analysis adding passive surveillance and undefined cases is a related sensitivity analysis (lower estimates for Australia, France, Italy and the USA), but the drinking estimates on which all modelled FAS figures rest were not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations paragraph discusses non-representative sampling, unvalidated tools, self-report under-reporting, diagnostic inconsistency, prediction error and FAS studies done where high prevalence was expected.
Heterogeneity tests are reported only in the appendix (pp 20 and 35); the article neither reports nor discusses heterogeneity.

Funnel plots, a rank correlation test and a weighted regression test were run, with results only in the appendix; the article does not discuss the likelihood or likely impact of publication or small-study bias.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Institutional funding stated, no external funding sought, no competing interests declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional, because item 8 could be judged only from the unread appendix; the rating would not change. Four critical items are not met (2, protocol registered after the searches; 7, no list of excluded studies; 11, combining unjustified and heterogeneity unreported; 15, publication bias not discussed), and two are partly met (4 and 9), which by the AMSTAR 2 rule gives critically low confidence in the pooled and modelled figures. This is a judgment on how far the numbers can be taken as unbiased summaries, not on the effort: searches were broad and language-unrestricted, selection and appraisal were duplicated, and the limitations are stated plainly. The practical point for claims is that most country, regional and global figures are model outputs, and the FAS figures outside seven countries are a fixed fraction of the drinking estimates.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol use in pregnancy: of 23,470 records, 328 studies were retained, with general-population data from 50 countries in all six WHO regions. FAS: of 11,110 records, 62 studies were retained, with data from 19 countries in four WHO regions (African, Americas, European, Western Pacific).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Summary › Findings

key_findings.finding: Drinking prevalence was estimated by random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries and by fractional response regression for 158 countries with one or no study; FAS prevalence by meta-analysis for 7 countries and, for 180 countries, by applying the quotient of women who drank per FAS case to the country's drinking prevalence.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Methods › Meta-analyses, 2nd and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population in 2012, weighted by live births: global 9.8% (95% CI 8.9-11.1); European region 25.2% (21.6-29.6), highest; Americas 11.2% (9.4-12.6); African region 10.0% (8.5-11.8); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5-11.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9-5.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1-0.9), lowest.
key_findings.locator: Table; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Country extremes for drinking in pregnancy: Ireland 60.4% (42.8-76.8), Belarus 46.6% (42.4-50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9-61.2), UK 41.3% (from 32.9; upper limit misprinted), Russia 36.5% (18.7-56.4); 0% (predicted) in Oman, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: FAS prevalence in the general population per 10,000 people: global 14.6 (95% CI 9.4-23.3); European region 37.4 (24.7-54.2); Americas 16.6 (11.0-24.0); African region 14.8 (8.9-21.5); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7-19.4); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3-8.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2-0.9).
key_findings.locator: Table; Results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Highest country FAS estimates per 10,000: South Africa 585.3 (430.7-761.7), Croatia 115.2 (34.8-236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4-142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1-134.6), Belarus 69.1 (42.1-103.5; predicted); below 0.05 (predicted) in Oman, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: From the seven countries with both indicators (Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea, USA), one in every 67 women who drank during pregnancy delivered a child with FAS; applied to 81,536,534 live births, about 119,000 children with FAS are born each year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: An aggregate ratio of two prevalences, not an individual risk; editors' arithmetic: 14.6 per 10,000 times 81,536,534 is about 119,000.

key_findings.finding: Editors' arithmetic from the Table: the regional and global FAS estimates equal, within rounding, the regional drinking prevalence divided by 67: global 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000 (printed 14.6); European 25.2% / 67 = 37.6 (37.4); African 10.0% / 67 = 14.9 (14.8); Americas 11.2% / 67 = 16.7 (16.6); Western Pacific 8.6% / 67 = 12.8 (12.7); South-East Asia 1.8% / 67 = 2.7 (2.7).
key_findings.locator: Table
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic; it shows the FAS figures outside the seven meta-analysed countries carry no independent FAS information.

key_findings.finding: The secondary FAS analysis, which added passive-surveillance studies and studies without a stated diagnostic definition, gave lower point estimates for Australia, France, Italy and the USA; values are in the appendix (p 36).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Discussion compares the quotient with Abel's estimate that 4.3% of children born to pregnant women who drink heavily (an average of two or more drinks a day, or five to six per occasion) have FAS, about 1 in 23, three times the general-population quotient; and cites a ratio of FAS to FASD of about 1 to 9 or 10, calling FAS the tip of the iceberg.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: some included drinking studies used non-representative samples or unvalidated tools; self-reported drinking may be under-reported, so drinking and FAS prevalence may be underestimated; drinking patterns not analysed; FAS diagnostic guidelines inconsistent or unspecified; predictions carry measurement error and omit variables such as alcohol policies; FAS studies were mostly regionally confined to areas of expected high prevalence; WHO member states only.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Both PROSPERO records (CRD42016033835 for drinking in pregnancy, CRD42016033837 for FAS and FASD) were registered on 31 January 2016; the drinking record, with a review start date of 1 January 2013, marks searching, screening and data extraction as already completed and plans binge-drinking prevalence, Indigenous and low-socioeconomic-status subgroups and exact intervals for single-study countries.
key_findings.locator: PROSPERO CRD42016033835 and CRD42016033837: Timeline of the review; Stage of the review; Planned data synthesis; Analysis of subgroups

key_findings.finding: The version read is the corrected online version of 25 January 2017. The correction (doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30032-3) concerns only figures 2 and 4: the maps had been printed in the wrong order, and values for Australia and China (drinking map) and Australia, Jamaica, Kazakhstan, Lesotho, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan (FAS map) were corrected to match appendix tables A2 and A7.
key_findings.locator: Correction to Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e290-99 (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e276); article page, note after the Discussion
key_findings.note: No number on this card comes from the maps, so none is affected by the correction.

reporting_issues.issue: The UK's drinking prevalence is printed as 41.3% with an interval of 32.9 to 49.%, the upper limit incomplete.
reporting_issues.consequence: The UK interval cannot be quoted from the main text; the appendix (not read) would be needed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives FAS in children in a Brazilian orphanage (Strömland et al.) as 3191 per 10,000, more than 14 times the general population; that multiple implies a Brazilian general-population FAS prevalence of about 228 per 10,000 (editors' arithmetic), far above the Americas average of 16.6. The companion paper by the same team (Lange et al., 2017, Figure 2 legend) gives FASD in the same orphanage as 170.2 per 1000 (1702 per 10,000), lower than the FAS figure here although FAS is a subset of FASD.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the two figures, and the stated multiple, is wrong; neither should be cited without checking the primary study. One reading that fits both the stated multiple and the FASD figure is a decimal misprint, 319.1 per 10,000 (31.9 per 1,000) for 3191 (second reader's suggestion; not checked against the primary study).

reporting_issues.issue: FAS prevalence is described as per 10,000 people in the Summary, Results and Discussion, and as per 10,000 livebirths in the Research in context panel; the 119,000 annual births apply the former to live births.
reporting_issues.consequence: Prevalence measured in general-population samples of children of various ages is treated as birth prevalence; the annual-births figure should be cited as a model estimate under that assumption.

reporting_issues.issue: The main text does not name the seven countries with meta-analysed FAS estimates. South Africa's estimate (585.3 per 10,000, the highest) is not marked as predicted, so it presumably comes from a meta-analysis, yet South Africa is not among the seven countries named for the quotient (Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea, USA); how the two sets of seven relate, and why South Africa's data did not enter the quotient, is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The derivation of the 1-in-67 quotient, which drives 180 of the 187 FAS estimates, cannot be reconstructed from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered protocols planned binge-drinking prevalence, special-population and ascertainment-method subgroups and exact intervals for single-study countries; the paper drops these and introduces prediction models not in the protocols, without comment.
reporting_issues.consequence: Undeclared departures from the protocol; the reasons can only be inferred (the limitations say patterns were inconsistently reported).

reporting_issues.issue: The correction notice cites the original as Lancet Glob Health 2016, published online 12 January, while the article was published online in January 2017.

design_detail: Comparative risk assessment, following the WHO Comparative Risk Assessment (CRA) methods of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2000 study, estimating deaths and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) attributable to alcohol in 2004 by sex, seven age groups and 14 WHO subregions (results shown for six WHO regions), with profiles of ten populous countries, plus a separate literature review of national cost-of-illness studies of which six were compared. Inputs: recorded and unrecorded adult per-capita consumption for 2003 (WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol 2004 and the WHO Global Information System on Alcohol and Health); survey-based prevalence of abstention and volume categories rescaled to per-capita consumption; drinking patterns for ischaemic heart disease and injuries; alcohol-attributable fractions taken from the CRA for 2002 (chronic diseases) and the CRA 2000 (injuries); WHO GBD 2004 deaths and DALYs for 136 causes; a new review of alcohol-use-disorder prevalence (37 studies). Counterfactual: no alcohol consumption; burden reported both as detrimental and as net of modelled protective effects. First of three papers in the Lancet Series on alcohol and global health. Design 'modelling' as the round brief directs for attributable-burden estimates: no risk-of-bias instrument applies, so the card states the design's limits with the editors' checklist (METHODS §5.3).
can_establish: Model estimates, under the WHO CRA assumptions and the stated inputs, of how many deaths and DALYs in 2004 were attributable to alcohol, globally and by sex, region, broad cause and ten countries, net of and before modelled protective effects; adult per-capita consumption by region in 2003; modelled one-year prevalence of alcohol-use disorders; and the costs reported by six national cost-of-illness studies on a common currency.
cannot_establish: Causal effects of alcohol beyond what the observational relative risks behind the attributable fractions support; how uncertain the estimates are (no uncertainty intervals are reported); the burden at any particular drinking level (the volume categories and relative risks are not given); trends since 2000 (methods and inputs changed between the 2000 and 2004 estimates); that poor or marginalised people suffer more harm per unit of alcohol (no within-population analysis); or economic costs in low-income countries (none of the six cost studies).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (modelling). Exposure: WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol 2004 and the WHO Global Information System on Alcohol and Health for 2003; recorded consumption from government taxation records, industry production and sales data and the Food and Agriculture Organization; unrecorded consumption mainly from expert opinion and general population surveys; abstention and volume distributions from large representative national surveys of the 2000s (Indicators of alcohol consumption, mortality, and burden of disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, pp. 2224–2225). Deaths and DALYs: WHO GBD 2004 update; population: United Nations 2006 revision (p. 2225). Cost studies: search of Ovid Medline, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsychINFO, Google Scholar and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, January 1992 to September 2007, with hand-searching of journal content pages and citations (Panel, 1st paragraph, p. 2228).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Alcohol-use-disorder review: studies done after 1990 using ICD-10, DSM-IIIR or DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence and the CIDI, SCAN or AUDADIS-ADR interview (p. 2225). Causes: categories meeting standard epidemiological criteria for a causal role (consistent association, chance, confounding and bias ruled out with reasonable confidence, plausible mechanism, with most weight on temporality, consistency, biological evidence and strength of association); the same as in the CRA 2000 plus colorectal cancer after the 2007 IARC assessment; infectious diseases not included (pp. 2226, 2231). Cost studies: of 29 studies from 18 countries and the European Union, only those estimating gross cost with a 6% discount rate (5% for South Korea), the most recent and comprehensive per country: France, the USA, Scotland and Canada (high income), South Korea and Thailand (middle income) (Panel, 3rd paragraph, p. 2228).
sample.demographics: Global population in 2004 by sex and age groups 0–4, 5–14, 15–29, 30–44, 45–59, 60–69 and 70 years and older, in 14 WHO subregions defined by child and adult mortality (pp. 2227–2228); country profiles for Brazil, China, Germany, India, Japan, Nigeria, Russia, South Africa, Thailand and the USA (Table 3, p. 2227).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The relative risks come mainly from meta-analyses of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries and are assumed to apply everywhere (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph, p. 2231). Drinking patterns were estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion where surveys were insufficient, and more than a quarter of global consumption is unrecorded and estimated mainly from expert opinion (p. 2231). The cost comparison keeps 6 of 29 identified studies, four from high-income countries, two from middle-income countries and none from low-income countries; two of the six are by authors of this paper (Canada, refs 50 and 51; Thailand, ref 45).

exposure.measurement: Modelled. Adult per-capita consumption (recorded plus unrecorded) for 2003; survey-derived volume of drinking adjusted to per-capita consumption, assuming that per-capita consumption is the most valid indicator of overall consumption and that surveys give correct proportions of volume by sex and age (pp. 2224–2225). Patterns of drinking (especially heavy drinking occasions) were used in addition to average volume for ischaemic heart disease and injuries (p. 2225).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure in litres of pure alcohol (100% ethanol) per adult per year (Figure 1; Findings › Exposure to alcohol, p. 2228); abstention = no drinking in the previous year (p. 2224). The average-volume categories used to compute attributable fractions, their gram thresholds and the relative risk at each are not given in this paper; 'adult' is not defined.
exposure.polysubstance: Not modelled. The authors note possible interactions between alcohol and poverty, malnutrition or hopelessness that would introduce error (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph, p. 2231).

comparison.controls: Counterfactual of no alcohol consumption, the same for detrimental and beneficial effects (Establishing risk relations, 2nd paragraph, p. 2227). The relative risks are those of each exposure category compared with no consumption in the source meta-analyses; whether those reference groups were lifetime abstainers or all non-drinkers is not stated here.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at model level; confounding and the make-up of abstainer groups in the studies behind the relative risks are not discussed in this paper.

outcomes.instruments: WHO GBD 2004 estimates of deaths and DALYs for 136 causes (p. 2225). Alcohol-related categories listed (p. 2226): perinatal disorders and low birthweight; cancers of the mouth and oropharynx, oesophagus, colon and rectum, liver and breast, and other neoplasms; diabetes; alcohol-use disorders; unipolar depression; epilepsy; hypertensive heart disease; ischaemic heart disease; haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke; cirrhosis of the liver; road traffic injuries, falls, drownings, poisonings, other unintentional injuries; self-inflicted injuries, violence and other intentional injuries. Costs: direct health care, law enforcement, other direct social costs and indirect (productivity) costs, converted to international dollars with the IMF purchasing-power-parity index and inflated to 2007 (Panel, p. 2228–2229).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors refer to general limitations of global mortality data and of DALY assumptions and weights, without quantifying them (Conclusions, 1st paragraph, p. 2231).
outcomes.operationalization: Alcohol-attributable fraction AF = Σ Pi(RRi − 1) / [Σ Pi(RRi − 1) + 1], with Pi the prevalence of exposure category i and RRi its relative risk against no consumption (pp. 2226–2227); conditions defined by alcohol (alcohol-use disorders, alcoholic liver disease, alcohol-induced pancreatitis) are wholly attributable. Net burden = detrimental minus prevented deaths or DALYs. Alcohol-use-disorder burden from prevalence, remission (0·175 a year), relative risk of death (1·80 men, 3·84 women) and disability weights of 0·122–0·137 (pp. 2225–2226). Costs are gross: only costs of harm were counted, with no offset for any benefit (Panel, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, p. 2228).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: estimation, no statistical tests. 25 counts the alcohol-related cause categories listed on p. 2226.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No uncertainty intervals are given for any estimate. Deaths in 2004 (Table 1, p. 2224; thousands): detrimental 2482 (men 2039, women 443), prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12), net 2255 of 58,738 deaths, 3·8% (men 6·3%, women 1·1%; CRA 2000 3·2%). Detrimental deaths by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. DALYs (Table 2, p. 2225; thousands): detrimental 73,231, prevented 2321, net 70,910 of 1,530,168, 4·6% (men 7·6%, women 1·4%; CRA 2000 4·0%); neuropsychiatric 26,682, unintentional injuries 18,604. Younger than 60: 5·3% of deaths (7·9% men, 1·9% women) (p. 2229). Regional share of deaths, both sexes: 0·5% eastern Mediterranean to 6·5% Europe; men in Europe 11·0% (Figure 2, p. 2225). One-year prevalence of alcohol-use disorders at 15–64 years: 3·6% globally (men 6·3%, women 0·9%), 10·9% in the eastern European subregion (Figure 4, p. 2226). Costs: I$122 (Thailand) to I$837 (USA) per head; 1·3% (Thailand) to 3·3% (South Korea) of GDP at purchasing-power parity (Table 4, p. 2230). Editors' calculation: detrimental deaths are 4·2% and detrimental DALYs 4·8% of the totals; cirrhosis is 15·0% of detrimental alcohol-attributable deaths.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. Attributable fractions are computed by sex, age group and region; patterns of drinking enter for ischaemic heart disease and injuries.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The relative risks, volume categories, exposure prevalences and cause-specific attributable fractions that produce every estimate are not shown; they are referred to earlier CRA reports (refs 12 and 34). Results are shown for six WHO regions rather than the 14 subregions modelled. The list of the 29 cost studies is in a web appendix, not on file. No sensitivity analysis is reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable. No uncertainty analysis is reported; the conclusions cite an earlier WHO report (World Health Report 2002, ref 7) for the uncertainty of alcohol estimates being fairly low compared with other risk factors (p. 2231).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under the WHO CRA assumptions, alcohol was estimated to account for 2·48 million deaths in 2004 before and 2·26 million after subtracting 0·23 million deaths it was modelled to prevent (3·8% of all deaths), and for 4·6% of net DALYs, with the burden concentrated in men, in Europe and the Americas, and in ages 15–59. Net burden varied from 28·1% of DALYs in Russian men to a small net benefit in German women (−0·4%). Six national cost-of-illness studies put alcohol's gross costs at 1·3% to 3·3% of GDP. None of these figures carries an uncertainty interval, and no sensitivity analysis is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that disease burden is closely related to average volume and, “for every unit of exposure, is strongest in poor people” and in people marginalised from society (p. 2223); the findings speak of alcohol-attributable mortality relative to volume being higher in developing countries, and of the proportion of alcohol-attributable deaths having increased since 2000, mainly because more women drink (pp. 2228–2229); the conclusions say the burden has not fallen since 2000 and probably increased, and that the uncertainty of the estimates is fairly low compared with other risk factors (p. 2231). Gaps: (1) the paper presents no estimate of burden per unit of alcohol by income or marginalisation, and its relative risks are the same in every population, so any per-unit difference in the model comes from modelled drinking patterns, abstention and cause-of-death structure rather than from measured vulnerability; (2) the comparison with 2000 mixes a real change with method changes (new alcohol-use-disorder prevalence and disability weights, colorectal cancer added, GBD 2004 cause revisions, attributable fractions from 2000 and 2002), so it cannot show that the burden rose or why; (3) no uncertainty is quantified in the paper; (4) that burden tracks average volume is built into the model, not found by it; (5) the abstract's cost statement uses gross national product, while the table uses GDP and the panel itself warns that expressing costs as a share of GDP poses a serious methodological problem.

timeline.event: Comparative Risk Assessment for 2000 (Rehm et al., in Ezzati et al., Comparative quantification of health risks; ref 12): 3·2% of deaths and 4·0% of DALYs attributable to alcohol, the comparison rows of Tables 1 and 2, and the source of the injury attributable fractions used here.
Comparative Risk Assessment for 2002 (Rehm et al., WHO report; ref 34), source of the chronic-disease attributable fractions used here.
IARC working group assessment of the carcinogenicity of alcoholic beverages (Baan et al., Lancet Oncol; ref 31), on which colorectal cancer was added to the causes.

This paper, first of three in the Lancet Series on alcohol and global health; the companion papers are Anderson, Chisholm and Fuhr (2009) on the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of alcohol policies and Casswell and Thamarangsi (2009), a call to action. The same issue carried an editorial (p. 2171), three comments (pp. 2173, 2174, 2176) and a perspective (p. 2191), which were not read.

Rehm et al. cirrhosis meta-analysis cites this paper for about 15% of alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004 being due to cirrhosis (Table 1 here: 373 of 2482 thousand detrimental deaths) and was done to supply cirrhosis relative risks to the GBD 2005 CRA (card sc_rehm_2010).

GBD 2016 alcohol analysis (Griswold et al.), with new relative-risk curves for 23 outcomes and an estimated theoretical minimum of zero drinks: 2·8 million attributable deaths in 2016 (card sc_griswold_2018, this round); the GBD 2020 analysis (Bryazka et al., 2022) revised it again (card sc_bryazka_2022).

replication.where_it_stands: A dated estimate (2004 deaths, 2003 exposure, attributable fractions from the 2000 and 2002 CRAs) built on the WHO CRA alcohol estimates for 2000 and 2002, whose support went to the first author. Later GBD rounds changed the relative-risk curves, the treatment of protective effects and the counterfactual (sc_griswold_2018), so its numbers should be cited only as 2004 WHO-CRA estimates, with their assumptions, and not compared directly with later estimates. Its cost comparison rests on six national studies from 1997 to 2006.

funding.funder: The comparative risk assessments for alcohol for 2000 and 2002 underlying the study were supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health to the first author; the specific work for this paper by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (Acknowledgments, p. 2231).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 2231).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the University of Toronto, the WHO Collaboration Centre for Substance Abuse (Zurich), TU Dresden, WHO's Department of Health Statistics (Geneva), and Thailand's Health Intervention and Technology Assessment Program at the Ministry of Public Health and Mahidol University (p. 2223). The model's inputs are largely the first author's group's earlier work (CRA 2000 and 2002, the alcohol-use-disorder review, ref 24), and two of the six cost studies compared are by authors of this paper (Canada and Thailand). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A re-estimation for the same year that propagates uncertainty in recorded and unrecorded consumption, drinking patterns, relative risks and cause-specific deaths into uncertainty intervals, with sensitivity analyses on the protective cardiovascular and diabetes relative risks and on the transfer of relative risks across countries; and cost-of-illness studies done to one protocol in low- and middle-income countries.

domains.note: Recorded consumption from taxation, industry and FAO data is a sound base, but more than a quarter of global consumption is unrecorded and estimated mainly by expert opinion, drinking patterns come from nearby countries or expert opinion where surveys were lacking, cause-of-death data are of uneven quality, and the exposure behind the attributable fractions dates from the 2000 and 2002 CRAs rather than 2004; regional and country figures for places with much unrecorded drinking carry more of this.

Taken from observational meta-analyses (via the CRA 2000 and 2002) that the authors describe as based mainly on middle-class cohorts in high-income countries and assume to hold in every population; not shown in this paper; the protective relative risks for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes, which subtract 227,000 deaths, come from the low-intake range where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed; no appraisal of the underlying studies.

No alcohol consumption, stated explicitly and applied to harms and benefits alike, and detrimental and net figures are both reported, which shows how much the protective estimates matter; but whether 'no consumption' in the source relative risks means lifetime abstention or all non-drinkers is not stated.

domains.domain: Uncertainty intervals: what they include and exclude
domains.note: No uncertainty intervals for any burden or cost estimate; the only intervals in the paper are for the relative risk of death with an alcohol-use disorder. The statement that uncertainty is fairly low rests on an earlier WHO report.
No sensitivity analysis is reported, for example to unrecorded consumption, drinking patterns, the protective relative risks or the transfer of relative risks between countries.

A described search with an explicit rule for comparability (gross cost, 6% discount rate, most recent study per country), but only six studies, none from a low-income country, from different years (1997 to 2006) and methods, two by the authors; gross costs only; population-weighted averages dominated by the USA; the list of 29 studies is in a web appendix not on file.

Tables 1 to 4 are complete and add up within rounding (editors' check), but the inputs that drive the estimates are only referenced, and several statements do not match the tables (neuropsychiatric shares, the alcohol-use-disorder age range, South Korea's income group, a net benefit in German women against the conclusion).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for burden-of-disease modelling (METHODS §5.3; the round brief sets design 'modelling' with no instrument). The editors' checklist is used with domains for the inputs, the relative-risk functions, the counterfactual, the uncertainty intervals, the sensitivity of the headline and the reporting, as in card sc_griswold_2018, with a domain added for the cost comparison; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The estimates are transparent model outputs whose tables add up, but they carry no uncertainty and no sensitivity analysis, and their net figures rest on protective relative risks from disputed low-intake studies. Citable as the WHO-CRA estimates for 2004 (deaths, DALYs, regional and country shares, the modelled prevalence of alcohol-use disorders) and for the costs reported by six national studies, always with these assumptions; not citable for trends since 2000, for greater harm per unit of alcohol in poor or marginalised people, or for the precision of the figures.

key_findings.finding: Exposure: worldwide average consumption in 2003 was 6·2 L of pure alcohol per adult per year, highest in the WHO European region (11·9 L) and the Americas (8·7 L) and lowest in the eastern Mediterranean region (0·7 L). Most adults abstained (no drinking in the previous year): 45% of men and 66% of women. Consumption rose with GDP per adult up to about I$10 000 and abstention fell with GDP up to about $7000.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 36·4% of all neuropsychiatric DALYs and 5·4% of all neuropsychiatric deaths were caused by alcohol (p. 2229). In Tables 1 and 2 these are the neuropsychiatric shares of the deaths and DALYs caused by alcohol, not alcohol's share of all neuropsychiatric deaths and DALYs (editors' calculation: 26,682 of 73,231 thousand DALYs and 135 of 2482 thousand deaths).

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure data are described for 2003 (p. 2224), but the attributable fractions applied to 2004 deaths were taken from the CRA for 2002 (chronic diseases) and the CRA 2000 (injuries) (p. 2227); yet the findings attribute the rise from 3·2% to 3·8% since 2000 mainly to more women drinking (p. 2229).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which year's drinking the 2004 estimates reflect is unclear, and the change since 2000 also reflects changed methods and inputs (alcohol-use-disorder prevalence and weights, colorectal cancer, the GBD 2004 cause revision); it cannot be read as a measured trend.

design_detail: Systematic review with dose–response meta-analysis of 17 observational studies (14 cohort, 3 case–control; published 1980–2003) of average alcohol intake and liver cirrhosis, analysed separately for women and men and for the two end-points, morbidity (clinically assessed) and mortality (death certificates). Random-effects meta-regression using the Greenland–Longnecker method for trend estimation (GLST procedure, Stata 10.1), with intake modelled two ways: first-degree fractional polynomials forced to be monotonic, and a categorical model with six intake categories (>0–12, >12–24, >24–36, >36–48, >48–60 and >60 g a day) against abstention. The reference group is lifetime abstainers: estimates from studies that used current abstainers were converted with a pooled relative risk for former drinkers. No protocol and no risk-of-bias appraisal of the primary studies. The stated purpose was to supply cirrhosis relative risks to the Comparative Risk Assessment for alcohol in the Global Burden of Disease 2005 study (p. 438).
can_establish: The average shape and size of the published association between average daily intake and the relative risk of liver cirrhosis up to January 2008, by sex and by end-point, relative to lifetime abstainers, and how much the morbidity and mortality studies differ from each other.
cannot_establish: That drinking causes the differences between intake categories beyond what the underlying observational studies can show (no study was appraised for confounding or bias); that alcohol affects death from cirrhosis more than the onset of cirrhosis (the end-point comparison is between different sets of studies, which also differ in design and country); that women are more susceptible than men (no test of the sex difference, and each sex's relative risk is against its own abstainers); whether low intake is safe for the liver (the categories below two drinks a day give contradictory estimates, including a significantly lower risk in men); or absolute risks (none reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Database search of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CINAHL, PsychINFO, ETOH and Google Scholar from January 1980 to January 2008, with key words for alcohol, alcohol consumption, alcohol intake, heavy drinking, liver diseases and liver cirrhosis, plus hand-searching of the content pages of major epidemiological journals and the reference lists of relevant articles and reviews; no language restriction (Methods › Literature search, p. 438). The included studies are general-population or occupational cohorts (for example Kaiser-Permanente, Framingham, American Cancer Society, Japanese physicians, Shanghai men) and three Italian case–control studies of liver disease (Table 1, p. 440; reference list, pp. 444–445).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cohort or case–control design; hazard ratios, relative risks or odds ratios with 95% CIs, or the information to compute them; end-point liver cirrhosis morbidity (clinical assessment) or mortality (death certificates), self-reports not accepted; three or more intake categories, one of them abstention. ICD codes considered: 581 (ICD-7), 571 (ICD-8 and ICD-9), K70 and K74 (ICD-10); no ICD-10 study was found. Excluded: reports not published in full (conference abstracts, letters to editors), cross-sectional designs, studies reporting intake only as a continuous measure or in two categories. Where a cohort had several reports, the one with the most comprehensive alcohol data was used (Methods › Case definition and Inclusion and exclusion criteria, pp. 438–439).
sample.demographics: Nine studies from the USA, four from Italy, two from Denmark, one each from Japan and China. Seven reported women and men separately, two women only, five men only and three both sexes combined (Results › Characteristics of the included studies, p. 440). Study sizes range from 369 to 548,185 participants and from 15 to 611 cases; the largest are Garfinkel et al. (1988; 548,185 women), Thun et al. (1997; 457,423) and Boffetta and Garfinkel (1990; 239,462 men) (Table 1, p. 440). Ages, follow-up and settings are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within primary studies is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Only studies that reported at least three intake categories including abstention were eligible, so studies reporting intake only continuously or in two categories were lost. The search began in 1980 and excluded conference abstracts and letters without a stated reason. The end-point comparison is confounded by study type: all four morbidity-only studies are Italian (three case–control studies and one cohort), the two studies with both end-points are Danish cohorts, and all eleven mortality-only studies are cohorts, nine of them American (Table 1, p. 440). Three American cohorts (Garfinkel 1988, Boffetta and Garfinkel 1990, Thun 1997) contribute 1625 of the 3384 cases (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used, converted by the reviewers to grams of pure alcohol a day using the type of beverage and the country's standard drink size, taken from the WHO International Guide for Monitoring Alcohol Consumption and Related Harm or an ICAP overview where a standard drink was not 12 g. Category ranges were represented by their midpoint; for an open top category, 75% of the width of the previous category was added to its lower bound (Methods › Standardisation of alcohol consumption, p. 439). Baseline intake in cohort studies is taken as an indicator of drinking over time (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph, p. 443).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average volume only, in grams of pure alcohol a day; the text equates one drink with 12 g (for example five drinks with 60 g, p. 438, and 'one to two drinks' with the >12–24 g category, p. 441). Categories: 0 (reference), >0–12, >12–24, >24–36, >36–48, >48–60 and >60 g a day (Methods › Statistical analysis, p. 439). Drinking pattern (binge drinking, drinking over time) and beverage type could not be analysed because the included studies lacked the information (Strengths and limitations, 4th paragraph, p. 443).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level. Tobacco, viral hepatitis and other drug use enter only through whatever adjustment each primary study made; which adjustments were made was extracted but is not reported (Methods › Data extraction, p. 439).

comparison.controls: Lifetime abstainers of the same sex (Table 2 footnotes, p. 442). For studies that reported risks only against current abstainers, the reviewers pooled the relative risk of former drinkers against lifetime abstainers from the studies that reported both, estimated the ratio of former drinkers to lifetime abstainers, and adjusted each such study's relative risks to a lifetime-abstainer reference, to avoid the sick-quitter effect (Methods › Data extraction, 1st paragraph, p. 439). The pooled former-drinker relative risk, the ratio and the number of studies adjusted are not reported.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed: no appraisal of how the primary studies handled confounders (hepatitis B and C, obesity, smoking, socioeconomic position) or measurement of intake over time. The discussion argues that lifetime abstainers should be combined with very light, infrequent drinkers as the reference group (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 442), but the analysis does not do this.

outcomes.instruments: Liver cirrhosis morbidity by clinical assessment and cirrhosis mortality by death certificate, coded by ICD-7 581, ICD-8 and ICD-9 571, or ICD-10 K70 and K74 (Methods › Case definition, p. 438). The outcome is cirrhosis of any cause as coded, not alcoholic cirrhosis alone.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed. The reviewers argue on biological grounds that alcohol should affect mortality more than morbidity, because drinking worsens existing liver disease and impairs immunity (Introduction, 4th paragraph, p. 438).
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk of cirrhosis morbidity or mortality at each intake level against lifetime abstainers, by sex; odds ratios, relative risks and hazard ratios were all treated as relative risks (Methods › Data extraction, p. 439).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 24 counts the categorical estimates in Table 2 (six intake categories × two end-points × two sexes), each with its own P value, plus 12 mortality-versus-morbidity interaction P values; the continuous models add two fractional-polynomial fits and two interaction tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Extraction was done independently by two investigators; a third investigator re-extracted a random sample of 15 articles and agreed on 95.6% of 710 data points (Methods › Data extraction, p. 439). Whether screening was done in duplicate is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: All relative to lifetime abstainers of the same sex; intake in grams of pure alcohol a day (one drink = 12 g). Categorical random-effects model (Table 2, p. 442). Women, mortality: >0–12 g 1.9 (95% CI 1.1–3.1); >12–24 g 5.6 (4.5–6.9); >24–36 g 7.7 (6.3–9.5); >36–48 g 10.1 (7.5–13.5); >48–60 g 14.7 (11.0–19.6); >60 g 22.7 (17.2–30.1). Women, morbidity: 0.4 (0.1–1.2); 1.0 (0.5–1.9); 2.4 (1.8–3.2); 1.9 (1.4–2.6); 5.9 (3.7–9.3); 6.1 (4.6–8.0). Men, mortality: 1.0 (0.6–1.6); 1.6 (1.4–2.0); 2.8 (2.3–3.4); 5.6 (4.5–7.0); 7.0 (5.8–8.5); 14 (11.7–16.7). Men, morbidity: 0.3 (0.1–0.9); 0.3 (0.2–0.4); 0.7 (0.5–1.0); 2.0 (1.5–2.7); 2.3 (1.7–3.2); 5.0 (3.9–6.4). Continuous (fractional polynomial) model: best fit power 0.5 in women (deviance 76.12 lower than the linear model) and linear in men; for women, mortality RR 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g a day, morbidity 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7) (Results › Dose–response meta-analyses, pp. 441). Heterogeneity in the continuous models: women Q = 200.59, I² 72% (63–78%); men Q = 305.22, I² 78% (72–82%). Dose × end-point interaction: women χ² 7.89, 1 df, P = 0.005; men χ² 17.06, 1 df, P ≤ 0.001. No absolute risks.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Primary-study adjustments were extracted but are not reported, and the paper does not say whether the most-adjusted estimate of each study was used. End-point (mortality or morbidity) entered the continuous model as an interaction with dose.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The continuous-model estimates are given in the text only for women at 24 and 60 g a day; men's values and all curves (Figure 2) are shown without intervals. The sensitivity analysis restricting to studies with sex- and end-point-specific results is described as giving a very similar pattern, with no numbers (p. 442). Residual heterogeneity after adding end-point to the model, and heterogeneity in the categorical model, are not reported. The significantly lower morbidity risks in men drinking up to 36 g a day appear in the results and limitations but not in the abstract. Table 2 gives no number of studies, datasets or cases behind any cell (p. 442).
analysis.power: Not discussed. The morbidity estimates rest on six studies (four Italian, two Danish) in each sex; Egger and Begg tests on 12 and 15 datasets have limited power to detect small-study effects (editors' observation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 17 mostly American and Italian studies, the relative risk of cirrhosis rose steeply with average intake in both sexes and both end-points, reaching 14 to 22.7 for death and 5.0 to 6.1 for morbidity above 60 g a day against lifetime abstainers. Mortality studies gave larger relative risks than morbidity studies at every level. Below about two drinks a day the estimates diverge: women in mortality studies already had a raised risk at up to 12 g a day (1.9), while men in morbidity studies had significantly lower risks than lifetime abstainers up to 36 g a day (0.3, 0.3, 0.7), and women's morbidity risk was not raised up to 24 g a day and was lower at 36–48 g than at 24–36 g. Women's relative risks exceeded men's at the same intake, without a formal test.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports "some indications for threshold effects" and a significantly larger effect of alcohol on mortality than on morbidity (p. 437), and the conclusions call the biological hypothesis for this "confirmed" (p. 443). Gaps: (1) the mortality–morbidity contrast is a comparison between two sets of studies that also differ in design (case–control against cohort) and country (Italy and Denmark against mainly the USA), and the same data were entered in both sets when a study did not separate end-points, so it cannot confirm a biological mechanism; (2) the 'threshold' for morbidity includes significantly lower risks in men drinking up to three drinks a day, which the authors themselves call a protective effect without a biological pathway (p. 443) and which suggests a problem with the reference groups of the morbidity studies, but the abstract does not mention it; (3) the statement that women have a higher risk at the same intake compares relative risks against each sex's own abstainers, without a test; (4) the public-health advice that no drinking can be recommended where cirrhosis is concerned and that people with any liver problem should abstain (p. 442) goes beyond the data, which concern average intake in general populations. The discussion does caution that the pooled estimates should be read in the light of the primary studies' limitations (p. 442).

timeline.event: English et al., an Australian report on drug-caused morbidity and mortality (this review's ref 8): more than ninefold risk of cirrhosis above 40 g a day in both sexes against abstainers, so no sex difference in relative risk at heavy intake, though risks differed between women and men at 20–40 g a day (as summarised in this review's introduction, p. 438).

Corrao et al., meta-analyses of 1998, 1999 and 2004 (this review's refs 5–7): a continuous, almost exponential rise in cirrhosis risk without an evident threshold, a significant increase from 25 g a day against abstainers, and high heterogeneity that this review suspected came from the end-point (Introduction, pp. 437–438).

Kamper-Jørgensen et al. (Danish cohort, J Hepatol): a threshold above about five drinks (60 g) a day, with 27-fold (men) and 35-fold (women) mortality from alcoholic cirrhosis against the Danish general population, and no further dose–response, as summarised in this review's introduction (p. 438).
Rehm et al. (Lancet), the global burden estimate cited here for about 15% of alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004 being due to cirrhosis (p. 437).
This review; its relative risks were intended for the Comparative Risk Assessment for alcohol in the Global Burden of Disease 2005 study (p. 438).

Askgaard et al., Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort: cites this review for a raised alcoholic-cirrhosis risk at one to two drinks a day, which holds for the review's mortality estimates but not its morbidity estimates, and notes the review's different morbidity and mortality risk functions; deaths were only 11% of its cases, too few to compare the end-points (card sc_askgaard_2015).

Roerecke et al. (Am J Gastroenterol), dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cirrhosis with sex differences, the update listed on the round's Tier A evidence map (card sc_roerecke_2019). Six of its nine studies are among the 17 here (Garfinkel et al., 1988; Boffetta and Garfinkel, 1990; Fuchs et al., 1995; Klatsky et al., 2003; Corrao et al., 1993 and 1997), so the two reviews are not independent.

replication.where_it_stands: The steep rise of cirrhosis risk with average intake is consistent with the earlier Corrao meta-analyses it updates. Its two distinctive claims, a larger relative risk for cirrhosis death than for cirrhosis onset and a threshold for morbidity, rest on between-study contrasts in four Italian and two Danish morbidity datasets and should be checked against the 2019 update (Roerecke et al.) before a claim relies on them. Two Danish cohorts (Becker et al., 1996 and 2002) are among its 17 studies; the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort (Askgaard et al., 2015) is not, so the two can be cited together without double counting.

funding.funder: NIAAA (contract HHSN267200700041C, 'Alcohol- and Drug-Attributable Burden of Disease and Injury in the US', to the first author) and the Global Burden of Disease and Injury 2005 Project provided financial and/or technical support; the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care supports salaries and infrastructure at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Acknowledgements, p. 443).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors are at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (the first author also at the University of Toronto and TU Dresden). The review was done to supply relative risks to the alcohol Comparative Risk Assessment of the Global Burden of Disease 2005 study, whose core group is thanked for comments (p. 443), and its introduction cites the first author's global burden paper (Rehm et al., 2009). No author is an author of an included study. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A dose–response meta-analysis of individual-participant data from prospective cohorts that record both incident cirrhosis (hospital records) and cirrhosis death (death registers) in the same people, with lifetime abstainers separated from former and occasional drinkers and with absolute incidence by sex, so that the morbidity–mortality and sex comparisons are made within cohorts rather than between different kinds of study.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Exposure (average intake in at least three categories including abstention), comparator (abstention, converted to lifetime abstention), outcomes (cirrhosis morbidity by clinical assessment and mortality by death certificate, with ICD codes) and designs are specified (pp. 438–439).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Cohort and case–control studies were chosen as giving stronger control than cross-sectional studies (Inclusion and exclusion criteria, pp. 438–439).

Seven databases including Google Scholar, key words given, hand-searching of journal content pages and reference lists, no language restriction (p. 438); but the search was limited to 1980 onwards and reports not published in full (conference abstracts, letters) were excluded, without a stated reason; no study registries or experts consulted. Applied as written (decision p-amstar2-item4); a lenient reading would give partial yes. The search ended in January 2008, about two and a half years before publication.
Who screened records and assessed eligibility, and whether two people did, is not stated; only extraction is described as duplicate.
Independent extraction by two investigators, with a third re-extracting a random sample of 15 articles (95.6% agreement on 710 data points) (p. 439).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives only numbers excluded (109 after screening articles, 41 after applying the inclusion criteria), without a list or reasons (p. 440).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives author, country, sex, design, cases, sample size and end-point (p. 440). The exposure measure and categories, the reference group used (current or lifetime abstainers), covariates, ages, setting and follow-up are not described for any study, so the five elements needed even for partial yes are not all present.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of the included studies. The conversion of current-abstainer references to lifetime abstention addresses one bias (sick quitters) analytically but is not a study-level assessment, and confounding is not assessed at all.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects dose–response meta-regression with Greenland–Longnecker trend estimation is an appropriate technique (p. 439), but the paper does not say that adjusted estimates were combined; odds ratios, relative risks and hazard ratios are pooled as one measure; results reported for both sexes combined were entered in both sexes' datasets, and results combined across end-points in both end-point datasets, so the same data appear twice (p. 439); and current-abstainer references were converted with an unreported pooled former-drinker relative risk.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact; the only sensitivity analysis concerns studies without sex- or end-point-specific results and is reported without numbers (p. 442).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: One general sentence asks readers to interpret the estimates in the light of the primary studies' strengths and limitations (p. 442); the interpretation of the mortality–morbidity difference and of the thresholds does not consider bias in the primary studies.

Q and I² with confidence intervals are reported for the continuous models (p. 441), and end-point and sex were examined as sources of heterogeneity and discussed; residual heterogeneity after adding end-point is not reported.

Begg–Mazumdar and Egger tests in each sex (women P = 0.837 and 0.215; men 0.767 and 0.196) and a discussion of publication bias (pp. 440–441, 443); the funnel plots are not shown and the tests have limited power with 12 and 15 datasets.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding is reported in the acknowledgements, but there is no conflict-of-interest statement and no description of how conflicts were managed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six of the seven critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, unjustified limits on date and publication type; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk of bias of included studies; 11, pooling of unstated adjusted estimates with data entered twice; 13, bias not considered in interpretation); only item 15 is met. Under AMSTAR 2 this gives critically low confidence, and it would do so under the lenient reading of item 4 as well. The review is useful as a quantitative summary of the cirrhosis dose–response in published studies to 2008, kept apart by sex and end-point and referenced to lifetime abstainers; its numbers can be cited as what these 17 studies show, relative to lifetime abstainers, with the steep rise at higher intakes as its most robust result. It cannot be cited on its own for a safe threshold, for a biological difference between cirrhosis onset and death, for a protective effect of light drinking in men, or for greater female susceptibility.

key_findings.finding: Selection: 3,238 records, 167 left after screening abstracts for liver cirrhosis, 58 articles assessed against the inclusion criteria and 17 studies included (14 cohort, 3 case–control; mortality end-point 11, morbidity 4, both 2); 109 and 41 articles were excluded at the last two steps, without reasons.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (flow diagram); Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The numbers are printed inside the Figure 1 image and are not in the text extraction; they were read on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: The 17 studies (published 1980–2003; 9 USA, 4 Italy, 2 Denmark, 1 Japan, 1 China) provided 12 datasets for women and 15 for men, with 1 477 887 participants and 3384 cases of cirrhosis in total; seven reported women and men separately, two women only, five men only and three both sexes combined.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The total is printed as 1477 887. Editors' check: the sample sizes and case counts in Table 1 sum to the totals in the text (1,477,887 and 3384). The three studies without sex breakdown entered both sexes' datasets (p. 439), which is why 12 + 15 datasets come from 17 studies.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Methods that shape every estimate: search of seven databases from January 1980 to January 2008 without language restriction; intake converted to grams a day using each country's standard drink (12 g as the base), category midpoints, and for open top categories the lower bound plus 75% of the previous category's width; current-abstainer references converted to lifetime abstention with a pooled former-drinker relative risk; results combined across sexes or end-points entered in both datasets.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Literature search (p. 438); Data extraction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Standardisation of alcohol consumption (p. 439)
key_findings.note: The pooled former-drinker relative risk, the former-drinker to lifetime-abstainer ratio and the studies that were converted are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Continuous models: of eight first-degree fractional polynomials, power 0.5 fitted best in women (deviance 76.12 lower than the linear model) and the linear model fitted best in men; marked heterogeneity remained (women Q = 200.59, P ≤ 0.001, I² 72%, 95% CI 63–78%; men Q = 305.22, I² 78%, 72–82%). key_findings.finding: Thresholds as the authors read them: in women's morbidity studies one to two drinks a day carried the same risk as lifetime abstention (RR 1.0, 0.5–1.9) and two to three drinks was the lowest category with a raised risk (2.4, 1.8–3.2); men drinking one to two drinks a day in morbidity studies had a lower risk than lifetime abstainers (0.3, 0.2–0.4), described in the limitations as a protective effect with no biological pathway; in women's mortality studies risk was raised from one drink a day on average. The authors conclude the results point to a threshold for morbidity but not mortality.

reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the reference group is modelled rather than observed. Because the conversion raises the relative risks of every converted study by an unknown factor, the size of the correction behind each pooled estimate cannot be checked.
