design_detail: Two-part review. (1) A narrative review of meta-analyses and selected studies on alcohol and ischaemic heart disease (IHD): the reference group, average intake, drinking pattern, confounding by age, smoking and other factors, short-term experimental and Mendelian randomization evidence. (2) A systematic review and DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analysis of seven observational studies comparing drinkers averaging under 30 g/day, with and without episodic heavy drinking, against lifetime abstainers. Searches from 1980 to August 2014 following PRISMA; the databases, search strings, protocols and details of the seven studies are only in Additional file 1 (not read). As the round brief directs, AMSTAR 2 is applied to the systematic part; the narrative part is described in the reasoning against the editors' narrative-review checklist.
can_establish: From part 2: the pooled IHD association, against lifetime abstainers, of drinking under 30 g/day on average without heavy drinking occasions and of the same average intake with such occasions, in seven published observational studies. From part 1: the authors' reading of the meta-analytic literature to 2014, much of it their own.
cannot_establish: That drinking without heavy episodes lowers IHD risk (observational studies without a risk-of-bias appraisal; the experimental evidence cited is short-term and on surrogate markers); which studies, designs, participants and heavy-drinking thresholds lie behind the pooled estimates (given only in the supplement); and, from part 1, any systematic or appraised synthesis (meta-analyses are selected and summarized without a stated method).

sample.recruitment: Two searches of electronic databases from 1980 to the second week of August (2014 according to the abstract): one for meta-analyses on alcohol and IHD, one for original articles (letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments excluded), plus hand-searching of the references of identified papers and of relevant reviews and meta-analyses. The databases and search terms are given only in Additional file 1 (Methods › Searches).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Meta-analysis: adult (18 or over) population samples; IHD as a separate outcome (ICD-9 410–414, ICD-10 I20–I25); case-control, prospective or historical cohort design; average intake over a reference period of more than 2 weeks; a drinking group averaging under 30 g/day that specifically excluded or included episodic heavy drinking; a risk measure against lifetime abstainers with its variability (or data to compute it); English, German or Spanish. Excluded: self-reported IHD and samples of people with IHD-related conditions (Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article (Table S1 of Additional file 1, not read). All seven studies adjusted for age and smoking, five for education or other socio-economic indicators, and four each for body mass index and marital status (Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Single-author search and data extraction; languages limited to English, German and Spanish without a stated reason; grey literature excluded; primary authors not contacted when data were missing. Only seven studies met the criteria, and their identities, designs, settings and sizes are not given in the article. The legend of Figure 2 marks one of its entries as taken from the authors' 2010 meta-analysis; how far the seven studies overlap with that review is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported average intake over more than 2 weeks, with a measure of heavy drinking occasions, as defined by each primary study; the threshold for a heavy drinking occasion is not stated in the article (Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Two exposure groups, each against lifetime abstainers: average under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions, and the same average with such occasions. In the narrative, chronic heavy drinking means an average of 60 g/day or more; the conclusions speak of one to two drinks per drinking day without heavy episodes, without defining a drink.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking was adjusted for in all seven studies; smoking as an effect modifier is discussed narratively (the evidence in smokers is called mixed). Other drug use is not addressed.

comparison.controls: Lifetime abstainers (former drinkers not included). Where needed, within-study estimates were re-expressed against lifetime abstainers by the method of Hamling et al., with priority given to estimates already comparing drinkers with lifetime abstainers (Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction and Statistical analysis).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Differences between lifetime abstainers and drinkers beyond the covariates listed (health, social position, reasons for not drinking); the narrative itself cites a US study showing that non-drinkers differ in their reasons for not drinking in ways that the lifetime-abstainer and former-drinker split may not capture (Results and discussion › Lifetime abstainers and former drinkers).

outcomes.instruments: IHD (ICD-9 410–414; ICD-10 I20–I25), mortality and morbidity combined, called IHD incidence (Figure 2 legend; Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias assessment of the seven studies is described; the article calls them high-quality and well adjusted.
outcomes.operationalization: Hazard ratios, odds ratios and relative risks treated as equivalent; the most-adjusted estimate was used, giving priority to comparisons with lifetime abstainers, and information from related papers on the same cohort was used where possible (Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction and Statistical analysis).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two pooled estimates (without and with heavy drinking occasions) and their ratio.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The first author performed the literature search and abstracted the data; full-text articles of potential eligibility were discussed by both authors until consensus (Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction).

analysis.effect_sizes: DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling on the natural log scale, Cochran's Q and I², Egger's test, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis (Methods › Meta-analysis › Statistical analysis). Against lifetime abstainers: drinkers averaging under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions, RR 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.71), I² 10%; with heavy drinking occasions, 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37), I² 0%; Egger P = 0.35 and 0.58; no single study had a large influence. Ratio between the two groups 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25). The numbers of participants and events are not given in the article.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; most-adjusted estimates, all adjusted at least for age and smoking.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The article does not mention registration; Additional file 1 is described as containing the systematic review protocols for the narrative and quantitative reviews (not read), and the authors' contributions mention protocol design.
analysis.selective_reporting: The meta-analysis is reported in two paragraphs, with the study details in the supplement. In the narrative, the authors' own 2012 meta-analysis is represented by its all-studies estimates only (see interpretation gap).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With seven studies, Egger's test has little power to detect small-study effects (editors' note), which the article does not discuss.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Part 2: in seven observational studies, drinkers averaging under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions had a lower pooled IHD risk than lifetime abstainers (0.64), while those with the same average intake and heavy drinking occasions did not differ from lifetime abstainers (1.12, 0.91 to 1.37). Part 1 reports, mostly from the authors' own meta-analyses: higher IHD mortality in former drinkers than in lifetime abstainers (women 1.54, men 1.25); no lower IHD risk in men drinking 60 g/day or more against lifetime abstainers (mortality 1.00, 0.74 to 1.36); and higher IHD mortality in people treated for alcohol use disorder than in the general population (men 1.62, women 2.09).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the epidemiological evidence for a beneficial effect of low intake without heavy drinking episodes is strong and corroborated by experiments, and the conclusions say the alcohol–IHD relationship fulfils all of Hill's criteria for causation (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph). Gaps: (1) the quantitative support is a seven-study meta-analysis with single-author selection and extraction and no risk-of-bias assessment, whose studies are not named in the article; (2) the experimental evidence is short-term studies of surrogate markers such as HDL cholesterol, which, as the authors note, is highest in people with alcohol use disorder; (3) the narrative reports the authors' 2012 meta-analysis through its all-studies estimates (0.69 to 0.81, all significant, at 1–2 drinks a day) and does not mention that its sex- and end point-stratified estimates for men's IHD mortality at about 1 and 2 drinks were not significant, or that its abstract said cardioprotection could not be assumed for all drinkers; (4) the Mendelian randomization study of Holmes et al. (2014), which found no protective effect, is set aside because the genetic variant was also associated with less binge drinking, and readers are referred to the authors' own rapid response to that paper; (5) the evidence on confounding is a selection of stratified studies, not a systematic synthesis. The conclusions also say that no amount of drinking is safe and that starting to drink should not be considered as prevention, which stands beside the causal claim without resolving it.

timeline.event: Roerecke & Rehm (American Journal of Epidemiology): among current drinkers who were not chronic heavy drinkers, heavy drinking occasions were associated with higher IHD risk than regular moderate drinking (RR 1.45, 1.24 to 1.70); the legend of Figure 2 of this review marks an entry as taken from it.
Ruidavets et al. (BMJ), the PRIME study of drinking patterns and IHD in France and Northern Ireland, cited here as showing similar findings.
Roerecke & Rehm (American Journal of Epidemiology): former drinkers had higher IHD mortality than lifetime abstainers (women 1.54, men 1.25).
Roerecke & Rehm (Addiction): average intake and IHD against lifetime abstainers by sex and end point (read in this round; card sc_roerecke_2012).
Roerecke & Rehm (Open Heart): chronic heavy drinking (60 g/day or more) showed no lower IHD risk than lifetime abstention (mortality 1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; incidence 1.04, 0.83 to 1.31).

Holmes et al. (BMJ) Mendelian randomization analysis concluding there was no protective effect; Rehm & Roerecke posted a rapid response to it on the BMJ site, cited here as ref. 97. Holmes et al. is read in this round by another reader.
This review: drinkers under 30 g/day without heavy episodes 0.64 against lifetime abstainers; with heavy episodes 1.12.

replication.where_it_stands: The pattern finding, that heavy drinking occasions remove the lower IHD risk seen in light drinkers, rests on this team's own meta-analyses (2010 and this one, which may share studies) and was not independently replicated in the sources read. The causal reading of the low-intake association is contested by genetic studies. The review can be cited for its pattern contrast, with its comparator (lifetime abstainers) and its limits, and as a pointer to the authors' other meta-analyses; its narrative conclusions are the authors' judgment, not findings.

funding.funder: European Community's Seventh Framework Programme (FP7/2007-2013), Grant Agreement no. 266813, Addictions and Lifestyle in Contemporary Europe – Reframing Addictions Project (ALICE RAP); the views are stated to be the authors' only (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests (Competing interests). In the same authors' 2012 meta-analysis, J. Rehm had declared taking part in scientific meetings organized or sponsored by the alcohol industry with financial support for that participation; no such statement appears here.
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the University of Toronto (Dalla Lana School of Public Health, Institute of Medical Science, Department of Psychiatry), and TU Dresden. The narrative rests mainly on the authors' own meta-analyses (refs 15, 26, 33, 39 and 42); Figure 1 is built from three of them (refs 15, 33 and 39) plus the Russian studies.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts with lifetime drinking histories and repeated measures of both average intake and heavy drinking occasions, separating lifetime abstainers, former and occasional drinkers, pooled at the individual level under a registered protocol; with genetic analyses designed to separate average volume from drinking pattern. Causation at low intake would need a long-term trial, which the authors consider unavailable.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adult population samples), exposure (drinking under 30 g/day with or without heavy drinking occasions), comparator (lifetime abstainers), outcome (IHD by ICD codes) and designs are specified.
Provisional: the article does not say whether a protocol was registered or fixed in advance; Additional file 1, not read, is described as holding the review protocols.
Case-control and cohort designs; the background explains that long-term randomized trials are missing and will remain so.

The databases and search terms are only in the supplement, but the article itself shows an unjustified restriction to English, German and Spanish and the exclusion of letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments; no grey literature or expert contact, and primary authors were not contacted for missing data. Under the project's reading of item 4 this is no whatever the supplement shows.
The first author performed the literature search; only full texts of potential eligibility were discussed by both authors.
The first author abstracted the data alone.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies in the article, and the supplement's described contents (protocols, two search-results figures, a table of the seven included studies, two forest plots) do not include one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the included studies are described only in Table S1 of the supplement (not read); the article gives only the covariates adjusted for.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No method for assessing the risk of bias of the included studies is described; the studies are called high-quality and well adjusted without an appraisal.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling on the log scale of most-adjusted estimates against lifetime abstainers, with within-study re-referencing by the method of Hamling et al.; heterogeneity was low. The method behind the ratio of 1.75 between the two groups, whose estimates share reference groups, is not described.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias on the pooled estimates; only leave-one-out analyses.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The abstract calls the evidence strong and the conclusions call the relationship causal by Hill's criteria, without considering the risk of bias of the seven pooled studies, which was never assessed; the narrative discussion of confounding concerns the literature in general. A close call, since confounding is discussed at length.
Heterogeneity was low (I² 10% and 0%).
Egger's test for both pools (P = 0.35 and 0.58), reported as no evidence of publication bias; with seven studies the test has little power, which is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (EU Seventh Framework Programme, ALICE RAP) and a statement of no competing interests are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Systematic part (the meta-analysis of drinking pattern): four critical items are not met (4, search; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk-of-bias assessment; 13, interpretation), so confidence is critically low. Items 2 and 8 are provisional (judged no information because they depend on a supplement not read), but they cannot change the overall rating, which is therefore not provisional. Single-author screening and extraction and a description of the studies only in the supplement add to the concern. Narrative part (not scored by AMSTAR 2; the editors' narrative-review checklist, for information): systematic search and explicit selection, some concerns (a search for meta-analyses is reported, but which ones are discussed, and why, is not explained); appraisal of the cited studies, high concerns (none); reliance on the authors' own studies, high (most quantitative statements and Figure 1 come from the authors' own meta-analyses); separation of evidence from speculation, some concerns (the Russian adjustments are labelled speculation, but causal conclusions are stated as findings); balance between evidence for and against a protective effect of low intake, some concerns, with the evidence against (the authors' own stratified 2012 estimates; the genetic study) under-represented. The review can be cited for its pattern contrast as reported, with its comparator, and for pointers; its causal statements are the authors' judgment.

key_findings.finding: Methods of the systematic part: searches from 1980 to August 2014 following PRISMA; inclusion of adult population samples, IHD by ICD codes, case-control or cohort designs, a drinking group under 30 g/day defined by the presence or absence of episodic heavy drinking, and a comparison with lifetime abstainers; English, German or Spanish only; search and data abstraction by the first author, with eligibility of full texts agreed by both authors; primary authors not contacted.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Methods › Searches; Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria; Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction

key_findings.finding: Seven studies met the criteria. Against lifetime abstainers, IHD incidence (mortality and morbidity combined) was lower in drinkers averaging under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions, RR 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.71), and not different in drinkers with the same average intake and heavy drinking occasions, 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (legend)
key_findings.note: The interval 0.53 to 0.71 is not symmetric around 0.64 on the log scale (see reporting issues). Figure 2 and the forest plots in the supplement were not read for values.

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity was low (I² 10% without and 0% with heavy drinking occasions); Egger's test P = 0.35 and 0.58; no single study had a large influence; all seven studies adjusted for age and smoking, five for education or other socio-economic indicators, four each for body mass index and marital status.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The relative risk between the two drinking groups (with against without heavy drinking occasions) was 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), higher than the 1.45 of the authors' 2010 meta-analysis; the authors read this as the impact of episodic heavy drinking being greatest at low average intake.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 2nd paragraph; Results and discussion › Drinking pattern, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 1.75 equals 1.12 divided by 0.64 (editors' arithmetic); how its interval was computed is not described. The printed interval is reproduced exactly (1.361 to 2.250; editors' calculation) by combining the two printed intervals on the log scale as if the two pooled estimates were independent; they share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within studies, a positive correlation that would make the correct interval for the ratio narrower, so the printed interval is, if anything, conservative.

key_findings.finding: From the authors' 2011 meta-analysis of 54 studies, as reported here: former drinkers had higher IHD mortality than lifetime abstainers, women 1.54 (1.17 to 2.03) and men 1.25 (1.15 to 1.36); the definition of lifetime abstention did not change this.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Lifetime abstainers and former drinkers, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand from the authors' own earlier meta-analysis (ref. 33).

key_findings.finding: From the authors' 2014 Open Heart meta-analysis, as reported here: men drinking 60 g/day or more had IHD mortality similar to lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36) and IHD incidence 1.04 (0.83 to 1.31). Against current non-drinkers, Ronksley et al. (2011) had reported 0.76 (0.52 to 1.09) for IHD incidence and 0.75 (0.63 to 0.89) for IHD mortality above 60 g/day, which the authors attribute to the choice of reference group.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand (refs 18 and 39). The Ronksley incidence estimate cited is itself not significant.

key_findings.finding: From the authors' 2014 meta-analysis of people treated for alcohol use disorder, as reported here: IHD mortality against the general population, men 1.62 (1.34 to 1.95), women 2.09 (1.28 to 3.41); the abstract summarizes this as a 1.5- to 2-fold risk.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The comparator is the general population, not lifetime abstainers.

key_findings.finding: The narrative summarizes the authors' 2012 meta-analysis as clearly showing a beneficial association against lifetime abstainers when all studies were included, with all pooled IHD estimates significant at one to two drinks a day (point estimates 0.69 to 0.81), and with women showing slightly stronger associations and an earlier upturn than men.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: These figures match Table 4 (all studies) of the 2012 paper; its fully stratified Table 2, with non-significant estimates for men's mortality at about 1 and 2 drinks, is not mentioned (card sc_roerecke_2012).

key_findings.finding: Russian studies, taking low-level drinkers rather than lifetime abstainers as the reference, report substantially raised IHD risk in heavy drinkers; the authors' speculative re-scaling, assuming the Russian reference group (about 4.6 g/day) has the risk of low-level drinkers elsewhere (0.81), gives 1.58 (1.48 to 1.69), and assuming benefit in 25% of the population gives 1.36 (1.13 to 1.64) for men treated for alcohol use disorder.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Figure 1 (legend)
key_findings.note: Labelled by the authors as speculation; the method is not described.

key_findings.finding: On confounding, the narrative states that adding confounders changed pooled estimates little (citing Ronksley et al. and a pooled analysis of eight cohorts), that an inverse or J-shaped relation was seen in never or non-smokers in all but one population study, that evidence in smokers is mixed, and that evidence by physical activity and body mass index is sparse.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Confounding from other risk factors for ischemic heart disease, 1st paragraph; › Smoking, 2nd paragraph; › Other confounding factors, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Experimental evidence: no long-term randomized studies of alcohol and IHD exist; short-term studies show dose-dependent effects on surrogate markers (higher HDL cholesterol, less platelet activation, lower fibrinogen, anti-inflammatory effects), with HDL also raised by regular heavy drinking and highest in people with alcohol use disorder. The Mendelian randomization study of Holmes et al. (2014), using the ADH1B variant rs1229984, concluded there was no protective effect; the authors argue it is hard to compare with the epidemiology because the variant was also linked to less binge drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Experimental evidence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The conclusions state that using current abstainers as the reference leads to systematic bias, that against lifetime abstainers the relation follows a J-curve that turns detrimental at lower intakes in women, that episodic and chronic heavy drinking negate any beneficial association, that the relationship fulfils all of Hill's criteria, that uptake of drinking should not be considered for preventing IHD, and that for public policy no amount of drinking is safe.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The authors' conclusions, appraised in the interpretation gap.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled estimate for drinkers without heavy drinking occasions, 0.64 (0.53 to 0.71), given identically in the abstract and the results, is not symmetric on the log scale: the geometric midpoint of the interval is 0.61, and a lower limit of 0.53 would imply an upper limit of about 0.77 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Results); Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The point estimate or one of the limits is probably misprinted; Figure 2 (image) and the supplement could not be checked. Claims should quote the figures as printed and note the inconsistency.

reporting_issues.issue: How the ratio of 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) between the two drinking groups was obtained is not described; it equals the ratio of the two pooled estimates, which share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within studies.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Meta-analysis › Statistical analysis
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval of the ratio cannot be checked and may not allow for the correlation between the two estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Essential details of the systematic part are only in Additional file 1: the databases searched, the search strings, the definition of a heavy drinking occasion, the identities, designs, settings and sizes of the seven studies, and their forest plots; the Methods also omit the year of the search end date (August 2014 is given only in the abstract).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Searches; Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph; Additional file 1 (description)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimates cannot be appraised from the article; the exposure (what counted as heavy drinking occasions) cannot be stated in a claim without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's Methods describe comparisons against lifetime abstainers, and its Results give a 1.5- to 2-fold IHD risk in people with alcohol use disorder; the text's figures (men 1.62, women 2.09) are against the general population.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Methods, Results); Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim based on the abstract would misstate the comparator of the alcohol-use-disorder estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The narrative says a beneficial association among chronic heavy drinkers appears only with current abstainers as the reference and gives Ronksley et al.'s estimates as the example, but one of the two, 0.76 (0.52 to 1.09) for IHD incidence, is not significant.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the mortality estimate (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) illustrates the point.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference list errors: ref. 33 (the authors' former-drinker meta-analysis, source of the 1.54 and 1.25) is printed as American Journal of Epidemiology 2011, volume 73, while the same article is cited with volume 173 in the authors' 2012 review; ref. 36 is dated 2012 although its DOI carries a 1998 identifier.
reporting_issues.consequence: Bibliographic only; no effect on the numbers.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 156 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4203905 (BMC Medicine 2014;12:182, the published version; DOI 10.1186/s12916-014-0182-6 matches the assigned DOI). All sections read, including acknowledgements, competing interests, authors' contributions and the reference list; the article has no tables; Figures 1 and 2 are images and no values were taken from them beyond those stated in the text; Additional file 1 (a PDF with the protocols, search-results figures S1 and S2, Table S1 of the seven studies and forest plots S3 and S4) was not read. The PMC page links no correction notice.

disagreements.first_pass: 1.75 equals 1.12 divided by 0.64 (editors' arithmetic); how its interval was computed is not described.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 196 (key finding 3, confirmed with an addition; missed): the printed interval 1.36-2.25 is reproduced exactly by combining the two printed intervals as if independent; the pooled estimates share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within the same seven studies, so they are not independent.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after recomputing (1.361 to 2.250); modified: with a shared reference group the covariance between the two log relative risks is positive, so treating them as independent overstates, not understates, the ratio's uncertainty; the note says so.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 196 (blind second reading) and AI reader 221 (adjudication)

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (MOOSE; no registered protocol) of the sex-specific association between average alcohol intake and liver cirrhosis (all cirrhosis, alcoholic and other) relative to long-term or lifetime abstainers. Seven cohort studies (outcome mostly cirrhosis death) and two Italian hospital case–control studies (first diagnosis of symptomatic cirrhosis): 2,629,272 participants, 5,505 cases. Intake categories converted to g/day and pooled in standard drinks of 12 g/day (cohorts: occasional, 1, 2, 3–4, 5–6, 7 or more drinks/day; case–control: 1–4, 5–8, 9–13, 13 or more). Estimates from studies whose reference group was current non-drinkers were corrected upward for former drinking. Restricted cubic splines tested non-linearity. Read from the PMC author manuscript.
can_establish: The pooled association, in the few published sex-specific cohort and case–control studies up to March 2019, between categories of average daily alcohol intake and cirrhosis (in cohorts, mostly cirrhosis death) relative to long-term abstainers, and how much it varies between studies.
cannot_establish: Whether a threshold exists at low intake (two to seven estimates per category, intervals that include 1 at several levels, I² up to 99%); whether women are at higher risk than men at the same intake (no formal test, overlapping intervals); the effect of drinking pattern (single studies only); causation by itself; or low-intake contrasts free of the upward correction for former drinking, which rests on two studies.

sample.recruitment: Medline and Embase from inception to 6 March 2019 (strategy in Supplementary Table 1, not read), plus reference lists of identified articles, meta-analyses and reviews; no language restriction (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria). Figure 1 (flowchart, read on the rendered page): Medline 1,035, Embase 2,536 and hand search 18 records, 2,977 unique; 2,592 excluded on title and abstract; 385 full texts; full-text exclusions listed by reason; 7 cohort studies (4 with results for men, 5 for women) and 2 case–control studies included. Primary studies: four US cohorts (American Cancer Society men and women, 1959–60; Nurses' Health Study; Kaiser Permanente), the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort, the UK Million Women Study, a national cohort of Chinese men, and two Italian hospital case–control series (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cohort and case–control studies with sex-specific results for average intake, adjusted at least for age, with at least two quantified intake categories against non-drinkers (or former drinkers against long-term abstainers), and more than 50 cirrhosis cases. Excluded: studies limited to alcoholic cirrhosis, or counting alcoholism (the source's term) as part of the outcome, because alcoholic cirrhosis cannot occur in lifetime abstainers; qualitative intake descriptions; studies in which all participants had alcohol use disorder or cirrhosis at baseline; duplicate reports; studies with no abstainer group (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Exposure and outcome assessment, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Table 1: baseline years 1959–2005; mean or median age at baseline about 40 to 59 years; follow-up 6.1 to 20 years in cohorts; four studies from the USA, two from Italy, one each from China, the UK and Denmark. The Million Women Study contributes 1,280,737 women and 2,078 of the 5,505 cases.
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Only nine studies qualified, and the male forest plot contains three cohorts (Figure 3). The highest-intake estimates draw heavily on the American Cancer Society cohorts recruited in 1959–60 (Garfinkel 1988, women, adjusted for age only and rated at serious risk of bias; Boffetta 1990, men). Several well-known studies were excluded because they reported only alcoholic cirrhosis (Discussion, 6th paragraph). The proportion of non-drinkers ranges from 0.002% (lifetime abstainers among Danish men, as printed) to 80% (current abstainers, ACS women) (Results, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported intake measured once at baseline in every cohort; lifetime intake recalled retrospectively in the case–control studies. The reviewers converted each category to g/day by its midpoint (open-ended categories: lower limit plus three quarters of the preceding category's range), used each study's own conversion where intake was given in standard drinks (8 to 14 g by country), and reported results in standard drinks of 12 g (Methods › Exposure and outcome assessment, 1st paragraph). Primary-study units ranged from drinks per day or week to g/week and UK units per week (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average daily volume. Cohort categories: occasional, 1, 2, 3–4, 5–6 and 7 or more drinks/day; case–control: 1–4, 5–8, 9–13 and 13 or more drinks/day (Figures 2–5; one drink = 12 g/day). Category bounds are not stated beyond the rule that categories with a mean up to 12 g count as one drink. Drinking frequency and drinking with or without meals are reported from single studies; heavy drinking occasions are not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking was adjusted in six of seven cohorts (not in Garfinkel 1988) and in neither case–control study; hepatitis B and C status only in one case–control study (Corrao 1997), and the Million Women Study excluded women with viral hepatitis (Table 1). From the Million Women Study, the authors report that risk rose with intake similarly in never-smokers and current smokers (Results › Subgroup analyses, 1st paragraph). Other drug use is not considered.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Reference groups: lifetime or long-term abstainers in Askgaard, Klatsky, Fuchs and both case–control studies; current abstainers, who include former drinkers, in Boffetta, Garfinkel, Liu and Yang (Table 1), whose estimates were corrected as described under comparison.

comparison.controls: Long-term abstainers (cohorts) or lifetime abstainers (case–control studies). Where a study used current non-drinkers, the log RR of each drinking category was increased by 0.23 × ln 2.52, that is, the pooled RR of former drinkers vs long-term abstainers from two cohorts (2.52 in the Methods; 2.56, 95% CI 0.93–6.79, in the Results) weighted by the mean proportion of former drinkers among current non-drinkers in those two cohorts (23%) (Methods › Exposure and outcome assessment, 1st paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph). Editors' calculation: this multiplies each such RR by about 1.24; it applies to four of the seven cohorts (Boffetta 1990, Garfinkel 1988, Liu 2009, Yang 2012), including the Million Women Study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable; the most adjusted estimates were used, adjusted at least for age.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genetic susceptibility, body-mass index and metabolic risk, diabetes, viral hepatitis (adjusted in one study), drinking pattern across the life course and coffee intake; the authors name several of these as likely confounders or effect modifiers that the literature does not capture (Discussion, 2nd to 4th paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: Cirrhosis as defined in the primary studies: ICD-7 581, ICD-8 571 and ICD-10 K70, K73, K74, plus unspecified cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.9, 456.0, 785.3; ICD-10 I85.0, I85.9, K74.6, R18.9) (Methods › Exposure and outcome assessment, 2nd paragraph). Cohorts: cirrhosis mortality from death records, with hospital records added in the Million Women and Danish cohorts; case–control: first diagnosis of symptomatic or decompensated cirrhosis, biopsy-confirmed in 319 cases of one study (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study risk of bias assessed with ROBINS-I (Supplementary Table 2, not read): all but one cohort rated moderate, mainly for single baseline measurement of intake and observational design; Garfinkel 1988 rated serious (adjusted only for age); case–control ratings not given in the main text (Results, 1st paragraph). GRADE: moderate certainty for a causal effect; low certainty for the absence of a threshold (Results › Subgroup analyses, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Adjusted relative risk (RR, HR, OR or SMR) of cirrhosis by intake category against long-term or lifetime abstainers, pooled separately for cohort and case–control studies and by sex; estimates by sex treated as independent samples (Methods › Data extraction).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 22 counts the pooled categorical estimates in Figures 2–5 (6 all-cohort, 6 male, 6 female, 4 case–control); the paper also reports two spline tests of non-linearity, one Egger test and the pooled former-drinker estimate.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. At least two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts and abstracted the data, with a third reviewer for discrepancies (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, last paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled RRs (95% CI; number of sex-specific estimates; I²), vs long-term abstainers, one drink = 12 g/day (Figures 2–5, read on the rendered page). All cohorts (Figure 2): occasional 1.11 (0.77–1.59; 6; 70.6%); 1 drink/day 1.40 (1.00–1.97; 7; 78.2%); 2 drinks 3.02 (1.95–4.70; 7; 91.7%); 3–4 drinks 3.27 (0.90–11.87; 5; 98.6%); 5–6 drinks 6.26 (2.38–16.50; 6; 96.7%); 7 or more 10.70 (2.95–38.78; 5; 98.3%). Men (Figure 3): occasional 1.23 (0.46–3.28; 2; 80.4%); 1 drink 0.91 (0.31–2.64; 2; 86.7%); 2 drinks 1.97 (0.89–4.37; 3; 91.2%); 3–4 drinks 2.62 (0.42–16.21; 2; 99.1%); 5–6 drinks 3.80 (0.85–17.02; 3; 98.1%); 7 or more 6.93 (1.07–44.99; 3; 98.9%). Women (Figure 4): occasional 0.95 (0.77–1.16; 4; 13.7%); 1 drink 1.64 (1.07–2.51; 5; 78.9%); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59–7.25; 4; 89.1%); 3–4 drinks 3.87 (0.80–18.83; 3; 92.6%); 5–6 drinks 12.44 (6.65–23.27; 3; 53.3%); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77–40.90; 2; 30.0%). Case–control studies vs lifetime abstainers (Figure 5): 1–4 drinks 1.19 (0.58–2.43; 4; 59.7%); 5–8 drinks 3.42 (1.31–8.96; 4; 79.0%); 9–13 drinks 7.36 (1.91–28.34; 4; 86.3%); 13 or more 5.71 (2.87–11.33; 2; 0%). Former drinkers vs long-term abstainers: 2.56 (0.93–6.79; 2 studies). Non-linearity: P=0.24 (men), 0.27 (women). Egger's test for 1–2 drinks/day: P=0.94. No tau-squared, prediction intervals or absolute risks.
analysis.covariates: Most-adjusted estimates as reported; adjustment sets range from age only (Garfinkel 1988) to age, smoking, BMI and several clinical and dietary factors (Fuchs 1995) (Table 1). A sensitivity analysis of the four female cohorts adjusted for age, BMI or waist circumference and smoking gave a similar, linearly increasing relationship from 1 drink a day (Results, 3rd paragraph; Supplementary Figure 3, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol registration reported; MOOSE guidelines followed (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract says meta-regressions were conducted, but the only dose–response results are the spline non-linearity tests, shown in supplements. Small-study and influence analyses were restricted to the 1–2 drinks/day categories. No analysis without the former-drinker correction is reported in the main text. All pooled categorical estimates appear only in the forest-plot images; the text gives a few.
analysis.power: Acknowledged as low for the non-linearity tests and for sex-specific estimates at low intake; male categories rest on two or three cohorts.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In cohort studies, cirrhosis risk (mostly cirrhosis death) rose with intake relative to long-term abstainers: no excess with occasional drinking, RR 1.40 (1.00–1.97) at about one drink a day and 10.70 (2.95–38.78) at seven or more, with I² of 70% to 99%. In women one drink a day gave 1.64 (1.07–2.51); in men 0.91 (0.31–2.64), from two cohorts pointing in opposite directions. Male estimates rest on three cohorts that differ more than tenfold at the highest intake, and the female estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one 1959–60 cohort adjusted only for age. In the two case–control studies 1–4 drinks a day showed no increase (1.19, 0.58–2.43).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that risk of cirrhosis increases exponentially with intake and that women “may be at higher risk compared to men even with little alcohol consumption”; the Study Highlights say risk increased exponentially among women with any alcohol consumption; the GRADE paragraph claims “high confidence in a causal dose-response relationship”. Gaps: (1) no test of a sex difference is reported, and the discussion concedes the intervals overlap; (2) 'any alcohol consumption' contradicts the null estimate for occasional drinking in women (0.95, 0.77–1.16); (3) the abstract calls the male RR at 5–6 drinks a day (3.80) a substantially increased risk although its interval includes 1 (0.85–17.02); (4) the women's high-intake estimates depend mainly on the one study rated at serious risk of bias; (5) the low-intake contrasts depend on a uniform upward correction for former drinking based on a non-significant RR from two studies, with no sensitivity analysis without it in the main text; (6) the high confidence in causation rests on a citation of a mechanistic review, not on trials of alcohol exposure; (7) the discussion reports some evidence for a threshold in men, whereas the results section finds no clear indication of a threshold and the non-linearity tests were null.

timeline.event: Liu et al., Million Women Study: alcohol, smoking and cirrhosis in middle-aged women; the largest contributor to this review (1,280,737 women, 2,078 cases).

Rehm et al., the same group's earlier meta-analysis: some evidence of a protective association at low intake in men (as summarised in this paper's introduction). This review, with a stricter outcome definition and the former-drinker correction, finds no protective association at any level.
Askgaard et al., Danish cohort included here; daily drinking vs drinking on 2–4 days a week at the same weekly intake: men RR 2.25 (1.68–3.00), women 1.28 (0.82–2.02) (as reported in this paper).

Exchange in the Journal of Hepatology on whether safe limits for liver disease can be set from a single measure of intake in late adolescence (letter by Askgaard, Tolstrup and Leon; reply by Hagström et al.), cited in this paper's introduction as the current threshold debate.
Simpson et al., Million Women Study drinking patterns: daily vs non-daily drinking RR 1.61 (1.40–1.85); drinking with meals vs outside meals 0.69 (0.62–0.77) (as reported in this paper).

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent sex-specific dose–response meta-analysis on the list for alcohol and cirrhosis of any cause, updating Rehm et al. (2010) from the same group. Heavy intake is consistently associated with very large relative risks of cirrhosis. Whether there is a threshold at low intake, and whether women carry a higher risk at the same intake, remain open: the low-intake evidence rests on few studies with extreme heterogeneity and on an upward correction for former drinking, which is this group's answer to the abstainer-bias problem and differs from the earlier review's approach. Claims should state the reference group (long-term abstainers, partly by correction), the 12-g drink, that cohort outcomes are mostly cirrhosis deaths, and the number of estimates behind each category.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), National Institutes of Health, award R21AA023521 to MR; the sponsor had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Financial support; Role of funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: MR and JR report grants from National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), during the conduct of the study. MR designed the study and conducted the literature review, extraction and analysis (Authors' contributions). The 2010 meta-analysis this review updates (first author JR) is called 'our earlier meta-analysis', and JR and MR wrote several of the cited reviews on drinking pattern and on reducing drinking (references 51, 64, 79, 83). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pooled individual-participant analysis of prospective cohorts in which lifetime abstainers are identified directly rather than by correction, with repeated intake measures, incident cirrhosis from hospital and death records, adjustment for BMI, diabetes, viral hepatitis and smoking, a formal test of whether the intake–risk slope differs by sex at low intake, and cohorts from outside the USA and Europe.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adults in cohort and case–control studies, by sex), exposure (average intake in quantified categories), comparator (long-term or lifetime abstainers), outcome (cirrhosis) and designs are stated (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria).
No protocol or registration reported; MOOSE guidelines followed.
Cohort and case–control studies were included without a stated reason; the quality-assessment paragraph treats design as a quality component but does not explain the choice.

Medline and Embase from inception to 6 March 2019, strategy in Supplementary Table 1 (not read), reference lists of identified articles and reviews, no language restriction, no stated publication-type limit, and publication within 24 months of the search. No grey-literature, registry or expert searches, so not 'yes'.
At least two reviewers independently excluded articles on title and abstract or full text, with a third reviewer for discrepancies.
The same reviewers independently abstracted the data.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives counts of full-text exclusions by reason (which sum to 375, not the stated 349), and the text names a few excluded studies with reasons (references 28–30 and 77), but no list of excluded studies is provided or referred to.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives, for each study, baseline years, setting and exclusions, sex, age, country, cases, participants, follow-up, intake categories and reference group, outcome definition and adjustments.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: ROBINS-I, whose domains cover confounding, selection, exposure classification, missing data, outcome measurement and selective reporting, was applied to each study (ratings in Supplementary Table 2, not read). The main text reports the ratings for the cohorts (six moderate, one serious) but not for the two case–control studies; the tool was built for interventions and is adapted here to exposures.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

The techniques are appropriate in themselves: inverse-variance DerSimonian–Laird random effects on adjusted estimates, cohort and case–control studies pooled separately, and splines that allow for the covariance of estimates sharing a reference group. But categories were pooled despite I² of 89% to 99% (single-study RRs at 3–4 drinks/day range from 1.04 to 14.21) with no stated justification and no prediction intervals; and every estimate from studies with current non-drinkers as reference was shifted upward by a fixed factor (about 1.24, editors' calculation) derived from two studies, with nothing to show that its uncertainty entered the intervals. Judged not met, consistent with the reading recorded for pooling at I² near 99% without a stated reason (SENIOR-DECISIONS, decision 25).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis restricted to the four female cohorts adjusted for age, BMI or waist and smoking, which leaves out the age-adjusted study rated at serious risk, gave a similar relationship (Supplementary Figure 3, not read); influence analysis at 1–2 drinks/day found no dominant study. No equivalent analysis for men.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion attributes the moderate quality to confounding and selection bias, single baseline measurement of intake (regression dilution), recall bias and coarse categories in the case–control studies, and outlying studies; GRADE ratings are given (Results › Subgroup analyses, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd and 5th paragraphs).

I² is reported for every pooled estimate, and heterogeneity is discussed at length as reflecting unmeasured risk factors and effect modifiers (genetics, BMI, drinking frequency and meals), study design and outcome (mortality vs morbidity); too few studies for meta-regression by study characteristics.

Egger's test (P=0.94) and a funnel plot (Supplementary Figure 1) were run only for the 1–2 drinks/day categories, with at most nine estimates, and the likely impact of small-study effects on the higher-intake estimates is not discussed. A close call.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: NIAAA funding and the authors' declarations are printed (Financial support; Declaration of interests).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2 protocol, 7 list of excluded studies, 11 statistical methods, 15 publication bias, the last a close call), item 4 is partly met, and items 9 and 13 are met: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. This rates how far the pooled numbers can be taken as unbiased summaries, not the paper's usefulness. In practice: each category rests on two to seven sex-specific estimates with I² mostly above 89%; in women the estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one 1959–60 cohort adjusted only for age (Garfinkel 1988: 52% and 77% of the weight); the three male cohorts differ more than tenfold at the highest intake (1.80 in Chinese men vs 22.39 in the American Cancer Society cohort); and the low-intake contrasts depend on a fixed correction for former drinking. The direction (risk rising steeply at high intake) is consistent across designs and sexes. The low-intake shape, any threshold and the sex difference are not established by this review.

key_findings.finding: Seven cohort and two case–control studies met the criteria (four US, two Italian, one each from China, the UK and Denmark), with 2,629,272 participants (579,592 men, 2,049,680 women) and 5,505 cirrhosis cases (2,196 men, 3,309 women). All cohort studies included cirrhosis mortality as the outcome (with hospital records added in the Danish and Million Women cohorts); the case–control studies used first diagnosis of symptomatic cirrhosis against lifetime abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Former drinkers vs long-term abstainers (2 cohorts): pooled RR 2.56 (95% CI 0.93–6.79); former drinkers were 23% of current abstainers. These figures were used to correct upward the estimates of studies whose reference group was current non-drinkers (log RR + 0.23 × ln RR for former drinking).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Exposure and outcome assessment, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Methods give 2.52; the interval 0.93–6.79 is centred on 2.51 on the log scale (editors' calculation), so 2.56 is probably a misprint. The correction multiplies affected RRs by about 1.24 (editors' calculation) and applies to four of the seven cohorts.

key_findings.finding: All cohorts, RR of cirrhosis vs long-term abstainers (one drink = 12 g/day): occasional drinking 1.11 (0.77–1.59); 1 drink/day 1.40 (1.00–1.97); 2 drinks 3.02 (1.95–4.70); 3–4 drinks 3.27 (0.90–11.87); 5–6 drinks 6.26 (2.38–16.50); 7 or more drinks 10.70 (2.95–38.78). I² ranged from 70.6% to 98.6% across categories.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Only the 7-or-more estimate and the I² range are in the text; the others were read from Figure 2 on the rendered page. Each category pools 5 to 7 sex-specific estimates. Editors' sums from Figure 2 (as read on the figure page by AI readers 158 and 199, whose readings agree): occasional drinking 5 cohorts and 458 cases; 1 drink a day 6 and 1,111; 2 drinks 6 and 574; 3–4 drinks 5 and 203; 5–6 drinks 5 and 281; 7 or more 4 and 276.

key_findings.finding: Men, cohorts, RR vs long-term abstainers: occasional 1.23 (0.46–3.28); 1 drink/day 0.91 (0.31–2.64); 2 drinks 1.97 (0.89–4.37); 3–4 drinks 2.62 (0.42–16.21); 5–6 drinks 3.80 (0.85–17.02); 7 or more 6.93 (1.07–44.99). Two or three cohorts per category (Boffetta 1990, Klatsky 2003, Yang 2012); I² 80.4% to 99.1%.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: Values other than those in the abstract were read from Figure 3 on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Women, cohorts, RR vs long-term abstainers: occasional 0.95 (0.77–1.16); 1 drink/day 1.64 (1.07–2.51); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59–7.25); 3–4 drinks 3.87 (0.80–18.83); 5–6 drinks 12.44 (6.65–23.27); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77–40.90). Two to five cohorts per category; I² 13.7% (occasional) to 92.6% (3–4 drinks).
key_findings.locator: Figure 4; Results, 3rd paragraph; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: At 5–6 and 7 or more drinks a day, Garfinkel 1988 (American Cancer Society women, 1959–60, adjusted only for age, rated serious risk of bias) carries 52.49% and 77.38% of the weight (Figure 4).

key_findings.finding: Spread between cohorts: at 7 or more drinks a day the male estimates were 1.80 (1.38–2.36) in Chinese men (Yang 2012), 8.30 (3.97–17.34) in Kaiser Permanente men (Klatsky 2003) and 22.39 (17.45–28.72) in American Cancer Society men (Boffetta 1990); at 3–4 drinks a day the cohort estimates ranged from 1.04 (0.87–1.25) to 14.21 (10.77–18.75).
key_findings.locator: Figures 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Case–control studies vs lifetime abstainers: 1–4 drinks/day 1.19 (0.58–2.43); 5–8 drinks 3.42 (1.31–8.96); 9–13 drinks 7.36 (1.91–28.34); 13 or more drinks 5.71 (2.87–11.33). One study (Corrao 1997) showed large increases for both sexes and the other (Corrao 1993) none or marginal ones.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Figure 5

key_findings.finding: No evidence of a non-linear dose–response on the log scale in men (P=0.24) or women (P=0.27); the authors note the low number of studies gave little power to detect non-linearity.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Small-study bias, tested only at 1–2 drinks a day: Egger's P=0.94; no single study had an overly large influence on those estimates.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the four female cohorts adjusted for age, BMI or waist circumference and smoking, risk rose linearly from 1 drink a day, similar to the main analysis.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Values are in Supplementary Figure 3, not read.

key_findings.finding: Drinking pattern, single studies: daily drinking vs drinking on 2–4 days a week, adjusted for weekly intake, men RR 2.25 (1.68–3.00), women 1.28 (0.82–2.02) (Danish cohort); among women who drank, daily vs non-daily 1.61 (1.40–1.85) and with meals vs outside meals 0.69 (0.62–0.77), associations said to be similar in strata of BMI, smoking and beverage type, with no adjustment set stated, and daily and outside meals together 2.47 (1.96–3.11), adjusted for amount and type of beverage (Million Women Study).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subgroup analyses, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Danish figures are not in the main text of the cohort paper (Askgaard et al., 2015; card sc_askgaard_2015), whose Table 2 gives daily drinking against 2–4 days a week as 3.65 (2.39–5.55) in men and 1.73 (0.85–3.52) in women, adjusted for age, amount, smoking, education and waist, and 4.83 and 1.6 adjusted for age and amount. This review may have used another analysis of the cohort (its supplement is not on file); claims should cite the cohort paper's own figures. The review's Table 1 lists this cohort with 393 cases in men and 229 in women and an outcome that includes unspecified cirrhosis: these are the counts of the cohort paper's supplementary analysis of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis (Askgaard et al., p. 2, Statistical analysis, 7th paragraph, and pp. 5–6), so the review's figures probably come from that analysis (editors' reading; the supplement is not on file).

key_findings.finding: Other subgroups from single studies: risk rose with intake similarly in never-smokers and smokers (Million Women Study); results were similar after excluding people positive for HBsAg or anti-HCV (Italian case–control series); risk was greatest after 10 or 20 years of heavy drinking but not 30 (the authors suggest survivor bias) and stronger at age 60 or younger.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subgroup analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (ROBINS-I): all but one cohort rated moderate, mainly for single baseline measurement of intake and observational design; one cohort (Garfinkel 1988) rated serious because it was adjusted only for age. GRADE: moderate certainty for a causal effect of alcohol on cirrhosis; low certainty for the absence of a threshold, because of imprecision and few sex-specific estimates at low intake.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Subgroup analyses, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Studies limited to alcoholic cirrhosis, or counting alcoholism (the source's term) in the outcome, were excluded because that outcome cannot occur in lifetime abstainers; the authors note this excluded some of the best-known studies in the field.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Exposure and outcome assessment, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The RR for former drinkers vs long-term abstainers is 2.52 in the Methods and 2.56 (0.93–6.79) in the Results; the interval is centred on 2.51 (editors' calculation). The Study Highlights call it a three-fold risk of cirrhosis incidence, although its interval includes 1 and both contributing cohorts measured mainly cirrhosis deaths.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Exposure and outcome assessment, 1st paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph; Study Highlights
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure on which the correction of four cohorts rests is imprecise and is overstated in the highlights; a claim about former drinkers' risk should use 2.5 with its interval.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1: the listed reasons for full-text exclusion (26, 130, 144, 9, 8, 20, 17, 13, 6 and 2) sum to 375, not the stated 349; 385 retrieved minus 349 would leave 36 articles for 9 included studies, whereas 385 minus 375 leaves 10 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection cannot be reconciled from the flowchart as printed; the total of 349 is probably wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 reports four cohort studies with results for men, but only three male cohorts (Boffetta 1990, Klatsky 2003, Yang 2012) appear in Figures 2 and 3; the Danish cohort's men (393 cases, Table 1) contribute no estimate, and no reason is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The male results rest on three cohorts; possibly the Danish men could not be compared with lifetime abstainers, who are reported as 0.002% of them (issue 4).

reporting_issues.issue: Lifetime abstainers are said to be 0.002% of the men in the Danish study; 0.002% of 26,696 men is about half a person (editors' arithmetic), so the figure is probably 0.2% (about 53 men) or a proportion of 0.002.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error, but it signals that the reference group in that cohort was tiny.

reporting_issues.issue: The text refers to 'the three case-control studies from Italy', while two case–control studies were included (Corrao 1993 and 1997; Figure 1, Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; possibly a reference to the three hospital series pooled in Corrao 1997.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (manuscript and version of record) says studies needed more than two drinking categories, while the Methods require at least two quantified categories in relation to non-drinkers and the flowchart excludes studies with fewer than two.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Figure 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the stated inclusion criterion.

reporting_issues.issue: The objective, abstract and flowchart frame the outcome as incidence of cirrhosis (one exclusion reason is that the outcome was not incidence), but all seven cohorts used cirrhosis mortality, with hospital records added in two.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Objectives; Figure 1; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The cohort estimates, including all the headline RRs, are mainly for cirrhosis death; claims should not describe them as incidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says all categories showed heterogeneity with P-values below 0.001, but Figure 2 gives P=0.004 for occasional drinking.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The results section finds no clear indication of a threshold and null non-linearity tests, while the discussion reports some evidence for a threshold effect in men.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Subgroup analyses, 2nd paragraph; Results, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper can be quoted on either side of the threshold question; the male basis is two cohorts with opposite estimates at one drink a day (0.50 and 1.50).

reporting_issues.issue: In the reference list, reference 64 (Rehm and Roerecke, 2015, on drinking patterns and cirrhosis) carries the same journal, volume and pages (J Hepatol 62:1061–1067) as reference 20 (Askgaard et al., 2015).
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation error; the editor should not build a reference record from reference 64 as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort with 393 cases in men and 229 in women and an outcome that adds unspecified cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.9, 456.0, 785.3; ICD-10 I85.0, I85.9, K74.6, R18.9) to alcoholic cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.0, ICD-10 K70.3), under the heading of cirrhosis mortality although the patient register was used; these are the counts of the cohort paper's supplementary combined outcome, not of its main analysis (257 men and 85 women with alcoholic cirrhosis; card sc_askgaard_2015). Only the cohort's women appear in the forest plots (144, 41 and 38 cases at 1, 3–4 and 5–6 drinks a day).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's Danish data are not the cohort paper's alcoholic-cirrhosis results; claims should not describe them as alcoholic cirrhosis only, and the review's daily-drinking figures for this cohort (key finding 10) probably come from the same supplementary analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say women's relative risks were higher than men's across all consumption levels, and the abstract that women's risk was consistently higher, but at occasional drinking the women's pooled estimate (0.95, 0.77–1.16) is below the men's (1.23, 0.46–3.28) (Figures 3 and 4).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 3rd paragraph; Figures 3 and 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the text overstates the sex contrast; at occasional drinking the estimates point the other way, with wide intervals.
