design_detail: Narrative clinical review in NEJM's Review Article series, by a single author, on recognizing and managing alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens): mechanism and course of withdrawal, the DSM-5 criteria, prevalence, case fatality, predictors and treatment, with three tables (the CIWA-Ar scale, the DSM-5 criteria and a suggested treatment protocol) and 33 references. No search strategy, dates or inclusion criteria are stated, beyond a mention of a PubMed search for uncontrolled studies after a 2004 guideline; there is no quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: What one clinician-researcher, drawing on DSM-5, a 2004 evidence-based guideline and selected later studies, presented in 2014 as the recognition, course, risk factors and recommended management of alcohol withdrawal delirium, and how weak he judged the treatment evidence to be.
cannot_establish: The incidence, case fatality or predictors of withdrawal delirium (all figures are second-hand, given without the designs, sample sizes or periods of their sources and, beyond hospitalized patients for the 3 to 5% and 1 to 4% figures, without their settings), the comparative effectiveness or safety of any drug or route (no trial is appraised), or the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). 33 references chosen by the author: DSM-5; reviews and guidelines, including the 2004 guideline on withdrawal delirium (Mayo-Smith et al.), Cochrane reviews of benzodiazepines (Amato et al., 2010) and of magnesium (Sarai et al., 2013) for alcohol withdrawal, and the Royal College of Physicians guidance on Wernicke's encephalopathy; and primary studies of predictors and of individual drugs, some of them retrospective by their titles (refs 13 and 16) (references, p. 2113).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the author's own. The treatment evidence named as the best is old (nine controlled trials conducted from 1959 to 1978, summarized in a 2004 guideline); later evidence is from uncontrolled studies found in a PubMed search whose terms and dates are not given (p. 2111); the prevalence, case-fatality and predictor figures come from cited studies whose settings and designs are not described (p. 2110). Three of the 33 references are the author's own.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable as an exposure study. The condition reviewed is alcohol withdrawal and withdrawal delirium after stopping or reducing heavy, prolonged drinking (DSM-5, Table 2, p. 2111); the drinking that precedes withdrawal is not quantified.
exposure.polysubstance: Recent misuse of other depressant drugs (the review's term) is named as a predictor of withdrawal delirium (p. 2110); other drug use is not otherwise discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Withdrawal symptoms are described as beginning within 8 hours of falling blood alcohol, peaking at about 72 hours and markedly reduced by days 5 to 7 (p. 2109); delirium as beginning about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear (p. 2110).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no comparison of groups).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Described, not applied: the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, revised (CIWA-Ar; 10 clinician-rated items, total 0 to 67) for withdrawal severity (Table 1, p. 2110), and the DSM-5 criteria for alcohol withdrawal and for delirium (Table 2, p. 2111).
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal delirium is DSM-5 alcohol withdrawal together with delirium (Table 2 footnote, p. 2111); withdrawal severity is banded by CIWA-Ar total score (Table 1 footnote, p. 2110).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Descriptive figures as cited: lifetime alcohol use disorder in 20% of men and 10% of women in most Western societies; withdrawal symptoms in about 50% of people with an alcohol use disorder who cut down or stop, with seizures, delirium or both in 3 to 5% of them (p. 2109); withdrawal delirium in 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal; case fatality about 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium; recent withdrawal seizures in 20% of people with delirium (p. 2110). No relative risks or intervals are given for any predictor.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The studies of alternatives to benzodiazepines are cited for the amounts given, not for their results; harms are named for the alternative and adjunctive drugs but not for high-dose benzodiazepines; the PubMed search mentioned is not described (pp. 2111–2112).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review is a clinical synthesis. Its descriptive figures (3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for withdrawal develop withdrawal delirium; about 1 to 4% of those die; onset about 3 days after withdrawal begins; duration usually 2 or 3 days) and its predictors are second-hand from cited studies, and its treatment advice rests, by its own account, on nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 summarized in a 2004 guideline and on later uncontrolled studies; no benzodiazepine has been shown superior to another, and the alternatives are less studied.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say withdrawal delirium is "best treated with intravenous benzodiazepines" (p. 2112), while also stating that all doses in the review are approximations based on uncontrolled studies and that data on the most effective care are lacking. Gaps: (1) the body cites no evidence comparing intravenous with other routes, or benzodiazepines with other drug classes, in withdrawal delirium; the preference rests on the 2004 guideline and clinical reviews; (2) Table 3 presents its regimens as suggested treatment without grading the evidence for each element, although the Conclusions concede they rest on uncontrolled data; (3) the statement that case fatality could be reduced by timely diagnosis and adequate treatment comes without data on the size of the reduction (p. 2110); (4) the dangers of the alternative and adjunctive drugs are named (heart block, QT prolongation, seizures) but the harms of the high benzodiazepine amounts the review describes are not, beyond recommending hospital or intensive care and vital-sign monitoring (pp. 2111–2112). The explanation offered for the lack of trials (low prevalence, cost, no profit motive) is hedged as a possibility. Because the review is candid about the weakness of the evidence, the gap is minor.

timeline.event: Schuckit et al. (1995), Addiction: histories of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens in 1648 people with alcohol dependence; the author's own study, cited among the sources of the predictor list (ref. 17).

Mayo-Smith (1997), JAMA meta-analysis and evidence-based practice guideline on the pharmacological management of alcohol withdrawal (on the project's Tier A list); not cited in this review, which relies on the same first author's 2004 guideline on withdrawal delirium.

Mayo-Smith et al. (2004), Archives of Internal Medicine: evidence-based practice guideline on managing alcohol withdrawal delirium (ref. 9; on the project's Tier B list), which this review names as the best evidence, a review of nine prospective controlled trials conducted from 1959 to 1978.

Amato et al. (2010), Cochrane review of benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal (ref. 12; on the project's Tier A list, read by another first reader in this round), cited for benzodiazepines as the mainstay and for no single benzodiazepine being superior.

Eyer et al. (2011), Alcohol and Alcoholism: predictors of seizures and delirium tremens in the course of withdrawal (ref. 10; on the project's Tier B list), one of the cited sources of the prevalence and predictor statements.
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: A clinical review rather than an evidence synthesis. By its own account the treatment evidence for withdrawal delirium is thin (nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 and later uncontrolled studies), and it calls for publicly funded trials. Its descriptive figures should be cited from the primary sources it names (for example Eyer et al., 2011, the 2004 guideline and Amato et al., 2010). Later trials or reviews of treatment for withdrawal delirium were not searched for in this reading, and letters in reply were not searched (no browser in this round).

funding.funder: Not reported (the article has no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest relevant to this article was reported; the author's disclosure forms are available with the full text at NEJM.org and were not read (p. 2113).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, University of California, San Diego, School of Medicine (p. 2109). Three of the 33 references are the author's own: a 2009 Lancet review of alcohol use disorders (ref. 2), a textbook chapter on ethanol and methanol (ref. 5) and the 1995 study of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (ref. 17), which supports part of the predictor list. Published in NEJM's Review Article series (editor Dan L. Longo).

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials in patients with DSM-5 withdrawal delirium comparing benzodiazepine-based treatment with alternatives (for example phenobarbital, or dexmedetomidine as an adjunct) on mortality, complications and length of intensive care, together with prospective multicentre cohorts using standardized diagnosis to establish the incidence, case fatality and validated predictors of withdrawal delirium in each care setting.

domains.note: No search strategy, dates or inclusion criteria; a PubMed search for uncontrolled studies after 2004 is mentioned without terms or dates (p. 2111); 33 references chosen by the author (p. 2113).

The evidence base is characterized candidly in general terms (few double-blind trials; the best evidence nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978; doses approximations from uncontrolled studies; alternatives less well studied; pp. 2111–2112), but no cited study is appraised: the prevalence, case-fatality and predictor figures are given without the designs or settings of their sources, some of which are retrospective by their titles (refs 13 and 16).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 33 references are the author's own (refs 2, 5 and 17), and one of them supports part of the predictor list; the treatment recommendations rest mainly on others' guidelines and reviews (refs 9, 12 and 18 to 22).

The explanation for the lack of trials is hedged, and the Conclusions state that doses are approximations from uncontrolled studies and that data on the best care are lacking; but Table 3 sets out specific regimens as suggested treatment without grading their evidence, the Conclusions name intravenous benzodiazepines as the best treatment without cited comparative evidence, and the statement that alcohol use disorders shorten life by a decade carries no citation (pp. 2109, 2112).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on drug treatment of withdrawal delirium (benzodiazepines against alternatives)
domains.note: The dangers of the alternatives and adjuncts are named (heart block with dexmedetomidine; QT prolongation and seizures with antipsychotics) and they are said to offer few advantages, but the harms of high-dose benzodiazepines are not discussed and the studies of alternatives are cited for amounts, not results. The under-represented side is the evidence on the alternatives and on the harms of the recommended benzodiazepine approach (pp. 2111–2112).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used (model card sc_kish_2017), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain (search and selection, high). The review is candid about the thin evidence for treating withdrawal delirium and does not lean on the author's own work, but its selection is unsystematic and its figures are second-hand. It may be cited for the definitions it reproduces (the DSM-5 criteria; the structure and score bands of the CIWA-Ar, attributed to their sources), for the author's characterization of the evidence base (few controlled trials, the best being nine from 1959 to 1978; doses resting on uncontrolled studies) and for what it recommends in general terms, attributed to the author. Figures on incidence, case fatality, timing and predictors should be cited from the primary sources it names; a claim resting only on this review stays at draft (METHODS §5.3).

key_findings.finding: The review states that about 50% of people with an alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop drinking and that in 3 to 5% of them grand mal seizures, a delirium or both develop (citing DSM-5); lifetime prevalence of alcohol use disorder in most Western societies is given as 20% of men and 10% of women, and alcohol-related conditions as affecting more than 20% of patients in most medical settings.
key_findings.locator: Opening section (before States of Alcohol Withdrawal), 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures (refs 1 to 3). The statement in the same paragraph that these conditions can shorten life by a decade carries no citation.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2109 (text)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol is described as a central nervous system depressant that increases GABA release, with prominent effects at GABA-A receptors, and inhibits NMDA glutamate-receptor activity; with repeated exposure the brain adapts (tolerance), and falling blood alcohol then produces symptoms broadly opposite to the acute effects: insomnia, anxiety, raised pulse, respiration rate, body temperature and blood pressure, and hand tremor. Withdrawal symptoms usually begin within 8 hours after blood alcohol falls, peak at about 72 hours and are markedly reduced by days 5 to 7 of abstinence.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Mild and Moderate Withdrawal, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Cited to reviews and a textbook chapter (refs 4 to 7), not to primary studies.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2109 (text)

key_findings.finding: The CIWA-Ar is presented as a clinician-rated 10-item scale (9 items scored 0 to 7, and orientation and clouding of sensorium scored 0 to 4) with totals from 0 to 67: below 8 mild withdrawal that rarely needs medication, 8 to 15 moderate, above 15 severe, with a danger of grand mal seizures, delirium or both; some studies use 10 as the cut-off between mild and moderate. The table is taken from a review by Kosten and O'Connor (ref. 4).
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Mild and Moderate Withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 2109, continuing on p. 2110); Table 1 and its footnote (p. 2110)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2109–2110 (text; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal delirium is defined, following DSM-5, as alcohol withdrawal (stopping or reducing heavy, prolonged drinking, with at least two of eight symptoms: autonomic hyperactivity, hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, generalized tonic–clonic seizures) together with delirium, a rapid-onset, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness and cognition that is a change from normal, without coma or another evolving neurocognitive disorder.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 1st paragraph (p. 2110); Table 2 and its footnote (p. 2111)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2110–2111 (text read on the rendered pages; Table 2 checked)

key_findings.finding: Prevalence is said to be hard to establish, because clinicians differ in how closely they follow the criteria and rates depend on the setting (outpatient, general medical or psychiatric inpatient, intensive care); most studies estimate that 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal meet the criteria for withdrawal delirium, and retrospective chart reviews based on general clinicians' diagnoses give higher but less reliable rates.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand (refs 7, 10 and 11); beyond patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal, the settings, designs and periods of these estimates are not given.

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal delirium usually begins about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear and lasts from 1 to 8 days or more, usually 2 or 3 days. About 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium die, a rate the author says could be reduced by timely diagnosis and adequate treatment; death usually results from hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, complications of withdrawal seizures or concomitant medical disorders.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the case-fatality range is cited to four sources (refs 7, 9, 11 and 13) without their settings or periods, and the possible reduction is not quantified.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2110 (text read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Predictors of delirium during withdrawal named in the review: CIWA-Ar scores above 15 (especially with systolic blood pressure above 150 mm Hg or pulse above 100 beats per minute), recent withdrawal seizures (seen in 20% of people with delirium), prior withdrawal delirium or seizures, older age, recent misuse of other depressants, and concomitant medical problems, including low potassium or magnesium, low platelet counts, and respiratory, cardiac or gastrointestinal disease.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: No effect sizes or designs are given. The sources (refs 7, 10, 11, 13, 16 and 17) include two retrospective studies by their titles (refs 13 and 16) and the author's own 1995 study of 1648 people with alcohol dependence (ref. 17, reference list p. 2113).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2110 (text read on the rendered page); reference list p. 2113

key_findings.finding: The author states that few double-blind, controlled, prospective trials of treatment exist, offering the low prevalence of the condition, high treatment costs and a lack of commercial incentive as possible reasons; the best evidence is a 2004 review of nine prospective controlled trials conducted between 1959 and 1978 (Mayo-Smith et al., 2004), together with later uncontrolled studies identified in a PubMed search.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 1st paragraph (p. 2110, continuing on p. 2111)
key_findings.note: The PubMed search's terms, dates and selection criteria are not given.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2110–2111 (text read on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: The review's treatment goals are to control agitation and to lower the risk of seizures, injury and death. It recommends care in a locked inpatient ward or an intensive care unit, because agitation is common and outcomes can be fatal; a physical examination and blood tests to find and treat contributing medical problems; the general supportive care used for any delirium (reorientation, a well-lit room, reassurance, frequent vital-sign checks, adequate hydration); caution with glucose because of the risk of precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy; and care to avoid overhydration in people with alcohol-related cardiac compromise.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2111); Table 3 (p. 2112)

key_findings.finding: The review recommends thiamine and multivitamins, with more thiamine when Wernicke's encephalopathy is suspected, and finds little support for giving magnesium routinely. The amounts it gives are not recorded on this card.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepines are called the mainstay of drug treatment, and no single benzodiazepine has been shown superior to another; Table 3 gives example regimens for a long-acting and a shorter-acting benzodiazepine. The amounts needed vary greatly between patients and can be very large, which the author gives as a reason for treatment in hospital, preferably intensive care, directed by well-trained clinicians. The regimens and doses are not recorded on this card.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 4th paragraph (p. 2111); Table 3 (p. 2112)

key_findings.finding: Phenobarbital, clomethiazole, midazolam, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine have been proposed for uncomplicated withdrawal, but data on their use in withdrawal delirium are lacking. Propofol (especially in intubated patients) and dexmedetomidine (an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used in intensive care; not usable with heart block, and requiring close monitoring of blood pressure and heart rate) are named for patients who do not respond to high benzodiazepine doses. None of these has been studied as well as benzodiazepines, and each is said to carry additional dangers and few advantages for most patients. Haloperidol is listed as an adjunct for severe agitation or hallucinosis, with the warning that antipsychotics can prolong the QT interval and make seizures more likely.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 5th paragraph (p. 2111, continuing on p. 2112) and 6th paragraph (p. 2112); Table 3 (p. 2112)
key_findings.note: Cited to reviews and small or uncontrolled studies (refs 7, 13, 20 to 22 and 25 to 33); no results of these studies are given in the review.

key_findings.finding: The Conclusions call withdrawal delirium an uncommon, serious complication of withdrawal that is best treated with intravenous benzodiazepines; they state that all doses described in the review are approximations based on uncontrolled studies and that data on the most effective care are lacking, and call for treatment trials sponsored by the National Institutes of Health because the low profit potential may deter pharmaceutical companies.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 3 to 5% range is given for two different quantities: on p. 2109 for grand mal seizures, delirium or both among people with an alcohol use disorder who have withdrawal symptoms (citing DSM-5), and on p. 2110 for withdrawal delirium among patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal (refs 7, 10 and 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators (everyone with withdrawal symptoms against hospitalized patients) and the outcomes (seizures or delirium against delirium) differ; a claim must keep them apart and should cite the primary sources.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that alcohol use disorders can shorten life by a decade carries no citation; the reference markers in that paragraph belong to the sentences before and after it.

design_detail: Systematic review with mixed-effects meta-regression of 87 cohort studies (523 relative-risk estimates) of alcohol consumption and all-cause mortality, testing whether ‘abstainer biases’ (former and/or occasional drinkers counted in the abstainer reference group) and other study characteristics explain the J-shaped curve. Three strategies: all studies pooled with study-level covariates (Tables 2 and 3); studies stratified by type of abstainer bias (Table 4); and a subset of ‘higher quality’ studies with strictly defined lifetime abstainers (Table 5). Protocol approved as a US National Institutes of Health R01 grant application, presented as online Appendix A (not read); no registry record.
can_establish: How much the pooled association between low-volume drinking and all-cause mortality in published cohort studies (to 2014) depends on how each study defined its abstainer reference group and on other study characteristics, and what studies with strictly defined lifetime abstainers show.
cannot_establish: Whether low-volume drinking causes or prevents deaths (the data are observational and the adjustment is at study level, that is ecological); a pooled risk that applies to any defined population (the adjusted estimates are model predictions whose covariate reference levels are not stated); outcomes other than all-cause mortality; the shape of the curve below 25 g/day (a single low-volume category); or the absence of a modest effect in either direction (the adjusted low-volume interval, 0.88 to 1.07, includes both).

sample.recruitment: Database search: PubMed (last searched 25 February 2015) and Web of Science for English-language articles published up to 31 December 2014, plus the reference lists of two earlier meta-analyses (Fillmore et al., 2006; Ronksley et al., 2011). 2,662 records identified, 87 studies included (Method › Data sources; Study selection; Results › Study selection; Figure 1, an image).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original English-language peer-reviewed cohort studies quantifying all-cause mortality by level of alcohol consumption in human populations, any sex, age, ethnic group or region. Excluded: studies whose mortality outcome could not be separated from morbidity, and samples defined by pre-existing illness or poor health. Where a cohort had several publications, the most recent or the most comprehensive in its handling of bias and confounding was used (Method › Inclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Of the 87 studies, 30 reported separate estimates for men and women, 31 men only, 7 women only, 19 both combined; median cohort age at intake 54.5 years (SD 10.5); 77 from North America, Europe or Australia and 10 from Japan, China or India; mean follow-up 13.4 years (SD 6.6); 34 excluded unhealthy participants; 64 used an intake measure coded as adequate (Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English only, two databases, no grey literature or registries, search ending in December 2014. The included cohorts are mostly from high-income, mainly white populations. Choice of one publication per cohort, and the rules for converting categories to grams, could change estimates; per-study data are in online appendices B and D (not read).

exposure.measurement: Mean daily intake in grams of ethanol at baseline, self-reported in every primary study, converted from each study's categories with the study's drink size or a country-specific estimate (8 g in the UK to 19.75 g in Japan) and category midpoints; open-ended top categories set at the lower bound plus three quarters of the width of the next-lower category. An intake measure was coded ‘adequate’ if quantity and frequency were assessed over at least one week (64 of 87 studies) (Method › Measures of alcohol consumption; Quality assessment).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories in g/day: lifetime abstainers (reference, strictly zero lifetime consumption); former drinkers (now completely abstaining); occasional, less than 1.30 (up to one drink a week); low volume 1.30 to 24.9 (up to two drinks); medium 25 to 44.9 (up to four); high 45 to 64.9 (up to six); higher, 65 or more. Low volume was set in advance from the Australian NHMRC limit of 20 g/day and operationalized as up to 24 g because studies reported whole drinks (Method › Measures of alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph; Analyses, 4th paragraph). For orientation, 25 g/day is 175 g/week (editors' arithmetic).
exposure.polysubstance: Whether the primary study controlled for smoking is coded as a study-level covariate; no other substance is considered.

comparison.controls: Each study's own ‘abstainer’ group: in 74 of 87 studies it included former and/or occasional drinkers (41 both, 24 former only, 9 occasional only); 13 studies used strictly defined lifetime abstainers. Alternative reference: occasional drinkers (Table 2, right-hand columns; method in Appendix A, Box 1, not read).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Study-level covariates in the meta-regression: median age at intake, sex, mainly Caucasian population or not, adequacy of the intake measure, former-drinker bias and occasional-drinker bias (six-covariate model), then also follow-up years, exclusion of ill participants and whether the study controlled for race and smoking (full model).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within the cohorts, drinking history before baseline, reasons for abstaining, earlier health, socio-economic position, diet and physical activity are handled only by whatever each study adjusted for; apart from smoking and race control, these are not among the meta-regression covariates.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality as reported by each cohort: hazard ratios or rate ratios used as relative risks (RR), RRs computed from rates where only rates were reported, and estimates recalculated against abstainers when a study used occasional drinkers as its reference (Method › Summary measures of outcome).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death is an objective outcome; ascertainment methods of the cohorts are not described.
outcomes.operationalization: RR of death for each drinking category against the study's reference group, natural-log transformed; summary RRs are inverse-variance-weighted mixed-model estimates (fixed effects for drinking category and covariates, random intercept for study).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, but six drinking categories estimated in at least ten models (Tables 2 to 5), each tested at p < .05 with t tests; covariates entered on bivariable p < .20.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two trained reviewers read all titles; abstracts were then reviewed (by whom is not stated) and full texts checked for eligibility with cross-checking by senior investigators; two reviewers extracted and coded the data, disagreements resolved by discussion, and the coding was double-checked by the first two authors (Method › Study selection; Data extraction).

analysis.effect_sizes: All RRs for all-cause mortality. Table 2 (weighted for precision and between-study variation only), against each study's abstainers: former drinkers 1.22 (95% CI 1.14 to 1.31), 21 studies, 42 estimates, I2 65%; occasional 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), 15 studies, I2 61%; low volume 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90), 81 studies, 229 estimates, I2 65%; medium 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00), p = .031, I2 80%; high 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17), I2 82%; higher 1.29 (1.22 to 1.36), I2 83%; all drinkers combined 1.00 (0.85 to 1.17). Against occasional drinkers: abstainers 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27); former 1.45 (1.33 to 1.59); low 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10); medium 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22); high 1.33 (1.24 to 1.44); higher 1.52 (1.40 to 1.66); all drinkers 1.24 (1.08 to 1.42). Table 3, six covariates: former 1.26 (1.17 to 1.35); occasional 0.86 (0.80 to 0.92); low 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94); medium 0.98 (0.92 to 1.04); high 1.13 (1.06 to 1.20); higher 1.32 (1.23 to 1.41). Table 3, all covariates: former 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54); occasional 0.95 (0.85 to 1.05); low 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07); medium 1.07 (0.97 to 1.18); high 1.24 (1.12 to 1.37); higher 1.44 (1.30 to 1.60); all drinkers 1.15 (0.97 to 1.36). Table 4, 13 studies with lifetime abstainers only (adjusted for median age, sex and country): former 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57); occasional 0.94 (0.71 to 1.25), 4 estimates; low 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), 50 estimates; medium 0.95 (0.80 to 1.13); high 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32); higher 1.42 (1.15 to 1.75); in the three groups of studies with abstainer biases, low volume 0.91 (0.83 to 1.00), 0.86 (0.78 to 0.95) and 0.86 (0.82 to 0.91). Table 5, seven higher-quality studies against lifetime abstainers (sampling and between-study variation only): low 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), higher 1.58 (1.05 to 2.38), former 1.14 (0.77 to 1.69); without the influential Friesema et al. (2007) study: low 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15), medium 1.29 (1.06 to 1.56), former 1.31 (1.11 to 1.55), higher 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27). Egger tests: no significant publication bias for any category.
analysis.covariates: Study-level only: median age at intake (continuous), sex, mainly Caucasian population or not, adequacy of the intake measure, former-drinker bias, occasional-drinker bias; full model adds follow-up years, exclusion of ill participants and whether race and smoking were controlled in the study. Candidates were screened by bivariable p < .20 and pruned for intercorrelations above .30. No significant interaction with median age, sex or Caucasian status. The paper does not state at which covariate values (reference levels or averages) the adjusted category RRs are evaluated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the protocol was first approved as an NIH R01 grant application (Award 1RO1AAO19939-02) and present it as online Appendix A (not read); there is no registry record. PRISMA followed (Method › Overall approach).
analysis.selective_reporting: Results excluding outliers are said to be the same but are not reported; forest plots, influence analyses and per-study data are in Appendices B to F (not read). The Discussion emphasizes the Table 5 estimates after removal of the influential study. Outcome-specific results (CHD) are outside this paper.
analysis.power: Strata are small where the conclusion rests: 4 occasional-drinker estimates in the bias-free studies, 6 or 7 higher-quality studies (low-volume interval 0.62 to 1.29 with Friesema et al.). The authors argue that two estimates per covariate suffice for linear regression (Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling 87 cohorts with only precision and between-study variation accounted for reproduced the J-shape (low volume RR 0.86, occasional 0.84, against each study's abstainers). Adding study-level covariates for abstainer biases and other characteristics moved the low-volume RR to 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) while former drinkers (1.38) and people drinking 45 g/day or more (1.24; 1.44) stayed at higher risk. In the 13 studies with strict lifetime abstainers, low-volume RR was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06); in the higher-quality subset, 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), or 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) after removing one study. Occasional drinkers had RRs like low-volume drinkers in every model, and against occasional drinkers low-volume RR was 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10) while abstainers had 1.19.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that low-volume consumption “has no net mortality benefit compared with lifetime abstention or occasional drinking”. Gaps: (1) non-significance is read as absence: the fully adjusted interval (0.88 to 1.07) is compatible with up to 12% lower or 7% higher mortality, and in the bias-free stratum the point estimate is 0.90; (2) the adjusted RRs come from an ecological meta-regression, with covariates chosen partly by bivariable p-values and evaluated at unstated reference levels, so they are not the risk in any defined set of studies; (3) the higher-quality conclusion leans on the analysis that drops an influential study after the fact (both versions are non-significant); (4) the occasional-drinker reference, which the authors favour, also shows abstainers at higher risk (1.19), which fits abstainer bias but confirms that the choice of reference group drives the conclusion; (5) the Discussion concedes that even the 13 bias-free studies had other serious problems that could bias results in either direction. The paper's own summary, that a sceptical position about net benefit is warranted, is proportionate to these results, and the authors are open that occasional-drinker bias could not be confirmed.

timeline.event: Shaper et al.: the ‘sick quitter’ explanation of the U-shaped curve in British men (cited in the background).
Naimi et al.: 27 of 30 potential confounders of coronary heart disease more common among US non-drinkers than moderate drinkers (cited; Naimi is a co-author of this review).

Fillmore et al.: the original meta-analysis classifying studies by abstainer definition, whose codebook this review refines (Stockwell and Chikritzhs are co-authors). The project list also holds Di Castelnuovo et al. (2006), a J-curve meta-analysis of 34 studies, which this review does not cite.

Ronksley et al. meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes, whose reference list was searched and whose conclusion is cited as the case for advising abstainers to drink (carded in this round by another reader).
Holmes et al. Mendelian randomization study, cited in the conclusions as consistent with this review (carded in this round by another reader).
Chikritzhs et al. editorial arguing the protective hypothesis had collapsed, cited in this review's first sentence; three of its authors wrote this review (card sc_chikritzhs_2015, this round).
Same issue of the journal: commentaries by Greenfield, by Connor and by Rehm, Roerecke and Room, with the authors' response (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 77:199–207; titles from PubMed, not read).

Letter by Barrett-Connor and 16 co-signatories, ‘Comments on Moderate Alcohol Consumption and Mortality’, letters by Gow and by Braillon, and a reply by Stockwell, Chikritzhs, Naimi and Zhao whose title frames the critique as coming from ISFAR and industry sympathizers (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 77:834–841; not read).
Commentary by Xuan in Evidence-Based Medicine (21:194), listed on PubMed (not read).
Wood et al. individual-participant analysis of 599,912 current drinkers, which avoids the abstainer reference group altogether (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Zhao et al. update by the same group (107 studies, the same 87 plus 20): fully adjusted low-volume RR 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).
Stockwell et al. review of study characteristics that may bias low-volume mortality estimates, on the project list (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The review is the base dataset of a series of meta-analyses by one group. Its central result, that counting former drinkers in the reference group lowers drinkers' relative risks and that the low-volume association moves towards 1 when study characteristics are taken into account, was reproduced by the group's own update (Zhao et al., 2023), which is not independent and whose adjusted estimate (0.93, 0.85 to 1.01) sits further from 1 than this one. Critiques and replies were published in the same journal in 2016 and have not been read. The question cannot be settled by study-level meta-regression; individual-participant analyses with lifetime drinking histories and genetic studies (carded separately) approach it differently.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the PMC version; only the funding footnote.
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addictions Research of BC, University of Victoria; National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University; Institute for Scientific Analysis, San Francisco; Boston University Schools of Medicine and Public Health. (2006), whose classification this review refines, and three of the authors (Chikritzhs, Stockwell, Naimi) had argued in a 2015 editorial that the protective hypothesis had collapsed, so the authors test a position they had already taken in print. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant analysis of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories, so that former drinkers can be reassigned to the levels they drank, with strictly defined lifetime abstainers, repeated intake measures and common adjustment for socio-economic and health confounders; or a long-term randomized trial of low-volume drinking against abstention.

Two databases with the key words printed and reference lists of two meta-analyses, but English only without justification, no grey literature, no registries and no experts consulted; search ended February 2015 for a 2016 paper.

Two trained reviewers read all titles, and full-text eligibility was cross-checked by senior investigators; who reviewed the abstracts, and whether screening was independent, is not stated, so this is a close call.

Inverse-variance-weighted mixed models with a random study intercept, the combination justified by the aim; reported hazard or rate ratios were used and crude rates converted only when nothing else was reported. Met on balance, a close call: whether the most-adjusted estimate was taken is not stated, the correlation between categories sharing a reference group is handled only by the random intercept, and the adjusted RRs are evaluated at unstated covariate levels.

domains.note: The review's purpose: bias covariates in the meta-regression, stratification by abstainer bias and a higher-quality subset.

Q and I2 reported (all above 50%), meta-regression and stratification explore sources, and the reduced heterogeneity in the higher-quality subset is reported (Appendix F).
Funnel plot (Appendix C) and Egger tests for each category and for all drinkers; no significant bias found.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items fail (item 4, English-only search without justification; item 7, no list of excluded studies), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; item 2 is provisional (appendix not read) but cannot change the rating. This rates how far the pooled numbers can be taken as an unbiased summary, not the value of the idea: the review is transparent about its coding, tests a clearly stated hypothesis in three ways and reports unadjusted estimates beside adjusted ones. The card may be cited for the finding that abstainer definitions and study characteristics move the low-volume RR from about 0.86 towards 1, for the higher mortality of former drinkers and of drinkers of 45 g/day or more in every model, and for the counts of studies by type of reference group. It should not be cited for a demonstrated absence of benefit, or for any adjusted RR as the risk in a real population.

key_findings.finding: 87 cohort studies were included from 2,662 records (PubMed and Web of Science, English-language articles published to 31 December 2014, plus reference lists of two earlier meta-analyses): 523 relative-risk estimates from 3,998,626 participants with 367,103 deaths.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Method; Method › Data sources; Results › Study selection; Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias

key_findings.finding: Of the 87 studies, 65 counted former drinkers in the abstainer reference group and 50 counted occasional drinkers (41 both, 24 former only, 9 occasional only); only 13 studies (127 estimates) used strictly defined lifetime abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Summary of evidence, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias

key_findings.finding: Weighted only for precision and between-study variation, against each study's abstainers: low-volume drinkers (1.30 to 24.9 g/day) RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.90), occasional drinkers (under 1.30 g/day) 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), former drinkers 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31), medium volume (25 to 44.9 g/day) 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00), high (45 to 64.9) 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17), higher (65 or more) 1.29 (1.22 to 1.36). Heterogeneity significant in every category, I2 61% to 84%; Egger tests showed no publication bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality with limited adjustment, 1st paragraph; Table 2

With the six first covariates only, low volume was 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94).

key_findings.finding: As the bias and quality covariates are removed from the full model, the low-volume RR falls from 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) to 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90); the authors' Appendix E is said to confirm the importance of former-drinker bias and to suggest that occasional-drinker bias matters less.

key_findings.finding: In the 13 studies with strictly defined lifetime abstainers (adjusted for median age, sex and country): low volume RR 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), 50 estimates; occasional 0.94 (0.71 to 1.25), 4 estimates; medium 0.95 (0.80 to 1.13); high 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32); higher 1.42 (1.15 to 1.75); former drinkers 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57). In the three groups of studies with abstainer biases, low volume was 0.91 (0.83 to 1.00) in the 41 studies with both former- and occasional-drinker bias, 0.86 (0.78 to 0.95) in the 24 with former-drinker bias only and 0.86 (0.82 to 0.91) in the 9 with occasional-drinker bias only; the bias-free point estimate (0.90) is about the same as that of the studies with both biases (0.91), with a wider interval.

key_findings.finding: Seven higher-quality studies (lifetime abstainers only, adequate intake measure, median age under 60 at intake and at least 55 at follow-up), against lifetime abstainers: low volume RR 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), medium 1.08 (0.72 to 1.62), high 0.95 (0.62 to 1.46), higher 1.58 (1.05 to 2.38), former 1.14 (0.77 to 1.69). Leave-one-out analysis found Friesema et al. (2007) highly influential (6 of its estimates were outliers); without it: low volume 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15), medium 1.29 (1.06 to 1.56), high 1.07 (0.83 to 1.36), former 1.31 (1.11 to 1.55), higher 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27), with I2 below 50% for former, low and medium categories.

In the bias-free and higher-quality subsets the 45 to under 65 g category was never significantly raised (1.11 in key finding 6; 0.95 and 1.07 here), while 25 to under 45 g was in the model without Friesema et al. (1.29): in these small subsets the intake at which risk rises is not well defined.

key_findings.finding: Outliers (log RR beyond the category mean plus or minus 2 SD): 11 estimates below (RR 0.1 to 0.46) and 18 above (1.89 to 4.57); removing them made no substantive difference, so all models include them. key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: imperfect, mostly under-reported self-reported intake and unreliable classification of lifetime abstainers; few studies in some stratified analyses; too few studies controlling for heavy episodic drinking to examine it; findings apply to all-cause mortality only.

design_detail: Subgroup meta-analyses of the 107 prospective cohort studies of alcohol and all-cause mortality assembled for the same group's earlier review (Zhao et al., 2023: the 87 studies of Stockwell et al., 2016, plus 20 added; search to 31 July 2021). Studies were grouped by characteristics predicted by the authors' theory of lifetime selection bias (Naimi et al., 2017) to make low-volume drinkers look healthier than abstainers: primarily a median cohort age of 55 or younger at enrolment (with follow-up to at least 56) and no former or occasional drinkers in the abstainer reference group, secondarily an intake measure covering at least 30 days, exclusion of people with prior illness, and control for smoking and for socio-economic status (SES). Low-volume intake (1.30 to under 25 g ethanol a day) against abstainers was pooled by mixed-effects regression of log relative risks with a random study effect (SAS PROC MIXED), preceded by bivariate comparisons of mean relative risks between study subgroups (Table 1). Presented as a response to a critique of Zhao et al. (2023) by the International Scientific Forum on Alcohol Research (ISFAR). Protocol described as preregistered on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/tnhd3; not read).
can_establish: How the pooled relative risk of death for low-volume drinking (1.30 to under 25 g a day) against abstainers differs between subgroups of published cohort studies defined by cohort age and by whether former and occasional drinkers were counted as abstainers, and how few published cohorts meet both criteria.
cannot_establish: Whether low-volume drinking lowers, raises or does not change mortality (pooled observational cohorts; restriction does not remove confounding); whether the difference between subgroups is caused by the biases named rather than by other features of the studies (a study-level comparison, six unnamed studies in the decisive subgroup, no test of the difference reported); the shape of risk within the 1.30 to 25 g range; or anything firm about nonsmokers (an exploratory, unadjusted mean of six studies for one intake category).

sample.recruitment: Review-level: PubMed and Web of Science for articles published up to 31 July 2021, with reference lists of earlier meta-analyses checked; the search and flowchart belong to Zhao et al. (2023) and the supplement (Figure A2, not read). The cohorts came from North and Central America (40 studies), Europe and Australia (48) and Asia (12) (Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English-language original research in peer-reviewed journals; prospective cohort studies relating at least two levels of alcohol consumption to all-cause mortality in general populations of any age. Excluded: reviews, letters, editorials, commentaries, unpublished work, dissertations, government reports, books, conference proceedings and meeting abstracts, guidelines; cohorts selected for a specific illness or for heavy, problematic or dependent drinking. Where several publications came from one data set, the most recent was coded unless populations differed (Method › Inclusion and exclusion criteria; Data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Study level only: median cohort age at baseline 19 to 55 in 61 studies and 56 to 78 in 44; result sets for men only (66), women only (45) and both sexes (29), counts overlapping because some studies report by sex (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the primary cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English only, peer-reviewed only, two databases, no grey literature; the search closed three years before publication. The decisive subgroup holds six or seven studies that are not named in the main text, with no count of their participants or deaths. The grouping variables come from the authors' own theory, and the paper responds to a critique of the authors' previous analysis of the same studies.

exposure.measurement: Baseline self-reported intake as each cohort measured it, over periods from 2 or 3 days to a lifetime, converted to grams of ethanol a day from category midpoints; open top categories were set at the lower bound plus three quarters of the width of the next category down. Where a study did not define its drink, national sizes were assumed: 8 g (United Kingdom), 10 g (Australia, Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Netherlands, New Zealand, Poland, Spain, Sweden), 11 g (Finland), 12 g (Denmark, Germany, Italy, South Africa, Switzerland and other countries), 12.5 g (China), 13.45 g (Canada), 14 g (United States), 19.75 g (Japan). Only 27 of 99 studies measured typical intake over at least 30 days (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories (g ethanol a day): former drinkers; occasional, under 1.30 (up to one 10-g drink a week); low volume, 1.30 to under 25 (up to two drinks); medium, 25 to under 45; higher, 45 or more (Tables 2 and 3; printed bounds vary, reporting issues 1 to 3). Lifetime abstainers: never one drink; current drinkers: at least one 10-g drink in the past year (p. 443).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking handled only as a study characteristic: 83 studies controlled for it by adjustment or stratification and 18 did not; 6 reported results for nonsmokers and 7 for smokers (Table 1). Other drugs not addressed.

comparison.controls: Abstainers as defined by each cohort, coded for contamination: both former and occasional drinkers counted as abstainers (46 of 99 studies), former drinkers only (27), occasional drinkers only (8), neither (18). 'Neither' requires a strict lifetime-abstainer reference: never one drink, with any occasional lifetime or past-year drinking (for example fewer than 12 drinks, or 'rarely') disqualifying; studies measuring usual drinking over a week or a month were assumed to include occasional drinkers among their abstainers (pp. 442-443; Table 1).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Lifetime drinking histories, health-related reductions in drinking before baseline, and the ways lifetime abstainers differ from drinkers (health, religion, socio-economic position) are not available at review level; restricting to lifetime-abstainer reference groups removes former drinkers from the comparison but not these other differences.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking in the reference groups not reported.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality: hazard ratios and rate ratios used as relative risks; where only mortality rates were reported they were converted to relative risks; estimates were re-referenced to abstainers where needed (Method › Data extraction, Outcomes).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death ascertainment as in each cohort (not described).
outcomes.operationalization: A 'health benefit' is a relative risk below 1 for low-volume drinkers against the abstainer reference group.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, but Table 1 reports 17 bivariate p values and Tables 2 and 3 report 15 pooled estimates, each in two model versions, all judged at p < .05 (bold in the tables).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Three coders extracted and coded each study independently, resolving disagreements with the principal investigator and investigators (Method › Data extraction, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Low volume (1.30 to under 25 g a day) against abstainers, random study effect ('adjusted' for between-study variation), with the estimate without it ('partially adjusted') second (Table 3): all 107 studies 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88) and 0.85 (0.82 to 0.88), 99 studies, 306 estimates; older cohorts 0.84 (0.81 to 0.87); both abstainer biases 0.85 (0.81 to 0.89); older cohorts with both biases 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), 18 studies; plus a poor intake measure 0.83 (0.77 to 0.90), 15 studies; younger cohorts only 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92), 51 studies; no abstainer bias only 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95), 18 studies; younger cohorts and no abstainer bias 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) and 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24), 6 studies, 38 estimates; plus a 30-day measure 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) and 1.14 (1.00 to 1.29), 5 studies. Higher-quality subgroup, other categories against lifetime abstainers (Table 2, random effect): former drinkers 1.32 (1.13 to 1.54); medium 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40); higher, 45 g or more, 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82). Bivariate unadjusted means (Table 1): younger 0.93 vs older 0.83 (p = .0085); poor health excluded or controlled 0.97 vs not 0.84 (p = .0004); 30-day measure 0.99 vs 0.86 (p = .0026); neither abstainer bias 0.99 vs both 0.82 (p = .0004); no smoking control 1.01 vs control 0.86 (p = .0010); no SES control 0.97 vs control 0.85 (p = .0010); nonsmokers 1.16 (0.91 to 1.41) vs smokers 0.93 (0.71 to 1.16) (p = .1817). No heterogeneity statistic, prediction interval or absolute rate is reported. Editors' calculation: ratio of the higher-quality (0.98) to the lower-quality (0.84) subgroup estimate 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), z = 2.23, p of about .03, treating the two disjoint sets of studies as independent.
analysis.covariates: None at review level beyond the random study effect: 'adjusted' in Tables 2 and 3 means adjusted for between-study variation, not for confounders. Covariates differ between the primary studies; whether the most-adjusted estimate of each study was used is not stated here (methods referred to Zhao et al., 2023).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework, osf.io/tnhd3 (Stockwell et al., 2021), not read. The paper says the two primary criteria (cohort age, abstainer bias) are those of the preregistered protocol and calls the smoking and SES analyses exploratory; it does not say whether the intake-measure and baseline-illness criteria or the nonsmoker analysis were registered, nor whether the registration preceded the search (which closed on 31 July 2021). Zhao et al. (2023) have a different registration (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G, according to card sc_zhao_2023).
analysis.selective_reporting: Absent from the main text: heterogeneity statistics, the names and sizes of the decisive studies, a test of the difference between higher- and lower-quality subgroups, and any check for publication bias. Medium and higher categories for the lower-quality studies appear only in Figure 2; the contrast of 5 against 15 studies (Figure B5) and the forest plots (Figures B1 to B4) are in the supplement (not read).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The decisive subgroup has 6 studies and 38 estimates; its interval (0.87 to 1.11) runs from a 13% lower to an 11% higher risk. The authors say more higher-quality studies are needed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the 6 cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger and using lifetime abstainers as the reference, low-volume drinkers (1.30 to under 25 g a day) had an RR of 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), and 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without the random study effect; former drinkers (1.32) and people drinking 45 g a day or more (1.51) had higher mortality. Cohorts meeting neither criterion gave 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), and cohorts meeting only one criterion 0.88. In bivariate, unadjusted comparisons, cohorts that controlled for smoking or SES showed lower low-volume RRs than those that did not, and the six cohorts reporting nonsmokers separately gave 1.16 (0.91 to 1.41) for nonsmokers against 0.93 for smokers (p = .18).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports that the higher-quality studies estimated "similar mortality risk for low-volume drinkers" as abstainers and that RRs in nonsmoking cohorts were above 1.0 (p. 441); the Discussion says the findings support lifetime selection biases creating the false appearance of benefit (p. 448); the Conclusions say that studies of nonsmokers find no J-shaped curve (p. 450). Gaps: (1) the decisive estimate rests on 6 unnamed studies whose participants and deaths are not counted, and its interval is compatible with a 13% lower risk; (2) no test of the difference between higher- and lower-quality subgroups is reported in the main text (the editors' calculation gives p of about .03), and the comparison is between groups of studies, which differ in more than the two criteria: cohorts recruited at younger ages, even if followed to 56, contribute deaths at ages and from causes different from older cohorts, and lifetime abstainers differ from drinkers in other ways, so the difference is consistent with, but not specific to, the selection bias named; (3) the nonsmoker statement rests on an exploratory, unadjusted mean of six studies, not restricted by the quality criteria as far as the paper says, for one intake category, so no curve was estimated and the interval includes 0.91; (4) the suggestion that adjustment for smoking or SES creates the J-curve comes from comparing studies that did or did not adjust, which differ in other ways; the paper presents it as a question for future research, but the Conclusions state the nonsmoker finding as a result. The main estimate itself is reported accurately, with its interval, and the Discussion states the main limits.

timeline.event: Fillmore et al.: meta-analysis grouping cohort studies by abstainer definition and analysing higher-quality studies separately; this paper follows its definitions (Stockwell is a co-author, according to the reference list).
Di Castelnuovo et al.: J-shaped meta-analysis of 34 cohorts, not cited by this paper; the project list pairs them (card sc_di_castelnuovo_2006, this round).
Stockwell et al.: 87-study review whose studies and codebook are reused here (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round).
Naimi et al.: the authors' theory of lifetime selection biases, which this paper tests; Zhao et al.: CHD mortality meta-analysis described here as finding younger cohorts less prone to bias.
Wood et al.: pooled analysis restricted to current drinkers, which avoids the abstainer reference group; not cited here (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Ortolá et al.: older Spanish cohort in which apparent protection vanished when lifetime drinking was taken into account (as described here, p. 442; among the 20 added studies).
Open Science Framework protocol, osf.io/tnhd3 (Stockwell et al., 2021), not read.
Zhao et al.: the 107-study review with study-level adjustment; low-volume RR 0.93 there against 0.98 here (p. 446) (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).

ISFAR Critique 264 of Zhao et al. (web critique, not read), described by the authors as coming from a group with significant ties to the alcohol industry (citing a blog post by Siegel, 2023); Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health final report (Paradis et al., 2023), co-authored by Naimi and Sherk and cited here for the view that mortality cohorts are too bias-prone to ground guidelines.

Stockwell, Zhao and Naimi, reply to ISFAR (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 85:133-135), cited as the fuller response (not read); Stockley, Hendriks and Ellison, ISFAR's rejoinder (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 85:136-140), listed on PubMed as a comment on Zhao et al. according to card sc_zhao_2023 (not read).
This paper (received 10 September 2023, revised 22 January 2024; July 2024 issue). No correction is mentioned in the PDF; the reference record's retraction check is clear.

replication.where_it_stands: The third analysis by one group of an overlapping set of studies (Stockwell et al., 2016: 87 studies; Zhao et al., 2023: 107; this paper: subgroups of the same 107), so the three are not independent confirmations. That very few published cohorts both recruit before age 56 and use lifetime abstainers as the reference, and that these few show no lower mortality at 1.30 to under 25 g a day, stands as reported; whether the gap from other cohorts is caused by selection bias is argued between the authors and ISFAR (exchange not read). Claims should cite 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) with its six-study basis and lifetime-abstainer reference, alongside the individual-participant (Wood et al., 2018) and Mendelian randomization studies carded in this round.

funding.funder: Partly funded by the Canadian Centre of Substance Use and Addiction (so spelled in the footnote) as part of a contract to assist with the development of the new Canadian Guidance on Alcohol and Health (p. 441, footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: Stockwell, Sherk and Naimi declare previous funding from government alcohol monopolies in Finland, Sweden and Canada to conduct public-health-oriented alcohol research; Stockwell and Naimi also received personal fees from these bodies in the past for the same purposes, and travel support from IOGT-NTO, described as a not-for-profit non-governmental organization that advocates against alcohol use, to prepare reports on alcohol and health (Conflict-of-Interest Statement, p. 450).
funding.affiliations_note: Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research, University of Victoria (Stockwell, Zhao, Clay, Sherk, Naimi), Dalhousie University (Clay) and the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (Levesque, Sanger), which is also the funder. Naimi and Sherk are co-authors of the Canadian guidance report the contract supported (Paradis et al., 2023, reference list). The authors wrote the theory tested here and the two earlier reviews of the same studies, and the paper answers a critique of their own previous analysis. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant analysis of cohorts recruited in early adulthood with repeated, lifetime measures of drinking, comparing low-volume drinkers with lifetime abstainers and with stable occasional drinkers, reporting cause-specific deaths and absolute rates under a pre-specified adjustment set; genetic analyses able to estimate risk at low intake would test the same question without the abstainer reference group.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: General-population cohorts, intake in grams a day by category, abstainers (with their contamination coded) as comparator, all-cause mortality.

Provisional: the paper cites an OSF protocol (osf.io/tnhd3, 2021) and says the two primary criteria come from it, but the registration was not read, so its content, its timing relative to the search (closed 31 July 2021) and any deviations cannot be checked.
The question is about why some cohort studies find benefits, so cohorts are the designs at issue.

Two databases with keywords printed and reference lists, but English and peer-reviewed publications only without justification, no grey literature or registries, and a search closed three years before publication (project reading of item 4, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Provisional: selection is not described in the article, which refers to Zhao et al. (2023) and to the supplement flowchart (Figure A2), not read.
Three coders extracted and coded each study independently, disagreements resolved with the investigators (Method › Data extraction, 1st paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list in the article; the supplement contents the article names (Figures A1, A2, B1 to B5; Tables A1, A2) include a flowchart but no list of excluded studies; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article describes no study individually, not even the six that decide the main result; Table A1 (supplement, not read) lists the 20 added studies and Figures B1 to B4 hold forest plots.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No formal tool, but every study was coded for the selection and confounding problems at issue (abstainer contamination, cohort age, baseline illness, intake measure, control for smoking and SES); outcome ascertainment and selective reporting were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Inverse-variance-weighted mixed models of log relative risks with a random study effect, reported beside the fixed version. Met on balance, a close call: whether the most-adjusted primary estimates were used is not stated, crude rates were converted and pooled with adjusted ratios, correlation between estimates sharing a reference group is handled only by the random effect, and the Table 1 means appear to be computed on the untransformed scale (reporting issue 8).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The paper's purpose: pooled estimates are compared across subgroups defined by the bias-related characteristics (Tables 1 to 3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Results are interpreted through the bias subgroups, and the Discussion names residual problems in the higher-quality studies (the 55-year cut-off, former drinkers not reallocated).
Sources of between-study variation are the subject of the analysis and are discussed, although no Q or I2 value is reported despite the Methods (reporting issue 5).
Not mentioned for any subgroup; according to card sc_zhao_2023 the parent review ran funnel plots and Egger tests on the full pool.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding footnote and conflict-of-interest statement printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are 'no' (4, 7 and 15), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence whatever the provisional items (2, 5 and 8) turn out to be. The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not the value of the question: grouping studies by the features that could bias the abstainer comparison is a reasonable design, and the authors report the main estimate with its interval and state its limits. The practical consequences: the decisive estimate rests on six unnamed studies, heterogeneity and publication bias are unexamined, and the subgroup contrast is a comparison between groups of studies. The paper may be cited for the RR of 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) in younger cohorts with lifetime-abstainer references and for how rarely published cohorts meet those criteria; not for the claim that nonsmokers show no J-curve, nor as proof that the protective association is wholly bias.

key_findings.finding: Study pool: the 107 prospective cohort studies of alcohol and all-cause mortality assembled for Zhao et al. (2023): 87 from Stockwell et al. (2016) and 20 added, found by searching PubMed and Web of Science for articles published up to 31 July 2021 plus reference lists; English-language, peer-reviewed, general-population cohorts. The abstract gives 724 risk estimates, 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths; 99 studies gave estimates for low-volume drinking (306 estimates).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Method; Method › Overview; Search strategy for relevant studies, 1st paragraph; Inclusion criteria (p. 442); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 444); Table 3, row 'All 107 studies' (p. 447)

key_findings.finding: Exposure definitions: grams of ethanol a day at baseline; occasional drinkers under 1.30 g a day (up to one 10-g drink a week); low volume 1.30 to under 25 g a day (up to two drinks); medium 25 to under 45; higher 45 or more. Where a study did not define its drink, national sizes from 8 g (United Kingdom) to 19.75 g (Japan) were assumed (10 g for Australia, New Zealand and nine European countries, 13.45 g Canada, 14 g United States). Lifetime abstainers: never one drink; former drinkers: stopped completely by baseline; studies measuring usual drinking over a week or a month were assumed to include occasional drinkers among their abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Inclusion criteria, last bullet (p. 443); Method › Data extraction: Measures of alcohol consumption; Drinking categories; Misclassification of former and occasional drinkers as abstainers, both paragraphs (p. 443); Tables 2 and 3 row labels (p. 447)

key_findings.finding: Quality criteria and how many studies meet them: of the 99 studies with low-volume estimates, 18 had neither former nor occasional drinkers among their abstainers, 46 had both, 27 former drinkers only and 8 occasional drinkers only; 27 measured typical intake over at least 30 days and 72 did not; 83 controlled for smoking (18 did not), 65 for SES (35 did not), and 44 excluded or controlled for poor health (56 did not). The primary criteria, said to be those of the preregistered protocol, were a median cohort age of 55 or younger at enrolment (with follow-up to at least 56) and no abstainer bias.
key_findings.locator: Method › Criteria for selecting studies of higher or lower quality for separate meta-analyses, items (a) to (f) and last paragraph (p. 444); Table 1 (p. 445)

key_findings.finding: Main result: in the 6 studies (38 estimates) with a median baseline age of 55 or younger, followed beyond 55, and with neither former nor occasional drinkers among the abstainers, low-volume drinkers (1.30 to under 25 g a day) had an RR for all-cause death of 0.98 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.11) against lifetime abstainers with a random study effect, and 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without it. With a 30-day intake measure required as well (5 studies, 34 estimates): 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15), and 1.14 (1.00 to 1.29; p = .047) without the random effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The bounds of the low-volume category are printed differently in different places: more than 1.30 to under 25 g a day (abstract), 1.3 to 24 g (Method › Overview), 1.30 to 24 g (Drinking categories), 1.35 to 25 g (Results, 2nd paragraph), 1.30 to under 25 g (Tables 1 to 3) and 1.30 to 24 g (Figure 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables' 1.30 to under 25 g a day should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The occasional-drinker cut-off is given as up to one 10-g drink a week, under 1.30 g a day; one 10-g drink a week is 1.43 g a day (editors' arithmetic). The drink sizes implied by the other categories also vary (two drinks for 25 g, four for 45 g, six for 65 g).
reporting_issues.consequence: Category labels in drinks are approximate; claims should use grams a day.

reporting_issues.issue: The high-volume category is printed as up to 6 drinks or 25 to 64 g a day, overlapping the medium category (25 to 44 g); the analysed category in Tables 2 and 3 is 45 g a day or more.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typographical error for 45 to 64 g; no effect on the tabulated results.

reporting_issues.issue: The age criterion is described as a mean cohort age of 55 or younger, followed up beyond 55 (abstract); a median age at enrolment of up to 55, followed to at least 56 (Method, item b); followed until over 55 (Table 2 note); and followed up to at least 55 (Table 3 note).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Method's median age with follow-up to at least 56 is presumably what was applied.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I2 and that mixed models were used because significant heterogeneity was detected, but no Q, I2, tau-squared or prediction interval is reported for any pooled estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: How consistent the six decisive studies were with one another cannot be judged from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Table 2 presents outcomes for six studies, while Table 2 lists 7 studies for all drinkers, former drinkers, current drinkers and the highest category and 6 for the low and medium categories; neither the six nor the seven studies are named in the main text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup has 7 studies, 6 with low-volume estimates; the decisive studies can be identified only from the supplement's forest plots (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 51 of 97 studies as 52.28%; 51/97 is 52.58%, and the printed percentages of that panel sum to 99.71% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on results.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's 'unadjusted mean RR' intervals are symmetric on the untransformed scale (for example 1.16, 0.91 to 1.41; 0.89, 0.74 to 1.04), unlike the log-scale intervals of Tables 2 and 3 and the log-scale method described in the Methods; and Table 1's means for the same subgroups differ from Table 3's (cohorts aged 55 or younger, 51 studies and 169 estimates: 0.93 against 0.88; no abstainer bias, 18 studies and 78 estimates: 0.99 against 0.88).
reporting_issues.consequence: The bivariate comparisons, including the nonsmoker estimate quoted in the abstract, come from a computation the Methods do not describe; on the meta-analytic method the subgroup without abstainer bias still shows a significantly lower risk (0.88), as the Discussion acknowledges.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results contrast the higher-quality (0.98) and lower-quality (0.84) subgroups as if they differed, but no test of the difference is given in the main text; the supplement's Figure B5 (5 against 15 studies) is said to show significantly greater risk in the higher-quality studies at each level.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editors' calculation from the printed intervals gives p of about .03 (ratio 1.17, 1.02 to 1.34), so the contrast is nominally significant but not strongly so.

reporting_issues.issue: One of the 20 added studies, Kaprio et al. (2019), is cited as European Neuropsychopharmacology 29, S804, a supplement page of the kind used for congress abstracts, with a DOI carrying the year 2017; meeting abstracts are an exclusion criterion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a meeting abstract included against the stated criteria; one study of 107, and whether it is among the decisive studies is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Lifetime abstention is defined in the text as never drinking one drink, and in the Table 1 note as never having drunk more than one drink.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor ambiguity in the reference-group definition that decides the main result.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results (1st paragraph) list 'assessed alcohol use over less than 30 days' among the study characteristics with significantly higher low-volume relative risks, but Table 1 gives the higher relative risk to studies whose intake measure covered at least 30 days (0.99, 0.92 to 1.05, against 0.86, 0.82 to 0.90; p = .0026), and the Discussion lists measures covering less than 30 days among the characteristics that go with lower risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 and the Discussion agree, so the Results sentence is the error; claims should cite Table 1.
