design_detail: Pooled analysis of individual-participant data from 83 prospective studies in 19 high-income countries, not chosen by systematic search: the cohorts are the three data sources available to the investigators' consortium, namely the 81 Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration (ERFC) cohorts that recorded the amount drunk (of 102 with drinking status), EPIC-CVD (a case-cohort study nested in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition, 22 of 23 centres) and UK Biobank. The literature search in the Research in context box was for background only. Main analysis restricted to 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease (CVD) at baseline; Cox models fitted within each study and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; hazard ratios (HRs) corrected for regression dilution with 152,640 repeat alcohol assessments from 71,011 participants in 37 studies, so that they refer to long-term average (‘usual’) intake.
can_establish: How all-cause mortality and first cardiovascular events vary with self-reported alcohol intake among current drinkers, mostly aged 40 to 80 and without known CVD, in high-income countries, relative to the lightest current drinkers, with large numbers and a common analysis across 83 cohorts.
cannot_establish: Whether drinking any amount carries more or less risk than not drinking (never and former drinkers were excluded from the main analyses); that alcohol causes the associations (observational data, main models adjusted only for age, sex, smoking status and diabetes, and residual reverse causation from people who cut down because of illness, which the authors acknowledge); the effect of reducing intake within a person; a precise threshold (it is read from category HRs plotted in a figure, with no interval of its own); risks in low- and middle-income countries; or outcomes the cohorts did not generally record (non-fatal liver disease, injuries, psychiatric conditions).

sample.recruitment: Registry/cohort: existing population cohorts pooled by the consortium. ERFC: 81 studies in 19 countries, recruited 1964 to 2008, follow-up to 2013; EPIC-CVD: 22 centres in 10 European countries, recruited 1990 to 2002, follow-up to 2009, case-cohort design (all-cause deaths only from the 13,670-person random subcohort); UK Biobank: England, Scotland and Wales, recruited 2006 to 2010, follow-up to 2016 (Table 1; Methods › Study design, data sources, and participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Required: recorded amount drunk and drinking status (non-drinker or current drinker), age, sex, history of diabetes and smoking status; at least 1 year of follow-up after baseline; no known baseline CVD (coronary heart disease, other heart disease, stroke, transient ischaemic attack, peripheral arterial disease or cardiovascular surgery). Main analyses restricted to current drinkers. For each outcome, studies with fewer than five incident cases were excluded (Methods › Study design, data sources, and participants, 3rd paragraph; Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Current drinkers: mean age 57 (SD 9); 265,910 (44%) women; 128,085 (21%) current smokers; recruitment years 1964 to 2010. Median baseline intake 96 g/week (5th to 95th percentiles 6 to 448); by source, median 87.7 g/week in ERFC, 61.9 in EPIC-CVD and 103.9 in UK Biobank; current smokers 35%, 32% and 10% respectively; history of diabetes 3 to 4% (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1). Ethnicity is mentioned only as differing between never and current drinkers (appendix, not read).
sample.attrition: Median follow-up 7.5 years (5th to 95th percentiles 5.0 to 18.4), 5.4 million person-years. Loss to follow-up is not reported in the main text. Analyses are complete-case; a multiple-imputation analysis for current drinkers with a missing amount is said to give similar results (appendix p 32, not read). The text gives 786,787 participants with sufficient information but not how many were excluded for insufficient information.
sample.selection_effects: Cohorts were those available to the consortium, not found by search, and UK Biobank supplies 54% of the current drinkers (326,372 of 599,912; editors' arithmetic). Participants enter in mid-life as prevalent current drinkers: people who had stopped (including because of illness) are excluded by design, but people who had cut down because of illness stay in the lighter categories, and people harmed by drinking, or who died, before recruitment are not represented. Requiring 1 year of follow-up and no baseline CVD selects healthier participants. The 71,011 with repeat measures (about 12%; editors' arithmetic) were younger, more often men and drank slightly more than the rest, yet supply the correction applied to everyone (Results, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported intake from each cohort's own instrument (self-administered or interviewer-led questionnaires; food-frequency questionnaires or dietary recall), harmonised to grams of pure alcohol per week with 1 UK unit = 8 g (conversion in appendix pp 1 to 2, not read). No biological verification. Long-term average (‘usual’) intake estimated by multilevel regression calibration from repeat surveys (ERFC, UK Biobank) or lifetime-intake measures (EPIC-CVD); regression dilution ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.52), similar to systolic blood pressure (0.52) and lower than HDL cholesterol (0.74) in the same participants (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Eight predefined baseline categories in g/week: >0 to ≤25 (reference category), >25 to ≤50, >50 to ≤75, >75 to ≤100, >100 to ≤150, >150 to ≤250, >250 to ≤350 and >350. Linear analyses per 100 g/week of usual intake (12.5 UK units). The authors equate 100 g/week with about 5 to 6 standard UK glasses of wine or pints of beer, and the US limit for men (196 g/week) with about 11. Frequency dichotomized at up to 2 versus more than 2 drinking days a week; episodic heavy drinking as 100 g or more per occasion; beverage type wine, beer or spirits (exploratory). Life-expectancy groups: >0 to ≤100 g/week (reference; mean usual 56 g), >100 to ≤200 (123 g), >200 to ≤350 (208 g), >350 (367 g).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking status (current or not) adjusted in all models; smoking amount (pack-years) only in subsets, where it abolished the association of alcohol with lung cancer (appendix p 16, as reported in Results, 4th paragraph). Use of other drugs not measured or not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (intake at baseline, outcomes during follow-up).

comparison.controls: The lightest current drinkers (>0 to ≤25 g/week) for the category analyses (Figures 1 and 2); along the intake gradient within current drinkers for the per-100 g/week HRs (Figure 3, Table 2); drinkers of >0 to ≤100 g/week for life expectancy (Figure 4). Never drinkers and former drinkers were excluded from the main analyses; analyses including them, which reproduce U-shaped curves, are only in the appendix (p 31, not read).
comparison.matching: None. Stratified by sex and study or centre; adjusted for age, smoking status and history of diabetes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Drinking history before baseline (apart from the EPIC-CVD lifetime measures used for calibration), why people drank at their current level (including having cut down because of illness), and, in the main models, socio-economic position, physical activity, diet, mental health and general health; some cohorts did not record chronic disease other than CVD at baseline (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality (40,310 deaths, including 11,762 vascular and 15,150 neoplastic); first incident CVD events (39,018): myocardial infarction (MI, 14,539), coronary disease excluding MI (7,990), stroke of all subtypes (12,090), heart failure (2,711), and deaths from other CVD (1,121: dysrhythmia, hypertensive disease, sudden death, aortic aneurysm), as recorded by each cohort; definitions in appendix p 5 (not read). Cancers of the digestive system and lung cancer are reported from the appendix.
outcomes.validity_norms: How deaths and events were ascertained (registries, records, adjudication) is not described in the main text and differs between cohorts; the authors note that outcome misclassification would dilute dose-response associations (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is a higher hazard of death or of a first CVD event. The ‘threshold for lowest risk’ is the intake above which category HRs for all-cause mortality rise in Figure 1 (an image); no formal threshold estimate or interval is given. Years of life lost were modelled by applying age-at-risk-specific HRs for baseline intake categories to US death rates for 2007 to 2010 (CDC WONDER), not observed in the cohorts (Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the main outcomes. 11 counts all-cause mortality, total CVD, MI, coronary disease excluding MI, stroke, heart failure, other CVD deaths and its four components named in the Methods; cancers, stroke subtypes, fatal and non-fatal splits and many subgroup and sensitivity analyses are in the appendix. Interaction tests used a 0.1% significance level and the choice of second-order fractional polynomials a 1% level (Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; outcomes were recorded by the contributing cohorts independently of this analysis.

analysis.effect_sizes: HR per 100 g/week higher usual intake within current drinkers, adjusted for age, smoking and diabetes and stratified by sex and centre: stroke 1.14 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.17); coronary disease excluding MI 1.06 (1.00 to 1.11); heart failure 1.09 (1.03 to 1.15); fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15 to 1.33); fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28); MI 0.94 (0.91 to 0.97) (Abstract; Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3). All-cause mortality: positive and curvilinear, lowest at or below about 100 g/week relative to >0 to ≤25 g/week (Figure 1; category HRs not given as numbers in the text). Table 2, subsets with the covariate measured, per 100 g/week, basic then further adjusted: systolic blood pressure subset, stroke 1.16 (1.11 to 1.22) to 1.10 (1.06 to 1.14), MI 0.95 (0.91 to 0.99) to 0.91 (0.87 to 0.94), coronary excluding MI 1.06 (1.00 to 1.12) to 1.03 (0.97 to 1.10), heart failure 1.11 (1.04 to 1.18) to 1.08 (1.02 to 1.15), other CVD deaths 1.16 (1.06 to 1.27) to 1.14 (1.03 to 1.25); HDL cholesterol subset, stroke 1.16 (1.10 to 1.23) to 1.17 (1.11 to 1.22), MI 0.93 (0.88 to 0.97) to 1.00 (0.96 to 1.04), coronary excluding MI 1.07 (0.98 to 1.17) to 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22), heart failure 1.09 (1.00 to 1.19) to 1.14 (1.01 to 1.27), other CVD deaths 1.22 (1.06 to 1.40) to 1.22 (1.08 to 1.38); body-mass index subset, little change (for example MI 0.95 to 0.94). Heterogeneity I2: stroke 12%, MI 12%, coronary excluding MI 26%, heart failure 4%, other CVD deaths 33%. Life expectancy at age 40 compared with >0 to ≤100 g/week: about 6 months shorter for >100 to ≤200 g/week, 1 to 2 years for >200 to ≤350 and 4 to 5 years for >350 (no intervals in the text); men above 112 g/week 1.6 years shorter (1.3 to 1.8), above 196 g/week 2.7 years (2.4 to 3.1); women above 112 or 98 g/week about 1.3 years (1.1 to 1.5).
analysis.covariates: Main models: age, smoking status (current or not) and history of diabetes, stratified by sex and study or centre; EPIC-CVD case-cohort analysed with Prentice weights. In subsets, usual levels of body-mass index, systolic blood pressure, HDL and LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol and fibrinogen, and baseline pack-years, education, occupation, physical activity, self-rated general health, red meat intake and antihypertensive drug use (Methods › Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph); results for most of these are only in the appendix (pp 15, 30, not read). Blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, other lipids and fibrinogen are potential mediators rather than confounders, as the authors treat them.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is cited. The principal analysis of current drinkers is described as prespecified (Results, 1st paragraph) and the eight intake categories as predefined (Methods › Study design, 3rd paragraph), without a reference to a protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The category-specific HRs for all-cause mortality on which the headline threshold rests appear only in Figure 1 (an image) and appendix p 25, not as numbers in the article, and the threshold is stated only in words. The analyses that include never and former drinkers, and most sensitivity analyses, are summarized as similar or as reproducing earlier findings with the numbers in the appendix (pp 18, 31 to 37). Results modelled on EU death rates are described as similar, data not shown.
analysis.power: Very large: 40,310 deaths and 39,018 first CVD events. Precision is lower for heart failure (2,711 events) and other CVD deaths (1,121), and for the subsets with HDL cholesterol (UK Biobank lipids were not yet available).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 599,912 current drinkers in 83 cohorts, all-cause mortality was lowest in the categories up to about 100 g/week and rose above that, relative to people drinking more than 0 and up to 25 g/week. Higher intake went roughly linearly with more stroke, heart failure, coronary disease other than MI, fatal hypertensive disease and fatal aortic aneurysm, and log-linearly with less MI (HR 0.94 per 100 g/week), an inverse association that disappeared after adjustment for HDL cholesterol (1.00, 0.96 to 1.04). Modelled life expectancy at 40 was lower in heavier-drinking groups, with about 20% of the difference in men attributed to CVD deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the conclusion state that among current drinkers “the threshold for lowest risk of all-cause mortality was about 100 g/week” and that the data support lower guideline limits; the Research in context box calls this the chief implication for policy. Gaps: (1) the threshold is lowest risk among current drinkers only, because the comparison is with the lightest drinkers; the analysis says nothing about drinking up to 100 g/week against not drinking, although a guideline limit is read that way; (2) the discussion says that long-term reduction from 196 to 100 g/week or below was associated with 1 to 2 years longer life expectancy for men, which describes a change within people that the study did not observe: the figure compares different people by baseline intake and is modelled on US death rates; (3) the threshold is read from plotted category HRs, without an interval, and the plotted values are not printed; (4) the main models adjust only for age, sex, smoking status and diabetes, and the authors concede residual reverse causation; (5) the suggestion that HDL-related pathways mediate the lower MI risk is a hypothesis drawn from how the HR changed with adjustment. The abstract does restrict its conclusion to current drinkers in high-income countries, and the discussion lists the main limitations and calls for randomized trials.

timeline.event: Ronksley et al. meta-analysis of alcohol and cardiovascular outcomes, cited among the earlier literature on risk thresholds (carded in this round by another reader).
Holmes et al. Mendelian randomization analysis, cited by the authors as concordant with their cardiovascular findings (carded in this round by another reader).
Stockwell et al. meta-analysis of 87 cohorts referenced to abstainers (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round): a different comparison, which Wood et al. do not cite.
This analysis, with a linked Lancet comment by Connor and Hall, ‘Thresholds for safer alcohol use might need lowering’ (Lancet 391:1460–1461; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30545-2; not read).
Correction (Lancet 391:2212; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31168-1): one author's affiliation corrected; no data changed (read).

Letters titled ‘Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption’ by Astrup, Costanzo and de Gaetano, by Schernhammer and by Thompson (Lancet 392:2165–2167), listed on PubMed as comments on this paper (not read).
Commentary by Xuan in BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine (24:117–118), listed on PubMed (not read).
Zhao et al. update of the abstainer-referenced meta-analysis (card sc_zhao_2023, this round); Wood et al. is not among its included studies.

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication of the threshold within current drinkers was identified in what was read this session, so the status reflects only that reading. The study answers a narrower question than the abstainer-referenced meta-analyses (Stockwell et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2023) and the burden-of-disease and genetic studies carded by other readers, and the numbers are not interchangeable: 100 g/week is about 14 g/day (editors' arithmetic), inside the 1.3 to 25 g/day ‘low-volume’ category of those meta-analyses. The divergence between MI and the other cardiovascular outcomes is the study's most distinctive result, and its linked letters and comment have not been read.

what_would_settle_it: A long-term randomized trial of moderate drinking against abstention or reduction (the authors cite a proposal for one); failing that, pooled cohorts that record drinking from early adulthood with repeated, biomarker-checked measures and correctly classified never and former drinkers, analysed together with genetic methods able to estimate the shape of the curve at low intake.

domains.note: Main models adjust only for age, smoking status (current or not) and diabetes, stratified by sex and centre. Socio-economic position, physical activity, diet and self-rated health were added only in subsets reported in appendix pages not read; the authors say further adjustment changed little except for the mediators blood pressure and HDL cholesterol. Smoking amount explained the lung-cancer association, which shows residual confounding by smoking at this level of adjustment. Reverse causation from people who had cut down because of illness remains, as the authors say, and some cohorts did not record chronic disease other than CVD.

Single baseline self-report from heterogeneous instruments harmonised at 8 g per UK unit; the regression dilution ratio of 0.50 shows large within-person variation, corrected from the 12% with repeat measures, who differed from the rest. Error is probably non-differential with respect to later outcomes, but under-reporting would mean that 100 g/week reported corresponds to more drunk.

Prevalent current drinkers entering in mid-life: former drinkers removed by design, earlier casualties of drinking absent, survival of at least 1 year and absence of CVD required. Cohorts chosen by availability to the consortium, with UK Biobank 54% of participants.

Changes in drinking and medical treatment during follow-up (for example antihypertensive drugs, adjusted for only in subsets) are not modelled beyond calibrating baseline intake to its long-term average; advice to cut down after diagnoses could attenuate associations.

Complete-case analysis; the number excluded for missing intake or covariates is not reported in the main text; multiple imputation reportedly agreed (appendix p 32, not read). EPIC-CVD deaths come from its random subcohort only.

Death is reliably recorded, so the risk is low for all-cause mortality; ascertainment of CVD subtypes differs across 83 cohorts and is described only in the appendix, and hypertensive disease and aortic aneurysm are fatal events only.

No protocol or registration cited for a principal analysis described as prespecified; the threshold is read from plotted categories rather than estimated; many outcomes, subgroups and sensitivity analyses, most reported only in the appendix; beverage-type and pattern results are labelled exploratory.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The gradient of rising mortality above about 100 g/week among current drinkers is estimated with unusual precision and consistency (83 cohorts, individual data, low heterogeneity, stable in sensitivity analyses), and the current-drinker design avoids the former-drinker problem of abstainer-referenced analyses. Attributing the gradient to alcohol, and above all locating the threshold and interpreting the lower MI risk, requires accepting minimal adjustment and residual reverse causation from illness-related reduction, hence high risk of bias overall. The card may be cited for the shape of the associations of self-reported intake with mortality and with cardiovascular subtypes among current drinkers in high-income countries, for the divergence between MI and other cardiovascular outcomes, and for modelled life-expectancy differences between intake groups. It should not be cited for any comparison of drinking with not drinking, for a causal or ‘safe’ threshold, or for the effect of cutting down.

key_findings.finding: Of 786,787 participants with sufficient information for inclusion, 186,875 reported not drinking at baseline, leaving 599,912 current drinkers (ERFC 247,504; EPIC-CVD 26,036; UK Biobank 326,372). Over 5.4 million person-years (median follow-up 7.5 years) there were 40,310 deaths (11,762 vascular, 15,150 neoplastic) and 39,018 first CVD events (12,090 stroke, 14,539 MI, 7,990 coronary disease excluding MI, 2,711 heart failure, 1,121 other CVD deaths).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The text gives the non-drinkers as 19%, but 186,875 is 23.8% of 786,787 (editors' arithmetic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: About 50% of current drinkers reported more than 100 g/week and 8.4% more than 350 g/week; median 96 g/week (5th to 95th percentiles 6 to 448). Intake was lower in more recent recruitment periods and weakly positively correlated with male sex, smoking, systolic blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, fibrinogen and lower socio-economic status.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: Table 1 counts give 8.7% above 350 g/week (52,429 of 599,912; editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Regression dilution ratio for alcohol 0.50 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.52) from 152,640 repeat assessments in 71,011 participants of 37 studies (median interval 5.6 years, 5th to 95th percentiles 1.04 to 13.5); those with repeat measures were younger, more often men and drank slightly more. All per-100 g/week HRs refer to long-term average (usual) intake estimated this way.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality rose with intake in a positive, curvilinear association, lowest for categories below 100 g/week, relative to current drinkers of >0 to ≤25 g/week (reference); similar in men and women, weaker at older ages. The aggregate of CVD outcomes showed a J-shaped association.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image and its category HRs were not extracted; the numbers are in appendix p 25 (not read). The threshold has no interval.

key_findings.finding: Per 100 g/week higher usual intake within current drinkers: stroke HR 1.14 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.17), coronary disease excluding MI 1.06 (1.00 to 1.11), heart failure 1.09 (1.03 to 1.15), fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15 to 1.33) and fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), roughly linear; MI 0.94 (0.91 to 0.97), approximately log-linear inverse. Adjusted for age, smoking and diabetes, stratified by sex and centre.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Abstract › Findings

key_findings.finding: In the subset with HDL cholesterol measured (61 cohorts, 9,911 MI events), adjustment for usual HDL cholesterol moved the MI HR per 100 g/week from 0.93 (0.88 to 0.97) to 1.00 (0.96 to 1.04) and strengthened coronary disease excluding MI from 1.07 (0.98 to 1.17) to 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22) and heart failure from 1.09 (1.00 to 1.19) to 1.14 (1.01 to 1.27). In the systolic blood pressure subset, adjustment weakened stroke from 1.16 (1.11 to 1.22) to 1.10 (1.06 to 1.14) and strengthened the inverse MI association from 0.95 (0.91 to 0.99) to 0.91 (0.87 to 0.94). Body-mass index changed little.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: When never drinkers and former drinkers were included, the analysis reproduced the U-shaped associations with total CVD and all-cause mortality reported previously; never drinkers differed from current drinkers in sex, ethnicity, smoking and diabetes, which the authors take as supporting the restriction to current drinkers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Values only in the appendix (pp 12, 31; not read). This is the only place the study touches non-drinkers.

key_findings.finding: Results were described as similar with multiple imputation, fractional polynomials, fixed-effect pooling, inclusion of studies with fewer than five events, separate analyses of men and women, omission of the first 5 years of follow-up, exclusion of people with diabetes or other known chronic disease, and restriction to studies recording fatal and non-fatal events.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: No numbers in the main text (appendix pp 17, 18, 26, 32 to 37, not read).

key_findings.finding: Exploratory: at the same weekly amount, all-cause mortality associations were stronger in people drinking beer or spirits than wine and in those drinking on fewer days, including people drinking 100 g or more per occasion, but these groups smoked more and had other markers of lower socio-economic status; for CVD subtypes, beer and spirits HRs were not significantly higher than wine in direct comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Little heterogeneity between studies: I2 12% for stroke, 12% for MI, 26% for coronary disease excluding MI, 4% for heart failure, 33% for other CVD deaths. HRs for the CVD outcomes were broadly similar across regions, decades of enrolment, data sources and alcohol assessment methods, generally higher at younger ages, and did not vary substantially by sex, diabetes, lipids, body-mass index or smoking; no evidence of small-study effects or of non-proportional hazards.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Modelled life expectancy at age 40, compared with reported intake of >0 to ≤100 g/week (mean usual 56 g): about 6 months shorter for >100 to ≤200 g/week (mean usual 123 g), 1 to 2 years for >200 to ≤350 (208 g) and 4 to 5 years for >350 (367 g). Men above the UK limit of 112 g/week: 1.6 years shorter (1.3 to 1.8); above the US limit of 196 g/week: 2.7 years (2.4 to 3.1); women above 112 or 98 g/week: about 1.3 years (1.1 to 1.5). About 20% of the difference in men (slightly less in women) was attributed to CVD deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Model-based: HRs for baseline intake categories applied to US death rates for 2007 to 2010; reference is light drinkers, not non-drinkers.

key_findings.finding: The association of alcohol with cancers of the digestive system was confirmed and unchanged by further adjustment; adjustment for smoking amount abolished the apparent association with lung cancer.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Values in appendix p 16 (not read).

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations: self-reported intake that is hard to harmonise; no measurement across the whole life course; outcome misclassification diluting associations; no access, in general, to non-fatal liver disease, injuries or psychiatric outcomes, so that benefits of lower intake were probably underestimated; and residual reverse causation from people who cut down because of illness, with some cohorts not recording other chronic disease; they call for randomized trials.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The published correction (Lancet 2018;391:2212, doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31168-1) corrects only the affiliation of one author (Makoto Daimon); no numbers were changed, so all values on this card are unaffected.
key_findings.locator: Department of Error notice, single paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 186,875 non-drinkers were 19% of 786,787 participants, but 186,875 is 23.8% of 786,787 (editors' arithmetic); 19% would fit a denominator of about 973,700.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of non-drinkers in the source cohorts cannot be stated from the article with certainty; quote counts, not the percentage.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives total participants of 356,819 (ERFC), 30,702 (EPIC-CVD) and 358,833 (UK Biobank), summing to 746,354, whereas the text starts from 786,787 participants with sufficient information (editors' arithmetic); the 40,433 difference is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The flow from eligible participants to the 599,912 analysed current drinkers cannot be reconstructed from the main text.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 8.4% drank more than 350 g/week, but the Table 1 counts for that category (25,432 + 1,796 + 25,201 = 52,429 of 599,912) give 8.7% (editors' arithmetic). Table 1 also labels the top category ≥350 g/week while the predefined categories are >250 to ≤350 and >350.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Study design, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the table counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 all-cause mortality events (32,813 + 784 + 6,720) sum to 40,317, against 40,310 deaths in the text and abstract (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the estimates; cite 40,310 as the authors' total.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 defines the CVD aggregate as MI, coronary heart disease and stroke, but the first-event counts for those outcomes sum to 34,619 (38,451 with heart failure and other CVD deaths), against 39,018 total CVD events (editors' arithmetic); the composition of the total is not stated in the main text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The J-shaped ‘total CVD’ association cannot be tied to a defined outcome from the article alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The numerical category HRs behind the all-cause mortality threshold, the study's headline result, are given only in an image (Figure 1) and the appendix; the text describes the threshold in words.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims cannot quote the size of the mortality excess at given intake levels from the article; they should cite the per-100 g/week HRs, the life-expectancy estimates, or the appendix once read.

reporting_issues.issue: The life-expectancy method is described in two ways: the Methods (Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph) apply age-specific hazard ratios for cause-specific mortality to the CDC WONDER death rates, while the Figure 4 legend applies hazard ratios for all-cause mortality by baseline intake category to US death rates.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph; Figure 4 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Which method produced the 6-month to 5-year estimates cannot be settled from the main text (appendix pp 6-7 not read); the Results' attribution of about 20% of the men's difference to cardiovascular deaths fits the cause-specific version.

reporting_issues.issue: Two intake scales are used: the hazard ratios per 100 g a week and the all-cause mortality curve (Figure 1, plotted against the mean usual intake in each baseline category) refer to usual, regression-calibrated intake, whereas the life-expectancy groups are defined by reported baseline intake (mean usual intake 56, 123, 208 and 367 g a week in the four groups).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend; Figure 4 legend; Results, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims giving '100 g a week' should say which scale they use and should not mix the threshold (usual intake) with the life-expectancy groups (reported intake).

design_detail: Systematic review with mixed-effects meta-regression updating Stockwell et al. (2016): 107 cohort studies (the 87 of 2016 plus 20 published from 2015 to 2021) with 724 relative-risk estimates for all-cause mortality by level of alcohol intake, pooled with study-level adjustment for abstainer biases and other characteristics, repeated with occasional drinkers as the reference group, and stratified by cohort median age at enrolment (under 56 versus 56 or older) and by sex. Described as preregistered on the Open Science Framework; the registration (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G, registered 3 November 2021) was read for this card.
can_establish: Whether the 2016 finding (a low-volume relative risk close to 1 after study-level adjustment) holds with 20 more studies, and how pooled estimates in the cohort literature to mid-2021 differ by cohort age and by sex.
cannot_establish: Causation; that low-volume drinking has no association with mortality (the fully adjusted interval, 0.85 to 1.01, includes a reduction of up to 15%); the risk in any defined population (the adjusted estimates are study-level model predictions at unstated covariate values); outcomes other than all-cause mortality; or precise sex-specific risks at heavier intake in women, which rest on 11 to 17 studies.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed and Web of Science for studies published from January 1980 to 31 July 2021, stated to be regardless of language, plus reference lists of earlier meta-analyses; staff of the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) ran a preliminary search (Abstract › Data Sources; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Article Information). Flow chart and search details in Supplement 1 (eFigure 1, eAppendix; not read). The registration describes the new search as covering 1 July 2016 to 30 June 2021 and requires English-language publication (registry record).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort studies of alcohol consumption and all-cause mortality; details in the eAppendix (not read). The registration specifies original peer-reviewed cohort studies in English, any age, sex, ethnicity or location, reporting at least three levels of daily consumption, and excludes cohorts selected for illness or for heavy, problematic or dependent drinking.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (counts of studies, some counted more than once): published 1980 to 2004, 51; 2005 to 2014, 36; 2015 to 2021, 20. Median age at enrolment 19 to 55 in 67, 56 to 78 in 46. Men only 73, women only 48, men and women 31. North and Central America 41, Europe and Australia 53, Asia 14. Follow-up 3.7 to 10.5 years in 45, 11 to 41 years in 62. Primary studies controlled for smoking in 91, socio-economic status in 69, body-mass index in 61, diet in 17.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: The 87 earlier studies come from an English-only search ending in December 2014. The paper says the update was made regardless of language, but the registration requires English. The registered search starts on 1 July 2016, and the paper does not say how studies published between January 2015 and June 2016 were found (at least two of the 20 new studies, refs 14 and 15, appeared in 2015 and in the first 2016 issue of their journal). Cohorts are mostly from high-income countries.

exposure.measurement: Mean daily intake in grams of ethanol as reported or converted from each study's categories with country-specific drink definitions where not stated (refs 33 and 34; the registration lists, for example, 8 g per UK unit, 13.45 g per Canadian and 14 g per US drink); self-report in all primary studies (Methods, 3rd paragraph; registry record).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories: lifetime abstainers (reference), former drinkers (now completely abstaining), occasional more than 0 and under 1.3 g/day (under 9.1 g a week), low volume 1.3 to 24.0 g/day (1.30 to under 25 in the tables), medium 25 to 44, high 45 to 64, highest 65 g/day or more (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2). The Key Points equate under 25 g/day with about two Canadian standard drinks. For orientation, 25 g/day is 175 g/week (editors' arithmetic).
exposure.polysubstance: Whether the primary study controlled for smoking is a study-level covariate; no other substance considered.

comparison.controls: Abstainers as defined in each study: 21 of 107 studies used strictly defined lifetime abstainers (zero consumption or never one drink); 50 included both former and occasional drinkers, 28 former drinkers only and 8 occasional drinkers only (Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1). Table 2 repeats the analysis with occasional drinkers as the reference.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Fully adjusted model, study-level covariates: abstainer biases, median age, sex, country, publication year, follow-up years, drinking pattern, and whether the study controlled for heart problems, social status, race, diet, exercise, body-mass index and smoking (Table 2, footnote c). The registration describes candidate selection by univariate p < 0.20, change in estimate and collinearity checks.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within the cohorts, earlier drinking history, reasons for abstaining, earlier health, socio-economic position and lifestyle are handled only by whatever each study adjusted for; the meta-regression codes whether such adjustment was made, not its adequacy.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality relative risks (hazard ratios or rate ratios) from each cohort, log-transformed; variance from reported standard errors, confidence intervals or numbers of deaths (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death is an objective outcome; ascertainment in the cohorts is not described.
outcomes.operationalization: RR for each drinking category against the study's reference group. The ‘unadjusted’ column is an unweighted mean of log RRs; ‘partially adjusted’ is weighted and allows for between-study variation; ‘fully adjusted’ adds the study-level covariates (Table 2 footnotes).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, estimated for eight rows at three levels of adjustment and two reference groups (Table 2), then in age and sex strata (Tables 3 and 4) and a young-cohort subgroup (eTable 3), each by t test at .05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Three coders (J. Z., F. A., J. C.) extracted and coded data independently (Methods, 3rd paragraph). The registration states that those who searched for studies were unaware of the hypotheses and that coders were blind to each other's coding.

analysis.effect_sizes: All RRs for all-cause mortality, unadjusted / partially adjusted / fully adjusted, against lifetime nondrinkers as modelled (Table 2): former drinkers 1.22 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.33) / 1.17 (1.08 to 1.26) / 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42), 28 studies, 56 estimates; occasional 0.92 (0.84 to 1.01) / 0.89 (0.83 to 0.95) / 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06), 24 studies; low volume 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88) / 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88) / 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01), 99 studies, 306 estimates; medium 1.02 (0.96 to 1.08) / 0.97 (0.92 to 1.02) / 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14); high 1.07 (0.99 to 1.16) / 1.11 (1.03 to 1.21) / 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32); highest 1.35 (1.26 to 1.46) / 1.24 (1.16 to 1.32) / 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47); current (active) drinkers 0.97 / 0.93 / 1.02 (0.93 to 1.13). Occasional drinkers as reference, fully adjusted: abstainers 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); low 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); medium 1.09 (0.96 to 1.25); high 1.24 (1.07 to 1.44); highest 1.41 (1.23 to 1.61); former 1.31 (1.13 to 1.52). Age strata, fully adjusted (Table 3): low volume 0.93 (0.86 to 1.01) under 56 and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.02) at 56 or older; high 1.24 (1.10 to 1.40) and 1.15 (1.02 to 1.30); highest 1.38 (1.23 to 1.55) and 1.32 (1.18 to 1.47). Sex strata, fully adjusted (Table 4): men low 0.94 (0.88 to 1.01), medium 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10), high 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), highest 1.34 (1.23 to 1.47); women low 0.99 (0.90 to 1.10), medium 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36), high 1.34 (1.11 to 1.63), highest 1.61 (1.44 to 1.80); current female drinkers 1.03 (0.92 to 1.15); any female drinkers including former 1.22 (1.02 to 1.46). Heterogeneity Q (723 df) = 5314.80, I2 above 85.87% in every category; no publication bias by funnel plot or Egger test.
analysis.covariates: Study-level only (Table 2, footnote c); the Figure shows the low-volume RR after removing each covariate or covariate set (values not extracted). The paper does not state at which covariate values (reference levels or averages) the adjusted category RRs are evaluated; Table 1's reference categories for its bivariable tests (for example Asian cohorts, follow-up of 3.7 to 10.5 years, publication 2015 to 2021, median age 56 to 78) show that such choices are not neutral.
analysis.preregistration_detail: OSF Preregistration doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G, registered 3 November 2021 (the paper's reference 11 gives https://osf.io/tnhd3/, an author's OSF profile page that links to it). It was registered after the search ended (30 June or 31 July 2021) and, by the paper's own dates, after analysis began (September 2021), although the registration says no analyses for the new plan had been run and that the patterns relevant to hypotheses 1 to 3 were already known from the earlier dataset. Registered but not reported in the paper, with no deviation noted: hypothesis 5 (studies with lifetime drinking measures); a meta-analysis restricted to studies with lifetime abstainers; the strict subset recruited before 46 and followed to 60 or older; strata by Caucasian population and by control for heart health; CHD mortality, a registered outcome. The young-cohort subgroup was redefined (registered: recruited under 55 and followed to 55 or older, or under 45 and followed to 60 or older; reported: recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60). The registration requires English-language studies; the paper says regardless of language.
analysis.selective_reporting: Registered analyses missing as listed above. The low-volume estimate for the 21 studies with lifetime abstainers, the analogue of the 2016 paper's key stratified result, is not given in the main text. The young-cohort subgroup is reported only in words in the main text (eTable 3, not read).
analysis.power: Women's heavier-drinking categories rest on 11 to 17 studies; occasional drinkers on 24 studies (57 estimates). The authors argue that two estimates per covariate suffice for linear regression (Limitations, 2nd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With 20 more studies the 2016 pattern recurred, with a point estimate further from 1: low-volume RR 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88) unweighted, 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88) weighted and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) fully adjusted; occasional drinkers 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06); former drinkers 1.26; 45 to 64 g/day 1.19 and 65 g/day or more 1.35. Against occasional drinkers the fully adjusted low-volume RR was 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11). Fully adjusted low-volume estimates were identical in younger and older cohorts (0.93). Risk at 25 to 44 g/day was raised in women (1.21) but not in men (1.01).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points conclude: “Low-volume alcohol drinking was not associated with protection against death from all causes.” Gaps: (1) the fully adjusted low-volume RR is 0.93 with an upper limit of 1.01 (P = .07 in the text, .08 in Table 2), which is compatible with a reduction of up to 15%; the Discussion itself calls it a nonsignificant protective association, so the Key Points overstate a borderline null result as an absence of association; (2) the models are presented as prespecified and the protocol as preregistered, but the registration post-dates the search and the stated start of analysis, acknowledges prior knowledge of the main patterns, and planned analyses the paper does not report; (3) the abstract's statement that female drinkers had larger mortality risks (RR 1.22) uses the ‘any drinker’ row, which includes former drinkers; for current female drinkers the RR was 1.03 (0.92 to 1.15), and the excess is confined to 25 g/day or more; (4) the Discussion says risk was increased from 25 g/day, which holds for women but not for the pooled estimate (1.05, 0.96 to 1.14) or for men; (5) the abstract does not say that the adjusted estimates are study-level model predictions. The Discussion and Limitations do describe the dependence of results on modelling choices and the weakness of self-reported intake.

timeline.event: Stockwell et al.: the 87-study review this paper updates, fully adjusted low-volume RR 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round), followed in 2016 by commentaries, a critical letter from Barrett-Connor and co-signatories and the authors' replies.
Zhao et al.: CHD mortality meta-analysis by the same group, described in this paper's introduction as showing no significant cardioprotection in young cohorts followed to older age (not read).
Naimi et al.: paper on selection biases across the life course, named in the registration as the hypothesis this update tests (not read).
Wood et al. pooled analysis of current drinkers, not among the included studies (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
OSF preregistration, 3 November 2021 (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G), read for this card.
Biddinger et al. Mendelian randomization study in UK Biobank, cited in the introduction as finding no cardioprotection (carded in this round by another reader).

This paper, and its correction (JAMA Netw Open 6:e2315283; doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.15283): incorrect 95% CIs in the Figure and the Supplement were corrected; the text and tables were not listed as changed (read).

Stockley, Hendriks and Ellison, ‘ISFAR Reiterates Its Defense of Moderate Alcohol Consumption's Health Benefits’ (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 85:136–140), listed on PubMed as a comment on this paper (not read).
Stockwell et al. review of study characteristics that may bias low-volume mortality estimates, on the project list (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: An update by the authors of the 2016 review on largely the same studies, so it does not replicate that review independently. Its adjusted low-volume estimate (0.93, 0.85 to 1.01) is closer to a protective association than the 2016 estimate and its interval touches 1, so it supports ‘no detectable net reduction’ rather than ‘no association’. It was funded partly through the process that produced Canada's guidance on alcohol and health, and it has drawn a published critique from ISFAR (2024, not read).

funding.funder: Partly funded by the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) as a subcontract for a Health Canada grant to develop guidance for Canadians on alcohol and health; the larger guidance project contributed some funds. Health Canada had no role in the study; CCSA staff ran a preliminary literature search but did not take part in inclusion decisions, coding, analysis, interpretation or approval of the manuscript (Article Information › Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor; Additional Contributions).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Dr Stockwell reported personal fees from the Ontario Public Servants Employees Union for expert witness testimony and personal fees from Alko outside the submitted work. Dr Sherk reported grants from the CCSA during the conduct of the study. No other disclosures.
funding.affiliations_note: Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research, University of Victoria; Department of Psychology, University of Portsmouth. The co-chairs of Canada's guidance development process are acknowledged. Zhao, Stockwell and Naimi wrote the 2016 review being updated, and Stockwell and Naimi the 2015 editorial arguing that protective effects had collapsed (card sc_chikritzhs_2015). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant analysis of cohorts recruited in early adulthood with lifetime drinking histories, strictly defined lifetime abstainers and former drinkers reassigned to the levels they drank, with common adjustment and sex-specific estimates, run to a protocol registered before the data are assembled; or a long-term randomized trial of low-volume drinking against abstention.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Cohort populations, intake level, lifetime abstainers or occasional drinkers as comparators, all-cause mortality.

An OSF preregistration with hypotheses, search, criteria, coding of biases and an analysis plan exists, but it was registered after the search was completed and after the stated start of analysis, with the main patterns admittedly known; deviations (unreported registered analyses, redefined subgroups, language) are not acknowledged in the paper.
Cohort studies chosen to compare studies with and without controls for abstainer biases (Abstract › Study Selection).

Two databases and reference lists; no grey literature, registries or expert consultation beyond a preliminary search by funder staff; the search strategy is only in the eAppendix (not read). The paper says regardless of language, but the registration requires English and the 87 carried-over studies come from an English-only search, without justification; the registered search window starts on 1 July 2016, leaving the capture of 2015 to mid-2016 publications unexplained.
Provisional: the article refers selection details to the eAppendix (not read); the registration plans two reviewers for titles and abstracts and three investigators for eligibility.
Three coders extracted and coded data independently (Methods, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list in the article; the listed supplement contents (eAppendix, eFigures 1 to 4, eTables 1 to 3) include a flow chart but no list of excluded studies; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article gives aggregate characteristics only (Table 1); eTable 1 describes the 20 new studies and the 87 earlier ones are described in the 2016 paper's appendix; neither supplement was read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No formal tool; each study coded for abstainer biases, exclusion or control of baseline illness, follow-up, cohort age, intake measure and control for smoking, socio-economic status, race, diet, exercise and body-mass index; selection of reported results not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Inverse-variance-weighted mixed models with a random study effect, as registered. Met on balance, a close call: the ‘unadjusted’ column is an unweighted mean, correlation between categories sharing a reference group is handled only by the random effect, whether the most-adjusted primary estimates were used is not stated, and adjusted RRs are evaluated at unstated covariate values.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Bias covariates in the meta-regression, removal of each covariate (Figure), and age and sex strata.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion interprets the shift between unadjusted and adjusted estimates as the effect of abstainer and selection biases and says results depend on the modelling strategy.
Q and I2 reported (I2 above 85.87% in every category) and sources explored by meta-regression and strata; discussion of its impact is brief.
Funnel plot and Egger tests for each study group, all P > .05 (eFigure 2, eTable 2, not read; result stated in the text).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and individual disclosures are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items fail (item 4, a search restricted in practice to English without justification and with an unexplained gap in its window; item 7, no list of excluded studies), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; items 5 and 8 are provisional (supplement not read) but non-critical and cannot change the rating. Beyond AMSTAR, the late registration and unreported registered analyses weaken the claim that the main models were prespecified. The card may be cited for the pooled estimates by intake category with their reference groups, for the elevated risk of former drinkers and of drinkers of 45 g/day or more, and for women's elevated risk from 25 g/day. It should not be cited for an absence of association at low volume, for the female ‘any drinker’ estimate as a risk of current drinking, or for any adjusted RR as the risk in a real population.

key_findings.finding: 107 cohort studies (87 from Stockwell et al., 2016, and 20 new) contributed 724 relative-risk estimates from 4,838,825 participants with 425,564 deaths; search of PubMed and Web of Science to 31 July 2021.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The search covered January 1980 to July 2021 (abstract); by the reference list, the earliest included studies are from 1981 (refs 79, 110 and 122) and two are cited with 2022 print issues (refs 30 and 31).

key_findings.finding: Reference groups: 21 studies (220 estimates) used strictly defined lifetime abstainers; 50 (265 estimates) included former and occasional drinkers among abstainers, 28 (177) former drinkers only and 8 (62) occasional drinkers only.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: By the reference lists, 14 of the 87 earlier studies are now classed as bias-free and 8 as occasional-bias only, against 13 and 9 in the 2016 paper (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted mean RR of any drinking (including former drinkers) by study characteristic: studies with lifetime abstainers only 1.19 (1.12 to 1.25) against 0.98 (0.92 to 1.04) for studies with both biases; follow-up of 11 to 41 years 1.12 (1.07 to 1.16) against 0.98 (0.92 to 1.03) for 3.7 to 10.5 years; baseline illness excluded or controlled 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17) against 1.01 (0.97 to 1.06); no control for socio-economic status 1.16 (1.10 to 1.22) against 1.01 (0.97 to 1.06) with control; quantity-frequency intake measure 1.18 (1.12 to 1.25) against 1.01 (0.97 to 1.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No evidence of publication bias (funnel plot; Egger tests, all P > .05); significant heterogeneity in every drinking category (Q with 723 df = 5314.80, P < .001; I2 above 85.87%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against lifetime nondrinkers as modelled, fully adjusted: occasional drinkers (under 1.3 g/day) RR 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06); low volume (1.3 to under 25 g/day) 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01); medium (25 to 44) 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14); high (45 to 64) 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32); highest (65 or more) 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47); former drinkers 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42). Unadjusted, low volume was 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88) and former drinkers 1.22 (1.11 to 1.33), against abstainers as defined in each study.
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 2, upper panel
key_findings.note: The low-volume P value is .07 in the abstract and text and .08 in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: With occasional drinkers as the reference, fully adjusted: abstainers RR 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); low volume 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); medium 1.09 (0.96 to 1.25); high 1.24 (1.07 to 1.44); highest 1.41 (1.23 to 1.61); former drinkers 1.31 (1.13 to 1.52).
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, lower panel

key_findings.finding: Removing study-level covariates from the fully adjusted model mostly lowered the low-volume RR, that is, moved it towards apparent protection.
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 1st paragraph; Figure caption
key_findings.note: The Figure is an image and its values were not extracted; its 95% CIs were corrected in May 2023.

key_findings.finding: Cohort median age interacted with mortality risk (P = .02). Fully adjusted, low-volume RR was 0.93 (0.86 to 1.01) in cohorts with median age under 56 and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.02) at 56 or older, although unadjusted it was 0.88 (0.84 to 0.93) and 0.79 (0.74 to 0.84); high volume 1.24 (1.10 to 1.40) and 1.15 (1.02 to 1.30); highest 1.38 (1.23 to 1.55) and 1.32 (1.18 to 1.47). In cohorts recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60, RRs were higher for all drinking groups against lifetime abstainers and significant except for low volume.
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk on the Basis of Median Age of Study Cohorts at Baseline; Table 3
key_findings.note: The young-cohort subgroup values are only in eTable 3 (not read); the subgroup is defined differently in the Introduction, Results and Discussion.

key_findings.finding: Sex interacted with risk (P = .001). Fully adjusted, against lifetime nondrinkers of the same sex: men, low volume 0.94 (0.88 to 1.01), medium 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10), high 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), highest 1.34 (1.23 to 1.47); women, low volume 0.99 (0.90 to 1.10), medium 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36), high 1.34 (1.11 to 1.63), highest 1.61 (1.44 to 1.80). For women, any drinking including former drinkers 1.22 (1.02 to 1.46), current drinking 1.03 (0.92 to 1.15).
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers by Sex; Table 4

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: imperfect, mostly under-reported intake, often measured once; unreliable classification of lifetime abstainers, so that risks relative to presumed lifetime abstainers may be underestimated; few studies in some strata; binge drinking not controllable; all-cause mortality only.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Correction (JAMA Netw Open 2023;6:e2315283, doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.15283): incorrect 95% CIs were shown in the Figure and the Supplement, and the article was corrected. The numbers on this card come from the text and Tables 1 to 4, which the notice does not list as changed.
key_findings.locator: Errors in Figure and Supplement, single paragraph

key_findings.finding: The OSF preregistration (registered 3 November 2021) states five hypotheses, an English-language inclusion criterion, a new search from 1 July 2016 to 30 June 2021 having found 31 new cohort studies, and planned analyses including studies with lifetime drinking measures, studies with lifetime abstainers only, a strict subset recruited before 46 and followed to 60 or older, and strata by sex, age, ethnicity and control for heart health, for all-cause and CHD mortality; it says no analyses for the plan had been run and that the patterns for hypotheses 1 to 3 were already known from the earlier dataset.
key_findings.locator: OSF Preregistration doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G (https://osf.io/pf95g): Study Information › Hypotheses; Design Plan › Study design; Sampling Plan › Explanation of existing data; Analysis Plan › Statistical models

reporting_issues.issue: P values differ between places: low volume, fully adjusted, P = .07 (abstract, text) against .08 (Table 2); any drinking in women P = .03 (abstract, text) against .04 (Table 4); abstainers against occasional drinkers P = .44 (text) against .45 (Table 2). The abstract gives the low-volume RR without its interval.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results; Tables 2 and 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the abstract alone hides that the interval reaches 1.01.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 study counts exceed 107 in most rows (median age 67 + 46 = 113; sex 73 + 48 + 31 = 152; countries 108; smoking control 109), with percentages computed on those totals; the text's sex lists name 39 + 33 + 8 + 30 = 110 studies, only 105 distinct, with refs 13, 21, 26, 29 and 84 in two lists and refs 60 and 131 in none (editors' count).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition of the sex strata cannot be reconstructed from the article; study counts per stratum should be taken from Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 counts 436 and 281 estimates for the two age strata (717 in all), whereas Table 1 gives 438 and 286 (724) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Seven estimates are unaccounted for in the age-stratified models.

reporting_issues.issue: Labels: Table 2 heads all three columns ‘Reference group = lifetime nondrinker’, although the unadjusted and partially adjusted estimates are against abstainers as defined in each study (most not lifetime abstainers), as the text says; in its lower panel rows are labelled ‘vs abstainer’ under the occasional-drinker reference; Table 4's first column is headed by median age though it is stratified by sex.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take the unadjusted 0.85 as a comparison with lifetime abstainers; cite it as against study-defined abstainers.

reporting_issues.issue: The young-cohort subgroup is defined three ways: recruited before median age 51 and followed to median age 60 or more (Introduction), recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60 (Results), enrolled at 50 or younger and followed for at least 10 years (Discussion); the registration specified other cut-offs.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Results › Median Age; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup result, already available only in a supplement, cannot be attributed to a defined set of studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper states the protocol was preregistered and the models prespecified, and dates the analysis from September 2021, but the cited registration was made on 3 November 2021, after the search, and itself says no analyses had yet been run; the reference given (https://osf.io/tnhd3/) opens an author's profile page rather than the registration.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Abstract; reference 11; registry record
reporting_issues.consequence: The degree of prespecification cannot be taken at face value; claims should not describe the main models as preregistered without this qualification.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says studies were sought regardless of language, but the registration requires English-language publication and describes the combined sample as close to all such studies ever published in English.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 2nd paragraph; registry record (Design Plan › Inclusion criteria; Sampling Plan › Sample size rationale)
reporting_issues.consequence: The review should be treated as English-only.

reporting_issues.issue: The interaction of cohort age with risk is reported as F601 = 2.93, P = .02, with a single degrees-of-freedom value; F(1, 601) = 2.93 gives P of about .09, whereas P = .02 fits 4 numerator degrees of freedom (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Median Age, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the test cannot be checked as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: One of the 20 new studies, and one of the 21 classed as free of abstainer bias, is cited as a journal supplement page (ref 13, Kaprio et al., Eur Neuropsychopharm 2019;29 Suppl 3:S804, with a 2017 DOI), the format of a congress abstract; the registration excludes meeting abstracts and requires peer-reviewed original articles.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, reference 13; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph; registry record (Design Plan › Exclusion criteria)
reporting_issues.consequence: If it is an abstract, a bias-free study rests on unreviewed summary data; the editor should check the source before the bias-free count is quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give the drinking categories as 1.3-24.0, 25.0-44.0 and 45.0-64.0 g a day, leaving gaps between them, while Tables 2 to 4 use 1.30 to under 25, 25 to under 45 and 45 to under 65 g a day; the abstract uses 1.3-24.0.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Abstract; Tables 2 to 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; claims should use the tables' bounds.
