design_detail: Prospective population-based twin cohort (Minnesota Twin Family Study; same-sex pairs born 1977–1984), assessed at target ages 11 (intake, n=1512), 14 (FU1, n=1404) and 24 (FU4, n=1328). Two self-reported early exposures by the age-14 assessment (FU1, mean age 14.8: any alcoholic drink without parental permission; ever intoxicated) were related to 12 adult outcomes at about 25 in two ways: inverse-probability weighting on a propensity score built from 29 intake covariates (GEE for twin clustering), and co-twin control, which estimates the within-pair effect in pairs discordant for the exposure (all pairs, then MZ and DZ separately).
can_establish: Whether drinking and intoxication by about 14 go with adult substance-related and social outcomes at about 25 after balancing 29 measured childhood characteristics, and after holding constant what co-twins share (rearing environment, and all or half of their genes), in a Minnesota twin cohort born 1977–1984.
cannot_establish: That early drinking causes the adult outcomes: within-pair differences can still reflect confounders that differ between co-twins (for example a twin's own experimentation with tobacco or other drugs before 14, or different peers) and exposure measurement error; the within-MZ-pair estimates, the cleanest test, were significant for only a few outcomes and rest on small numbers of discordant pairs; nothing about amount or frequency of early drinking (two binary exposures) or about mechanism.

sample.recruitment: Population-based longitudinal study of twins born in Minnesota and their families (called community-based in the abstract); this analysis uses same-sex pairs from the cohort born 1977–1984, first assessed at a target age of 11 and followed every three or four years (Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Same-sex twin pairs of the 1977–1984 birth cohort; other criteria are in earlier MTFS reports and not restated here.
sample.demographics: Intake: mean age 11.72 (SD 0.43), 50.3% female; FU1: 14.8 (0.53), 50.6% female; FU4: 25.29 (0.74), 51.4% female; 64% MZ and 36% DZ twins (Methods › Participants). Ethnicity and socioeconomic status entered the propensity model (Tables 1A and 1B) but their distributions are not reported in the main text.
sample.attrition: 1404 of 1512 (92.9%) assessed at 14 and 1328 (87.8%) at 24 (editors' arithmetic). How missing outcome data were handled, and whether those lost differed from those retained, is not reported in the main text; 'additional statistical and data-related considerations' are in the supplement, which was not read.
sample.selection_effects: A population-based twin sample from one US state, with 12% loss by 24. The co-twin analyses use only pairs discordant for the exposure: 20% of MZ and 26% of DZ pairs for early use, and 9% and 12% for early intoxication. If those percentages apply to all 486 MZ and 270 DZ pairs, about 97 MZ and 70 DZ pairs were discordant for early use and about 44 MZ and 32 DZ pairs for early intoxication (editors' arithmetic; the paper gives no pair counts).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at the age-14 assessment, recorded at the time rather than recalled in adulthood: ever having had an alcoholic drink without parental permission by FU1 (505 exposed) and ever having been intoxicated by FU1 (212 exposed). Rates were similar by zygosity (χ2(1)=0.192, p=0.66; χ2(1)=0.691, p=0.41) and are said to approximate national rates for adolescents of the same cohort and age (Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: both exposures are binary, with no amount, frequency or age within the window; drinking with parental permission counts as unexposed.
exposure.polysubstance: The twin's own tobacco or other drug use before 14 is not among the 29 propensity covariates, which are all measured at 11 and include parental alcohol, tobacco and drug use (Tables 1A and 1B); adult tobacco, cannabis and other drug use are outcomes.

comparison.controls: Propensity-score analyses: twins without the early exposure, weighted by 1/(1-PS), against exposed twins weighted by 1/PS. Co-twin control: the unexposed co-twin in exposure-discordant pairs, through the within-pair (individual-level) coefficient (Methods › Statistical Analyses).
comparison.matching: Weighting on 29 intake covariates (9 individual-level, such as IQ, puberty, school performance, externalizing symptoms and delinquency; 20 family-level, such as sex, age, ethnicity, parental education, income, psychopathology and substance use) reduced the mean absolute standardized difference from 0.23 to 0.03 for early use and from 0.29 to 0.07 for early intoxication, all below the 0.25 threshold used. Within discordant pairs, individual-level covariates were balanced except puberty in DZ pairs discordant for intoxication (0.31) (Results › Propensity Score and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights; Tables 1A and 1B).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Factors that differ between co-twins and precede the exposure but were not measured (own early tobacco or drug use, peer group, traits beyond the measured externalizing, school and family variables); in DZ pairs half of the genetic variation; prenatal and perinatal differences.

outcomes.instruments: Twelve outcomes at FU4, described only in the supplement (not read): alcohol use quantity and frequency index; alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms; tobacco use quantity and frequency index; number of times used marijuana; number of drug classes ever used; drug abuse or dependence symptoms; adult antisocial behavior symptoms; dependent stressful life events; family relationships; interpersonal problems; social engagement; adult independence (Tables 2A and 2B).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Standardized regression coefficients (β) for each binary exposure on each outcome; the scaling of the 'standardized estimates' is not explained in the main text. Alcohol 'problems' are symptom counts of abuse or dependence, not diagnoses.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 12 outcomes × 2 exposures × 5 analyses (unweighted, weighted, co-twin all pairs, MZ, DZ) give 120 coefficients judged at p<0.05, plus zygosity moderation tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Tables 2A and 2B, β (SE) as printed. Early alcohol use: alcohol use index, unweighted 0.63 (0.06), propensity-weighted 0.57 (0.06), co-twin all pairs 0.21 (0.09), MZ 0.22 (0.10), DZ 0.20 (0.14); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms 0.46, 0.36, 0.24 (0.11), MZ 0.17 (0.14), DZ 0.34 (0.16); tobacco index 0.63, 0.49, 0.21 (0.09), MZ 0.09, DZ 0.39; times used marijuana 0.54, 0.43, 0.28 (0.10), MZ 0.22 (0.11), DZ 0.38; drug classes 0.73, 0.60, 0.44 (0.10), MZ 0.41 (0.12), DZ 0.50 (0.17); drug abuse or dependence symptoms 0.51, 0.40, 0.27 (0.11), MZ 0.18, DZ 0.42; antisocial symptoms 0.52, 0.38, 0.19 (0.09), MZ 0.08, DZ 0.37; dependent stressful life events 0.35, 0.26, 0.26 (0.10), MZ 0.26 (0.11), DZ 0.26. Early intoxication: alcohol use index 0.62, 0.57, 0.37 (0.13), MZ 0.26 (0.17), DZ 0.54 (0.23); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms 0.53, 0.31, 0.29 (0.15), MZ 0.15, DZ 0.51; tobacco 0.68, 0.50, 0.25 (0.12), MZ 0.16, DZ 0.38; marijuana 0.60, 0.31, 0.43 (0.17), MZ 0.27, DZ 0.66; drug classes 0.84, 0.62, 0.50 (0.16), MZ 0.38 (0.15), DZ 0.68; drug abuse or dependence symptoms 0.68, 0.38, 0.47 (0.16), MZ 0.26, DZ 0.78; antisocial 0.60, 0.43, 0.18 (0.16), MZ 0.08, DZ 0.35; dependent stressful life events 0.47, 0.40, 0.38 (0.15), MZ 0.43 (0.18), DZ 0.30. Family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement and adult independence were not associated with either exposure after weighting or within pairs. Zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect. Significance in this card is taken from β and SE, not from the printed p-values (see reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Propensity score from 29 intake covariates (Tables 1A and 1B; full list and descriptions in supplementary Table S1, not read); co-twin control removes factors shared within pairs.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 12 outcomes are reported for every analysis in Tables 2A and 2B. The text's summaries of those tables are partly inaccurate (see reporting issues), and outcome definitions and data handling are only in the supplement.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Co-twin estimates rest on roughly 97 MZ and 70 DZ discordant pairs for early use and 44 MZ and 32 DZ pairs for early intoxication (editors' estimate from the discordance percentages), so most MZ-only estimates are imprecise and their non-significance is not evidence of no effect.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Drinking and intoxication by 14 were associated with adult alcohol use, other substance use, antisocial symptoms and stressful life events of the person's own making, after propensity weighting and, attenuated, within discordant twin pairs; the unweighted associations with interpersonal problems and adult independence lost nominal significance after weighting (for adult independence through a larger standard error, the coefficient barely changing), and no social-functioning outcome was associated within pairs. Within MZ pairs, which control for all genes and the shared environment, the association reached significance for the alcohol-use index (early use), number of drug classes used and dependent stressful life events, was borderline for marijuana use (early use), and was not significant for alcohol or drug abuse and dependence symptoms, tobacco or antisocial symptoms.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that early alcohol exposures 'predict adult alcohol problems and related outcomes' despite stringent adjustment, and that propensity-score estimates were likely biased by unmeasured confounding; the Discussion says the analyses support a causal effect of early alcohol use on adult functioning. Gaps: (1) for alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms the within-pair association held only for early use across all discordant pairs (β 0.24), not within MZ pairs (0.17, SE 0.14) and not for early intoxication (0.29, SE 0.15); (2) 'adult functioning' overstates a result that was null for every social-functioning outcome; (3) the inference that propensity estimates were biased rests on within-pair estimates being smaller, which exposure measurement error can also produce (as the authors note), and which did not hold for early intoxication with marijuana use and drug abuse or dependence symptoms (larger within pairs than after weighting); (4) causal wording is used although non-shared confounding is not excluded. The final paragraph is more cautious, saying effects may be causal only in the absence of such confounding and that more research is needed.

timeline.event: Prescott & Kendler, twins: the association of age at first drink with alcoholism judged largely non-causal and attributed to common genetic effects (as cited in the introduction).
Grant J.D. et al., twin design: adolescent alcohol use a risk factor for adult alcohol and drug dependence, not wholly explained by familial factors (as cited).
Odgers et al., Dunedin cohort: after propensity-score matching, substance use before 15 kept associations with adult substance dependence and convictions (as cited).
Deutsch et al., Australian twins: age at first drink associated with adult alcohol involvement beyond shared familial factors, moderated by family context (as cited).
Maimaris & McCambridge, systematic review of prospective general-population cohorts (read in this round): sparse and mixed evidence, with no twin or sibling design among the five included reports.
This study (online October 2014): propensity weighting and co-twin control in the Minnesota Twin Family Study.

replication.where_it_stands: The study agrees with the earlier co-twin reports it cites (Grant et al., 2006; Deutsch et al., 2013) that associations of early drinking with adult alcohol and drug outcomes are reduced but not removed within twin pairs, against the earlier non-causal reading of Prescott & Kendler (1999). The within-MZ-pair results are mostly imprecise, and residual non-shared confounding is not excluded. The round's reading list names Richmond-Rakerd et al. (2016) as the other DOI-bearing twin test; it was not read here.

funding.funder: Not reported: the author manuscript on PMC carries no funding or acknowledgments statement (the published version was not read).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declaration of interests: None.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the Department of Psychology, University of Minnesota, which runs the Minnesota Twin Family Study; the second and third authors are authors of several of the cited earlier MTFS and twin-method papers (refs 5, 11, 17, 20, 21).

what_would_settle_it: Pooled analyses of MZ twin pairs discordant for early drinking across several twin registries, large enough to estimate within-MZ-pair effects on DSM alcohol and drug use disorders with precision, with early drinking measured repeatedly (age, amount, intoxication) and the twins' own behaviour and substance use before the exposure measured; together with natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person.

domains.note: Propensity weighting balanced 29 measured childhood covariates, and the co-twin design removes everything shared within pairs (all genes in MZ pairs, half in DZ pairs); confounders that differ between co-twins, including the twin's own early tobacco or drug use, are not addressed.

Two binary self-reports at 14, recorded close to the time; drinking with parental permission counts as unexposed, and random misclassification, which the authors note, biases within-pair estimates toward zero.
Population-based twin cohort entered at 11, before the exposure.
No interventions relevant to the exposure–outcome relation are described.
12% of the intake sample was not assessed at 24; handling of missing data and the comparison of those lost with those retained are only in the supplement (not read).
Adult outcomes are self-reported symptom counts and indices, described only in the supplement; whether assessors knew the adolescent data is not reported.

All 120 coefficients are tabulated, which is good, but none are corrected for multiplicity, the printed p-values are wrong (see reporting issues) and the text's summary departs from the tables in places.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A strong design for this question: exposure measured at 14 in a population-based cohort, balanced on a rich set of childhood measures, and tested within twin pairs. The remaining threats are non-shared confounding, small numbers of MZ discordant pairs, attrition handled only in the supplement, and reporting errors in the p-values and in the text's summary of the tables. Cite it for the attenuated but persisting association of early drinking with adult alcohol use and with the number of drug classes used within twin pairs, including MZ pairs, and for the absence of associations with adult social functioning; not for a causal effect on alcohol use disorder, which within MZ pairs was not shown.

key_findings.finding: Minnesota Twin Family Study, same-sex pairs born 1977–1984: 1512 twins at 11 (50.3% female; 972 MZ, 540 DZ), 1404 at 14 and 1328 at about 25. By the age-14 assessment (FU1, mean age 14.8), 505 had drunk alcohol without parental permission and 212 had been intoxicated.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants; Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14

key_findings.finding: Before weighting, 13 of 29 childhood covariates differed by a standardized difference of about 0.25 or more between twins who had drunk by 14 and those who had not (19 of 29 for intoxication), notably delinquent behaviours (0.51; 0.79) and parental tobacco and alcohol use; weighting reduced the mean absolute difference from 0.23 to 0.03 (use) and from 0.29 to 0.07 (intoxication).
key_findings.locator: Results › Propensity Score and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights, 2nd paragraph; Tables 1A and 1B

key_findings.finding: After propensity weighting, early alcohol use remained associated with the adult alcohol-use index (β 0.57, SE 0.06), alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.36), tobacco (0.49), marijuana (0.43), number of drug classes (0.60), drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.40), antisocial symptoms (0.38) and dependent stressful life events (0.26). The unweighted associations with interpersonal problems and adult independence lost nominal significance after weighting, in different ways: for interpersonal problems the coefficient fell (0.15, SE 0.06, to 0.08, SE 0.08); for adult independence it barely changed (0.16, SE 0.07, to 0.15, SE 0.08) and the standard error grew (for early intoxication, 0.18 before and after weighting, Table 2B).
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2A; Table 2B (adult independence)

key_findings.finding: Within all exposure-discordant pairs, early alcohol use was associated with the alcohol-use index (β 0.21, SE 0.09), alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.24, 0.11), tobacco (0.21, 0.09), marijuana (0.28, 0.10), drug classes (0.44, 0.10), drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.27, 0.11), antisocial symptoms (0.19, 0.09) and dependent stressful life events (0.26, 0.10), all with β/SE of about 2 or more.
key_findings.locator: Table 2A, Cotwin control: All discordant pairs; Results › Estimated Effects…, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within MZ pairs discordant for early use, associations with β/SE of about 2 or more were found for the alcohol-use index (0.22, SE 0.10), number of drug classes (0.41, 0.12) and dependent stressful life events (0.26, 0.11), with marijuana borderline (0.22, 0.11); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.17, 0.14), tobacco (0.09), drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.18) and antisocial symptoms (0.08) were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2A, Cotwin control: Discordant MZ pairs
key_findings.note: Judged from β and SE because the printed p-values are not valid (see reporting issues); the MZ estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs (editors' estimate).

key_findings.finding: For early intoxication, within all discordant pairs: alcohol-use index 0.37 (SE 0.13), tobacco 0.25 (0.12), marijuana 0.43 (0.17), drug classes 0.50 (0.16), drug abuse or dependence symptoms 0.47 (0.16) and dependent stressful life events 0.38 (0.15) were associated; alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.29, SE 0.15) and antisocial symptoms (0.18, 0.16) were not. Within MZ pairs only drug classes (0.38, 0.15) and stressful life events (0.43, 0.18) were.
key_findings.locator: Table 2B, Cotwin control columns

key_findings.finding: Zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect, but several substance-related within-pair estimates were larger in DZ than in MZ pairs (for example drug abuse or dependence symptoms after intoxication, DZ 0.78 vs MZ 0.26), which the authors read as partial genetic confounding in DZ pairs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimated Effects…, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph; Tables 2A and 2B

key_findings.finding: Neither exposure was significantly associated with family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement or adult independence after weighting or within pairs. After weighting, the adult-independence estimates were not near zero but missed significance (early use 0.15, SE 0.08; early intoxication 0.18, SE 0.11); within pairs they were 0.00 and 0.01.
key_findings.locator: Tables 2A and 2B, lower four rows; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that the co-twin design cannot separate causal effects from confounders not shared by co-twins, and that random error in the exposure also shrinks within-pair estimates relative to unpaired ones.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The p-values in Tables 2A and 2B cannot be two-sided p-values from the coefficients and standard errors shown. Coefficients of zero or nearly zero carry p-values of about 0.39 to 0.40 (for example 0.00, SE 0.12, p=0.396; 0.01, SE 0.15, p=0.396; -0.02, SE 0.25, p=0.397), where a Wald test would give values near 1. Across the tables the printed values match the standard normal density at β/SE, which peaks at 0.399, rather than tail probabilities (editors' check: 0.09/0.12 gives density 0.30 and two-sided p 0.45, printed 0.291; 0.08/0.11 gives 0.31 and 0.47, printed 0.312; -0.06/0.10 gives 0.33 and 0.55, printed 0.332; 0.08/0.08 gives 0.242 and 0.32, printed 0.242). One printed value fits neither reading: MZ pairs, number of drug classes after early use, 0.41 (SE 0.12), printed p=0.004, where the density is about 0.001 and the two-sided p about 0.0006 (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: No printed p-value should be quoted, including the abstract's p=0.031 for the co-twin alcohol-use estimate (two-sided p about 0.02 from 0.21 and 0.09, editors' calculation, imprecise because of rounding). Above |z| of about 1.6 the density is slightly larger than the true p, so the paper's significance calls are, if anything, slightly conservative: for example MZ marijuana after early use (0.22, SE 0.11, printed 0.055) has a two-sided p near 0.05.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that within-pair effects of both exposures were attenuated relative to the weighted estimates and remained significant for the alcohol and substance-use outcomes, with only antisocial behavior lost for intoxication. In Table 2B, early intoxication's within-pair association with alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms was not significant (0.29, SE 0.15, printed p=0.061), and its within-pair estimates for marijuana (0.43 vs 0.31 weighted) and drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.47 vs 0.38) were larger than the weighted ones.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table 2B
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion that propensity-score estimates were biased by unmeasured confounding rests on a uniform attenuation that the table does not show for early intoxication, and the claim that early exposures predict adult alcohol problems within pairs holds only for early use, in all pairs, not in MZ pairs.

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure counts are given as 36% (505) and 15% (212) of the 'total sample', but the percentages correspond to the 1404 assessed at 14, not to the 1512 at intake (33% and 14%) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; prevalence statements should name the FU1 sample as the denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's Findings say that after propensity weighting several adult outcomes related to substance use or social functioning remained significantly associated with early alcohol exposure, but in Table 2A none of the outcomes the Results call social functioning or independence (family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement, adult independence) remained significant after weighting; besides the substance outcomes, the ones that did were antisocial symptoms and dependent stressful life events, which the Results describe separately.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Findings; Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2A
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract should not be cited for effects on social functioning; the Results and the Discussion's last paragraph report no reliable effects on social functioning or independence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion attributes the loss of significance for adult independence after weighting to confounding, but the coefficient hardly changed (early use 0.16, SE 0.07, unweighted against 0.15, SE 0.08, weighted; early intoxication 0.18 in both, SE 0.09 and 0.11): the weighting widened the standard error rather than removing the association. The unweighted association was with more independent adult functioning, not less.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Tables 2A and 2B, row 'Adult independence'
reporting_issues.consequence: The weighted data show this association estimated less precisely, not explained by confounding; within twin pairs the estimates were 0.00 and 0.01.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of two independent US national cross-sectional surveys pooled into one data set: the National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey (NLAES, 1991–1992) and the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC, 2001–2002), both sponsored by NIAAA, with Census Bureau fieldwork and the same AUDADIS-IV interview. US-born respondents aged 18–57 (N=53,238) were grouped into five 10-year birth cohorts (born 1934–1943 to 1974–1983). Three 'telescoping' landmarks were reconstructed from ages recalled at a single interview: age at first drink, time from first drink to onset of DSM-IV alcohol dependence, and time from dependence onset to first alcohol treatment. Analyses: within-cohort comparisons of mean times (t tests), life tables with log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards models with cohort-by-gender and cohort-by-gender-by-time interactions, weighted for both complex sample designs (SUDAAN). A general-population sample, not a treatment sample.
can_establish: For US-born adults aged 18–57 in two national household surveys, how the recalled timing of first drink, onset of alcohol dependence and first alcohol treatment differed between men and women and between birth cohorts, and whether the sex pattern reported from treatment samples (later first drink but faster progression to dependence and to treatment in women) shows up in a general-population sample.
cannot_establish: Whether the timing differences are real rather than products of recalling ages years or decades later (nothing was recorded as it happened); why men and women differ (biological sex and gender roles are not separated, and the authors' explanation of cohort convergence by changing norms was not tested); how fast people progress once they are on the way to dependence as distinct from whether they become dependent at all (the survival and hazard analyses among all drinkers combine the two); and anything about people over 57, people born outside the US, people outside the households and group quarters sampled, or people who died before the surveys.

sample.recruitment: General-population sample: two US national multistage probability surveys of households and group quarters, interviewed face to face by trained lay interviewers; response rates 90% (NLAES) and 81% (NESARC); no person took part in both surveys (Method › Sources of Data, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: US-born respondents aged 18–57. Excluded: people older than 57 (to limit the effect of alcohol-related deaths) and people born outside the US (to limit changes in cohort make-up from immigration) (Method › Sources of Data, 2nd paragraph). Lifetime drinkers were people who had ever had more than 12 drinks (Method › Measures). The 258 people whose first treatment came before dependence onset were left out of the treatment analysis (Table 1 footnote a).
sample.demographics: Unweighted: 23,113 men and 30,125 women (Table 1). Cohorts 2–4 contribute respondents from both surveys, interviewed 10 years apart; cohort 1 comes only from NESARC (aged 18–27) and cohort 5 only from NLAES (aged 48–57) (Method › Sources of Data, 4th paragraph). Race and ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity were covariates, but their distributions are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview per person). Item-level missing data are not reported, and the analysed numbers differ between Table 1 and the figures and Table 2 without explanation (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: A general-population sample, unlike the treatment samples in which telescoping was first described. Survivors only: capping age at 57 limits but does not remove the loss of people with severe dependence who died young, a loss that grows with cohort age. Each cohort is seen at different ages (cohort 1 only at 18–27, cohort 5 only at 48–57), so the youngest cohort can contribute only early transitions to dependence and treatment, and cohort, age and survey year are partly bound together. Treatment is uncommon (24.6% of people with dependence had ever had any alcohol treatment, per the Discussion), so the treatment comparisons rest on 3,056 treated people, including only 72 and 65 women in cohorts 1 and 5.

exposure.measurement: The groups compared are men and women (the paper uses 'gender' throughout and does not separate biological sex from gender roles) and birth cohort (five 10-year groups). The landmark ages were all self-reported at a single AUDADIS-IV interview: age at first drink (people counted at risk from age 5, the youngest age the surveys accepted), age at onset of DSM-IV alcohol dependence (three or more of seven criteria clustering within one year) and age at first alcohol treatment. All timing was recalled, none recorded as it happened.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed: quantity and frequency of drinking are not in the models. The paper does not spell out whether 'initiation' means the first drink or the point of having had more than 12 drinks; the Figure 1 legend counts years to the first drink.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: other drug use and other drug use disorders are neither described nor adjusted for.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women within each birth cohort; successive birth cohorts compared with each other, separately in men and in women.
comparison.matching: None. The Cox models adjusted for survey (NLAES vs NESARC), race/ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity, and for age at first drink in the dependence and treatment models; whether age itself stayed in the final models is stated inconsistently (see reporting issues). Birth cohort was a five-level categorical variable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of alcohol problems, childhood adversity, conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, body size and composition, amount drunk and other drug use were not included. Income and education were measured at the interview, years after many of the events being timed, so they may be consequences of drinking rather than prior characteristics.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV (structured lay-administered interview with DSM-IV criteria); the authors cite good to excellent reliability and validity of its alcohol diagnoses (refs 19–21). 'First treatment' is described as first engagement with treatment, or any type of alcohol treatment; which services counted is not defined in this paper.
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability of the diagnosis is cited; the reliability of the recalled onset ages is not reported. The authors' recall check compared, within each birth cohort, the prevalence of dependence that began at age 25 or later between the two surveys (no difference found; Discussion, 6th paragraph); it tests forgetting of later-onset episodes over 10 years, not whether men and women recall timing differently.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping was defined as a later age at first drink in women together with shorter times from first drink to dependence and from dependence to first treatment (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). Times were analysed three ways: (a) mean times among people who had the event (Table 1; the authors warn these are distorted because older people have had more time); (b) survival curves among everyone at risk (all lifetime drinkers for dependence, all people with dependence for treatment), censored at current age; (c) hazard ratios for men against women by cohort, with two-way and three-way interactions.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The three landmarks were tested with t tests in 18 cells, log-rank tests for each cohort and for adjacent cohorts in each sex, and Cox main effects and two-way and three-way interactions: several dozen tests without correction (editors' count).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (structured interview; interviewers knew respondents' sex).

analysis.effect_sizes: Hazard ratios, men compared with women, with 95% CIs (Table 2). First drink: cohort 1 1.50 (1.37–1.64), cohort 2 1.50 (1.43–1.57), cohort 3 1.62 (1.55–1.70), cohort 4 2.01 (1.91–2.12), cohort 5 2.19 (2.01–2.39). Time from first drink to dependence, among lifetime drinkers: 1.56 (1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02), 1.71 (1.34–2.20). Time from dependence to first treatment, among people with dependence: 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1.38 (0.84–2.26). Interactions (Table 2 footnotes): first drink, two-way F=16.7, df=4, p<0.01, three-way F=0.10, df=6, p=0.84; dependence, two-way F=2.51, df=4, p=0.04, three-way F=54.1, df=6, p<0.01; treatment, two-way F=0.92, df=4, p=0.46, three-way F=0.02, df=6, p=0.98. Mean times among people with the event (Table 1), men vs women overall: first drink 17.8 vs 19.0 years; first drink to dependence 5.8 vs 5.6 years (ratio 1.04, not significant); dependence to first treatment 7.0 vs 6.1 years (ratio 1.15, p<0.05). The coefficients of the three-way interactions are not shown.
analysis.covariates: Survey, race/ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity in all models; age at first drink in the dependence and treatment models; age reported as not retained in the Methods but as controlled in the Results and in the Table 2 footnote. Cohort, age and survey year are close to collinear (age is roughly survey year minus birth year), so cohort effects are identified only through within-cohort age spread and the two survey years; the paper does not discuss this.
analysis.selective_reporting: The direction of the three-way interaction on which the abstract's main new claim rests (men faster to dependence, especially in younger cohorts) is 'data not shown'; the 5-year-cohort sensitivity analyses and the survey-by-survey post hoc analyses are described only as similar, without numbers.
analysis.power: The authors state that the treatment analyses lacked power to detect small cohort differences because treatment is rare (24.6% of people with dependence ever treated); each cohort had at least 4,600 people (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this general-population sample, women reported a later first drink than men in every cohort (overall means 19.0 vs 17.8 years; the gap shrank from 3.0 years in the oldest cohort to 0.4 in the youngest), and the men-to-women hazard ratio for a first drink fell from 2.19 to 1.50. Among all lifetime drinkers, men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every cohort (HR 1.36–1.79), and among people with dependence men had a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in cohorts 2 and 3, HR 1.55 and 1.42). Among the people who did become dependent, however, mean time from first drink to dependence was about the same in men and women overall (5.8 vs 5.6 years) and shorter in women in cohort 2 (3.7 vs 4.2 years, p=0.02); among people treated, women's mean time from dependence to first treatment was shorter overall (6.1 vs 7.0 years, p<0.05) and in the oldest cohort (19.4 vs 23.5 years).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports little evidence of telescoping in women and says a three-way interaction suggests men have a shorter time to dependence, especially in younger cohorts; the conclusion states that "A telescoping effect is not evident in the general population" (Abstract, Conclusions). Gaps: (1) in the survival and hazard analyses 'time to dependence' is computed among all lifetime drinkers, so a higher male hazard largely reflects men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent, not faster progression among those who do; the mean times among people who became dependent, which correspond to what treatment-sample studies measured, show no male advantage and a shorter time in women in one cohort; (2) the direction of the three-way interaction behind 'especially in younger cohorts' is not shown, and the youngest cohort can only contribute transitions completed by age 27; (3) the Discussion (2nd paragraph) says that, on mean times as well as survival curves, women had neither a shorter time to dependence nor a shorter time to treatment, which Table 1 contradicts in part; (4) all timing is recalled, and the recall check does not test differences in recall between men and women; (5) the explanation of convergence by changing gender norms is offered as consistent with other research, and the authors say they know of no formal test of it. The limitations paragraph is candid about recall and power, and 'full' or 'complete' telescoping is the wording used in the Discussion and Conclusions.

timeline.event: Telescoping first described in women in treatment for alcohol problems (Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager, 1989; ref. 1 of this paper).
Project MATCH treatment sample: telescoping of drinking landmarks in women compared with men (cited by Keyes et al. as ref. 4).
Women entering treatment for opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence progressed faster to treatment (Hernandez-Avila, Rounsaville and Kranzler, 2004; ref. 3 of this paper).

Review of women's treatment entry and outcome states as established that women progress faster from use to regular use to first treatment (alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence), citing treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996); in that paragraph the label of a most reproducible finding belongs to women's vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences, not to faster progression.

This study: first test in two pooled US general-population surveys; women later to first drink, men higher hazards of dependence and treatment; mean times among people with the event similar or shorter in women.
Review cites this study as the population-based analysis that did not replicate telescoping and explains the discrepancy by sample (treatment vs population).
Critique of the telescoping concept summarizes this study as finding no telescoping in the general population and recommends discarding the term.

replication.where_it_stands: Telescoping was described in treatment samples, which this paper cites (refs 1–6), and this general-population analysis did not find the full pattern; later reviews on this round's list (mchugh_2018, marks_2018) treat it as the main general-population counter-evidence and explain the difference by sample. Whether telescoping is a feature of women's drinking careers or of who reaches treatment, and when, remains open, and the speed-versus-probability point in this card's interpretation gap is not raised in either review. No prospective cohort designed to test telescoping is cited in this paper.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young men and women followed from before their first drink with repeated interviews (or linked records) that record drinking, dependence criteria and treatment as they happen, analysed with methods that separate the chance of ever becoming dependent from the speed of progression among those who do (for example mixture-cure or competing-risks survival models), with measures of body composition, gender roles and access to treatment so that sex and gender can be told apart.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National probability frames of households and group quarters suit a general-population question, but the analysis keeps only US-born people aged 18–57 who survived to interview, which removes the oldest people and early deaths from severe dependence.
Multistage probability samples; the two surveys' weights and design variables were combined and analysed in SUDAAN.

53,238 people and at least 4,603 per cohort, but the treatment comparisons rest on 3,056 treated people (65–72 women in cohorts 1 and 5), and the authors say they lacked power for small treatment differences.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Survey designs described by reference, sex and cohort counts given; no table of race, income or education by sex or cohort, and 'treatment' is not defined.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Analysed numbers differ between Table 1 and the figures and Table 2 (38,812 vs 38,309 drinkers; 7,752 vs 8,564 with dependence), and the handling of missing ages is not described.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-IV alcohol dependence from the AUDADIS-IV, with cited reliability; but the measures analysed are onset ages recalled at one interview, up to decades later, whose reliability is not reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same instrument and diagnostic rules in both surveys and for all respondents.

Weighted survival analysis with censoring is appropriate for onset data, but hazards among everyone at risk combine the chance of the event with its speed; age, cohort and survey are near-collinear and the age adjustment is described inconsistently; income and education measured at interview are adjusted for; the three-way interaction coefficients are not shown; no correction for many tests.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Response rates 90% (NLAES) and 81% (NESARC), with weights adjusting for the designs.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is moderate risk. The descriptive numbers (ages at first drink by sex and cohort; who ever became dependent or entered treatment) come from large probability samples with good response and a standard interview. The analytic conclusions about telescoping are weaker than the data handling: every timing is recalled; the main estimand (hazard among all at risk) is not the quantity telescoping refers to (speed among those who reach the landmark); the youngest cohort is observed only to age 27; and several table and text values disagree. The paper may be cited for the absence of the full telescoping pattern in two US general-population surveys of US-born adults aged 18–57 interviewed in 1991–1992 and 2001–2002, for women's later first drink and its narrowing across cohorts, and for men's higher hazards of dependence and treatment; it should not be cited as showing that men progress faster from first drink to dependence among people who become dependent, and its treatment figures should be cited with the inconsistencies noted.

key_findings.finding: Pooled sample of 53,238 US-born adults aged 18–57 from NLAES (1991–1992, response 90%) and NESARC (2001–2002, response 81%): cohort 1 (born 1974–1983) 5,845, cohort 2 (1964–1973) 13,555, cohort 3 (1954–1963) 16,329, cohort 4 (1944–1953) 12,906, cohort 5 (1934–1943) 4,603. A general-population sample; timing of every landmark was recalled at one interview.
key_findings.locator: Method › Sources of Data, 1st–4th paragraphs; Method › Measures

key_findings.finding: Mean age at first drink, men vs women (Table 1): overall 17.8 (SE 0.03) vs 19.0 (SE 0.04) years; cohort 1 17.1 vs 17.5; cohort 2 17.2 vs 17.7; cohort 3 17.5 vs 18.5; cohort 4 18.4 vs 20.5; cohort 5 19.1 vs 22.1. Women were older at first drink in every cohort (t from −2.80, p=0.007, in cohort 1 to −19.58, p<0.001, in cohort 4); the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in the oldest to 0.4 years in the youngest cohort (editors' subtraction).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Alcohol use initiation

key_findings.finding: Hazard of a first drink, men vs women (Cox, Table 2): cohort 5 2.19 (95% CI 2.01–2.39), cohort 4 2.01 (1.91–2.12), cohort 3 1.62 (1.55–1.70), cohort 2 1.50 (1.43–1.57), cohort 1 1.50 (1.37–1.64); cohort-by-gender interaction F=16.7, df=4, p<0.01, read by the authors as a narrowing gender gap; three-way interaction with time F=0.10, df=6, p=0.84.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnote b; Results › Multivariate Results: Two-Way Interaction of Gender and Birth Cohort on Event Hazard

key_findings.finding: Mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent, men vs women (Table 1): overall 5.8 (SE 0.12) vs 5.6 (SE 0.15) years, ratio 1.04, not significant; cohort 1 2.8 vs 3.1; cohort 2 4.2 vs 3.7 (women shorter, t=2.36, p=0.02); cohort 3 6.4 vs 5.5 (not marked significant); cohort 4 7.9 vs 8.6; cohort 5 10.4 vs 11.8.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from initiation to dependence onset
key_findings.note: These conditional means are the closest analogue to the treatment-sample measure of telescoping; the authors set them aside because mean durations depend on age at interview.

key_findings.finding: Time from first drink to dependence among all 38,309 lifetime drinkers: survival curves fell faster for men in every cohort (log-rank 46.7, 69.6, 110.8, 181.8 and 36.3 for cohorts 1–5, all p<0.01); Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, 1.56 (1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for cohorts 1–5. The authors read this as men becoming dependent at a faster rate, contrary to telescoping.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Gender difference (Figure 2); Table 2
key_findings.note: A hazard among all drinkers mixes the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of progression; see the interpretation gap.

key_findings.finding: Three-way interaction of cohort, gender and time for time from first drink to dependence: F=54.08 (Table 2: 54.1), df=6, p<0.01; its direction is 'data not shown' and is described as men having a shorter time to dependence than women, and than men in earlier cohorts, in more recent cohorts. Three-way interactions were not significant for first drink or for time to treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariate Results: Three-Way Interaction of Gender, Birth Cohort, and Time to Event on Event Hazard; Table 2 footnote c

key_findings.finding: Time from dependence to first treatment among people with dependence (N=8,564): men had a shorter time in cohorts 2, 3 and 4 (log-rank 15.1, 19.5 and 7.0, p<0.01), no difference in cohorts 1 and 5; Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1.38 (0.84–2.26) for cohorts 1–5; no cohort-by-gender (F=0.92, p=0.46) or three-way (F=0.02, p=0.98) interaction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Gender difference (Figure 3); Table 2 and footnote d

key_findings.finding: Mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated after dependence onset, men vs women (Table 1): overall 7.0 (SE 0.28) vs 6.1 (SE 0.37) years, ratio 1.15, p<0.05 (women shorter); cohort 5 23.5 vs 19.4 years (t=3.2, p=0.002); no significant difference in cohorts 1–4.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from dependence onset to first treatment utilization
key_findings.note: The overall means cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows (reporting issue 2); cite the cohort-5 comparison rather than the overall one.

key_findings.finding: Main effects in the Cox models: men had a higher hazard of first drink (F=1,536.9), of dependence among drinkers (F=223.2) and of treatment among people with dependence (F=22.7), each df=1, p<0.001; later cohorts had higher hazards of first drink (F=82.95, df=4) and of dependence among drinkers (F=227.7, df=4), with no cohort effect on treatment. In life tables, each successively younger cohort progressed faster from first drink to dependence (pairwise p<0.01 in both sexes), while the youngest cohort was later to first drink than cohort 2 (log-rank 37.7 in men; the results in women are described as analogous).
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariate Results: Effect of Birth Cohort and Gender › Gender difference and Cohort effect; Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Cohort effect

key_findings.finding: 24.6% of people with alcohol dependence in these data had ever used any type of alcohol treatment; the authors say this left too little power to detect small cohort differences in treatment.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 counts give 3,056 treated after onset of 8,564 with dependence, about 36% unweighted (editors' arithmetic); the 24.6% may be weighted, which the paper does not say.

key_findings.finding: Recall check: within each birth cohort, the prevalence of dependence beginning at age 25 or later did not differ between respondents interviewed in NLAES and those interviewed 10 years later in NESARC, which the authors take as evidence of limited recall bias; post hoc analyses run separately by survey were described as similar in direction and size.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest, as a possibility, that the narrowing gender gap in the overall hazard of dependence reflects protective social factors (for example, social sanctions on women's drinking) that weakened as gender norms shifted; they cite research consistent with changing norms (greater acceptability of women drinking, advertising exposure among adolescent women, cross-national surveys) and state that they know of no formal test of this possibility. They recommend more screening of younger women for alcohol use disorders and further study of the apparent faster progression to dependence in younger men.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 7th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 2,634 cohort-1 men in the age-at-first-drink column, more than the 2,553 cohort-1 men in the sample; the column sums agree with the totals, so one of the two cohort-1 figures must be wrong (the corresponding share for cohort-1 women, 1,667 of 3,292, is also out of line with the other cohorts).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1, cohort 1 rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of drinkers in the youngest cohort cannot be taken from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the total-sample mean times from dependence to first treatment (men 7.0, women 6.1 years) cannot be averages of its cohort rows: cohorts 3–5 hold 1,491 of the 2,088 treated men and have means of 14.8–23.5 years, and the printed numbers give about 14.8 years for men and 13.2 for women (editors' arithmetic; survey weights could not plausibly bring this down to 7.0). The total row's ratio (1.15) matches its own means.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1, time from dependence to treatment column
reporting_issues.consequence: The overall finding that women reached treatment sooner (6.1 vs 7.0 years, p<0.05) should not be cited until the discrepancy is resolved; the cohort-specific rows are internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Analysed numbers differ without explanation: the Table 1 counts of drinkers sum to 38,812, against 38,309 lifetime drinkers in Figure 2 and Table 2; Table 1 lists 7,752 people with a time from first drink to dependence, against 8,564 people with dependence (after excluding 258) in Figure 3 and Table 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1; Figure 2 and 3 titles; Table 2 column heads
reporting_issues.consequence: Missing data on onset ages, and how they were handled, are not described; the denominators of the conditional means and of the survival analyses are not the same people.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance markers in Table 1 disagree with the text: for age at first drink in cohort 1 the text gives t=−2.80, p=0.007, while Table 1 marks p<0.001; for time to treatment in cohort 5 the text gives t=3.2, p=0.002, while Table 1 marks p<0.001. The cohort-3 difference in time to dependence (6.4 vs 5.5 years, SEs 0.21 and 0.31) is not marked although the printed means and SEs give t of about 2.4 (editors' approximation ignoring within-design covariance; the same approximation gives 2.2 for cohort 2, where the paper reports 2.36).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1 footnotes c and d; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort
reporting_issues.consequence: Small, but the cohort-3 point bears on telescoping: by the printed numbers women who became dependent may also have done so faster in cohort 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The cohort-by-gender interaction for time from first drink to dependence is given as F=2.8 (text) and F=2.83 (Figure 2 legend), p=0.03, but as F=2.51, p=0.04 in the Table 2 footnote.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Results › Multivariate Results: Two-Way Interaction; Figure 2 legend; Table 2 footnote c
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the interaction is significant in all versions.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the men-to-women hazard ratio for a first drink in cohort 4 as 2.10; Table 2 gives 2.01 (1.91–2.12).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Results › Multivariate Results: Two-Way Interaction, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Transposed digits; use the table value.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say age was evaluated as a confounder but not kept in the final models; the Results and the Table 2 footnote say the models controlled for age.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Method › Statistical Analysis, 5th paragraph; Results › Multivariate Results; Table 2 footnote a
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which model produced the hazard ratios; with age, cohort and survey near-collinear, the choice matters for the cohort estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The three-way interaction tests are given 6 degrees of freedom, which does not match a five-level cohort by two-level gender by time term (4 df if time is continuous); how time entered the interaction is not described, and the coefficients are not shown.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 2 footnotes b–d; Method › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's claim that men progress faster especially in younger cohorts cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that, on mean times as well as survival curves, women had neither a shorter time to dependence nor a shorter time to first treatment, but Table 1 shows significantly shorter mean times in women to dependence in cohort 2 and to treatment overall and in cohort 5.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary in the Discussion is stronger than the table; the evidence against telescoping rests on the hazard analyses, not on the conditional means.

design_detail: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (no meta-analysis), reported as guided by PRISMA, of general-population prospective cohort studies in which the age of first drink (AFD; more than a few sips) was measured in adolescence at least 3 years before alcohol outcomes at 18 or older. Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice were searched from inception to 10 January 2013, with citation searching and expert contact. Five reports from four cohorts (two US, two Norwegian; n 447 to 1311) were included; risk of bias and confounding were appraised narratively.
can_establish: What the prospective general-population cohort literature up to January 2013 showed about whether an earlier first drink, measured in adolescence, goes with adult drinking and alcohol problems, and how the reported associations changed with adjustment for confounders.
cannot_establish: Whether delaying the first drink would reduce adult alcohol problems (every included study is observational and none controls for unmeasured familial factors); a pooled size of any association (no meta-analysis); anything about drugs other than alcohol or about countries outside the USA and Norway; or the effects of first intoxication or of early regular drinking, which were excluded as exposures.

sample.recruitment: Database search of Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice from inception to 10 January 2013, without language or date restrictions but limited to peer-reviewed studies; backward searching of reference lists and forward citation searching of included studies; 20 experts on young people's drinking contacted; the references of a related review (McCambridge, McAlaney & Rowe, 2011) screened (Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Box 1 gives the PsycInfo strategy). The included cohorts were school-based (Oslo; Seattle; a national Norwegian school cohort) or community-based (Rutgers Health and Human Development Project, USA) (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: general-population cohort studies; AFD defined as a first drink of more than a few sips (studies measuring only first intoxication or the start of regular drinking were excluded); AFD measured in adolescence with at least 3 years between the initial AFD measurement and the outcome; outcomes at 18 or older (consumption, DSM- or ICD-defined dependence or non-dependent problems, or other harmful use such as fights while drinking); a reported magnitude of association; peer-reviewed. Excluded: special populations such as children of alcoholics; cross-sectional and case-control studies, because of recall and reporting bias in retrospective AFD (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Included cohorts (Table 1): Pedersen & Skrondal 1998, Oslo school cohort, n=522, follow-up 89%, AFD charted at five waves from 12–15 to 18–21, outcomes at 18–21; Warner & White 2003, Rutgers project, n=447, 83%, AFD at 12, 15 and 18, outcomes to 30–31; Guttmannova et al. 2011, Seattle Social Development Project, n=808, 92%, AFD in four bands up to 18–20, outcomes every three years from 21 to 33; Guttmannova et al. 2012, same cohort, subset of 706, AFD before 11 or not; Rossow & Kuntsche 2013, Young in Norway, n=1311, 82.4%, any drinking by 13–14, one outcome wave at 26–27. Sex and other participant characteristics are not tabulated. No study came from a low- or middle-income country or a Mediterranean culture (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Follow-up in the included cohorts was 82.4% to 100% (Table 1); the Warner & White sample was restricted to people who provided data at every wave, and the 100% given for the Seattle 2012 report describes an analytic subset (706 of the cohort's 808 in the 2011 report).
sample.selection_effects: Only five reports from four cohorts met the criteria, three of them (2011 to 2013) published within the 3 years before the review. Abstract screening was done by one author; grey literature was excluded by the peer-review restriction; the authors judge publication bias a 'profound threat' and note that no birth cohort had reported on this question (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Two of the five reports share one cohort, so the evidence is four cohorts, not five studies.

exposure.measurement: Age of first drink of more than a few sips, self-reported prospectively in adolescence, with study-specific definitions: half a bottle of beer, 100 mL of wine or 25 mL of spirits, used as a continuous variable (Pedersen & Skrondal); a first drink before 11, separately at a family gathering or elsewhere (Warner & White); four bands, under 11, 11–14, 15–17 and 18–20, with 11–14 as reference (Guttmannova 2011), and before 11 or not (Guttmannova 2012); any drinking by 13–14, from questions about the most recent drinking occasion (Rossow & Kuntsche) (Results, 2nd to 6th paragraphs; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: the exposure is the age of the first drink, not amount or frequency.
exposure.polysubstance: Only the Seattle analyses adjusted for adolescent use of other substances (tobacco, marijuana and other illicit drugs in 2011; tobacco, marijuana and heavy episodic drinking in one 2012 model); the other studies did not (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Within each cohort, people who started drinking later: continuous AFD (Pedersen & Skrondal); first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering (Warner & White); first drink at 11–14 (Guttmannova 2011); first drink at 11 or older (Guttmannova 2012); no drinking by 13–14 (Rossow & Kuntsche).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjustment sets differ widely (Table 1): parental and peer norms and use (Pedersen & Skrondal); gender, religion, parental status, features of the first drinking episode, family history of alcoholism, family and friends' drinking, parental relationship, delinquency, school performance and psychiatric symptoms (Warner & White); gender, ethnicity, childhood poverty and adolescent substance use (Guttmannova 2011), plus parental drinking, family factors and four sets of mediators (2012); gender and conduct problems (Rossow & Kuntsche).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review assessed control for socioeconomic status, family history of alcohol problems, mental health and early behaviour problems (Methods, 5th paragraph); only Warner & White adjusted for family history and psychiatric symptoms. No included study used a twin, sibling or adoption design, so familial and genetic liability was not controlled. The authors also raise overadjustment, for example peer variables that may lie on the causal path (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: As used by the primary studies (Table 1): past-month consumption and the Rutgers Alcohol Problem Index (Pedersen & Skrondal); lifetime problem drinking, abuse or dependence (Warner & White); past-year alcohol misuse and DSM-IV dependence at each wave, and the number of waves with a diagnosis (chronicity) (Guttmannova 2011, 2012); intoxication 10 or more times in the past year and an AUDIT score of 8 or more (Rossow & Kuntsche).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review judges outcome measurement reliable and generally validated (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); no formal appraisal tool was used.
outcomes.operationalization: An adult alcohol outcome was any of the measures above at 18 or older; associations were taken as reported (odds ratios, regression or structural-equation coefficients) without conversion to a common metric.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the narrative synthesis; 10 counts the outcome measures across the five reports in Table 1, several of them examined in more than one model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Abstracts were screened by the first author alone; selected full texts were reviewed independently by both authors; data were extracted with a dedicated form, but who extracted them, and whether in duplicate, is not stated (Methods, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate: meta-analysis was judged inappropriate because of heterogeneous methods and outcomes. Study results as reported (Table 1; Results): Pedersen & Skrondal, structural coefficients of -3.465 for alcohol debut age on consumption and -13.828 on the problem index (both p<0.0001), described as roughly a 35% reduction in consumption for a 10% delay in debut, with weak control of confounding. Warner & White, a first drink before 11 at a family gathering OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10 to 5.20) and elsewhere OR 5.75 (1.53 to 21.54), both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 31, in a model adjusting for features of the first drink, gender, socioeconomic status and religion; in the fully adjusted model AFD was not significant (coefficient -0.0631, p>0.05), while feeling drunk at the first drink was (0.3848, p<0.0001). Guttmannova 2011, no association of AFD with alcohol misuse (ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64 against 11–14, all p>0.05) or with dependence at any follow-up (1.49, 1.16 and 0.35, all p>0.05), but a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the follow-up interviews (OR 1.68, p<0.05); starting regular drinking at 15–17 was consistently associated with misuse and dependence. Guttmannova 2012, early AFD and chronicity of dependence, β=0.44 (p<0.05) unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models. Rossow & Kuntsche, drinking by 13–14 and frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2 to 1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more OR 1.6 (1.3 to 2.1), adjusted for gender; after adding adolescent conduct problems, 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) for both.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; each study's adjustment set is listed in Table 1.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The review states it is guided by PRISMA; no protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Every included report's main results are summarized, including null ones. Several primary estimates are given without confidence intervals (all Seattle odds ratios and coefficients carry p-values only), and one Seattle cell (AFD 18–20, chronicity of dependence) gives a p-value without an estimate (Table 1).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Five reports of 447 to 1311 participants, with the main exposure contrasts often small subgroups (for example a first drink before 11).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Four cohorts in the USA and Norway. An earlier first drink went with adult drinking or problems in some analyses (Pedersen & Skrondal, with weak confounder control; Warner & White before full adjustment; Rossow & Kuntsche adjusted for gender only; chronicity of dependence in the Seattle cohort, which did not change across four adjusted models in the 2012 report) and not in others (misuse and any dependence in the Seattle cohort; Warner & White and Rossow & Kuntsche after broader adjustment or adjustment for conduct problems). Feeling drunk at the first drink and early regular drinking had larger associations than the age of the first drink.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that rigorous control for confounding 'markedly attenuates or eliminates any observed effects' and concludes that there is no strong evidence that starting earlier leads to adult problems, so that policy makers should reconsider delaying initiation as a strategy against adult problems. Gaps: (1) the generalization does not hold for the Seattle 2012 report, whose association with chronicity of dependence was unchanged by adjustment (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted), and the Discussion itself notes that this report rejected a marker explanation, yet its last paragraph lists it among the studies supporting the absence of an effect; (2) a lack of strong evidence from four small cohorts, which the authors fear are distorted by publication bias, is turned into a policy recommendation that reads as evidence of no effect, while the review's own final sentence says we do not yet know; (3) the Discussion's caution that adjustment for peer variables may be overadjustment, which would make attenuation after adjustment weaker evidence of confounding, does not reach the abstract. The review is otherwise explicit about how small and uncertain the evidence base is.

timeline.event: Grant & Dawson, NLAES: the cross-sectional association between age at onset of alcohol use and DSM-IV abuse and dependence, with ages recalled in adulthood (cited by this review among the mostly cross-sectional studies behind US and UK guidance).
Prescott & Kendler, twin study: age at first drink and alcoholism, described in its title as a non-causal association (cited for the marker hypothesis).

King & Chassin, prospective study of children of alcoholics (excluded as a special population): earlier first drink unrelated to alcohol dependence after confounders were taken into account (as summarized in the Discussion).

Two NESARC analyses (Hingson et al., 2006; Dawson et al., 2008), excluded because AFD was recalled in adulthood, both found small associations of AFD with adult outcomes (as summarized in the Discussion).
This review (online November 2013): five reports from four cohorts, mixed results.

Irons, Iacono & McGue, Minnesota twin cohort (read in this round): drinking by 14 associated with the adult alcohol-use index within exposure-discordant twin pairs, including MZ pairs, attenuated but not eliminated relative to propensity-weighted estimates; no significant within-MZ-pair association with alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms.

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of prospective cohorts on this question named in the round's reading list, and for alcohol only. Its core message, that prospective general-population evidence was sparse and mixed in 2013, stands; its abstract overstates how consistently adjustment removes the association. Later co-twin evidence (Irons et al., 2015) found associations of early drinking with adult alcohol use that survived control for shared familial factors, so the question remains open, as the review's own last sentence says. No later systematic review was searched here.

funding.funder: The work of the second author was supported by a Wellcome Trust Research Career Development Fellowship in Basic Biomedical Science (WT086516MA) (Footnotes, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none. Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed.
funding.affiliations_note: The second author wrote the related review whose references were screened and which informed the design (McCambridge, McAlaney & Rowe, 2011), and the papers on publication bias cited to support the publication-bias concern (refs 25 and 26); none of the five included studies is by the review authors.

what_would_settle_it: Individual-participant analyses of several large birth or school cohorts, with the first drink recorded as it happens, harmonized adult DSM or ICD outcomes and the same confounder set, combined with designs that control familial liability (MZ twins or siblings discordant for early drinking) and with natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person (for example changes in minimum legal drinking ages).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (no protocol; no list of excluded studies; a search limited to peer-reviewed publications without justification, under the project's strict reading of item 4), which gives critically low confidence by the AMSTAR 2 rule even without item 4. Single-reviewer abstract screening and unverified extraction add to the risk that eligible reports were missed in a field of five. The review is nonetheless careful about the limits of its evidence, restricts itself to the right design for the question, and states that the answer is unknown. Cite it for the scarcity and mixed direction of prospective general-population evidence up to January 2013 (alcohol only) and as a pointer to the five reports; do not cite its abstract's statement that adjustment eliminates the association, which one of its own included reports contradicts.

key_findings.finding: Only five reports met the criteria: three from two US cohorts and two from two Norwegian cohorts, with samples of 447 to 1311, all school- or community-based; three of them (2011 to 2013) were published within the 3 years before the review.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Search: Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice from inception to 10 January 2013, no language or date limits, peer-reviewed studies only, with backward and forward citation searching, 20 experts contacted and a related review's references screened; abstracts screened by the first author, full texts independently by both authors.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Box 1

key_findings.finding: Oslo cohort (n=522): later alcohol debut was strongly associated with lower consumption and fewer problems at 18–21 (structural coefficients -3.465 and -13.828, p<0.0001), estimated as about a 35% reduction in consumption for a 10% delay, after control for parental and peer influences only; the original authors expected stricter control to weaken it.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Rutgers cohort (n=447, completers only): a first drink before 11 went with lifetime problem drinking by 31 (at a family gathering OR 2.39, 95% CI 1.10 to 5.20; elsewhere OR 5.75, 1.53 to 21.54; both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering) after adjustment for features of the first drink, gender, socioeconomic status and religion, but not after adjustment for further risk factors (coefficient -0.0631, p>0.05); feeling drunk at the first drink remained a strong predictor (0.3848, p<0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Seattle cohort, 2011 report (n=808 who started before 21): AFD was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with any dependence to 33 (against a first drink at 11–14, for a first drink before 11, at 15–17 and at 18–20: misuse at any follow-up OR 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64; dependence at any follow-up 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35; chronicity of misuse 1.20, 1.13 and 0.77; all p>0.05), but a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the follow-up interviews (every 3 years from 21 to 33) than a first drink at 11–14 (OR 1.68, p<0.05); starting regular drinking at 15–17 was consistently associated with misuse and dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1, Guttmannova et al 2011 row
key_findings.note: No confidence intervals are given for the Seattle estimates.

key_findings.finding: Seattle cohort, 2012 report (subset of 706): a first drink before 11 was associated with chronicity of dependence (β=0.44, p<0.05), and the association was essentially unchanged in four models adding peer, school, behavioural and substance-use factors (β 0.45 to 0.53); none of the three explanations tested (confounding by other risk factors, developmental impairment, more adolescent substance use) was supported.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Young in Norway cohort (n=1311): drinking by 13–14 went with frequent intoxication (OR 1.5, 1.2 to 1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more (OR 1.6, 1.3 to 2.1) at 26–27 when adjusted for gender, and both fell to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) after adjustment for adolescent conduct problems.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Follow-up exceeded 80% in every included study; the authors consider selection in sample construction, not attrition, the larger threat to generalizability.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The authors judge publication bias a profound threat to any inference, noting that no birth-cohort study had reported on the question, and that the evidence comes only from high-income countries without a Mediterranean drinking culture.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Excluded studies pointing the same way: a prospective study of children of alcoholics found earlier AFD unrelated to dependence after adjustment, and two NESARC analyses with recalled AFD found small associations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Feeling drunk at the first drinking episode and the start of regular drinking showed larger associations with adult problems than the age of the first drink itself.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the sensible position is that it is not yet known whether starting to drink earlier leads to adult alcohol problems, and that prevention should be justified by the acute harms of drinking in young people.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The last paragraph of the Discussion lists the second Seattle report (Guttmannova et al., 2012) among the studies supporting the absence of an effect of AFD, but the review's own summary of that report says the association with chronicity of dependence was unchanged across four adjusted models and that none of the explanations tested, including confounding, was supported, and the Discussion's 7th paragraph says the report rejected a marker hypothesis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 10th paragraph; Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The tally of supporting and non-supporting studies is misstated: on the review's own summaries, two of the four cohorts show an association that survived the adjustment made (Seattle chronicity; Oslo, under weak control) and two do not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's Results state that rigorous control for confounding markedly attenuates or eliminates any observed effects, which is contradicted by the Seattle 2012 report (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted) summarized in the same review.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Results); Results, 5th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's generalization should not be cited; attenuation after adjustment was seen in two of the four cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: The criteria require AFD measured in adolescence, with at least 3 years between the initial adolescent AFD measurement and the adult outcome, but the Seattle 2011 report's exposure bands include a first drink at 18–20 with outcomes measured from 21, Table 1 lists AFD collection in that cohort up to 27 (up to 24 in the 2012 report) overlapping the outcome waves, and the Oslo cohort charted AFD up to the outcome wave (18–21).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The 3-year rule applies to the first wave of AFD measurement, not to each person's first drink; for late starters in two of the four cohorts the first drink was neither adolescent nor 3 years before the outcome, which weakens the protection against recall and reverse timing that the review claims for its design.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives a follow-up rate of 100% for the Seattle 2012 report, which analysed a subset of 706 from a cohort reported as 808 in the 2011 report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 100% describes an analytic subset rather than retention; about 13% of the earlier analytic sample is not in it (editors' arithmetic). It does not change the review's conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract counts 'five studies', but two of the five reports come from the same Seattle cohort.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base is four independent cohorts; claims should say so.
