design_detail: Secondary analysis of the two waves of NESARC, a US nationally representative household survey (Wave 1 2001–2002, n=43,093; Wave 2 2004–2005, n=34,653 re-interviewed). Past-12-month DSM-IV alcohol dependence (AD; AUDADIS-IV) at Wave 2 was split by Wave 1 status into new onset (no lifetime AD at Wave 1), persistence (past-12-month AD at Wave 1) and recurrence (lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1). The share of each in Wave 2 prevalence, and the rate of each among the people at risk, were estimated by age group (seven groups) with weighted logistic regressions adjusted for sex and race. A second set of weighted logistic regressions related three life transitions between the waves (becoming a parent, change in marital status, change in employment) to each transition, with two- and three-way interactions with age (21–37 vs 38+) and sex.
can_establish: How past-year alcohol dependence among US adults in 2001–2005 was made up of new, persistent and recurrent cases at each age, how often each transition happened over about three years among the people at risk, and whether life transitions between the interviews went with these transitions after adjustment for sex, race and age group.
cannot_establish: Whether life transitions cause changes in alcohol dependence (they were measured over the same interval as the outcome, people select into roles, and few confounders were adjusted); whether the age gradient reflects ageing rather than birth cohort (different age groups were followed over one three-year window); what happened to people who died or were not re-interviewed; whether 'offset' means lasting recovery (anyone below the full three-criterion threshold in the year before Wave 2 counted as offset); or what part treatment played (treatment between the waves is not reported).

sample.recruitment: General population, not a treatment sample: NESARC, funded by NIAAA and conducted by the US Census Bureau, a weighted representative sample of US civilians aged 18 and over, with Black and Hispanic people and young adults aged 18–24 oversampled; face-to-face interviews at both waves (Method › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All Wave 2 respondents enter the age decomposition: the six groups of Table 2 sum to 34,653 (editors' arithmetic), so the population at risk of new onset includes people who had never drunk alcohol. The life-transition models drop people with missing transition data (Table 3, note; footnote 5) and use two age groups, 21–37 and 38+ (Results › Role Transitions…, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Wave 2 (weighted): mean age 48 (SE 0.17); 52% women; 71% White non-Hispanic, 11% African American, 12% Hispanic, 4% Asian, 2% American Indian (Method › Participants). The groups with past or present AD were 65–72% men against 44.7% in the consistent non-diagnosis group, and their mean age at Wave 1 ranged from 30.4 (offset) to 41.8 (non-recurrent) against 46.4 in the consistent non-diagnosis group (Table 2).
sample.attrition: 34,653 of 43,093 Wave 1 respondents were re-interviewed (80.4%, editors' arithmetic; approximately 80% according to the Limitations). Retention was higher in women (82.7% vs 80.2% in men), at ages 30–59 than at 18–20 (79.0%), and in people with prior-to-past-year AD (85.6% vs 81.2% with no diagnosis); it was lower in Black (79.2%), Asian (73.3%) and Hispanic (73.4%) than in White respondents (83.6%), and among age groups lowest at 21–24 (76.4%) and 60 and over (76.9%) (Table 1). Wave 2 weights adjust for attrition and Wave 1 lifetime psychiatric disorders, and all analyses were repeated with multiple imputation (Method › Analysis; Results, 1st paragraph). The life-transition models lost a further 10–15% of each at-risk group to missing transition data (Table 3 against Table 2, editors' arithmetic).
sample.selection_effects: A general-population household sample re-interviewed after about three years. Age comparisons are between birth cohorts followed over the same three-year window, so age is confounded with cohort and period, which the authors set aside explicitly together with differential mortality (Introduction › The Relative Importance of Onset, Recurrence, and Persistence on Maturing Out, 1st paragraph). People who died between the waves are not in the Wave 2 sample; if mortality is higher among people with persistent AD, persistent cases would be lost preferentially at older ages (editors' inference; the paper does not examine it). The at-risk groups are defined from lifetime histories recalled at Wave 1, so forgotten earlier episodes move people from 'recurrence' into 'new onset'.

exposure.measurement: Age group: Wave 1 age plus three years, an approximation of age at Wave 2 because the interval between interviews varied; seven groups for the decomposition (the text names 21–23, 24–27, 28–32, 43–52 and 63+; the full set is printed only in the figures) and two groups (21–37, 38+) for the life-transition models. Life transitions between the waves, by self-report: becoming a parent (any own, adopted, foster or step children since the last interview); change in marital status (became married, including starting to live with someone as if married; stable; separated, divorced or widowed); change in employment (unemployed or retired at Wave 1 and employed at Wave 2; employed at Wave 1 and unemployed or retired at Wave 2; stable), coded from the two waves (Method › Measures › Life Transitions; footnotes 2–4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the exposures. Alcohol consumption and heavy drinking were not analysed (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph); age at first drinking ('not counting small tastes or sips') was used only to describe the groups (Method › Measures › Other variables).
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or adjusted in this analysis: no variable for tobacco, other drug use or drug use disorders enters any model.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (household survey of alcohol-dependence status).

comparison.controls: For each transition, the people at risk who did not make it: offset (past-12-month AD at Wave 1, none at Wave 2) against persistence; non-recurrence (lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1, none at Wave 2) against recurrence; consistent non-diagnosis (no lifetime AD at Wave 1, none at Wave 2) against new onset (Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 1st paragraph). For the life transitions the references were not becoming a parent, stable marital status (married, single or divorced at both waves) and stable employment (employed or unemployed at both waves).
comparison.matching: None. The age-group models adjust for sex and race (White against all other groups); the life-transition models contain sex, race, age group, the three transitions, and their two- and three-way interactions with age and sex (Table 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Traits related to negative emotionality and impulsivity (named by the authors as unavailable in the data set), drinking level and heavy drinking, family history of alcohol problems, other psychiatric and substance use disorders, education and income, treatment for alcohol problems between the waves, and the timing of each transition within the interval.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV, the NESARC interview, scoring DSM-IV alcohol dependence (at least 3 of 7 criteria) for the past 12 months and for the period before it; prior-to-past-year dependence required the criteria to cluster within the same year (Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 1st paragraph). Reliability is supported by citation (Grant et al., 1995; Grant et al., 2003).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability is cited, not re-examined here. The authors note that lifetime diagnoses have poor test–retest reliability (Discussion › Rethinking…, 2nd paragraph), and lifetime status at Wave 1 is what separates new onset from recurrence.
outcomes.operationalization: New onset: past-12-month AD at Wave 2 with no lifetime AD at Wave 1. Persistence: past-12-month AD at both waves; this includes episodic courses with a remission between the interviews that did not reach the year before Wave 2. Recurrence: past-12-month AD at Wave 2 after lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1. Offset, the complement of persistence and the closest this paper comes to 'maturing out' or remission: past-12-month AD at Wave 1 and not meeting full criteria in the 12 months before Wave 2, about three years later, which can include people with one or two remaining symptoms. Rates were computed among the people at risk and shares as fractions of all Wave 2 cases (Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). Whether anyone had treatment is not reported. Sensitivity analyses redefined persistence as AD at Wave 1 plus at least one dependence symptom at Wave 2, or as continuous diagnosis across the interval, and recurrence as no dependence symptom in the year before Wave 1 (Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three transition outcomes, each tested across seven age groups (three Wald tests) and in a life-transition model of 22 odds ratios (66 in Table 3), plus sensitivity analyses, all judged at p<0.05 without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: face-to-face survey interviews with the AUDADIS-IV for the US Census Bureau; whether Wave 2 interviewers knew Wave 1 answers is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Shares of Wave 2 past-12-month AD (Figure 1, given in the text only for the youngest and oldest groups): persistence 29% at ages 21–23 and 27% at 63+; new onset 66% and 58%; recurrence 5% and 15%. Rates among the people at risk (Figure 2), age-group differences adjusted for sex and race: new onset Wald F=44.22, 6 df, p<.0001, and recurrence Wald F=6.64, 6 df, p<.0001, both falling with age; persistence Wald F=2.28, 6 df, p=.047, rising with age, not significant with multiple imputation. Persistence over the interval: 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at 43–52 (Discussion); the other age-specific rates and all prevalences are printed only in Figures 1 and 2 (images, not extracted). Editors' calculation from the unweighted counts of Table 2, all ages: 422 of 1,172 people with past-12-month AD at Wave 1 (36%) met criteria again at Wave 2, so about 64% showed offset; 767 of 30,696 without lifetime AD (2.5%) had a new onset; 244 of 2,785 with earlier AD (8.8%) had a recurrence. Life-transition models (Table 3; odds ratios with 95% CIs; because the interactions are in the model, each main effect is the odds ratio in the reference groups, women aged 21–37): new onset, becoming a parent 0.39 (0.18–0.83), new job 2.79 (1.19–6.55), men vs women 1.87 (1.29–2.73), age 38+ vs 21–37 0.22 (0.14–0.34); persistence, becoming a parent 0.22 (0.06–0.82), sex × parenthood 4.56 (1.09–19.08), age × parenthood 9.56 (1.14–79.78), sex × age × parenthood 0.02 (0.00–0.28), sex × age × new job 0.03 (0.00–0.48); recurrence, no term significant (age 38+ 0.47, 0.22–1.01). Change in marital status was not significant in any model.
analysis.covariates: Age-group models: sex and race. Life-transition models: sex, race, age group, the three transitions and their interactions with age and sex. Not adjusted: drinking level, other substance use, psychiatric comorbidity, education, income, family history, treatment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of survey data; no protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 3 prints every term of the three models, and three alternative definitions are reported with their effect on the results. But several analyses are 'not shown' (the replication of Grant's 1997 persistence definition with Wave 1 data; the marital-status analysis in the whole sample), imputation results are mentioned only where they differ, and the age-specific prevalences and rates are printed only in figure images.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The authors state that subsamples become small when baseline diagnosis, age, sex and transition are crossed, and that they collapsed age into two groups and merged 'stable' categories for this reason (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph); the widest intervals in Table 3 (0.00–0.28; 1.14–79.78; 0.42–83.46; 0.55–204.78) show sparse cells.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a US general-population sample followed for about three years, the lower prevalence of past-year alcohol dependence at older ages went with steeply falling rates of new onset and of recurrence, while the persistent share of cases stayed near 27–29% and persistence rates were somewhat higher in middle age (44.5% at 43–52) than at 21–23 (32.4%), an age difference of borderline significance that disappeared with multiple imputation. Offset was common at every age. Becoming a parent went with lower odds, and getting a job with higher odds, of new onset in the reference group of women aged 21–37; the persistence findings rest on three-way interaction terms from sparse cells, one of which (new job) was not significant with multiple imputation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract speaks of the 'effects' of life transitions varying across the lifespan and between men and women. The Results call becoming a parent 'a protective factor against persistence' for older men (OR 0.02) and report a new job lowering persistence in older men (OR 0.03); the Discussion calls the onset associations 'consistent across gender and age'. Gaps: (1) 0.02 and 0.03 are the three-way interaction terms of Table 3, not odds ratios for older men; under the table's reference coding the implied odds ratios for men aged 38+ are about 0.2 and 0.1 (editors' arithmetic from rounded values; no interval can be computed); (2) 'consistent across gender and age' is inferred from non-significant interactions with wide intervals, which do not show that the associations are the same; (3) 'protective' and 'effects' are causal words, while the Limitations say the results should not be taken to imply a causal effect, because transitions were measured over the same interval and people select into roles; (4) the abstract reports that persistence increased with age without saying that the result was marginal (p=.047) and absent with imputation and with a continuous-diagnosis definition; (5) offset is called only a minor contributor to the age gradient from shares and rates by age, without a formal decomposition of the prevalence difference. The descriptive headline, that falling onset and recurrence rather than a peak of offset in the twenties drive the age gradient, follows from the results, subject to the cohort confounding the authors set aside; the overstatements are confined to the life-transition analysis.

timeline.event: Chilcoat & Breslau: members of a health maintenance organization aged 21–30 followed for 3.5 years; onset of DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence was higher in those stably single and persistence lower in those who married (as summarized in this paper's introduction). This paper found no association with change in marital status.

Grant, NLAES cross-sectional data: the youngest cohort had the highest past-year persistence among people with earlier dependence. This paper reproduced that result with Wave 1 NESARC data using Grant's retrospective definition (results not shown) and attributes the conflict with its own two-wave finding to the definition.
Crum et al., Baltimore Epidemiologic Catchment Area follow-up: incidence of DSM-III-R alcohol dependence over 12.6 years fell with age (as cited in this paper's discussion).

Dawson, Goldstein & Grant, NESARC Waves 1–2: 5.1% of people in full remission at Wave 1 had a recurrence by Wave 2, and age was negatively associated with recurrence (as cited in this paper's introduction).
Kalaydjian et al., NCS-R: remission from dependence was more frequent at younger ages (as cited), in the same direction as this paper's lower persistence at 21–23.
This study (online November 2011): decomposition of the age-prevalence curve of DSM-IV alcohol dependence in the two NESARC waves.

Related, same survey: Lopez-Quintero et al., NESARC Wave 1, probability of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine (a different question: cumulative transition from first use, not course after onset).

replication.where_it_stands: Within the paper, the decline of new onset with age agrees with earlier cross-sectional and longitudinal reports, while the age pattern of persistence depends on the definition: a retrospective definition reproduces Grant's (1997) falling persistence with age, the two-wave definition does not. No direct replication is named in the reading list for this round, and later NESARC analyses were not searched here. Claims may use the paper for the decomposition (new onset dominates the age gradient; offset is common at every age) and must present the life-transition results as associations from sparse subgroups.

funding.funder: NIH grants K05AA017242 and R01AA016392 to Kenneth J. Sher, and P60AA011998 to Andrew C. Heath (Acknowledgments). The survey itself is described as funded by the "National Institute of Alcoholism and Alcohol Abuse (NIAAA)" (so printed) and conducted by the US Census Bureau (Method › Participants).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the author manuscript on PMC.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Missouri, Brown University and Washington University School of Medicine, most also with the Midwest Alcoholism Research Center. The Discussion's interpretation (age-related loss of vulnerability linked to personality maturation) draws on the senior author's own earlier analyses (Littlefield, Sher & Wood, 2009, 2010a, 2010b; Cicero, Epler & Sher, 2009), which this paper's data cannot test because the survey has no personality measures.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort-sequential study with yearly interviews of several birth cohorts from adolescence into old age, recording DSM symptoms, drinking, treatment and deaths (by record linkage) at every wave, would separate ageing from cohort, count onsets and recurrences without relying on lifetime recall, and show whether offset is lasting remission; for life transitions, within-person analyses that date each transition relative to the change in symptoms.

domains.note: The life-transition models adjust only for sex, race and age group; drinking level, other psychiatric and substance use disorders, education, income and family history are not adjusted, and people with alcohol dependence may be less likely to marry or become parents (selection into roles, acknowledged by the authors). The age gradient in transition rates is confounded with birth cohort and period, which the authors set aside.

Transitions are self-reported, coarse and coded from two time points: 'stable' merges married, single and divorced people (and employed and unemployed people), becoming a parent includes step, foster and adoptive parenthood, and changes of employment within the interval are missed (the authors expect this to underestimate employment effects). Age at Wave 2 is approximated as Wave 1 age plus three years.

A representative household sample, but the analysis includes only people alive and re-interviewed at Wave 2; the Wave 1 response rate is not reported in this paper; the at-risk groups depend on lifetime histories recalled at Wave 1.
Treatment for alcohol problems between the waves is neither reported nor adjusted, so offset may partly reflect treatment, and treatment could itself follow some transitions.

About 20% of Wave 1 respondents were not re-interviewed, with differences by sex, age, race and AD history; weights and multiple imputation gave similar results except that the persistence age effect and the new-job interaction lost significance; a further 10–15% of each at-risk group lacked transition data.

Self-reported AUDADIS-IV diagnoses. Persistence, offset and recurrence depend on a fixed 12-month window and the three-criterion threshold (the sensitivity analyses changed which age and interaction effects were significant), and new onset versus recurrence depends on recall of lifetime episodes at Wave 1, which the authors say may differ by age.

All Table 3 terms are printed and the sensitivity analyses are described, but 66 odds ratios were tested without correction, the text emphasises the significant three-way interactions, several analyses are 'not shown', and imputation results are given only where they differ.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the associations of life transitions with the course of alcohol dependence the risk of bias is high: confounding is barely addressed, transitions and outcome were measured over the same interval, and the authors themselves rule out a causal reading. The descriptive decomposition (shares and rates of onset, persistence and recurrence by age) is not a causal estimate and is better protected by a representative sample, a standard interview and weighting for attrition; its main threats are cohort confounding of the age gradient, survivor-only follow-up, recall-based definitions of new onset and recurrence, and the 20% attrition. The paper may be cited for the descriptive picture (onset and recurrence fall steeply with age; offset is common at every age; about a third of cases persisted over three years in the early twenties and under half in middle age), always with the definition of offset, and not for effects of parenthood, employment or marriage.

key_findings.finding: NESARC Wave 1 (2001–2002) interviewed 43,093 US adults; 34,653 were re-interviewed at Wave 2 (2004–2005). Of the 1,433 with past-12-month DSM-IV alcohol dependence at Wave 2, 767 were new onsets (no lifetime AD at Wave 1), 422 persistent (past-12-month AD at Wave 1) and 244 recurrent (lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1).
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants; Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Among Wave 2 cases, the persistent share stayed about the same across age (29% at ages 21–23, 27% at 63+), the new-onset share fell (66% to 58%) and the recurrent share rose (5% to 15%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (Figure 1)
key_findings.note: Only the youngest and oldest groups are given in the text; the values for the other age groups and the age-specific prevalences are printed only in Figure 1 (image, not extracted).

key_findings.finding: Among the people at risk, and adjusted for sex and race, the rates of new onset (Wald F=44.22, 6 df, p<.0001) and recurrence (Wald F=6.64, 6 df, p<.0001) fell significantly with age, while persistence rose (Wald F=2.28, 6 df, p=.047), a result not significant in the multiple-imputation analyses. The authors conclude that most of the age decline in prevalence comes from less onset and recurrence.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (Figure 2)

key_findings.finding: Persistence of dependence over the roughly three-year interval was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52, and the authors describe the persistence rate as relatively stable through the third decade while prevalence falls steeply.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Persistence here means meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the 12 months before each interview; the remainder (offset) includes people with one or two remaining symptoms and is not a remission definition. Treatment between the waves is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the unweighted counts in Table 2, all ages together: 422 of 1,172 people with past-12-month AD at Wave 1 (36%) met criteria again at Wave 2, so about 64% showed offset; 767 of 30,696 people without lifetime AD at Wave 1 (2.5%) had past-year AD at Wave 2 (new onset); 244 of 2,785 people with earlier AD (8.8%) had past-year AD again at Wave 2 (recurrence).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, column sample sizes
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, unweighted and not age-standardised; the paper does not print weighted totals for the three rates. The new-onset denominator includes people who had never drunk alcohol. New onset and recurrence count only dependence in the 12 months before Wave 2 (the authors call their approach 'time-sampling'): dependence that began or recurred and then remitted earlier in the roughly three-year interval is not counted, so 2.5% and 8.8% are past-year statuses at follow-up among the people at risk, not three-year cumulative incidences, and they understate onsets and recurrences over the interval.

key_findings.finding: With persistence redefined as AD at Wave 1 plus at least one dependence symptom at Wave 2, persistence rose in every age group with a similar age pattern, but the drop at 63+ made the age effect significant; with persistence redefined as continuous diagnosis across the interval, persistence showed no significant change with age. A stricter definition of recurrence gave a similar age pattern. The interaction results changed with the definition: under the at-least-one-symptom definition only the sex × age × new-job interaction was significant, and under the continuous-diagnosis definition only the parenthood interaction remained.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for the sensitivity analyses.

key_findings.finding: New onset between the waves: becoming a parent went with lower odds (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18–0.83) and getting a new job with higher odds (OR 2.79, 1.19–6.55); men had higher odds than women (OR 1.87, 1.29–2.73) and people aged 38+ lower odds than those aged 21–37 (OR 0.22, 0.14–0.34). None of the interactions with age or sex was significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Onset column; Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Because interaction terms are in the model, these main effects are odds ratios in the reference groups (women aged 21–37, and for sex and age, people with no transitions), adjusted for race and the other terms. The sample is general-population; new onset was recorded prospectively across the waves, with the absence of earlier dependence taken from lifetime recall at Wave 1.

key_findings.finding: Persistence: becoming a parent went with lower odds of persistence in the reference group of women aged 21–37 (OR 0.22, 0.06–0.82), with significant sex × parenthood (4.56, 1.09–19.08), age × parenthood (9.56, 1.14–79.78) and sex × age × parenthood (0.02, 0.00–0.28) terms; the sex × age × new-job term was also significant (0.03, 0.00–0.48), but only the parenthood interaction remained significant with multiple imputation and with a continuous-diagnosis definition of persistence, while only the new-job interaction was significant with the at-least-one-symptom definition: neither survives every check. Sex was not associated with persistence (1.20, 0.67–2.15) or recurrence (1.00, 0.52–1.93), and no term was significant for recurrence.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Persistence and Recurrence columns; Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 3rd paragraph; Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The text presents 0.02 and 0.03 as odds ratios for older men; they are interaction terms (see reporting issues). The intervals reflect sparse cells in a persistence model of 993 people at risk.

key_findings.finding: Change in marital status (becoming married or becoming separated, divorced or widowed) was not associated with new onset, persistence or recurrence in any model.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Discussion › Life Transitions and the Course of AD, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The authors suggest the merged 'stable' reference group (married, single or divorced at both waves) may have hidden an association; a whole-sample analysis showing the expected marriage pattern is 'not shown'.

key_findings.finding: Mean age at first drinking was 19.9 years in the new-onset group, 16.7 to 17.3 in the four groups with dependence at Wave 1 (persistent, recurrent, offset and non-recurrent), and 21.7 in the consistent non-diagnosis group; 65–72% of the five groups with past or present dependence were men against 44.7% of the consistent non-diagnosis group.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows Age First Drinking and % Male
key_findings.note: Descriptive only: age at first drinking was recalled and did not enter any model.

key_findings.finding: Retention at Wave 2 was about 80% and differed by sex, age, race and AD history (for example 85.6% with prior-to-past-year AD vs 81.2% with no diagnosis; 73.3% Asian and 73.4% Hispanic vs 83.6% White respondents); analyses with multiple imputation were reported as similar.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that because life transitions were measured over the same interval as the changes in dependence and people can select into roles, the results should not be read as causal effects of the transitions.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors report that Grant's retrospective definition of persistence (past-year dependence among people with dependence before the past year) reproduces a decline of persistence with age in the Wave 1 data, unlike their two-wave definition, and argue that the retrospective definition gives younger people less time to desist.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The replication is 'not shown'.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results present 0.02 (0.00–0.28) as the odds ratio showing that becoming a parent protects older men against persistence, and 0.03 (0.00–0.48) as the odds ratio for a new job in older men. In Table 3 these are the sex × age × parenthood and sex × age × new-job interaction terms. Under the reference coding the table states (female, 21–37, not a parent, stable job), the implied odds ratios for men aged 38+ are the products of the main effect and the three relevant interaction terms: 0.22 × 4.56 × 9.56 × 0.02 ≈ 0.19 for parenthood and 0.84 × 2.14 × 1.90 × 0.03 ≈ 0.10 for a new job (editors' arithmetic; with the rounding of the printed terms, about 0.14 to 0.25 and 0.08 to 0.12).
reporting_issues.consequence: The implied associations are much weaker than the printed terms suggest: about ten times for parenthood (0.19 against 0.02) and about three times for a new job (0.10 against 0.03). Their intervals cannot be computed from the table, and the printed values must not be quoted as odds ratios for older men.

reporting_issues.issue: The onset main effects (parenthood 0.39; new job 2.79) are described as applying 'regardless of the age or sex' of participants, and in the Discussion as consistent across gender and age, but with interaction terms in the model they are the odds ratios for women aged 21–37; the absence of a significant interaction (for example age × parenthood 0.55, 0.11–2.86) does not show that the association is the same in other groups. Conversely, the significant persistence main effect of parenthood (0.22, 0.06–0.82, women aged 21–37) is not mentioned in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should state the onset associations for the reference group or as average associations with unknown heterogeneity, and should not describe the parenthood–persistence association as limited to older men.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions attribute most of the decrease in dependence over the life course to the reduction of onset and recurrence 'in addition to the increase in persistence', but a rise in persistence with age would raise prevalence, not lower it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A wording error in the Conclusions; the Results and Discussion make clear that falling onset and recurrence, not persistence, account for the decline. The sentence should not be paraphrased as written.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 (retention at Wave 2) is headed N=28,482, a number that matches neither the Wave 1 sample (43,093) nor the Wave 2 sample (34,653) and is not explained in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the retention percentages is unclear; the overall retention can be taken only as 'approximately 80%', which agrees with 34,653 of 43,093 (80.4%, editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the persistent group had a smaller proportion of married people 'at both waves' and the offset group fewer parents 'at both waves', but by the table's own subscripts the persistent group did not differ from the offset group in marriage at Wave 1 or from the onset and offset groups at Wave 2, and the offset group did not differ from the persistent and onset groups in parenthood at Wave 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Descriptive overstatement of group differences; use the subscripted table, not the text, for these comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The persistence result is described as an 'increasing trend with age', but the test reported is a 6-df Wald F test of any difference among seven age groups, not a trend test, and in one sensitivity analysis persistence fell at 63+.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 3rd paragraph; Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction and shape of the age pattern of persistence come from Figure 2 (an image) rather than from a test; together with its loss of significance under imputation and under the continuous definition, persistence should be described as roughly stable with age.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites Crum et al. (2005) as reporting that the incidence of DSM-III-R dependence over 12.6 years fell from 52.7% at ages 18–29 to 4.3% at 65 and over. A cumulative incidence above one half in a general-population cohort would be far above this paper's own onset figures (2.5% over three years, unweighted, all ages).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit of the cited figures (percentage or a rate per person-years) should be checked in the primary paper before they are reused; they do not affect this paper's own results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Method gives SUDAAN 'version 10' with a 2004 citation, while the reference list cites SUDAAN Version 9.0 (2004).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Method › Analysis; References (Research Triangle Institute, 2004)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no effect on the results.

design_detail: Randomized five-condition crossover pharmacokinetic study in 9 healthy non-smoking men in Linköping, Sweden. Each man received the same ethanol dose (0.30 g per kg body weight) on five occasions at least 7 days apart: drunk a few minutes after a breakfast rich in fat, in carbohydrate or in protein (about 3000 kJ each, eaten in 15 min), drunk after a 10-hour overnight fast, or infused intravenously over 30 min. Venous blood ethanol was measured by headspace gas chromatography for 210 min (sometimes 300 min). Outcomes: peak blood alcohol concentration (BAC), time to peak, and area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 210 min (AUC); elimination rate, back-extrapolated intercept and volume of distribution for the fasting and intravenous conditions only. How the order was randomized is not described.
can_establish: Whether, in a few healthy young men given one small fixed amount of ethanol in the laboratory, a breakfast eaten just before drinking lowers the peak and the area of the blood alcohol curve compared with drinking on an empty stomach and with intravenous delivery, and by roughly how much.
cannot_establish: Whether the composition of the meal matters (the meal comparison had post hoc power of 0.22 to 0.25); what happens with larger amounts, in women, after other meals or other intervals between eating and drinking, or in everyday drinking; whether a lower BAC means less impairment (no effect measure); or by what mechanism (first-pass metabolism was inferred, not measured).

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers; how they were recruited is not reported (Methods › Subjects and conditions, 1st paragraph, pp. 521–522). Hospital departments of forensic toxicology, clinical pharmacology and internal medicine in Linköping, Sweden.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy men, all non-smokers (p. 521). No other criteria are stated: usual drinking, medicines, health screening and liver tests are not reported.
sample.demographics: Mean age 24.6 years (SD 4.8), body weight 75.8 kg (SD 9.0), height 183 cm (SD 4.6) (pp. 521–522). No women.
sample.attrition: None reported; Table 1 gives n = 9 for every condition (p. 524).
sample.selection_effects: Nine young, healthy, non-smoking paid male volunteers whose drinking histories are not described. The results cannot be assumed to hold for women, older people, people who drink heavily, people with liver disease or people taking medicines.

exposure.measurement: Ethanol was given by the investigators: ethanol diluted with orange juice to 20% v/v and finished within exactly 15 min, or a 6% w/v solution in saline infused at a constant rate over 30 min by pump (Methods › Subjects and conditions, 1st paragraph, p. 522). Breakfasts of ordinary Swedish foods chosen with a dietician were eaten in 15 min and the drink was taken a few minutes later (2nd paragraph, p. 522; acknowledgement, p. 525).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one dose of 0.30 g ethanol per kg body weight in every session. Fat-rich meal 2908 kJ (fat 55%, carbohydrate 33%, protein 12% of energy); carbohydrate-rich meal 2924 kJ (9%, 86%, 6%); protein-rich meal 3188 kJ (24%, 45%, 31%); fasting condition after a 10-hour overnight fast; intravenous infusion over 30 min on an empty stomach (p. 522; Table 1, p. 524). Sessions at least 7 days apart, intervals differing between participants (p. 522).
exposure.polysubstance: All participants were non-smokers; other drug use, usual alcohol intake and medicines are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Overnight fast of 10 hours before the fasting and intravenous sessions (p. 522); whether alcohol was avoided before sessions is not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person: every man completed all five conditions, so the overnight-fast and intravenous sessions are the reference conditions for the three meal conditions.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person design). The meals were meant to be of similar energy, but the protein-rich meal provided about 9 to 10% more energy than the other two (editors' calculation from Table 1, p. 524).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Usual drinking, liver function, gastric emptying and the activity or genotype of alcohol-metabolizing enzymes were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within-person comparison); other drug use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Venous blood through an indwelling catheter before dosing and at 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180 and 210 min, sometimes to 300 min; ethanol by headspace gas chromatography with n-propanol as internal standard, limit of quantification 1 mg/dl, SD 0.8 mg/dl (coefficient of variation under 1%) at 100 mg/dl, accuracy checked against purchased known-strength standards of 50, 100 and 150 mg/dl (Methods › Sampling of blood, p. 522). Peak BAC and time to peak read from the data; AUC by the linear trapezoidal rule from 0 to 210 min; for the fasting and intravenous conditions only, the zero-order disappearance rate (ko), the back-extrapolated intercept (Co) and the apparent volume of distribution (Vd) (Methods › Pharmacokinetics of ethanol, p. 522).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard pharmacokinetic quantities and a forensic analytical method. The authors state that bioavailability cannot be computed as an AUC ratio because ethanol elimination is saturable, so AUC is used only to compare conditions given the same dose (p. 522).
outcomes.operationalization: Systemic availability of ethanol was represented by peak BAC and AUC in each meal condition compared with the fasting and intravenous conditions. No measure of impairment, subjective effect or harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Seven tests: two five-condition ANOVAs (peak BAC, AUC), two ANOVAs across the three meals, and three fasting-versus-intravenous comparisons (ko, Co, Vd). The shorter elimination time in the fed state was not tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported and not possible for participants (meal, fast or infusion obvious); the outcome is an objective laboratory measure.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mean (SD), n = 9 (Table 1, p. 524). Peak BAC, mg/dl: fat-rich 16.6 (4.0), carbohydrate-rich 17.7 (7.1), protein-rich 13.3 (4.0), fasting 30.8 (4.3), intravenous 54.3 (6.4). AUC 0–210 min, mg/dl·min: 1767 (549), 1619 (760), 1270 (406), 3210 (527) and 4786 (446). Five conditions: F = 98.7 (peak) and 88.9 (AUC), df 4 and 32, P < 0.001; three meals: F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05 (pp. 523–524). Editors' calculation: the meal peaks were 43% to 57% of the fasting peak and the meal AUCs 40% to 55% of the fasting AUC; the fasting peak and AUC were 57% and 67% of the intravenous values. No meal-versus-fasting test is printed; using the five-condition residual SD (5.1 mg/dl; 465.2 mg/dl·min), each meal-fasting difference is about 5 to 9 times its approximate standard error (editors' calculation, assumes sphericity). Between meals, the protein-rich meal gave a peak about 20% and 25% lower than the fat-rich and carbohydrate-rich meals, and an AUC about 28% and 22% lower (editors' calculation), not significant. Fasting versus intravenous: ko 10.3 (1.8) versus 9.8 (1.2) mg/dl per hour, 95% CI of the difference −2.27 to 1.25; Co 37 (4.9) versus 40 (3.9) mg/dl, CI −1.6 to 7.0; Vd 0.81 (0.11) versus 0.75 (0.08) l/kg, CI −0.154 to 0.033 (p. 523).
analysis.covariates: None; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests (SigmaStat) (p. 522).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (1997). The protocol was approved by the local ethics committee (p. 522).
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods say paired t-tests were used when two treatments were compared, but no meal-versus-fasting test is reported; the only test including the fasting condition is the five-condition ANOVA, whose result is driven partly by the intravenous condition. The shorter elimination time in the fed state is stated as 1 to 2 hours without measured values. No elimination rate could be fitted for the meal conditions (p. 522).
analysis.power: No calculation in advance. Post hoc power was 1.0 for the five-condition ANOVAs and 0.22 (peak) and 0.25 (AUC) for the three-meal comparison, which the authors say calls for caution (p. 523; Table 1 footnotes, p. 524).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 healthy young men given 0.30 g ethanol per kg, drinking a few minutes after a breakfast of about 3000 kJ roughly halved the peak BAC (13 to 18 mg/dl against 31 mg/dl after an overnight fast) and the AUC over 210 min (1270 to 1767 against 3210 mg/dl·min), with larger differences between people after food (coefficients of variation 24% to 47%). The three meals did not differ significantly, but the protein-rich meal gave the lowest values and the comparison had power of about 0.2. Even on an empty stomach, peak and AUC were lower than with intravenous infusion of the same dose (57% and 67%). The fed-state curves could not be fitted, so no fed-state elimination rate was estimated.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that drinking after a meal, regardless of its composition, decreases the systemic availability of ethanol, and explains this by hepatic first-pass metabolism (p. 521); the final paragraph calls composition not so important (p. 525). Gaps: (1) the composition statement rests on a non-significant comparison that the authors themselves say had low power (p. 523), and differences of 20% to 28% between meals were seen but could not be tested reliably; (2) first-pass metabolism and the alternative two-pool absorption mechanism were not measured; the authors offer both (pp. 524–525); (3) the statement that elimination took 1 to 2 hours less in the fed state (abstract, p. 521; Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 523) and that disposal was boosted is not quantified; a lower curve reaches zero sooner even at an unchanged elimination rate, and the fasting curves were still above zero when sampling ended (Figure 1, p. 523); (4) a more pronounced effect when the meal is closer to drinking is cited as unpublished work (p. 525). The central result, lower peak and AUC after food at this small dose, is reported accurately.

timeline.event: Welling (1977) and Wilkinson et al. (1977): earlier fasted and fed studies of small ethanol doses, cited by the paper as showing a lower peak and BAC profile after food (refs 7 and 11); not read.

Rogers et al. (1987): cited as finding carbohydrate-rich food more effective than fat or protein in accelerating ethanol metabolism, by an unexplained mechanism (ref 28); not read. This conflicts with the present null comparison of meals.
Jones and Jönsson (1994): the same group's earlier study of food-induced lowering of peak BAC and faster elimination immediately after a meal (ref 10); not read.
Fraser et al. (1995): variability of ethanol profiles with ingestion before or after an evening meal (ref 6); not read.
This study: five-condition crossover in 9 men at 0.30 g/kg.
Ramchandani et al. (2001): food and food composition and alcohol elimination rates in healthy men and women, listed as a further study on the BeforeDuring reading list; not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The lowering of peak BAC and AUC by food before drinking agrees with the earlier fed-versus-fasting studies the paper cites, none of which was read for this card. Whether macronutrient composition matters is unsettled: this study was underpowered for it and a cited study found a carbohydrate effect on metabolism. The evidence is from small laboratory studies at small doses; the BeforeDuring list records that no naturalistic study of food before drinking was found.

funding.funder: Supported in part by grants from the Swedish National Board of Forensic Medicine and the Forensic Science Centre, Linköping (acknowledgement, p. 525).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: First author from the Department of Forensic Toxicology, National Laboratory of Forensic Chemistry, Linköping; co-authors from clinical pharmacology and internal medicine. The paper frames its question around estimating BAC in medicolegal casework (pp. 521, 525). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover study in women and men, at several doses including amounts typical of a drinking occasion, with meals that differ in composition at matched energy and volume and at several intervals before drinking, blood sampled until BAC reaches zero, and measures of impairment as well as BAC.

domains.note: A randomized crossover order is stated (abstract; Methods, p. 522), but how the order was generated and concealed, and which order each man received, are not reported; with five conditions and nine men the orders cannot have been balanced.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: At least 7 days between sessions after a single small dose eliminated within hours (Figure 1), so carryover is implausible; period was not in the analysis and intervals varied between men.
Supervised laboratory sessions with fixed meals, timed drinking and pump infusion; no deviations reported. Open conditions, but the outcome does not depend on expectations.
All 9 men contribute to every condition in Table 1 (p. 524). The printed degrees of freedom for the three-meal ANOVA (2 and 17) do not match complete data from 9 men (2 and 16); see reporting issues.

Blood ethanol by a validated headspace gas chromatography method with stated precision (p. 522). AUC stops at 210 min while fasting and intravenous concentrations were still above zero, which if anything understates the fed-fasting difference.

No protocol; the meal-versus-fasting comparisons that the Methods imply (paired t-tests) are not reported; the fed-state elimination time is asserted without values; the sampling times visible in Figure 1 do not match the stated schedule.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The outcome is objective, the design is within-person and the fed-fasting difference is large relative to its variability, so bias is unlikely to explain it; concerns come from an undescribed randomization and incomplete reporting of the planned comparisons. The main limits are precision and directness rather than bias: 9 young men, one small dose, breakfasts eaten just before drinking. Citable for: lower peak BAC and AUC after a meal than on an empty stomach at 0.30 g/kg in healthy men, with values (Table 1). Not citable for: meal composition having no effect, the mechanism, the size of the effect at larger doses or in women, or any effect on impairment.

key_findings.finding: Nine healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6 years, SD 4.8; weight 75.8 kg, SD 9.0) each received ethanol 0.30 g/kg in five sessions at least 7 days apart, in randomized order: after a fat-rich, a carbohydrate-rich or a protein-rich breakfast, after a 10-hour overnight fast, or by intravenous infusion over 30 min.

key_findings.finding: The breakfasts provided 2908 kJ (fat-rich: 55% of energy from fat), 2924 kJ (carbohydrate-rich: 86% from carbohydrate) and 3188 kJ (protein-rich: 31% from protein, 45% from carbohydrate); each was eaten in 15 min and the drink was finished within 15 min a few minutes later.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Subjects and conditions, 2nd paragraph (p. 522); Table 1 (p. 524)

key_findings.finding: Peak BAC, mean (SD), mg/dl: 16.6 (4.0) after the fat-rich meal, 17.7 (7.1) after the carbohydrate-rich meal, 13.3 (4.0) after the protein-rich meal, 30.8 (4.3) after an overnight fast and 54.3 (6.4) with intravenous infusion.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 521); Table 1 (p. 524)

key_findings.finding: AUC from 0 to 210 min, mean (SD), mg/dl·min: 1767 (549) fat-rich, 1619 (760) carbohydrate-rich, 1270 (406) protein-rich, 3210 (527) fasting and 4786 (446) intravenous.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 521); Table 1 (p. 524)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: meal peaks 43% to 57% of the fasting peak, meal AUCs 40% to 55% of the fasting AUC.

key_findings.finding: Across all five conditions the differences were significant (F = 98.7 for peak BAC and 88.9 for AUC, df 4 and 32, P < 0.001, post hoc power 1.0); no test of each meal against fasting is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 522, F values on p. 523); Table 1 and footnote 3 (p. 524)

key_findings.finding: The three meals did not differ significantly (F = 2.22 for peak BAC and 2.42 for AUC, P > 0.05); post hoc power was 0.22 and 0.25, and the authors say the result should be read with caution.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 523); Table 1 and footnotes 1–2 (p. 524)
key_findings.note: The protein-rich meal gave the lowest peak and AUC; the authors call this a non-significant tendency (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 524).

key_findings.finding: Time to peak ranged from 30 to 90 min after the fat-rich and carbohydrate-rich meals, 30 to 60 min after the protein-rich meal and on an empty stomach, and was 30 min (end of infusion) intravenously.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, tmax column

key_findings.finding: Variability between people was greatest after food: coefficients of variation 24% to 40% for peak BAC and 31% to 47% for AUC after the meals, against 14% and 16% fasting and 12% and 10% intravenous.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 523); Table 1 (p. 524)

key_findings.finding: Fasting and intravenous conditions did not differ in disappearance rate (10.3, SD 1.8, versus 9.8, SD 1.2 mg/dl per hour; 95% CI of the difference −2.27 to 1.25), intercept (37 versus 40 mg/dl; CI −1.6 to 7.0) or volume of distribution (0.81 versus 0.75 l/kg; CI −0.154 to 0.033).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: After food, individual peaks were often below 10 to 15 mg/dl and some curves showed a secondary peak hours after drinking, so curves could not be fitted and no elimination rate was estimated for the meal conditions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Pharmacokinetics of ethanol, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The statement that elimination from blood took 1 to 2 hours less in the fed state comes from inspection of Figure 1, not from a measured or tested quantity. Editors' reading of the mean curves (Figure 1f): the meal curves reach about zero at roughly 190 to 200 min; the fasting curve's last plotted point is at about 190 min, with a dashed extension reaching zero at roughly 235 min; the intravenous curve is still about 1 mg/dl at 300 min.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 521); Discussion, 1st paragraph and Figure 1 (p. 523)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 600-dpi crop of Figure 1f and approximate. On this reading the fed-fasting difference in time to zero is under an hour and partly extrapolated.

key_findings.finding: The authors explain the lower BAC after food by slow, variable gastric emptying allowing hepatic first-pass metabolism under Michaelis-Menten kinetics, or by a two-pool model in which part of the dose is bound to the meal; neither was measured in this study.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 524); 6th and 7th paragraphs (p. 525)

key_findings.finding: The disappearance rate in the fasting and intravenous conditions (about 10 mg/dl per hour) was lower than the 15 mg/dl per hour the authors say is often cited for moderate drinkers; they attribute this to the 10 to 12 hour fast, citing earlier work.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The three-meal ANOVA is printed with 2 and 17 degrees of freedom; with 9 men measured under 3 conditions a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA has 2 and 16 (the five-condition ANOVA's 4 and 32 is correct).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the p-values are about 0.14 (peak) and 0.12 (AUC) with either df (editors' calculation), so the conclusion is unchanged, but a value may be missing or the df mistyped.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list blood samples at 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180 and 210 min (sometimes 300 min), but in the editors' reading of Figure 1 the individual curves in panels a–d end at about 190 min and the mean curves in Figure 1f show points at roughly 10-minute intervals from 150 min onwards (and from 210 to 300 min for the intravenous condition); AUC is said to run from 0 to 210 min.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sampling actually behind the AUC and the elimination-time statement cannot be reconstructed. Fasting and intravenous concentrations were still above zero at the end of the window, so their AUCs are truncated, which makes the reported fed-fasting contrast conservative rather than inflated.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes large inter- and intra-individual variation, but each condition was given once to each man, so variation within a person under the same condition was not measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only between-person variation (the coefficients of variation in Table 1) is supported by the data.

reporting_issues.issue: The meals are described as similar in volume and energy (abstract; Table 1 title), but meal volume or weight is not reported and the protein-rich meal provided 3188 kJ against 2908 and 2924 kJ, about 9 to 10% more (editors' calculation); it also took more of its energy from carbohydrate (45%) than from protein (31%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The meal with the lowest BAC was also the largest in energy, and the macronutrient contrast is weaker than the labels suggest; any composition effect, or its absence, is confounded with meal size.

reporting_issues.issue: The coefficient of variation for the intravenous AUC is printed as 10%, but by the editors' calculation 446/4786 is 9.3%; the other coefficients match their means and SDs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial rounding or transcription error; no effect on interpretation.

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of the 1992 National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey (NLAES), a US national multistage probability sample of 42,862 adults aged 18 and older in the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US and the District of Columbia, interviewed face to face by Census Bureau interviewers with the AUDADIS, a structured interview designed for lay interviewers. Among the 27,616 current and former drinkers, the weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence, and of lifetime alcohol abuse without dependence, was tabulated for each year of recalled age at first drink (12 or younger to 25 or older), overall and by sex and race; logistic regression estimated the change in odds per year of later onset, adjusted for sex, race, age group, duration of drinking, family history of alcoholism and current vs former drinking.
can_establish: That in a 1992 US household sample of people who had ever drunk alcohol, those who recalled starting to drink younger were much more likely to have met DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence or abuse at some time in their lives, and that the association remained after adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history, duration of drinking and current drinking status.
cannot_establish: Whether starting to drink early causes later alcohol-use disorders rather than shared family, genetic, behavioural or psychiatric factors; the analysis does not adjust for most such alternatives. The source does not establish that the survey never measured them, and its cited reliability work covered alcohol and drug interview modules. Two adjustment variables may follow the disorder. Household sampling and recalled ages limit generalization and temporal interpretation.

sample.recruitment: General-population household sample: the NLAES, sponsored by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, fieldwork by the US Bureau of the Census in 1992; multistage design with primary sampling units selected with probability proportional to size and oversampling of Black and young adult (18–29) respondents; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents took part (p. 104, Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Current drinkers (drank in the past year) and former drinkers (drank in the past but not in the past year); lifetime abstainers, who have no onset age, are not analysed (p. 106). No minimum amount of drinking is stated in this paper.
sample.demographics: Among drinkers, 51% men and 49% women, 88.9% nonblack and 11.1% Black (p. 106, Results, 1st paragraph); these shares equal the unweighted counts (13,990 and 13,626; 24,554 and 3,062). Age, education and income distributions are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview). The numbers of drinkers missing an onset age or a diagnosis, and the number at each onset age, are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Household survivors only: people who had died (including from alcohol-related causes), were institutionalized or were homeless were not sampled, and early-onset, severe drinking may be over-represented among them. Respondents were aged 18 to over 65, so lifetime diagnoses cover very different lengths of drinking; age group and duration of drinking were adjusted for.

exposure.measurement: Age at onset of drinking: one recalled question asking how old the respondent was when they first started drinking, not counting small tastes or sips; test-retest reliability 0.72 (p. 105, Method › Measures, 3rd paragraph). Asked of adults of all ages in the same interview as the diagnostic questions; nothing recorded at the time.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Quantity and frequency of drinking were not analysed. Duration of drinking (years from onset to the last drink for former drinkers, or to the interview for current drinkers; set at 0.5 when onset and last drink were at the same age) was a covariate (p. 105).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use was neither measured in this analysis nor adjusted for.

comparison.controls: Drinkers with later recalled onset: prevalence tabulated for each year from 12 or younger to 25 or older (Tables 1 and 2, p. 107); regression per year of later onset, with onset entered as a continuous term (p. 108).
comparison.matching: None. Adjusted for sex, race (Black vs nonblack), age (18–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+), duration of drinking, family history of alcoholism (any first- or second-degree relative reported as an alcoholic or problem drinker, asked about 18 types of relative) and current vs former drinking (pp. 105–106).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood conduct problems, other psychopathology, childhood adversity, peer and family environment, genetic liability beyond the family-history question, and other drug use were not taken into account in this analysis; whether each was measured in the survey is not established here. Current vs former drinking, and duration of drinking up to the last drink in former drinkers, may themselves follow from having had the disorder.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS DSM-IV alcohol abuse and dependence, measured for the past year and before the past year with the DSM-IV clustering and duration criteria; lifetime = an episode in either period; the two diagnoses are mutually exclusive (lifetime abuse = abuse without lifetime dependence); test-retest reliability 0.76 (past year) and 0.73 (before the past year) (p. 105, Method › Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliabilities come from an independent general-population test-retest study (Grant et al., 1995) (p. 105); the recalled onset age has only a test-retest reliability (0.72), no validation.
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence; lifetime DSM-IV alcohol abuse among people without lifetime dependence.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two outcomes, each also estimated in four subgroups).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (structured lay interview; onset and diagnostic questions asked in the same interview).

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted prevalence by onset age (Tables 1 and 2, p. 107; see key findings). Adjusted: odds of lifetime dependence 14% lower and of lifetime abuse 8% lower per year of later onset; by subgroup, dependence 14.7% (men), 13.2% (women), 14.5% (nonblack), 8.1% (Black); abuse 7.0% (men), 9.1% (women), 6.7% (Black), 7.8% (nonblack) (p. 108). No odds ratios, confidence intervals, p values or unadjusted estimates are given. Editors' conversion: per-year odds ratios of about 0.86 (dependence) and 0.92 (abuse).
analysis.covariates: Sex, race, age group, duration of drinking, family history of alcoholism, current vs former drinking (p. 106, Statistical Analysis).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only percentage reductions in odds are reported: no regression table, no confidence intervals, no estimate before adjustment, no test of the sex or race differences in slope, and no number of drinkers at each onset age.
analysis.power: Not reported; 27,616 drinkers overall; cell sizes per onset age unknown (standard errors reach 9.9 points for Black respondents starting at 13).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Lifetime alcohol-dependence criteria were met by 40.6% to 47.3% of drinkers who recalled starting at 14 or younger, 24.5% at 17, 16.6% at 18, about 10% at 21 to 22 and 7.9% at 25 or older, with a rise to 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24; lifetime abuse without dependence peaked at 13.8% for onset at 14 and fell to 2.5%. After adjustment, the odds of dependence were 14% and of abuse 8% lower for each later year of onset.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion opens by calling age at first use "a powerful predictor of lifetime alcohol abuse and dependence" (p. 108); the Results call it a major contributor to the development of abuse and alcoholism (p. 108); the Discussion identifies ages 16 and younger as a particularly vulnerable period for starting to drink and suggests prevention aimed at delaying onset until after 18 or 19, while saying this should be considered cautiously (pp. 108–109). The authors also state that a prospective study is needed to learn whether the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors explain the association, whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker, and to reduce the recall bias of cross-sectional designs including this one (p. 109). Gaps: (1) 'contributor to the development' and 'vulnerable period' are causal readings of a cross-sectional association with recalled onset, which the authors' own closing paragraph concedes; (2) the per-year figures come without confidence intervals or unadjusted estimates, and one linear term summarizes a curve that is steep before 18 and irregular after 20; (3) the thresholds of 16 and of 18 or 19 are read from the crude curve, not tested; (4) adjustment for current drinking status and, in former drinkers, for duration up to the last drink may remove part of the association or add bias, since both can follow from the disorder.

timeline.event: This study: cross-sectional NLAES association between recalled age at first drink and lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence and abuse.
Same survey and authors, for drugs among people who had used a drug at least 12 times: adjusted odds about 5% (abuse) and 4% (dependence) lower per year of later onset (read in this round).

Systematic review of prospective cohorts of age at first drink and adult alcohol problems: four cohorts, associations in some analyses and not others, often shrinking with adjustment; it cites this study among the mostly cross-sectional evidence behind guidance (as recorded on the library's card sc_maimaris_2014).

Minnesota twins: drinking by 14 stayed associated with adult alcohol outcomes after propensity weighting and within discordant pairs, but within identical pairs the association with alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms was not significant (as recorded on the library's claim on early drinking, which cites the study).

replication.where_it_stands: This cross-sectional association is the usual starting point for the question; whether early drinking causes later disorders has since been tested with prospective cohorts (maimaris_2014: few cohorts, inconsistent and attenuated associations) and co-twin designs (irons_2015), both in the library, and the authors themselves considered other associated factors the more likely explanation. The steep gradient is not in doubt as a description of what US adults reported in 1992; its causal reading remains open.

funding.funder: No funding or acknowledgment statement. Both authors were at the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (Division of Biometry and Epidemiology), which sponsored the NLAES (pp. 103–104).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Government researchers analysing their institute's own survey; no commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: Designs that separate the effect of early drinking from shared liability: prospective cohorts that measure conduct problems, family environment and genetic risk before the first drink and record drinking and disorders as they happen; comparisons of twins or siblings who differ in age at first drink; and long-term follow-up of randomized prevention programmes that succeed in delaying first drinking.

domains.note: Adjusted for sex, race, age group, family history and duration of drinking; conduct problems, other psychopathology, childhood adversity, peer and family environment and other drug use were not taken into account in this analysis; whether each was measured in the survey is not established here; adjustment for current vs former drinking (and, in former drinkers, for duration up to the last drink) may itself be affected by the disorder.

One recalled question asked of adults of all ages; test-retest reliability 0.72; recall error, possibly differing between people with and without the disorder, cannot be ruled out; the authors acknowledge recall bias (p. 109).
Household survivors with good response (about 90%); deaths, institutions and homelessness, plausibly related to both early onset and severe disorder, are outside the frame.
Lifetime diagnoses; treatment after onset cannot remove a past diagnosis.
Numbers missing an onset age or a diagnosis, and cell sizes per onset age, are not reported.
Structured lay interview with fair to good reliability (0.73–0.76); lifetime episodes recalled in the same interview as the onset age; abuse counted only in people without dependence.
Only percentage reductions in odds are reported, without intervals, unadjusted estimates or model details; subgroup slopes compared without tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The steep crude gradient (Tables 1 and 2) is a sound description of what US drinkers reported in 1992, from a large probability sample with good response and a standard interview. As evidence that early drinking causes alcohol use disorders it is weak: the exposure was recalled in the same interview as the outcome, the main competing explanations (shared behavioural, psychiatric, family and genetic liability) were not included in this analysis, two covariates may follow from the outcome, and the adjusted estimates come without intervals. Cite it for the cross-sectional association and its size in 1992 (lifetime dependence above 40% for onset at 14 or younger against about 8% to 11% for onset at 20 or later, outside the bump at 23 and 24; 14% lower adjusted odds per year); do not cite it as showing that delaying the first drink prevents alcohol use disorders.

key_findings.finding: NLAES 1992: face-to-face Census Bureau interviews with 42,862 adults aged 18 and older in the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US, with oversampling of Black and young adult respondents; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents took part. The analysis used the 27,616 current (18,352) and former (9,264) drinkers: 13,990 men and 13,626 women; 3,062 Black and 24,554 nonblack respondents.
key_findings.locator: Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 104); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 106); column heads of Tables 1 and 2 (p. 107)
key_findings.note: The text calls the drinkers 66% of the sample; 27,616 of 42,862 is 64.4% unweighted (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Age at onset was one recalled question (how old the respondent was on first starting to drink, not counting small tastes or sips), with test-retest reliability 0.72. Lifetime DSM-IV dependence and abuse came from the AUDADIS (reliability 0.76 for past-year and 0.73 for earlier diagnoses), abuse being counted only in people without lifetime dependence.
key_findings.locator: Method › Measures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
Table 1, Total column
key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer misreads the onset-13 total as 41.3; the rendered page shows 47.3, which lies between the men's (49.4) and women's (43.2) values. Numbers of drinkers per onset age are not given.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime dependence was higher in men than women at every onset age, for example 41.3% vs 39.1% (12 or younger), 49.4% vs 43.2% (13), 19.4% vs 12.5% (18), 14.7% vs 7.4% (20) and 9.7% vs 6.9% (25 or older); in Black respondents it ranged from 44.4% (onset 13, SE 9.9) to 9.5% (onset 22).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Male, Female and Black columns
key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer misreads three values in Table 1 (men 25 or older 9.7 as 9.1; Black onset 15, 27.4 as 21.4; nonblack 25 or older 7.7 as 1.7) and one in Table 2 (Black onset 15, 9.7 as 9.1); the values here are from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of lifetime alcohol abuse without dependence by age at first drink, all drinkers (SE): 12 or younger 8.3% (1.1); 13, 11.5% (1.8); 14, 13.8% (1.5); 15, 11.9% (0.9); 16, 10.6% (0.7); 17, 9.5% (0.6); 18, 7.8% (0.4); 19, 6.3% (0.6); 20, 4.8% (0.5); 21, 4.8% (0.4); 22, 4.9% (1.0); 23, 3.6% (0.9); 24, 3.1% (1.0); 25 or older, 2.5% (0.4). Editors' sums with Table 1 (the two diagnoses are mutually exclusive): any lifetime alcohol use disorder 48.9% (12 or younger), 58.8% (13), 54.6% (14), 24.4% (18), 16.2% (20) and 10.4% (25 or older).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 106); Table 2, Total column (p. 107)

key_findings.finding: After adjustment for sex, race, age group, duration of drinking, current vs former drinking and family history of alcoholism, with onset entered as a continuous term, the odds of lifetime alcohol dependence were 14% lower and the odds of lifetime abuse 8% lower for each later year of onset; no odds ratios, confidence intervals or p values are printed. Editors' conversion: odds ratios of about 0.86 and 0.92 per year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starting p. 106, continuing p. 108)

key_findings.finding: By subgroup, the odds of dependence fell 14.7% (men), 13.2% (women), 14.5% (nonblack) and 8.1% (Black) per year of later onset, and the odds of abuse 7.0% (men), 9.1% (women), 6.7% (Black) and 7.8% (nonblack); no test of the differences between subgroups is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The decline in dependence was interrupted by a rise from 9.5% (onset at 22) to 14.7% and 13.6% (onset at 23 and 24); the authors suggest, without data, that unusually late first drinking may mark other psychopathology and self-medication.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors identify ages 16 and younger as a particularly vulnerable period for starting to drink and say their results suggest prevention aimed at delaying onset until after 18 or 19, but that this recommendation should be considered cautiously because why onset relates to the disorders is not understood.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors call for a prospective study to find out whether the delay of drinking itself or, more likely, other associated factors explain the inverse relationship; whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker of disorders that would develop anyway; whether delaying onset has unintended effects such as more drug experimentation; and to reduce the recall bias of cross-sectional designs, including this one, and separate onset from duration of drinking.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The regression results are reported only as percentage reductions in odds: no coefficients, confidence intervals, p values, model sample size or unadjusted estimates, and no number of drinkers at each onset age.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the 14% and 8% figures, and how much adjustment changed them, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results put the rise in dependence at onset ages 22 and 23 (p. 106), the Discussion at 23 and 24 (p. 108); Table 1 shows 9.5% at 22 and 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table settles it (23 and 24).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's pooled figures (abuse just over 11% for onset at 16 or younger and about 4% at 20 or older; dependence about 10% at 20 or older) do not appear in the tables, whose single-year values range from 8.3% to 13.8% (abuse, 16 or younger), 2.5% to 4.9% (abuse, 20 or older) and 7.9% to 14.7% (dependence, 20 or older).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the pooled values cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The drinkers are said to be 66% of the sample, but 27,616 of 42,862 is 64.4%; the sex and race shares given (51% and 49%; 88.9% and 11.1%), said to mirror the general population, equal the unweighted counts although Black respondents were oversampled (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; weighted and unweighted figures appear to be mixed without saying which is which.

reporting_issues.issue: The covariates include current vs former drinking and, for former drinkers, the duration of drinking up to the last drink (pp. 105–106), both of which can follow from developing a disorder; the effect of including them is not shown. Duration is calculated from onset to interview or last drink, and age group is also adjusted for; the onset coefficient is therefore conditional on linked time variables. The authors explicitly say onset and duration still need to be disentangled (p.109).
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted per-year estimates may be biased in either direction relative to the total association.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group for the reported abuse regression is not stated: the paper does not specify whether it excludes dependence or includes everyone without abuse.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reported 8% lower odds per later onset year cannot be assigned an exact diagnostic reference group from this report.
