design_detail: Retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of the baseline data of Project MATCH, a multisite randomized trial that matched people seeking treatment for alcohol problems to treatments (recruited 1991–1993 at nine US clinical research units; an outpatient arm recruited from the community by newspaper advertisements and from outpatient programmes, and an aftercare arm recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes). Ages at four drinking landmarks (first getting drunk regularly; first alcohol-related problems; first difficulty stopping drinking before intoxication, called loss of control; onset of the worst period of drinking) were recalled at baseline. Landmark ages, the intervals between successive landmarks, and the time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment (only for the 735 people for whom MATCH was their first treatment, so that first treatment is the treatment at which they were recruited) were compared between women and men in 2 (arm) × 2 (gender) × 5 (current-age quintile) between-subjects ANOVAs. A treatment sample, not a general-population sample.
can_establish: Whether, in this sample of US adults with DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence who volunteered for a treatment trial, women recalled reaching drinking landmarks at later ages than men and recalled shorter intervals between some landmarks, and how these differences varied with current age.
cannot_establish: Whether women in general progress faster than men. The whole analysis sample entered the trial at similar ages, but the 735-person first-treatment subgroup has no sex-specific entry ages reported; a recruitment-age explanation for its interval difference is conditional, not measured decomposition. All ages were recalled, no age at first drink or first intoxication was asked, and people who never sought treatment or met the exclusions are not represented. No biological or social mechanism was measured.

sample.recruitment: Treatment-seeking volunteers for a randomized trial (Project MATCH), recruited over 2 years, 1991–1993, at nine clinical research units across the US. Outpatient arm (688 men, 264 women): recruited from the community through newspaper advertisements and from outpatient clinical programmes. Aftercare arm (619 men, 155 women): recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes in private, public and Veterans Affairs facilities. All were seeking treatment for alcohol problems (p. 253, Method › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence; age 18 or over; willing to accept random assignment. Excluded: current dependence on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana (in the 90 days before enrolment, per the Discussion; a history of drug dependence was allowed), suicidal or psychotic patients, and people unable to name a contact for follow-up (p. 253, Method › Subjects, 2nd paragraph; p. 259, Discussion, 10th paragraph). The analysis sample was the 1,589 of 1,726 participants with all four landmark ages (p. 253, Procedure, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Analysis sample (Table 1, p. 254), women aftercare/outpatient vs men aftercare/outpatient: n 148/231 vs 576/634; mean age 41.7 (SD 12.17)/38.3 (10.70) vs 41.5 (10.68)/38.5 (10.51); employed 75/73% vs 82/87%; White 83/79% vs 80/81%; Black 13/9% vs 14/4%; more than 12 years of education 49/62% vs 51/54%; married or cohabiting 36/36% vs 37/48%; alcohol-dependent 97/98% vs 96/96%; SCID alcohol symptoms 6.5/5.9 vs 6.9/5.9 (maximum 9). Women were 24% of the analysis sample (editors' arithmetic). Mean current age by quintile, sexes combined: 26.6, 33.2, 38.2, 44.3 and 56.9 years (p. 254, Statistical methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (baseline data). 137 of 1,726 enrolled (7.9%) lacked one or more landmark ages, almost always the two self-administered DrInC items near the end of a long questionnaire (p. 253). By the editors' arithmetic from p. 253 and Table 1: 40 of 419 women (9.5%) and 97 of 1,307 men (7.4%) were left out; 33 of 264 outpatient women (12.5%), 7 of 155 aftercare women (4.5%), 54 of 688 outpatient men (7.8%) and 43 of 619 aftercare men (6.9%). Included and excluded participants were not compared. The treatment analysis kept only the 735 people (46% of 1,589) for whom MATCH was the first treatment; their sex split is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A treatment sample of trial volunteers, the kind of sample in which telescoping was first described, not a general-population sample. Table 1 gives similar trial-entry ages for the full analysis sample, not the 735 first-treatment subgroup. If that subgroup also entered at similar ages, a later recalled start would mechanically shorten its interval to treatment; the needed subgroup ages are not reported. the worst period of drinking was also reached at the same age by both sexes (35.2 vs 35.0 years, Table 2). People who never sought treatment, people dependent on other drugs, and people with psychosis or suicidality are not represented. Grouping by current age means the youngest participants could only report landmarks at young ages and are a subset who reached treatment quickly, which the authors acknowledge (p. 258).

exposure.measurement: The groups compared are women and men (the paper uses 'gender' and does not separate biological sex from social roles), within study arm and current-age quintile. Landmark ages were self-reported at the baseline assessment: first problems and worst problems from questions in the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID); drunk regularly (age at which the person first started getting drunk regularly) and loss of control (age at which the person first had difficulty stopping drinking before intoxication) from two items of the self-administered Drinker Inventory of Consequences (DrInC). Age at first treatment was the age at entry to MATCH for those for whom it was the first treatment. All timing was recalled; none was recorded as it happened (p. 253, Procedure, 2nd paragraph; p. 256).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed: drinking amounts and patterns were not part of the analyses; severity is described only by SCID symptom counts (Table 1, p. 254).
exposure.polysubstance: Current dependence on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana was an exclusion; past drug dependence was allowed (pp. 253, 259). Other drug use was not described or adjusted for; the authors say the results may not apply to people dependent on several drugs (p. 259).

comparison.controls: Women compared with men within each study arm and current-age quintile; the treatment-interval analysis compared women and men among the 735 people for whom MATCH was the first treatment.
comparison.matching: None. Study arm and current-age quintile were factors in the ANOVA; no other characteristic was adjusted for, although men were more often employed and more often married or living with a partner (p. 254, Results › Subject characteristics, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, childhood conduct problems, psychiatric comorbidity (raised by the authors as a possible explanation, p. 258), body size and composition, drinking quantity and other drug use were not measured or not used. Nothing was recorded before treatment entry.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The same drug-dependence exclusion applied to both sexes; other drug use not reported for either.

outcomes.instruments: Quick Screen interview (demographics); Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID: count of alcohol dependence symptoms, age at first alcohol-related problems and at onset of the worst drinking period); Drinker Inventory of Consequences (DrInC: five domains of negative consequences, plus the two age questions). The full baseline battery took three sessions of 6 to 8 hours in all (p. 253, Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: No reliability or validity data are given for the recalled landmark ages; the authors recommend test-retest validation and linking the questions to periods of life (p. 258, Discussion, 7th paragraph). The two DrInC landmarks are single questions whose interpretation may vary, as the authors note.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping was operationalized as later landmark ages but shorter intervals between successive landmarks in women. Intervals were differences between recalled ages taken in the average order of the landmarks, so negative values were possible; only 53% of participants reported the full assumed order (p. 254, Statistical methods, 1st paragraph; p. 256). Time to first treatment = age at entry to MATCH minus age at getting drunk regularly, for the 735 for whom MATCH was the first reported treatment (p. 256).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: univariate tests at .05 divided by the number of variables in each set (four landmark ages; three intervals), with interpretation limited to effects significant in both the univariate and the multivariate analyses (p. 254, Statistical methods, 3rd paragraph); the multivariate results are not reported. Simple main effects within quintiles used error terms computed within each quintile and Dunn's procedure (p. 255); their statistics are not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report questionnaire and structured interview by research assistants who knew participants' sex).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD), women vs men (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 255–256): age at getting drunk regularly 26.6 (10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96); first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87); loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95); worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93). Gender main effects F(1, 1,569) = 83.62, 32.35 and 38.67 for the first three (p ≤ .001), ω² = .03, .01 and .01; no gender effect for worst problems. Intervals: drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04), F(1, 1,569) = 13.04, ω² = .01; first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), no gender effect reported; loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67), F = 20.95 (df printed as 1/1,589), ω² = .01. Drunk regularly to first treatment (n = 735): 11.6 (9.01) vs 15.8 (9.67), F(1, 715) = 44.5, ω² = .04. Editors' calculation, unadjusted standardized differences (women minus men, pooled SD): landmark ages 0.42 (drunk regularly), 0.25 (first problems), 0.25 (loss of control), 0.02 (worst problems); intervals −0.21, 0.02 and −0.27; time to first treatment about −0.43 to −0.47 (the sex split of the 735 is not reported, so the pooled SD is bracketed by the two group SDs).
analysis.covariates: Study arm and current-age quintile as factors, with all interactions; nothing else.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of a trial's baseline data; no analysis plan for this question is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: Multivariate test results, the simple-main-effect statistics by quintile, the cell sizes and SDs for the 735-person treatment analysis, and the similar results said to hold for first problems to first treatment (p. 258) are not shown. Arm × age-quintile interactions are given only as F values, described as not shown (pp. 255–256).
analysis.power: Not reported. 379 women in all, 66 to 85 per quintile; the treatment analysis has 735 people of unknown sex split.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1,589 people entering alcohol treatment in a trial, women recalled reaching three of four drinking landmarks 2.5 to 3.9 years later than men but reached their worst period of drinking at the same age (35.2 vs 35.0 years). Recalled intervals were shorter in women from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 vs 2.3 years) and from loss of control to worst problems (5.5 vs 7.8), but not from first problems to loss of control (2.3 vs 2.2); among 735 people in their first treatment, women reported a shorter time from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 vs 15.8 years). Gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance (ω²), and age interactions were reported for landmark ages and time to first treatment. Such an interaction is not reported for each shorter successive-landmark interval; Results and Discussion disagree for loss of control.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "Telescoping is a relatively robust phenomenon in treatment-seeking alcoholics" and that women are more likely to progress faster through the landmarks (p. 252); the Discussion speaks of strong support (p. 257), recommends identifying women at the loss-of-control stage for intensive intervention and alerting women that they are more likely than men to develop alcohol problems and dependence rapidly (p. 259), and offers biological explanations (higher blood alcohol from body size and composition, gastric first-pass metabolism, organ toxicity, hormones) and social or psychiatric ones, none of which was measured (p. 258). Gaps: (1) a recruitment-age explanation is plausible but conditional: Table 1 similar entry ages refer to all 1,589, while the treatment interval concerns735 with no sex-specific entry ages. The comparisons below use different samples and do not decompose the observed treatment difference: in the editors' reading of Figure 1, the men–women gaps in time to treatment by quintile (about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7 and 6.5 years) are close to the gaps in age at getting drunk regularly in Table 2 (0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1 and 7.1); the interval ending at the worst period, reached at the same age by both sexes, is affected in the same way; (2) the effects are small (ω² .01 to .04), which the authors acknowledge (pp. 255, 259), and absent in the youngest quintile, so 'relatively robust' overstates them; (3) alerting women in general extends a treatment-sample finding to all women; (4) the landmark ages were recalled, and only 53% of participants reported the assumed order. The limitations paragraph names the exclusion of people dependent on other drugs (p. 259) but not the selection at treatment entry.

timeline.event: Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager: telescoping studied across first drink, first intoxication, first drinking problem and first treatment; a gender difference only from first problem to first treatment (as described by Randall et al., pp. 252 and 258).
Blankfield, age-matched inpatient women and men in Australia: telescoping for some landmarks only in the older group (as described by Randall et al., pp. 253 and 257).
This study: Project MATCH treatment sample; shorter recalled intervals in women for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment, concentrated in older participants.
Two pooled US general-population surveys do not find the full telescoping pattern; this study is cited as ref. 4 (as recorded on the library's card sc_keyes_2010).
US general-population analysis of cannabis use disorder cites this study among treatment-sample findings for alcohol (Khan et al., PDF pp. 2 and 6, read in this round).
Review cites this study for faster progression in women with alcohol problems and explains the discrepancy with population surveys by sample (as recorded on the library's card sc_mchugh_2018).
Critique places this study among larger samples with discrepant results and fewer telescoping effects (as recorded on the library's card sc_marks_2018).

replication.where_it_stands: The two descriptions of this study already in the library are each partly right: in the full text women had shorter recalled intervals for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment overall (as Keyes et al. and McHugh et al. cite it), but the differences were small and minor or absent in the youngest participants (closer to Marks and Clark's reading). The general-population analysis in the library (keyes_2010) did not find the full pattern. Whether telescoping is a feature of women's drinking careers or of who reaches treatment, and when, remains open; no prospective test is cited here.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective general-population cohort of young women and men followed from before regular drinking, with landmarks and treatment recorded as they happen, analysed with survival methods that separate the chance of reaching a landmark from the speed of getting there; or, in treatment samples, comparisons that do not end intervals at the recruitment visit, with body composition, psychiatric comorbidity and access to treatment measured so that sex and gender can be told apart.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Volunteers for a treatment trial, with exclusions (other drug dependence, psychosis, suicidality): suitable only for treatment-seeking people of this kind, not for the question of whether women in general progress faster.
Recruited by advertisement and from treatment programmes for a randomized trial, not sampled; how many were screened, eligible or declined is not reported in this paper.
1,589 people, but only 379 women (66 to 85 per quintile); the treatment analysis has 735 people of unknown sex split.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 by arm and sex; recruitment and setting described (pp. 253–254).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 92% of enrolled participants analysed; missingness higher among outpatient women (12.5%); included and excluded people not compared.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The quantities analysed are recalled landmark ages from single questions (two from a self-administered questionnaire) with no reported reliability or validity; 47% of participants did not report the assumed order.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same instruments in both arms and both sexes, delivered by trained and monitored research assistants (p. 253).

A factorial ANOVA with current-age quintiles handles age crudely; intervals ending at treatment entry are fixed by the sampling; nothing else was adjusted for; multivariate and simple-effect statistics are not shown; several printed p values do not match their test statistics.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Participation among those approached is not reported in this paper.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is high risk for the site's question (do women progress faster than men?). The descriptive numbers, recalled landmark ages and intervals by sex and current age in this treatment sample, are clearly reported in Tables 2 and 3. But the sample was selected at treatment entry, which ties the intervals ending at treatment (and, in practice, at the worst period) to the recruitment age and could partly create a shorter interval in women if entry ages in the first-treatment subgroup were similar; that subgroup’s sex-specific ages are not reported; all ages were recalled; the effects were small and absent in the youngest participants; and several statistics are inconsistent. The paper may be cited for what women and men entering this alcohol treatment trial recalled: later landmark ages in women, the same age at the worst period, and shorter recalled intervals for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment, concentrated in older participants. It should not be cited as showing that women in general progress faster from drinking to problems or to treatment.

key_findings.finding: Project MATCH enrolled 1,307 men and 419 women seeking treatment for alcohol problems (1991–1993, nine US clinical research units): outpatient arm 688 men and 264 women, recruited by newspaper advertisement and from outpatient programmes; aftercare arm 619 men and 155 women, recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes. The analysis sample was the 1,589 with all four landmark ages: 379 women and 1,210 men.
key_findings.locator: Method › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Method › Procedure, 3rd paragraph (p. 253); Table 2, N column (p. 255)
key_findings.note: Table 1 (p. 254) gives the analysed cells: women 148 aftercare and 231 outpatient; men 576 aftercare and 634 outpatient.

key_findings.finding: Landmarks were recalled at baseline: ages at first alcohol-related problems and at onset of the worst period of drinking from the SCID interview; ages at first getting drunk regularly and at first difficulty stopping drinking before intoxication (loss of control) from two items of the self-administered Drinker Inventory of Consequences. Missing ages were almost always these two items, asked near the end of a long questionnaire.
key_findings.locator: Method › Procedure, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Women and men entered treatment at similar ages (aftercare 41.7 vs 41.5 years; outpatient 38.3 vs 38.5); 96% to 98% of each group were alcohol-dependent. Men were more often employed (82% and 87% vs 75% and 73%; χ² = 21.66, 1 df) and more often married or living with a partner (χ² = 4.97, 1 df).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Subject characteristics, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The partner difference is printed with p ≤ .001, but χ² = 4.97 with 1 df gives p of about .03 (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Mean recalled ages, women vs men: getting drunk regularly 26.6 (SD 10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96); first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87); loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95); worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93). Gender effects F(1, 1,569) = 83.62, 32.35 and 38.67 (p ≤ .001) for the first three, with ω² = .03, .01 and .01; the authors call these small relative to total variation but, at 2.5 to 3.9 years, clinically meaningful. No gender effect for worst problems. Editors' calculation, unadjusted standardized differences: 0.42, 0.25, 0.25 and 0.02.
key_findings.locator: Results › Age-of-onset data, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Gender differences in landmark ages depended on current age: Gender × Age Quintile F(4, 1,569) = 6.81 (drunk regularly), 4.37 (first problems) and 3.32 (loss of control), each ω² = .01. In the youngest quintile women vs men were 18.8 vs 18.0, 19.2 vs 18.8 and 20.6 vs 20.4 years; in the oldest, 37.8 vs 30.7, 39.2 vs 34.3 and 42.4 vs 37.5. Current age itself explained far more variance (ω² .25, .26, .30 and .43 for the four landmarks), because younger patients reported each landmark at younger ages.
key_findings.locator: Results › Age-of-onset data, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: The Discussion says the loss-of-control interaction was not significant (pp. 257–258), and F = 3.32 with 4 and 1,569 df gives p of about .01, not ≤ .001 as printed (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: On average the landmarks came in the order drunk regularly, first problems, loss of control, worst problems (mean within-person ranks 1.6, 2.0, 2.7 and 3.7; order kept in 19 of 20 design cells by means and 18 of 20 by ranks), but only 53% of individual participants reported this order.
key_findings.locator: Results › Order of landmark events, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recalled intervals, women vs men: drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (SD 5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04) years, gender F(1, 1,569) = 13.04, p ≤ .001, ω² = .01; first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), no gender effect; loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67), gender F = 20.95, p ≤ .001, ω² = .01, with intervals lengthening with current age (3.6 years, SD 4.31, in the youngest quintile to 9.9, SD 12.66, in the oldest; age-quintile F = 16.60, ω² = .04).
key_findings.locator: Results › Progression through successive landmark events, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: The error df for the loss-of-control to worst-problems ANOVA are printed as 1,589 (the sample size) instead of 1,569 (reporting issue). Editors' calculation, standardized differences: −0.21, 0.02 and −0.27.

key_findings.finding: Among the 735 people for whom MATCH was the first treatment, the time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment was 11.6 (SD 9.01) years in women vs 15.8 (9.67) in men: gender F(1, 715) = 44.5, p ≤ .001, ω² = .04; age quintile F(4, 715) = 48.41, ω² = .17; Gender × Age Quintile F(4, 715) = 3.76, p ≤ .005, ω² = .01. Simple-effect tests (statistics not given) found no gender difference in the youngest quintile and significant differences in the other four.
key_findings.locator: Results › Progression from drunk regularly to first treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The numbers of women and men among the 735 are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows mean time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment by sex and quintile, without cell sizes or SDs. Editors' reading of a 300-dpi crop (approximate, to about 0.2 years), men vs women: quintile 1 8.0 vs 7.2; quintile 2 13.1 vs 11.1; quintile 3 16.2 vs 11.7; quintile 4 18.9 vs 11.2; quintile 5 25.0 vs 18.5. The men–women gaps (about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7 and 6.5 years) are close to the gaps in age at getting drunk regularly in Table 2 (0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1 and 7.1), consistent with a recruitment-age explanation if women and men in the 735-person subgroup entered at similar ages; those subgroup ages are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 257); Table 2 (p. 255)
key_findings.note: Figure values are approximate and are the editors' reading; Table 2 is for the full 1,589, not the 735.

key_findings.finding: No significant interaction of study arm with gender was found for any landmark age or interval, which the authors read as outpatients and aftercare patients showing the same pattern of gender differences.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors offer two explanations for the absent gender differences in the youngest participants, which their data cannot distinguish: the youngest patients are a subset of fast progressors whose speed masks differences, or social norms have changed so that both sexes now seek treatment earlier.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that some participants reported first problems before getting drunk regularly, possibly from different interpretations of the questions or recall bias, and recommend standardized landmark definitions, test-retest validation of the self-reports and questions linked to periods of life.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Possible causes are offered as hypotheses, none measured in this study: higher blood alcohol in women from smaller body size, more fat and less body water and possibly lesser gastric first-pass metabolism; greater organ toxicity (corticosterone findings in female rats, tissue penetration, receptor sensitivity); alcohol–estrogen interactions; sex differences in reward neurobiology; women being more readily identified as having alcohol problems; and more depression and anxiety in women.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors grant that the gender differences are small relative to total variation but call them clinically meaningful, recommend identifying women at the loss-of-control stage for intensive intervention, and say women should be alerted that they are more likely than men to develop alcohol problems and dependence rapidly.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitation: conclusions are limited to the Project MATCH sample, which excluded people dependent on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana in the 90 days before enrolment; whether telescoping occurs in people dependent on several drugs, on other drugs or not yet dependent is unknown.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The questionnaire did not ask ages at first drink or first intoxication. Its first timing landmark was getting drunk regularly, so it cannot directly estimate progression from first use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning The progression between landmarks

reporting_issues.issue: Two chi-square tests are printed with p ≤ .001 although their values give larger p: education by arm χ² = 7.41 with 1 df (p about .006) and living with a partner by sex χ² = 4.97 with 1 df (p about .03) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the differences in sample characteristics are less certain than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Gender × Age Quintile interaction for loss of control (F = 3.32, 4 and 1,569 df) is printed with p ≤ .001 and called significant in the Results (p. 255), but these values give p of about .01 (editors' calculation), and the Discussion states there was no significant interaction for this landmark (pp. 257–258).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the age dependence of the loss-of-control difference met the authors' own rule (univariate at .05/4 and multivariate) cannot be determined; the multivariate results are not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The ANOVA of the loss-of-control to worst-problems interval is reported with error df of 1,589 (F = 20.95, 1/1,589; F = 16.60 and 3.86, 4/1,589), equal to the sample size; with 20 design cells the error df should be 1,569, as in the other analyses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor typographical inconsistency; conclusions unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Interpretation was to be limited to effects significant in both the univariate and multivariate analyses (p. 254), but no multivariate statistic is reported, and the simple-main-effect tests by quintile behind the statements that gender differences were absent in the youngest and present in the older quintiles are given without statistics (pp. 255, 257).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claims about which quintiles show a gender difference cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment analysis of 735 people reports neither how many were women and men nor the cell sizes and SDs behind Figure 1; the Discussion also reports similar results for first problems to first treatment without data (p. 258).
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the treatment-interval comparison, and its unreported companion, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the sample as 1,307 men and 419 women, but every analysis uses 1,589 people (379 women, 1,210 men); exclusions for incomplete landmark ages were more frequent among outpatient women (12.5%) than in the other cells (4.5% to 7.8%) (editors' arithmetic from p. 253 and Table 1), and included and excluded participants were not compared.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; a small, unexamined selection within the women's outpatient group.

reporting_issues.issue: Intervals were computed in the average order of the landmarks, so they could be negative, yet only 53% of participants reported that order (p. 256); mean intervals therefore mix people whose landmarks came in different orders.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mean interval between two landmarks is not the time between events experienced in that order for nearly half the sample.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 entry ages and Table 2 onset ages describe the 1,589-person analysis sample; first-treatment intervals and Figure 1 concern735. Sex-specific entry ages for that subgroup and the handling of the index inpatient/day-hospital episode in aftercare participants are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat comparisons between the 3.9-year whole-sample onset gap and 4.2-year subgroup interval gap as approximate cross-sample comparisons, not a measured explanation of the entire interval difference.

disagreements.first_pass: A treatment sample of trial volunteers, the kind of sample in which telescoping was first described, not a general-population sample. design_detail: Meta-analysis of 36 balanced-placebo experiments (34 articles published before September 1985 in eight journals, listed in the Appendix) in which an alcohol-versus-placebo beverage was crossed with an alcohol-versus-placebo expectancy instruction. 144 main effects of alcohol and 144 of expectancy were coded; multiple indicators of one dependent variable were averaged within each study, giving (by the editors' count from the degrees of freedom) 56 study-by-measure units across 11 types of dependent variable. Effects were expressed as Hedges' g between marginal means, signed by the predicted direction, and pooled as unweighted mean g with an unweighted Stouffer Z and Rosenthal's diffuse-comparison heterogeneity chi-square; Alcohol × Expectancy interactions were counted by statistical significance.
can_establish: How often, and in which direction, alcohol content and the belief of having drunk alcohol were reported to change behaviour in balanced-placebo laboratory experiments published before September 1985, and for which types of behaviour each manipulation showed a significant pooled effect.
cannot_establish: The size of either effect in any defined population or at any dose (participants, sample sizes and doses are not extracted; means are unweighted with unreported effects set to zero; no confidence intervals); whether alcohol and expectancy truly do not interact (a count of significant interaction tests in small factorial experiments cannot show that interactions are absent); or effects at higher blood-alcohol levels, at which, in the editors' view (the paper gives no doses and does not discuss it), a placebo deception could not be kept up.

sample.recruitment: Published balanced-placebo studies of alcohol consumption before September 1985; no databases, search terms or other search methods are described. The authors wrote to researchers whose reports gave effects only as non-significant, asking for fuller results (pp. 347–349).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized factorial designs crossing an alcohol–placebo beverage manipulation with an alcohol–placebo expectancy manipulation. Excluded: studies that manipulated expectations about alcohol's effects (for example more vs less arousal) or about the type of beverage (spirits vs beer) (footnote 2, p. 348). Only variables of primary interest to each study's authors were coded; indirectly related variables were dropped (footnote 3, p. 348).
sample.demographics: Not extracted. Participants' sex, age, drinking history, sample sizes and the alcohol doses are not reported for the included experiments. The text mentions a women-only physiology study contrasted with five men-only studies (p. 352), and describes the three studies of drinking as studies in people with alcoholism (p. 354), although one of them (Marlatt et al., 1973) also tested social drinkers.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.
sample.selection_effects: Published studies only, located by an undescribed search, in eight journals; effects reported only as non-significant and not supplied by the authors were set to zero (50 of 144 alcohol and 65 of 144 expectancy effects). Several effect types rest on three studies. The first author is an author of one included study (Hull, Levenson, Young & Sher, 1983; Appendix).

exposure.measurement: As manipulated in each experiment (alcohol vs placebo beverage; told alcohol vs told placebo). The authors rated each experiment's expectancy manipulation from 0 to 3 on three criteria taken from Marlatt and Rohsenow (1980): taste masking, mixing in front of the participant from appropriately labelled bottles, and a significant effect on the manipulation check (independent ratings by both authors, 97% agreement) (p. 349).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted: no doses, blood-alcohol levels or drinking periods are reported for the included experiments.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Within each experiment: the placebo beverage (for the alcohol effect) and the told-placebo instruction (for the expectancy effect), each compared on marginal means across the other factor.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized factorial designs by inclusion criterion).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; participant characteristics were not extracted, so moderators such as sex, drinking history and dose could not be examined except post hoc in single contrasts.

outcomes.instruments: Eleven types of dependent variable: aggression, alcohol consumption, physical sensations, mood, attentional focus, locus of control, helping, motor performance, information processing (memory), physiology (heart rate, skin conductance, skin temperature, pulse transit time) and sexual arousal (penile tumescence, vaginal pressure pulse or self-report) (pp. 349, 352–353).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study measures were not appraised. Signs were set by predictions drawn from the literature: alcohol predicted to increase aggression, drinking, specific physical sensations, positive mood, helping, locus of control and external attention and to impair motor performance, information processing, certain physiological responses and sexual arousal; expectancy predicted to act like alcohol except to increase sexual arousal and to reduce helping (p. 349).
outcomes.operationalization: Each main effect as g = (M1 − M2)/S pooled between marginal means and as a z from its one-tailed p; positive when in the predicted direction. Behaviours were grouped, following Marlatt and Rohsenow's attributional account, into illicit social behaviours (sexual arousal, drinking, aggression, being unhelpful) and other behaviours (pp. 348–349).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 22 counts the pooled estimates (2 overall, 4 in Table 1, 16 in Tables 2–9); several post hoc contrasts are added (humorous vs neutral settings, women-only vs men-only studies, physiological vs self-report measures, blind vs non-blind experimenters).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Both authors classified manipulation quality (97% agreement) and experimenter blindness (94% agreement) independently; who extracted the effect sizes, and whether in duplicate, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unweighted mean g, unweighted Stouffer Z, diffuse-comparison chi-square; no confidence intervals, weights or sample sizes. Overall (56 units by the editors' count): alcohol mean g 0.18 (absolute 0.35), Z = 5.10, p < .001, chi-square(55) = 136.49; expectancy 0.08 (absolute 0.27), Z = 2.03, p = .04, chi-square(55) = 98.49 (p. 349). Illicit social vs other behaviours: expectancy 0.17 (Z = 2.32, p < .05) vs 0.03 (Z = 0.81); alcohol 0.09 (Z = 1.26) vs 0.23 (Z = 5.42, p < .001) (Table 1, p. 350). By type (alcohol; expectancy): information processing, 5 studies, 0.5344 (z = 3.618, p < .001); −0.002. Physical sensations, 3 studies, 0.6440 (Z = 4.549, p < .001); 0.0450. Mood, 14 units, 0.209 (Z = 3.026, p < .01); 0.061 (chi-square(13) = 22.38, p < .05). Physiological arousal, 8 studies, −0.225 (Z = −1.193; chi-square(7) = 46.48, p < .001; 0.10 without one suspect study); 0.046. Motor performance, 3 studies, 0.6360 (Z = 3.725, p < .001); 0.1230. Sexual arousal, 9 studies, −0.017; 0.306 (Z = 2.861, p < .01). Aggression, 7 units, 0.255 (Z = 1.764, p < .10); −0.131 (Z = −1.194). Drinking, 3 studies, −0.040; 0.523 (Z = 2.870, p < .01) (Tables 2–9, pp. 350–355). Interactions: 7 of 137 tests significant at .05 (5.1%) (p. 354). Editors' calculations: assuming the heterogeneity chi-squares partition additively (55 = 19 + 35 + 1), the difference between illicit social and other behaviours gives chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39 (p ≈ .24) for expectancy and ≈ 4.93 (p ≈ .03) for alcohol; 6.85 of 137 interaction tests would be significant by chance alone.
analysis.covariates: None. Moderators examined at study level: quality of the expectancy manipulation (correlation with expectancy g), experimenter blindness to expectancy, and post hoc single contrasts (setting of mood studies, participants' sex in physiology studies, type of sexual-arousal measure).
analysis.selective_reporting: Analyses excluding the effects set to zero are said never to have changed a conclusion about whether an effect exists, but their estimates are not shown. Helping, locus of control and attentional focus enter Table 1 (by the editors' count 1 and 3 units) but have no table or pooled estimate of their own.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Physical sensations, motor performance and drinking each rest on 3 studies; with unweighted means and no intervals, the precision of every pooled g is unknown.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In balanced-placebo experiments published up to 1985, the alcohol actually drunk had significant pooled effects on information processing, physical sensations, mood (mean g 0.21) and motor performance, and none on physiology, sexual arousal or drinking; a near-significant effect on aggression (0.26, p < .10). Believing one had drunk alcohol had significant pooled effects on sexual arousal (0.31) and on drinking (0.52, 3 studies), none elsewhere, and a non-significant negative effect on aggression (−0.13). Heterogeneity was substantial for several types. Seven of 137 interaction tests (5.1%) were significant.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says expectancy had "strong effects on relatively deviant social behaviors" and minimal effects on nonsocial ones, with alcohol showing the opposite pattern; the conclusion says expectancy increases illicit social behaviours and that the two factors rarely interact (pp. 347, 358). Gaps: (1) the expectancy effect on illicit social behaviours averaged g 0.17, and the difference from other behaviours was not tested (editors' partition chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39, p ≈ .24), so the support for the attributional account rests on a significant result beside a non-significant one; (2) expectancy did not increase aggression (g −0.13), so the claim about illicit social behaviours rests on sexual arousal and drinking; (3) from a count of significant interaction tests the discussion concludes that alcohol's effects are the same whatever people expect and that the balanced-placebo design is no longer necessary (pp. 357–358), although such a count cannot show absence of interaction, and the authors' own finding that alcohol usually alters what participants believe they drank (18 of 20 studies without a prior beverage question) means the told-placebo, given-alcohol cell seldom tests alcohol without expectancy (the authors answer, p. 358, that alcohol and expectancy never both had significant effects on the same measure, an argument that again rests on which tests reached significance); (4) setting 35% to 45% of effects to zero, unweighted means and no intervals make every pooled g a rough lower bound of unknown precision; (5) the alcohol effects called strong and homogeneous (p. 356) include mood at g 0.21; (6) the recommended alternative, adjusting for reported expectancy as a covariate, adjusts for a variable that alcohol itself changes, which can bias the alcohol estimate (editors' note).

timeline.event: Marlatt, Demming & Reid: balanced-placebo taste-task experiment on drinking in men with and without alcoholism; one of the three studies in Table 9.

Marlatt & Rohsenow, chapter on cognitive processes and the balanced placebo design: source of the attributional hypothesis and of the manipulation-quality criteria used here (as described in this meta-analysis; not read).

Steele & Southwick meta-analysis of alcohol and social behaviour: 8 of its 35 studies overlap with this one; it reported an expectancy mean effect size of .38 for those eight and an alcohol mean effect size of .49 for all 35, without heterogeneity statistics (footnote 5, p. 356).
This meta-analysis.
McKay & Schare, meta-analysis of alcohol and alcohol-expectancy effects on subjective reports and physiological reactivity; on the project's General list, not yet appraised.
Testa et al., symposium report revisiting the placebo condition in alcohol expectancy research; on the project's General list, not yet appraised.

replication.where_it_stands: The first meta-analysis restricted to balanced-placebo experiments, and still the source usually cited for the split between alcohol effects and expectancy effects. Its methods predate weighted random-effects pooling and confidence intervals, so it supports statements about the direction and pattern of effects by type of behaviour in laboratory studies up to 1985, not about their size. Later syntheses on the project's list (McKay & Schare, 1999; Testa et al., 2006) remain to be appraised.

funding.funder: No funding statement printed; the authors thank alcohol researchers who provided previously unreported results (author note, p. 347).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Dartmouth College (Hull) and Connecticut College (Bond). The first author is an author of one included study (Hull, Levenson, Young & Sher, 1983; Appendix, p. 359). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A modern systematic review with a reproducible search, duplicate extraction of sample sizes, doses or blood-alcohol levels and participant characteristics, a weighted random-effects synthesis with confidence and prediction intervals, risk-of-bias assessment including blinding integrity, and interactions estimated as effect sizes with intervals; and adequately powered factorial experiments estimating the alcohol × expectancy interaction at more than one dose, with blinding of beverage content checked rather than assumed.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Intervention and comparator are defined by the design criterion, but the population is left open (social drinkers and people with alcoholism, men and women pooled) and the outcomes were identified from the included studies rather than specified beforehand.
No protocol (1986).
The restriction to balanced-placebo designs is explained (to compare alcohol and expectancy within the same experiments), and other expectancy manipulations are excluded with a reason (footnote 2).
No databases, search terms or dates beyond a September 1985 cut-off; published studies only. The authors did write to researchers for unreported results.
Not reported.
Not reported for the effect sizes; only the manipulation-quality and experimenter-blindness ratings were made independently by both authors (97% and 94% agreement).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list; only a category of excluded designs is described (footnote 2).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Studies appear by name with their g values and in the Appendix; sample sizes, participants, doses, settings and outcome measures are not tabulated.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two features were rated: the quality of the expectancy deception (0–3) and whether the experimenter was blind to the expectancy condition (7 of 36 studies). Randomization, allocation concealment and selective reporting were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Unweighted mean g and unweighted Stouffer Z, no confidence intervals, no model allowing for the significant heterogeneity, and effects of unknown size set to zero; heterogeneity was tested and explored.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The two rated features were tested against effect sizes: manipulation quality did not correlate with expectancy g (r = .07, −.05, .14), and experimenter blindness did not change mean effects (t < 1.00) though non-blind studies varied more. Other sources of bias were not assessed, so this covers only part of the item's intent.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion takes up experimenter blindness, a study with incorrect degrees of freedom (with a sensitivity analysis) and the failure of the told-placebo, given-alcohol deception, and recommends blinding of experimenters.
Heterogeneity is tested for every pooled estimate and explored by type of behaviour, setting, sex and measure type, mostly post hoc and with single studies in some contrasts.
Not investigated; only published studies were included.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Neither funding nor conflicts are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 15), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. This is a 1986 meta-analysis judged against standards written later; the judgment concerns how far its pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries, not its historical importance. It is transparent about its choices (zero imputation, unweighted pooling, the post hoc status of several contrasts) and tests two bias-related features. Citable for: the direction and pattern of alcohol versus expectancy effects by type of behaviour in balanced-placebo experiments up to 1985, the frequency of significant interactions, the low rate of experimenter blinding to expectancy, and the finding that alcohol usually changes what participants believe they drank. Not citable for: effect magnitudes, absence of interaction, or any dose or population.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 34 articles (36 experiments) published before September 1985 in eight journals, each crossing an alcohol-versus-placebo beverage with an alcohol-versus-placebo expectancy instruction; 144 main effects of alcohol and 144 of expectancy were coded from the variables of primary interest to each study's authors.
key_findings.locator: Sample of Studies; Data Extracted From Each Study, 1st paragraph (p. 348); Appendix (pp. 359–360)
key_findings.note: The text says the earliest article was dated 1972; the earliest in the Appendix is Marlatt, Demming & Reid (1973).

key_findings.finding: Effects reported only as non-significant and not obtainable from the original authors were set to zero: 50 of 144 alcohol and 65 of 144 expectancy main effects. Analyses excluding them are said never to have changed a conclusion about whether an effect exists; their estimates are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Data Extracted From Each Study, 2nd paragraph (p. 348, continuing on p. 349)

key_findings.finding: Methods: each main effect as Hedges' g between marginal means, positive when in the predicted direction, and as a z from its one-tailed p; multiple indicators of one dependent variable averaged within each study; pooled as an unweighted mean g and an unweighted Stouffer Z, with a diffuse-comparison chi-square for heterogeneity; interactions counted by whether they reached p < .05.
key_findings.locator: Data Extracted From Each Study, 2nd to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Overall, the mean signed g was 0.18 for alcohol and 0.08 for expectancy (mean absolute g 0.35 and 0.27); both were significant (Z = 5.10, p < .001; Z = 2.03, p = .04) and heterogeneous (chi-square(55) = 136.49, p < .0001; chi-square(55) = 98.49, p < .001).
key_findings.locator: General Analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Fifty-six study-by-measure units is the editors' count from the degrees of freedom (55 = 19 + 35 + 1, Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Illicit social behaviours (sexual arousal, drinking, aggression, being unhelpful) vs other behaviours: expectancy mean g 0.17 (absolute 0.40), Z = 2.32 (p < .05), heterogeneity chi-square(19) = 53.27 (p < .001), vs 0.03 (absolute 0.20), Z = 0.81, chi-square(35) = 43.83; alcohol 0.09 (absolute 0.29), Z = 1.26, chi-square(19) = 26.68, vs 0.23 (absolute 0.38), Z = 5.42 (p < .001), chi-square(35) = 104.88 (p < .001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; General Analyses, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The difference between the two categories was not tested. Editors' calculation, assuming the heterogeneity statistics partition additively: between-category chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39 (p ≈ .24) for expectancy and ≈ 4.93 (p ≈ .03) for alcohol; the categories hold 20 and 36 study-by-measure units (editors' count from the degrees of freedom).

key_findings.finding: The quality of the expectancy manipulation (0–3 on taste masking, mixing in front of the participant from labelled bottles and a significant manipulation check; 97% agreement between the authors) was not related to expectancy effect sizes: r = .07 overall, −.05 for social and .14 for nonsocial behaviours, all non-significant.
key_findings.locator: General Analyses, 4th paragraph (p. 349) and 7th paragraph (p. 350)

key_findings.finding: Information processing (memory; 5 studies): alcohol mean g 0.5344 (impairment), z = 3.618 (p < .001), heterogeneity chi-square(4) = 4.69; expectancy −0.002, z = −0.004, chi-square(4) = 0.79.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Meta-Analyses of Nonsocial Behaviors, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Physical sensations (3 studies): alcohol mean g 0.6440, Z = 4.549 (p < .001), chi-square(2) = 0.20; expectancy 0.0450, Z = 0.305, chi-square(2) = 0.33.
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Self-reported mood (14 units; improvement positive): alcohol mean g 0.209, Z = 3.026 (p < .01), chi-square(13) = 12.31; expectancy 0.061, Z = 1.084, chi-square(13) = 22.38 (p < .05). Post hoc, expectancy improved mood more in the one study with a humorous setting than in neutral settings (g 0.67 vs 0.00; contrast Z = 2.89, p < .01), with no difference between anxiety-arousing and neutral settings (Z = 0.38, ns).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 351); paragraph beginning 'In order to explain' (p. 352, 1st paragraph)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: the four neutral-setting studies in Table 4 average −0.025, not 0.00.

key_findings.finding: Physiological arousal (8 studies; decreased arousal positive): alcohol mean g −0.225, Z = −1.193, chi-square(7) = 46.48 (p < .001); expectancy 0.046, Z = 0.333, chi-square(7) = 16.77 (p < .05). Without one study whose test had incorrect degrees of freedom (Briddell et al., 1978), alcohol g 0.10, Z = 0.91, chi-square(6) = 5.22, ns; expectancy heterogeneity chi-square(6) = 14.54, p < .05. A post hoc contrast of the one women-only study with five men-only studies gave Z = 2.56, p < .02 for expectancy.
key_findings.locator: Table 5; paragraphs beginning 'Table 5 displays' and 'A potential explanation'

key_findings.finding: Motor performance (3 studies): alcohol mean g 0.6360 (impairment), Z = 3.725 (p < .001), chi-square(2) = 6.90 (p < .05); expectancy 0.1230, Z = 0.645, chi-square(2) = 0.98.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Three studies have been conducted' (p. 352, right column); Table 6 (p. 353)

key_findings.finding: Sexual arousal (9 studies): expectancy mean g 0.306 (increase), Z = 2.861 (p < .01), chi-square(8) = 20.64 (p < .01); alcohol −0.017 (positive meaning reduced arousal), Z = −0.056, chi-square(8) = 10.04. Expectancy effects did not differ between physiological and self-report measures (g 0.41 vs 0.33, Z = −0.45, ns), nor did alcohol effects (0.00 vs 0.10, Z = 0.58, ns).
key_findings.locator: Table 7; Meta-Analyses of Social Behaviors, paragraph beginning 'Nine studies'

key_findings.finding: Aggression (7 units; increase positive): alcohol mean g 0.255, Z = 1.764 (p < .10), chi-square(6) = 12.88 (p < .05); expectancy −0.131, Z = −1.194, chi-square(6) = 18.40 (p < .01). The authors conclude that expecting alcohol did not increase aggression and may lower it.
key_findings.locator: Table 8; paragraph beginning 'Seven studies'

key_findings.finding: Drinking or desire to drink (3 studies: Marlatt et al., 1973; Maisto et al., 1977; Berg et al., 1981): expectancy mean g 0.523 (study values 0.66, 0.52, 0.39), Z = 2.870 (p < .01), chi-square(2) = 0.32; alcohol −0.040 (−0.17, not significant, 0.05), Z = −0.315, chi-square(2) = 0.30.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Three studies have investigated' (p. 354); Table 9 (p. 355)
key_findings.note: Maisto et al. (1977) reanalysed data first reported by Engle & Williams (1972) (p. 354). For Marlatt et al. (1973), the editors reproduce Table 9's values by averaging that study's three measures (total amount, sips, amount per sip): about 0.66 for expectancy and −0.17 for alcohol, whereas its expectancy effect on total amount alone is about 1.1 (editors' calculation from its F ratios and means).

key_findings.finding: Interactions: 7 of 137 Alcohol × Expectancy tests (5.1%) were significant at .05 (137 rather than 144 because one study did not report interactions for seven measures); five of the seven were significant by narrow margins, and they had no consistent shape. The authors conclude that alcohol and expectancy interact no more often than chance.
key_findings.locator: Interactions of Alcohol and Expectancy, 1st paragraph (p. 354, continuing on p. 355); footnote 4 (p. 354)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 6.85 of 137 tests would be significant by chance alone; a count of significant tests shows only that interactions were seldom detected.

key_findings.finding: Only 7 of 36 studies kept the experimenter blind to the expectancy condition (classification agreement 94%). Mean effect sizes did not differ by experimenter blindness (t < 1.00), but effects varied more when the experimenter was not blind (alcohol effects F = 3.76, p < .01; expectancy effects on nonsocial behaviours F = 5.07, p < .03).
key_findings.locator: Other Issues: The Use of Blind Techniques

key_findings.finding: Among studies with a manipulation check, 59% found that the alcohol actually given changed what participants believed they had drunk: 1 of 12 (8%) when participants were first asked which beverage they had received, 18 of 20 (90%) when they were not. The authors read this as alcohol almost always altering expectancy, so that the design seldom provides a condition in which people drink alcohol without believing they have.
key_findings.locator: Utility of the Balanced-Placebo Design, paragraph beginning 'The above conclusion' and the next paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors' answer to this point is key finding 19 (p. 358).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that for alcohol and the behaviours reviewed the balanced-placebo design is no longer necessary, and recommend using participants' reported expectancies as a covariate when the aim is to estimate the effect of alcohol alone.
key_findings.locator: Utility of the Balanced-Placebo Design, last paragraph (p. 357, continuing on p. 358)

key_findings.finding: Overlap with Steele and Southwick (1985): 8 of their 35 studies are among these 36; they reported an expectancy mean effect size of .38 for those eight and an alcohol mean effect size of .49 for all 35, without heterogeneity statistics.
key_findings.locator: Footnote 5

key_findings.finding: The authors accept that the balanced-placebo design did not give an unconfounded manipulation of alcohol and expectancy, but argue that it still separated their effects: for no dependent variable in Tables 2–9 did alcohol and expectancy both show significant effects, still less in the same direction, so they conclude that the alcohol effects did not come about through expectancy.
key_findings.locator: Utility of the Balanced-Placebo Design › 'Success of the balanced-placebo design' (run-in heading), left column
key_findings.note: The authors' answer to key finding 16; like the interaction count (key finding 14), it rests on which tests reached significance.

reporting_issues.issue: The Lang studies are labelled the wrong way round in two tables: Table 7 (sexual arousal) lists Lang, Goeckner, Adesso & Marlatt (1975), which the Appendix gives as the aggression study, and Table 8 (aggression) lists 'Lang, Searles, Lauerman, & Adesso (1975)', a combination that matches no Appendix entry; the text cites Lang, Searles, Lauerman & Adesso (1980) for sexual arousal and Lang et al. (1975) for aggression.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study lists in the text match the table contents, so the values probably belong to the right studies, but a reader matching table rows to the Appendix would attribute them to the wrong papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Effects of unknown size were set to zero (50 of 144 for alcohol, 65 of 144 for expectancy), means are unweighted, and no sample sizes, weights or confidence intervals are given; the analyses excluding the zero values are described but not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Pooled g values are shrunk towards zero by an unknown amount and their precision cannot be computed; cite them for direction and pattern, not size.

reporting_issues.issue: The central contrast between illicit social and other behaviours (Table 1) is drawn from a significant expectancy effect in one category beside a non-significant one in the other, without a test of the difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation from the printed heterogeneity statistics (assuming additive partition): chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39, p ≈ .24 for the expectancy difference; the attributional reading of Table 1 is less secure than the text implies, while the alcohol difference (≈ 4.93, p ≈ .03) is larger.

reporting_issues.issue: Multiple indicators of one dependent variable were averaged within studies; for Marlatt et al. (1973) the Table 9 values (expectancy 0.66, alcohol −0.17) are reproduced only by averaging total amount drunk with sip frequency and amount per sip (editors' reconstruction from that paper's means and F ratios).
reporting_issues.consequence: The drinking category mixes amounts drunk with counts of sips, so the 0.66 entered for that study is lower than its expectancy effect on total amount alone (about 1.1; 0.66 is about 58% of 1.13); the pooled 0.523 is not an effect on quantity drunk.

reporting_issues.issue: Helping, locus of control and attentional focus contribute units to Table 1 (by the editors' count 1 unit among illicit social behaviours, 20 minus 19, and 3 among other measures, 36 minus 33) but have no table or pooled estimate of their own.
reporting_issues.consequence: These effects cannot be checked, and they are inside the Table 1 estimates.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract says expectancy had "strong effects on relatively deviant social behaviors" and minimal effects on nonsocial ones, with alcohol showing the opposite pattern; the conclusion says expectancy increases illicit social behaviours and that the two factors rarely interact (pp. 347, 358). Gaps: (1) the expectancy effect on illicit social behaviours averaged g 0.17, and the difference from other behaviours was not tested (editors' partition chi-square(1) ≈ 1.39, p ≈ .24), so the support for the attributional account rests on a significant result beside a non-significant one; (2) expectancy did not increase aggression (g −0.13), so the claim about illicit social behaviours rests on sexual arousal and drinking; (3) from a count of significant interaction tests the discussion concludes that alcohol's effects are the same whatever people expect and that the balanced-placebo design is no longer necessary (pp. 357–358), although such a count cannot show absence of interaction, and the authors' own finding that alcohol usually alters what participants believe they drank (18 of 20 studies without a prior beverage question) means the told-placebo, given-alcohol cell seldom tests alcohol without expectancy; (4) setting 35% to 45% of effects to zero, unweighted means and no intervals make every pooled g a rough lower bound of unknown precision; (5) the alcohol effects called strong and homogeneous (p. 356) include mood at g 0.21; (6) the recommended alternative, adjusting for reported expectancy as a covariate, adjusts for a variable that alcohol itself changes, which can bias the alcohol estimate (editors' note).
