design_detail: Randomized between-subjects balanced-placebo laboratory experiment, 2 × 2 × 2: beverage given (vodka and tonic, or tonic only) × instructions (told the drinks were vodka and tonic, or tonic only), with each of the four cells run in two non-randomized groups of men: 32 classified by the study as alcoholic from their history (treatment admissions, drunkenness arrests, Alcoholics Anonymous or a vocational rehabilitation programme for alcoholism; called here the alcoholism group) and 32 social drinkers. Drinking was measured during a 15-minute ad-lib 'taste-rating' task used as a cover story. Madison, Wisconsin; received December 1971, published 1973.
can_establish: Whether, in this short laboratory taste task, the belief that the drinks contained alcohol and the actual presence of alcohol each changed how much men with and without alcoholism drank in 15 minutes, at the modest blood-alcohol levels the task produced.
cannot_establish: Whether alcohol triggers uncontrolled drinking over longer periods, at higher blood-alcohol levels or outside a taste test (the authors name these limits, pp. 240–241); whether the alcoholism group's heavier drinking is caused by alcoholism (that comparison is not randomized and the groups differed in age and social class); whether a moderate pharmacological effect was missed (8 men per cell); or anything about women.

sample.recruitment: Community recruitment in and around Madison, Wisconsin. Alcoholism group: sign-up sheets left with hotel desk clerks and bartenders in areas the authors describe as frequented by people with alcoholism, inviting volunteers to a taste study that might involve sampling alcohol; names supplied by a former treatment patient of local people believed to be drinking again; and friends and acquaintances of these men. Social drinkers: the same sign-up sheets in hotels, bars, a university workplace and with taxi drivers, a newspaper advertisement for male social drinkers aged 21 or over, and friends of other participants. Paid five dollars; the consent form said alcohol might or might not be consumed (pp. 234–235).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All: men; a 30-minute screening interview on demographics, drinking pattern, treatment history and arrests for drunken conduct; candidates were not told the criteria for group assignment (p. 235). Alcoholism group: at least one of (a) one or more admissions to an alcoholism treatment centre, (b) five or more arrests for drunk and disorderly conduct, (c) past membership of Alcoholics Anonymous or the local vocational rehabilitation programme for alcoholism (all but 7 of 32 met two or more); and alcohol drunk within the previous 2 weeks with no immediate intention to stop, so that men trying to stay abstinent were not involved (p. 235). Social drinkers: did not abstain and did not meet the alcoholism criteria; excluded if they reported heavy drinking or called their drinking a problem (p. 235). Breath test on arrival: readings above 0.06% led to a new appointment; participants had been asked not to drink for 12 hours beforehand (p. 235). No diagnostic instrument was used.
sample.demographics: Alcoholism group: age 24–65 (mean 46.75); 23 had been treated for alcoholism (mean 5.5 admissions), 21 had drinking-related arrests (mean 21.5 arrests), 18 reported past Alcoholics Anonymous membership and 10 the vocational rehabilitation programme. Social drinkers: age 23–63 (mean 37.19); the age difference was significant (p < .01). Hollingshead social class index 59.2 vs 52.2, both within Social Class IV. Education (other than as part of the index), ethnicity, usual drinking quantity and other drug use are not reported (p. 235).
sample.attrition: None reported; the degrees of freedom of every analysis (1/56) fit complete data on 64 men in 8 cells. The numbers screened, rejected, or sent home after a positive breath test are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Men recruited through bars, hotels and a former patient's contacts who were currently drinking and not trying to abstain, compared with younger social drinkers recruited partly by newspaper advertisement; the groups differ in age (9.6 years on the printed means) and social class index, and the group comparison is not randomized. Excluding men who wanted to abstain means the results do not describe people in recovery. A taste-study invitation may have selected men willing to drink in a laboratory.

exposure.measurement: Manipulated. Beverage: vodka and tonic, or tonic only; instructions: told the beverage was vodka and tonic, or tonic only (four cells within each group). The alcoholic mixture was chosen in a pretest in which 25 student social drinkers could not tell it from tonic better than chance (44% judged it alcoholic) (p. 234). All participants rinsed with a mouthwash to which alcohol had been added, described as dulling taste and creating an alcohol sensation in the mouth (p. 236). Manipulation check: after the task each man was asked whether any drink had contained alcohol and, if yes, what percentage (p. 236). Blood alcohol was not measured after the task; for men given alcohol it was estimated from body weight and alcohol drunk with a published formula (American Medical Association, 1959) (pp. 237, 239).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions, oral: a primer drink about 20 minutes before the task (in the alcohol conditions described as equivalent to one bar mixed drink; tonic only in the others), then free access for 15 minutes to three decanters, with the instruction to sample as much as needed to rate the drinks (pp. 236–237). The amount drunk was self-selected. Mean estimated end-of-task blood alcohol: alcoholism group .093% (told alcohol) and .056% (told tonic); social drinkers .044% and .031% (p. 239).
exposure.polysubstance: Not assessed or reported (other drugs, tobacco).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Asked not to drink for 12 hours before the session; breath test on arrival, readings above 0.06% sent home to return sober; the authors state all but a few eligible men read zero (p. 235).

comparison.controls: For the randomized factors, the other beverage and instruction cells within the same group (8 men per cell, implied by the degrees of freedom). For the group factor, 32 male social drinkers.
comparison.matching: Age matching was attempted but failed (mean 46.75 vs 37.19 years, p < .01); age was not significantly correlated with any consumption measure (coefficients not printed, p. 239). Social class index 59.2 vs 52.2. No matching on usual drinking.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Usual quantity and frequency of drinking, tolerance, craving before the session, other drug use, smoking, psychiatric comorbidity and body weight (used for the blood-alcohol estimates) are not measured or not reported.

outcomes.instruments: (1) Total amount drunk in fluid ounces (the 72 ounces in the decanters minus what remained, allowing for the 6-ounce primer); (2) number of sips, counted in 3-minute blocks by a rater behind a disguised one-way mirror; (3) amount per sip (total divided by sips; an approximation by the authors' account); (4) post-task estimates of the percentage of alcohol in the drinks; plus formula-estimated blood alcohol in the given-alcohol cells and informal remarks heard over an intercom (pp. 236–237, 240).
outcomes.validity_norms: The taste-rating task adapts a procedure from a study of eating (Schachter, Goldman & Gordon, 1968); no validation of it as a measure of drinking is reported. The authors call the per-sip index and the per-block values of Figure 1 approximations (pp. 237–238).
outcomes.operationalization: Loss of control was operationalized as greater, and progressively increasing, drinking by men actually given alcohol, especially in the alcoholism group. The progressive-increase part was judged only by inspecting Figure 1 (3-minute blocks); no statistical test of the time course is reported (pp. 238–240).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four 2 × 2 × 2 fixed-effects analyses of variance (seven effects each, 28 F tests) plus correlations of age with each measure; only significant F values are printed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The rater counting sips was unaware of the condition (p. 236). The experimenter (the second author) prepared the drinks in front of each participant, read the instructions and returned midway through the task, so she knew the assignment (p. 236).

analysis.effect_sizes: As printed (no standard deviations anywhere). Total amount: instructions F = 20.59, df = 1/56, p < .01 (told tonic 9.12 vs told alcohol 17.77 fl oz in the text; Table 1 gives 18.77); beverage F = .50 (given tonic 14.69 vs given alcohol 13.19); group F = 7.22, p < .01 (alcoholism group 16.80 vs social drinkers 11.08); interactions not significant, F not printed (p. 237). Sips: group F = 5.68, p < .025 (21.59 vs 29.81); beverage F = 4.01, p < .05 (alcohol 22.25 vs tonic 29.16) (p. 237). Amount per sip: group F = 10.65 (.92 vs .48 oz) and instructions F = 11.89 (.94 vs .46 oz), both p < .01 (p. 238). Alcohol-content estimates: instructions F = 44.49, p < .01 (about 1% vs 27.6%) (p. 239). Editors' calculations (from the printed means and F ratios, 32 men per level, df 56): the three F ratios for total amount imply the same within-cell SD of about 8.5 fl oz (8.46 to 8.52); instructions d ≈ 1.13 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.64 treating the SD as known; 0.60 to 1.66 by the noncentral t); beverage d ≈ −0.18 (95% CI −0.68 to 0.33; difference −1.5 oz, 95% CI −5.8 to +2.8); within the alcoholism group, given alcohol minus given tonic −1.2 oz (95% CI −7.2 to +4.8; 16 vs 16 men); group d ≈ 0.67; group × instructions F(1,56) ≈ 1.7, p ≈ .20 (instruction effect 12.4 oz in the alcoholism group, 6.9 oz in social drinkers); within the told-alcohol cells, alcoholism group minus social drinkers 8.5 oz, t(56) ≈ 2.8, p ≈ .007. Within-cell SDs implied for sips about 13.8 and for amount per sip about 0.55 oz.
analysis.covariates: None; age was correlated with the dependent measures instead of being adjusted for (p. 239).
analysis.selective_reporting: No standard deviations, standard errors or mean squares; cell sizes not printed; non-significant F values omitted, including the group × instructions interaction that bears on the discussion's claim about the alcoholism group; the time course in Figure 1 is described but not tested.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 8 men per cell, the editors' 95% interval for the effect of alcohol on total amount runs from about two-thirds of a standard deviation less to one-third more, so a moderate pharmacological effect cannot be excluded.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 64 men in a 15-minute laboratory taste test, being told the drinks contained vodka roughly doubled the amount drunk (about 18.8 vs 9.1 fl oz from Table 1; editors' d ≈ 1.1), while actually receiving vodka made no detectable difference (13.2 vs 14.7 oz), in both groups. The alcoholism group drank more overall and in larger sips but sipped less often; drinking mostly fell across the session; estimated end-of-task blood alcohol averaged .031% to .093%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports these results accurately and says loss of control did not occur during the task. The discussion calls the findings opposed to the view that alcohol's physiological effects alone drive increased drinking, and "strong support for the role of cognitive factors" in loss of control (p. 240). It also states that the alcoholism group told alcohol drank significantly more than the social drinkers and attributes this to a greater expectation of reinforcing effects (p. 240); no such test is printed (an editors' simple-effect test would probably support the difference), the group × instructions interaction was not significant, and expectation of reinforcement was not measured. The same discussion names the limits that restrict the inference (a short task, blood alcohol below the level at which loss of control may begin, demand characteristics of a taste test) and closes by saying the study does not discount physiological factors (pp. 240–241). The authors also name a taste-discrimination explanation of the main finding, which their data do not rule out, and argue against it (p. 240). The null effect of alcohol rests on 8 men per cell and is imprecise.

timeline.event: Engle & Williams, effect of an ounce of vodka on desire for alcohol in people with alcoholism (as titled in Hull & Bond's reference list); reanalysed in balanced-placebo form by Maisto, Lauerman & Adesso (1977), according to Hull & Bond (1986, p. 354).
This experiment: told-alcohol instructions, not alcohol itself, increased drinking in a 15-minute taste task in men with and without alcoholism.
Maisto, Lauerman & Adesso: expectancy g 0.52, alcohol effect not significant, as coded by Hull & Bond (1986, Table 9); primary paper not read.

Berg, LaBerg, Skutle & Ohman, instructed versus pharmacological effects of alcohol in alcoholics and social drinkers (title as listed): expectancy g 0.39, alcohol g 0.05, as coded by Hull & Bond (1986, Table 9); primary paper not read.

Hull & Bond meta-analysis: across these three studies of drinking or desire to drink, expectancy g 0.523 (Z = 2.870, p < .01) and alcohol g −0.040. It codes this experiment as expectancy g 0.66 and alcohol g −0.17, values the editors reproduce by averaging total amount, sip count and amount per sip, so 0.66 understates the expectancy effect on the amount drunk (about 1.1).
Testa et al., symposium report revisiting the placebo condition in alcohol expectancy research; on the project's General list, not yet appraised.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the finding (expectancy, not alcohol content, raised drinking) was seen in all three balanced-placebo studies of drinking or desire to drink pooled by Hull & Bond (1986), who do not report their doses, session lengths or settings. This experiment speaks against alcohol at low doses triggering escalating drinking within a short laboratory task; it does not test loss of control at higher blood alcohol, over longer periods or in natural settings, the limits the authors themselves named.

funding.funder: Supported in part by Grant MH-17982 from the National Institutes of Mental Health to the senior author (footnote 1, p. 233; funder's name as printed).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement printed.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the University of Wisconsin for the study; the first author had moved to the University of Washington and the third to the Oregon Research Institute (footnotes 2 and 3, p. 233). The second author was the experimenter who prepared the drinks and gave the instructions (p. 236). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A balanced-placebo or placebo-controlled experiment in people with alcohol use disorder diagnosed with a standard instrument, women included, with longer self-paced access in a more natural setting, blood alcohol measured rather than estimated across a range of levels under medical supervision, craving rated before and after the first drink, drinks prepared and instructions given by staff blind to the beverage, and enough participants to estimate the alcohol × group interaction with a useful confidence interval.

domains.note: Participants were randomly assigned to the four cells within each group, but sequence generation, allocation concealment and baseline characteristics by cell are not reported. The group factor (alcoholism group vs social drinkers) is not randomized and lies outside RoB 2: it is confounded by age, social class and recruitment route.

The experimenter knew each assignment and interacted with the participant (instructions, a midway check). The alcohol-laced mouthwash given to everyone may have weakened the told-tonic instructions. The manipulation check suggests the deception held: men told tonic but given alcohol estimated 0% (alcoholism group) and 3.5% (social drinkers) alcohol.
Complete data implied for all 64 men (df 1/56 in every analysis).
Amount drunk was measured as volume left in the decanters; sips were counted by a rater unaware of the condition. The secondary blood-alcohol values were estimated by formula, not measured.
No protocol (1973). All four measures are reported, but without standard deviations and with non-significant F values omitted; the time-course hypothesis was judged from a figure without a test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applies to the randomized comparisons (instructions and beverage). Their main outcome, volume drunk, is objective and complete, so the instruction effect is credible within this task; concerns come from unreported randomization details, an experimenter who knew the assignment and dealt with participants, and incomplete statistical reporting. The comparison of the alcoholism group with social drinkers is observational and confounded by age, social class and recruitment, and is citable only as a descriptive difference. The null effect of alcohol is imprecise (8 men per cell). Citable for: in a 15-minute laboratory taste task at low estimated blood alcohol, what men with and without alcoholism believed they were drinking, not what they drank, determined how much they drank. Not citable for: absence of loss of control at higher doses, over longer periods or in natural settings, or for women.

key_findings.finding: Being told the drinks contained vodka increased the total amount drunk in 15 minutes: 9.12 fl oz in the told-tonic cells vs 17.77 fl oz (as printed in the text) in the told-alcohol cells, F = 20.59, df = 1/56, p < .01, in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount of Beverage Consumed, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: Table 1 implies 18.77, not 17.77, for the told-alcohol mean ((23.00 + 14.53)/2; also twice the grand mean 13.94 minus 9.12). Editors' calculation: d ≈ 1.13 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.64), using the within-cell SD of about 8.5 oz implied by the printed F ratios and treating it as known; the exact noncentral-t interval (t = 4.54, df 56) is 0.60 to 1.66.

key_findings.finding: The beverage actually given did not change the amount drunk: 14.69 fl oz when given tonic vs 13.19 when given vodka and tonic, F = .50, df = 1/56; the instructions × beverage interaction was not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount of Beverage Consumed, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: difference −1.5 oz (95% CI −5.8 to +2.8), d ≈ −0.18 (−0.68 to 0.33); within the alcoholism group alone −1.2 oz (95% CI −7.2 to +4.8), 16 vs 16 men.

key_findings.finding: Cell means for total amount drunk: alcoholism group told tonic 10.94 (given tonic) and 10.25 (given alcohol), told alcohol 23.87 and 22.13; social drinkers told tonic 9.31 and 5.94, told alcohol 14.62 and 14.44 fl oz; grand mean 13.94.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: The alcoholism group drank more than the social drinkers overall (16.80 vs 11.08 fl oz, F = 7.22, df = 1/56, p < .01); the group × instructions interaction is reported only as not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount of Beverage Consumed, 1st paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: the instruction effect was 12.4 oz in the alcoholism group and 6.9 oz in social drinkers, interaction F(1,56) ≈ 1.7, p ≈ .20. The group comparison is not randomized; the groups differ in age and social class.

key_findings.finding: Sips: social drinkers took more sips than the alcoholism group (29.81 vs 21.59, F = 5.68, df = 1/56, p < .025), and all men sipped more often when given tonic than when given vodka and tonic (29.16 vs 22.25, F = 4.01, p < .05); instructions and interactions were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sip Rate; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Amount per sip: the alcoholism group drank more per sip than social drinkers (.92 vs .48 fl oz, F = 10.65, df = 1/56, p < .01), and men told alcohol drank more per sip than men told tonic (.94 vs .46 fl oz, F = 11.89, p < .01); the beverage given and the interactions were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount Consumed Per Sip, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Post-task estimates of alcohol content depended only on the instructions (F = 44.49, df = 1/56, p < .01): about 1% in the told-tonic cells vs 27.6% in the told-alcohol cells. Told and given alcohol: 21.3% (alcoholism group) and 23.1% (social drinkers); told alcohol but given tonic: 28.7% and 37.2%; told tonic but given alcohol: 0% and 3.5%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimates of Alcohol Content, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Estimated end-of-task blood alcohol (formula from weight and alcohol drunk; not measured) in the given-alcohol cells: alcoholism group .093% (told alcohol) and .056% (told tonic); social drinkers .044% and .031%. The authors place the alcoholism group within, and the social drinkers below, a borderline-intoxication range of .05% to .15%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Postexperimental Blood-Alcohol Concentrations, 1st paragraph (continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: A pen mark in the scan crosses the last digit of .056; it reads as 6 on a high-resolution crop (the text layer gives .055).

key_findings.finding: Drinking did not rise progressively in men given alcohol: in most cells consumption was highest in the first 3-minute block and fell over the remaining 12 minutes; the exception the authors name is the social drinkers told tonic but given alcohol, whose drinking stayed low and stable.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 238); Results › Amount Consumed Per Sip, 2nd paragraph (p. 238, continuing on p. 239); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 240)
key_findings.note: No test of the time course is reported, and the authors call the per-block values approximations. Editors' reading of Figure 1 on a high-resolution crop (approximate): in the alcoholism group told and given alcohol, about 7.9 oz in the first block falling to about 2.0 in the fourth, then about 2.9 in the last.

key_findings.finding: Age was not significantly correlated with any consumption measure (coefficients not printed), which the authors take to show that the age gap between the groups did not drive drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Postexperimental Blood-Alcohol Concentrations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Informal observation only: several men told alcohol but given tonic, in both groups, volunteered that they felt a buzz or a bit tipsy; no systematic measure of intoxication or craving was taken, and the authors propose such measures for future work.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors list limits to generalizing: the task may have been too short; loss of control may begin only above the blood-alcohol levels reached; the taste-test framing may have discouraged drinking, since participants may have thought intoxication would spoil their ratings. They propose longer sessions, instructions encouraging heavy drinking and observation in natural drinking settings, and say the study does not discount physiological factors.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 240, right column) and 5th–6th paragraphs (pp. 240–241)

key_findings.finding: Participants: 32 men classified as alcoholic from their history (all but 7 meeting two or more criteria; 23 with treatment admissions, mean 5.5; 21 with drinking-related arrests, mean 21.5; 18 past Alcoholics Anonymous members) who had drunk in the past 2 weeks and did not intend to stop, and 32 male social drinkers; mean age 46.75 vs 37.19 years (p < .01); social class index 59.2 vs 52.2.
key_findings.locator: Method › Subjects, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors say their findings do not rule out that men in the told-alcohol conditions sampled more because detecting vodka in a mixed drink is harder than judging tonic alone, a taste-discrimination effect rather than an expectation of alcohol's effects; they argue against it because the alcoholism group drank more than the social drinkers in the told-alcohol cells and because the social drinkers sipped more often.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: Relevant data already on this card: the instructions did not change the number of sips (key finding 4) but nearly doubled the amount per sip (key finding 5). The alcoholism-group comparison the authors rely on is not printed as a test (interpretation gap).

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the told-alcohol mean for total amount drunk as 17.77 fl oz, but Table 1 implies a different value (condition means 23.00 and 14.53; grand mean 13.94 with the told-tonic mean 9.12); editors' arithmetic: 18.77 from the condition means, 18.76 from the grand mean.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in the text; the table value (about 18.8 oz) should be cited, which makes the instruction effect slightly larger than the text states.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion of age describes the alcoholism group as on average 6 years older (p. 239), but the printed means (46.75 and 37.19 years, p. 235) differ by more (editors' arithmetic: 9.6 years).
reporting_issues.consequence: The groups differed in age more than the age check says; that check (no significant correlation of age with the drinking measures) prints no coefficients and cannot be weighed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say up to 72 fluid ounces were available during the 15-minute task, but the Method states that the 6-ounce primer was drawn from the same three decanters (2 ounces from each) and allowed for in the total.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 66 ounces were available during the task. No cell mean approached either limit (highest 23.87), so the comparisons are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: No standard deviations, standard errors or mean squares are reported, cell sizes are not printed (8 per cell is implied by df 1/56), and non-significant F values are omitted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes and intervals must be back-calculated. The within-cell SD for total amount implied by the three printed F ratios (instructions, group, beverage) is the same, about 8.5 oz (editors' calculation), which supports the internal consistency of the printed means and F values.

reporting_issues.issue: The four estimated blood-alcohol means are not proportional to the amounts drunk in the same cells of Table 1: per fluid ounce of beverage, about .0042% and .0055% in the alcoholism group and .0030% and .0052% in social drinkers (editors' arithmetic); body weights and the inputs to the formula are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimates cannot be checked, and they were estimated rather than measured; the authors' suggestion that blood alcohol stayed below the level at which loss of control might begin rests on them.

reporting_issues.issue: The text summarizes Figure 1 as highest drinking in the first block and decline afterwards, with one exception, but the figure also shows rises in two alcoholism-group cells; editors' approximate reading: told and given alcohol, about 2.0 to 2.9 oz in the last 3-minute block; told tonic but given alcohol, about 3.1 to 3.5 oz from the first to the second block.
reporting_issues.consequence: Single-block fluctuations in 8 men, not the progressive increase the authors looked for; the narrative is smoother than the figure, and no statistical test of the time course was made.

design_detail: Self-described systematic review with narrative synthesis (no pooling, no appraisal of included studies) of published numeric estimates of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018: 124 estimates from 27 studies, 71 of them calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data (marked 'a' in Tables 1–3). Its aim was explicitly not to produce rates but to map how the choice of starting sample (all people with alcohol problems, untreated people, or people already in remission) and the definitions of an alcohol problem, of remission and of treatment shape the estimates, for use in treatment-service planning (p. 61). Because it maps without appraising, it is rated with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief requires, not with AMSTAR 2; it does have a systematic search and explicit selection, which the first checklist domain records.
can_establish: That estimates of untreated remission from alcohol problems drawn from published studies (71 of the 124 calculated by the reviewers, including the 2.7% minimum) span 2.7% to 98.3% and that much of this spread follows from which denominator is used and how an alcohol problem, remission and treatment are defined, with worked within-study examples.
cannot_establish: How many people with alcohol problems remit without treatment (no pooled or appraised estimate, by design), whether treatment changes the chance of remission (no treated comparison is analysed), or how far the figures apply outside North America or to recent years (24 of 27 studies are North American and 24 were published before 2010, editors' count).

sample.recruitment: Medline, PsycINFO and EMBASE searched on 10 November 2016 by one author with an expert librarian; further searches through Google Scholar, reference harvesting, the CORK Bibliography and consultation within the team, and checks by two authors up to April 2018; limits: human studies, English language, published after 1975 (p. 61, Methods › 2.2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: published journal articles giving a numeric estimate of untreated remission from alcohol problems, with no restriction on definitions, measures or design (p. 62, Methods › 2.4). Removed at screening: alcohol not the main focus (528), not about reducing alcohol use (146), formal treatment only (472), biological (357), no original data (48). Excluded at eligibility: self-help only as an adjunct to treatment (263), no separation of treated from untreated remission (51; for example Vaillant, 2003), substance use disorders without alcohol-specific data (29), mechanisms of change (127), stability of remission (2), no quantitative estimate (53). Dissertations, books and book chapters excluded (Fig. 1; pp. 61–62).
sample.demographics: Participant characteristics are not reported in the article (the study details are in the Supplementary Material, not read). Studies published 1976 to 2018; 24 of 27 (89%) North American, the others from Germany, the Netherlands and Poland; 12 longitudinal; 20 (74%) convenience samples, 1 probability sample (Kelly et al., 2018) and 6 population-based representative samples from the US, Canada, Germany and the Netherlands (p. 63, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the longitudinal studies is not reported in the article.
sample.selection_effects: English-language journal articles only, mostly North American convenience samples, and a dated literature, as the authors note (pp. 61, 70). Several included papers draw on one source cohort (Timko et al., 1993: people who had had a single detox episode or had contacted an information and referral centre, without other treatment), which contributes estimates to all three methods (Tables 1–4 footnote b, pp. 64–67). Studies that did not separate treated from untreated remission, including some long natural-history cohorts, were excluded (p. 62).

exposure.measurement: 'Untreated' as each study defined treatment, from formal alcohol treatment only to a definition counting formal treatment, self-help groups, informal help (for example clergy, college recovery programmes, employee assistance) and medical care; 27% of estimates used that broadest definition (p. 69, Results › 3.2.3; Table 5 note 3, p. 68). Some studies counted treatment for other mental-health problems as treatment; in the Timko-based studies, people seen once for detox or at an information and referral centre counted as untreated (Table 5 note 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Rarely addressed in the included studies, as the authors note; whether people who remit from alcohol without treatment seek treatment for another drug is unknown (p. 71, Discussion › 4.3, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Remission as each study defined it: abstinence only (41% of estimates), abstinence or moderate drinking (27%), no diagnosis (9%), no consequences (4%), and combinations; most studies used a one-year window; others used windows from six months to five years, or several follow-ups (pp. 68–69; Tables 1–3, 5).

comparison.controls: Not applicable: a descriptive review of proportions. The three 'methods' differ in their denominator: all people with an alcohol problem (method 1), untreated people with an alcohol problem (method 2), and people already in remission (method 3) (p. 63, Results › 3.1.1).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity, psychiatric comorbidity and other drug use were rarely reported by the included studies (p. 71).

outcomes.instruments: Each study's own definitions, tabulated by method: alcohol problem by diagnosis (39% of estimates), consequences (20%), assumed from service contact (19%), consumption (9%) or consumption and consequences (12%); remission and treatment definitions as above (Tables 1–5, pp. 64–68; p. 69).
outcomes.validity_norms: No assessment of methodological quality or bias, by design (p. 70, Discussion › 4.2). Estimates marked 'a' in Tables 1–4 were calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data; how is described only in the Supplementary Material, not read.
outcomes.operationalization: Untreated remission expressed three ways: the share of all people with an alcohol problem who remitted without treatment (method 1); the share of untreated people with an alcohol problem who remitted (method 2); the share of people in remission who had not been treated (method 3) (p. 63).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests; summaries are ranges, medians and unweighted means of estimates.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Who screened, judged eligibility and extracted data is not stated; one author ran the database search and two authors ran further searches and checks (p. 61).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling (the literature was judged too heterogeneous, p. 62). All 124 estimates ranged from 2.7% to 98.3% (p. 63). In the nine studies with estimates for all three methods (23 estimates each, Table 4): method 1 2.7% to 63.6% (median 12.4, mean 21.5); method 2 6.5% to 77.9% (median 38.9, mean 40.9); method 3 4.3% to 94.2% (median 43.9, mean 42.7) (pp. 63, 67–68). Editors' calculation: these summaries reproduce from Table 4 as printed; with Table 3's method-3 values for Timko et al. (2000), the method-3 minimum becomes 6.4% and the mean 44.0, the median unchanged.
analysis.covariates: None. Effects of definitions are shown narratively, mainly through within-study contrasts in which the same sample is counted under different definitions.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA guidelines were applied to the search (p. 61).
analysis.selective_reporting: Study details are only in the Supplementary Material. The narrative reads one key within-study contrast against its own table (Cunningham, 1999; see reporting issues). A preliminary comparison of longitudinal and cross-sectional designs is reported only as showing no meaningful difference, without data (p. 70).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Published estimates of untreated remission from alcohol problems range from 2.7% to 98.3%. Estimates that start from people already in remission (method 3, the commonest kind) run highest; those that start from everyone with an alcohol problem (method 1) run lowest, with a median of 12.4% in the nine studies that allow all three methods. Broader remission definitions raise estimates under every method; narrower treatment definitions raise methods 1 and 3; stricter problem definitions can lower or raise estimates depending on method and remission definition.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract opens by stating that untreated remission from alcohol problems is common (p. 60), a premise the review does not quantify: the method that answers 'how many people with an alcohol problem remit without treatment' (method 1) gives mostly low figures over mostly one-year windows (editors' calculation from Table 1: median of the 37 method-1 estimates 14.8%, 28 of them below 30%). The text and discussion state that method-1 estimates are robust to the definition of an alcohol problem (pp. 69–70), which Table 1 contradicts for the one study that varied that definition (Cunningham, 1999: 6.7% rising to 25.9%). The suggestion that the findings apply across countries with established treatment systems rests on two population studies said not to deviate from the rest, without analysis (p. 71). Against this, the authors are explicit that the review was not designed to yield rates and did no quality appraisal (pp. 61, 70), and their main conclusion, that planners must choose the denominator and definitions to match the question and that remitted-sample estimates do not suit planning (pp. 70–71), follows from the tables.

timeline.event: Sobell, Cunningham & Sobell, two Canadian population surveys: 78% of people in remission had not been treated, the review's example of a 'remitted sample' figure (included study; pp. 61, 63; Table 3).

Sobell, Ellingstad & Sobell, methodological review of natural-recovery research, cited here for definitional variability and methodological weaknesses (p. 61; General list #24; not read for this card).

Dawson et al., NESARC 2001–2002: untreated-sample estimates of 12.4% with abstinence only and 32.6% with abstinence or moderate drinking (included study; p. 69; General list #22; not read for this card).

Fleury et al., meta-analysis of long-term remission in mostly treatment-recruited cohorts (35% to 54% after a mean 17 years); not cited by this review, and it classes the source cohort of Moos and Moos (2007) as a clinical sample.
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: A methodological map, not an estimate. It explains why figures such as 'most people recover without treatment' (a remitted-sample ratio) and much lower figures for the share of all people with an alcohol problem who remit untreated in a given year can both be correct. Any figure the encyclopedia quotes should come from a primary study, with its denominator, its definitions of problem, remission and treatment, and its time window.

funding.funder: The Drug Policy Modelling Program is funded by the Colonial Foundation Trust and located at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, which is funded by the Australian Government; the Centre for Social Research in Health is supported by a grant from the Australian Government Department of Health. Alison Ritter holds a National Health and Medical Research Council Fellowship (APP1136944), Kari Lancaster a UNSW Scientia Fellowship, and Richard Mellor a National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre PhD Scholarship. The funders had no role in design, analysis, write-up or the decision to submit (p. 71).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declarations of interest: none (p. 71).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at UNSW Sydney (Drug Policy Modelling Program; Centre for Social Research in Health). The review serves the authors' work on treatment-planning models, and the introduction quotes their own planning paper (Ritter, Mellor et al., 2019) (p. 61); none of the 27 included studies is by the authors. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Population cohorts that assess alcohol use disorder with a standard interview at repeated, fixed intervals and record every form of help (formal treatment, mutual help, primary care, informal help), reporting all three ratios for the same people under stated definitions and windows; an individual-participant reanalysis of existing surveys named in the review (NESARC, the Netherlands Mental Health Survey and Incidence Study-2, the German TACOS) under common definitions is the achievable version.

domains.note: Three databases plus Google Scholar, reference harvesting and a specialist bibliography, with stated terms and limits and a PRISMA flow with counts and reasons (pp. 61–62); but English-language journal articles only, the database search was run by one author, and no duplicate screening or extraction is described.

No assessment of methodological quality or bias, by design (p. 70); estimates from convenience samples and from national surveys are tabulated side by side, and estimates calculated by the reviewers are explained only in the Supplementary Material.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 27 included studies is by the authors; only the motivation draws on their own planning work (p. 61).

Most conclusions are tied to tabulated contrasts, but the robustness of method-1 estimates to the problem definition is asserted against Table 1, the abstract's premise that untreated remission is common is not quantified, and cross-national applicability is suggested from two studies without analysis (pp. 60, 69–71).

domains.domain: Balance of populations and settings represented
domains.note: All numeric estimates were included whatever their size, so the range is not cherry-picked; but 24 of 27 studies are North American, 20 used convenience samples and 24 were published before 2010 (editors' count), so population-based and recent data from elsewhere are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument fits a review that maps estimates without appraising them; under the round brief it is rated with the editors' narrative-review checklist rather than AMSTAR 2. (Had AMSTAR 2 been applied, confidence would be critically low: no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no appraisal of included studies.) The overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of any appraisal. The review may be cited for the spread of published estimates (2.7% to 98.3%), for the three denominators and why they give different answers, and for within-study examples of how definitions move the estimates (for example NESARC: 12.4% with abstinence only vs 32.6% with abstinence or moderate drinking). It should not be cited for a rate of untreated remission (the authors disclaim this), for the claim that method-1 estimates are robust to the problem definition, or for its unweighted medians and means as if they described a population.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 2,103 texts screened (2,081 from databases, 22 from other searches); 1,551 removed at screening and 525 at eligibility (263 self-help only as an adjunct to treatment, 51 no separation of treated from untreated remission, 29 no alcohol-specific data, 127 mechanisms of change, 2 stability of remission, 53 no quantitative estimate), leaving 27 studies. Databases searched on 10 November 2016; further searches and checks to April 2018; English, human studies, published after 1975.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.2 Search strategy (p. 61); 2.3 and 2.4 (pp. 61–62); Fig. 1 (p. 62)

key_findings.finding: No assessment of the methodological quality or bias of included studies was done, by design; synthesis was narrative because the literature was too heterogeneous for meta-analysis; study details are given only in the Supplementary Material.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.5 (p. 62); Discussion › 4.2 Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 70)

key_findings.finding: 27 studies published 1976–2018: 24 (89%) North American, 12 longitudinal, 20 (74%) convenience samples, 1 probability sample and 6 population-based representative samples (US, Canada, Germany, Netherlands). The 124 estimates of untreated remission ranged from 2.7% to 98.3%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Three starting samples give three different quantities: method 1, the share of all people with an alcohol problem who remit without treatment (37 estimates from 11 studies, only 2 of which reported it directly, the rest calculated by the reviewers; for example 36.9% of people with non-comorbid and 42.6% with comorbid DSM-IV alcohol dependence in the German TACOS survey); method 2, the share of untreated people who remit (36 estimates from 16 studies); method 3, the share of people in remission who were never treated (51 estimates from 19 studies, the commonest approach; for example 78% in two Canadian population surveys, Sobell et al., 1996).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Tables 1–3 (pp. 64–66)
key_findings.note: Sobell et al.'s 78% is the abstinence-or-moderate-drinking figure (Table 3, p. 66: 77.7% Ontario, 77.5% national); with abstinence only, 56.0% and 65.7%.

key_findings.finding: In the nine studies with estimates under all three methods (23 each): method 1 ranged 2.7% to 63.6% (median 12.4, mean 21.5), method 2 6.5% to 77.9% (median 38.9, mean 40.9) and method 3 4.3% to 94.2% (median 43.9, mean 42.7).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.2, 1st paragraph (starting p. 63, ending p. 68); Table 4 (p. 67)
key_findings.note: Unweighted summaries of estimates, several per study. Table 4's method-3 values for Timko et al. (2000) repeat its method-1 values; with Table 3's values the method-3 minimum is 6.4% and the mean 44.0 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Studies drawing on one cohort of untreated people (seen after a single detox episode or at an information and referral centre; Timko et al., 1993) found 14.0% to 52.9% remitting (method 2). In Moos and Moos (2007), 36.0% of the untreated sample were in remission at both the 1-year and 3-year follow-ups, and 14.0% (marked as the reviewers' own calculation) when remission also had to hold at the 16-year follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.1, 2nd paragraph (p. 63); Table 2 (p. 65); Results › 3.2.2, 2nd paragraph (p. 69)

key_findings.finding: Definition of remission: 41% of estimates used abstinence only and 27% abstinence or moderate drinking; broader definitions raised estimates under all three methods (for example NESARC, Dawson et al., 2005, method 2: 12.4% with abstinence only vs 32.6% with abstinence or moderate drinking), and 'no diagnosis' definitions sat at the top of each method's range. Most studies used a one-year window; a six-month abstinence window gave 63% in one study (Tucker and Gladsjo, 1993).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5 (p. 68)

key_findings.finding: Definition of an alcohol problem: diagnosis 39% of estimates, consequences 20%, assumed from service contact 19%, consumption 9%, consumption and consequences 12%. In the Netherlands (Tuithof et al., 2016), 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, but 40% of those with a moderate or severe disorder. In Cunningham (1999), the method-3 estimate with abstinence or moderation fell from 87.5% (one or more consequences) to 80.7% (two or more), 74.5% (three or more) and 53.7% (six or more).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (starting p. 68); Tables 3 and 5 (pp. 66, 68)
key_findings.note: For Cunningham (1999), the method-3 estimates with abstinence only rose from 46.5% to 80.5%, and the method-1 estimates rose from 6.7% to 25.9% (abstinence) and 13.8% to 31.8% (abstinence or moderation) (Tables 1 and 3).

key_findings.finding: Definition of treatment: 27% of estimates counted formal treatment, self-help groups, informal help and primary care as treatment. Narrower definitions raised method-1 and method-3 estimates: in the Dutch survey, counting only alcohol treatment gave 63.6% (method 1) and 94.2% (method 3), against 42.9% and 63.5% when general treatment for other mental-health problems also counted; method-2 estimates changed little.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.3, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 1 and 3 (pp. 64, 66)
key_findings.note: The text describes the narrower Dutch definition as formal alcohol treatment alone; Tables 1 and 3 label it formal plus medical alcohol treatment.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: remitted-sample estimates (method 3), the commonest in the literature, are not useful for treatment planning because they start from people no longer in need; method-1 estimates suit planning for the total number needing treatment in a year, method-2 estimates the number of additional places needed for people not in treatment; a majority of studies defined remission over 6 to 12 months, so the estimates suit planning over about one year, and longer planning horizons need studies with repeated assessments.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.1, 2nd and 5th paragraphs (p. 70); 5. Conclusions (p. 71)

key_findings.finding: Context cited by the authors: about 20% of people with alcohol use disorders receive treatment in Europe and in the US, and 22% in Australia (from Probst et al., 2015; Grant et al., 2015; Teesson et al., 2010).
key_findings.locator: Introduction › 1.1, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; cite the primary sources.

key_findings.finding: Further points from the discussion: in a preliminary analysis, longitudinal and cross-sectional studies did not differ meaningfully (no data shown); population estimates from Germany and the Netherlands did not deviate from the rest; other drug use and mental-health comorbidity were rarely addressed, and in TACOS untreated remission did not differ significantly between people with and without comorbidity (as cited).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.3, 1st paragraph (starting p. 70), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 71)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that, in Cunningham (1999), varying the definition of an alcohol problem did not affect method-1 estimates, and the review concludes that method 1 is more robust to that definition (pp. 69–70); Table 1 shows the method-1 estimates rising from 6.7% to 25.9% (abstinence) and from 13.8% to 31.8% (abstinence or moderation) as the definition tightens from one to six or more consequences (p. 64).
reporting_issues.consequence: The robustness claim, one reason given for preferring method 1, is not supported by the only study that varied the problem definition within method 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites Cunningham (1999) as showing that stricter problem definitions lower method-3 estimates (87.5%, 80.7%, 74.5% and so on), which holds for abstinence or moderation; for abstinence alone, Table 3 shows the method-3 estimates rising from 46.5% to 80.5% (pp. 66, 69).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the effect of the problem definition depends on the remission definition; the general statement that stricter problem definitions lower method-2 and method-3 estimates rests partly on one half of this study's data.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 repeats Timko et al. (2000)'s method-1 values (4.3%, 11.2%, 7.3%, 16.1%) in the method-3 column, while Table 3 gives that study's method-3 values as 8.0%, 20.9%, 12.5% and 27.6% (pp. 66–67).
reporting_issues.consequence: The method-3 range (from 4.3%) and mean (42.7) quoted in the text derive from the error; with Table 3's values the minimum is 6.4% and the mean 44.0 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 prints 15 (13.5%) for method-1 estimates defining remission as abstinence and 11 (18.9%) for the total of estimates using 'formal alcohol treatment excludes detox and I&R'; by the editors' arithmetic, 15 of 37 is 40.5% and 11 of 124 is 8.9%. Dawson et al. (2006)'s treatment definition is printed with 'AA' twice in Tables 1–4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the counts are consistent and the text's percentages are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The summaries (ranges, medians, means) treat each estimate as one unit although studies contribute between 1 and 12 estimates drawn from the same participants (Cunningham, 1999 alone gives 12 of the 37 method-1 estimates), and no weighting by sample size is used (pp. 63, 68).
reporting_issues.consequence: The medians and means describe the set of published estimates, not any population, and should not be quoted as rates.

reporting_issues.issue: Most method-1 estimates and many method-3 estimates are the reviewers' own calculations ('a' in Tables 1–4; by the counts of AI readers 341 and 371, 31 of 37 method-1, 14 of 36 method-2 and 26 of 51 method-3 estimates, 71 of the 124, including the 2.7% minimum), described only in the Supplementary Material; the abstract reports 2,103 texts identified and Fig. 1 2,103 screened, although duplicates are said to have been removed, so the number of duplicates is not given (pp. 60, 62).
reporting_issues.consequence: The calculated estimates cannot be checked from the article; the Supplementary Material (at the article's DOI) is needed.

Its aim was explicitly not to produce rates but to map how the choice of starting sample (all people with alcohol problems, untreated people, or people already in remission) and the definitions of an alcohol problem, of remission and of treatment shape the estimates, for use in treatment-service planning (p. 61). Because it maps without appraising, it is rated with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief requires, not with AMSTAR 2; it does have a systematic search and explicit selection, which the first checklist domain records.
