design_detail: Post-mortem comparison of necropsy brains: 11 men with a long and severe history of heavy drinking who met DSM-III-R criteria for alcoholism (the paper's term), from brains collected at 18 Danish hospitals in 1986–1990, against 11 control men without a history or tissue signs of heavy drinking, whose source is not described, matched for age and height. Total neocortical neuron number was estimated by design-based stereology (optical disector with systematic uniform random sampling) in one hemisphere per brain, alternating sides; volumes of neocortex, white matter, ventricles, archicortex and central grey structures by Cavalieri's principle, also expressed as volume-to-brain-weight ratios (Vw). Unadjusted two-tailed unpaired t tests.
can_establish: That in these 22 brains the total number of neocortical neurons, overall and in each lobe, did not differ detectably between men with long-standing heavy drinking and matched control men, with enough precision to exclude a group difference larger than about 10% (editors' calculation), and that white-matter and archicortex volumes relative to brain weight were lower in the alcohol group.
cannot_establish: That heavy drinking never kills brain cells: neurons were not counted in the hippocampus, subcortical limbic structures, cerebellum (removed before sampling) or individual cortical areas and layers; the sample excluded women and men with Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, prolonged hepatic coma or other neurological disease; and one post-mortem comparison cannot show change within a person, cognitive consequences (nobody was tested) or whether white-matter differences reverse with abstinence.

sample.recruitment: Necropsy brains from Danish hospital pathology and forensic departments. Alcohol group: 55 brains of people with chronic heavy drinking were collected consecutively over 4 years (1986–1990) from 18 hospitals, and 11 met the study criteria (p. 1201, Subjects and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Controls: 11 brains selected by the same criteria but without any history or histological signs of heavy drinking; how and where the control brains were identified is not described further (p. 1202, left column, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Alcohol group: a severe and lasting history of excessive drinking, DSM-III-R criteria for alcoholism, and pathoanatomical evidence of alcohol-related disease at necropsy (most had liver cirrhosis and oesophageal varices; ascites, pancreatitis and alcoholic cardiomyopathy were also found). Excluded: women; age over 67; hepatic coma lasting more than 5 days; signs of infarction or of neurological disease other than those associated with alcoholism; medication acting on the central nervous system; disseminated cancer; severe lung disease; a history of severe head injury; withdrawal seizures; delirium tremens; diabetes; and a history of clinical Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis. Nobody in the alcohol group had been neuropsychologically tested (p. 1201).
sample.demographics: All white men. Mean (range) age: alcohol group 46.8 (36–64), controls 46.9 (34–67) years; height 178.8 (167–190) vs 176.5 (162–186) cm; mean brain weight 1443 g (CV 0.083) vs 1415 g (CV 0.14), not significantly different (p. 1202, Results, 1st paragraph). Causes of death: alcohol group, 3 acute pancreatitis, 2 bleeding oesophageal varices, the others septic shock, cardiomegaly, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, lung cancer or colon cancer (p. 1201); controls, 8 acute myocardial infarction, 1 aortic aneurysm, 1 violent death, 1 myocardial infarction with pulmonary cancer (p. 1202). The authors state that all but 2 of the alcohol group died of consequences of their drinking (p. 1203).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one post-mortem measurement per brain). 44 of the 55 collected brains from people with heavy drinking were not used because they did not meet the criteria.
sample.selection_effects: Strong and directional. Only 11 of 55 consecutively collected brains were used, and the criteria removed the men in whom brain damage from drinking is most expected (Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, prolonged hepatic coma, other neurological disease); women were excluded. Both groups are necropsy cases at a mean age of 47 (the alcohol group from 18 Danish hospitals; where the control brains came from is not described, and one control was killed violently): the alcohol group died mostly of liver, pancreatic and septic complications, the controls mostly of acute myocardial infarction. Neither group represents living people who drink heavily or people who do not.

exposure.measurement: Group membership from clinical and pathological data: a severe and lasting history of excessive drinking, DSM-III-R criteria for alcoholism (how the criteria were established after death is not described) and alcohol-related pathology at necropsy (p. 1201). Controls: no history and no histological signs of heavy drinking (p. 1202).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported for either group: no amount, duration or pattern of drinking is given.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported. Dependence on other drugs and smoking are not described; medication acting on the central nervous system was an exclusion criterion.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported: time since the last drink before death is unknown, so the reversibility the authors discuss cannot be examined in this sample.

comparison.controls: 11 men whose brains came to necropsy (where and when the control brains were obtained is not described; one man was killed violently), 9 with acute myocardial infarction (8 as the only cause), without a history or histological signs of heavy drinking, selected with the same exclusions (p. 1202). The 2 controls who did not die of infarction had neuron totals within the control range.
comparison.matching: Group means matched for age and height; all white men; brain weight similar. Not matched for cause of death, liver disease, smoking or nutrition.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure from before heavy drinking began. Neuron number varies between people (coefficient of variation 0.12 within each group), so only a group difference can be detected, not an individual's loss. Education, cognitive ability, smoking, nutritional (thiamine) status, liver function and the agonal state are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls' drinking was not quantified (only the absence of a recorded history and of histological signs); other drug use is not reported for either group.

outcomes.instruments: Optical disector counting at a final magnification of 3900× (100× oil-immersion objective) in one 35 µm Giemsa-stained section per bar, with 6 to 10 bars per region sampled systematically and uniformly from transcortical wedges taken from every second 7 mm slice; on average about 400 neurons were counted in about 200 disector samples per brain, coefficient of error 0.05 for each brain's total (p. 1202). Volumes by Cavalieri's principle (on average 270 points on neocortical sections, CE 3%): neocortex, white matter, ventricles, archicortex (defined to include uncus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, gyrus fornicatus, subcallosal area and amygdala) and central grey structures, each also divided by brain weight (Vw). Cerebellum and brainstem were detached before sampling.
outcomes.validity_norms: Design-based stereology estimates total number without assumptions about cell size, shape or orientation (pp. 1201–1202). Measurement variance was 17% of the between-brain variance (CE² / CV² = 0.05² / 0.12²). Neurons were told from glia by a defined cytoplasm, a membrane-bound convex nucleus with even chromatin and a clear nucleolus; doubtful cells (under 3% in each group) were left out (p. 1203). Tissue swelling between the volume and the density estimates was 7.5% and 6.1% in the two groups, which the paper describes as the same (p. 1202).
outcomes.operationalization: ‘Neuron loss’ was operationalized as a lower mean total (or lobar) neocortical neuron number in the alcohol group than in controls, and ‘white-matter loss’ as a lower mean volume or Vw; both at one time point after death, with no within-person change measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 16 counts the group comparisons reported with a p value or a significance statement: neuron number in 4 lobes and in total (5); volume and Vw of neocortex, white matter, ventricles, archicortex and central grey (10); brain weight (1). The two significant results (white-matter Vw p=0.013, archicortex Vw p=0.028) would not pass a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/16 = 0.003 (editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported: the paper does not say whether the person counting neurons or delineating regions knew which group a brain came from.

analysis.effect_sizes: Total neocortical neurons: controls 23.2 × 10^9 (CV 0.12), alcohol group 23.4 × 10^9 (CV 0.12), p=0.86. By lobe, controls vs alcohol group (× 10^9): frontal 8.22 vs 8.05 (p=0.82), temporal 5.34 vs 4.93 (p=0.27), parietal 5.25 vs 5.64 (p=0.33), occipital 4.42 vs 4.83 (p=0.28) (Table, p. 1202). Editors' calculation from the printed means and CVs (SD = CV × mean; Student t, df 20): difference +0.2 × 10^9 (alcohol minus control), 95% CI −2.3 to +2.7 × 10^9, that is −10% to +12% of the control mean; these data gave 80% power for a difference of about 3.5 × 10^9 (15%) and 90% power for about 4.1 × 10^9 (18%). Volumes, controls vs alcohol group: neocortex 486 vs 498 cm³ (p=0.66), Vw 0.1729 vs 0.1727 (p=0.99); white matter 502 vs 459 cm³ (9% lower, p=0.21), Vw 0.18 vs 0.16 (11% lower, p=0.013); ventricles 18.2 vs 24.7 cm³ (p=0.13), Vw 0.0065 vs 0.0087 (p=0.16); archicortex 38.6 vs 30.7 cm³ (p=0.053), Vw 0.014 vs 0.011 (called a 30% reduction, p=0.028; about 21% relative to controls and 27% relative to the alcohol group's value, editors' calculation); central grey 47.0 vs 51.4 cm³ (p=0.31), Vw 0.033 vs 0.036 (p=0.29) (pp. 1202–1203).
analysis.covariates: None: unadjusted two-tailed unpaired t tests at p<0.05. Brain size was handled by matching on height and by dividing volumes by brain weight.
analysis.selective_reporting: Neuron counts are reported in full (each lobe and the total, with CVs and p values). For volumes, the summary and discussion emphasise the two significant Vw ratios (white matter and archicortex) rather than the non-significant raw volumes (white matter p=0.21; archicortex p=0.053), and the summary presents the white-matter result as confirmed loss.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors argue that the precision of each brain's estimate (CE 0.05) is far better than needed (p. 1202), but the power of the group comparison depends on between-brain variation (CV 0.12) and on n=11 per group: by the editors' calculation the study could detect only a difference of about 15% with 80% power. The authors concede that 22 brains were too few to detect the 2% brain-weight difference that Torvik found in 545 necropsies, or to settle the ventricular difference (p. 1203).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 11 men with long-standing heavy drinking and 11 matched control men, total neocortical neuron number was almost identical (23.4 vs 23.2 × 10^9) and no lobe differed; the data exclude a group difference larger than roughly 10% (editors' calculation). White-matter volume was 9% lower (not significant) and 11% lower relative to brain weight (p=0.013); the archicortex ratio was lower (p=0.028; reported as 30%, a figure that fits only the alcohol group's value as the base; about 21% relative to controls from the printed means). Nobody was tested in life, neurons were not counted in the hippocampus or subcortical structures, and the men with the most severe alcohol-related neurological illness were excluded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says the study "confirms that chronic alcoholics lose white matter" (p. 1201), suggests this could explain their functional impairment, and infers that the damage is potentially reversible because preserved nerve-cell bodies might let lost connections be re-established after abstinence or treatment (pp. 1201, 1203); the discussion argues that, because neocortical neuron numbers did not differ, neocortical neuron death is unlikely to explain alcohol-related dementia (p. 1203, Discussion, 7th paragraph). Gaps: (1) white-matter volume itself did not differ significantly; only its ratio to brain weight did, in brains that were 2% heavier in the alcohol group, and one post-mortem comparison cannot show loss within a person; (2) function was not measured in anyone; (3) reversibility is a hypothesis, since abstinence, treatment and recovery were not studied; (4) the dementia inference rests on a sample from which the men most likely to have dementia (Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis) were excluded, a limit the authors partly acknowledge by naming the uncounted hippocampus and subcortical limbic structures (p. 1203, Discussion, 8th paragraph). A headline version, ‘alcohol does not kill brain cells’, overstates the paper: it shows no detectable loss of neocortical neurons in a selected group of men, not that drinking spares every brain region or every person.

timeline.event: Harper, Kril and Daly described loss of frontal-lobe nerve cells with gliosis in chronic alcoholism, based on two-dimensional counts (as cited by this paper, p. 1201); this study set out to test that belief with three-dimensional stereology.
Torvik's necropsy series of 545 people with and without alcoholism showed a 2% difference in brain weight (as cited, p. 1203), far smaller than a difference 22 brains can detect.
De la Monte reported disproportionate atrophy of cerebral white matter in chronic alcoholism compared with non-alcoholic liver cirrhosis (as cited, p. 1203).
This study: no difference in total neocortical neuron number; lower white-matter and archicortex volume-to-brain-weight ratios.

Topiwala et al. (MRI in a non-dependent community cohort, not neuron counts): heavier average drinking associated with visually rated hippocampal atrophy and lower white-matter integrity; read in the same dispatch.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication of the stereological neocortical count appears in the sources read for this card, and later stereological studies were not searched by this reader. What the paper supports is narrow: no detectable loss of neocortical neurons in men with long-standing heavy drinking who had no Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis or other neurological complication. It is silent on the hippocampus, cerebellum and subcortical nuclei, on women, and on people with alcohol-related dementia, which the authors name as open questions (p. 1203).

funding.funder: Direktør Emil Hertz and wife Inger Hertz Foundation; Ferdinand and Ellen Hindsgaul Foundation; Foundation for Neurological Research (acknowledgements, p. 1203).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Neurological Research Laboratory, Bartholin Instituttet, Kommunehospitalet, Copenhagen, and Stereological Research Laboratory, Århus University (p. 1201). The counting method follows earlier method papers, one of them first-authored by the second author (ref. 21).

what_would_settle_it: Stereological counts made blind to group, of neurons in the hippocampus, cerebellum, subcortical nuclei and individual neocortical areas and layers, in larger post-mortem samples of women and men with documented drinking histories (including people with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol-related dementia), compared with controls whose drinking was quantified, and linked to cognitive testing in life.

domains.note: Age, sex and body size (height) were matched and brain weight was similar, which covers the main determinants of neuron number; but causes of death (liver and septic complications vs myocardial infarction), liver cirrhosis, smoking, nutrition and agonal state differ or are unknown, and nothing is adjusted.

Group membership is probably right (history plus alcohol-related pathology), but amount and duration of drinking are not reported, how DSM-III-R criteria were applied after death is not described, and controls' drinking was not quantified.

11 of 55 brains were used; the criteria excluded men with Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, prolonged hepatic coma or other neurological disease. Selection was thus related to both exposure and outcome and would bias towards finding no neuron loss.
No interventions were studied; abstinence or treatment before death is unknown, which matters for the volume results (which may change with abstinence) more than for neuron number.
All 22 brains contributed to all measures.

Design-based stereology is unbiased and precise (CE 0.05), but blinding of the counter to group is not reported, telling neurons from glia involves judgment (doubtful cells, under 3%, excluded), and the authors found the archicortex hard to delineate (p. 1203).

For the neuron result, all lobes and the total are reported. The volume results raise concerns not scored here: 16 unadjusted comparisons and emphasis on the significant ratios over the non-significant raw volumes.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judgments refer to the main result, total neocortical neuron number. The counting method is design-based and precise, and the null result is informative within its sample (95% CI −10% to +12% of the control mean, editors' calculation). The overall judgment is high because of selection: 11 of 55 brains were used, and the criteria removed the men most likely to have lost neurons. The paper can be cited for no detectable loss of neocortical neurons in this selected group of men; not for the claim that heavy drinking does not kill brain cells. The white-matter and archicortex results carry further concerns: ratios rather than volumes, unadjusted multiple comparisons, a 30% figure reproducible only relative to the alcohol group's value (about 21% relative to controls), and different causes of death between groups.

key_findings.finding: Total neocortical neuron number was almost identical in the two groups: 23.2 × 10^9 (CV 0.12) in 11 control men and 23.4 × 10^9 (CV 0.12) in 11 men with long-standing heavy drinking (p=0.86).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table (Total neocortex row)
key_findings.note: The OCR text layer of this scanned PDF drops decimal points (it reads 0 86 for 0.86); all values were read on the rendered page (300 dpi). The same means appear in the summary (p. 1201).

key_findings.finding: No lobe differed (controls vs alcohol group, × 10^9): frontal 8.22 vs 8.05 (p=0.82), temporal 5.34 vs 4.93 (p=0.27), parietal 5.25 vs 5.64 (p=0.33), occipital 4.42 vs 4.83 (p=0.28).
key_findings.locator: Table (Mean (CV) total neurons in four regions of neocortex)

key_findings.finding: Could the study have detected a loss? Editors' calculation from the printed means and CVs (n=11 per group, Student t, df 20): difference +0.2 × 10^9 (alcohol minus control), 95% CI −2.3 to +2.7 × 10^9, which excludes a loss larger than about 10% of the control mean; 80% power corresponded to a difference of about 15%. Smaller or localized losses (single areas, layers, the hippocampus) could not be examined.
key_findings.locator: Table; Results, 1st paragraph (editors' calculation)
key_findings.note: Approximate: means and CVs are printed to one or two decimals.

key_findings.finding: Measurement precision: on average about 400 neurons were counted in about 200 disector samples per brain; each brain's total had a coefficient of error of 0.05, so measurement error was only 17% of the between-brain variance (0.05² / 0.12²).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The groups were similar in mean age (alcohol group 46.8 years, range 36–64; controls 46.9, range 34–67), height (178.8 vs 176.5 cm) and brain weight (1443 vs 1415 g; not significantly different); all were white men.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; left column, 1st paragraph (white men)

key_findings.finding: Neocortical volume did not differ (controls 486 cm³, CV 0.15; alcohol group 498 cm³, CV 0.11; p=0.66), nor did its ratio to brain weight (0.1729 vs 0.1727, p=0.99).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: White matter: volume 9% lower in the alcohol group (459 vs 502 cm³; p=0.21, not significant); white matter relative to brain weight 11% lower (0.16 vs 0.18; p=0.013).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure
key_findings.note: Only the ratio was significant, and the alcohol group's brains were slightly heavier (1443 vs 1415 g), which lowers the ratio; the result would not survive correction for the 16 comparisons (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Ventricles: 24.7 cm³ in the alcohol group vs 18.2 cm³ in controls (p=0.13, not significant); ratio to brain weight 0.0087 vs 0.0065 (p=0.16). The paper calls this 26% larger, which matches the difference divided by the alcohol group's volume; relative to controls the printed volumes give 36% (editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 1202, right column, continuing at the top of p. 1203)

key_findings.finding: Archicortex (uncus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, gyrus fornicatus, subcallosal area, amygdala): volume 38.6 cm³ in controls vs 30.7 cm³ in the alcohol group (p=0.053); ratio to brain weight 0.014 vs 0.011 (p=0.028), described as a 30% reduction. Neurons were not counted in this region.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (left column); archicortex definition in Subjects and methods (p. 1202)
key_findings.note: Relative to the control mean the printed ratios give about 21% (at most about 28% allowing for rounding) and the volumes 20%; 30% is reachable only relative to the alcohol group's value (27% from the printed means, up to about 38% with rounding), the base that reproduces the paper's 26% for the ventricles (editors' calculation). The authors say the archicortex is hard to demarcate macroscopically, which limits interpretation (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Central grey structures did not differ: 47.0 vs 51.4 cm³ (controls vs alcohol group; p=0.31); ratio to brain weight 0.033 vs 0.036 (p=0.29).
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Who was studied: 11 of 55 consecutively collected brains of people with heavy drinking (18 Danish hospitals, 1986–1990) met the criteria; women, men over 67, and people with Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, hepatic coma over 5 days, signs of infarction, other neurological disease, central nervous system medication, diabetes, disseminated cancer, severe lung disease or severe head injury were excluded; nobody had been neuropsychologically tested.
key_findings.locator: Subjects and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Causes of death differed between groups: in the alcohol group 3 acute pancreatitis, 2 bleeding oesophageal varices and the rest septic shock, cardiomegaly, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, lung or colon cancer, most with liver cirrhosis; among controls 9 had acute myocardial infarction (8 as the only cause), 1 an aortic aneurysm and 1 a violent death.
key_findings.locator: Subjects and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1201); left column, 1st paragraph (p. 1202)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: a total count may miss small localized losses (in areas or layers) but excludes a major loss; neurons were not counted in the hippocampus or subcortical limbic structures, where loss could underlie alcoholic dementia; telling the largest glia from the smallest neurons is "not a trivial problem", so stated criteria were applied and doubtful cells (under 3% in each group) were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 8th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Ventricular enlargement is given as 26% in the summary, Results and Discussion, but the printed volumes (18.2 cm³ in controls, 24.7 cm³ in the alcohol group) are 36% larger relative to controls; 26% is the difference expressed relative to the alcohol group's value (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper understates the relative difference; cite the volumes, or ‘about a third larger, not statistically significant’.

reporting_issues.issue: The archicortex Vw reduction is given as 30% (summary, Results, Discussion). Relative to the control mean, the printed means (0.014 vs 0.011) give about 21% (at most about 28% allowing for rounding) and the archicortex volumes 20%; 30% can be reached only with the alcohol group's value as the base (0.003/0.011 = 27%, up to about 38% allowing for rounding), the base that also reproduces the paper's 26% for the ventricles (editors' calculation; the paper does not state its base).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 30% figure probably expresses the difference relative to the alcohol group's value and overstates the reduction relative to controls (about 21%); claims should cite the means and p=0.028, with the authors' caveat that the region is hard to delineate.

reporting_issues.issue: The volume-to-brain-weight ratios in the text (neocortex 0.1729 vs 0.1727; white matter 0.18 vs 0.16; archicortex 0.014 vs 0.011) are about half the values plotted in the Figure, whose group means lie near 0.34, 0.35 vs 0.32 and 0.027 vs 0.021 cm³/g (read approximately from a 300-dpi crop); the printed volumes divided by the printed brain weights match the Figure (for example 486/1415 = 0.34; editors' calculation). One hemisphere per brain was studied, and the paper does not say how one-hemisphere estimates were scaled to the whole-brain volumes, ratios and neuron totals it reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: Relative group differences are unaffected, but absolute ratio values should not be quoted without saying which scale they use.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary presents white-matter loss as confirmed, but the white-matter volume difference was not significant (459 vs 502 cm³, p=0.21); only the ratio to brain weight was (p=0.013), in a group whose brains were slightly heavier (1443 vs 1415 g).
reporting_issues.consequence: The white-matter finding depends on the choice of the ratio and would not survive correction for 16 comparisons; it should be cited as a lower white-matter ratio, not as demonstrated loss.

design_detail: Whitehall II imaging substudy (UK civil servants). Weekly alcohol intake was self-reported at about five-year intervals from 1985–88 to 2011–12 (up to six phases) and averaged across phases; verbal fluency and recall were tested repeatedly from 1991–93; one 3T MRI scan was made in 2012–15. 550 scanned, 527 analysed (511 for diffusion imaging). Outcomes: grey-matter density (voxel-based morphometry) and white-matter microstructure (tract-based spatial statistics) as primary outcomes; visually rated hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens score above 0) and automated hippocampal volume as post hoc confirmatory tests; decline in lexical and semantic fluency and word recall; cognitive tests at the scan. Exposure was measured prospectively; the brain was measured once, at the end.
can_establish: How 30-year average self-reported drinking relates to brain measures taken around age 70 in this mostly male, educated, non-dependent civil-service sample, after adjustment for measured confounders: a graded association of heavier drinking with visually rated hippocampal atrophy, smaller hippocampal volume and lower white-matter integrity.
cannot_establish: That drinking caused brain shrinkage (one scan, no earlier brain measure, so ‘atrophy’ is a single rating, not observed loss); how large the risk is in absolute terms for the general population (a selected cohort of survivors, with 37 abstainers as the reference); effects in women (103 women, few drinking heavily); or clinically meaningful cognitive harm (one of three repeated tests declined faster, and no test at the scan differed).

sample.recruitment: Whitehall II cohort (established in 1985; 10,308 non-industrial civil servants, phase 1 in 1985–88). From the 6306 phase-11 participants, a random list of 1380 who had taken part in phase 11 or the phase 10 pilot and had consented was drawn, sampled across high, intermediate and low socioeconomic groups; 550 had a structural scan in Oxford in 2012–15 (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph, p. 2; Fig 2, p. 15). Why the other 830 on the list were not scanned is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Safe to undergo MRI and able to consent; not alcohol dependent by the CAGE questionnaire (no score of 2 or more at any phase with data; 75 participants lacked CAGE data at one phase or more, p. 6). Excluded: incomplete or poor-quality imaging, a gross structural abnormality (for example a cyst), alcohol data missing for more than two phases, missing sociodemographic, health or cognitive data (23 excluded); a further 16 lacked usable diffusion images (pp. 2, 4; Fig 2).
sample.demographics: Mean age 43.0 (SD 5.4) at phase 1 and about 70 at the scan (the age the paper uses for its typical participant). 424 men and 103 women (summed from Table 2). People above vs within the pre-2016 limits (n=99 vs 428): men 85.9% vs 79.2% (p=0.13); estimated full-scale IQ 120.0 vs 117.4 (p=0.009); smokers at the scan 11.1% vs 2.6% (p<0.001); median education 14.8 vs 14.0 years (p=0.2); median Framingham stroke risk score 11 vs 9 (p=0.5) (Table 1, p. 10). Compared with the larger cohort, more men, slightly less educated, higher blood pressure and fewer depressive symptoms (appendix table A, not read; stated on p. 4).
sample.attrition: From 550 scanned to 527 analysed (4%), and 511 for diffusion analyses; excluded participants did not differ significantly on the reported characteristics (data available on request). 75 participants (14.2%) lacked CAGE data at one phase or more. Losses before the substudy (death or dropout of cohort members before phase 11; 830 of the 1380 invited not scanned) are not analysed.
sample.selection_effects: A survivor sample: people had to remain in the cohort for about 27 years, stay healthy enough for MRI and agree to a scan; people who drank heavily and died, became dependent (screened out by CAGE) or dropped out are absent. Mostly educated, middle-class men, as the authors note (p. 6). The reference group is 37 people averaging under 1 unit a week, and whether they had always abstained or had stopped drinking is not stated. Few women drank heavily, and none averaged 30 units or more.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported units of alcohol per week (with frequency of drinking) at phases 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 (1985–88 to 2011–12), averaged across phases; 1 UK unit = 8 g of alcohol (Fig 1, p. 14). Categories: abstinent, under 1 unit a week; light, 1 to <7; moderate, 7 to <14 (women) or 7 to <21 (men); above the pre-2016 limits, more than 14 (women) or 21 (men); further split at 14, 21 and 30 for the logistic models (pp. 2–3). CAGE at each phase to exclude dependence.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Median of the 30-year average: men 11.5 units a week (IQR 6.2–18.8), women 6.4 (2.8–11.9). Intake was stable over time (change per 10 years 0.15 units a week, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.51); people drinking more at baseline reduced more (intercept–slope r=−0.43) (p. 4). Averages above the pre-2016 limits: 20.0% of men and 13.6% of women. Drinking pattern (for example heavy single occasions) was not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking was recorded and entered the models only within the Framingham stroke risk score; the number of psychotropic medicines at the scan was adjusted for; illicit drug use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable as such: the exposure is the average over the phases up to 2011–12, before the 2012–15 scan.

comparison.controls: People averaging under 1 unit a week across the study (n=37; 22 men, 15 women) were the reference for the odds ratios and for the cognitive-decline contrasts; the voxel-wise and volume analyses used alcohol as a continuous variable.
comparison.matching: No matching; regression adjustment (see covariates).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No MRI before or early in the drinking history, so hippocampal size before exposure is unknown; the authors judge reverse causation (people with smaller hippocampi drinking more) unlikely but could not test it (p. 6). ‘Premorbid IQ’ was estimated with a reading test at the scan. Diet, APOE genotype, head injury and the reasons for abstaining were not measured or not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for any group beyond smoking and psychotropic medicines.

outcomes.instruments: 3T MRI (Siemens Verio, Oxford, 2012–15): voxel-based morphometry of grey-matter density and tract-based spatial statistics of fractional anisotropy and mean, radial and axial diffusivity (primary outcomes, corrected across voxels with threshold-free cluster enhancement); hippocampal atrophy rated visually on the 4-point Scheltens scale by three clinicians who reached a consensus, dichotomized at 0 vs above 0; FIRST automated hippocampal volume as a percentage of intracranial volume, squared for analysis. Cognition: lexical and semantic fluency (phases 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and at the scan), 20-word recall (phases 3–11); at the scan MoCA, trail making A and B, Rey-Osterrieth complex figure, Hopkins verbal learning test, Boston naming test, digit span and digit symbol substitution; TOPF-UK for premorbid IQ (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Visual ratings correlated with automated hippocampal volumes (Spearman r=−0.4, p<0.001); mean hippocampal volumes lay within published ranges (appendix table D, not read) (p. 5).
outcomes.operationalization: ‘Hippocampal atrophy’ was any Scheltens score above 0 on one scan, described as abnormal for clinical use (p. 3). It was common: right-sided in 293 of 527 participants and left-sided in 351, including 13 and 19 of the 37 abstainers (editors' arithmetic from Table 2). ‘Cognitive decline’ was a faster fall in a test score over repeated testing than in abstainers. No within-person change in brain structure was measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Voxel-wise imaging analyses were corrected across voxels (TFCE). For cognitive decline, overall Wald tests were used and lexical fluency was said to survive Bonferroni correction across the three decline tests (threshold 0.017). The hippocampal odds ratios (5 drinking categories × 2 sides × 3 sex groupings), the volume regression and the tests at the scan carry no reported correction. 23 counts the outcome measures: grey-matter density 1, diffusion indices 4, atrophy ratings 2, hippocampal volume 1, decline measures 3, tests at the scan 12.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported whether the visual raters knew participants' drinking.

analysis.effect_sizes: Right hippocampal atrophy, adjusted odds ratios against abstainers (all 527; Table 2, p. 11): 1 to <7 units a week 1.5 (95% CI 0.7 to 3.4); 7 to <14 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4); 14 to <21 3.4 (1.4 to 8.1), p=0.007; 21 to <30 3.6 (1.4 to 9.6), p=0.009; 30 or more 5.8 (1.8 to 18.6). Left side: 1.3 (0.6 to 3.0), 1.4 (0.6 to 3.2), 1.9 (0.8 to 4.6), 1.9 (0.7 to 4.9), 5.7 (1.5 to 21.6). Crude proportions rated atrophic on the right rise from 35% (13/37) in abstainers to 65% (63/97) at 14 to <21 and 77% (24/31) at 30 or more units; crude risk ratios about 1.85 and 2.2 (editors' calculation). Hippocampal volume (squared, % of intracranial volume) per 10 units a week: −0.26 (−0.37 to −0.15) unadjusted and −0.19 (−0.30 to −0.08) adjusted, both p<0.001 (Table 3, p. 12). Lexical fluency declined 0.5%, 0.8% and 0.6% a year faster than in abstainers at 7 to <14, 14 to <21 and more than 21 units (Wald χ²=14.4, p=0.006); semantic fluency (χ²=10.0, p=0.04) and recall (χ²=9.8, p=0.04) were judged not significant after correction; no association with tests at the scan (p. 5). Post hoc structural equation model (511): alcohol to hippocampal volume −0.572 (−0.800 to −0.353), alcohol to corpus callosum mean diffusivity 0.038 (0.017 to 0.064), direct alcohol to lexical decline −0.002 (−0.005 to 0.000), p=0.08; 2% of lexical-decline variance explained (Table 4, p. 13; Fig 7, p. 20).
analysis.covariates: Brain analyses: age, sex, premorbid IQ, education, social class, Framingham stroke risk score, number of psychotropic medicines, lifetime major depressive disorder (SCID), exercise, club attendance, voluntary work and social visits (marital status also in Table 3); trait impulsivity in a subset of 179. Cognitive-decline models: time, alcohol category, age, sex, education, social class, premorbid IQ and Framingham score, with terms for practice effects. Smoking enters only through the Framingham score, and several covariates were measured at the scan, decades after drinking began.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported. The imaging substudy has a published protocol (Filippini et al., 2014, BMC Psychiatry, ref. 30), not read, so whether these analyses were planned cannot be checked; the paper itself calls the hippocampal regression tests and the structural equation model post hoc (pp. 3–4, 6).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 2 reports every drinking category for both sides and by sex, and null cognitive results are stated. But the abstract reports right-sided estimates only (on the left, only 30 or more units a week differed significantly), the headline odds ratios come from post hoc tests, and the Results text attaches the 14 to <21 estimate (3.4) to the 7 to <14 category, whose own estimate (2.0, 0.9 to 4.4) was not significant.
analysis.power: Not reported. The reference group has 37 people (15 women), so the odds ratios are imprecise (upper limits up to 18.6 in the whole sample and 55.2 in women). The authors say the study was underpowered for women and for people whose intake changed substantially (pp. 6–7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 527 mostly male civil servants scanned once around age 70, higher average drinking over 30 years went with lower hippocampal grey-matter density and volume, higher odds of a visual hippocampal atrophy rating above 0 (right side from 14 units a week: adjusted odds ratio 3.4; crude 65% vs 35% of 37 abstainers) and lower corpus callosum white-matter integrity, after adjustment for measured confounders. Lexical fluency fell slightly faster at 7 units a week or more (0.5% to 0.8% a year relative to abstainers), semantic fluency and word recall did not after correction, and drinking was not related to any cognitive test at the scan. Light drinking (1 to <7 units) did not differ from abstinence (right odds ratio 1.5, 0.7 to 3.4).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title presents moderate drinking as a risk factor, and the abstract concludes that drinking, "even at moderate levels, is associated with adverse brain outcomes" (p. 1), supporting the lower UK guidance and questioning the US limits (abstract; p. 7). Gaps: (1) the brain was scanned once, so ‘atrophy’ is a single visual rating above 0 that more than half of participants had, including 35% of abstainers on the right; neither shrinkage over time nor its cause was observed; (2) the abstract's moderate category of 14–21 units a week is moderate only for men under the paper's own definition, and the Results text attaches the 3.4 estimate to 7 to <14 units, where the actual estimate was 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4); (3) three times the odds is not three times the risk: with so common an outcome the crude proportions were 65% against 35% (risk ratio about 1.85, editors' calculation); (4) ‘cognitive decline’ rests on one of three repeated tests, a difference of under 1% a year from abstainers who started lower (Fig 6), with no difference on any test at the scan; (5) ‘no protective effect’ of light drinking is a null comparison against 37 abstainers whose interval (0.7 to 3.4) does not exclude a modest benefit; (6) a guideline recommendation goes beyond one observational cohort of survivors. The authors themselves acknowledge cross-sectional imaging, self-reported drinking, residual confounding and the post hoc model (p. 6).

timeline.event: Jensen and Pakkenberg (post-mortem stereology, 11 men with long-standing heavy drinking): no neocortical neuron loss; lower archicortex (including hippocampus) volume ratio, where neurons were not counted; read in the same dispatch.

Den Heijer et al. (alcohol measured cross-sectionally, hippocampus traced manually) reported a protective association of moderate drinking with hippocampal size compared with abstinence, as described in this paper (p. 6), which conflicts with these results.
This study: graded association of 30-year average drinking with hippocampal atrophy ratings, hippocampal volume and corpus callosum microstructure in 527 Whitehall II participants.
Sabia et al. analysed alcohol and dementia over 23 years in the same Whitehall II cohort (BMJ; on the project's alcohol list, not read for this card).
Daviet et al. examined drinking and grey- and white-matter volumes in UK Biobank (Nat Commun; on the project's alcohol list, not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication appears in the sources read for this card. The paper cites one earlier hippocampal study in people without dependence that found the opposite (cross-sectional) and calls for replication in other populations (pp. 6–7). Larger imaging cohorts on the project's alcohol list (Daviet et al., 2022) should be appraised before any claim treats the hippocampal association, or its threshold of about 14 units a week, as replicated.

funding.declared_conflicts: ICMJE form: grant support as listed above; in the previous three years no financial ties to any organisation with a possible interest in the work, and no other relationships or activities that might appear to have influenced it (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and FMRIB Centre, University of Oxford; Department of Epidemiology and Public Health, University College London. Open access (CC BY 4.0).

what_would_settle_it: Repeated MRI of the same people from midlife onward with an unchanged scanner protocol, drinking measured prospectively with lifelong abstainers separated from people who used to drink, enough women and people who drink heavily, and confounding addressed by designs such as genetic instruments or within-family comparisons; with cognitive outcomes that have clinical meaning.

domains.note: A broad set was adjusted (age, sex, premorbid IQ, education, social class, Framingham score, depression, psychotropic medicines, social and physical activity), but smoking only through the Framingham score; diet and APOE were not measured; several covariates were measured at the scan and may lie on the causal path; the 37 abstainers may include people who stopped drinking for health reasons.

Prospective, repeated self-report is a strength, but under-reporting is likely (the authors' caveat), an average over 30 years hides patterns such as heavy single occasions, and CAGE data were missing at one phase or more for 14.2%.

Survivors to phase 11 (6306 of 10,308), then 550 of 1380 invited were scanned with no reasons given; MRI safety and a CAGE screen excluded people. Selection plausibly relates to both drinking and brain health; its direction is uncertain, though survival of people who drank more and kept healthier brains would more likely weaken the association.
No interventions; changes in drinking are part of the averaged exposure.
23 of 550 excluded (4%) and 16 more from the diffusion analyses; the excluded did not differ on reported characteristics.

Visual ratings by consensus without reported blinding to drinking, at a low threshold (any score above 0) that makes the outcome very common; the automated volume and voxel-wise measures are objective and agree in direction.

The hippocampal odds ratios and the structural equation model are post hoc; many outcomes, sides, categories and sex strata are tested without correction; the abstract reports the right side, where results were stronger; the Methods list of categories omits 7 to <14 units, and the Results text attaches the 14 to <21 estimate to it.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judgments refer to the association of average drinking with hippocampal atrophy ratings and hippocampal volume (Tables 2 and 3). Drinking was measured prospectively and repeatedly, which the paper notes most earlier imaging studies lacked (p. 2), and the main confounders were adjusted; but the brain was scanned once, the headline odds ratios come from post hoc analyses reported selectively in the abstract, the reference group is 37 abstainers of unknown history, and the cohort is a selected group of surviving, mostly male civil servants. The study can be cited for an association between heavier average drinking (about 14 units a week and above) and smaller or visually atrophic hippocampi around age 70 in this cohort; not for ‘moderate drinking shrinks the brain’ or for cognitive harm at moderate levels.

key_findings.finding: Who was studied: from a random list of 1380 Whitehall II participants (UK civil servants first examined in 1985–88; 6306 took part in phase 11), 550 were scanned in 2012–15; 527 were analysed (23 excluded for brain abnormality, poor images or missing data) and 511 in the diffusion analyses. Mean age 43.0 (SD 5.4) at the start; none screened positive for dependence on the CAGE questionnaire. Men and women, summed from the rows of Table 2 (editors' arithmetic): 424 and 103.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Participants (p. 1); Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › Participants/descriptive data, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Table 2, sex totals (p. 11); Fig 2 (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: How much they drank: the median 30-year average was 11.5 units a week for men (IQR 6.2–18.8) and 6.4 for women (2.8–11.9), a UK unit being 8 g of alcohol; 20.0% of men and 13.6% of women averaged above the pre-2016 UK limits (21 and 14 units a week). Intake was stable across the study (change per 10 years 0.15 units a week, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.51).
key_findings.locator: Results › Participants/descriptive data, 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Fig 1, unit definition (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: What ‘hippocampal atrophy’ meant: a visual rating above 0 on the 4-point Scheltens scale, on one scan, agreed by three clinicians. It was common (editors' arithmetic from Table 2): right-sided in 293 of 527 participants (56%) and left-sided in 351 (67%), including 13 of the 37 abstainers (35%) on the right and 19 (51%) on the left.
key_findings.locator: Methods › MRI analysis, paragraph at the top of the left column (p. 3; the section begins on p. 2), and Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 2 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Right hippocampal atrophy, adjusted odds ratios against 37 abstainers (all 527): 1 to <7 units a week 1.5 (95% CI 0.7 to 3.4); 7 to <14 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4); 14 to <21 3.4 (1.4 to 8.1), p=0.007; 21 to <30 3.6 (1.4 to 9.6), p=0.009; 30 or more 5.8 (1.8 to 18.6). Proportions rated atrophic, from the printed counts 13/37, 67/140, 87/165, 63/97, 39/57 and 24/31 (editors' arithmetic): 35%, 48%, 53%, 65%, 68% and 77%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Total rows, right hippocampal atrophy
key_findings.note: Odds ratios overstate risk ratios when an outcome is this common: the crude risk ratio for 14 to <21 units against abstainers is about 1.85 (65% vs 35%), not 3.4 (editors' calculation; adjusted risk ratios are not reported).

key_findings.finding: Left hippocampal atrophy, adjusted odds ratios for the same categories: 1.3 (0.6 to 3.0), 1.4 (0.6 to 3.2), 1.9 (0.8 to 4.6), 1.9 (0.7 to 4.9) and 5.7 (1.5 to 21.6), p=0.01; only 30 or more units a week differed significantly from abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Total rows, left hippocampal atrophy (p. 11); Results › Grey matter, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: By sex: in men (22 of them abstainers) right-sided odds ratios were 3.2 (1.1 to 9.3) at 14 to <21, 3.9 (1.3 to 12.0) at 21 to <30 and 5.2 (1.4 to 19.0) at 30 or more units a week; in women (15 of them abstainers) no estimate was significant (for example 4.2, 0.6 to 28.8, at 14 to <21). From the counts in Table 2 (editors' arithmetic): 424 men and 103 women, only 14 women averaging 14 units or more, and none 30 or more.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Men and Women rows (p. 11); Results › Grey matter, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Hippocampal volume (automated, as a percentage of intracranial volume, squared) was lower with more drinking: change per 10 units a week −0.26 (−0.37 to −0.15) unadjusted and −0.19 (−0.30 to −0.08) adjusted, both p<0.001. Visual ratings correlated with these volumes (Spearman r=−0.4, p<0.001).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 12); Results › Grey matter, 3rd paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The squared, intracranial-volume-scaled unit has no direct anatomical reading; the paper gives no difference in cm³ or as a percentage of hippocampal volume.

key_findings.finding: Whole-brain imaging: higher average drinking correlated with lower grey-matter density, especially in both hippocampi and extending into the amygdalae, with frontal regions unaffected (voxel-based morphometry, 527, corrected across voxels), and with lower fractional anisotropy and higher radial, axial and mean diffusivity, concentrated in the front of the corpus callosum (genu and anterior body) (tract-based spatial statistics, 511).
key_findings.locator: Results › Grey matter, 1st paragraph (pp. 4–5) and White matter (p. 5); Figs 4 and 5 (pp. 17–18)
key_findings.note: Figures 4 and 5 are brain images with p-value colour scales; no effect sizes were extracted from them.

key_findings.finding: Light drinking did not differ significantly from abstinence: at 1 to <7 units a week the right-sided odds ratio was 1.5 (0.7 to 3.4) and the left 1.3 (0.6 to 3.0), and there was no evidence that light drinkers were protected from cognitive decline; the authors conclude that light drinking showed no protective effect compared with abstinence. Only the atrophy ratings and cognitive decline compared light drinking with abstinence: the voxel-wise, hippocampal-volume and at-scan test analyses treated drinking as a continuous measure.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 11); Results › Grey matter, 2nd paragraph, and Alcohol and cognitive function, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Discussion › Principal findings (p. 5); Methods › Statistical analysis, alcohol as a continuous variable in the voxel-wise, volume and at-scan analyses (pp. 3–4)
key_findings.note: A null comparison against 37 abstainers; the interval does not exclude a modest benefit.

key_findings.finding: Cognitive change: lexical fluency (words beginning with a given letter in one minute) declined faster than in abstainers by 0.5% a year at 7 to <14, 0.8% at 14 to <21 and 0.6% at more than 21 units a week (overall Wald χ²=14.4, p=0.006); semantic fluency (χ²=10.0, p=0.04) and 20-word recall (χ²=9.8, p=0.04) were not significant after correction for three tests.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol and cognitive function, 1st paragraph (p. 5); test definitions in Methods (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: No cognitive test given at the time of the scan (MoCA, trail making, Rey-Osterrieth figure, Hopkins verbal learning, Boston naming, digit span, digit symbol substitution) was significantly related to drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol and cognitive function, 4th paragraph (p. 5); tests listed in Methods (p. 2)
key_findings.note: The detailed results are in appendix table H, which was not read.

key_findings.finding: Behind the lexical result (Fig 6, model predictions for a typical man): the abstainers' line starts lowest (about 19 words) and ends highest (about 17.6 at 30 years), while the drinking categories start higher (about 20 to 21.5) and end lower (about 16.3 to 16.8); the paper reports a non-significant trend to higher baseline lexical fluency and recall in people who drank.
key_findings.locator: Fig 6 (p. 19); Results › Alcohol and cognitive function, 3rd paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Values read approximately from the figure (150 dpi). The legend names three tests, but only lexical scores are plotted.

key_findings.finding: Post hoc structural equation model (511): drinking predicted smaller hippocampal volume (−0.572, 95% CI −0.800 to −0.353) and higher corpus callosum mean diffusivity (0.038, 0.017 to 0.064), and diffusivity predicted faster lexical decline (−0.011, −0.022 to −0.003); the direct path from drinking to lexical decline was −0.002 (−0.005 to 0.000), p=0.08. The model explained 2% of the variance in lexical decline.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 13); Fig 7 (p. 20); Results › Modelling alcohol consumption and brain structure and function, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: excluding the three people who drank most (more than 60 units a week) did not substantially change the hippocampal results, nor did adding trait impulsivity in the 179 with personality data.
key_findings.locator: Results › Grey matter, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The figures are in appendix table E, which was not read.

key_findings.finding: People above the pre-2016 limits (n=99) differed from those within them (n=428) in estimated IQ (120.0 vs 117.4, p=0.009) and in smoking at the scan (11.1% vs 2.6%, p<0.001); they were also more often men (85.9% vs 79.2%, p=0.13) and had a higher median Framingham stroke risk score (11 vs 9, p=0.5), but neither of these differences was significant, although the Results text (p. 4) lists both as differences.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 10); Results › Participants/descriptive data, 1st paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The reference group was small and undefined: 37 people (22 men, 15 women) averaged under 1 unit a week across the study, and the paper does not say whether they had always abstained or had stopped drinking.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd paragraph (p. 2, right column); Table 2 (p. 11)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text attributes the odds ratio 3.4 (1.4 to 8.1; P=0.007) to moderate drinking of 7 to <14 units a week, but Table 2 gives 3.4 for 14 to <21 units and 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4; p=0.1) for 7 to <14; the abstract (14–21) and the Discussion (14 to <21) agree with the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim that 7 to 14 units a week significantly raised the odds of hippocampal atrophy would rest on a mislabelled number; that category was not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list of drinking categories for the logistic regression omits 7 to <14 units a week (p. 3), which Table 2 includes; the abstract and Methods say over 30 units while Table 2 says 30 or more.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but it adds to the confusion around the moderate category.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the women's 30-or-more row repeats the reference-row counts (4 of 15 and 7 of 15), but the total row (24 of 31, identical to the men's row) shows that no woman averaged 30 units or more, as do the sex totals (editors' arithmetic: 424 men and 103 women make 527).
reporting_issues.consequence: The row should read zero; the women's data say nothing about drinking 30 units or more.

reporting_issues.issue: The right-sided odds ratio for 30 or more units, 5.8 (1.8 to 18.6), is printed with P<0.001 (P≤0.001 in the abstract and Results), while the other p values in the total rows agree with their intervals; editors' calculation on the log scale: this interval implies p of about 0.003.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the association remains significant, but the abstract's p value overstates it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels as ‘OR’ statistics that are percentage-point or median differences (for example men 6.7, −2.5 to 14.1; smokers 8.5, 2.7 to 16.5; Framingham score 2.0, −4.2 to 10.3); an odds ratio cannot have a negative confidence limit. Social class 1 among people within the limits is printed as 62 (15.5%), but 62 of 428 is 14.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote Table 1 differences as percentage points or medians, not odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Lexical fluency: the 0.8% greater yearly fall at 14 to <21 units is translated as 17% over 30 years, whereas 0.5% and 0.6% a year become 14% and 16%; 0.8% a year compounded over 30 years gives about 21% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two figures for 14 to <21 units is wrong; cite the yearly figure with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The 40.3% said to exceed the 2016 guideline of 14 units a week matches men only (editors' arithmetic from Table 2: 171 of 424 men; for all 527 participants, 185 or 35.1% at 14 units or more). The gram equivalents of the median intakes (11.5 units = 85.8 g; 18.8 units = 154.3 g; 11.9 units = 103.6 g) do not follow the paper's own 8 g per unit (Fig 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote 40% as men only, and quote intake in units, the measure the categories used.

reporting_issues.issue: Structural equation model: the Methods call hippocampal volume and corpus callosum diffusivity endogenous variables (p. 4), the Results call them exogenous (p. 5); the title of Table 4 refers to fig 6, though the model is Fig 7; Fig 7 prints −0.017 for age to hippocampal volume where Table 4 gives −0.020 (−0.021 to −0.013), and shows no value on the alcohol to hippocampal volume path; the Results say drinking predicted faster lexical decline through a direct path, but that path's p is 0.08 (Table 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The post hoc model's direct link from drinking to cognitive decline is not significant; only the indirect path through corpus callosum diffusivity is.

reporting_issues.issue: The one earlier study of the hippocampus in people without dependence (Den Heijer et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2004, ref. 19) is cited as ref. 51 at its first mention, which is a meta-analysis of hippocampal volume in depression (Videbech and Ravnkilde, 2004); two sentences later it is cited correctly as ref. 19, and a later sentence on confounders that the Den Heijer study did not control, such as depression, cites ref. 51 again, where the depression meta-analysis may be the intended source.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation error; anyone tracing the conflicting study should use ref. 19.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text lists a higher estimated IQ, more men, more smokers and higher Framingham stroke risk scores as differences between people above and within the pre-2016 limits (p. 4), but in Table 1 only IQ (120.0 vs 117.4, P=0.009) and smoking at the scan (11.1% vs 2.6%, P<0.001) differed significantly; the share of men (85.9% vs 79.2%, P=0.13) and the median Framingham score (11 vs 9, P=0.5) did not.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only IQ and smoking should be cited as significant differences between the two drinking groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say 550 people were randomly selected for the imaging substudy (p. 2), but the random step was the list of 1380 cohort members invited to it (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Fig 2, p. 15); how the 550 who were scanned came from that list, and why the other 830 were not scanned, is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The scanned sample should not be called random: it is the scanned part of a random invitation list, selected in ways the paper does not report.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say CAGE scores were below the screening cut-off of 2 for all participants at all phases (p. 4), but the Discussion reports that 75 participants (14.2%) lacked CAGE data at one phase or more, each with at least three of five CAGE measurements, that some who screened negative reported drinking heavily, and that people who were alcohol dependent at times may have been included (p. 6). The Methods describe CAGE as collected at each phase (p. 2), whereas the Discussion counts five CAGE measurements in all.
reporting_issues.consequence: Describing the sample as not alcohol dependent means no positive CAGE screen among the measurements available, not a verified absence of dependence.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled two-period crossover trial (NCT02541422) at a US level 1 trauma centre: 49 healthy adults who completed both sessions drank beer under supervision to a set breath alcohol level and were given N-acetylcysteine (NAC) or identical lactose placebo capsules (doses and timing in the exposure field), the other treatment at the second session; the next morning they rated hangover symptoms at home on the Hangover Symptoms Scale. Primary outcome total symptom score; secondary headache, nausea, weakness and a comparison by sex. The PubMed Central version includes an author correction to the Introduction (Sci Rep 2021;11:15262).
can_establish: Whether NAC capsules taken during a supervised session of beer drinking, at the low doses and the one timing used (exposure field), made a large difference to next-morning hangover symptom scores in healthy young adults, compared with placebo in the same people.
cannot_establish: Whether NAC has a small or moderate effect (no intervals reported; medians only), whether higher doses or other timing would differ, whether the apparent benefit in women is real (a subgroup comparison among several tests, called post hoc in the Discussion, with men faring worse on NAC), and whether results hold for longer, unsupervised drinking without a fixed stopping point, or for drinking after leaving the site, which was not controlled.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers aged over 21 at St. Luke's University Health Network, Pennsylvania; how they were recruited is not described. Predominantly white; most aged 20 to 30 according to the Limitations.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults over 21 without alcohol use disorder (self-report). Excluded: diabetes, kidney or bladder stones, kidney or liver disease, stomach ulcers, organ transplant or dialysis, allergy to alcohol, egg, milk or wheat, pregnancy (urine test), and a list of medications (including several antibiotics, carbamazepine, nitroglycerine and activated charcoal).
sample.demographics: 31 men and 18 women, predominantly white, mostly 20 to 30 years old; no means or SDs reported.
sample.attrition: 62 enrolled, 49 completed (13 lost, 21%): scheduling conflicts (number not given), one could not tolerate the amount of beer, one withdrew; analysis of completers only. The five-item analysis in Table 1 has 91 observations (45 NAC, 46 placebo) instead of 98, without explanation.
sample.selection_effects: Young, mostly white volunteers willing to drink to intoxication twice in a hospital setting; completers only.

exposure.measurement: Supervised drinking of the same beer, one bottle at a time, with breath alcohol measured 15 minutes after each until the target was reached; capsules given by staff, with vapour rub under the nose to mask the capsule's smell.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 12 oz beers of 5.2% alcohol by volume until breath alcohol reached 0.1 g/210 L (plus or minus 0.005), in sessions starting in the early afternoon; then one, two or three capsules of 600 mg NAC or lactose placebo by mouth, according to the number of beers drunk (1 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 or more). Participants stayed until breath alcohol was below 0.08 g/210 L and were driven home; drinking after leaving was not controlled. The interval between the two sessions is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Listed interacting medications excluded; smoking and other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; symptoms were rated within an hour of waking the next morning, unsupervised.

comparison.controls: The same participants after identical-looking lactose placebo capsules at the other session, drinking to the same breath alcohol target.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover; order assigned by random number generator by a person who kept the allocation from the investigators.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant within person. Number of beers per session, sleep and drinking after leaving the site were not reported or not controlled.

outcomes.instruments: Hangover Symptoms Scale (Slutske et al., 2003): 13 symptoms rated on a five-point agreement scale (thirst, tiredness, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, difficulty concentrating, sensitivity to light and sound, sweating, trouble sleeping, anxiety, depression, trembling); a general hangover visual analogue scale (results not reported); and a subset of five items described as valid, summed.
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper calls the scale previously verified (validated in college students) in the Limitations, and technically not validated in the Methods, where it adds the five-item subset for that reason.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcome: total symptom score, NAC against placebo within person. Secondary: headache, nausea and weakness; difference scores (NAC minus placebo) compared between women and men.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and investigators blinded; capsules identical; smell masked. Symptoms were self-rated at home without supervision.

analysis.effect_sizes: Medians only, no intervals: total score NAC 10 against placebo 13 (P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum score); headache 1 against 1 (P = 0.93); nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11); weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); five-item subset 5 (range 0 to 19) against 5.5 (0 to 20), P = 0.86. Difference scores (NAC minus placebo) by sex: women −3.5, men +2 (P = 0.04); nausea P = 0.05, weakness P = 0.03, headache P = 0.32.
analysis.covariates: None; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for NAC against placebo, Mann-Whitney tests for sex comparisons and for the five-item subset.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02541422, registered 4 September 2015 according to the paper. The registry record was not read, so registered and reported outcomes were not compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: The general hangover visual analogue scale is described but no result is given. The Discussion calls the symptom-specific comparisons post hoc, while the Methods list headache, nausea, weakness and the sex comparison as secondary outcomes. The legend of Figure 1 says the results suggest benefit in people with high alcohol intake or high symptom scores, an analysis that is not reported anywhere.
analysis.power: Calculated in advance (PASS 11): 41 participants for a 20% reduction at alpha 0.05 and 90% power; 49 completed. The variability assumed is not stated. A survey of 69 medical professionals put the smallest clinically meaningful reduction at 69.4%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 49 young adults, NAC capsules taken during supervised beer drinking did not change next-morning hangover symptoms detectably compared with placebo (median totals 10 against 13 out of 52; P = 0.45), nor headache, nausea or weakness. Comparing difference scores by sex, women scored lower on NAC than placebo (median −3.5) and men higher (+2), P = 0.04, with no correction for the several tests. Side effects were few and mild on both NAC and placebo.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say the study was "suggestive of gender specific susceptibility" with women's symptoms improved after NAC. Gaps: (1) the primary outcome was null, and the sex difference is a subgroup comparison among several uncorrected tests that the Discussion itself calls post hoc for the individual symptoms; (2) the abstract does not say that men scored worse on NAC than on placebo; (3) the Figure 1 legend asserts benefit in people with high alcohol intake or high symptom scores without any reported analysis; (4) the title speaks of prevention, but when the capsules were taken (exposure field) limits what prevention can mean here. The Limitations are candid about dose, timing of drinking and self-administration of the scale.

timeline.event: Trial registered (NCT02541422).
Results presented as posters at three conferences.
Full report published; an author correction the next month replaced an inaccurate passage on ethanol metabolism in the Introduction and one reference, with no change to methods or results.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small trial of NAC for hangover. The authors cite an earlier trial of an L-cysteine-containing supplement (Eriksson et al., 2020) as positive; that is a different product and was not read here.

funding.funder: In part, a research scholarship from the St. Luke's University Health Network Women's Auxiliary Group.
funding.declared_conflicts: The corresponding author has recently begun consulting for Galephar Pharmaceuticals on a hangover medication, which she states started years after the study was completed; no other conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors from St. Luke's University Health Network; the drinking protocol was the same as in another study by the same group (Kelly et al., 2020).

what_would_settle_it: A larger preregistered randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with a validated hangover severity scale as the primary outcome, a prespecified test of the treatment-by-sex interaction, more than one dose, realistic drinking sessions with sleep recorded and no unmonitored drinking afterwards, and effect sizes with confidence intervals.

domains.note: Order assigned by random number generator; allocation kept from investigators by the person assigning treatments.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: NAC is short-acting, so carryover is unlikely, but the interval between sessions is not reported and period effects were not examined; the number of beers needed to reach the target in each period is not reported.
Blinding was well designed (identical capsules, smell masked). Drinking after leaving the site was not controlled, as the authors note, and could differ between periods.
13 of 62 enrolled (21%) did not complete, mostly for scheduling, and only completers were analysed; 7 of 98 expected observations are missing from the five-item analysis without explanation.
Blinded self-ratings on an established symptom scale; completed at home within an hour of waking without supervision, which adds noise but not bias between conditions.

Registered, but the registry was not checked here; the five-item re-scoring, the unreported visual analogue scale, and a figure legend asserting an unreported analysis suggest flexible analysis around the null primary result.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomization, concealment and blinding were done well, so the null primary result is credible as far as its precision allows; concerns come from completers-only analysis with 21% loss, unreported session interval, uncontrolled drinking after leaving, and analyses beyond the primary outcome that are inconsistently described. The card may be cited for no detectable effect of NAC on next-morning symptom scores at these doses and this timing. It should not be cited for a benefit in women: that comparison is a subgroup test among several, with men scoring worse on NAC, and the analysis treats the sex difference rather than testing an interaction prespecified with adequate power.

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: total Hangover Symptoms Scale score did not differ between NAC and placebo (median 10 against 13, P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum score) in 49 completers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
key_findings.note: The percentages correspond to a maximum of 52 (13 items scored 0 to 4), while the Methods describe items scored 1 to 5 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Secondary symptoms did not differ: headache median 1 against 1 (P = 0.93), nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11), weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); the five-item subset 5 (0 to 19) against 5.5 (0 to 20), P = 0.86.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: By sex, the difference score (NAC minus placebo) was −3.5 in women and +2 in men (P = 0.04), with sex differences for nausea (P = 0.05) and weakness (P = 0.03) but not headache (P = 0.32); the Discussion calls the symptom comparisons post hoc.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Side effects participants attributed to the pill: after NAC, gastrointestinal symptoms (4), headache (2), rash (1), muscle twitches (1) and insomnia (1); after placebo, headache (3) and gastrointestinal symptoms (1); no serious adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 62 participants were enrolled and 49 completed (31 men, 18 women, predominantly white); losses were mostly for scheduling, one could not tolerate the beer and one withdrew.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations that the low doses may have been below a therapeutic level, that the supervised sessions, which ended at a breath alcohol target, may have produced milder hangovers than unrestricted drinking, that participants may have drunk more after leaving, and that the scale was self-administered without supervision.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe each symptom rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), which with 13 items gives a minimum total of 13; the reported median totals of 10 and 13 and the percentages of 19% and 25% of the maximum match items scored 0 to 4 (maximum 52), as in the sample-size section.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 5th paragraph; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Scores should be described on the 0 to 52 scale; the Methods description is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 compares NAC with placebo, and women with men, using Mann-Whitney tests for independent groups, although each participant contributed to both conditions; its sample sizes (45 and 46; 34 women and 57 men) do not match 49 completers in two periods (98 observations; 36 and 62).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and its footnote; Methods, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The five-item analysis ignores the paired design and has unexplained missing observations.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 1 legend states that the results suggest improvement in people with high alcohol intake or high symptom scores; no such analysis is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a finding of this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the symptom-specific sex differences post hoc, while the Methods name headache, nausea, weakness and the sex comparison as secondary outcomes.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 7th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether these analyses were planned is unclear; they should be treated as exploratory.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the scale is technically not validated, the Limitations that it was previously verified in college students; and the Limitations say participants mostly ranged from 20 to 30 years, although only people over 21 were eligible.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 6th paragraph; Limitations, 1st paragraph
