design_detail: Narrative review with a reported literature search (PubMed and cross-references, 6 July 2024; 13 publications: 10 experimental studies and 3 surveys) on whether the alcohol hangover is caused by dehydration and whether drinking water prevents or relieves it, from the Utrecht hangover research group. It summarizes old biomarker studies of diuresis, hormones and electrolytes, student surveys of remedy use, and adds the authors' own re-analysis of an earlier naturalistic study (people walking the Samaria Gorge in Crete the day after drinking), correlating the amount of water drunk with hangover severity and thirst in the 176 walkers who had a hangover.
can_establish: As summarized, what small physiological studies found about fluid balance during hangover, how students rate water as a remedy, and, from the authors' re-analysis of their own data, whether the amount of water people drank on a hangover day was associated with how their hangover and thirst changed over that day.
cannot_establish: Whether drinking water prevents or relieves a hangover: no randomized trial existed by the authors' own account, the survey figures are respondents' ratings of how well water worked, and the re-analysis is correlational, with people who felt worse drinking more water.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Re-analysed study: 307 people who completed the 15.8-km Samaria Gorge walk and filled in surveys on the bus before and after it (Verster, Anogeianaki et al., 2020, as described) (p. 14). Surveys: 462 and 826 Dutch students (p. 14). Experimental studies: 1 to 19 men in 1942 to 1982, plus 13 men (2018), 90 volunteers (2019) and 214 participants (2020) (pp. 12-15).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Human studies investigating water consumption or dehydration in relation to hangover; reviews, commentaries, animal studies and non-English articles excluded; conference abstracts included because of the paucity of literature (p. 12).
sample.demographics: Walkers with a hangover had drunk a mean of 3.0 (SD 1.8) alcoholic drinks the evening before (p. 14); other demographics not given.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: A small, partly unpublished literature (two conference abstracts) dominated by the authors' own group; the walkers were tourists doing a long hike in the heat, with many more ways to lose and drink fluid than on an ordinary hangover day.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported amount of water drunk during the walk (re-analysis); self-reported use of water as a remedy (surveys); measured fluid intake or hormones in the old experiments.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: walkers drank a mean of 2.7 (SD 0.7) litres of water during the walk (p. 14); in the naturalistic hangover study the evening before averaged 12.4 (SD 4.4) drinks (p. 13); the experimental studies gave, for example, 1.5 to 2.3 g of ethanol per kg or six pints of beer (pp. 13-14).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: None in the re-analysis (correlation across walkers); an alcohol-free control day in the naturalistic study; control conditions in some of the old experiments.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Food, sleep, heat, exertion and the amount of alcohol were not accounted for in the correlations; the authors note that most studies did not control for food, physical activity or sleep (p. 15).

outcomes.instruments: Single-item hangover severity and thirst ratings from 0 (absent) to 10 (extreme); survey ratings of remedy efficacy from 0 to 10; urine flow, plasma hormones, electrolytes and acid-base measures in the experiments (pp. 12-15).
outcomes.validity_norms: Single-item ratings; no validated hangover scale in the re-analysis.
outcomes.operationalization: Dehydration indexed by thirst, urine output, hormones and electrolytes; benefit of water indexed by correlations between water drunk and changes in hangover and thirst ratings.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None in the re-analysis (more than a dozen correlations at p < 0.05).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Re-analysis (Spearman, n = 176): water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk r = 0.176 (p = 0.019), 0.243 (p < 0.001) and 0.229 (p = 0.002); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst r = -0.028, -0.001 and 0.059, and against change in thirst r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046, all non-significant (pp. 14-15; signs checked on the rendered page). Survey ratings of water as a remedy: 5.8 of 10 for water while hungover; 5.2 (SD 2.4, N = 618) for water during drinking and 5.6 (SD 2.6, N = 502) for water before bed (p. 14).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Narrative review; the re-analysis was not prespecified.
analysis.selective_reporting: The re-analysis restricted to walkers with a hangover is presented as more appropriate than the original full-sample analysis; the choice was made after the original publication.
analysis.power: Not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Signs of dehydration (thirst, hormonal changes) after drinking were mild and short-lived in small old studies, while hangover lasted all day; students rate water as a moderately effective remedy; and among walkers with a hangover, those who drank more water had worse hangovers but the amount drunk was not related to how their hangover or thirst changed during the day.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions (pp. 9, 17) state that water was not effective in relieving the hangover and that water during or directly after drinking is not effective in preventing it, and that hangover and dehydration are independent consequences of drinking caused by different mechanisms. No trial of water was available (the authors say so on p. 16), the survey figures are ratings rather than measured effects, and the correlational re-analysis cannot separate the effect of water from the fact that people who felt worse drank more; the mechanistic statements in the conclusions go beyond the evidence reviewed.

timeline.event: Jayawardena et al., systematic review of interventions for hangover (cited in the Introduction)
Verster, van Rossum and Scholey on the unknown safety and efficacy of hangover treatments (cited in the Introduction)
This review: no trial of water for hangover found; authors' re-analysis of the Samaria Gorge data.
Imai et al.: first randomized crossover trial of water drunk during drinking, 13 men, no detectable effect on next-morning symptoms (not part of this review)

replication.where_it_stands: Whether water prevents or relieves hangover remains untested in adequately sized trials; the one later trial was small and found no detectable effect.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (p. 17).
funding.declared_conflicts: A.S. has held research grants from many food, supplement and drinks companies, including Red Bull and Nutricia-Danone, has consulted for several, and is Chief Scientific Officer for Arepa Nootropics; J.G. is a part-time employee of Nutricia Research and has received grants from several companies and funders; J.C.V. has consulted for Eisai, KNMP, Med Solutions, Mozand, Red Bull, Sen-Jam Pharmaceutical and Toast! in the past three years; the other author declares none (pp. 17-18).
funding.affiliations_note: Utrecht University, TU Dresden, Danone Global Research and Innovation Center, Monash University and Swinburne University; the senior author leads the research group that produced most of the surveys and naturalistic studies reviewed.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people drinking as they normally would, comparing a specified amount of water after drinking or on the hangover morning with no added water, with a validated hangover scale, blinded assessment where possible and adequate power for a modest effect.

domains.note: A reproducible PubMed search with two search strings, cross-references and stated exclusions, but one database, English only, and no duplicate screening described.
No formal appraisal; general limitations (old, small, retrospective, uncontrolled) are named in the Limitations section.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The surveys, the naturalistic study and the re-analysed walking study come from the authors' own group, and the key correlations are a new analysis of their own data.
The conclusion that water is not effective is stated as a finding although no trial existed, and causal mechanisms (oxidative stress, inflammation) are asserted in the conclusions.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against water as a hangover remedy
domains.note: Evidence that water changes hormonal markers is discounted, and the possibility that people with worse hangovers drink more water (which would hide a benefit) is not weighed against the conclusion.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The search is reported, which is better than most narrative reviews, but the evidence is thin and largely from the authors' group, and the conclusions on water go beyond correlations and survey ratings. Cite it for the absence of trials up to July 2024, the student survey figures, and the re-analysis as a correlational finding; any claim resting only on it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand or the authors' own re-analysis.

key_findings.finding: Three searches on 6 July 2024 (PubMed with alcohol hangover and dehydration, 12 records, 3 eligible; alcohol hangover and water, 44 records, 2 eligible; then cross-references, 6 articles and 2 abstracts) identified 13 publications, 10 experimental studies and 3 surveys.
key_findings.locator: Literature search; Limitations and future research, 1st paragraph (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: In the authors' re-analysis of 176 walkers with a hangover (mean 3.0, SD 1.8, drinks the evening before; mean 2.7, SD 0.7, litres of water during a 15.8-km walk), more water drunk went with worse hangover before (r = 0.176, p = 0.019), during (r = 0.243, p < 0.001) and after the walk (r = 0.229, p = 0.002), but the amount of water was not related to change in hangover severity (r = 0.103, p = 0.174; r = 0.017, p = 0.828; r = 0.066, p = 0.388).
key_findings.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 3rd study (right column, p. 14); continued, 1st paragraph (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: The amount of water drunk during the walk was not correlated with thirst before (r = -0.028), during (r = -0.001) or after (r = 0.059), nor with changes in thirst (r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046); hangover severity and thirst correlated before the walk (r = 0.511, p < 0.001) but not during it (r = 0.066).
key_findings.locator: Left column, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered page; the text extraction drops them.

key_findings.finding: In the naturalistic study (mean 12.4, SD 4.4, drinks the evening before), hangover severity was higher than on an alcohol-free control day at every hourly rating from 09:30 to 15:30, while thirst was higher only at 09:30 and 10:30.
key_findings.locator: Left column, 1st paragraph; Fig. 5

key_findings.finding: In a survey of 462 Dutch students, drinking water was the most used hangover remedy (55.8%), followed by sleeping (55.2%), breakfast (52.2%), drinking more alcohol (47.2%), tea (47.0%), coffee (45.5%), paracetamol (45.0%), aspirin (43.1%), vitamins (40.5%) and hangover products (30.7%); water while hungover was rated 5.8 out of 10 for efficacy.
key_findings.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 1st study; Fig. 6 (percentages printed as labels; efficacy bars not extracted)

key_findings.finding: In a survey of 826 Dutch students (conference abstract), water during drinking was rated 5.2 (SD 2.4, N = 618) and water before going to bed 5.6 (SD 2.6, N = 502) out of 10 for preventing the next-day hangover; the amount of water was not recorded in either survey.
key_findings.locator: Right column, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Old experimental studies found extra urine output mainly in the first two hours of drinking (one person, 1942), hormonal changes in renin, aldosterone and vasopressin during hangover (6 to 10 men), no change in electrolytes during hangover (19 men in 1974; 90 volunteers in 2019) and, in a placebo-controlled trial of 214 people, no change in skin water content.
key_findings.locator: Studies investigating the nexus between alcohol hangover and dehydration (pp. 12-14); right column of p. 15

key_findings.finding: The authors state that no experimental study had specifically tested whether water intake counteracts dehydration or the alcohol hangover.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and future research, end of 2nd paragraph (left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The correlation between hangover severity and thirst after the walk (r = 0.160, p = 0.034) is described as not significant, although p is below 0.05 and no other threshold is stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pattern of hangover-thirst correlations is reported more one-sidedly than the numbers allow.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says there is a rise in blood pH during hangover and, in the same sentence, cites a significant decrease in pH.
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal contradiction; the cited data indicate a decrease (metabolic acidosis).

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that electrolyte imbalance plays no role is attributed to Linkola et al. (1978) while describing the study by Ylikahri et al. (1974).
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error at the top of the left column.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Fig. 7 refers to Fig. 6a when crediting the map.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling error.

design_detail: Single-author critical review (accepted author manuscript, NIHMS518366) of 62 published quantitative studies of alcohol protective behavioral strategies (PBS) in college-student samples. Searches of APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar with stated terms, plus reference lists and forward citations of the measure-development papers, ended in early February 2013. Narrative synthesis in four parts: how PBS were measured (Table 1: 11 measures and their variants), putative antecedents of PBS use, moderators of PBS–outcome relationships, and evidence for PBS as a mechanism of change; a one-line summary of each study in the Appendix. No protocol, no flow diagram, no per-study risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling (the author states that a meta-analysis is still needed). Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist: the search is described, but the review has none of the other features of a systematic review.
can_establish: How alcohol protective behavioral strategies were defined and measured in college-student research up to February 2013, which measures had passed which psychometric tests, and which associations (antecedents, moderators, mediation in trials, within-person daily associations) had been reported, how often, and with what designs.
cannot_establish: Whether using any protective strategy reduces drinking or harm (the studies summarized are mostly cross-sectional, retrospective, self-reported and between-person, and no effect is pooled), how large any association is (sizes are printed for only a few studies), or whether the findings hold outside college students (non-college samples were excluded; countries of the samples are not reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies used college-student samples, including incoming students and subgroups (student athletes, women, mandated students, lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender students), recruited as each study did (random samples from the National College Health Assessment, multi-university surveys, trial samples). Sources: APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar searched with terms for protective behavioral strategies or drinking control strategies combined with alcohol or drinking; reference lists; studies citing any measure-development paper; searches ended early February 2013 (Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Published quantitative studies in college-student samples whose measure unambiguously assessed PBS use and allowed PBS–variable relationships to be examined. Excluded: qualitative papers; non-college samples (few, and measured differently); measures limited to alcohol-avoidance strategies; PBS analysed only in combination with non-PBS variables (for example restraint or legal risk behaviours); PBS in other domains such as condom use (Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported in aggregate. The Appendix describes most samples only in words (large, modest, small); counts are printed for a few, for example two halves of a five-university sample of 6139 and 6658 students who drank (Benton et al., 2008) and a 15-day diary study of 40 students (Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013) (Antecedents › PBS descriptive norms; Identifying Gaps › Recall bias).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: One author searched, selected and summarized; the search terms were those the author knew to describe PBS; no count of records screened or excluded and no flow diagram. Published studies only. Some studies held several samples and some samples appeared in several reports, so the number of independent samples is unknown (Identification of Studies, 2nd paragraph). Seven of the 62 studies are co-authored by the reviewer (editors' count: Appendix nos. 11, 18, 44–48), among them the only head-to-head comparison of measures, the response-scale study and the only daily-diary study, on which several of the review's judgments rest. Restriction to college students is described as pragmatic (Conclusion).

exposure.measurement: In the included studies, PBS use was self-reported on questionnaires: at least 11 measures (PBSS, NCHA, CAS, PSQ, PBSM, SQ, SCQ and four unnamed), most in several variants differing in number of items, response scale (contingent frequency, that is how often a strategy is used when drinking; absolute frequency; degree of truth; yes or no for a day or occasion) and time window (none stated for most PBSS studies; past 24 hours, past week, past 2 weeks, past 3 months, past 12 months, last school year, since arriving on campus) (Measurement of PBS, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Strategies measured, as the review describes item content: setting a limit or leaving at a predetermined time; alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks; drinking water while drinking alcohol; eating before or during drinking; avoiding drinking games, mixing types of alcohol or keeping up with others; keeping track of drinks; using a designated driver or planning transport; going home with a friend; not leaving a drink unattended; asking a friend to say when one has had enough; and, in broad measures only, avoiding situations with alcohol (Protective Behavioral Strategies, 1st paragraph; Measurement of PBS › PBSS, PSQ, PBSM and SQ subsections).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: the review concerns alcohol only, and other drug use in the included samples is not mentioned.

comparison.controls: No comparison group at review level. Designs summarized: mostly cross-sectional between-person correlations, regressions and mediation models; randomized trials of brief alcohol interventions in which PBS change was tested as a mediator (Larimer et al., 2007; Barnett et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2012) or did not change (Kulesza et al., 2010; Neighbors et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2009); one experiment instructing students to drink less or to use more strategies (Sugarman & Carey, 2009); one assessment-reactivity experiment (Walters et al., 2009); panel and single-group pre–post studies; two studies separating within-person from between-person effects (Lewis et al., 2012; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review's own antecedent sections show that people who report more PBS differ in sex, drinking motives, personality and self-regulation, mental health and family history of alcoholism, all of which also relate to drinking; with mostly cross-sectional data, PBS use cannot be separated from these characteristics.

outcomes.instruments: Included studies: self-reported alcohol use (frequency, typical and heaviest quantity, heavy episodic drinking, estimated blood alcohol concentration) and alcohol-related problems (composite scales or single consequences such as injury or regretted acts). The review itself compares the measures' factor analyses (exploratory and confirmatory), response scales and time windows (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Only two measures have factor structures replicated in independent samples with both exploratory and confirmatory analyses: the PBSS (Martens et al., 2005) and the PSQ (DeMartini et al., 2013); the PBSM and the SQ failed a confirmatory analysis in an independent sample (Pearson, Kite & Henson, 2012a). Only one study tested measurement invariance by sex before comparing means (DeMartini et al., 2013) (Measurement of PBS › PBSM, SQ and Measurement summary; Antecedents › Gender).
outcomes.operationalization: PBS are conventionally defined by the harm they are presumed to reduce, a definition the author calls tautological. He proposes the narrow definition, strategies used immediately before, during or after drinking, and would treat avoidance of drinking as a separate, complementary construct (Measurement of PBS, 1st paragraph; Measurement summary; Conclusion).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no quantitative synthesis). The author notes that most antecedent and moderator findings come from single, unreplicated tests (Identifying Gaps in Knowledge, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling. Numbers are printed for a few studies only: descriptive norms of PBS correlated with own PBS use r=.32 and .33 in two halves of a five-university sample (n=6139 and 6658; Benton et al., 2008); same-sex norms r=.35, .26 and .49 for the three PBSS subscales and opposite-sex norms r=.02, −.01 and −.08 (Lewis, Rees & Lee, 2009) (Antecedents › PBS descriptive norms); in LaBrie et al. (2011) the path from drinking motives to alcohol use fell from β=.58 to β=.17 when PBS were added, about 70% of the total effect (Antecedents › Drinking motives, 2nd paragraph). Most other findings are described as significant or not, without sizes or sample sizes.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; covariates are named for some individual studies (for example gender and alcohol use).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Appendix summarizes what the author judged the most distinctive significant PBS findings of each study, not all its findings, because PBS were not the main focus of every study (Summarizing the Nomological Network, 1st paragraph); non-significant results are therefore under-represented in the summaries.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The author notes that two of the three studies finding that PBS buffer the link between drinking and problems had samples large enough to detect very small interactions (Moderators › Alcohol use).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The PBS literature in college students up to February 2013 is mostly cross-sectional, retrospective, self-reported and between-person, and uses many variants of 11 measures. People who report more PBS report drinking less and fewer problems. In the two studies separating within-person from between-person effects, some strategies (the Serious Harm Reduction subscale, such as using a designated driver or going home with a friend, and day-to-day Limiting/Stopping) went with more drinking on the days they were used. PBS mediated intervention effects in three trials and did not change in three others, and an instruction to use more strategies raised reported strategy use without reducing drinking (one study).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and most of the discussion are cautious about designs, but the Conclusion ends by calling PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its negative consequences. The section on trials calls the three mediation findings some of the strongest evidence for a causal relationship between PBS use and alcohol outcomes (Review of Evidence › Randomized controlled trials), although PBS were not the randomized factor, were self-reported, and none of the interventions mainly targeted PBS (as the author concedes in Identifying Gaps › Weak tests of PBS use as a mechanism of change); the same paragraph argues that trials in which PBS did not change do not question the PBS–outcome relationship. The Highlights say PBS are consistently negatively correlated with alcohol-related problems, while the body reports positive associations for some strategies (daily-report studies; absolute-frequency scales; some items in Frank et al., 2012).

timeline.event: Prince, Carey & Maisto (2013) is cited as a recent methodological review of PBS measurement (Purpose of the Present Review); not read here.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of protective behavioral strategies among adults, on the editors' reading list for this topic; not read or appraised here.

replication.where_it_stands: In 2013 the association between PBS and drinking was consistent between people but rested on cross-sectional self-report; within-person, prospective and experimental evidence was sparse and mixed. The author called for intensive longitudinal studies (daily diaries, ecological momentary assessment, objective alcohol measures) and a meta-analysis. A 2026 meta-analysis of randomized trials (Van Nhat et al.) addresses the trial evidence and should be read for the current state.

funding.funder: No official funding for the review; the author was supported by a National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism training grant, T32-AA018108 (Acknowledgments, 1st paragraph). A second acknowledgment sentence breaks off after the words supported in part by, with no funder named (Acknowledgments, 2nd paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Center on Alcoholism, Substance Abuse, & Addictions, University of New Mexico. The author co-wrote 7 of the 62 included studies (editors' count), including the measure comparison (Pearson, Kite & Henson, 2012a), the response-scale study (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013) and the daily-diary study (Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials that target one named strategy at a time (for example alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, or arranging a safe way home) against a control, with outcomes recorded at the event level in real time (daily diary or ecological momentary assessment with breath or transdermal alcohol) and harms such as injuries and blackouts as outcomes, in college and non-college samples; and a meta-analysis that separates within-person from between-person associations.

domains.note: Databases, terms, citation searching, end date and criteria are stated, which is more than most narrative reviews give; but one author did everything, the terms were those known to him, one of the three databases was Google Scholar, there is no count of records screened or excluded, and the exclusion of measures not unambiguously assessing PBS is a judgment.

No study-level appraisal, and sample and effect sizes are mostly not given; but the review appraises the measures' psychometric testing in detail and names the design problems that affect nearly all studies (cross-sectional between-person data, recall bias, common-method bias, weak tests of mediation).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Seven of 62 included studies are the author's; the judgments that the PBSS outperforms other measures, that absolute-frequency scales produce spurious positive correlations, and much of the within-person evidence come from them.

Limitations and the ecological fallacy are discussed explicitly, but trial mediation is described as among the strongest causal evidence, null trials are set aside as failures of method, and the final sentence calls PBS a promising way to reduce drinking.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a protective effect of PBS
domains.note: Counter-evidence (positive within-person associations, the null instruction experiment, trials that did not change PBS) is reported, but the framing favours a protective effect. Qualitative studies and non-college populations are excluded by design and so are not represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This one is more transparent than most: its search is described and it is explicit about the weaknesses of the literature it summarizes. Its limits are a single reviewer, no study-level appraisal or effect sizes, reliance on the author's own studies for key judgments, and a conclusion more favourable than the designs allow. Had it been rated as a systematic review, AMSTAR 2 would give critically low confidence (no protocol, no risk-of-bias assessment of included studies). It may be cited for how PBS were measured, for the design profile of the literature to 2013 and for pointers to primary studies; claims about whether a strategy reduces harm should rest on the primary trials and on a systematic review of them, not on this review.

key_findings.finding: 62 published studies met the criteria; some contained more than one sample and some samples were reported in several papers, so the number of independent samples is unknown.
key_findings.locator: Identification of Studies, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Search: APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar, with terms for protective behavioral strategies or drinking control strategies combined with alcohol or drinking; reference lists; forward citations of measure-development studies; college samples only; qualitative studies excluded; searches ended early February 2013.
key_findings.locator: Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: At least 11 PBS measures were used (PBSS, NCHA, CAS, PSQ, PBSM, SQ, SCQ and four unnamed), most in several variants of items, response scale and time window. The PBSS was the most used (36 studies, about 58%, in at least nine variants).
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Measurement of PBS › Variants of the PBSS, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text's own subtotals for the PBSS (24 + 5 + 4 studies by time window) and the PBSS rows of Table 1 (33 listings) do not reach 36; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Only the PBSS and the PSQ have factor structures replicated in independent samples with both exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis; the PSQ in that form had been used in one published report. The PBSM and the SQ failed a confirmatory analysis in an independent sample.
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS › Measurement summary; PBSM; SQ

key_findings.finding: The response scale changes the direction of results: with an absolute-frequency scale (number of times a strategy was used), the SQ subscale of strategies used while drinking correlated positively with drinking, because it also counts drinking occasions; with a contingent-frequency scale (how often when drinking), correlations were negative (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013, three studies).
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS, 3rd paragraph; Measurement of PBS › SQ

key_findings.finding: 13 of the 62 studies (about 21%) used a broad definition that includes avoiding drinking altogether; the author recommends the narrow definition (strategies used immediately before, during or after drinking).
key_findings.locator: Measurement of PBS › Broad vs. narrow operational definition; Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Women reported more PBS than men in nearly every study that compared them; only four studies reported any non-significant sex difference, and only one tested whether the measure worked the same way in both sexes before comparing means.
key_findings.locator: Antecedents/Predictors of PBS Use › Gender

key_findings.finding: Perceived norms of PBS use predicted own PBS use: r=.32 and .33 in two halves of a five-university sample (n=6139 and 6658); same-sex norms r=.35, .26 and .49 across the three PBSS subscales, opposite-sex norms r=.02, −.01 and −.08; both held in regressions adjusted for sex, drinking and problems (the review does not state these two studies' designs).
key_findings.locator: Antecedents/Predictors of PBS Use › PBS descriptive norms

key_findings.finding: Three cross-sectional studies found that PBS use statistically mediated part of the link between some drinking motives (for example social and enhancement motives) and drinking or problems, motives going with lower PBS use; in LaBrie et al. (2011) the motives–alcohol use path fell from β=.58 to β=.17 with PBS in the model (about 70% of the total effect). The author notes that cross-sectional data do not allow full tests of mediation.
key_findings.locator: Antecedents/Predictors of PBS Use › Drinking motives, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In three studies, people reporting more PBS showed a weaker association between how much they drank and their problems (Benton et al., 2004, 2006; Borden et al., 2011). Other moderators (mental and physical health, refusal self-efficacy, motives, negative urgency, self-esteem, self-regulation) come mostly from single studies; the author calls the pattern of stronger associations in higher-risk groups very preliminary.
key_findings.locator: Moderators of the Relationships between PBS Use and Alcohol-Related Outcomes › Alcohol use; Health variables; Other variables

key_findings.finding: Trials: in three randomized trials of brief interventions with college students, change in PBS statistically mediated the intervention's effect on drinking or problems (Larimer et al., 2007, mailed personalized feedback, 12 months, an effect described as fully mediated; Barnett et al., 2007, brief motivational interview with mandated students, PBS at 3 months and drinks per day at 12 months, per drinking day in the Appendix; Murphy et al., 2012, small trial with a behavioral economic supplement, 6 months). In three other trials the intervention did not change PBS (Kulesza et al., 2010; Neighbors et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2009). None of the interventions mainly targeted PBS.
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Randomized controlled trials; Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Weak tests of PBS use as a mechanism of change

key_findings.finding: Students instructed to use more strategies reported using more, but their drinking did not fall, and changes in strategy use were not correlated with changes in drinking (Sugarman & Carey, 2009). Students assessed at baseline and at 3, 6 and 12 months reported more PBS and less drinking than students assessed only at 12 months, suggesting that being asked about PBS changes reports (Walters et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Other experimental designs

key_findings.finding: Longitudinal studies without randomization gave mixed results: after a brief intervention, strategy use rose at 6 weeks but its change was not correlated with drinking outcomes (Martens et al., 2007, single group); in data from a peer intervention that had no significant effect (Cimini et al., 2009, analysed by Martens et al., 2011; baseline, 6 and 12 months), prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones while those with problems were weaker (3 of 9 non-significant); with the other subscales controlled, change in Manner of Drinking strategies predicted fewer drinks per week and change in Serious Harm Reduction strategies predicted alcohol problems at 6 and 12 months (direction not stated in the text; Appendix no. 35 says changes in two of the three subscales predicted less use or problems), and change in each subscale correlated negatively with change in one to three alcohol outcomes (Appendix no. 7); in women, strategy use did not predict drinking or problems at the same time point (baseline or 4 months), but baseline use predicted fewer problems 4 months later, adjusted for age, baseline problems, quantity and frequency of drinking and risk-amplifying behaviours (Luebbe et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Non-experimental longitudinal designs; Appendix nos. 7, 31 and 35

key_findings.finding: Within-person evidence (two studies: 7-day recall around the 21st birthday, Lewis et al., 2012; 15-day daily diary of 40 students, Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013): Manner of Drinking strategies went with less drinking both between people and on the days used; on days when Limiting/Stopping strategies were used, people drank more; Serious Harm Reduction strategies (such as a designated driver or going home with a friend) went with more drinking between people and on the days used, and with more problems on those days. The author suggests such strategies may be used mainly when heavy drinking is planned.
key_findings.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Designs with daily PBS reports

key_findings.finding: Nearly all included studies measured both PBS and outcomes by retrospective self-report, often with no time window; three studies limited recall to one occasion or used a daily diary (Frank et al., 2012; Neighbors et al., 2009; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013).
key_findings.locator: Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Recall bias
key_findings.note: The abstract says two such studies; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The abstract states that 80% of the 62 reports gave only cross-sectional data and that two studies examined both within-person and between-person effects.
key_findings.locator: Abstract
key_findings.note: The 80% figure is not derived anywhere in the body or Appendix; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The author concludes that intervention, experimental and longitudinal studies give mixed evidence for PBS as a mediator of intervention effects and as a prospective predictor of outcomes, calls for intensive longitudinal designs and a meta-analysis, and ends by calling PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its consequences.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion; Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Moving forward

key_findings.finding: The author's own summary of the cross-sectional evidence: nearly every reviewed study supports that students who report using more strategies also report drinking less and/or fewer alcohol-related problems (negative correlations with drinking frequency, quantity, heavy episodes, estimated blood alcohol concentration and problem measures, with examples cited); he calls the support for these negative correlations between self-reported strategy use and self-reported drinking or problems strong, and the Highlights say strategy use is consistently negatively correlated with problems. No effect sizes are given.
key_findings.locator: Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph; Purpose of the Present Review, 1st paragraph; Highlights
key_findings.note: The body also reports positive associations for some strategies (daily-report studies, absolute-frequency scales), so 'consistently' in the Highlights overstates (see interpretation gap).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says only two studies tried to reduce recall bias, but the Recall bias section names three (Frank et al., 2012 and Neighbors et al., 2009, single occasion; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley, 2013, daily diary).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the body's count of three, with its named studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's figure that 80% of the 62 reports gave only cross-sectional data is not derived in the body, and the Appendix does not state each study's design consistently. An editors' rough count of Appendix summaries that describe a trial, experiment, follow-up or daily design gives 14 to 16 of 62 (about 74–77% otherwise).
reporting_issues.consequence: The proportion cannot be checked exactly; cite it as the author's estimate (about three-quarters to four-fifths of studies cross-sectional), not as a verified count.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 36 studies (about 58%) used the PBSS, with 16 using a 5-point and 15 a 6-point scale, and by time window 24 with none stated, 5 with 3 months and 4 with a single day or occasion. The time-window subtotals add to 33, the scale subtotals plus the 4 yes/no studies to 35, and Table 1's PBSS rows list 33 (16 five-point, 13 six-point, 4 yes/no).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the number of PBSS studies is between 33 and 36. Cite as about 33 to 36 or as the author's figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The note to Table 1 says studies with a factor analysis are in bold and scale-development papers are underlined, but the PMC author manuscript renders neither mark (the HTML table contains no bold or underline).
reporting_issues.consequence: These two attributes can be read from this version only through the Factor Analysis column and the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation inconsistencies: Novik & Boekeloo appears once as 2012 (Measurement of PBS, 4th paragraph) but as 2011 elsewhere and in the reference list; Nguyen et al. is 2011 in the text and Table 1 but 2010 in the Appendix, with two co-authors' names spelled inconsistently (Wyatt or Syatt; DeJong or DeLong). A moderation finding on drinking refusal self-efficacy (Moderators › Other variables) is reported without naming its study (the Appendix attributes it to Ehret, Ghaidarov & LaBrie, 2013).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; check the primary paper's year and identity before citing any of these through the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The second paragraph of the Acknowledgments ends mid-sentence after the words supported in part by, with no funder named.
reporting_issues.consequence: The funding statement of the author manuscript may be incomplete; the published version was not read.

(locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Non-experimental longitudinal designs)

(2009) strategies were unrelated to both drinking and problems at the same time point (baseline and 4 months); in Martens et al. (2011) prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones. 'Missed': change-score findings favouring strategies (Cimini et al., 2009, Appendix no. 7; Manner of Drinking change predicting fewer drinks per week at 6 and 12 months, Martens et al., 2011).

disagreements.first_pass: Trials: in three randomized trials of brief interventions with college students, change in PBS statistically mediated the intervention's effect on drinking or problems (Larimer et al., 2007, mailed personalized feedback, 12 months; Barnett et al., 2007, brief motivational interview with mandated students, PBS at 3 months and drinks per day at 12 months, per drinking day in the Appendix; Murphy et al., 2012, small trial with a behavioral economic supplement, 6 months). In three other trials the intervention did not change PBS (Kulesza et al., 2010; Neighbors et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2009). None of the interventions mainly targeted PBS.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (blind second reading): confirmed; refinement: the body says Larimer et al.'s effect was fully mediated.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed (Review of Evidence › Randomized controlled trials, 1st paragraph); added.

disagreements.first_pass: (recorded only in the interpretation gap)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (blind second reading), 'missed': no key finding records the review's own summary of the cross-sectional evidence (nearly every study: more strategies, less drinking and/or fewer problems); the claim omits it.
disagreements.resolution: True and it matters (the claim cl_alc_protective_strategies understated it); checked at the stated places and added as the last key finding so that earlier indexes do not move.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD420251148669) of randomized controlled trials in adults in which protective behavioural strategies (PBS) were actively taught, prompted or reinforced: limiting or stopping drinking (for example drink limits), manner of drinking (for example pacing) and harm-reduction strategies (for example a designated driver), alone or inside multi-component interventions, against no intervention, assessment only, education or other behavioural interventions. 15 trials published 2007–2023, all in young adults, 13 at US universities. Separate pools of Hedges' g from post-intervention means at the longest follow-up for alcohol quantity (9 trials), drinking frequency (6), alcohol-related problems (7) and PBS use (6); influence diagnostics with sensitivity analyses; subgroups by follow-up (3 months or less versus more) and by the role of PBS in the intervention. Mediation and moderation summarized narratively.
can_establish: The average effect, mostly in US university students, of interventions that teach or prompt bundles of protective drinking strategies on self-reported drinking quantity, frequency, alcohol-related problems and strategy use, compared with a mix of control conditions.
cannot_establish: The effect of any single strategy such as eating, pacing or alternating drinks (no trial tested one strategy domain alone); effects in older, community, treatment or non-Western populations; effects on harms measured other than by self-report; whether strategies are the mechanism of change (mediation tested in six trials, with inconsistent results); or, in multi-component trials, whether the effect comes from the strategies or from the other components.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL and ProQuest from inception to December 2025, limited to peer-reviewed English articles, plus citation tracking, reference lists and earlier reviews (Methods 2.2–2.3, pp. 2–3). Participants of the included trials were mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 at US universities; one trial in Sweden (university) and one pilot in Australia (campus and social media) (Results 3.1, p. 3; Table 1, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: individual or cluster RCTs in adults (18 or older) who reported alcohol use, in which PBS were a primary or clearly identifiable component directly delivered by instruction, skills training, practice or prompting, with at least one quantitative alcohol outcome. Excluded: trials in which PBS were only an outcome, correlate, mediator or moderator; interventions aimed at norms, attitudes, motivation or identity without delivering PBS; non-randomized designs; reviews, protocols, conference abstracts and other non-peer-reviewed reports; under-18s without separate adult data (Methods 2.2, pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Randomized sample sizes 45 to 9,277; mean ages about 18 to 23 (two trials of people turning 21; one up to age 35); 41% to 100% women; risk profiles from universal samples to heavy episodic drinkers, students in counselling and 21st-birthday drinkers (Table 1, p. 6). Editors' calculation from Table 1: 15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed across the 15 trials.
sample.attrition: Trial-level attrition 0% to 95%, highest in large digital trials (p. 5; Table 1). At review level, 20 of 79 reports sought were not retrieved (12 full text unavailable, 8 abstract only) (Fig. 1, p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature; 20 possibly relevant reports were not retrieved. The evidence comes almost entirely from young US university students, so community, older, clinical and non-Western drinkers are not represented, as the authors state (p. 11).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drinking and problems in every trial (the authors list reliance on self-report as a limitation, p. 11); PBS use measured by self-report scales where assessed. The instrument behind each pooled outcome is not identified trial by trial.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to alcohol amounts. Interventions were mostly single-session or brief and digital (web feedback, email, SMS, smartphone apps, mailed postcards, interactive voice response); four had a face-to-face component; repeated formats ran from 3 days to 10 weeks (Results 3.2, p. 5; Table 2, p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; other drug use is not reported for any included trial.

comparison.controls: Assessment only (4 trials), no intervention (1), active or attention controls (study skills, health education, alcohol education, electronic brochure, control app, self-monitoring, differently framed messages), and in three booster trials the same computer-delivered intervention without the PBS booster (Table 2, p. 7).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials. Comparator types were pooled together without stratification.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level.

outcomes.instruments: Pooled outcomes: alcohol quantity, drinking frequency, alcohol-related problems and PBS use, each as Hedges' g with 95% CI from post-intervention group means, SDs and sample sizes, standard errors converted to SDs (Methods 2.7, p. 3). Trial risk of bias with RoB 2 by two independent reviewers (Methods 2.5, p. 3; Fig. 2, p. 5). Publication bias by funnel plots, rank correlation and Egger's test where feasible (p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Hedges' g corrects for small samples; negative values favour the intervention for alcohol outcomes and positive values for PBS use. Post-intervention values were pooled without adjustment for baseline.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit was lower self-reported quantity, frequency or problems, or more self-reported PBS use, in the intervention arm at the longest follow-up, which ranged from 3 days to 12 months (Table 3, p. 8).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 4 counts the primary pooled analyses; there are also 2 influence-based sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses by follow-up and by role of PBS (reported in the text for at least 8 estimates; supplementary figures S6–S16 not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening, extraction, classification of PBS role and risk-of-bias assessment were each done by two independent reviewers with a third for disagreements (Methods 2.4–2.6, pp. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects (Jamovi 2.6.44, MAJOR module), one effect per trial per model. Quantity: g −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), p = 0.162, 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07. Frequency: g −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), p = 0.014, 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001. Alcohol-related problems: g −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%; without Larimer et al. (2007) g −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01), p = 0.034. PBS use: g 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), p = 0.152, 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63; without the O'Donnell et al. (2019) pilot g 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), p = 0.005, I² 49.9% (pp. 6–7). Subgroups (p. 7; intervals and numbers of trials only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity g −0.12 (p = 0.004) and frequency g −0.13 (p = 0.003); no significant effect at 3 months or less; adjunct role, quantity g −0.10 (p = 0.040) and frequency g −0.13 (p < 0.001); core or primary role, no significant effect on quantity, problems g −0.11 (p = 0.091), PBS use g 0.91 (p = 0.128). No test of the difference between subgroups is reported.
analysis.covariates: None at review level.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD420251148669, described as prospectively registered (Methods 2.1, p. 2). The registry record was not read; the paper reports no deviations. The influence-based exclusions that produce the abstract's headline PBS-use estimate and the significant problems estimate are not described as prespecified; the subgroup analyses are.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives the PBS-use effect only after removal of an outlier (g 0.23) and calls the problems effect significant in sensitivity analysis, while both prespecified pooled estimates were non-significant (p. 1 versus p. 6). Subgroup estimates are reported without confidence intervals or numbers of trials. Which arms of multi-arm trials were compared is not stated.
analysis.power: Not formally assessed; the authors state that 6 to 9 trials per pool and fewer per subgroup limit power and make subgroup findings exploratory (Discussion 4.1, p. 11).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 trials, mostly of US university students, interventions that taught or prompted bundles of protective drinking strategies did not detectably change self-reported drinking quantity (g −0.05, −0.13 to 0.02), produced a very small reduction in drinking frequency (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; prediction interval reaching 0.001) and a borderline reduction in alcohol-related problems (g −0.07, upper limit 0.0007, p = 0.052). Effects on reported strategy use were highly heterogeneous (I² 97.8%) and not significant until one pilot trial was removed. No trial isolated a single strategy; 14 of 15 trials were at some concerns or high risk of bias; mediation through strategy use was found in some trials and not others.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's first result is the outlier-excluded effect on strategy use (g 0.23, p = 0.005), and it reports the problems effect as significant in sensitivity analysis; that analysis removed the largest and most precise trial, Larimer et al. (2007) (p. 6; Fig. 5, p. 9). The abstract and discussion say effects were greater at longer follow-up and when strategies were part of multi-component interventions (pp. 1, 10), but no between-subgroup test is reported, the subgroups differ in trial size and type, and three of the four adjunct trials paired the strategies with personalized normative feedback (Table 2, p. 7), so the larger effects cannot be credited to the strategies, a point the authors partly make (p. 10). The results section summarizes risk of bias as low to moderate (p. 5) although only one trial was low risk. The abstract's statements on alcohol outcomes (modest, no change in quantity, small reduction in frequency) and on mechanism (limited and inconsistent) match the results, and the discussion calls the subgroup findings exploratory.

timeline.event: Earliest included trial (Larimer et al., 2007, mailed personalized feedback with PBS, 1,488 students, 12-month follow-up), the largest weight in the problems pool.
Pearson (2013): critical review of PBS use among college students, cited as an earlier review mostly of observational evidence (card sc_pearson_2013).

Greń and Ostaszewski (2023), and Cox et al. (2024), a systematic review of associations between PBS and heavy drinking in young adults: earlier reviews cited as based largely on observational evidence; not read.
Latest included trial (Arazan et al., 2023, emailed e-card for students turning 21; 88% to 95% attrition).
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analysis restricted to RCTs delivering PBS as an active component.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of randomized trials of taught or prompted protective drinking strategies on the reading lists; the BeforeDuring list records that no trial of any single strategy on its own was found, which this review confirms (no trial isolated a strategy domain). Its estimates rest on 6 to 9 trials per outcome in US students. Primary trials cited here were not read; claims should not cite them as independent support alongside this review.

funding.funder: Ratchadapiseksomphot Endowment Fund, Chulalongkorn University (The Review Article Grant; Grant No. RA68011) and the Research grant for Systematic reviews and Meta-analyses from the Faculty of Nursing, Chulalongkorn University (p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to this work and state that the manuscript was completed independently of any commercial or financial relationships (pp. 11–12).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from nursing faculties in Vietnam (Thai Nguyen) and Thailand (Chulalongkorn, Burapha). The authors state that ChatGPT 5.3 was used to improve clarity and readability, with the authors reviewing and editing the text (p. 11).

what_would_settle_it: Pre-registered factorial or dismantling randomized trials that test single strategies (for example eating before drinking, pacing, alternating with non-alcoholic drinks, arranging transport) against each other and against a common control, in non-student adults as well as students, with event-level and objectively verified outcomes, including injuries and other harms, and follow-up beyond 6 months.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adults who drink), intervention (actively delivered PBS), comparators and outcomes specified (pp. 2–3).

Prospectively registered on PROSPERO (p. 2); the registry record was not read and the paper does not compare its methods with the protocol or report deviations; the role classification was developed for this review.
RCTs only, justified as a more rigorous test than the observational evidence of earlier reviews (pp. 2, 10).

Five databases, citation and reference-list searching, strategy in Appendix 1 (not read); but limited to peer-reviewed English articles without a stated reason, and no trial registries or grey literature. Applied as written per senior decision 21 (2026-10-25).
Titles, abstracts and full texts screened independently by two reviewers (p. 3).
Independent extraction by two reviewers with a piloted form (p. 3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: reasons for exclusion are said to be documented in Appendix 2 (p. 3), which is a supplement not among the files; the PRISMA diagram gives only counts by reason (Fig. 1, p. 4).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–3 give country, setting, design, randomized and analysed numbers, sex, age, risk profile, attrition, content, delivery, intensity, role, comparator, outcomes and follow-up (pp. 6–8); the instrument behind each pooled outcome is not identified.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 in duplicate with domain-level judgments for every trial (Fig. 2, p. 5); reasons for the judgments are not given, and the missing-data judgment for Arazan et al. (2023) looks lenient (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of Hedges' g with one effect per trial, I², prediction intervals and influence diagnostics (p. 3). A close call: the handling of multi-arm trials is not described, assessment-only, active and booster-design comparators are pooled together, and a pool with I² of 97.8% is summarized by one estimate (with its prediction interval).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis; the authors say it was not feasible because only one trial was low risk (p. 3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: A close call: the limitations state that high-risk trials were retained without sensitivity analysis and the estimates should be read cautiously, and discuss attrition, self-report and adherence (pp. 11); but the results describe overall risk of bias as low to moderate and miscount the high-risk trials (p. 5), and the abstract does not mention risk of bias.
Q, I² and prediction intervals reported, influence analyses run, and heterogeneity of PBS use discussed (pp. 6–7, 10).

Funnel plots, rank correlation and Egger's test for every pool, with no asymmetry found (p. 6; plots in supplementary figures S1–S4, not read). With 6 to 9 trials per pool these tests have little power, which the paper does not note.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Review funding and author declarations reported (pp. 11–12).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: one critical item is not met (item 4: English and peer-reviewed limits without justification, no registries or grey literature), which gives low confidence under the AMSTAR 2 rules; item 7 could not be judged without Appendix 2, and if that appendix lists no excluded studies with reasons the rating becomes critically low. Items 11 and 13 are close calls; a 'no' on either would also give critically low confidence. Otherwise the review is registered, duplicated at every step, uses RoB 2 and reports prediction intervals. Citable for: pooled effects of PBS-teaching interventions in mostly US students (no detectable effect on quantity; a very small effect on frequency; a borderline effect on problems; heterogeneous effects on strategy use) and for the absence of any trial of a single strategy. Not citable for: effects of any individual strategy such as eating before drinking, effects outside student populations, or strategies being the mechanism of change.

key_findings.finding: 15 RCTs published 2007–2023 were included: 13 in the United States and one each in Sweden and Australia, nearly all at universities, with randomized samples of 45 to 9,277; participants were mainly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 and attrition ranged from 0% to 95%.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 3, 5); Table 1 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: 15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed in total.

key_findings.finding: Searches of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL and ProQuest from inception to December 2025 were limited to peer-reviewed English articles; after removing 58 duplicates, 456 records were screened, 79 reports sought, 20 not retrieved (12 full text unavailable, 8 abstract only), 59 assessed and 14 included, plus 1 of 12 found by reference and citation searching.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2.2 (Publication restrictions) and 2.3 (pp. 2–3); Fig. 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The flow-chart counts are in Fig. 1, a drawing without a text layer; they were read from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: No trial evaluated a single PBS domain in isolation, so effects of individual strategies could not be analysed; 11 interventions are said to have combined limiting, manner-of-drinking and harm-reduction strategies and 4 emphasized selective avoidance and alternatives.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Table 2 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: Table 2 shows two of the eleven (Andersson 2015; Arazan 2023) with only two of the three domains; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: PBS had a core role in 4 trials, a primary role in 4, a booster role in 3 and an adjunct role (inside multi-component interventions, often with personalized normative feedback) in 4; most interventions were single-session or brief and digital, and four had a face-to-face component.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 2nd–4th paragraphs (p. 5); Table 2 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (RoB 2): one trial low risk in all domains (Martens et al., 2013); Fig. 2 shows four trials at high risk overall (Arazan 2023; Braitman and Henson 2016; Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018; Dvorak 2015) and the remaining ten at some concerns; concerns arose mainly from deviations from intended interventions and missing outcome data.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 2
key_findings.note: The text says three trials were high risk; the figure shows four. Trial names and judgments were read from Fig. 2, an image.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol quantity: pooled g −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), p = 0.162, 9 trials, I² 22.0%, 95% prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; no influential outliers or publication bias detected.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.4.1
key_findings.note: Fig. 3 (p. 9, image): trial estimates range from −0.54 (Leeman 2016) to +0.30 (Sugarman and Carey 2009, more drinking in the intervention arm, not significant); values read from the figure.

key_findings.finding: Drinking frequency: pooled g −0.09 (95% CI −0.17 to −0.02), p = 0.014, 6 trials, I² 11.85%, 95% prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001.

key_findings.finding: At trial level, 11 of 15 trials reported increased, maintained or mixed improvements in PBS use; 6 reported clear reductions in drinking, 1 partial and 1 mixed; 3 reported reductions in alcohol-related harms (one only after adjusting for consumption).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Mechanism: 6 trials ran mediation analyses, with significant indirect effects through PBS in three according to the text; 3 trials examined moderation, one finding stronger effects in people with lower baseline PBS use.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); Table 3 and Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 8)
key_findings.note: Table 3 and the Discussion list four trials with indirect effects (Dvorak 2015, Kenney 2014, LaBrie 2015, Larimer 2007); see reporting issues.

reporting_issues.issue: In the PRISMA diagram the database counts (PubMed 94, Embase 237, Scopus 117, CINAHL 71, ProQuest 45) sum to 564, but the total is printed as 514; the following boxes (58 duplicates, 456 screened) follow 514.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a database count or the total is wrong; 50 records are unaccounted for, which weakens the audit trail of the search. (Fig. 1 has no text layer; counts read from the rendered page.)

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says three trials were at high risk of bias and describes overall risk of bias as low to moderate, but Fig. 2 shows four trials at high risk overall, ten at some concerns and one at low risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates the risk of bias of the evidence; claims should use the figure (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk).

reporting_issues.issue: Arazan et al. (2023) has 88% to 95% attrition and 658 of 9,277 analysed (Table 1), yet its missing-outcome-data domain is judged low risk in Fig. 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one domain judgment looks lenient, and this trial contributes to the problems and PBS-use pools.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives analysed numbers equal to randomized numbers for Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018 (537/537 with 70–79% attrition), Braitman 2022 (528/528 with 31–45%), Larimer 2007 (1,488/1,488 with 33%) and Martens 2013 (365/365 with 5–6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: These trials presumably analysed all randomized participants with missing-data methods, but the review does not say which numbers and means entered its pooled post-intervention comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text reports significant indirect effects through PBS in three of six mediation trials, while Table 3 and the Discussion list four (Dvorak 2015, Kenney 2014, LaBrie 2015, Larimer 2007). Table 2 gives no mechanism test for Braitman 2022, Table 3 a non-significant moderation test. Table 3 marks Larimer 2007's PBS change as not assessed while concluding that its effects were mediated by increased PBS use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The narrative synthesis of mechanism cannot be reconciled with the tables; the count of trials supporting mediation is three or four depending on the source.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says eight trials showed clear increases in PBS use, but Table 3 marks nine as 'Yes' (with one mixed and one maintained, giving the stated eleven); the text says eleven interventions combined all three strategy domains, but Table 2 lists two of them (Andersson 2015; Arazan 2023) with two domains.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting errors in the descriptive synthesis.

reporting_issues.issue: Five trials had three to five arms (Table 1), but the review does not say which arms were compared or whether control groups were split, and the subgroup analysis prespecified as core/primary versus adjunct/booster (p. 3) is reported as adjunct versus core or primary without saying where the three booster trials went (p. 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled and subgroup estimates cannot be reproduced from the paper, and the adjunct subgroup's composition is unclear.
